Landscape and Jurisdictional Approaches - City of Atlanta's Carbon Credit Program: The City of Atlanta launched its urban forest carbon credit program in 2022 with the Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve Carbon Credit Project. This initiative preserves 196 acres of ecologically high value forest and has issued 36,265 Carbon Plus credits through a 40 year urban tree preservation protocol. The program is designed to generate revenue over more than four decades that supports preservation and stewardship, delivering co benefits in public health, air quality, stormwater management, and energy savings. Currently 27,717 credits are available for purchase, with credits issued annually at approximately 9,239 per year for 2023, 2024, and 2025.

Building on this success, the City is now expanding the program to include four newly acquired forested nature preserve properties: Southwest Nature Preserve, Utoy Creek Nature Preserve, Mount Zion Nature Preserve, and South River Nature Preserve, totaling approximately 252 acres. These areas were acquired between late 2022 and 2023 through deed, park impact fees, and tree trust funds.

This expansion continues the strategy of leveraging carbon credit revenue to preserve mature urban canopies from development pressures, bolster climate resilience, and fund ecosystem stewardship. It aligns with broader City goals of enhancing equitable greenspace access within walking distance for all residents, advancing greenhouse gas reduction efforts, and strengthening resilience through nature based strategies. Importantly, this carbon credit model is structured to continue scaling across all future forested property acquisitions the City makes, encouraging ongoing preservation while also generating additional revenue that can be reinvested to compound environmental and community impact over time.

The City is actively seeking partners to purchase these premium Carbon Plus credits and help spread the word about their availability. By connecting with buyers who value high quality, community centered offsets, the City can accelerate reinvestment in further preservation and resilience projects. At the same time, Atlanta hopes that showcasing this model will inspire other local governments to launch similar initiatives, demonstrating how urban forest preservation can serve as both a climate mitigation tool and a revenue generating pathway to fund long term adaptation.

Project documentation and credits available for purchase can be found here. Lake Charlotte Nature Preserve Carbon Credit Project Page : https://www.cityforestcredits.org/carbon-credits/carbon-registry/atlanta-forest-carbon-offsets/

City of Atlanta's Carbon Credit Program Expansion: https://www.cityforestcredits.org/carbon-credits/carbon-registry/city-of-atlanta-carbon-credit-program-2024/

Buildings - WeatheRISE Atlanta: The City of Atlanta has invested $2 million through the American Rescue Plan Act funds, which has aided in updating around 100+ homes with lighting, HVAC, insulation, and other issues with specific energy burdened neighbors and old buildings. This program has shifted to be run by three non-profits instead of the City: Greenlink Analytics, Sustainable Georgia Futures, and Partners in Action for Healthy Living (PAHL) to move this project forward to reduce energy burden in the city. 

Solar for All termination impacts: The City of Atlanta was expecting to receive an additional $2 million to support and scale WeatheRISE Atlanta's audits, energy efficiency retrofits, and pairing these with solar. However, just a few weeks ago the EPA terminated their contracts for all Solar For All grant recipients, so this is detrimental to scaling the impact and continued capacity to support this program. More funding is needed to reach the 10% energy burden reduction goal, but Google has donated $300,000 to support WeatheRISE Atlanta and the City has recently also invested an additional $200,000 from the Atlanta Community Energy Fund. However, new funding, partners, and models are needed to replace the funding gap in the wake of the sudden Solar For All contract terminations. 

Link: https://www.100atl.com/weatherise-atl

project_info: Transport - Moving Atlanta Forward: 2022 Infrastructure Package: Atlanta voters approved three ballot measures on May 24, 2022, that will make significant investments in the city's infrastructure and economy. The measures — two bonds and the renewal of a special sales tax — will put $750M toward vital transportation, recreation, public safety and arts projects across the city. The City of Atlanta has identified major infrastructure needs across streets, sidewalks, parks, recreation centers and public safety facilities. To make progress against these needs, the City of Atlanta has prepared a $750M infrastructure program for the next five years. Of this $750 million, $540 will be going to support increase and maintenance of bike and pedestrian infrastructure along with greenspace acquisition and maintenance, trails and transportation, complete streets and bridges. The comprehensive project list can be found at: https://www.atlantaga.gov/government/mayor-s-office/2022infrastructure

project_info: Water management - City of Atlanta Department of Watershed Management Environmental Impact Bond for Green Infrastructure: The EIB has provided $14M to implement green infrastructure and resilience projects on the city's west side, specifically in the Proctor Creek watershed. Redevelopment of disinvested urban areas, such as the Proctor Creek watershed, has the potential to create more impervious surfaces that contribute to stormwater runoff, water quality issues, and flooding during rainfall events. project_info: Renewable energy - BESS Emergency Backup: A goal for the Office of Sustainability & Resilience is to deploy resilience hubs by transitioning municipal facilities from fossil gas to PV & battery storage backup. Funding is currently being applied to through state Hazard Mitigation funding from FEMA. Currently, there is one resilience hub in Atlanta at a church that serves the community, Vicars Community Church of God, but not yet for a municipal facility. If awarded, the FEMA funding will go towards critical facilities in the City of Atlanta that need to continue operations in the case of an outage, such as warming and cooling centers. Additional funding is needed for facilities to transition to 100% clean energy and include a battery storage need.

project_info: Renewable energy - Solar Atlanta: Solar Atlanta is the City's municipal solar power program on City-owned sites. Currently, looking to expand this across Atlanta's portfolio to reach 100% clean energy by 2035, specifically seeking funding for a capped landfill solar community energy project. This would be an alternative model to our Solar Energy Procurement Agreement (SEPA) and would include upfront capital needed to launch. The cost of the project would be $2.68M with Direct Pay incentives, without them the cost would drive up to $6.7M.

Scope is a 50-port DC fast-charging hub at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport to serve rental fleets, rideshare, hotel shuttles, airport employees, City fleet (light-heavy duty), and the traveling public on adjacent interstates. Status: In early 2025, federal EV-charging funds were paused/frozen. Atlanta's CFI award remains treated as “frozen” pending clear federal direction on Georgia resumption, so the City is maintaining project readiness while the pause is resolved.

3rd Party owned charging on City owned property model: A cost-neutral (potentially revenue-generating) partnership in which a private EV charging provider owns, finances, installs, operates, and maintains DCFC and L2 chargers on City sites and eligible right-of-way; the City grants site access/licenses and receives revenue share or site-host fees. This approach is consistent with established right-of-way licensing and public-private EVSE best practices used by peer cities. This is currently in the process of the City's procurement Department to move forward.

Under this grant, the City will deploy seven medium- and heavy-duty zero-emission vehicles (including refuse and utility trucks, a street sweeper, and transit-style shuttles) and seven 150-kW DC fast chargers across four priority municipal sites. An earlier proposal to electrify four Department of Aviation buses was deemed ineligible, reducing the total scope to seven vehicles and seven chargers. The project, known as EcoFleet ATL, will deliver measurable reductions in greenhouse gas and criteria pollutant emissions, improve air quality in overburdened neighborhoods, and build workforce capacity through mechanic and operator EV training. It also represents the City's first dedicated heavy-duty EV and DC fast charging deployments, serving as a foundation for scaling electrification across Atlanta's municipal fleet. However, rising tariff prices on both EVs and charging infrastructure have significantly increased project costs, making external funding (like Georgia Power's Make Ready Program) important to closing budget gaps and maximizing successful implementation.

Transport - Trails ATL: The City of Atlanta formally adopted the Trails ATL master plan on June 16, 2025, through unanimous City Council approval, integrating it into the City's Comprehensive Development Plan and establishing the policy framework needed to move into implementation. As part of this bold 30 year vision, the plan targets a total network of 535 miles of multi use trails designed to connect neighborhoods, parks, schools, transit corridors, and greenways, ultimately enabling 95 percent of residents to access an 'all ages, all abilities' trail within a 10 minute walk or wheelchair ride by 2052.

Phase I of Trails ATL is scoped to deliver approximately 35 miles of new greenways and protected street trails spanning neighborhoods like Lakewood Heights, South Atlanta, Buckhead, and southwest Atlanta over a buildout decade from 2027 to 2037. This first phase carries an estimated price tag of $252 million, reflecting December 2024 labor and materials pricing, with some trails to include lighting but excluding costs for security cameras, real estate acquisition, easements, etc.

To date, while more than 100 miles of trails have already been completed or are currently funded through existing infrastructure, the Trails ATL plan remains reliant on securing dedicated funding. Proposed sources include local bonds or levies such as a Transportation Special Local Option Sales Tax (TSPLOST) anticipated for 2027, alongside state and federal grants, philanthropic contributions, and partnerships. These funding pathways are essential to launch Phase I and sustain the ongoing project conveyor belt strategy, ensuring design, permitting, and construction phases are continuously active.

climate_hazard: Extreme cold: In January 2023, winter storm Mara hit Central Texas causing the temperature to stay below zero for three days. However, the ice accumulated took almost a week to thaw and for the temperature to go back to normal. This resulted into increased collisions, power outages in cold weather shelters, hospitals and energy stations affecting 166,000 customers. | Extreme heat: The year 2023 was Austin's hottest year on record with the hottest meteorological summer- defined as the months of June, July and August- even recorded at Austin's airport. The city hit triple digits temperature for the first time on June 9 which was about a month ahead of normal and stayed in similar ranges for about 80 days. This trend was observed last in 2011. | Drought: 2011 was the worst single-year Texas drought since record keeping began — and, until Hurricane Harvey, may prove to be one of most devastating economic events in Texas history.Estimates by the Texas AgriLife Extension Service put Texas agricultural losses for the year at $5.2 billion. A December economic analysis by BBVA Compass Bank foundthat indirect drought losses to the state's agricultural industries could add another $3.5 billion to the toll. Impact were substantial on agriculture, trees and plants, industry, power generation, water supply, and residents. Although this year was unusually wet, we do not know if next year, or the following year, will bring extreme flooding or drought.. or both.Austin is currently impacted by severe drought. The combined storage level of water in Lakes Travis and Buchanan is currently at 1.409 million acre-feet and is projected to drop below 1.4 million acre-feet . Austin's Drought Contingency Plan sets a trigger at this storage level at which the City Manager will order the implementation of Stage 1 conservation measures. To give the community notice that these new restrictions are coming and consistent with the City's Water Conservation Code, City Manager Spencer Cronk has ordered implementation of Stage 1, effective June 6, 2022. This comes after over a 3-year stretch at Conservation Stage, the lowest stage of the Water Conservation Code.In Central Texas, droughts cause shifting soils, resulting in damage to roads, bridges, building foundations, and underground utilities. The highly elastic soils are primarily a long-term maintenance issue for roadways, given the potential for roadway damage resulting from extreme variations in precipitation and soil moisture (i.e. drought followed by heavy rainfall). | Extreme cold: In February, 2021, winter storm Uri struck Texas, causing temperatures to plunge to record lows for over a week. This triggered a cascading series of systemic failures that led to over 4.5 million Texan homes and businesses losing power during that period. Approximately half of all homes lost access to running water for an average of two days. It was the single largest insurance claim event in state history, causing an estimated $295 billion in damages. Increased extreme weather resilience planning is already under way at the City.The storm exposed vulnerabilities at multiple points in water distribution, including access to drinking water and sources for flushing toilets and hygiene. Low temperatures caused water mains to break, home and apartment complex pipes to rupture, and water loss resulting in storage and pressure failures. Hospitals lost access to water to supply boilers for heating. Community groups and elected officials mobilized to fill gaps. The City and County operated a community-wide distribution of drinking water. Austin Water purchased water totes, leased water tanker trucks, and deployed fire hydrant adapters to provide water. These efforts were hampered by road conditions, lack of pre-stocking supplies, coordination with food distribution, and shortfalls in targeting needs of vulnerable communities.Winter Storm Uri had a disproportionate impact on individuals that lack access to appropriate and nutritious food. Residents with greater resources were generally able to sustain access to food, especially if they had personal transportation and had strong social connections with neighbors and local familial networks who could provide support. The disruption in food supply chains, closure of grocery stores, hazardous road conditions, and other factors created additional barriers, worsening underlying food insecurity. Community-based organizations and individuals mobilized to meet unmet needs, as did City and County departments. But there were significant gaps in planning, response coordination, and staffing. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): In addition to being incredibly hot, the summer of 2023 was also very dry. These conditions contributed to several wildfires across Central Texas. With warmer, drier fire seasons and significant population growth in the wildland-urban interface (WUI), wildfire risk in Austin, Texas is increasing. Wildfire potential exists not just in the more forested portions of west Austin, but all around the city. On August 8, a 37-acres wildfire sparked in Cedar Park, a metro city in west Austin. Though they may exhibit less intensity than west-side crown fires, east-side grass and shrub fires can move extremely fast and pose significant threats to human health and safety, buildings, infrastructure, and water quality. Austin's most vulnerable populations largely are concentrated on the east side, a result of early 20th-century segregation policy and the legacy of discriminatory practices. Like other disasters, wildfires disproportionately affect the most vulnerable populations who are more likely to experience adverse outcomes because of their socioeconomic status, race, ethnicity, and age. Vulnerable populations are more likely to lack resources to prepare for, respond to, and recover from disasters, and they may experience cultural and institutional barriers, have limited mobility, and have compromised physical health. Increase in respiratory and cardiovascular illness and deaths caused by smoke from heat and drought-related wildfires. Based on climate change projections, the extreme heat, drought, and wildfires of the summer of 2011 will become less exceptional, resulting in changes to the way we plan for and respond to extreme weather events. | Urban flooding: In April of 2023, north Austin received more than 4 inches of rain within just one hour. Walnut Creek received 1.52 inches in just 15 minutes causing flash flooding. The City's Fire department conducted 10 water rescues, while emergency crews saved 16 people from cars stuck in rising water.

project_info: Transport - Project Connect: Project Connect will expand and improve our public transportation network for the entire Central Texas region, including new light rail, a subway under downtown and an accessible bus system to better connect neighborhoods in and outside our great city. Project Connect is designed to improve access to essential jobs, health care and education-making our communities more livable, equitable and sustainable. In 2023, after five options for a light rail plan were released, City Council, ATP, and CapMetro agreed on an initial alignment.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Local carbon farming: Explore the ability of food forests and community gardens on public lands to use low-carbon and carbon farming practices. This agricultural practice can improve carbon sequestration rates in agricultural systems and aid in plant growth, reduce fertilizer use and improve soil water retention. Support local research on carbon farming practices, especially in partnership with local higher education institutions or organizations that work with individuals from low-income communities and communities of color. Provide basic oversight, technical assistance, startup resources, and ongoing maintenance at these gardens. This could be done by funding outside groups, community-based organizations, or Stewardship Councils/Ambassadors to provide these services. Encourage private residents to implement similar food production and carbon farming practices in their yards through education and incentives.

project_info: Buildings - Lead by example, capture and destroy old refrigerants at City buildings: We propose to work in two phases: first, to build a complete, robust inventory of refrigerant and refrigerant-bearing equipment within the portfolio of buildings the City owns or controls. The results of the inventory will be used to calculate the scope of Austin's emissions risk posed by these gases. This phase is currently in progress, and a consultant has been retained to support its completion. Second, we will use this inventory analysis and inputs drawn from direct engagement with Austin stakeholders to develop a strategy for efficiently and responsibly managing those refrigerants. This strategy will focus on accelerating the transition from high Global Warming Potential (GWP) cooling systems to low GWP alternatives. project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Central Texas Árbol Equity Collective: East Austin and surrounding communities in Central Texas bear a legacy of systemic disinvestment and environmental inequities now reflected in disproportionate exposure to climate risks and high rates of chronic disease. These communities lack access to urban tree canopy: tree canopy cover falls below the regional average and is declining further. The Central Texas Árbol Equity Collective (CTAEC), a partnership of 15 different organizations, including the City of Austin, aims to address these inequities by expanding the urban forest and access to its climate resilience, public health, and workforce benefits. By championing work that is evidence-based and informed by the lived experiences of community members, this regional coalition will invest in Central Texas' forests, remove barriers to participation, elevate community priorities, leverage the expertise of local universities, and build the local forestry workforce. While not officially operating under the umbrella of CTAEC, a coalition of organizations is submitting a proposal to the EPA's Community Change Grants Program that meets many of the intents of CTAEC in Summer 2024.

climate_hazard: River flooding: The sanitation network would be one of the infrastructures most affected as a result of climate change in the most extreme scenario. These impacts would mainly lead to an increase risk of flooding from rivers, in urban areas or due to rising sea level. Overflows may be affected, but data on these overflows is not available to determine the specific extent to which they would be affected. It would also aggravate the impact on the drinking water network and, to a lesser extent, on the phreatic network. It could also lead to the entry of sea water, rendering the aquifer unusable (saline intrusion). Road and railway networks are particularly exposed to floods, particularly river and urban flooding. | Other forms of climate-induced landscape shift/degradation: High level of pollution increases the health problems to all inhabitants but specially affects to chilhood and elderly people | Heavy precipitation: The general trends observed indicate that, among other things, there are two impacts associated with climate change that may affect flood risk: changes in rainfall patterns and rising sea levels. Regarding the former, most projections indicate that there may be an increase in rainfall intensity and a greater concentration of extreme episodes. Increased rainfall intensity may cause certain areas of the city to flood, as it will increase the flow of circulating water and test the city's drainage system to its limits. The second aspect is higher sea levels, which may condition the functioning of the drainage system in extreme situations. Under extreme conditions, an increase in sea level would mean that the overflow channels would not work properly, causing higher water levels in the network that could cause overflow at the surface, and therefore flooding in the street. The risk of flooding would affect some areas of the city more than others. For current situations, the conclusion is that for rainfall with a return period of 10 years (T10), The drainage system can function correctly (although it functions under pressure in some sections), but the two future scenarios under analysis both forecast flooding in some locations.The results obtained by the RESCCUE project shows that intensity of heavy rainfall events will increase from 20 to 40 % depending on the climate change scenario considered, RCP 4.5 or RCP 8.5 respectively. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Regarding the Barcelona coastline, although there are still not many studies that analyse the specific effect of climate change on the coastal dynamics of the area, approximations have been carried out that show that there is likely to be a triple impact on the coast as a result of climate change: an increase in flooding, morphological changes to the beaches and greater exposure of port infrastructures. The results obtained form the RESCCUE project predict a 30cm increase of mean sea level rise by 2050 and 50 cm increase of mean sea level rise by 2100By january 2020 th city was affected by Gloria Storm causing important damages to beaches and port infrastructures | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Although there are other factors associated with global change that directly impact on fire risk, the increase in temperatures and decrease in precipitation caused by the effects of climate change, which will lead to plants suffering increased hydric stress, increasing their flammability, will favour an increase in the risk of forest fire. The future danger of fire shows us a situation similar to current danger, but with a slight overall increase in danger. In 2018 first autoctonus case of dengue was detected in Barcelona. In 2020 soma cases of authoctonus WNV were also detected in Spain. | Drought: The effect that climate change can have on the water cycle, as the different projections seem to indicate, is a slight decrease in resources, especially towards the end of the century, and above all greater variability in the availability of water resources, with increases in both periods of drought and possible flooding in extreme periods. A slight increase in demand is also forecast. This will aggravate the deficit in the supply that the city is already suffering today. Specifically, a reduction of 12% in surface resources and a reduction of 9% in underground resources are forecast by 2050. On the other hand, increased demand on the part of different city uses is estimated to be around 4%. Regarding 2019, no drought events have been suffered in Barcelona and Catalonia region.The results obtained by the RESCCUE project shows that the increase of evapotranspiration and the decrease of snowfall will reduce the watershed resources from 9% to 11% . | Biodiversity loss: The change in climate dynamics would lead to changes in the composition of biodiversity, so involve to the changes of adaptation in the vegetal and animal species that thrive in the city. | Storm: In order to study flooding caused by the sea, the height of flooding is calculated. This is determined by three factors: the rise in sea level that causes a permanent flood; the tide and pressure and wind changes that generate a potential flood; and finally the effect of waves, which cause extreme flooding. Waves are currently responsible for causing major problems along the Barcelona coastline during extreme storm conditions. Climate projections show that there will be a general rise in sea level as a result of melting polar ice caps and heat expansions, and this increase will bring changes depending on the region. In addition, extreme events are predicted to be more frequent, although their magnitude will not change much. In the case of Barcelona, which previously was associated with return periods of 50 years, periods of 35 years are forecast by 2050. Regarding the Barcelona coastline, althoughthere are still not many studies that analyse the specific effect of climate change on the coastal dynamics of the area, approximations have been carried out that show that there is likely to be a triple impact on the coast as a result of climate change: an increase in flooding, morphological changes to the beaches and greater exposure of port infrastructures. | Extreme heat: Barcelona currently has an average annual temperature of 17.6ºC. Barcelona may experience a 1.6ºC increase in average annual temperature by the middle of the century and 1.7ºC by 2100, in the case of global emissions being reduced in accordance with the Paris agreements (committed scenario or RCP 4.5). This forecast could get worse if the current levels of emissions continue (passive scenario or RCP 8.5), producing a 2ºC temperature increase by the middle of the century and 3ºC by 2100. With regard to hot days (temperatures above 30ºC), Barcelona currently has an average of 22 days a year. Current models suggest an increase to 50 days a year by the end of the century for the committed scenario and 80 days a year for the passive scenario. In both scenarios, the areas most affected by high temperatures are those furthest from the sea, as its thermoregulatory effect does not reach them. Similarly, simulations carried out also suggest that in coming years heat waves may be more numerous, more severe and have a longer duration. Barcelona currently suffers an average of 1 heat wave every 4 years. In coming years, this number will increase, reaching 1 heat wave a year in the pledgedcommitted scenario and 4 or 5 heat waves a year in the passive scenario. Another major aspect is the foreseeable increase in the duration of these heat waves. An average increase of 3 days for the committed scenario and between 6 and 8.6 days for the passive scenario. In 2019 the city suffered a heat wave that lasted 3 days. From 2015 to 2019 the city registered 4 heat wave event which represents 4 heat waves every 5 years.The results obtained by the RESCCUE project confirm the trends of climate change showed by the Climate Plan. The new climate projections developed within the project framework foresee that temperatures will increase progressively during the next years, been more heavily increased in summer. Also heat waves are expected to be more intense, lasting and long.

Climate projections show that there will be a general rise in sea level as a result of melting polar ice caps and heat expansions, and this increase will bring changes depending on the region. In addition, extreme events are predicted to be more frequent, although their magnitude will not change much. In the case of Barcelona, which previously was associated with return periods of 50 years, periods of 35 years are forecast by 2050. Regarding the Barcelona coastline, althoughthere are still not many studies that analyse the specific effect of climate change on the coastal dynamics of the area, approximations have been carried out that show that there is likely to be a triple impact on the coast as a result of climate change: an increase in flooding, morphological changes to the beaches and greater exposure of port infrastructures. | Extreme heat: Barcelona currently has an average annual temperature of 17.6ºC. Barcelona may experience a 1.6ºC increase in average annual temperature by the middle of the century and 1.7ºC by 2100, in the case of global emissions being reduced in accordance with the Paris agreements (committed scenario or RCP 4.5). This forecast could get worse if the current levels of emissions continue (passive scenario or RCP 8.5), producing a 2ºC temperature increase by the middle of the century and 3ºC by 2100. Current models suggest an increase to 50 days a year by the end of the century for the committed scenario and 80 days a year for the passive scenario. In both scenarios, the areas most affected by high temperatures are those furthest from the sea, as its thermoregulatory effect does not reach them. Similarly, simulations carried out also suggest that in coming years heat waves may be more numerous, more severe and have a longer duration. Barcelona currently suffers an average of 1 heat wave every 4 years. In coming years, this number will increase, reaching 1 heat wave a year in the pledgedcommitted scenario and 4 or 5 heat waves a year in the passive scenario. Another major aspect is the foreseeable increase in the duration of these heat waves. An average increase of 3 days for the committed scenario and between 6 and 8.6 days for the passive scenario. In 2019 the city suffered a heat wave that lasted 3 days. From 2015 to 2019 the city registered 4 heat wave event which represents 4 heat waves every 5 years.The results obtained by the RESCCUE project confirm the trends of climate change showed by the Climate Plan. The new climate projections developed within the project framework foresee that temperatures will increase progressively during the next years, been more heavily increased in summer. project_info: Renewable energy - Més Barcelona: The Barcelona Sustainable Energy Mechanism (MES Barcelona), a tool to support and accelerate the city's energy transition alongside private investors. The tool is intended to encourage investment in solar panelling and energy renewal in the city.The mechanism's priority aim is to boost the production of photovoltaic energy in the city based on private initiatives, focusing on projects that use both large spaces (the roofs of industrial buildings and warehouses, of office buildings or of other places in the city) and roofs and flat rooftops of residential buildings by grouping together several residential buildings which, together, can make the entire investment manageable as well as scalable. In addition, investments are expected to be made in energy renovation projects for buildings with a high energy consumption, such as hospitals, hotels and sports facilities. Finally, MES Barcelona also intends to invest in projects to boost innovation in the renewable energy economic sector.MES Barcelona is a financial investment mechanism from Barcelona City Council. This €50-million municipal endowment will therefore be used for investment projects proposed by City Council-approved investors. These approved investors are a group of investors with experience investing in photovoltaic installations and energy renovation. When it comes to selecting investments, the City Council will require these to focus on either photovoltaic solar panel installations or energy renovation where the business model does not require co-funding from the owners of the buildings. Investors will contribute 100% of the investment, which they will recover through the surplus energy or energy savings resulting from the operations funded by them. In the case of investors specialising in photovoltaic energy, among other criteria, there will be a guarantee that these funds diversify the installation of photovoltaic solar panels in several types of building (residential, tertiary and industrial buildings) and encourage self-consumption, energy communities and the installation of electric vehicle charging points and so on. Private investors will be able to suggest improvements regarding the use and exploitation of community roofs.In March 2021, Barcelona City Council's Economy and Tax Office Commission approved the first companies and business groups that can be approved investors in the Barcelona Sustainable Energy Mechanism (MESBarcelona). These companies are: Endesa; GVC; Accelera Energia; Iberdrola; Naturgy Iberia, SA; Suma Capital SGECR, SA; Hengdian Group / ENERparking Sunstroom, i Intermoney Titulización SGFT, SA. The diversity of companies enables very diversified investment strategies to be proposed, encompassing different types of buildings and actions: residential buildings, offices, industrial warehouses, car parks, and public infrastructures and buildings committed to implementing clean energy (solar panels), building renovation, and even the possible production of green hydrogen. The investor approval process is open-ended, so start-ups will be able to join the MESBarcelona project in upcoming calls. Initially, there will be two calls per year, in addition to the new approval calls that will emerge.

In 2023, 24% of the 443,703 households across Birmingham are classed as being in fuel poverty - the second highest in the whole country (where the average was 12.4%). Data published in Dec 2024 (2022 data) shows the Parliamentary Constituency area of Hodge Hill was the most fuel poor, at an incidence of 32.1%. This is then followed by Hall Green at 29.5%, Perry Barr 28.6%, Ladywood 26.8%, Yardley 25.3%, Selly Oak 24%, Erdington 23%, Edgbaston 19.9%, Northfield 18.8% and Sutton Coldfield 11.9%. There were 1,170 excess winter deaths across Birmingham in between August 2020 and July 2021 (most recent verified data available as of Jul 24). Early estimates predict this figure to be 1,600 for 2021/2022. | Extreme wind: Disruption to services, telecommunications/ digital infrastructure; also transport infrastructure and services; and localised energy-electrical power outages. The city's response to these events is covered by our Civil Contingencies Plan; working with partners and community agencies, to ensure local knowledge of those most affected.. | Urban flooding: Events have highlighted vulnerable zones in the city - in Selly Oak, Witton and Northfield; for large scale events (10,000 residents). The West Midlands Combined Authority's Summary of Climate Change Impacts highlights several direct risks to Birmingham and its citizens, including the increased risk of fires, floods and damage to property and infrastructure. The impact of flooding alone is significant, with the current annual cost of flood damage across the UK exceeding £700m, and the repairs for a flooded home costing £30,000 on average. More frequent localised events, continue to occur across the city through local storm events. The two most significant impacts are over-heating and flood risk. We have now mapped those impacts on vulnerable communities. Public Health has an Emergency Heat Plan; and our Flood Risk team work with the Environment Agency & local water companies for both flood risk and drought; both through our Civil Contingencies Plan. A further impact of urban heat can also be that of air quality peaks; we now have a Ward based Tool that again is able to map both the physical risk and the human impact. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat can have negative impacts on local infrastructure. For example, solar panels make less electricity when they become too hot. Extreme heat could lower the ability of transmission lines to carry power, transformers are more likely to fail too; one study by MIT found that for every 1-degree rise in temperature, the lifetime of a transformer decreases by four years. Telecommunications companies and internet providers face difficulties with infrastructure such as telecoms towers, servers, and data centres. Transport infrastructure is at risk too - extreme heat damages roads, rail tracks, bridges, and railway and streetcar power cables. In the last heat wave Birmingham had issues with railway tracks warping. We found that cars are more likely to break down and that truck refrigeration units can fail, threatening food supplies. The 2022 summer heatwave resulted in 1/5 of operations scheduled in Birmingham being cancelled across the three hottest days. In terms of vulnerable populations, some groups of the populations are more exposed to, or more physiologically or socio-economically vulnerable to physiological stress, exacerbated illness, and an increased risk of death from exposure to excess heat. These include the elderly, infants and children, pregnant women, outdoor and manual workers, athletes, and those on low incomes.

Snow and ice: Hundreds of millions are spent by the City for snow removal, and winter storms present a threat to life and safety. Particularly vulnerable groups of residents living in sub-standard housing, and with limited access to warming centers, are especially impacted by major winter storms.

The Office of Emergency Management and Communications works closely with other city departments to orchestrate preparedness and response strategies including opening a network of warming centers across the city, snow removal, and direct support services to unhoused Chicagoans who may need shelter. | Heavy precipitation: The most frequent impacts from flooding are basement groundwater infiltration, sewer back-ups, and road flooding. CSO outfall releases during major storms also significantly impact water quality and ecosystem stability. The City notes the disproportionate burden on low-income and BIPOC communities in terms of flooding damage and severity. | Extreme heat: Chicago experienced a terrible heat wave in 1995 when over 700 people died in a short period of time. Impacts from heat wave are primarily social and public health risks. Increasingly severe and frequent heat events continue to harm and kill Chicago residents. Economic impacts are minimal except when this hazard invokes energy problems. 

A critical challenge about this hazard is that the level of personal variability in perception of need and ability to adapt to the temperatures. Personal health sensitivities, access to cooling, energy affordability, and environmental factors collectively impact personal and community-level vulnerability. Some people medically struggle to regulate their body's internal temperature thus they may experience greater, or more extended heat stress. Additionally, those who work or do strenuous activity outside, work in hot or poorly ventilated indoor conditions, or spend extended hours outside also are exposed to greater periods of heat. Energy affordability is a critical concern because access to indoor climate-control is increasingly important for homes, especially during warm evenings in communities that don't see cooling effects at night. | River flooding: Few areas of Chicago are mapped riverine floodplains, and river flooding risk was once deemed minimal since the Chicago River can backflow as needed to Lake Michigan. However, recent storms and flooding events have been cause for serious concern. A recent New York Times article detailed the six foot swing in Lake Michigan's surface level that took place over the last seven years. High Lake levels in 2020 caused engineers to consider whether the river would overflow into the central business district (which has not happened in modern history). River flooding is becoming a more severe issue as the effects of climate change materialize. On a more regular basis, basement flooding in low-income and BIPOC communities has become more frequent. | Urban flooding: Much of Chicago's stormwater infrastructure was built over a century ago as a combined sewer system. Chronic flooding—corroding the sewer system's capacity—has repeatedly impacted residents with basement overflows, electric fires, and smoke damage. This highlights systemic infrastructure inadequacies compounded by climate change. Underserved areas—especially on the South and West Sides—face disproportionate flooding risks. Legacy factors like high impervious surfaces, low green space, and weakened infrastructure mean these communities bear the brunt of damage and slow recovery. | Extreme wind: Historically there have been minimal deaths and property damage from severe wind.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Community Garden Compost Pilot: In November 2022, the City of Chicago announced a pilot project to divert household food scraps into composting through six community garden sites. The project was implemented in collaboration with the nonprofit NeighborSpace and was partially funded through the National Resources Defense Council. The announcement embedded the project in the city's effort to explore waste reuse strategies that contribute to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Six gardens were chosen across Chicago in collaboration with the nonprofit NeighborSpace. 

All six gardens composted food scraps during 2023; gardens acted as environmental education
sites, introducing participants to the practice and importance of composting.
100+ food scrap participants participated in the program across six community gardens and
the majority of participants lived in proximity to their submission garden. Gardens established unique systems for collecting food scraps in ways that were culturally relevant to their community. 

Chicago has great potential to divert food scrap waste from landfills. A 2021 study of Chicago
waste generation estimated 522,510 tons of organic waste annually, almost half of which
originates in single-family households. The study recommends investment in residential
source reduction and community education programs. Evaluation data demonstrates that the
program addressed both recommendations (Delta Institute, 2021).
https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/chicago-recycles/home/compost.html

project_info: Buildings - Building Decarbonization Strategy: The City of Chicago seeks to advancing energy justice and climate resilience through efficiency and renewable energy investments. By strategically investing in moderate income (LMI), homes, affordable housing, neighborhood anchor buildings and institutions, public libraries, and historic protected landmarks. These projects will equitably decarbonize and retrofit LMI homes and units across the City to enhance resilience to climate change, lower utility costs, and improve livability. Further, funding for retrofits and renewable energy projects will be delivered to cornerstone neighborhood institutions (e.g., community centers and libraries), improving their long-term environmental and economic sustainability. project_info:
Transport - Community charging pilot: The transportation sector is the second highest source of GHG emissions in Chicago and is a major contributor to poor air quality in our region. CDOT and the City more broadly are focused on lowering emissions from the transportation sector while improving air quality, increasing residents' mobility and job access, lowering household transportation costs, and improving public health.
The Charge Up Chicago! Chicago Community Resources and Charging Infrastructure Implementation (CUC) project will bring unique community benefits to Chicago by enabling equitable access to electric vehicles and E-mobility options in the city. CUC will then invest in community developed and owned charging station projects in addition to City of Chicago owned public charging stations. Leveraging the geographic diversity and equitable access mission of the Chicago Public Libraries, City-owned stations will be deployed at libraries to fill gaps in existing charging infrastructure, support high density multifamily housing communities, and create shared-use charging access to expand the City's EV municipal fleet in addition to ride hail, taxi and rental EV fleets serving Midway Airport. 

Currently, there are 720 publicly available EV passenger vehicle chargers in Chicago. Every community has registered EVs, but 70% of all public charging stations are concentrated in just three Community Areas. Of the 77 total Community Areas in Chicago, 47 do not have any public charging stations. The South and West Sides of Chicago have few public locations for Level 2 charging and virtually no access to DC fast charging. 

This project will work to overcome past planning shortcomings by ensuring CBOs are funded and positioned as leaders in the identification of local needs, with technical advisors to support them. CNT acts as the convener and facilitator of the Transportation Equity Network, a coalition of CBOs who will be the primary beneficiaries of this project. CNT's role on this project is to convene the participating CBOs, including maintaining direct and personal connections with each of them to ensure they see the value in participating and continually look for opportunities to improve our engagement process. 

CNT, Forth, and IACT will convene the 2 CBO partners for the training series, spanning approximately 9 months. The technical assistance and capacity building training will start with building a foundation on electric mobility to allow participants to have the same baseline of knowledge on transportation decarbonization. Learnings will build on each other throughout the course of training. After a foundation is established, Forth and partners will work with the CBOs to identify what topics to focus deeper on and are the most relevant for the communities they serve.

climate_hazard:
Snow and ice: Hundreds of millions are spent by the City for snow removal, and winter storms present a threat to life and safety. Particularly vulnerable groups of residents living in sub-standard housing, and with limited access to warming centers, are especially impacted by major winter storms.

The Office of Emergency Management and Communications works closely with other city departments to orchestrate preparedness and response strategies including opening a network of warming centers across the city, snow removal, and direct support services to unhoused Chicagoans who may need shelter. | Heavy precipitation: The most frequent impacts from flooding are basement groundwater infiltration, sewer back-ups, and road flooding. CSO outfall releases during major storms also significantly impact water quality and ecosystem stability. The City notes the disproportionate burden on low-income and BIPOC communities in terms of flooding damage and severity. | Extreme heat: Chicago experienced a terrible heat wave in 1995 when over 700 people died in a short period of time. Impacts from heat wave are primarily social and public health risks. Increasingly severe and frequent heat events continue to harm and kill Chicago residents. Economic impacts are minimal except when this hazard invokes energy problems. 

A critical challenge about this hazard is that the level of personal variability in perception of need and ability to adapt to the temperatures. Personal health sensitivities, access to cooling, energy affordability, and environmental factors collectively impact personal and community-level vulnerability. Some people medically struggle to regulate their body's internal temperature thus they may experience greater, or more extended heat stress. Additionally, those who work or do strenuous activity outside, work in hot or poorly ventilated indoor conditions, or spend extended hours outside also are exposed to greater periods of heat. Energy affordability is a critical concern because access to indoor climate-control is increasingly important for homes, especially during warm evenings in communities that don't see cooling effects at night. | River flooding: Few areas of Chicago are mapped riverine floodplains, and river flooding risk was once deemed minimal since the Chicago River can backflow as needed to Lake Michigan. However, recent storms and flooding events have been cause for serious concern. A recent New York Times article detailed the six foot swing in Lake Michigan's surface level that took place over the last seven years. High Lake levels in 2020 caused engineers to consider whether the river would overflow into the central business district (which has not happened in modern history). River flooding is becoming a more severe issue as the effects of climate change materialize. On a more regular basis, basement flooding in low-income and BIPOC communities has become more frequent. | Urban flooding: Much of Chicago's stormwater infrastructure was built over a century ago as a combined sewer system. Chronic flooding—corroding the sewer system's capacity—has repeatedly impacted residents with basement overflows, electric fires, and smoke damage. This highlights systemic infrastructure inadequacies compounded by climate change. Underserved areas—especially on the South and West Sides—face disproportionate flooding risks. Legacy factors like high impervious surfaces, low green space, and weakened infrastructure mean these communities bear the brunt of damage and slow recovery. | Extreme wind: Historically there have been minimal deaths and property damage from severe wind.
project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - Food Scrap Drop Off Program: Chicago launched its first food scrap drop-off program in October 2023. Beginning with 15 collection sites, there will be continual expansion to sites across other communities. Currently, receptacles are sited a City facilities which streamlines waste pickup and bin replacement. The program is made possible by funding through the Chicago Recovery Plan via general obligation bonds.

From Oct-Dec 2023, 27.49 tons of food waste collected for composting, resulting in 17.97 MTCO2E emissions reductions. The program experienced minimal issues with waste stream contamination which may be due to significant educational material on the program's website. Further funding would allow for additional outreach and education, and program expansion to all 77 community areas.

project_info: Water management - Rain Readiness Program: In Summer 2023, two extreme rainfall events took place in Chicago, earning both state and federal disaster designation. Source: https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/oem/supp_info/flash-flood-declaration-status.html \n\nThe “rain readiness” program is currently in development and is expected to offer funding for homes to invest in infrastructure to improve resilience in the face of increasing storm intensity, heavy precipitation, and urban flooding. Improvements include, but are not limited to, leak detection and repair, foundation cracks, downspout disconnection and other remedies to reduce the likelihood of flooding at the site level. The City expects to prioritize household located in high flood risk communities on the City's far west and mid-south sides. The City anticipates the release of a request for proposals in early 2025. climate_hazard: Extreme heat: While temperatures are rising citywide, heat risk varies by neighborhood. As a result of systemic racism, lack of green space, limited access to air-conditioning and poor housing quality, heat exacerbated deaths are more common in neighborhoods that are home to a greater proportion of low-income and Black New Yorkers. Heat waves pose a serious threat to public health, to the electrical supply and distribution system, and to many critical infrastructure systems that rely on electricity. Elderly residents, New Yorkers with mental illness, communities of color as well as low-income are at most risk to underlying health disparities and be socially isolated or limited in mobility. They lack access to indoor cooling and a relative lack of greenery. New Yorkers in homeless shelters or City jails are also vulnerable, given that these facilities lack proper air-conditioning, ventilation and bear the brunt of both indoor and outdoor urban heat impacts. The NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) Heat Vulnerability Index (HVI) shows neighborhoods whose residents are more at risk for dying during and immediately following extreme heat. The 2024 Heat Mortality annual report describes the impact of extreme heat on the most vulnerable population and sectors in detail (https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/data-features/heat-report/#:~:text=As%20of%20January%202024%2C%20there,residents%20(2013-2022).&text=Notes:%20The%20number%20of%20heat,deaths%20for%202022%20is%20provisional.) | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): NYC experiences multiple types of flooding, including pluvial flooding, storm surge, tidal flooding, groundwater flooding, riverine and compound flooding. Hundreds of thousands of residents live in coastal flood zones (expected to increase over time). Many critical community infrastructure facilities are located in low-lying coastal areas like schools, libraries, spaces for youth and senior services and cultural sites. These spaces serve as support centers during and after storms. Services may be inaccessible to residents during or after a coastal surge event due to damage and potential power outages. Coastal flooding not only directly impacts public health and lives of people, homes and business in the floodplain but cascading impacts from flooding can impact critical city infrastructure such as power plants, hospitals or transportation networks in surrounding areas. The Flood insurance data and analytics can be found here --> https://nfipservices.floodsmart.gov/reports-flood-insurance-data\n | Heavy precipitation: Heavy rainfall and inland flooding pose a risk to residences in some neighborhoods, particularly those living in basement apartments as well as certain critical infrastructure facilities. Heavy precipitation and flood preparedness is a matter of life safety, particularly in immigrant, low-income, and rental communities, as well as for populations with limited mobility and the elderly. Thirteen New Yorkers lost their lives during Hurricane Ida in 2021 with most of those lives lost tragically in basement apartments. A decade before, we had lost forty-four New Yorkers during 2012's Hurricane Sandy. Some city residents are facing repeated flooding from either heavy precipitation or sea level rise that causes financial damages and puts their lives at risk. Stormwater flooding can also trigger new mental health challenges in a community due to high anxiety and stress. Extreme rainfall causes sewers to overflow, exposing New Yorkers and natural systems to contaminated water. Residents could also be at risk to mold exposure as a result of trapped water in houses or buildings after extreme rainfall. These risks are higher for low-income residents living in substandard housing. As climate change causes sea levels to rise, flooding that occurs during high tides (also called sunny-day flooding) will also become an increasingly chronic issue for shoreline communities. In March 2022, the City announced funding to support the long-term recovery efforts following Hurricane Ida. In January 2023, there was an announcement for additional funding that was used for disaster relief, long-term recovery, restoration of infrastructure and housing, economic revitalization and mitigation, in the most impacted and distressed areas. Some impact and learnings from Superstorm Sandy and Hurricane Ida can be found here--> https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/data-stories/flooding-and-health/

project_info: Renewable energy - Public Solar program: In collaboration with the NYC Comptroller's Office, the Public Solar NYC (PSNYC) program has secured $37.5 million in funding through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Solar for All competition under the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. PSNYC will install 31 megawatts of rooftop solar with the goal to serve at least 5,000 low- and moderate-income households over the next five years. With 4.5MM NYC residents living in federal Disadvantaged Communities, representing more than 59% of the State's DAC census tracts, PSNYC will address historic barriers to solar adoption for LMI residents. The program will provide pathways to solar with no upfront capital costs, leveraging multiple publicly financed models to deliver cost savings. Through multilingual outreach via trusted community organizations, PSNYC will recruit customers, reduce installation costs, and streamline the solar adoption process for New Yorkers. More information here -->https://comptroller.nyc.gov/services/for-the-public/confronting-the-climate-crisis/public-solar/

project_info: Health systems and services - Air Quality Program: In PlaNYC, the City's strategic plan, the City commits to developing a new air quality monitoring program by 2024 to support efforts to reduce air pollution. In 2023, the city acquired ten new particulate matter monitors, which are being used to evaluate air quality at specific locations including commercial cooking restaurants, distribution centers, and other locations that are major sites of PM pollution. This monitoring has helped inform what day of the week or time of day inspectors should conduct inspections and provides insight into the particulate matter levels in the evaluated areas. In place of launching a new air quality monitoring program at this time, the city will use its resources \nto advance legislation to establish an Indirect Source Rule. The policy will improve air quality by \nrequiring certain warehouses to take actions to reduce air pollution from their operations.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Climate change is set to lead to heatwave conditions every summer by the middle of the century, and the Urban Heat Island effect makes the centre of London up to 4.5C warmer than rural areas surrounding the city. Higher temperatures will lead to heat-related illnesses and can exacerbate existing health conditions, including on mental health. Vulnerable populations, such as the elderly; as well as low-income and minority populations, who often reside in areas more susceptible to heat impacts, are particularly at risk. London's heatwave in July 2022 saw the highest temperatures ever recorded in excess of 40C and triggered a Level 4 national emergency, the highest level in the UK government's \'heat-health alert system\' indicating extreme or severe heatwave impacts expected across multiple sectors. During this period, nighttime temperatures also remained high, peaking at a high of 23.6 degrees Celsius - recent studies show that the UK is now seeing more frequent occurrences of (tropical nights) these events, particularly during heatwaves. Across the five periods of heat experienced in summer 2022 London saw 387 excess deaths from heat. The extensive and intense heat impacted vulnerable populations with multiple sectors affected, including significant house and building fires as a concurrent risk. Analyses of regional temperature-mortality relationships indicate that the threshold at which excess deaths start to increase is 24.7C, above which there is a greater rate of increase in the number of deaths per degree Celsius rise in temperatures than in other regions at a similar level. London is uniquely exposed to rising temperatures compared to the rest of the country. Its dense building stock limited green space, and high levels of surface sealing contribute to a pronounced urban heat island effect. Over half of UK homes are at risk of overheating in English homes show that specific building types are more vulnerable (Lomas et al., 2021). Flats and small dwellings (<50m2) face the highest risks. Flats are twice as likely to overheat in living rooms compared to other housing types. Bedrooms show higher overheating rates than living rooms, likely driven by poor night time ventilation, exposure to rooftop solar gain, and heat retention in top-floor rooms Projected increases in average monthly temperatures in London until 2050 show a 5-6C increase in summer and winter averages. This will have an impact on health, infrastructure and city operations. | Urban flooding: The city is vulnerable to less predictable surface water and sewer flooding from heavy rainfall events. This is due to increasing areas of impermeable surfacing, such as roads, roofs, and pavements. London also has a Victorian drainage system that wasn't designed to cope with the demands of the current and future population. There are 543,500 properties at high/medium risk and 319,8000 properties at high risk of surface water flooding in London. In July 2021 London was hit by two serious flash floods, just two weeks apart. Some areas of the city received more than twice the average monthly rainfall in just two hours. The floods caused massive disruption with homes and properties flooded by rainwater and sewage. Many rail and underground stations and several schools closed. Some hospital wards were evacuated. But the impacts could have been even more serious had the circumstances been only slightly different. Parts of London's combined sewer system are close to reaching capacity, increasing the risk of surface water and sewer flooding. In several locations, areas that currently experience capacity issues are earmarked for significant growth in homes and jobs, which, without mitigation, risks making the problem worse. London's sewerage system was designed for a smaller London of four million people. As London has grown, the frequency and magnitude of stormwater discharges has increased, from occasionally in the late 19th century to more than once a week today. Stormwater discharge results in dilute sewage being released into the river Thames. Insufficient capacity in London's combined drainage networks means London's wastewater treatment and collection system is considered inadequate to meet EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive (UWWTD) requirements. The Tideway Tunnel and Lea Tunnel has been built to reduce combined sewer overflows into the River Thames and meet the requirements of the UWWTD. The Thames Tideway Tunnel will help to reduce combined sewer overflows (CSOs) in a typical year by 95%, it is currently being commissioned and will be operational by 2025. | Drought: London's growing population and business base is demanding more water. London is within the driest part of the country and is potentially at risk of drought if reservoirs and groundwater aquifers are not re-filled by regular rainfall. The cost of a severe drought to London's economy is estimated by Thames Water to be £330m per day, and would have severe economic, social and environmental consequences. This figure may be even higher when all cumulative and knock on impacts of a severe drought are considered. In the situation of a severe drought, there would be significant disruption to the delivery of health and care services with impacts on health. It is not possible for water companies to prioritise supply to critical infrastructure, such as hospitals. The Mayor has no statutory responsibilities in relation to water resources and their associated supply and distribution infrastructure. However, the Mayor can influence water use and supply, to some extent, through the London Plan. It is also essential that the GLA maintains an oversight of strategic water resource planning and demand management measures to ensure a resilient and affordable supply for Londoners. When faced with the prospect of water shortages, water companies work closely with the regulator, the Environment Agency. A phased approach starts with information provision, awareness raising, and voluntary measures to restrict water use. It then escalates to compulsory measures if resource pressures worsen. Drought measures reduce the amount of water that people use through, for example, temporary use bans, such as on washing cars. However, they also have environmental impacts, as the usual restrictions on the amount of water abstracted from rivers and groundwater may be temporarily relaxed. This can result in low flows in rivers and impacts on wetlands. It causes a related reduction in water quality, and damage to river and other water body ecosystems. In some places this can be dramatic, such as in the groundwater-fed chalk streams, a globally rare habitat. Many areas of the UK, including London, faced prolonged drought in 2022. This resulted in water companies supplying London to impose a hosepipe ban, requiring household customers to reduce their water consumption for non-essential activities (vulnerable populations are generally exempt). This ban lasted from August to November 2022. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Currently 51,100 properties 37,359 existing homes are at high or medium risk of tidal or fluvial flooding, from the National Flood Risk Assessment data published in 2024 by the Environment Agency and 1.3 million people are living and working in areas of tidal and fluvial flood risk. Part of London (approximately 15 per cent) sits in the natural tidal floodplain. Many parts of the city nearest the river would flood on virtually every high tide, were it not for the Thames flood defences. However, the current defences were not built to withstand the higher water levels expected in the future and left unmitigated, the tidal flood risk to London will increase as sea levels rise. A 0.9 metre rise in mean tide levels is projected by 2100 over pre-industrial levels. The current flood risk to London is highest when a spring tide coincides with a North Sea tidal surge. This is caused by a specific set of meteorological conditions, including low pressure over the North Sea and a northerly wind resulting in raised sea levels. The Thames Barrier is closing more frequently now than when it was first built, as sea level affect peak high tide and surge levels. The Thames Estuary 2100 Plan outlines how to manage the risk of flooding from the Thames as sea levels rise and sea defences are aging. The Plan sets out a deadline for upgrading flood defences downstream (east) of the Thames Barrier by 2040 and upstream (west) of the Thames Barrier by 2050. The latter was recently moved forward by 15 years as a result of a review of the Thames Estuary Plan. The Plan also considers different options for upgrading the Thames Barrier itself. The recent 10-year review brought forward the deadline for a decision on this upgrade from 2050 to 2040. | River flooding: London has many tributary rivers leading to the River Thames and the Thames itself is a fluvial river upstream of Teddington Lock. As with any river system there is a possibility that any of these rivers could flood. This could come from either particularly intense rainfall within the catchment or from a blockage or restriction to flow within the river channel. Currently 51,100 properties are at high or medium risk of tidal or fluvial flooding, and 1.3 million people are living and working in areas of tidal and fluvial flood risk. Within a predominantly urban area, London's rivers are often heavily modified from their natural state. The urbanised river environment contains many bridges, tunnels and culvert structures. These form potential flood risks as they can become blocked or restricted. Culverts present a particular difficulty in that it is difficult and expensive to determine their condition and to carry out maintenance and repairs. Fluvial flooding affects most London boroughs. Fluvial flooding has been more frequent than tidal flooding meaning that where the flood plain remains as parkland and/or undeveloped land (e.g. Lee Valley Regional Park), it should be protected. london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/regional_flood_risk_appraisal_sept_2018.pdf Over centuries, London has grown on the banks of the Thames, encroaching on the natural floodplain. As the city has become more built up, the river walls have been raised incrementally. There are already many Londoners, businesses, and properties in flood risk areas. These areas tend to include a higher proportion of people on low incomes. For these households, a flood can often be even harder to cope with and recover from. This is because poorer people and small businesses may lack appropriate insurance cover or the funds to properly repair the premises. They may also lack a wider support network to help them cope with, and recover from, flooding. In many cases the physical and mental health impacts of being flooded can last for many years. Flood risk management authorities must consider that the number of properties at low risk of flooding will increase as development happens in the floodplain, albeit in areas protected by the Thames tidal defences. The Thames Barrier is closing more frequently now than when it was first built, as sea level affect peak high tide and surge levels.

project_info: Other: Multiple - Net zero action: In excess of £75 billion of infrastructure investment is needed to achieve London's net zero target by 2030. To achieve decarbonisation on this scale, a mix of public and private investment is required, and far higher levels of private finance must be mobilized into climate projects. In recognition of this challenge, the Mayor committed to setting up a new green financing facility, and in June 2023, launched the London Climate Finance Facility. Current finance mechanisms available under the LCFF are: Mayor's Energy Efficiency Fund (MEEF): provides flexible & competitive finance to enable & accelerate the delivery of bankable low carbon projects across London; Green Finance Fund (GFF): provides low cost, flexible loan finance to accelerate investment into green projects developed by the GLA Group and other key public sector bodies across London. The latest bidding round was launched during the Climate Innovation Forum at London Climate Action Week on 25 June 2025 and to date, the GFF Credit Committee has approved more than 318m in finance to deliver decarbonisation projects in London, with an estimated annual carbon savings of 45,043tCO2e Round 5; London EDGE Fund (EDGE): an exemplar on how private finance and cities can work together to achieve decarbonisation goals, promote green jobs and support low-carbon infrastructure. Since 2018, the Mayor's green finance programmes have made 1.1 billion available to support the decarbonisation of buildings, energy systems and transport across the capital. Work is underway to identify further opportunities to accelerate private sector finance into London's programmes. \nA bankable pipeline of projects is essential for any green finance programme & the mayor has the Zero Carbon Accelerator providing Technical Assistance and/or Development Funding for developing climate related projects. There are a range of projects that are being developed that cover the three main sources of emissions: Buildings, Energy System; and Transport System. The projects include: Buildings: Retrofitting projects including public sector buildings and social housing that hope to attract grant funding where it is available and then also investment funding for bankable projects. Energy Systems: Energy projects including district heating, renewable energy and energy storage projects. Transport Systems: EVs & charging infrastructure projects that hope to attract grant funding and finance.

The risks increase if the heat is high throughout the day. If the heat carries on through the nights, the body has less possibilities to recover. Water management - Flood capital programme: Flooding is a key issue for many of our communities and can have a significant impact upon their quality of life. There is an urgency to protect properties and avoid the blight that flood incidents can place on local communities and economies. We are equipping communities with the skills, support, knowledge, and equipment to protect their own property and the investment from ECC forms a vital part of partnership funding from national through to regional and local levels. The Flood Prevention Capital Programme was instigated to reduce the level of surface water flood risk to properties. For the first seven years, the Flood Team have increased the number of properties protected year on year, culminating in over 1,800 by the end of 2022/23. climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Las Vegas is one of the fastest warming cities in the country as the average annual high and low temperatures have continued to increase over time. Over the next 30 years, if there are no mitigation techniques applied to the area, the average annual number of days when temperatures exceed 100 degrees will increase to 70 days. Extreme heat is further exacerbated by the urban heat island effect which can cause the following:-Delays, business risks, and health concerns for employees that work outside, especially at the City's resorts, construction and development labor. -Increased energy and water demand for air conditioning and cooling, as well as increased building operational costs, employee needs, and goods requiring refrigeration. -Poorer air quality through the greater incidences of inversion layers.Although Las Vegas is prepared for prolonged periods of intense heat, the impact of prolonged high temperatures in the western US will stress electricity supply, as well as deter tourists from visiting, impacting the local economy. The EPA predicts that hotter days will increase ground level ozone, which can produce smog and increase in respiratory infections. They also predict an increase in fine particulate matter, which could exacerbate a host of respiratory diseases. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): As the population of Las Vegas grows, more communities are being built on the outter parts of the city. Las Vegas is a valley and the further away communities are built, the closer they are to the mountains which contain a lot of trees. For example, Mt. Charleston is an area that many frequent to escape the city heat in the summertime or visit the snow in the winter time. This area is vulnerable to wildfires and there are homes within Mt. Charleston, and homes and electrical units nearby. Wildfire risks have increased due to the prolonged drought and extreme heat that Las Vegas experiences. Fires, including those that are local and those burn across the American West, also impact air quality and those that have respiratory sensitivities/illnesses may experiences exacerbated symptoms due to poor air quality from wildfires. | Drought: Southern Nevada continues through 20 years of drought. In the long-term, Southern Nevada's community, economy, and agricultural sector would be affected by the availability of water. The elevations in Lake Powell and Lake Mead are intended to rise and fall to capture excess water in high flow years and to buffer against dry years (or droughts). The Secretary of the Interior is responsible for delivering water from Lake Mead to the Lower Basin States and Mexico. Shortages and surpluses of water are based upon Lake Mead's elevation. If Lake Mead dips below 1,075 feet, the Secretary of the Interior could declare a shortage, meaning Nevada and the other Colorado River Basin states would be required to reduce its Colorado River allocation. The amount of allocation reduction depends upon Lake Mead's elevation level. As of July 2022, given conditions in the Colorado Rockies and the Colorado River Basin, the projected elevation has dropped below 1,050 feet, and has triggered shortage declarations. | Water stress: Similar to drought, Las Vegas is impacted by water, drought and water stress. Policies have been implemented to reduce the overall consumption of water. The City of LV is following guidelines in the Southern Nevada Water Authority's Conservation and Water Resources Plan to reduce the current consumption (~100 gallons per person, per day) to 85 Gallons Per Capita Per Day (GPCD) by 2035. | Increased water demand: Similar to drought and water stress. As the population in Las Vegas increases there will be more demand for water. Policies and conservation plans exist to reduce the consumption of water, and stricter policies are in draft mode to reduce the consumption of water even more. For example, in 2021, the Nevada Legislature passed Assembly Bill 356, which will make Las Vegas the first region in the U.S. to permanently ban \'non-functional\' grass. project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - City of Las Vegas C-PACE: The city of Las Vegas launched the state's first Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) program, a new effort designed to provide long-term investments in clean energy for commercial property owners. C-PACE was enabled by the 2017 Nevada Legislature and adopted in November 2018 by the Las Vegas City Council. Under this program, which is commonly found in other parts of the country, owners of existing commercial properties will be able to finance up to 100 percent of the cost of energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy projects for up to 25 years through a special assessment placed on the property. Project financing is provided by private capital providers in an open market and repaid through the assessment. Since the financing is tied to the property, the owner is not required to sign a personal guarantee and the C-PACE assessment can transfer to a new owner upon sale. For a project to be eligible, the project's estimated energy cost savings must exceed the financing amount, providing a positive cash flow for the property owner; property owners, in turn, reduce their energy costs and may improve the value of their building—all with no upfront, out-of-pocket costs. The City selected Sustainable Real Estate Solutions (SRS) to serve as the third-party administrator of the C-PACE program. SRS will handle outreach, education, project underwriting and quality assurance services and is launched the program in August 2019.
