project_info: Transport - Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure works: Newcastle's Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Strategy has been developed to respond to the current and expected future need for EV charging infrastructure across the city. The strategy sets out how Newcastle City Council (referred to as the 'Council') will support increasing uptake of electric vehicles (referred to as 'EV') on roads across the city. This strategy has a 5 year time horizon. Newcastle City Council (the Council) has provided a range of public charge points for Electric Vehicles (EVs) since 2015. However, under investment in the existing network of EV charge points over the years, as well as recent developments in EV technology and much greater demand for EVs has meant that our city-wide EV charging infrastructure needs renewing, upgrading and extending over the coming months and years. The Council's vision is to create a leading network of charging infrastructure in neighbourhoods and city destinations that will support and accelerate the transition towards EVs. There are 5 proposed Priority Actions in the strategy covering a range of charging infrastructure scenarios across the city - they are: -Action 1: Deliver an inclusive neighbourhood charge point roll-out -Action 2: Establish a network of publicly available destination EV charge points -Action 3: Deliver an EV car club model -Action 4: Accelerate EV transition within the Council and Your Homes Newcastle fleet-Action 5: Deploy rapid charging infrastructure for electric taxis. To deliver these actions and deploy several hundred publicly available residential and destination charge points across the city, an extensive capital programme is required for installation of the units and ancillary infrastructure, as well as ongoing maintenance and operations services.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Council operational assets (non-domestic public sector buildings owned by Newcastle City Council): Over the last five years Newcastle City Council has been bidding into a match funding grant scheme for decarbonisation measures for our non-domestic buildings such as our leisure centres, council buildings and libraries. The only funding pot to enable these services to meet Net Zero is the UK governments Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) which requires match funding from the Council. So far under PSDS round one we delivered works to 15 schools, 6 offices, 3 leisure centres 2 libraries, an entertainment hall, the Discovery Museum and several car parks. Measures installed included air source heat pumps, one district heat connection, solar panels, electric heating, ventilation, and electrical infrastructure upgrades, alongside business energy management system upgrades, insulation, double glazing, secondary glazing and LED lighting. Under PSDS round three we have installed works in 2 leisure centres, 1 children's social care site, 1 adult social care site and a district heat connection to a college building. The capital cost of the Non-Domestic Public Sector Buildings decarbonisation (full programme of Newcastle City Council buildings) is £90.5 million. However, in 2025 it was announced that PSDS has ended so the future of funding for our non-domestic buildings is unknown. We have developed a number of RIBA stage 4 designs for council operational assets but need to fund these.

project_info: Renewable energy - Byker Heat Network Decarbonisation: The Byker housing scheme was constructed in the 1970s and covers an area of approximately 80 hectares, comprising residential properties and community buildings. One of the most notable features is the Byker Wall, a 2km long continuous block of multi-storey maisonettes along the north boundary of the estate which contains 620 homes. The rest of the estate generally consists of a mixture of low-rise multi-storey blocks and terraced housing, all characterised by modernist architecture with the use of bright colours. There is one high-rise cluster to the north- western corner. Apart from some privately-owned houses, all of the estate and some community buildings is heated by the Byker district heating scheme (referred to as the Byker Heat Network). Newcastle City Council, together with project partners (Karbon Homes, Byker Community Trust and Your Homes Newcastle) is currently conducting a Strategic Feasibility Study for the Decarbonisation, Renewal and Reconfiguration of the Byker Heat Network. The purpose of this strategic feasibility study is to: a)Conduct an independent investigation into and an analysis of the causes of the primary side network failures that took place in late 2021 b)Undertake a detailed condition assessment of the primary side network including recommendations for repairs and renewals of end-of-life elements c)Assess the potential routes to full decarbonisation of the heat network d)Undertake a techno economic appraisal of the technologies available to achieve the decarbonisation e)Examine the options for the conversion and reconfiguration of the primary distribution network such that is compatible with those potential low carbon options identified in c b) and incorporate renewal of end-of-life elements of the network as identified in b) (expected to be most significantly the primary network and the back-up oil-fired boilers) f)Undertake an appraisal of potential alternative energy centre location(s) to the single Byker Heat Station which currently supplies heat to the network, and thereby improve system resilience g)Examine the potential expansion opportunities to the heat network including new and existing properties h)Provide an economic assessment (including capital costs, operational and maintenance costs, and lifecycle costs) of the potential scheme options identified in ca) to ge) and identify routes to funding such scheme.

Please note that Northumberland County Council is not seeking funding to develop this project, however this project is a planned climate-related project within the jurisdiction that is seeking funding through the North East Carbon and Nature Marketplace.: The Northumberland Peat Partnership are planning a project that would allow them to gather, analyse and use investment grade data on bogs within Northumberland, with the aim to attract more investment into peatland restoration. The project builds one work already active across sites in Northumberland, such as Whitelee Moor where upland blanket bog is being restored. Ongoing monitoring allows evidence of the long term effects of restorative works, and to plan for how to achieve more benefits. 
The investment would fund purchase and maintenance of equipment to gather high quality water table data, and the vital work of analysing that data and interpreting what it means for action. This intelligence is critical to understand what is required to restore the hydrological functioning of bogs. 
The project also plans to carry out communications work highlighting evidence on the relationship between healthier peatlands and the well-being of people in the North East. 
The project will also assist the Northumberland Peat Partnership to prepare for the launch of peatland biodiversity credits. It will allow completion of the preparation work necessary to make the most of this upcoming opportunity and potentially access new forms of financial support for restoration.

Water management - South Tyne Sediment Project. Please note that Northumberland County Council is not seeking funding to develop this project, however this project is a planned climate-related project within the jurisdiction that is seeking funding through the North East Carbon and Nature Marketplace.: Tyne Rivers Trust is leading a project that aims to reduce the fine sediment load of the South Tyne by at least 20% while reducing lead and zinc contamination. Using nature based solutions the work will also contribute to improved water quality, natural flood management, habitat restoration and carbon sequestration. An aligned project promoting regenerative farming will maximise the impact of the project while improving soil health, increasing carbon capture and water retention. 
The first phase of the project has been completed. This was a fine sediment fingerprinting study that was funded by Northumbrian Water and the Mining Remediation Authority, and delivered by Tyne Rivers Trust and Rothamsted Research. Through the study key locations were identified along the South Tyne where interventions to tackle fine sediment pollution will have the greatest impact. This has enabled identifying Wellhope Burn as a priority for the next phase of the project. 

Using measures such as riverbank stabilisation, woodland and wetland creation, ditch blocking and reconnecting the river to its floodplain and natural course, the pilot project will reduce the South Tyne fine sediment load by approximately 3.3%, reduce heavy metal load by approximately 1 tonne per year, create 7 hectares of woodland, 1 hectare of wetlands and ponds and lead to restoration of 2.5 hectares of floodplain. 


Project information and costs/investment costs have been obtained from information on the Carbon and Nature Marketplace. Further information is available on the link provided.

Mean summer temperature: Increase of up to 3.7C. Mean winter temperature: Increase of up to 2.9C. Mean daily maximum summer temperature: Increase of up to 4.5C. Risks and Impacts The rising temperatures, particularly during summer, pose significant threats, as evidenced by events such as the Summer 2022 heatwaves. 

Key concerns include: 

Built Environment: Higher temperatures may lead to heat-related damage to buildings and infrastructure, impacting the city's built environment. 

Transport and Energy Supply: Increased temperatures can disrupt the Council's transport networks and energy systems, necessitating adaptations to improve resilience. 

Urban Heat Island Effect: The intensification of this effect may lead to increased cooling demands, further straining energy systems. 

Public Health: Vulnerable groups are at heightened risk of heat-related discomfort, with potential knock-on effects for NHS services due to increased healthcare demands. 

Vulnerability Assessment Emerging research (subject to change as studies progress) highlights the following: 34% of Nottingham's population has a high vulnerability to extreme heat, considering both high exposure and sensitivity to heat. 

When focusing solely on areas with very high heat exposure (calculated from land surface temperature) and very high sensitivity (based on seven socio-economic factors), this decreases to 1.9% of the population. | Drought: Nottingham is expected to experience greater seasonality in rainfall patterns, with projections indicating more rainfall in winter and less in summer compared to the baseline average (1981-2000). 

Key Impacts on Water Availability

 Reduced Summer Water Availability: Declines in summer rainfall may result in increased water shortages, affecting the supply for various services, facilities, and communities across Nottingham. 

Regional Water Stress: Recent years have seen prolonged periods of hot weather combined with shorter rainfall seasons, creating significant regional water stress. 

Warmer weather has led to a surge in water usage, further exacerbating the strain on available water resources. 

These changes highlight the importance of implementing sustainable water management strategies to address the challenges posed by shifting rainfall patterns and ensure the resilience of Nottingham's water supply.

Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Domestic Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme: Large scale external fabric retrofit programme - Nottingham has around 5,500 solid brick or system built council houses that require external wall insulation and other fabric energy efficiency measures, and could benefit from solar PV on roofs.

Nottingham has been pioneering approaches utilising modern construction methods, such as panelisation and offsite manufacture through its Energiesprong programme, to deliver deep retrofit with high quality, guaranteed performance and low disruption to occupiers. However, these approaches need delivery at scale to truly realise their potential and drive down costs.

A programme at the scale of 1,000 properties per year would be a game changer in driving the development of a new locally-based industry to manufacture and install high quality external wall insulation and other measures, using modern construction methods and offsite manufacture.

Based on Nottingham's experience, there is currently a funding gap in the order of £25k between the cost of offsite manufacture external fabric measures and the investment that can be justified based on long-term maintenance savings, property value increases and other revenues. This will decrease through economies of scale and innovation in approach.

Given Nottingham's experience and current programme, and its in-depth knowledge of the supply chain, it is very well place to scale up fast. Our current projects have shown a lack of capacity and capability in the supply chain to deliver the required solutions at a cost effective price point, so our programme will need to start scaling up gradually, with a target of achieving 1000 per year once capacity is built.

Vegetation helps manage both urban heat and stormwater, reducing flood risk and mitigating temperature extremes. Green areas also support biodiversity—especially when they serve as corridors for species movement—making the city more adaptable and ecologically stable.

Other: Zoonotic disease: Models predict potential range expansions of ticks carrying pathogens such as Lyme borreliosis and tick-borne encephalitis in northern Europe, with milder winter conditions such as temperature increases. Such conditions can allow more ticks to survive the winter, and increase the probability of tick bites. Young children, the elderly and those with chronic health problems are at higher risk as well as migrants, refugees and populations living in poverty that might be less likely to have secure, air-conditioned homes and therefore become more susceptible to insect bites (Paz, 2020). | Other: Air pollution: Air pollution can cause, complicate, or exacerbate many adverse health conditions. It usually manifests as respiratory or cardiac symptoms and can lead to chronic health issues. Recent studies show that poor air quality can affect every organ in the body and even cause damage to cognitive performance. Exposure to poor air quality is directly related to diseases such as cancer, asthma, stroke, heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and dementia. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), air pollution kills an estimated 8 million people worldwide every year, of which 4.2 million are attributed to exposure to outdoor air pollution and 3.8 million to indoor air pollution. Currently nine out of 10 people in the world breathe air containing health impacting levels of air pollutants. Long term exposure to anthropogenic particulate air pollution in Oxford could be responsible for 6% of all deaths of people aged 25 and over. Air pollution also affects the global economy in several ways: it costs human lives, it reduces people's ability to work, it affects vital products like food, it damages cultural and historical monuments, it reduces the ability of ecosystems to perform functions societies need and it costs money in remediation or restoration. This is of particular importance given the current situation caused by the coronavirus pandemic, which has shown the important link between human health and the health of our economy. | Urban flooding: Flooding can have an impact on the natural environment, particularly regarding flooding of arable land and disruption to agriculture activities. Flooding can also increase soil runoff and erosion and force the migration of species. Furthermore, floods can cause damage to homes, disruption to transport, utilities and other services. Although rare, direct physical health impacts can arise from flooding. Such impacts include drowning, injury due to collision with debris, electrocution or fire exposure, infection, and heart attacks. | Other: Extreme weather: Ever changing weather conditions associated with climate change are likely to impact buildings and infrastructure in Oxford. For example, it is expected that the UK will see heavier rainfall events occurring more frequently (particularly in Winter), which raises the flood risk and associated damage to buildings and infrastructure. Additionally, rising temperatures are likely to disturb the historic building stock in Oxford, since increased heat and humidity can accelerate the chemical processes which cause the building materials to deteriorate. Furthermore, it's likely that storms and strong winds will increase in frequency and intensity over the coming years. This will increase the likelihood of fallen trees or flying debris causing damage to infrastructure and buildings. | Extreme heat: There is an evident higher current heatwave hazard in urban areas such as Oxford City due to greater urban and suburban areas, higher cooling degree days and lower proportion of green space. Key railway stations and routes are located in Oxford City which have a high heatwave hazard.Summertime overheating in both new and existing dwellings is widespread and increasing, even in temperate climates. Many buildings in Oxford are designed to retain heat, therefore periods of extreme heat bring increased risks of overheating for the building occupants. High temperatures in homes negatively impact people's lives. Sleep is disrupted, with knock on impacts on health and productivity. Even more seriously, overheating effects mortality and morbitity, with elderly and vulnerable populations particularly affected. | River flooding: Critical infrastructures are located in areas of high current flood hazard, including electricity transmission lines located along the River Thames path to the west of Oxford and to the east and west of Abingdon, south of Oxford City. The railway line from Oxford City to the Cotswolds in West Oxfordshire lies on an area of high flood hazard, as it lies in proximity to the River Evenlode. This is also true of the Oxford to Banbury rail line which is located in parallel to the channel of the River Cherwell. All other main rail lines in Oxfordshire are located at least partially within an area of high current flood hazard. | Extreme heat: Current heatwave risk as a function of vulnerability, exposure and hazard demonstrates high heatwave risk in Oxford City. Eight of the ten wards with the highest current heatwave risk in Oxfordshire County are located in Oxford City. Extreme heat can impact vulnerable groups which have a lower ability to adapt and the people at greatest risk from heat health impacts (morbidity and mortality), including: • Elderly people, chronically ill people and people taking certain medicines may have impairments in their thermoregulation, thus more likely to overheat. • Children under 5 years are unable to control their body temperatures as efficiently as adults and are more likely to overheat. • There is a link between increasing temperatures (resulting in dehydration) and increasing infections of Gram-negative bacteria, such as E. coli. (risk of such infectious diseases is greatest in elderly people). • People with alcohol or drug dependence and homeless people may be less able to adapt to extreme temperatures | Extreme wind: High winds and storms can cause damage to infrastructure cutting of roads and settlements with fallen trees and damaging electricity transmission lines causing power cuts. Additionally, high winds and storms can impact on communities, resulting in injuries and damage to buildings. The observed monthly mean wind speed at 10 m in 1991-2020 in Oxford city was 8.35 knots compared to a national average of 8.33 knots. project_info: Renewable energy - Project LEON: Project LEO (Local Energy Oxfordshire), the first phase of Project LEON has now been implemented. Project LEON was one of the UK's most ambitious, wide-ranging and innovative energy trials, seeking to accelerate the UK's transition to a zero-carbon energy system. Project LEO saw that a decentralised, or local energy solution, focused on balancing energy use at the grid edge, closest to homes and businesses, will be the most desirable approach to accelerating our transition to a zero-carbon energy system. Project LEO, as a partnership, ran trials in Oxfordshire to understand how new technologies and services, particularly at the 'edge' of the network - closest to the point where people are using energy - can benefit local people, communities, and the energy system. This cross sector collaborative project built a broad range of reliable evidence of the technological, market and social conditions needed for a greener, more flexible and fair electricity system. It also learned what changes need to happen within national and local policy to enable this to happen.Project LEO: -Tested new market and flexibility models-Advanced the capabilities of networks to manage smart, renewable, and storage technologies -Facilitated local participation in the energy systemWe are currently seeking funding for phase 2, Project LEON.

project_info: Other: Governance & stakeholder collaboration - Knowledge transfer platform between businesses and academia: An Oxford 'knowledge transfer platform' would look to unlock innovation, efficiency and productivity improvements by matching up: (i) academics with businesses that require their area of expertise, and (ii) businesses with other businesses that they can learn from. This would enable large and leading businesses in Oxford to provide guidance and support to smaller businesses. One element of this could be leading players in Oxford (e.g. BMW) sharing detailed case studies (e.g. installing a heat pump system in Plant Oxford, or completing an environmental management audit) for others to learn from and use as a guide. The matchmaking, case studies and associated communications would be delivered through existing networks, such as Oxford Greentech, with overall steer from the ZCOP Secretariat.The action could also seek to integrate part (i) of the matchmaking offer with the national-level Innovate UK scheme 'Knowledge Transfer Partnerships' (KTPs). 1.Complete a detailed design of the potential scheme, including whether it links to the Innovate UK scheme, how businesses will be made aware, and what the matchmaking process will be.2.Utilise an online form to gather information from businesses (and academics should the action not link with Innovate UK's KTPs) regarding the key questions they face and the learnings they have to share (including any case studies).3.Looking across the landscape of submissions, the agreed matchmaking process will result in introductions facilitated by the ZCOP, as well as a selection of a number of case studies to be developed based on expressed demand.4.Once the process is established, the matchmaking and selection and sharing of case studies can continue with ease as long as there is sufficient business demand and interest.

Urban flooding: While the State of Oregon found only a 50% probability of occurrence, Portland has dealt with flooding in the past, including major areas of downtown. Given this, Portland may be more susceptible to flooding, as the City is at the intersection of two major rivers - Columbia and Willamette. Risk of flooding is expected to increase in the future. Most areas of the city are within the FEMA 100 year floodplain maps. Populations effective are primarily in industrial areas and have lower income populations and communities of color in North Portland and downtown. | Extreme heat: For this risk the probability was estimated by the State of Oregon as a 90% probability of occurrence, meaning the probability is high. Portland is already experiencing more frequent high heat days. Summer 2024 included more early heat waves, with temps over 100 before mid August. This is expected to continue.

For this risk the magnitude of the impact is assessed as high because high heat days are increasing, heat impacts all residents and businesses, and already, since 2020, high heat events have led to numerous deaths in the City. Given the magnitude and high probability of this risk and the evidence of impacts from prior heat waves, it is known that Portland's most vulnerable communities will be most impacted, including low income populations, communities of color, elderly, and outdoor workers. | Mass movement: Probability of mass movement is estimated at 50%. Portland has always had risk of landslides in the City due to topography, logging and development practices. This is expected to continue with warmer winters and potential for more intense rain events, combined with increased spring and summer snow melt due to higher temperatures. Impacts of mass movement are limited, impacting fewer residents overall, except for risks to damage to transportation infrastructure which could have broader impacts on the region. The areas of the city most at risk for mass movement are in Portland's west hills, which have a higher per capita income than Portland as a whole. Whether or not vulnerable communities are impacted depends on where the mass movement occurs and what infrastructure is impacted. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfires probability in Oregon was estimated at 66% in 2014. Since this time Oregon has experienced more frequent wildfires, increasing in intensity and acreage burned. In Oregon fire season is typically occurs between July and October. As a result, in recent years Portland has experienced poor air quality days resulting from wildfires in the region. 

Wildfires can burn in the large natural areas located throughout Portland's urban area. Portland's considerable urban forest, natural parks and open space areas contribute to the potential for wildfires within the urban area. Portland's largest urban fires have occurred in and around Forest Park. Forest Park, is one of the largest urban forests in the United States at 5,200 acres and over 80 miles of trails, fire lanes, and forest roads. At a smaller scale, the vast majority of wildfires in Portland involve grasses and brush. Portland is at increased risk of wildfires due to hotter and drier summers. 

Vulnerable populations will include low income populations who have less ability to adapt to increasing wildfire threats and less ability to protect from poor air quality. In addition, elderly, children, and people with weakened immune systems or respiratory conditions will be most impacted.

River flooding: Exceptional rainfall in January 2024 saw the River Thames, which passes through Reading, reach its highest level since 1947 as a result of which flood conditions occurred, inundating 21 properties and 3 business premises. Reading experienced a major flood in 1947 when much of Lower Caversham was flooded. This flood was in part caused by snow melt across the Thames catchment but a flood of this size could also happen just from rainfall, as happened in 1894, when flood levels were even higher on the Thames. Flood modelling by the UK Environment Agency shows that over 700 properties are currently at risk of flooding from the River Thames in Caversham and north Reading area alone. With climate change this number will rise. This makes it the largest community at risk from the Thames without existing or proposed flood defences. Homes and businesses in low lying areas of Caversham flooded in 2014 and 2003. Houses were surrounded by floodwater and a number of roads were closed to vehicles. In 2003 several roads were closed, some for as long as 5 days. The wet winter of 2013/14 led to widespread flooding along Reading's waterways and floodplains (Thames, Loddon and Kennet). Sonning Bridge was closed on two occasions in January and for part of February, while Loddon Bridge Park & Ride was closed for much of January. In some areas, flooding due to rising groundwater levels was a problem and there was widespread travel disruption. Similarly, the wet period in late winter 2019-20 caused widespread travel disruption. January 2014 was the wettest January on record in Reading, with 151 mm of rail (251% the normal January rainfall). February 2014 was the wettest February on record in Reading, with 117 mm of rain (287 % of normal). Reading has also experienced recent summer flash flooding - in July 2007, 69 mm of rain fell in only 15 hours (the monthly mean rainfall for July in Reading is 46 mm), leading to flooding on many local rivers. The Reading Climate Change Adaptation Plan includes a summary of impact by area showing the potential spatial distribution of climate impacts on different parts of the Borough. We know from the UK Climate Projections that variability in rainfall is increasing. Wet winters will get wetter, but we can still expect some dry winters. Summer rainfall is expected to decrease significantly, but when it rains in summer there may be more intense rainfall events. | Drought: Summer 1976 saw the culmination of a prolonged drought which had started in April 1975. July/August 1976 saw barely any rain for 37 days, making it the longest period without measurable rainfall. Reading is a growing town which will place further pressure on water resources at the same time that climate change will be having an impact on water availability and water quality. It is therefore expected that drought risk will increase in the coming decades. As well as impacts on people, drought will have impacts on Reading's natural environment. Reading Borough Council's Local Plan and Biodiversity Action Plan identify Biodiversity Opportunity Areas, one of which, Kennet Valley East, has been highlighted as an area where measures to retain winter flood water in the flood plain of the River Kennet throughout the year could have benefits for biodiversity and carbon storage. The Council is therefore engaged with local partners in a project to take this forward. £20,000 has been allocated for a feasibility study. The first part of this study was completed in March 2024 and suggested significant potential, including income from Biodiversity Net Gain to fund ongoing maintenance, for a scheme. | Urban flooding: See also text above on river flooding much of which applies to urban (surface water) flooding. A Preliminary Flood Risk Assessment was completed for Reading in 2011, 2 years after the Flood Risk Regulations 2009 placed a duty on the Council to prepare such an assessment by June 2011. This estimated some 7,600 properties were at risk of flooding to a depth greater than 0.3m during a 1 in 200 annual chance rainfall event, out of a total of c. 65,410 households - giving the figure cited of between 10-20% of the population being exposed to the risk of flooding. Vulnerable groups will be inherently more exposed to flood risk in view of factors such as reduced mobility, availability of resources to adapt etc. | Extreme heat: Reading benefits from an excellent record of local weather observations dating from 1902, gathered by the University of Reading. Just from this record, it is possible to see indications of changes in climate. For example, the six warmest summers recorded in Reading all occurred since 1976 (with 2018 the warmest), while the five coldest summers all occurred before 1955. Since 1961, mean temperature in Reading has been rising at a rate of 0.26 °C per decade (J. Lowe, pers. com, 2019).June 1976 was the warmest June on record in Reading, until 2025 where the temperature exceeded the previous mean temperature record of 18.1 °C, at 18.3 °C (3 °C above the June average for 1981-2010). Like 1976, the very hot weather continued into July. After a dry start to the year, the hot dry conditions led to widespread forest and woodland fires in Berkshire (and many other places in south and south-east England). Maximum temperatures reached 30 °C or above every day for 14 days from end of June into July 1976, peaking at 34.0 °C on 26 June. Following a very hot summer in 2018, which saw temperatures in Reading reach a high of 32.9°C, with seven hot days where the temperature reached 30ºC or over, Reading also experienced record-breaking temperatures during 2019. Between 1908 and 2021, only five days have reached 35 °C or higher in Reading. The hottest day recorded in Reading was 36.4 °C on 10 August 2003 until a new (provisional) high of 37.6 °C was recorded at the University of Reading on 19 July 2022 during the heatwave which saw the UK national temperature record also broken. Looking ahead, hot summers are expected to become more common. In the recent past (1981-2000) the chance of a summer as hot as 2018 (one of the hottest on record) was less than 10%. The chance has already increased due to climate change and is now between 10% and 25%. With future warming, the chance of a summer as hot as 2018 is around 50% by mid-century. 2025 has so far proven to be the warmest summer on record in the UK.

project_info: Renewable energy - Heat Networks: An initial Heat Mapping and Masterplanning study commissioned by Reading Borough Council was completed in 2018/19. A further Feasibility Study identifying the most viable locations for a district heat network, using the Towns Rivers as a source of renewable heat, stepped up by heat pumps, was completed in 2023. The UK Government's Heat Network Investment Programme offers a structured process, supported by grant funding, to help local authorities develop heat network proposals, and Reading is following this process. The total cost of the project has been estimated at c£30 million. In 2024 the council has progressed the 'detailed project development' phase of the project completing packages of work which include network outline design, technoeconomic model, stakeholder engagement and outline business case. This work in budgeted at £325,000 which has been secured primarily through grant funding (66%), which will enable an appropriate commercial model to be identified. It is anticipated that Government funding of up to 50% will be available. The Council will take a committee decision on the project in 2025/6 and will proceed to commercialisation in 2026. The latest design includes the hospital, 2 regeneration projects (~1000 homes), 1 hotel, University campus, magistrates court, town hall and 2 schools. https://images.reading.gov.uk/2025/03/Reading-Heat-Network-Feasibility-Study_Rev03a-1.pdf\n(note previous stage feasibility shows north of station area)

climate_hazard: Heat stress: In June of 2021, Seattle experienced a significant heat dome event that caused numerous impacts on the City of Seattle's operations and public services. Throughout the city, draw bridges were shut down, highways buckled from heat expansion, city transfer stations were closed to prevent heat stress among workers, and other city resources were diverted to protect both worker and public health. Acute heat waves like this one, made more likely through climate change, present an ongoing climate risk to city operations. | Extreme heat: Increase in mean temperatures of 4.2 - 5.9 F by 2050s. increase in temperature of hottest days 6.5F. Not typically associated with heat, Seattle has averaged only a handful of 90 degree (F) days per year during the past few decades. By the end of this century, such events are expected to become more common, with more than two weeks of 90 degree (F) days likely each summer. Also certain to increase are nighttime temperatures and humidity. Increased temperatures will likely increase water demand, which SPU feels it can address through its comprehensive water conservation program. Frontline populations within Seattle are more likely to live within live within areas without urban tree cover and near industrial areas that concentrate extreme heat | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise of 1 foot by 2035 and 2 feet by 2060. The water along Seattle's Puget Sound shoreline has risen by more than 6 inches during the past century. Climate change is expected to accelerate rising sea levels during the next century. Central estimates indicate that Seattle will experience 10 inches of sea-level rise by 2050, and 28 inches by 2100, and 47 inches by 2150. While chronic inundation is a concern, sea-level rise impacts will first be noticed episodically with more frequent tidal flooding events. Water levels associated with storm surges and \'king tides\' (annually occurring extreme events) today will eventually become monthly, even daily events. Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) has developed tools to help visualize and evaluate impacts of sea-level rise scenarios. These storm surges will likely hit vulnerable communities most acutely, as several communities live near the Duwamish waterway that is acutely impacted by tidal surges. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Seattle obtains its water from two watersheds, which are either exclusively owned by SPU, or are administered in part by SPU. These watersheds provide natural services that purifies and preserves SPU's water supply. SPU has projected that an increasing climate will results in hotter, drier summers, which increases the risk of wildfires in our watersheds. A large wildfire within our watershed could impact the quality of the water in our supply, posing a serious risk to Seattle's essential infrastructure. Wildfire smoke also exacerbates existing health disparities caused by air pollution and heat events, with the impacts most acutely felt by people living in proximity to these industrial zones. | Urban flooding: More extreme precipitation 3-11% on average for the 2050s. Other: Utility Infrastructure, Drainage - Duwamish Valley Resiliency District: Over the next 10+ years, Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) will invest over $500+ million in water management (e.g., drainage) and water quality improvement (Superfund cleanup, combined sewer overflows control, source control sufficiency, etc.) infrastructure in the Duwamish Valley. Additionally, SPU will begin planning, designing, and delivery of flooding prevention infrastructure projects to protect the Duwamish Valley community—residents and businesses—from the impacts of extreme precipitation, high tides, and rising sea levels. Given the financial restrictions and need for utility nexus on spending ratepayer dollars, investments from SPU alone will not create transformative change and placemaking for the community. However, through creating alignment, with community, other government agencies and funders, the design of SPU investments can facilitate positive community outcomes.
Our planning and delivery of these projects will also focus on developing replicable and scalable community investment and engagement models suitable for our local and regional context.

ADDITIONAL CONTEXT
This 685 acre area is currently home to 4,154 residents and 6,426 jobs. It is the center of the City's Latino community with a population that is 47% Latino and more than 70% of residents are non-white. Median household income is 40% below the Seattle average with a third of residents below 200% of the poverty level. Due to historic land use practices and decisions, this area has disproportionate health inequities, environmental burdens; area residents have 13-year shorter life expectancy than other, wealthier and less diverse, areas of Seattle. The area is home to Seattle's only river and the City's largest Superfund site. If unaddressed, flooding related to climate change will threaten both industry and small residential parts of the community. At present, South Park experiences flooding associated with heavy rainfall with increased flooding due to both the sea-level rise and rainfall intensity impacts of climate change. Of the 120 acres in Seattle projected to experience daily water levels in 2060 that are 2' greater than today's high tide, the majority are located in the South Park industrial area. The defined outputs of this effort will contribute to improved health and avoid negative outcomes for both the residents and businesses. The water infrastructure will reduce the existing flooding in South Park associated with flooding from rainfall and deliver new infrastructure to manage the expected flooding associated with sea level rise and the rising Duwamish River. The management of sea level rise, delivered in a community-centered manner, will also address needed open space buffering for residents living in the industrial area, contributing positively to public health outcomes for those residents. Second, it provides an opportunity to bring together and leverage the investment of others including the Army Corps of Engineers, Port of Seattle, King County, US Forest Service, affordable housing providers, private property owners, community foundations, nonprofits, etc. Collaboration of that scale between government agencies working in South Park is unprecedented and will allow capital and program investments to be planned and delivered strategically rather than in individual government silos.

project_info: Buildings - Clean Heat Program: The Clean Heat program supports low-income and moderate income households convert from expensive and dirty heating oil to clean and energy-efficient heat pumps. Since 2017, Seattle has provided incentives and no-cost conversions to more than 2,000 households. As the program makes great progress in meeting its goals of eliminating all heating oil by 2030, residential natural gas use is widely used and the program currently does not provide incentives for gas to heat pump conversions given the large financial/budget need. The City is currently looking at window heat pump technology for affordable housing buildings and has launched an interdepartmental process to identify barriers and opportunities with the technology. The goal is to then develop a list of good candidate multifamily buildings to support the use of window heat pumps and learn from the NYCHA/NYSERDA program. Funding for the purchase and installation of the equipment for a pilot would be needed.

Heavy precipitation: Climate change hazards often most impact those facing systemic inequities; it can also exacerbate these inequities as these same populations often have the least resources to respond. 

For extreme rainfall, impacts that may particularly impact VULNERABLE POPULATIONS are:- 
- Increased costs for response actions and clean-up after heavy rain events
- Buildings may be maladapted in terms of water ingress, rain or snow loads
- Increase in landslide risk affecting public infrastructure and private property
- Transportation and mobility impacted by street flooding - particularly those with disabilities, relying on public transit, or relying on driving for their job.
- Property damage from flooding. There was significant flooding damage in neighboring jurisdictions in 2021, resulting in all road and rail links being severed between SW British Columbia and the rest of the country, which disrupted supply chains and gasoline supplies were rationed until pipelines were repaired. This increased the cost of goods and gasoline, making it harder for those with lower incomes or who rely on driving for their job or primary mode of transport.

Sectors most exposed: 
-Sewage, waste management and remediation activities: -Increases in private property sewer back-ups in combined sewer areas due to high rainfall volume in sewer system
-Human health and social work activities: flooding due to heavy rainfall can cause respiratory issues due to mold exposure. Furthermore, changes in precipitation patterns can alter the habitats of disease-carrying insects, potentially increasing the spread of vector-borne diseases. Finally, the stress and trauma associated with heavy precipitation can effects on mental health including anxiety, depression and PTSD.
-Electricity, gas, steam and ac supply: heavy precipitation can cause power outages and damage to infrastructure. Utilities may face increased operational strain as they work to repair damage assets and restore services. This can lead to higher operational costs and potential service disruptions. 
 | Storm: Storm events result in increase urban and coastal flooding, wind damage (see impacts detailed above) as well as limiting access to amenities and required services such as medical care, support services etc. and transportation. They can also result in utility interruptions which can be dangerous for some groups such as seniors or those relying on power for heat or medical reasons. In addition, renters and those on lower incomes may have the fewest resources to respond to storm damage to their home. | Extreme heat: Increased health and safety risks, especially to frontline communities during extreme heat events and air quality events; decreased thermal comfort in buildings in the summer due to lack of air conditioning or increasing electricity costs with air conditioning; increasing stress on green infrastructure in the summer time; water supply shortages felt in late summer due to a decreased spring snow pack and higher summer temps could result in increased costs for water and imperative conservation measures. There was an extreme heat event in late June 2021 that led to 117 deaths, in the jurisdiction, due to inadequate housing and insufficient emergency response (see: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/birth-adoption-death-marriage-and-divorce/deaths/coroners-service/death-review-panel/extreme_heat_death_review_panel_report.pdf ). | Urban flooding: Increased surface water flooding from ponding of rainfall in low-lying areas or heavy rainfall overcoming the capacity of drainage system; increase in landslide risk affecting public infrastructure and private property. Vancouver seawall experienced significant damage in 2021, which is a significant recreation destination for the region surrounded by high-density neighborhoods. | Other: Groundwater Issues: Saltwater intrusion is not a significant issue in Vancouver since we're already in close proximity to the ocean and we don't have internal rivers leading to the ocean. We also don't have agricultural land use that would draw water from the Fraser and be impacted by salt moving upstream with sea level rise. What we will experience is 'groundwater rise' due to sea level rise, but this will be more of a parkade and infrastructure issue. Risk to urban forest and native species. Recent example includes looper moth outbreak in coastal coniferous species in Vancouver, impacting nearly 160,000 trees within Stanley Park. | Drought: Water supply shortages felt in late summer due to a decreased spring snowpack and higher summer temperatures could result in increased costs for water, vegetation loss, and more stringent conservation measures. These impacts affect more vulnerable populations in a number of ways - limiting access to water from increased costs, and reducing shade available in public spaces for those that need it (e.g. those without cooling in their home or those without a home). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Increased health and safety risks, especially to frontline communities during air quality events (e.g., smoke from wildfires). Risk of wildfire in urban parks adjacent to jurisdiction (Central Park, Pacific Spirit Park) or within Jurisdiction (Stanley Park) during increasingly hot and dry summers.

Heavy precipitation: In the summer of 2011, in 2014 and again in 2015, there have been torrential downpours in Copenhagen. The same picture will increasingly occur in years to come. If the projections of the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) prove correct, there is a risk of the costs of damage in Copenhagen over the next 100 years totalling DKK 16 billion. This is a conservative estimate. Before the downpour in the summer of 2014, the cost of damage from extreme rainfall events already totalled DKK 6 - 9 billion over the past 6 years. Extreme heat: Coventry and Warwickshire was included in the Met Office's first ever Amber Extreme Heat Warning in June 2021. A number of moths previously considered vagrant or rare are now common. Water is being actively diverted from various water sources in an effort to sustain a sufficient supply for existing businesses and the population. Projections in population growth in coming years will increase the likely demand for water whilst Severn Trent are increasing capacity for water treatment and making significant investments in reducing leaks from the water distribution network. Operation Mighty Oak also recently identified the need to ensure sufficient energy supply as all of the City's water supply is electrically pumped around the City. despite these stresses every person has access to a supply of fresh water that meets the quality standards. It is the freshwater ecosystems that are most impacted upon.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Net Zero Neighbourhood: The Council are working with WMCA to try and access funding for a Net Zero Neighbourhood Demonstrator Project. The Net Zero Neighbourhood (NZN) Demonstrator Programme is aiming to develop a replicable financial and delivery model for creating low carbon energy communities on a street-by-street or neighbourhood-by-neighbourhood basis. The programme is aiming to demonstrate that a street-by-street approach to retrofit and neighbourhood regeneration to support communities to transition to a sustainable lifestyle. The programmes are therefore aiming to demonstrate the following:•Approaches to engaging the community across housing tenures to co-design a Net Zero Neighbourhood and opt-in to installing retrofit measures.•The economies of scale that can be achieved with suppliers by taking a street-by-street approach.•A replicable financial model to deliver a pipeline of neighbourhoods with increasingly less reliance on grant funding.It is expected that the Council will form a set of potential partners that will form part of the NZN Partnership. This would likely include commercial partners, housing associations, investors, various Council teams etc.

climate_hazard:
Storm: Storms are identified as a significant and recurring climate hazard in Cardiff, with increasing socio-economic impacts. The city has experienced multiple named storms in recent years, including Storm Darragh (2024), Storm Eunice (2022), and Storm Dennis (2020), each causing widespread disruption. Impacts have included power outages, transport cancellations, school and park closures, and extensive damage to infrastructure and property.

Current:
The coastal defences are in poor state of repair and therefore storm surges and sea level rise are starting to cause erosion to landfill site and potential environmental impact to Severn Estuary. 

Areas like Ely, Splott, and Butetown - which have high concentrations of ethnic minorities and lower-income households - are among the most socially vulnerable to flooding and storm damage. These communities often live in older housing stock, more prone to damage from high winds and rain.

Future:
Storm surges have the potential to cause flooding to gypsy traveller site and displacement of Cardiff Gypsy population. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Coastal flooding presents significant current and future risks for marginalised and minority communities in Cardiff, particularly those living in vulnerable areas such as Butetown, Grangetown, Splott, and parts of Cardiff Bay. These risks are compounded by social, economic, and infrastructural inequalities.

Current:
The coastal defences are in poor state of repair and therefore storm surges and sea level rise are starting to cause erosion to landfill site and potential environmental impact to Severn Estuary. Urban development in Cardiff Bay also limits the ability of coastal habitats (e.g. saltmarshes) to migrate inland, reducing natural flood protection.


Cardiff's Port and coastal infrastructure are critical for employment and supply chains -disruption affects jobs and access to goods, disproportionately impacting those in precarious work.

Neighbourhood Flood Vulnerability Index (NFVI) highlights Ely, Rhymney, and parts of Grangetown as having high social vulnerability to flooding.

Future: 
Storm surges have the potential to cause flooding to gypsy traveller site and displacement of Cardiff gypsy population.

Sea levels in Cardiff are projected to rise by up to 0.40 metres by the 2050s, with potential for 0.55 metres under extreme scenarios (UKCP18). Increased erosion and storm surges will threaten housing, infrastructure, and natural habitats—especially in Cardiff Bay, Rover Way, and Rhymney Great Wharf.

Rising flood risk may lead to displacement of residents in social housing or poorly maintained buildings. Insurance premiums and property devaluation could make housing unaffordable for low-income families, increasing inequality. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat poses growing risks to elderly people, children, and vulnerable health groups in Cardiff, both now and in the future. These risks are expected to intensify due to climate change, with hotter summers and more frequent heatwaves projected across the city.

Current:
Older adults (14% of Cardiff's population) are more susceptible to heat-related illnesses such as heatstroke, dehydration, and cardiovascular stress, whilst children, especially in schools without adequate ventilation or cooling, are vulnerable to overheating and fatigue. Furthermore, people with pre-existing health conditions (e.g. respiratory or cardiovascular diseases) face increased risks during hot weather.

Many homes, care facilities, and schools in Cardiff are not designed to cope with high temperatures. Care homes and hospitals are identified as key vulnerability hotspots in the Cardiff Climate Risk Assessment.

Flats and social housing - often occupied by lower-income or vulnerable residents - are particularly prone to overheating. Poor insulation and lack of ventilation exacerbate indoor heat stress.

Future:
By the 2050s, Cardiff is projected to experience an increase of hot weather days and posing serious risks to elderly people, children, and those with health vulnerabilities:
- 22 summer days annually with temperatures above 25°C
- 4 hot summer days above 30°C
- Up to 7 tropical nights (minimum temperature > 20°C)

Heat-related deaths in the UK are projected to triple by the 2050s. Vulnerable groups will be disproportionately affected, especially those in poorly ventilated buildings or without access to cooling. | River flooding: Cardiff faces disproportionate risks from river flooding, driven by a convergence of geographic, social, and infrastructural factors that heighten vulnerability for many of its communities. River flood is currently managed by historic and ongoing river flood management works (Flood Risk Management Plan). Increased rainfall may compound the issue however, meaning that current river flood management is not adequate.

Current:
Cardiff's rivers - Taff, Ely, and Rhymney - flow through areas with high concentrations of deprivation and ethnic diversity, including Ely, Splott, Butetown, and Adamsdown. These areas are identified in the Neighbourhood Flood Vulnerability Index (NFVI) as having Acute, Very High, or High vulnerability, meaning they are more likely to suffer severe impacts during flood events.

Temporary displacement due to flooding disproportionately affects renters and those in social housing, disrupting education, employment, and healthcare access. Older adults and disabled residents may struggle to evacuate or implement property-level flood protection.

By 2050, around 33,000 properties (17%) in Cardiff are projected to be at risk of flooding. Peak river flows are expected to increase by 20% by the 2050s, and 25% by the 2080s, intensifying flood risk in vulnerable neighbourhoods.
project_info: Renewable energy - The Heat Network: Cardiff's Heat Network is a low-carbon district heating project that uses waste heat from the Viridor Energy Recovery Facility to supply sustainable heating and hot water to key buildings in Cardiff Bay. Phase 1 connects sites such as the Senedd, Wales Millennium Centre, and County Hall, with future expansion planned. regions) than in England. There is also spatial variation within UK countries as socially vulnerable neighbourhoods
are less likely to have insurance, which leads to significant disadvantage when combined with lower household
incomes and exposure to more frequent flooding.
• Direct expected annual damages from flooding in Northern Ireland for residential properties are currently around
£21.3m, which equates to a high magnitude score.
Belfast is exposed to river flooding due to the large number of tributaries and rivers that connect into the city catchment area, many of which have been culverted over the years. Food bank usage in Belfast is increasing and the cost of living has increased, placing a greater strain on low income households. Supply chain disruption will affect areas with poor food access which have now been mapped in the city in terms of food deserts, food mirages and food swamps. | Other: urban heat island: Belfast has areas of low green cover and tree canopy and high levels of asphalt, concrete and hard surfaces that can exacerbate the urban heat island effect. Vulnerable populations live in housing that is poorly ventilated and streets where there is a lack of shading. Rivers have been culverted under the streets so the cooling effect of rivers is minimised. People with health problems and older people are particularly at risk. The increasing use of air conditioning in offices and glazing can increase the temperature on the street and further add to the urban heat island effect.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - 1 million trees: The One Million Trees project is a key programme to support climate adaptation across the city. project_info: Transport - Public EV Charging Infrastructure - FASTER Project: The FASTER Project is a joint cross border project across Scotland, the border Counties of Ireland and Northern Ireland to support the overarching ambition to transition to low carbon transport systems and to demonstrate how each of the three jurisdictions can provide early systems learning in relation to the electrification of transport.The FASTER Project aims to ensure that the availability of public charging stations is not a major obstacle to Electric Vehicle (EV) market penetration.The partnership will implement the physical rollout of 73 rapid charging stations in the programme area. The Project aims to ensure that the availability of charging stations is not a major obstacle to Electric Vehicle (EV) market penetration with the proposal to carry out the design, analysis, procurement, installation, and operation of 73 Rapid Chargers across the three programme jurisdictions. There must be cross compatibility between the three jurisdictions which may be achieved using contactless card payments or other methods.In Northern Ireland it is anticipated that up to 22 EV RAPID chargers will be installed through the FASTER project. RAPID chargers are 55kw chargers, capable of fully charging a vehicle in approximately 30 minutes. Belfast City Council is in the final stages of developing a Belfast EV Strategy, which will set out the city's requirements and recommended approach to be implemented through a partnership approach, aligned to the regional EV Infrastructure Action Plan https://www.infrastructure-ni.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/infrastructure/ev-infrastructure-action-plan-2022.pdf.

project_info:
Buildings - Belfast Retrofitting Programme: Belfast Retrofit Delivery Hub was established in September 2022 following the Belfast Net Zero Carbon Roadmap identifying buildings and transport as the two highest carbon emitting sectors in Belfast. The Hub takes a consortium approach to catalyse retrofit activity across the public and private building sectors in Belfast, engaging stakeholders from across the construction supply chain, funders, academics, public bodies, housing providers and consumer bodies. The Hub's work is informed by the National Retrofit Strategy produced by the Construction Leadership Council. 

There are almost 150,000 homes in the city of Belfast, half of them owned by the people who live in them. Terraced and semi-detached properties make up more than two thirds of the city's homes and mains gas dominates heating supply. Public, commercial and industrial buildings are also major players, accounting for almost a third of the city's emissions and just under a fifth of its energy spend each year. The city's commitment to tackling climate change means that these same homes need to be Net Zero by 2050. 
Belfast City Council has commissioned the Energy Systems Catapult to produce a Local Area Energy Plan (LAEP), which is a data-driven approach to map and model the whole energy system across the city covering production, consumption, demand. The process collates, for the first time, valuable data about housing stock condition, single glazing, Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs) and energy demand, highlighting that 63%of homes have an Energy Performance Certificate rating of D-G. LAEP priority projects include transitioning 500 homes from oil to low carbon heating systems supporting the retrofit of up to 2,000 homes through a cross tenure, area based retrofit programme.

Heavy precipitation: Glasgow and the West of Scotland commonly experience heavy rain with the most common weather events identified through local climate impacts profile being rain precipitation. This often leads to fluvial or pluvial flooding events which in turn impact many vulnerable population groups and sectors. 
• Climate change is a threat multiplier and therefore the impacts of climate change impact those in society who are already most vulnerable such as marginalised and minority communities, and women and girls.
• Children and youth may experience disruption to their education if schools and extracurricular activities are closed or operating at reduced capacity due to infrastructure or staffing issues as a result of heavy precipitation and subsequent flooding.

project_info: Buildings - Climate Neutral Innovation District: As part of the development of Glasgow City Innovation District, this project aims to create a 100% renewable climate neutral and climate resilient area within the district. The project aims to integrate heat, power, transport, climate adaptation and wellbeing solutions that will benefit everyone in the area of the Innovation District. Key aspects of the project are the potential for a heat network within the district served exclusively via a Water Source Heat Pump situated in the river Clyde. The district's streets will act as climate and energy corridors that will help the local community to benefit from low carbon heat, power, improved transport, cycling and walking options which will all help provide space for people to move safely and more easily. The project will improve air quality in the centre of Glasgow. A focus on greening the space and nature being allowed to flourish is part of the work.\n\nhttps://www.glasgowcityinnovationdistrict.com/

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: By the 2050s, the District will experience an annual average temperature increase by 3-5F from 2000 average temperatures. Projections show that annual average temperatures are expected to rise by between 5-9F between circa 2000 and 2080s. By the 2050s, the District will experience between 30 and 40 days per year of heat over 95F. In the coming decades, the frequency of extreme heat events is expected to increase, doubling by the 2030s and nearly quadrupling by the 2080s in the likely scenario. In the worst-case scenario, nearly 20% of the year or nearly 75% of the summer could exceed 95F. Heat waves are projected to be more frequent and last longer. Compared to a baseline of 3 average heat waves lasting 4-5 days ca. 2000, the District will experience 6-7 heat waves lasting 7-8 days by 2050 and 7-9 heat waves lasting 8-13 days by 2080. Vulnerable populations, including the elderly, unhoused residents, low income residents, and those with medical conditions are most at risk for heat stroke and other heat related health conditions due to exposure and limited mobility. Heat waves will also impact energy infrastructure as peak demand for cooling could strain the distribution system and transportation as existing roads and rail lines were not designed for the temperature extremes expected by the 2080s. | Urban flooding: An increase in the intensity and frequency of heavy rain events will contribute to an increase in the likelihood of flash flooding. The District's aging drainage infrastructure was not designed for these extreme rain events. Localized flooding of streets and buildings would impact residents and businesses while increased storm water runoff and combined sewer overflows would impact environmental quality. | River flooding: Situated along two tidal rivers and home to multiple streams, the District is currently at risk of riverine flooding. The risk will increase in the future as a result of increasingly frequent and severe rain events. Riverine flooding could impact large areas of the District disrupting critical infrastructure systems damaging public facilities homes and businesses and cultural resources. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Storm surge from hurricanes and nor'easters can have significant impacts on the District region, and will be exacerbated in the future by climate change due to sea level rise and storm intensification. Coastal storm surge coupled with riverine flooding driven by heavy rains could damage critical infrastructure including energy, transportation, and water systems. A large storm with significant impacts could also displace residents and put more stress on affordable housing supply. High winds could also cause widespread power outages. | Heavy precipitation: Storms of all durations and return intervals are expected to get more intense in the future. Daily extreme rainfalls are projected to be significantly more intense, with a 25-yr 24 hr. event producing 19% (1.15 in.) more rain and a 100-yr 24 hr. event producing 11% (0.92 in.) more by the late 21st century under the likely warming scenario. Multi-day extreme rainfall events may increase by multiple inches, and severe storms in the 90th percentile of potential size may exceed 20 inches of rain by 2050.Changes in rainfall volumes have a significant impact on drainage infrastructure. As precipitation patterns become more intense and frequent the effectiveness of new construction projects designed to alleviate flooding and/or upgrades to existing stormwater and wastewater infrastructure to mitigate flooding will need to be evaluated. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The District is located at the confluence of two tidal rivers. Local sea levels have risen an average of 3.2 mm per year over the last century due to a combination of global sea level rise and local subsidence. Relative sea level rise projections for the District range from 1.1 to 1.7 feet by 2050 and 1.4 to 4.4 feet by 2080, according to the District's climate change projections. Local sea level rise rates are higher than global rates, in part due to land subsidence; the District is projected to sink half a foot or more in the next 100 years due to natural and human causes. The District is already experiencing an increase in tidal nuisance flooding due to sea level rise. Higher sea levels coupled with more severe coastal storms will cause more serious coastal flooding in the future. Coastal floods pose a serious risk to the District's critical infrastructure systems including transportation and water systems, as well as significant cultural resources on the National Mall.

Urban flooding: Impacts include disruption to transport services, displaced people, damage to assets and private property, business interruption. Key public transport sector nodes within the city are vulnerable to urban flooding. Flinders st station at the bottom of the Elizabeth catchment is a key transport hub. There are several neighbourhoods within the city that are prone to flooding during both 1:20 and 1:100 ARI events. These includes Southbank, Fisherman's Bend, Kensington, Docklands, CBD and North Melbourne. There are a large number of residents and businesses within these areas that are impacted during flooding events of this scale. For example Melbourne's Arts precinct and key roads transporting goods across the city are located in Southbank which is highly flood prone. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise by 2030 is expected to be between 7-19cm, and by 2090 27-89cm. Communities living in neighbourhoods around the Yarra River and Maribynong River are expected to be impacted by sea level rise by 2100. Fisherman's Bend, West Melbourne, Docklands and Southbank are heavily impacted. These neighbourhoods consist of residential, business and industrial areas which will be vulnerable to coastal inundation in the future, however currently communities and sectors are not directly impacted by coastal flooding. | Heavy precipitation: More intense storms events are likely to increase flood frequency, damage to physical assets, disrupt public transport and the ability to deliver services. Heavy rainfall intensity is expected to increase by an average of 0.9 percent by 2030 and 5.9 percent by 2070 (large margins of error). The 5 per cent 1 in 20 year event could increase between 9-26 per cent by 2090. This increasing rainfall intensity will impact vulnerable people in the city. This includes outdoor workers and their related sectors who are vulnerable to disruptions and riskier working conditions due to more intense rainfall and storms. Weather in Melbourne is highly variable and can change quickly, vulnerable populations including the elderly and people experiencing homelessness have less capacity to find shelter from intense storms and heavy precipitation which is often unexpected. Unemployed individuals, marginalised communities and refugee and migrant peoples often live in low-quality housing which is vulnerable to intense rainfall and storm events. | Drought: Decreased water supply along with warmer temperatures are likely to increase drought risk and severity. Average rainfall could decline by 27 per cent or rise by 4 per cent over the years to 2090. Drought reduces ability to irrigate open space which impacts the health of our urban forest and other green assets and significantly warms the urban environment exacerbating the extreme heat impacts provided above. | Extreme heat: Melbourne has experienced several heat wave events over the last ten years. Impacts experienced as a result of these heat wave events include increased demand on health services, excess deaths due to heat stress, and revenue losses to businesses receiving less trade. Annual average number of hot days (35 degrees C) is expected to increase to 12-15 days by 2030 and between 15-32 by 2090. Vulnerable community groups including the elderly, children, marginalised/minority peoples and people experiencing homeless are highly sensitive to extreme heat and are more likely to experience heat health impacts. Public transport network disruptions increase during extreme weather events which further exacerbates impacts on vulnerable populations who often depend on these services to move around the city. Extreme heat also significantly impacts upon the events sector. Events such as the Australian Open, cricket and music festivals have had to change their schedules and/or implement heat plans to protect attendees.
project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Urban Forest Fund: The City of Melbourne's Urban Forest Fund enables partnerships and contributions towards new greening projects in the city, beyond Council's existing capital works program. Contributions to the Urban Forest Fund are welcomed from organisations or individuals wanting to create a greener and more liveable Melbourne into the future. The Urban Forest Fund will supports projects such as: • New parks • Urban forest projects• Green roofs• Green walls or facades• Water sensitive urban design projects. The City of Melbourne offers an annual, matched-funding grants program through the Urban Forest Fund, to support new greening projects on private property in the city. A range of projects may be funded including new green open spaces, tree planting, biodiversity projects, green roofs and vertical greening, and water sensitive urban design projects. Grant applications are assessed by a panel of greening experts and community members who prioritise projects that will provide the most benefit to the community and environment. Each round of funding differs in scope due to factors such as available funds, City priorities, and joint-funding arrangements. Trees, plants and green open spaces are essential infrastructure in our city. They help to cool the environment, reduce pollution, support biodiversity, improve both mental and physical health and wellbeing, and create a welcoming city for residents, workers and visitors. Additionally, green spaces support a thriving economy in a range of ways, such as boosting pedestrian traffic, improving productivity and increasing tourism. At a time when Melbourne is experiencing rapid population growth and increasing impacts of climate change, the green elements of our city are more important than ever. Approximately 75 per cent of the land within the City of Melbourne municipal area is privately owned or managed, so there is huge potential for the private realm to contribute towards greening our city. City of Melbourne created the Urban Forest Fund to accelerate greening across our city. The Urban Forest Fund aims to build partnerships between government and the private sector to deliver additional greening above and beyond existing Council capital works investment. Key public transport sector nodes within the city are vulnerable to urban flooding. Flinders st station at the bottom of the Elizabeth catchment is a key transport hub. There are several neighbourhoods within the city that are prone to flooding during both 1:20 and 1:100 ARI events. These includes Southbank, Fisherman's Bend, Kensington, Docklands, CBD and North Melbourne. There are a large number of residents and businesses within these areas that are impacted during flooding events of this scale. For example Melbourne's Arts precinct and key roads transporting goods across the city are located in Southbank which is highly flood prone. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise by 2030 is expected to be between 7-19cm, and by 2090 27-89cm. Fisherman's Bend, West Melbourne, Docklands and Southbank are heavily impacted. These neighbourhoods consist of residential, business and industrial areas which will be vulnerable to coastal inundation in the future, however currently communities and sectors are not directly impacted by coastal flooding. | Heavy precipitation: More intense storms events are likely to increase flood frequency, damage to physical assets, disrupt public transport and the ability to deliver services. Power Melbourne will make it easier for renters, people living in apartments and small businesses to access the benefits of renewable energy and energy storage. Council is working with an electricity retailer to establish a network of community batteries in the city and seeks to establish a renewable energy retail plan linked to battery storage assets, to be offered to residents and businesses within the municipality. An initial pilot phase will see the operation of 1.1MWh network of three batteries, with battery revenue flowing to a Community Energy Fund to support local renewable projects. Power Melbourne will test and build the business case for a viable battery network delivery model with potential to scale in excess of 5MW/10MWh. Based on the results of the pilot phase and with Council approval, we may seek further funding and joint investment to support the expansion of the battery network and development of the retail energy plan.

The attached document is not a proposal but a guide to community batteries in the urban context developed in partnership between City of Melbourne and two other local government partners. The guide is specifically targeted at other local governments and community groups seeking to create their own community battery project.

Total annual precipitation averaged 807 mm from 1971 to 2000, then decreased to 783 mm from 2011 to 2021. 2017 and 2020 were the least rainy years, with 527 mm and 601 mm, respectively, while 2014 was the wettest, with 1,116 mm.
