with negative consequences for managing these phenomena. | Drought: According to data from a study on the vulnerability of climate-risk areas in Italy, conducted by CREA, organic farming suffered 62% of the damage caused by drought between 2003 and 2012.
In 2017, the Lazio region experienced a severe drought in its countryside, which caused damage amounting to €200 million, including investments in planting, additional costs for diesel or electricity for irrigation, loss of direct fodder production for livestock, loss of revenue for fruit and vegetable companies, and loss of production in the wine and olive oil sectors.
The city of Rome, in 2018 and in recent years in general, also found itself having to deal with drought. That year, although ordinances had already been issued during the summer months to limit water use in gardens, swimming pools, vegetable gardens, and car washes, and some areas were subject to low water pressure in apartments, these initiatives were not enough to avoid a crisis, and water had to be drawn from Lake Bracciano. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): During summer there are frequent fires in many green areas and parks of the City. The most important recent Fire was in 2017 in the Castel Fusano pine forest.The city of Rome approved a fire prevention plan for these areas. According to Rome's Civil Protection records of activities carried out between 2013 and 2022, 34% of them were related to weather emergencies and 16% to interface fires. These percentages rise to 58% and 28% if interventions carried out for bio-sanitary emergencies are excluded, given the particular impact of the pandemic in the three-year period 2020-2022. Over 54% of the fires were concentrated in five municipalities. | Extreme heat: In Rome the highest risk is recorded in the summer months when the ground temperatures reach 31°C. The phenomenon mainly concerns the areas of the city center, but there is also a significant formation of the heat island towards the areas furthest from the sea. Furthermore, night temperatures above 20°C are increasing, which represent an established risk factor for the most fragile population groups and the associated proliferation of insects. Since a further increase in temperature is an almost certain forecast, heat waves must be considered as one of the most relevant risk factors throughout the municipal area. | Mass movement: The screening, carried out by combined intersection of the main historical databases available ranging from the end of the 19th century, for a total of approximately 800 events, identified approximately 400 failures. The most of the landslides occurred in the western sector, as a result of a different structure morphological and geological nature of the territory. The landslides are distributed where the slopes are greatest, i.e. on the slopes that follow one another along the Tiber Valley, both on the right and on the hydrographic left, and its tributaries. | Other coastal events: The Roman coastline is a delicate ecosystem that must be protected. Rome is one of the few European capitals with a stretch of sea, with urban, port, and natural features. Erosion has increased in recent years, and with sea level rise expected, coastline simulation models clearly indicate the areas at greatest risk, because they are below sea level, and those where salt wedge upwelling could intensify. | Soil degradation/erosion: The information on land consumption in Italy, published in the most recent ISPRA29 report, reveals that in 2021, land consumption
recorded its highest level in the last ten years: with an average of 19 hectares per day and a rate exceeding 2 square meters per second, land consumption reached nearly 70 km2 of new artificial cover in a single year.
In 2016, land use in the municipality of Rome was distributed as follows: agricultural land covered 64,950 hectares (equal to 50% of the municipal area), urban land covered 44,177 hectares (34% of the area), and natural land and water covered 19,423 hectares (15% of the municipal area).Land use changes between 2000 and 2016 mainly concerned the change from agricultural to urban use (4,854 hectares), followed by the change from urban to agricultural use (686 hectares) and the change from natural to urban use (355 hectares).

Increasing temperatures and changes in the spatiotemporal distribution of precipitation due to climate change may change the possible distribution areas and active periods of arthropods that transmit infectious diseases (such as mosquitoes), as well as the invasion and colonization rate of alien species that cause human damage, and may increase the risk of infectious diseases transmitted by arthropods. (Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P41)
 | Other: Impacts on forestry Forest and Forestry 
Climate change including changes in the growing environment such as rising temperatures and drying, may result in reduced growth and death of trees.
(Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P46)
Forests/Forestry
Climate change, including changes in the growing environment such as rising temperatures and dryness, may cause reduced growth and death of trees. (Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P46)
 | Other: Change of ecosystem Terrestrial ecosystem
As for natural and secondary forests, most of the component species in cool-temperate forests are expected to move to higher latitudes and higher elevations, resulting in a decrease in the optimal distribution range. is also predicted that the habitat of wild birds and animals such as Japanese deer will expand due to higher temperatures and shorter periods of snow cover etc. as well as soil runoff and a decline in water source cultivation functions. 
Freshwater ecosystem
 In lakes and rivers, the production rate of algae increases due to temperature rise and CO2 increase but in freshwater ecosystems where nutrient salts supply are poor, the higher order production is expected to decrease because the increase in algae decreases the quality of their food. 
Coastal and marine ecosystems 
In subtropical areas, coral bleaching has already occurred due to rising sea temperatures. In the future, it is predicted that the area suitable for reef-building corals may disappear by 2040 due to rising water temperatures and ocean acidification. In Tokyo Bay, a case of the southern green mussel native to Southeast Asia overwintering has been confirmed. In addition, changes have occurred, such as the southern butterflyfish, previously seen only in summer being able to be seen from autumn onwards. 
Phenology
The impact on various species such as the earlier flowering date of Yoshino Cherry is predicted. Furthermore, it is expected that the impacts will not only affect individual species but also affect various interactions among species. 
Distribution and population changes 
In addition to changes in distribution ranges and life cycles etc., there is a research case that changes in interspecies interactions caused by species migration and local extinction have further adverse effects, habitat fragmentation prevents migration in line with climate change, and changes in weather conditions such as wind, which may reduce survival rates and cause species extinction. It is assumed that climate change will lead to changes in the rate of invasion and establishment of non-native species
(Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P53)

In addition, due to the influence of high temperature and drying, poor growth in the early stage of growth tends to increase. Fruit failure and sunburn caused by high temperatures also occur in fruits and vegetables, especially in tomato cultivation at facilities. 
Fruit tree 
Fruit trees, such as Japanese pear, have been damaged by frost damage, such as death of flower buds and new treetops, due to earlier germination and flowering due to global warming from winter to spring. In addition, due to high temperatures in summer, problems such as coloring disorder of grapes and sunburnt fruits have occurred in Japanese pear and kiwifruit. flesh fruit Disorders (Water core, fruit cracking etc.) due to high temperature and low rainfall after the fruit enlargement stage also occurs. 
Livestock production 
Although it is possible to reduce the impacts of global warming by measures such as blowing air and sprinkling water in the barn, it is predicted that milk production will decrease in dairy cows and egg production rate will decrease and soft eggs will increase in hens. In addition, the areas where the growth of beef, pigs and meat chickens will decline will expand and the extent of the decline is expected to increase. 
Pests 
As for pests, there are many pests that prefer high temperatures such as spider mites, snow beetles and thrips and the generation period tends to be prolonged. Although there has been no clear increase in diseases due to climate change, there is a possibility that damage to agricultural crops will expand due to the increased occurrence of pests and the expansion of their distribution ranges.

The increase in extreme weather events such as heavy rains and droughts and impacts are predicted on farmland, which is the base of agricultural production, nationwide. In recent years, there have been frequent torrential rains and it is predicted that the risk of flooding of farmland will increase. (Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P46)

Changes in water temperature, changes in water quality and changes in the runoff characteristics of nutrients salts etc. from watersheds due to climate change is expected. With regard to rivers, an increase in heavy rain and short periods of heavy rain may lead to an increase in sediment runoff, resulting in an increase in turbidity. In addition, a decrease in the amount of dissolved oxygen due to a rise in water temperature, a promotion in the decomposition of organic matter by microorganisms and an increase in algae are also predicted. A rising trend in surface seawater temperature has been reported in closed waters. In addition, as the sea level rises, the saltwater run-up area in the coastal area is expected to expand.
(Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P49)
Water environment

Regarding closed water bodies, an increasing trend in surface seawater temperature has been reported. Additionally, as sea levels rise, the area of ​​salt water intrusion in coastal areas is expected to expand. (Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan P49)

climate_hazard: Storm: An increase in intense rainfall and hail events may result in damage to properties, causing displacement and disruption of the community, businesses and other activities while clean-up and recovery occurs. In the short term this may increase the need and cost for emergency housing or shelter, rebuild skills, disaster relief and social services. In the longer term this may impact productivity and reputation. The impacts are similar to those as flash flooding but with more prolonged and deeper felt impacts. | Oceanic events: Rising sea levels and coastal inundation could have the potential to reduce the accessibility and aesthetics of the City's iconic cultural and tourism precinct (eg Sydney Opera House forecourt, Circular Quay and public amenities such as the Royal Botanical Gardens). This includes the potential erosion of places of indigenous cultural or community significance along the Sydney Harbour foreshore.The effects on vulnerable communities are less significant in the City of Sydney jurisdiction as this primarly effects state land and buildings and has less coastal exposure. The City and residents is more impacted by flash flooding. | Extreme wind: High intensity of rainfall events and high winds which have the potential to increase storm surges and disrupt ferry, cruise ship and freight logistics entering and operating within Sydney ports. This risk addressees how the east coast low pressure systems can cause high seas resulting in: Grounding of or damage to freight ships (including oil tankers) resulting in environmental impacts within Sydney Ports. Disruption of ferry services with flow-on impacts for the broader transport network. Disruption to cruise ships docking in Sydney Harbour impacting tourist trade and reputation of Sydney as a safe tourist destination.Communities the city has identified as experiencing vulnerability primarily use public transport to navigate the city and connect social and for health and food services. High winds routinely take out water-based public transport in the City (harbour-based) and can result in issue with trains and buses sur to falling debris. This impacts their ability to access services and leads to increasing social isolation. Prolonged storms in other parts of Australia, which we have seen, also impact City residents and cause delays with freight leading to lack of availability of fresh, suitable food and can push prices up beyond the means of vulnerable residents. This puts pressures on health care and charity services provinding food relief. | Urban flooding: Flash flooding can cause overflow of stormwater drainage creating hazardous conditions for the community. Flash floods can cause storm water drainage systems to back up and cause localised flash flooding of roads, public spaces and property. This may result in an increase in localised traffic congestion, vehicular and pedestrian accidents, as well as loss of parking spaces in low lying areas and basements.A number of flash flood prone areas in the City of Sydney contain social/public housing and low income housing where communities that traditionally experience vulnerability live. Due to Sydney's high property prices and the number of hospitals, fire stations and police stations in the LGA, there is a propportion of front line workers that also live in these areas. Flash flooding can cause massive damage and require the displacement of communities away from their residence. Social isolation, high costs associated with moving and potentially extended travel are just some of the impacts from flash flooding on these communities.The City contains a large number of arts, entertainment and recreation locations including theatres, pubic galleries and hotels which will be both physically and economically affected if prolonged flash flooding causes damage to property and people cannot visit or stay. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat could put strains on the energy system, simultaneously decreasing system efficiency and performance of the energy network as system operators struggle to cool down facilities, and increasing electricity consumption due to a surge in peak demand for air conditioning. As a result demand can outstrip supply causing power outages. This risk may also increase water demand for cooling towers. An increase in extreme heat could lead to power supply disruptions from programmed load shedding and heat damage to network infrastructure, causing brownouts and blackouts. This in turn reduces the reputation of the City in having a reliable power supply for its community and visitors.The City of Sydney is a hyper-diverse city in terms of community demographics. We have a higher than average community of those who would be considered vulnerable to extreme heat. For communties experiencing vulnerability, poor quality housing and lack of residential cooling mechanisms (or inefficent cooling mechanisms) go hand in hand. Energy is expensive in Australia and this increases during a heat event - those with the ability in cool in their own homes may not do so due to high energy prices and potential heat-induced brown-outs - loss of electricity due to exsessive or loss of load. It also compunds social isolation and, if the heat event is long in duration, may impact access to food, medication top-ups and being able to travel (via public transport).Outdoor workers are more likely to suffer loss of working hours and income due to extreme heats due to laws regualting when people can work outdoors and in what temperatures it becomes and OHS issue. This impacts productivity, livliehoods and, if prolonged, economically. | Heat stress: Heat waves could lead to higher incidents of heat stress and other related illnesses amongst the community resulting in a decrease in comfort levels and an increase in hospital admissions, pressure on social services and morbidity. This increases strain on emergency and social services supporting this sensitive population due to increases in demand coupled with a decrease in staffing resources. An increase in extreme heat and associated impacts could reduce workforce productivity, as activities become too hot for people to work outside during parts of the day and the indoor thermal comfort is affected by pressures on cooling. It could lead to negative changes in behaviour in particular increases in violence and anti-social behaviour leading to an increase in demand for emergency and social services. An increase in the extreme heat could lead to increases in heat impacts to transport infrastructure - resulting in congestion, major delays and mass transit disruption with potential stranding of commuters. An increase in extreme heat could lead to changes in commuter behaviour opting to use private vehicles to access the CBD (rather than public transport) to avoid potential delays and discomfort resulting in increased congestion.As mentioned, the City of Sydney is hyper-diverse and has a number of communities throughout the city who are already experiencing vulnerability. Low quality housing means homes are hotter, cool down slower and are climate inefficient. This means, when the City experiences extreme heat, communities already experiencing vulnerability will be more likely to suffer heat injuries such as heat stroke, complications with medication and be unable to remedy the situation themselves i.e. travel to cooler locations, due to disability, inability to catch publc transport or a fear of leaving their homes and/or pets. This puts pressure on the health care sector, in particular emergency health and social work (mental health impacts are exasperated during times of heat stress). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): An increase in bushfire weather conditions across the Greater Sydney Region could lead to business interruption and economic loss within the LGA due to interrupted accessibility in and out the City and strain on resources and services. This risk addresses bushfires continuing to cause extensive property and infrastructure damage across the Greater Sydney Region with cascading impacts on the LGA, including: Damage to the transport network delaying or stranding CBD workers. Limited availability of emergency response and social services within the CBD due to transfer of capacity to regional disaster zones. Decrease in tourism due to reduced appeal of attraction on Sydney's fringe. Reduced productivity and economic loss due to CBD workers and LGA workforce taking leave to volunteer or defend property. Contaminated water supply. Poor air quality in the City LGA area resulting from fires outside the LGA.While the City does not suffer directly from fire, the poor air quality from backburning (hazard reduction) and bushfires has an effect and this is pronounced in communities experiencing vulnerability already, especially in terms of short and long term health implications. Homes become inundated by smoke and particles so offer no respite from external exposure. Respiritory and health impacts are felt widely leading to increase pressure on the health care service including emergency, doctors and medication provision. Bushfires and smoke are usually caused by prolonged drought and exteme heat events so these have compounding effects on communities. | Drought: Drought conditions could result in reduced water availability for gardens and open space areas, resulting in reduced scenic/social amenity and limited recreation and respite areas.As mentioned in extreme heat and heat stress categories, incidences of low housing quality mean peoples residences are too hot and they seek shelter in our parks, gardens and water features. During prolonged drought, it is hard to keep the green infrastructure watered and healthy enough to provide shade. Water restrictions mean that cooling water features not fed by recycled water have to be turned off futher reducing cooling opportunities of those who do not have sufficient cooling methods at home to excape the effects of the heat. | Heavy precipitation: Ability of heavy rainfall with hail can cause extensive damage to property;- Infrastructure (ie power lines, street lights, embankments)- Buildings (ie homes, PV installations and stations)- Trees (ie street trees)-This increases clean-up efforts, disposal and maintenance costs.Due to poor quality low-cost and social/public housing, increased precipitations impacts communities experiencing vulnerability as it does in the flooding section above and leads to extensive damp and mould which can take weeks and months to fix. We would also add renters as a vulnerable group here as they relay on a landlord to fix the issue and have no control over the process or outcome.
project_info: Sustainable food consumption/production - Community 'Food Hubs' for a sustainable food system: Funding - State funding opportunities.\nProject Description:A Food Hub is a physical space for meetings, classroom education, kitchen training, acommercial kitchen for prep and practice, and market/retail and café space for new andexisting/growing businesses to test their products and menus. Food Hubs are a means to grow inclusive, supportive and diverse communities, expandpeoples' networks, and provide opportunities for capacity building of community members,especially those from vulnerable communities. Such Hubs could be permanent, activatingunderutilised physical spaces, and hosting regular programs run in partnership with existingorganisations, network members, or event series.The hubs would facilitate the development of networks that are diverse (in terms of culture,finances, interests, food expertise, stages in business, industry history) while also involvingpeople who gather around common goals (food systems change, issues in local community,starting a business or social enterprise etc) and values (care, generosity, mutual aid).Such diversity, practiced in place, allows for people in new and existing local food businessesto expand their 'assets' (resources, connections, opportunities, knowledge and skills), buildcapacity, and problem solve within a community of experts. Common goals, values andproblems allow for communities of practices to form where people share knowledge, givefeedback, provide support and develop relationships based on mutual aid and mentorship.These relationships are crucial to the success of business, and the development of resilient foodsystems based on inclusivity, diversity, and justice.Physically, such Food Hubs could be developed in existing community centres, underutilised commercial properties, and/or be designed into new builds or refurbishments. Once established, such a model can be scaled out across the City and beyond.This project was scoped as a part of a recommendation by Food Lab Sydney as part of a review of food activities in the City of Sydney. Recommendation attached.

Water stress: Johannesburg is at risk of a prolonged drought that could result in significant water stress. The city's water infrastructure is under pressure due to high domestic and industrial consumption and insufficient maintenance. Recently, water losses have exceeded 40% due to neglected infrastructure, further aggravating the situation. | Other: Hail: Thunderstorms in the region may bring destructive hail. Johannesburg residents rely heavily on their vehicles for transport, and many vehicles are uninsured. In response, insurance companies have innovated by linking their customers to an early warning system for hail via mobile applications. | Urban flooding: Flooding causes significant damage to property and infrastructure, and can lead to personal injuries and loss of life. Vulnerable populations, particularly those living in informal settlements situated in floodplains, face heightened risk due to inadequate housing and limited access to emergency services.
Beyond flooding, the City's recent heat assessment study highlights that informal settlements and low-income communities experience disproportionately high exposure to extreme heat. This exacerbates health risks such as heat stress, respiratory illnesses, and cardiovascular problems, especially among the elderly, children, and those with pre-existing conditions.
Flooding and extreme heat both contribute to disruptions in essential services. Flood events exacerbate traffic congestion, increase road accidents, and damage critical electrical and IT infrastructure, while heatwaves strain water supply and energy systems.
The City's Water Security Strategy underscores that climate change will intensify water scarcity challenges, particularly affecting vulnerable populations who already face limited access to reliable water services. Floods damage water infrastructure and contaminate water sources, while prolonged droughts and heatwaves reduce water availability, compounding health and livelihood risks.
Secondary impacts of flooding include educational disruptions—students miss classes due to unsafe conditions—and economic interruptions, as employees leave work early or businesses close in response to storm warnings. In vulnerable communities, floods damage vital food stocks and personal possessions, such as identification documents, further jeopardizing socio-economic stability.
 | Drought: Rising water demand is placing significant strain on Johannesburg's water supply system, posing risks to urban agriculture and other vital sectors of the city's economy, including retail and commerce.
Drought conditions are expected to particularly impact water-intensive industries, potentially disrupting business operations and diminishing Johannesburg's attractiveness as an economic hub. The city's economy, which is largely driven by wholesale trade, financial services, and retail sectors, may face notable challenges as water shortages constrain production and consumer activity.
Johannesburg depends on a complex water supply system originating in Lesotho, a high-altitude, landlocked country, governed by intricate transboundary water agreements. This dependency adds an additional layer of vulnerability, as upstream factors can influence the volume and reliability of water flow into the city.
Health risks also arise from drought through threats to drinking water quality, including increased contamination and scarcity. In South Africa, drought events are often linked to the El Niño weather pattern, which intensifies water stress. While Johannesburg has not experienced a severe drought in recent memory, this lack of recent experience means residents and businesses may not be adequately prepared or have robust coping strategies in place.
 | Heat stress: A recent City of Johannesburg study on urban heat reveals that areas predominantly inhabited by Black populations are disproportionately affected by heat stress.
These communities often face multiple socio-economic challenges and lack adequate green infrastructure, such as parks and tree cover, which exacerbates urban heat island effects. Informal housing in these areas frequently relies on makeshift building materials that provide poor thermal regulation, intensifying exposure to extreme heat during summer months.
In addition to heat stress, these materials offer inadequate insulation against harsh winter cold, increasing residents' vulnerability to cold-related health risks. The use of open flames or braziers for heating—common in such housing—heightens the risk of shack fires, posing serious safety hazards.
This intersection of climatic, infrastructural, and socio-economic factors underscores the urgent need for targeted interventions that improve housing quality, expand green spaces, and enhance community resilience to extreme temperature fluctuations.
 | Extreme heat: Rising temperatures are expected to increase the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events and heatwaves, leading to higher rates of heat-related illness and fatalities.
Vulnerable groups—such as the elderly living in informal settlements, young children in kindergartens, and individuals with pre-existing health conditions—are particularly at risk. Animals in the city also face significant heat stress, necessitating focused care and interventions.
Recent urban heat assessments show that densely populated areas with limited vegetation and predominately hard, heat-absorbing surfaces are especially vulnerable to severe urban heat island effects. These neighborhoods often coincide with socio-economic challenges, and the widespread use of materials like corrugated iron in informal housing contributes to elevated indoor temperatures due to poor thermal regulation.
Outdoor workers performing heavy physical labour face increased risks of heat stress. For example, the City's waste management personnel work outdoors and may require adjusted schedules or protective measures as heatwaves become more intense and frequent. This vulnerability was tragically underscored in January 2023, when seven farm workers in Kakamas, Northern Cape, died from heatstroke during a severe heatwave.
 | Other: Lightning: The city is located in an area prone to frequent lightning, especially during the summer months from December to February, when afternoon thunderstorms are a common occurrence. A considerable number of workers and students, who are often on foot returning home or to bus stations in the afternoon, face a high risk from these dangerous lightning strikes. Homeless individuals often seek shelter in exposed areas, making them susceptible to lightning strikes, which can result in permanent injuries or even fatalities. Lightning is known to cause more deaths in this region than flooding and also causes significant damage to the city's electrical infrastructure. | Other: Tornadoes: The proliferation of smartphones has likely highlighted the regularity of tornadoes. In recent years, it seems rare for a summer rainy season to pass without a tornado sighting near the city and its surroundings. While most are not powerful enough to cause major damage, historical records indicate that destructive tornadoes have occurred. For instance, in December 2017, a tornado led to the city declaring the affected area a disaster after it left a path of destruction. | Extreme cold: New insights emerging from research by the South African Medical Council suggest that extreme cold weather leads to fatalities in the city. This is especially so for marginalised communities (eg., the homeless), people living with underlying illnesses and the elderly. Cold weather is also associated with shack fires which tend to lead many fatalities. Whereas climate models indicate a warming trend into the future, temperature variability between years and winter months is important to design adaptation strategies for colder days/nights in order to save lives.
project_info: Health systems and services - Developing a baseline for the impacts of heatwaves and extreme heat on human health.: In light of the city's urban heat study identifying critical hotspots, it has become clear that baselines must be established to understand the effects of heat on human health. Currently, the potential impacts of heatwaves on humans are largely deduced from anecdotal evidence, underscoring the need for a comprehensive extreme heat/heatwave data management system.

project_info: Renewable energy - Renewable energy (RE) development in the form of solar PV on disused and degraded mining land and city-owned land: The City of Johannesburg intends to repurpose disused and degraded mining land, as well as city owned land, for renewable energy (RE) development. Rehabilitation of disused mining land is an environmental solution for managing the dust, recycling water, and reconditioning soil as key interventions for addressing the long term environmental and social consequences of mining. Solar photovoltaic (PV) generation capacity has been identified as a feasible technology for generating RE given the abundant sunshine available to Johannesburg, while a belt of mining land that runs from east to west through the centre of Johannesburg (the Main Reef) provides a supply of currently unproductive land, in the form of mine dumps, that could be resuscitated as an economic asset through augmenting the city's electricity supply with RE (the city sources bulk electricity from Eskom at an increasingly costly and unreliable level). These mine dumps, in conjunction with city owned sites, offer the opportunity for the city to address the environmental impact of the dumps while simultaneously securing a cleaner, cheaper, and more reliable supply of electricity and possibly integrating urban agriculture on the solar farms that are developed.

project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - Diverting garden waste from landfill to compost in Johannesburg: From Waste to Value: A Garden Waste Diversion Initiative in Johannesburg

Context and Purpose
Garden waste makes up a significant portion of Johannesburg's municipal waste stream. Traditionally, this organic material has been sent to landfills, contributing to methane emissions, groundwater contamination, and public health risks. Recognizing the environmental and economic costs of this approach, the City of Johannesburg is exploring sustainable alternatives to transform garden waste from a liability into a resource.

 Strategic Vision
The initiative aims to:
- Reduce landfill pressure and associated health risks
- Lower greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions
- Create value through composting, mulching, biochar, and energy recovery
- Promote community participation and workforce inclusion in green jobs
Waste Diversion Pathways

The project outlines multiple pathways for garden waste processing:

- Drop-off & Collection: Community-based systems for gathering garden waste
- Composting & Mulching: Soil enrichment and urban agriculture support
- Biochar & Energy Recovery: Advanced technologies for carbon sequestration and renewable energy
- Reuse: Creative repurposing of organic materials

Each pathway is designed to maximize environmental returns while fostering local innovation and participation.

 Health Risks of Poor Landfill Management
The initiative also responds to the urgent need to mitigate the health impacts of unmanaged landfill.

 Inclusive Workforce Development
A key component of the project is building a more inclusive green workforce. In 2021, 41% of Conservation Corps participants came from demographic groups historically underrepresented in conservation jobs. The initiative seeks to expand these opportunities, ensuring that environmental stewardship also advances social equity.

In vulnerable communities, floods damage vital food stocks and personal possessions, such as identification documents, further jeopardizing socio-economic stability.
 | Drought: Rising water demand is placing significant strain on Johannesburg's water supply system, posing risks to urban agriculture and other vital sectors of the city's economy, including retail and commerce.
Drought conditions are expected to particularly impact water-intensive industries, potentially disrupting business operations and diminishing Johannesburg's attractiveness as an economic hub. The city's economy, which is largely driven by wholesale trade, financial services, and retail sectors, may face notable challenges as water shortages constrain production and consumer activity.

This dependency adds an additional layer of vulnerability, as upstream factors can influence the volume and reliability of water flow into the city.

In South Africa, drought events are often linked to the El Niño weather pattern, which intensifies water stress. While Johannesburg has not experienced a severe drought in recent memory, this lack of recent experience means residents and businesses may not be adequately prepared or have robust coping strategies in place.
 | Heat stress: A recent City of Johannesburg study on urban heat reveals that areas predominantly inhabited by Black populations are disproportionately affected by heat stress.

 | Extreme heat: Rising temperatures are expected to increase the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events and heatwaves, leading to higher rates of heat-related illness and fatalities.

Renewable energy - Solar (microgrids) solution for Informal 
Settlement in Johannesburg: Johannesburg's informal settlements lack safe, reliable energy, forcing households to rely on illegal connections and polluting fuels. At The View (144 households), residents spend about R137/week on energy, with poorer households paying more. Health and safety risks are widespread: 30-65% fire risk, 25% respiratory illness, and 20% electrocution risk.

Proposed Solution
Solar microgrid: 3 kWh/day per household (432 kWh/day total), with public lighting.
Impact per household/year:
0.35-0.42 tCO₂e avoided
0.7-1.0 kg PM2.5 avoided
R3,300-3,500 saved
Projected Benefits

Pilot (144 households): 110 tCO₂e + 0.25 t PM2.5 avoided/year.
City-wide (249,000 households): 95,400 tCO₂e + 172,450 kg PM2.5 avoided/year.
Case study (Amarasta): 2.65 MW solar, R60m cost, 18-month payback, 80 jobs created.

Equity & Health Gains
Lower costs for the poorest households.
Reduced exposure to air pollution, especially for women and children.
More time for education, work, and social activities.

Infectious disease: Vector-borne diseases are a concern for Toronto. In recent years, West Nile Virus and Lyme disease have migrated northward posing increased risk to human health and specifically for Toronto residents - blacklegged ticks which transmit Lyme disease have been found in Toronto. The disease can affect the central nervous system, brain, joints or the heart affecting any age group. West Nile Virus can affect anyone - however; the elderly, children and those with a weakened immune system are at greater risk. As the climate continues to warm, Toronto may experience an increased number of health implications linked to vector-borne diseases. Although the number of people affected currently is not high, the impact on individual people is considered sometimes to be extreme. Lyme disease in particular has the threat of changing how much people spend time outdoors which will have other health and psychological effects. (i.e. the benefits of being able to spend time in nature may decrease). The proportion of the population is not exactly calculated, but persons spending a lot of time outdoors will be more affected by insect borne disease. Also homes without proper window screens will let in more mosquitos that could carry disease. 

 Lyme disease is advancing into the Toronto area and into recreational areas where people travel for vacation. 

The public health sector (i.e. Toronto Public Health) is the group working to increase public education and to implement programs to reduce vector borne diseases. Programs such as tick mapping, and mosquito larvicide in catch basis act to reduce risk to residents. | Other: Smoke from wildfires: PM 2.5 particulate in wildfire smoke is linked to many short term health implications. Long term implications are note well understood. Persons with existing medical conditions and the elderly and persons needing to work outdoors are most likely to be affected. 

It is conceivable that the health care system (i.e. ambulance and emergency rooms and hospitals) could become overwhelmed due to emergency room visits during extreme smoke episodes. In 2023, Toronto experience smoke episodes, but 2024 air quality was not significantly impacted by smoke. | Heavy precipitation: In recent years, Toronto has experienced extreme rainfall resulting in widespread basement flooding; untreated sewage entering Lake Ontario; debris and hazardous material clean-up costing millions of dollars; electrical disruption affecting hundreds of thousands of Toronto residents; and, transportation disruption affecting thousands of commuters due to road closures, and public transport delays.

There is a concern that critical infrastructure could be affected by flooding. Cascade failure effects of infrastructure systems are not yet well understood (e.g. damage to telecom systems, electrical systems etc.) Basement flooding is increasingly a problem. Low income people may not afford insurance or the cost of cleaning up and rebuilding. 

 More people are living in basement second suites and this increases the exposure of these lower income people. Even if a basement is dried out, a key concern is the growth of mold which can has significant health implications. 

The electrical system can be affected by extreme precipitation when distribution equipment (e.g. transformers or switch gear / control systems get flooded. | Urban flooding: In recent years, Toronto has experienced extreme rainfall resulting in widespread basement flooding; untreated sewage entering Lake Ontario; debris and hazardous material clean-up costing millions of dollars; electrical disruption affecting hundreds of thousands of Toronto residents; and, transportation disruption affecting thousands of commuters due to road closures, and public transport delays. | Extreme heat: Toronto's climate is getting warmer - it is expected that by 2040, the number of hot days exceeding 30 degrees Celsius will increase threefold, from 20 to 66 days. This will pose problems for the elderly, young children, and those with pre-existing health conditions . An increase in the number of hot days will also exacerbate the need for air conditioning placing a greater burden on the electrical system which could result in a potential brownout or blackout affecting the health and wellbeing of thousands of Toronto residents. A key issue is persons living in high rise buildings without electricity during an extended power outage caused by extreme over heating of transformers or other factors. 

Infrastructure implications include buckling and melting of highways and roads, mechanical failures, delays in travel times for commuters and the goods and services sector affecting supply of goods due to transportation problems. As a lesser concern, but still an issue, urban agriculture will be stressed by extreme heat. | River flooding: River based flooding is fortunately confined to a relatively smaller percentage of our Toronto jurisdiction due to tight regulations on building in river flood planes. In recent years, including two major storm events in 2024, Toronto has experienced extreme rainfall resulting in thousands of basement floods; untreated sewage entering Lake Ontario; debris and hazardous material clean-up costing millions of dollars; electrical disruption affecting hundreds of thousands of Toronto residents; and, transportation disruption affecting thousands of commuters due to road closures, and public transport delays. There are 262 homes and roughly 650 people who live on the Island, including many seniors. In the case of coastal flooding many of the homes can be damaged or become inaccessible. Significant flood defenses were installed with some success in preventing damages after the 2018 flood. Prediction of lake levels and wind driven wave action makes long range flood forecasting difficult. | Extreme cold: There is a low probability scenario of an extended cold period near the end of the building heating season. Main issue is a major ice storm bringing down trees on top of electrical wires or the weight of ice on wires and electrical poles.

Heat stress: Through the answers to the electronic questionnaires made for the public consultation of Athens climate action plan, it is made clear that the increase of heat stress and heatwaves is believed to be most crucial threat for the city. This point of view comes as no surprise; approximately 230 deaths annually are related to high temperatures in Athens (Katsouyanni and Analytis, 2016). High temperatures can lead to uncomfortable thermal conditions in outdoors spaces, discouraging the use of public space, which has direct economic effects in commercial and leisure activities. There are strong negative effects on socialisation, such as children's need to play outdoors in playgrounds and open spaces. There is also the danger of the potential use of public spaces for illegal activities, due to their abandonment during high temperatures. Furthermore, due to the energy poverty that many households face in the Municipality of Athens and the lack of air conditioning in many dwellings, in relation to the aged building stock, thermal discomfort can be observed within many buildings. This can lead to high morbidity and mortality risks of vulnerable groups of the population .During the last decade, the hot period starts earlier in spring and finishes later in autumn, leading to an increased number of hot days. The decade 2011-2020 has been the warmest one that has been monitored, since the mid 19th century (Founda and Pierros, 2021). Several studies have shown that the number of days with temperatures of more than 37-40C has increased significantly after the 1990s. Electricity demand for cooling rises, while there are negative impacts mainly on vulnerable population's health and generally decrease in people's activities in the commercial city centre. These trends will deteriorate if appropriate measures are not taken. It is expected that the average annual temperature will rise from 0.28C to 1.60oC during the period 2031-2050 (Risk Assessment Athens, 2021/attached above).References: Katsouyanni, K., and Analytis, A. (2016) Mortality and High Temperatures, TREASURE Project. Presentation at the workshop: The impact of heatwave in the city of Athens: Synergies and actions for a cool Athens.Founda D., and Pierros F. (2021) The 'new' climate of Athens- period 1991-2020. Online scientific magazine of the National Observatory of Athens: http://magazine.noa.gr/archives/4446 | Urban flooding: Although the average annual precipitation will decrease, the number of days with intense rainfall will increase. This, in conjunction with the fact that locally, in some areas of the city, the drainage system is not adequate; the risks of flash/surface flood are serious. For instance, the intense rainfall of 14/10/2021 caused serious flooding incidents within the city, especially in areas where sewage systems are insufficient and also in areas where old streams have been transformed into streets. Damages were recorded due to this event in both residential and commercial buildings, as well as municipal infrastructure. If streams are not protected and no actions are taken for managing flood water, these phenomena will deteriorate the already aged building stock and infrastructure.

Intense rainfall and flooding can damage homes and small business leading to costly repairs that many residents may not afford. Also, the city's aging infrastructure, including drainage and sewage systems, is ill-equipped to handle sudden influxes of water. Ongoing damage could lead to increased maintenance costs and reduce overall urban resilience. | Drought: As a result of climate change, the average annual rainfall is expected to decrease by 6-12.5mm. This shall have a negative impact on the quality of underground water and there might be water scarcity incidents. | Extreme heat: In Athens, heat waves are exacerbated, due to the heat island effect. The intensity of heat waves also shows a growing trend. As a result, in periods of extremely high temperatures there is an increasing number of medical incidences, higher morbidity and mortality risks, increase of energy consumption for cooling and negative effects on the commercial sector due to the limited activities and commuting in the city centre. When these incidents coincide with high concentrations of particulate matter from the Sahara Desert, whose frequency has increased since 2000 (Bibi et al 2020), the result is excruciating for the population. Heat waves seem to increase both in frequency and duration, while they tend to appear earlier in summer through the country (Founda et al, 2021). The trend of heat wave increase in Athens is 3-5 days per decade (ibid). Apart from that, the number of nights that tourists spent within the city decreases due to high temperatures. It is interesting to note that from the COVID-19 lock-downs onward, the Athenians have rediscovered and reclaimed the public spaces of their neighborhoods. Parks, squares and hills that had been abandoned by the locals and often delinquent activities took place there. During the lock downs and afterwards, public spaces have been full of people, displacing delinquent activities. Thus, public spaces have been fulfilling their primary reason of existence, ie to offer spaces for communication and relaxation to the inhabitants and assist in the social cohesion of neighborhoods. All these trends will deteriorate if appropriate measures are not taken to transform public spaces into oases for the heat waves. References: Bibi M., Saad M., Masmoudi M., Laurent B., Alfaro S.C. (2020) Long-term (1980-2018) spatial and temporal variability of the atmospheric dust load and deposition fluxes along the North-African coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Atmospheric Research; 234:104689.Founda D., Katavoutas G., and Pierros F. (2021) June heat waves: from the exception to normality. Online scientific magazine of the National Observatory of Athens: http://magazine.noa.gr/archives/4496 | Water stress: According to the European Drought Observatory warnings, it is estimated that Greece will see a 10-30% reduction in rainfall by 2050, with 30% of the country possibly facing desertification within decades as a result. Greek households have the 4th highest consumption of water per capita in Europe, at 177 liters per day, yet pay one of the lowest costs per cubic meter of water in Europe, even after adjusting for cost of living. In 2024, the water level in the Mornos reservoir, which supplies the greater Athens-Piraeus area with much of its drinking water, has been 15% to 20% below the 14-year average, forcing Attica to start drawing water from other reserves and 17 boreholes to cover its needs.

The projected reductions in rainfall and the threat of desertification will have a significant impact on Athens, particularly for low income households and elderly and disabled individuals. These groups may face increased difficulties in accessing water sources, especially if supply becomes more erratic. They may also be more susceptible to health issues arising from heatwaves exacerbated by drought. Residents in informal or poorly connected areas of Athens may also face the most severe impacts, as they often rely on inadequate infrastructure. Water shortages could lead to significant public health issues, including hygiene-related diseases.

As a major economic driver for the City of Athens, tourism may suffer if water scarcity leads to environmental degradation or impacts the aesthetic appeal of the city. Tourists may be less inclined to visit a city facing severe drought conditions. Water shortages could also strain public services, including health care and sanitation. Increased demand on water supply systems may lead to higher operational costs, diverting funds from other essential services.

project_info:
Renewable energy - Energy Community of the Municipality of Athens (Faethon): The Municipality of Athens will develop an energy
community to produce clean energy and distribute it to citizens and, above all, to vulnerable households. The initial phase of the community will be implemented in the
Municipality of Athens. The Municipality will then offer the other municipalities of the Athenian Energy Alliance the opportunity to participate. The main objectives will be the following:
1) Production, storage, self-consumption or selling of electrical or thermal or cooling energy from RES or Hybrid stations.
2) Supply of energy products, devices, and services to its members, with the aim of reducing energy consumption and the use of conventional fuels as well as improving energy efficiency.
3) Promotion of electrification and supply for its members of electric vehicles, hybrid or otherwise, and in general vehicles that use alternative fuels.
4) Demand-side management to reduce the final use of electricity and representation of producers and consumers in the electricity market.
5) Network development, management, and exploitation of alternative fuel infrastructure or management of sustainable means of transport.

The Municipality is currently targeting the purchase of the first 20 MW. The total installed capacity required to achieve the Municipality's strategic priority for electricity produced by energy communities is approximately 270
MW.

climate_hazard:
Extreme heat: Health: The health of Berlin's population is affected by climate change by both the gradual change in average weather values in the form of a general increase in temperature and the increasing frequency of extreme weather events such as hot days, tropical nights, storms and heavy rainfall. Higher levels of UV radiation are also increasing people's risk of skin cancer.In addition to the direct risks to human health, there are also indirect risks. Plants' vegetation period is now lasting longer as a result of the increase in temperature. Consequently, plants are sometimes flowering for longer too, thereby increasing pollen concentrations. Around 700,000 pollen allergy sufferers living in Berlin are currently affected.

Urban development: Due to the density of buildings, reduced evaporation and the numerous barriers preventing air exchange, temperatures in cities are significantly higher than in surrounding rural areas. This phenomenon is known as the 'urban heat island effect'. In addition to high temperatures, the summer months are also likely to bring longer periods of drought in future. Berlin's urban green spaces will be particularly affected by this development. Hot summers with longer periods of drought place the city's urban green spaces under stress and make them more vulnerable to pest infestations. This leads to a reduction in the effectiveness of their climatic balancing functions, biotope functions and recovery function of the green spaces as well as causing them to become less attractive.

Forests: Berlin's forests provide numerous ecosystem services, which are absolutely essential, especially in the face of climate change. They help to keep the air clean, provide areas of cool air and allow the groundwater to recharge. This is of vital importance, as the majority of Berlin's drinking water comes from the groundwater. Just like the green spaces and recreational areas of the inner city, Berlin's forests are also placed under stress by long periods of heat and drought and grow more susceptible to pest infestations as a result. There is also a greater chance of wildfires occurring.(Source: diBEK) | Heavy precipitation: As it is so tightly closely interlinked with global and regional water cycles, the municipal water supply is directly affected by climate change. Around 522 million m3 of precipitation falls on the Berlin city area each year. Of this, approximately 310 million m3 evaporates, 142 million m3 seeps into the ground and nearly 70 million m3 is channelled away via the sewage system. As mentioned above, an increase in instances of heavy rainfall in areas of the city with large areas of sealed ground can result in flooding of and damage to infrastructure. Berlin's combined sewer system, through which rain water is channelled away along with waste water, represents an already widely acknowledged problem. Due to the above, it has been considered to implement a sustainable driving program that allows city drivers to maximize the benefits in air quality, road safety and economic benefits.

project_info: Transport - Environmental labeling of vehicles in use: The Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is structuring a national vehicle environmental labeling, in order to classify vehicles according to their emissions levels according to the emission standard they meet and the technology they have. In this sense, the territorial entities together with the Automotive Diagnostic Centers are responsible for the implementation of the labeling, the District is also responsible for establishing control and monitoring actions such as peak and plate according to the label level, access to low and zero emission zones, green corridors, among others, in order to unify the labeling tool with incentive actions for the use of cleaner technologies. By 2022 it is expected to have the labeling classification at the national level and at the district level it is expected to have a vehicle labeling pilot, subsequently it is expected to update the restrictions in circulation and other programs that can use environmental label levels as a categorization instrument. This will facilitate on-road control and vehicle restriction policies, which are currently defined for private vehicles according to the license plate number, which can be exempt from circulation restrictions if a full rate is paid regardless of the impact on air quality of the technology that circulates. For heavy-duty vehicles, the current restrictions are carried out according to the load capacity and model year of circulation, and historically from 2019 back there was a peak and environmental plate of one hour per day according to the plate. Over time, the aim is for the number of vehicles with zero and low emissions labels to increase in the city, and for labels with associated levels of higher emissions to be reduced, thus achieving a decrease in total emissions by the vehicle fleet that circulates. in the city.

project_info: Transport - On-road control of mobile sources through the implementation of remote sensors: One of the strategies to increase coverage in the control of mobile sources and determine their environmental state under real operating conditions is through the use of telematic control systems, such as remote sensors, which significantly increases the number of vehicles tested and presents typical emissions results of the operation. This technology is similar to lifesaving cameras that detect speeding, but focused on the detection of pollutant emissions in real vehicle operating conditions. In the case of the SDA, in 2019, pilot tests were carried out with remote sensors under real operating conditions. This study and others in the literature show that it is a viable option to increase coverage and vehicle environmental monitoring in the vehicle fleet, however, there are challenges to be solved for its application in the city. such as:-Regulations: There are no established emission limits to carry out control by this method and that it is comparable to a conventional measurement on the road. On the other hand, electronic reports for environmental measurements are not regulated.-Standardization: There is no standardization framework for this type of metrics at the national level.-Technological: It is a method that is in the process of development worldwide, which is why there may be technological variations in the measurement methods and metrics. -Operational: The operational framework for remote sensor control must be defined, associating operational personnel to guarantee continuity in measurements, supervision and analysis of results. as well as the definition of measurement points, among other parameters.-Economic: It is necessary to establish what is most appropriate to carry out control by remote sensors, from outsourcing or from the purchase of equipment. measurement of the city.-Integration: There is a challenge of integrating the data obtained and the information and technology systems of the SDA and the city. project_info: Buildings - Introduction of construction machinery with low emission levels: Objective: Carry out a technological upgrade in the construction machinery that operates in the city, to reduce its contributions of particulate matter and gases generated by the internal combustion of its engines Description: The emissions generated by the operation of construction machinery are not regulated in the country, which implies that new or used machinery enters that are not approved by international standards such as those defined by the Tier and Stage regulations, which seek to reduce fuel consumption and atmospheric emissions through the implementation of more efficient and environmentally friendly technologies. This situation implies that the machinery that is marketed and operated in the city does not meet the minimum standards regulated worldwide, evidencing technological lags. On the other hand, a large proportion operate with diesel cycle engines and have It has exceeded its useful life, a situation that does not favor the city's air quality. In accordance with the above, the result seeks to establish a minimum emission standard that all new or used machinery that operates in the city must meet. For this purpose, it was defined that, as of January 1, 2023, importers and/or assemblers must guarantee that their machinery complies with the Tier 4i standard, or its equivalent, Stage IIIB. Therefore, a staggered technological promotion was proposed to be implemented between the years 2021 and 2030, taking as a criterion that currently all machinery complies with the TierI emission standard. Thus, for the optimistic scenario, it was proposed that by 2030, 80% of the vehicle fleet will meet the defined standard. In the intermediate scenario, 60%, and in the pessimistic scenario, 20%. To execute the result, the following activities were defined: 1) Inventory and characterization of machinery, 2) selection and evaluation of minimum technological requirement, 3) regulation of implementation of minimum requirement, 4) regulation of economic and financial incentives, 5, implementation of the minimum requirement. Impacts: • Environmental: Estimated emission reductions for pollutants: NOx and PM10. • Health: Reduction in the number of deaths attributed to exposure to PM2.5 concentration • Economic: Savings in costs associated with the reduction of attributed deaths Estimated Budget: 11,697 million Colombian pesos

project_info: Transport - Electromobility - Financing: The project contemplates carrying out three works focused on electric mobility and its infrastructure. First deliverable: You will develop plausible scenarios to inform the establishment of a city-wide target for the adoption of zero-emission vehicles. The analysis takes into account electric vehicles and other low-emission technologies, such as the second generation. biofuels, fuel cells or vehicles with hydrogen internal combustion engines. Second deliverable: Assesses the needs and challenges for the development of charging infrastructure for electric vehicles in CABA, provides recommendations for the city government to plan an initial deployment of electric charging infrastructure, potentially from public and private sources, with a gradual expansion once there is greater demand for electric vehicles in the long term. In addition, it evaluates international experiences to provide a benchmark on charging infrastructure planning in comparable cities. Third deliverable: evaluate the potential to develop a manufacturing cluster in the southern area of ​​CABA oriented to electric mobility, including multiple small and medium-sized producers of light electric vehicles (VEV). The manufacturing cluster may also include electric vehicle retrofit workshops, vehicle charger manufacturing and sales, electric vehicle showroom, among other uses.

The InVEST Coastal Vulnerability model uses the geophysical and natural habitat characteristics of coastal areas to compare exposure to erosion and flooding during severe weather events. When the model's outputs are overlaid with data on coastal population density, they can be used to identify areas where people are at higher risk of damage from storm surges and waves.

The InVEST Coastal Vulnerability model distinguishes areas that are relatively highly or lowly exposed to erosion and flooding during storms, thereby producing a qualitative estimate of this type of exposure in terms of a vulnerability index arising from risks caused by climate change.

The map of costal vulnerability shows the coastal regions most at risk from floods and water surges due to wind and storms. The following factors were considered in the establishment of the map:

- types and strengths of wind
- physical structure and power of waves
- coastal shape. 

Among the most vulnerable areas in Istanbul are for example the Black Sea coastline, the Marmara coastline on the Asian side and the historic peninsula of Istanbul.

Nevertheless, the droughts experienced until today has been evaluated, and the strongest drought indices, which can best describe these droughts and enable the accurate, reliable and easy calculation of drought severity, has been determined with the help of drought indices accepted in the national and international literature. Through this determined drought index, the current and future drought risk has been determined as point and regional. Droughts under different recurrence times and the possible effects of these droughts on water resources have been examined, and the effects that may arise in case of a similar dry period in the future have been interpreted. In order to serve this purpose, the current and potential water resources of Istanbul have been modeled by using precipitation-flow modeling, and with the help of these models, the possible effects of climate change on water resources have been revealed through climate models and scenarios. Additively, a series of actions and measures have been put forward within the scope of the report to reduce the risk of drought and to mitigate the effects of possible severe droughts and water scarcity. climate_hazard: Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Using observed data from sea level gauges across the Vietnam coastline, the increase in sea level between 1993 and 2014 was approximately 3.34 mm/year (MONRE, 2016, page 36). The Southern region of Vietnam, including Ho Chi Minh City, experienced an even more pronounced rise of around 5.58 mm/year in this time period (MONRE, 2016, page 36). Following the RCP 8.5 scenario, the average sea level rise for coastal areas throughout Vietnam would be 250 mm by 2050 and 730 mm by 2100 (MONRE, 2016) | Mass movement: Overload the exit infrastructure, make more people subsidence to climate change. | Heat stress: In the South region, where Ho Chi Minh City is located, has experienced a steady rise in average annual temperature from 1960 to 2010 (Katzfey et al., 2014). In this period, annual temperature in the South Delta region has significantly increased from 0.04°C to 0.28°C per decade. Maximum and minimum temperatures have increased by up to 0.36°C per decade (Katzfey et al., 2014).For the southern Mekong Delta region, where Ho Chi Minh City is located, projections show a very clear warming signal, with an increase in average annual temperature of around 1.4°C to 2.8°C by mid-century and 2.8°C to 4.7°C by end-of-century under the RCP 8.5 scenario. The warming is approximately uniform over the year (MONRE, 2016).The amount of days with extreme temperatures will also increase. The Southern Delta and Ho Chi Minh City currently experience on average 30-60 extremely hot days per year (IPONRE, 2009). The Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE, 2016) projects 10 additional extremely hot days by 2050, under the RCP 8.5 scenario, for Ho Chi Minh City. | Heavy precipitation: Observed rainfall records from the last 50 years (1961-2010) do not show a significant trend in total rainfall (Katzfey et al., 2014). However, the story is different for heavy rainfall events. Between 1962 and 2001, Ho Chi Minh City and the surrounding region experienced only one “extremely heavy” precipitation event (i.e. 3-hour accumulated rainfall exceeding 100 millimeters) every 4 years. Nevertheless, heavy precipitation events have become more frequent (Khoi and Trang, 2016). From 2002 to 2017, heavy precipitation events occurred 3 times per year (C40, 2018). Projections for future rainfall show larger variations in the direction of change than were projected for temperature. Nevertheless, projections of the RCP 8.5 scenario show an increase in rainfall of 7.3 - 20.2% in 2050 compared to 1986-2005 for Ho Chi Minh City. The summer monsoon will lengthen and the monsoonal rainfall will increase by 11.6 - 18.9 % (MONRE, 2016). | Storm: Far from now, I haven't hear any storm that really cross Ho Chi Minh city. There are just thunderstorms and tornadoes that rarely cause human damage. But climate change happend. Extreme rainfall events will occur more often and become more intense through climate change. The average maximum 1-day rainfall will increase by 30-40 % in 2050 (RCP 8.5, compared to 1986-2005) (MONRE, 2016). In recent decades, tropical cyclones have become more common in Ho Chi Minh City (Ho Chi Minh City Atlas, 2013). Projections for the south region suggest that although the number of tropical cyclones may decrease in the East Vietnam Sea by mid-century, the intensity may increase by the end-of-century (Katzfey et al., 2014 ). Furthermore, tropical depressions and typhoons will likely occur at the end of the typhoon season. As a result, Ho Chi Minh City will become more vulnerable to extreme rainfall events during this period, which is one of the deadliest natural disasters affecting Vietnam (MONRE, 2016). | Water stress: Saline in The Mekong Delta already happened during the dry season of 2015-2016 and is expected to increase in the future because of sea level rise (Viet Dung Nguyen, 2019). The salinity concentration is expected to increase by 1.2% to nearly 10% in the future. This means that saltwater will move deeply inland in the future and have significant impacts on agricultural activities and livelihoods of farmers in the Mekong Delta (Ha, 2016).
project_info: Transport - Development of a charging station system for electric buses: In order to support the implementation of the policy on building a modern and environmentally friendly public transport system, Ho Chi Minh City is currently preparing to pilot five electric bus routes in the city. To successfully replicate the electric bus model, Ho Chi Minh City will need to plan and develop a system of charging stations for electric buses. The development of the charging station system is an indispensable piece to complete the implementation of the electric bus system, contributing to the construction of a modern and friendly public transport system, thereby reducing traffic congestion and pollution, environment.

project_info: Transport - Develop e-bus for Ho Chi Minh city: With limited financial and human resources, the city can consider and coordinate with stakeholders to study the option of building an electric bus rental model to move towards electrification of the public passenger transport system with the most economical cost. In this model, some, or all, of the electric bus parts manufactured by a third party will be leased by the public passenger transport system operator. The parts to be rented can be batteries or the whole bus. The bus operator will pay a flat monthly fee to the lessor based on specific conditions, possibly with a monthly surcharge based on the distance traveled. If the battery-only model is adopted, the upfront cost for electric buses will be significantly reduced and almost equivalent to the cost of buying a traditional diesel bus. As a result, the bus operator can purchase an electric bus without incurring any additional additional costs than usual. The transfer of operational risk and technology from the operator to the lessor will also facilitate fleet electrification.

project_info: Other: Climate change in general - EU-Mission 100% climate neutrality in cities: Heidelberg is part of the EU Mission „100 climate neutral and smart cities 2030“. The EU Mission's goal is to facilitate knowledge transfer between European cities and the EU Commission in order to accelerate local climate action towards climate neutrality. The initial step was the development of the Climate City Contract in 2023 together with over 40 different stakeholders in the city such as companies, scientific institutions and civil organisations. In March 2024, Heidelberg was rewarded with the Mission Label. In September 2024, Heidelberg started the EU Mission pilot project Climate City Dash 2.0 together with the City of Munich and the City of Dortmund. Climate City Dash 2.0 aims to tackle the stakeholders' engagement and further develop Heidelberg's ClimateView dashboard. Furthermore, the German EU Mission cities have founded the network stronGER Cities to share best practices and to start a process for better collaboration with the German Government.

Transport - REALLOCATE EU-Mission: REALLOCATE pilot project for vibrant traffic-calmed areas: As part of the EU REALLOCATE project, Heidelberg is developing approaches and measures to redistribute public space in favour of pedestrian and bicycle traffic as well as
public transport. In two districts redesigns will be implemented in 2025/2026. They have been developed in consultation with citizens,
local schools and businesses, as well as experts from the EU consortium. The aim is to reduce car traffic, increase safety, especially for children and older people, and create attractive, green recreational areas. The focus is on
land use conversion, traffic calming and sustainable mobility.

project_info: Renewable energy - Citizen Wind park: In October 2023, a bidding consortium consisting of the utilities companies Stadtwerke Heidelberg, Trianel and three regional energy cooperatives was awarded the contract to plan a community wind farm on state-owned forestry land. The total area covers 600 hectares and is only partly located in Heidelberg, with most of it in a municipality in the Rhine-Neckar district. The turbines would cover a large part of the electricity needs of all private households in Heidelberg. Citizens would not only benefit from affordable green electricity, but could also purchase shares in the community wind farm. Currently, ways of reconciling nature conservation concerns with the planned wind turbines are being examined.\nhttps://www.heidelberg.de/HD/entwickeln/buergerwindpark+lammerskopf.html\n

project_info:
Renewable energy - Construction of river and wastewater heat pumps: Generating regenerative heat from the Neckar River and from treated wastewater with the help of large-scale heat pumps is an important component of climate neutrality. 
A river heat pump is to be built on the south-western side of the approach to the Ernst Walz Bridge in Heidelberg-Bergheim. The site is technically well suited, but its inner-city location requires the building to be integrated attractively into the urban landscape. The aim is to upgrade this previously underused area, which is surrounded by traffic. The urban development concept envisages breaking up the area with several buildings featuring attractive, green façades. The idea of planning a small restaurant at the facility was also well received. There are also discussions about connecting the area to the Neckar river. The heat pump extracts up to five degrees of heat from the water taken from the Neckar. The temperature of the Neckar may not fall by more than one degree Celsius in total. This value is calculated by relating the cooled water volume to the volume flow of the Neckar. The plant will fall well below this legally prescribed value: when in operation, it will cool the Neckar by a total of around 0.3 degrees Celsius.
The wastewater heat pump will be built near the North Wastewater Treatment Plant in Neuenheimer Feld. Although the urban planning requirements here are less demanding than for the river heat pump, an attractive architectural concept has also been developed for this project: the plan is to construct a building whose visual design implies the waves of the Neckar River.
The heat pump will use the heat from the wastewater. The temperature of wastewater from households is higher than that of the Neckar, especially in the winter months. This means that the heat pump can cool the wastewater by up to seven degrees Celsius.
The heat pumps increase the temperature of the heat extracted from the river or wastewater to approx. 90 to 95 degrees Celsius, so that the heat can be fed into the district heating network. Each of the two plants will generate 130,000 to 240,000 megawatt hours of usable heat per year at an output of 30 megawatts. The plants are scheduled to go into operation by 2029.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: In 2022, DKI Jakarta Province will face quite extreme hot weather, reaching temperatures of 36 degrees Celsius in several days. The Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) provides the reasons. This condition occurs because Indonesia is currently entering the transition season or the transition period from the rainy to dry season. This incident has an impact on toddlers, the elderly and people who are vulnerable to hot temperatures. | Urban flooding: From a study of historical BMKG daily rainfall data for 150 years (1866 - 2015), there is a trend of increasingly frequent significant flooding events in Jakarta with an increase in the intensity of annual extreme rainfall. Meanwhile, in the Jabodetabek area (Jakarta, Bogor, Depok, Tanggerang, Bekasi) the highest daily rainfall per year shows a trend of increasing intensity of 10 - 20 mm per 10 years from the last 43 years of data. Analysis of statistical data from the 150 year series of the BMKG Jakarta Station Observatory for the probability of rainfall occurrence extreme rain causes flood events with recurrences such as the return period of 2014, 2015 and early 2020 in Jakarta showing an increase of 2-3% when compared to climate conditions 100 years ago | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): In 2017 a 200 cm high tide triggered tidal floods in the northern area of ââJakarta and caused losses of more than IDR 4.7 trillion. Currently the central government is building a giant embankment and starting to promote the rehabilitation of mangrove forests as natural, environmentally friendly fortifications on the Coast and Seribu Islands.. | Infectious disease: Based on BPS data for DKI Jakarta Province in 2021, there is information regarding the number of disease cases according to province/district/city and type of disease. The types of diseases related to the impact of climate change are dengue fever, diarrhea, Pneumoniahttps://statistik.jakarta. go.id/case-pesit-menular-di-dki-jakarta/ https://data.jakarta.go.id/dataset/data-jumlah-kasus-penyakit-menular-menurut-jenis-penyakit-dki-jakarta | River flooding: The 2007 Jakarta flood was a flood disaster that hit Jakarta and its surroundings since 1 February 2007 at night. Apart from the poor drainage system, the flood started from heavy rain which lasted from the afternoon of February 1 until the following day, February 2, plus the large volume of water from the 13 rivers that cross Jakarta originating from Jonggol-Bogor-Puncak-Cianjur area, and high tide, resulting in almost 60% of the DKI Jakarta area being submerged in floods with depths reaching up to 5 meters at several flood locations.
