project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Waste Infrastructure Development Strategy: Under this action, Lagos State will undertake an evaluation of the cur- rent status of waste management and develop a Waste Infrastructure Development Strategy by 2022. The evaluation will be based on data on tons of waste collected, waste composition and volumes processed by MRF and composting facilities. The strategy will aim to increase the capacity of Lagos's waste transfer, material recovery, bio- digester and composting facilities. It will mandate the construction of new waste infrastructure, including transfer loading stations, starting in Iberekodo, Agunlejika and Odogunyan. The strat- egy will build on the progress the State has made so far in establishing waste transfer stations and expanding the waste vehicle fleet. The new facilities will need to have the capacity to absorb the expected increase in the volume of recyclables diverted from landfill due to the launch of the Lagos Recycling Initiative. Implementation of the strat- egy is expected to require State funding and cooperation with the private sector through PPPs. The State could institute a levy on waste disposal to support infrastructure investments. A number of previous projects were abandoned because their operation was deemed unfeasible; demand must be confirmed in the planning phase and consideration must be given to how these projects can be made sustainable in the long term. For wastewater management, the State Government intends to develop an Outline Business Case (OBC) study and WIDP for the sector. The OBC study/ WIDP will cover the preparation of detailed engineering designs, drawings and specifications, construction and operational cost estimates, environ- mental and social impact assessments, and analysis of required land use for wastewater infrastructure provision for existing and projected population of the State, in line with Regional Masterplan of the State. The WIDP will further determine project implementation and phasing plan, set timelines and process to be followed for project procurement (either through government funding or through private sector participation), while the OBC study will specifically provide a well-developed and compre- hensive suite of project documents that will be made available to private inves- tors during the procurement process. This is a useful tool that will bring all the elements of the project together, so that any conflicts between factors can be resolved before approaching the pri- vate sector. This document will be used to form the basis on which the project will be assessed and approved for com- mencement of the procurement phase. It will also have served as an investment document to engender the interest of investors and facilitate the implemen- tation of wastewater treatment projects through public private partnerships (PPP) procurement routes. In addition to this, all existing wastewater treat- ment infrastructure in the State will be upgraded and expanded to cover more catchment areas, these include Alausa wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), Abesan WWTP, Oke-Afa WWTP and Iponri WWTP.

project_info: Transport - Non- Motorised Transport for Cycling Infrastructure: The NMTP was developed by the LAMATA on behalf of the Lagos State Government. The NMTP improves basic mobility, the affordability of transport, access to public transport and also pro- vides health and recreational benefits. Improving the convenience, comfort and safety of walking and cycling reduces the demand for personal motorised vehicle travel and can help to alleviate the critical traffic challenges the State faces. climate_hazard: Drought: Metropolitan Lima is characterized by a semi-warm-arid climate with a deficiency of precipitation and humidity. Although it has recorded several drought events in recent decades (e.g. the regional drought that occurred in 1992, which covered the three basins that supply Metropolitan Lima), its climatic condition makes it more pertinent to evaluate the change in aridity under Climate Change scenarios, instead of the danger of droughts through these indices. Regarding precipitation, there are four factors: Humboldt current, Andes Mountains, topography and the continental effect are what determine the desert condition of Metropolitan Lima, which is, in turn, affected by precipitation coming from the high basins. According to the reference climatology used for the SENAMHI (2015) study, the total annual precipitation generally presents a precipitation of less than 50 mm and increases with altitude, reaching maximum values ââof 178 mm. In the future climate projection it was found that the total annual precipitation shows average values ââof between 25 mm and 161 mm under the RCP 4.5 scenario and between 30 mm and 200 mm under the RCP 8.5 scenario (Figure 49). Its behavior is similar to that recorded during the historical period, since a gradual increase in precipitation is observed as the distance from the coast increases. Likewise, there is variability in the level of drought danger under the RCP 4.5 scenario. The reason is due to a variable behavior in precipitation under this scenario since the temperature shows a uniform increase throughout the province. Thus, the most dangerous areas are those areas where there is a decrease in precipitation with respect to the historical period; while the areas with less danger are those that show an increase in precipitation compared to the historical period. On the other hand, The RCP 8.5 scenario mostly shows a low or moderate level of risk mainly due to the fact that there is a greater increase in precipitation during this climate scenario. However, it should be noted that this variable presents high uncertainty in the territory; Therefore, the results obtained under this scenario are also subject to said uncertainty. | Mass movement: Mass movements, which refer to processes activated mainly by gravity, are the phenomena that have the greatest incidence in the territory with more than half of the total events recorded per year. project_info:
Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - LED in public lighting: Its purpose is to change to LED all the luminaires managed by the Municipality. They are located in public spaces and roads to reduce energy consumption and improve luminosity in different areas of the city.
Potential reduction of accumulated GHG due to energy efficiency for 1 year is approximately 206.31tCO2e, the same as that estimated in the city's Local Climate Change Plan. 

Within this framework, in 2024 the advancement of the technological renewal and modernization of public lighting was approved in the IOARR: "RENOVATION OF PUBLIC LIGHTING ASSEMBLY; ON PASEO DE LA REPÚBLICA AVENUE (PLAZA GRAU - AV. REPÚBLICA DE PANAMÁ) IN THE CENTRO POBLADO LA VICTORIA, DISTRICT OF LA VICTORIA, “LIMA PROVINCE, LIMA DEPARTMENT”. 

Paseo de la República Avenue currently has a total of 1,424 lights in poor condition, operational at an average level; however, the The public purpose of the development of this investment is to contribute to energy efficiency in the public lighting service. Therefore, it is of utmost importance to have the assembly of public lighting above the standard with special LED luminaire technology, a service that must be developed by the concessionaire of the public electrical service of the concession area corresponding to the DGE technical standard “LIGHTING OF PUBLIC ROADS IN DISTRIBUTION CONCESSION AREAS” approved with Ministerial Resolution No. 013-2003-EM/DM.

project_info: Public and green spaces - Implement a new intelligent irrigation system in the parks and gardens of the city of Lima.: A complete preliminary study will be developed to characterize the types of irrigation in parks and gardens, in order to implement a new management system for them, for that of an intelligent irrigation system in the city of Lima. The parks and gardens of Metropolitan Lima would be equipped with a system of sensors and controllers that measure climatic variables (temperature, precipitation, soil humidity and wind speed) and report on the plants' need for water. This information is transmitted to a GIS system (Geographic Information System) where municipal technicians manage irrigation in real time from their computer and detect incidents such as breakdowns or malfunctions.

It will affect a wide range of groups of population, activities and economic sectors. One of the main impacts will happen o health issues, increasing mortality and morbidity rates over the most vulnerable gropus, but also reducing the confort of quality of life of the whole population. Buildings - 'Emplea T Verde' Project: On July 27, 2023, Madrid City Council signed an agreement with the Public Organization “ECODES”, under the framework of the “TANDEM PROGRAMME OF TRAINING IN ALTERNITY WITH EMPLOYMENT, WITHIN THE FRAMEWORK OF THE RECOVERY, TRANSFORMATION AND RESILIENCE PLAN, REGULATED BY THE ORDER OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOR AND SOCIAL ECONOMY TES/ /1153/2021, OF OCTOBER 24”, with aim of taking part in the project 'Emplea T Verde'. The project has been selected by the National Public Employment Service (SEPE) and granted ECODES the appropriate funding for its development.
The aim of this project is to ensure that 64 unemployed citizens (young refugees) in the municipality of Madrid, benefit, after a professional training process, from a first work experience in a segment of the labor market where there is currently a great demand for professionals.
Through the “Emplea T Verde Project”, which has the support of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, UNHCR-Spain, the aim is to achieve a triple impact: 

1.Re-qualification and accompaniment towards green jobs for young people in a situation of unemployment.
2.Adaptation to climate change connecting with the climate strategy of the municipality and specifically with the following lines of work in the buildings subject to the action:
- The improvement of energy efficiency with one or more of these elements: by replacing windows, green surface or improving insulation.
- The installation of renewable energies.
3.Advice on energy efficiency to the residents of the neighborhood where the action is carried out, as well as environmental education programs if any intervention is carried out in schools.

Likewise, as a result of the “Emplea T Verde Project”, the city of Madrid and its citizens will benefit from the actions of energy advice to the citizens and sustainable rehabilitation carried out in public spaces.

Biodiversity loss: The conservation land, which represents 59% of the total territory of Mexico City, has shown constant deterioration, as a consequence of the expansion of the urban area, productive practices that degrade the ecosystem and the abandonment of the land. If the trend continues, an average loss of 219 hectares per year would be expected, which by 2040 would represent half of the forest that existed in 1986. In general, the forests and green areas of the city face constant degradation due to poor urban planning, the expansion of the urban sprawl, irregular human settlements, deforestation, illegal extraction of flora and fauna, forest fires and poor waste management. This has generated loss of biodiversity, presence of invasive species, loss of productive areas, erosion, contamination of water, air and soil, fragmented green areas, overexploitation of the aquifer, disappearance of bodies of water, decrease in areas of infiltration to recharge the aquifer, increased flooding, among other problems. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): In 2020, Mexico City ranked second nationally in terms of the number of wildfires. This affects both the animal and plant species that live on conservation land and the air quality of the entire metropolitan area. The city is not only the space made up of concrete and asphalt soils, it also has a huge and rich territory known as conservation land, made up of regions of high biodiversity framed mostly by pine and oak forests, scree areas, as well as lands of agricultural communities. Conservation land occupies more than half (59%) of the total area of ââthe city and the environmental benefits it brings to all inhabitants cannot be replaced; Some of these are, for example, the recharge of the aquifer, from which we obtain a large part of the water we consume on a daily basis. daily, generating oxygen, cleaning the atmosphere and regulating the climate, in addition to providing animal and plant food for the entire basin. It is relevant to mention that although forest fires contribute only 0.03% of CO2e emissions and 0.2% of the City's black carbon emissions, they are associated with negative effects on human health and the loss of biodiversity and, as they are exacerbated by global warming, their priority attention enhances synergies between mitigation and adaptation to climate change. | Urban flooding: Hydrometeorological phenomena such as rain, hail, added to the presence of bodies of water, topographic conditions, are some of the determinants of danger due to flooding. In Mexico City, the danger of flooding is determined by a combination of physical and anthropogenic factors. Among the main ones are the spatial distribution of precipitation, the topography, the characteristics of rivers and streams, the slope of the land, the loss of vegetation cover, changes in land use, the accumulation of waste on public roads, the occupation of flood zones and urban expansion without planning. These elements significantly increase exposure and risk in different areas of the city, the flood danger zones are concentrated in the region closest to the southern and western slopes, as well as in part of the central-eastern region of the City. With the constant rains, flooding in Mexico City has become a serious problem, affecting the population in such a way that their homes and businesses are often destroyed by water. In addition to this, the drainage system is overwhelmed so flooding can last for days. 

According to data from the Secretariat of Comprehensive Risk Management and Civil Protection of Mexico City, 27.8% of the territory in 14 Municipalities of CDMX present very high and high danger indices due to flooding. Through studies, it was found that these events showed damage or human losses due to flooding, falling trees and billboards, among others. In addition to this, there is the possibility of thunderstorms in 5 of the municipalities belonging to Mexico City.

Mexico City has a high population density, a large percentage of impermeable areas (asphalt, concrete) and drainage systems that, although modern, are insufficient in the face of extreme rainfall, which is why low areas or areas with land subsidence are particularly susceptible. Between 2024 and 2025, floods and flooding were recorded, affecting homes, road infrastructure, public transportation services and drinking water networks. Water stress: Climate change has led to a variation in the distribution of rainfall throughout the year: very intense rainfall alternate with long periods of drought.
At the moment drought does not threaten vulnerable population's (older adults aged 65 and above, children under 10, individuals with low education levels, those living in isolation, and people residing in overcrowded households) access to fresh/drinking water since the city is very rich in underground water, but it can be an issue for air quality, since rain captures air pollutants and cleans the atmosphere.
At the moment, water stress has not caused severe disruptions in exposed sectors, such as agriculture and green area maintenance. | Drought: As highlighted in the Local Climate Profile, the yearly overall amount of rain decreased by approximately 8 mm per decade, and it's expected to become even lower by 2050. This change does not threaten Milan's access to water resources since the city is very rich in underground water, but it can be an issue for air quality, since rain captures air pollutants and cleans the atmosphere, and for agriculture, biodiversity and natural environment. After a very dry 2022 and 2023 the first 6 months of 2024, quite the opposite, were exceptionally rainy with heavy accumulation of snow on the mountains, overflowing rivers and inner water basins which have reached their historical peaks. Nevertheless also this excessive water amount has damaged agriculture and flooded several locations in Milano (especially the usual flooded area in the north east side around the Seveso basin), in Lombardy and around Italy, proving once more that weather phenomena have become more and more extreme. | Urban flooding: Surface runoff is widely recognised as one of the main issues of contemporary cities, which are getting less permeable due to the high demand in space for buildings and infrastructures. Milan suffers from this problem as well, but, considering that the sewage network is very efficient, this issue in particular manifests itself through localized flooding, which slightly affect the mobility sector (traffic conditions and the viability of certain pedestrian areas) but do not cause severe damages as it happens for river flooding. This kind of phenomenon affects the sewage system as well, which has to treat more water than it's actually necessary and wears over time. | River flooding: The urban area of Milan is affected by the passage of three rivers with torrential regime (Lambro-Seveso-Olona) and several creeks and ditches (almost completely covered) that in case of rainstorm or intense precipitation events may overflow, invading streets, underground stations, and the lower level of buildings, therefore causing traffic interruption, damages to buildings, interruption of schools and commercial services. 
Milan water management policies are decreasing the impact of river floods thanks to an agreement for the hydraulic protection of the city signed in 1999 between different authorities (Lombardy Region, Metropolitan city of Milan, Interregional Agency for the Po River and the Municipality of Milan). Interventions have been planned and realized, including flood expansion basins along the rivers upstream of the city of Milan (basin of Parco Nord along the Seveso river and rehabilitation of Lambro river floodplain areas) and a diversion channel (Canale Scolmatore Nord Ovest) that intercepts flood waves before they enter the city. Milan has an efficient drainage network and several projects are in place to further reduce flood risk, namely: Safer Places, MSC, de-sealing projects and implementation of SuDS within the Air and Climate Plan.
Sectors most exposed: 
- Accomodation and food services, wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (tipically located at the ground or underground level can be flooded and their activity forced to stop)
- Sewerage (greatly stressed by the excessive water amount to treat) 
- Waste management and remediation activities (carried out at the ground level or in open spaces can be deeply affected by floods). 
- Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning networks (can be damaged and forced to shut down for some time).
- Health and social work activities (social workers might not be able to reach their users).
- Water supply (potable water network can be damaged and the supply interrupted).
- Agriculture (land can be invaded by streams of water and mud also transporting waste, even toxic waste).
- Administrative and support service activities (work under greater stress, affects their capacity to respond quickly and effectively).

People most exposed:
- Low-income households (live in lower levels, cannot escape their homes)
- Outdoor workers (directly exposed to danger)
- Vulnerable health groups and elderly (cannot be reached by medical assistance, difficulty to move) | Extreme heat: According to the IPCC Fifth ans Sixth Assessment Reports, heatwaves have an higher incidence on cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, especially in elderly people and children. A correlation seems to exist also between gender and mortality rates during heatwaves, in fact during 2003 Paris heatwave, mortality rates were greater among women, whilst a very high rate was discovered among working men, which suggests that the working environment influences vulnerability. Heatwaves also cause higher energy demand for cooling by creating a general discomfort. In the last years this fact forced the energy management agency of Italy (Unareti) to issue a warning to reduce energy consumption in order to prevent blackouts: in 2015, due to the high temperature, a peak in energy demand was registered in the city (1.625 MW), causing several failures in the energy distribution network. The same event occurred in 2021, when a sudden rise in temperatures in mid-June produced a 25% increase in electricity consumption leading to several blackouts.
Vulnerable populations most affected include: 
- Elderly/children/vulnerable health groups (more fragile and affected by heath connected diseases)
- Outdoor workers (directly exposed to heath stress)
- Frontline workers (more exposed to heath stress, e.g. armed forces, firefighters, and other security workers)
- Low income households (cannot afford air conditioning and quality home insulation, cannot leave the city).
Sectors most exposed:
- Agriculture (lack of water, crops suffering from high temperatures)
- Electricity, gas, steam, air conditioning supply (risk of blackouts)
- Water supply (risk of water rationing)
- Transportation and storage (can be affected by blackouts)
 | Heavy precipitation: There are several negative effects of heavy rainfall: one of the most obvious ones is the fact that heavy rainfall, which is becoming increasingly intense due to climate change, not only contributes to flooding of watercourses but also creates widespread flooding in urban areas as drainage systems are designed for shorter return period. 
Heavy rainfall damages house cellars, underground car parks and mobility infrastructures such as road gallery and subways. Another effect of intense rain is on the use of the different transportation means: when it rains, the use of private cars increases, filling the streets and increasing the vulnerability of the city to floods. Indeed, infrastructures are one of the most sensitive elements when exposed to floods and, considering that vehicle circulation slows down, emergency services are affected. | Infectious disease: According to the data provided by the SSN (National Health Service), in Milan's region (Lombardy) have been reported 225 cases of malaria (average per year between 2013 and 2017), 1 case of Chikungunya (2018), 13 cases of Dengue (2018) and a single case in the whole national territory of Zika (2018). All these diseases are related to mosquitos, which are expected to grow in number due to the rising of temperatures, therefore it is possible that the future reported number of cases per year is going to increase. In August 2023, a dengue outbreak occurred in a village in the Lombardy region. This event marked the largest confirmed cluster of locally transmitted dengue in Lombardy, leading to the implementation of vector control measures and intensive screening efforts. Due to Italian Healthcare system, the diseases are preventable, curable or at least the symptoms can be treated until the spontaneous healing, therefore the consequences of the hazard are not severe. Despite all, it is crucial to be aware that Milan is moving towards a tropicalization of the climate. Thus, although risk level remains low, biological hazards need to be kept under control in order to contain future risks. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: During the summers of 2022 and 2023 the climate change effects have shown themselves clearly, causing an increase in extreme weather events such as storms, hailstorm, and even tornadoes triggered by very high temperatures and high humidity rates. The weather, at least in the Po basin area (Padana valley), is moving towards a tropical model. Storms and hailstorms seriously wound and even impact on people's safety and exposed sectors such as agriculture (damage crops, trees) and mobility (cars, roads and railroads). | Extreme wind: Even though wind intensity is perceived as higher, ARPA's data regarding Milan is not old enough to make relevant climatic analysis or benchmarking, in fact, wind monitoring stations were installed between 2012 and 2014 in Brera and Lambrate's stations (respectively describing the city center and the suburbs). Data collected by those stations shows that wind intensity actually increased in average 1 m/s in Brera, with a frequency increase of six seasonal events over the 95th percentile (calculated on the wind intensity recorded in Brera between 01/01/2015 and 31/12/2018). Data also shows that the average wind intensity in Lambrate didn't change, while the severe wind events frequency actually decreased in the last five years, even though the frequency change was too small to be considered relevant: available data is not enough to make assumptions about wind in relation to climate change, but it could suggest that the wind intensity did not actually change and the change in Brera could have been caused by morphological factors. During the past three years, some episodes of strong wind happened, causing damages to trees (in this case, the municipal governement closes public parks and gardens), households and historical buildings' roofs. According to the Municipality records only 24 trees has been eradicated/damaged specifically by strong winds since 2008. Generally speaking, an increase in wind intensity and frequency of strong winds is expected in connection with more frequent extreme meterological events as seen in the summer of 2023 (particularly in occasion of the July 25th storm).

The cost of this measure may vary due to the specific characteristics of the areas to reforest and to the maintenance costs of the tree species. The aim of the project is to ensure that the population of the metropolitan area of Milan benefits from the positive ecosystem impacts of the reforestation program, from health benefits, to mitigation and water retention.
As of the agronomic season 2023/2024, the project has already planted 611.459 plants and trees in the Metropolitan City of Milano: 
-	58,534 were planted in 29 municipalities of the Metropolitan City directly from Forestami thanks to donations from private citizens and companies. 
-	13,100 plants were planted thanks to the SUPERB project (a European project Horizon 2020 by the University of Milan and Parco Nord Milano). The intervention involved, in the last two agronomic seasons (22-23 and 23-24), a total area of 15.22 hectares distributed among 4 Municipalities of the Metropolitan City of Milan;
-	7,800 trees and shrubs were planted, instead, by the National Biodiversity Future Centre (NBFC), in collaboration with the University of Milan-Bicocca, the Polytechnic of Milan and ERSAF - Lombardy Region. The intervention involved 3 Municipalities on a total area of 3.70 hectares in the agronomic season 23-24;
https://forestami.org/
NOTE: the total cost of project is not applicable due to its complexity and variability through time.

Other: All areas - Investment Plan of Milan's Climate City Contract: In the framework of the EU Mission 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, in March 2024 the City of Milan developed its Climate City Contract (CCC), including a Commitments document, an Action Plan and an Investment Plan. The Investment Plan outlines: 1. current state of climate investments 2. quantification of the funds needed to implement the CCC actions, highlighting the gap with investments and funding already acquired 3. cost scenario, with the breakdown of expenditure up to 2030, including those underway. 
The total costs of the planned interventions amount to approximately 6 billion euros investments, of which 2.6 billion by the Municipality of Milan and 3.3 billion by the signatory stakeholders.
The process of costing all actions involved internal dialogues within the Municipality as well as discussions with stakeholders. This multi-stakeholder approach added complexity to the process, as it required alignment of diverse interests and priorities. Furthermore, the emphasis on actions made possible by access to extraordinary EU funding introduced uncertainties regarding the availability and allocation of funds. The resulting portfolio of actions comprises a mix of clearly defined projects, some related to specific areas and sites, and others pertaining to the entire city or network infrastructure. This diversity in scope made the process even more complex, as each action requires a tailored approach. Additionally, enabling actions that support mitigation actions (e.g. citizen engagement) presented by both the Municipality and stakeholders contribute to a further 10% reduction in emissions. 
Priority areas of action include energy requalification of buildings, new infrastructures, tools aimed at promoting soft mobility, depaving, new plantings, reclamation and innovative projects for citizen involvement.

Milan has an efficient drainage network and several projects are in place to further reduce flood risk, namely: Safer Places, MSC, de-sealing projects and implementation of SuDS within the Air and Climate Plan.
Sectors most exposed: 
- Accomodation and food services, wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (tipically located at the ground or underground level can be flooded and their activity forced to stop)
- Sewerage (greatly stressed by the excessive water amount to treat) 
- Waste management and remediation activities (carried out at the ground level or in open spaces can be deeply affected by floods). 
- Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning networks (can be damaged and forced to shut down for some time).
- Health and social work activities (social workers might not be able to reach their users).
- Water supply (potable water network can be damaged and the supply interrupted).
- Agriculture (land can be invaded by streams of water and mud also transporting waste, even toxic waste).
- Administrative and support service activities (work under greater stress, affects their capacity to respond quickly and effectively).

People most exposed:
- Low-income households (live in lower levels, cannot escape their homes)
- Outdoor workers (directly exposed to danger)
- Vulnerable health groups and elderly (cannot be reached by medical assistance, difficulty to move) | Extreme heat: According to the IPCC Fifth ans Sixth Assessment Reports, heatwaves have an higher incidence on cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, especially in elderly people and children. A correlation seems to exist also between gender and mortality rates during heatwaves, in fact during 2003 Paris heatwave, mortality rates were greater among women, whilst a very high rate was discovered among working men, which suggests that the working environment influences vulnerability. Heatwaves also cause higher energy demand for cooling by creating a general discomfort. In the last years this fact forced the energy management agency of Italy (Unareti) to issue a warning to reduce energy consumption in order to prevent blackouts: in 2015, due to the high temperature, a peak in energy demand was registered in the city (1.625 MW), causing several failures in the energy distribution network. The same event occurred in 2021, when a sudden rise in temperatures in mid-June produced a 25% increase in electricity consumption leading to several blackouts.
Vulnerable populations most affected include: 
- Elderly/children/vulnerable health groups (more fragile and affected by heath connected diseases)
- Outdoor workers (directly exposed to heath stress)
- Frontline workers (more exposed to heath stress, e.g. armed forces, firefighters, and other security workers)
- Low income households (cannot afford air conditioning and quality home insulation, cannot leave the city).
Sectors most exposed:
- Agriculture (lack of water, crops suffering from high temperatures)
- Electricity, gas, steam, air conditioning supply (risk of blackouts)

 | Heavy precipitation: There are several negative effects of heavy rainfall: one of the most obvious ones is the fact that heavy rainfall, which is becoming increasingly intense due to climate change, not only contributes to flooding of watercourses but also creates widespread flooding in urban areas as drainage systems are designed for shorter return period. 
Heavy rainfall damages house cellars, underground car parks and mobility infrastructures such as road gallery and subways. Another effect of intense rain is on the use of the different transportation means: when it rains, the use of private cars increases, filling the streets and increasing the vulnerability of the city to floods. Indeed, infrastructures are one of the most sensitive elements when exposed to floods and, considering that vehicle circulation slows down, emergency services are affected. | Infectious disease: According to the data provided by the SSN (National Health Service), in Milan's region (Lombardy) have been reported 225 cases of malaria (average per year between 2013 and 2017), 1 case of Chikungunya (2018), 13 cases of Dengue (2018) and a single case in the whole national territory of Zika (2018). All these diseases are related to mosquitos, which are expected to grow in number due to the rising of temperatures, therefore it is possible that the future reported number of cases per year is going to increase. In August 2023, a dengue outbreak occurred in a village in the Lombardy region. This event marked the largest confirmed cluster of locally transmitted dengue in Lombardy, leading to the implementation of vector control measures and intensive screening efforts. Due to Italian Healthcare system, the diseases are preventable, curable or at least the symptoms can be treated until the spontaneous healing, therefore the consequences of the hazard are not severe. Despite all, it is crucial to be aware that Milan is moving towards a tropicalization of the climate. Thus, although risk level remains low, biological hazards need to be kept under control in order to contain future risks. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: During the summers of 2022 and 2023 the climate change effects have shown themselves clearly, causing an increase in extreme weather events such as storms, hailstorm, and even tornadoes triggered by very high temperatures and high humidity rates. The weather, at least in the Po basin area (Padana valley), is moving towards a tropical model. Storms and hailstorms seriously wound and even impact on people's safety and exposed sectors such as agriculture (damage crops, trees) and mobility (cars, roads and railroads). | Extreme wind: Even though wind intensity is perceived as higher, ARPA's data regarding Milan is not old enough to make relevant climatic analysis or benchmarking, in fact, wind monitoring stations were installed between 2012 and 2014 in Brera and Lambrate's stations (respectively describing the city center and the suburbs). Data collected by those stations shows that wind intensity actually increased in average 1 m/s in Brera, with a frequency increase of six seasonal events over the 95th percentile (calculated on the wind intensity recorded in Brera between 01/01/2015 and 31/12/2018). Data also shows that the average wind intensity in Lambrate didn't change, while the severe wind events frequency actually decreased in the last five years, even though the frequency change was too small to be considered relevant: available data is not enough to make assumptions about wind in relation to climate change, but it could suggest that the wind intensity did not actually change and the change in Brera could have been caused by morphological factors. During the past three years, some episodes of strong wind happened, causing damages to trees (in this case, the municipal governement closes public parks and gardens), households and historical buildings' roofs. According to the Municipality records only 24 trees has been eradicated/damaged specifically by strong winds since 2008. Generally speaking, an increase in wind intensity and frequency of strong winds is expected in connection with more frequent extreme meterological events as seen in the summer of 2023 (particularly in occasion of the July 25th storm).
project_info: Other: Energy poverty - Milan's Plan Against Energy Poverty and Precariousness \'Towards a Common Energy Well-Being\': Following the energy and cost of living crises, Milan has been registering an increase in the number of citizens in energy poverty condition but also of those experiencing temporary difficulties in addressing energy costs (energy precariousness). The Municipality has developed a plan to tackle energy vulnerability titled \'Towards a Common Energy Wellbeing\', aiming to provide relief to situations of poverty as well as to mitigate the risk factors aggravating insecurity. The Plan consists of four key actions: 1. Creation of a Municipal Observatory on Energy Wellbeing 2. Systematization, remodulation and provision of contributions for energy-vulnerable citizens 3. Reshaping of the Energy HelpDesk to address people in conditions of energy vulnerability 4. Creation of a framework of actions and stakeholder engagement. Each action builds on past experiences gained by the Municipality and local stakeholders, especially with the One Stop Shop and the social services provided to vulnerable citizens, and aims to enhance their strengths and address critical issues. To ensure continuity of the actions and engage local stakeholders, new approaches and human and financial resources are required.\nhttps://www.comune.milano.it/aree-tematiche/ambiente/energia/piano-per-il-contrasto-alla-poverta-e-precarieta-energetiche

climate_hazard: Infectious disease: The tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), capable of carrying viruses responsible for diseases like dengue fever, chikungunya, and zika, has been spreading in temperate regions. In Paris, the tiger mosquito was observed in 2015, leading to mosquito control operations. From 2016, reinforced entomological surveillance was implemented. The tiger mosquito became established in Paris by the end of 2018, but no cases of indigenous arbovirosis were reported due to low vector population concentrated in a single district on the outskirts of Paris.The common mosquito Culex sp., a potential vector of the West Nile virus, is already present in Paris, but the virus is not circulating there. However, the risk of its presence could increase due to climate change and other factors. Preventive actions, supervised by the Regional Health Agency (ARS), aim to monitor and control mosquito populations and limit the risk. The city has an expert entomologist responsible for coordinating surveillance and vector control, communicating with city employees and the public about mosquito control.The incidence of Lyme borreliosis in Île-de-France is relatively low compared to other French regions. Still, there is a risk of expansion in Paris due to climatic changes, like milder winters and hot, dry summers, which favor the northward movement of ticks, as well as the increase in nature in cities, creating a suitable environment for tick presence.Climate change also impacts public health directly, causing respiratory and cardiovascular diseases and premature deaths due to degraded air quality. The loss of biodiversity may lead to the spread of epidemics and pandemics like COVID-19. The presence of tiger mosquitoes and allergies is also increasing in the city. | Urban flooding: The increasing impermeability of the soil, the elimination of natural drainage, and the decline of vegetation significantly alter the natural water cycle. At the city scale, rainwater, unable to infiltrate, joins the wastewater, increasing health risks for the population. Certain heavy rain episodes saturate the sewer system and wastewater treatment plants, causing floods and discharge of polluted water into the Seine.The storm on August 16, 2022, caused localized flooding, including in certain metro stations.https://www.paris.fr/pages/comment-se-preparer-aux-risques-d-inondations-7276Floods can cause considerable damage to buildings, roads, bridges, and public infrastructure. Water can damage foundations, electrical systems, transportation systems, and other essential elements of urban infrastructure. Floods can disrupt essential services such as potable water supply, sanitation systems, electricity, and telecommunications. Distribution networks can be damaged, leading to service outages and difficulties for residents and businesses. Economic impacts are possible: businesses may incur material and financial losses due to damages to buildings, stocks, and equipment.Paris possesses a rich cultural heritage, and floods can damage historical sites, monuments, museums, and archives. Such damages can have lasting consequences for the preservation of the city's cultural heritage.In response to these impacts, local authorities implement flood prevention measures, such as building dams, creating flood expansion zones, and improving drainage systems. Additionally, emergency plans and early warning systems are in place to alert residents of flood risks and facilitate evacuation when necessary. | Drought: Authorities currently manage drought issues well due to the relatively low intensity of the phenomena in the region. However, studies indicate that droughts will become more frequent and intense in the future (medium and long term). By 2050, the Seine flow could decrease by at least 25%, and by 2080, it could decrease by 30%. This will also lead to a relative decrease in underground water resources and water pollution due to higher pollutant concentrations, potentially resulting in increased water use pressures and more frequent restrictions. Meteorological drought, characterized by prolonged precipitation deficits compared to seasonal norms, has various causes, including periods without rain leading to temporary droughts, low precipitation levels between September and March hindering groundwater replenishment, and high temperatures exacerbating drought episodes through increased water evaporation and plant evapotranspiration. Human practices, such as overexploitation of water resources from rivers and groundwater, also contribute to drought occurrences.Prolonged drought can have consequences on the watercourses of the Seine-Normandy basin, leading to dried-up rivers reaching their lowest level (low flow) typically at the end of summer. Urban systems may be affected, resulting in tensions on non-potable water networks, reduced soil water infiltration (leading to floods and inundations), decreased potable water production, and potential risks to fauna and flora. In the summer of 2020, restrictions were imposed in Paris and its surroundings, and Eau de Paris had to reduce withdrawals from the Yonne and Seine-et-Marne sources for drinking water production, compensating through other supply points. On August 2, 2022, Paris issued a drought vigilance alert. This marks the first level of drought alert, urging individuals and professionals to conserve water (with 4 levels of drought severity: vigilance, alert, reinforced alert, and crisis). When drought is confirmed, municipal services take measures to moderate water consumption: watering of parks and green spaces is done outside the hottest hours of the day to reduce water evaporation, floor and equipment washing is limited, and some ornamental fountains in closed circuits are closed. | Biodiversity loss: Nearly 2,800 wild species, both animals (dragonflies, ladybugs, crayfish, eels, pikes, frogs, newts, peregrine falcons, tawny owls, foxes, martens, red squirrels, hedgehogs, and 11 species of bats) and plants (orchids, ferns, mosses, as well as cultivated plants and trees), have been observed in Paris in recent years (observations between 2010 and 2020). The City has 500 parks and gardens, 200,000 avenue trees, the Seine, and canals.This regional biodiversity is present but very fragile and mostly declining (due to multiple pressures), and Paris has lost 73% of its sparrows between 2003 and 2016 due to intensive agriculture, habitat fragmentation, lack of breeding sites, and soil artificialization. Climate change is one of the five pressure factors on biodiversity and will lead to a hindrance to migration due to the speed of change, a trend towards homogenization of fauna and flora, alteration of supporting habitats, an increase in diseases, and the development of invasive species.Biodiversity provides numerous ecosystem services and is essential in Paris as it mitigates the effects of urban heat islands, improves the living environment, stormwater management, and soil preservation, and contributes to flood regulation and reduces potential damage to buildings and infrastructure. Biodiversity loss, among other consequences, favors the emergence of new diseases, such as the tiger mosquito, whose development is linked to rising temperatures.The Paris Biodiversity Plan for 2018-2024 sets short-term objectives, such as creating 20 biodiversity spaces by 2020 or demineralizing 35% of the territory with vegetated permeable surfaces by 2024. However, there is no long-term strategic scenario for the territory, and it is challenging to assess long-term developments. The City plans to establish ecological corridors to facilitate the movement of animal and plant species through green and blue corridors, complemented by brown and black corridors. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): In Paris, fires are generally associated with specific weather conditions that promote the spread of fire. Although Paris is not as prone to forest fires as some regions, urban fires can still occur in buildings, outdoor spaces, and public areas. These incidents can be caused by high temperatures and prolonged periods of heat and heatwaves, leading to dry vegetation and combustible materials. Strong winds can rapidly exacerbate the fire's spread from one building to another and can make firefighting challenging for firefighters. Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning can trigger fires when they strike areas where vegetation or buildings are particularly dry. | Heat stress: Thermal stress refers to the impact of extreme weather conditions, particularly heat, on the human body. When temperatures increase significantly, it can have considerable effects on the health and well-being of the population. Thermal stress increases health risks. During heatwaves, Parisian healthcare services may experience a significant rise in emergency room visits and hospitalizations related to heat-related health issues, putting additional pressure on healthcare professionals.Intense heat periods can worsen air pollution in Paris. High temperatures and stable weather conditions promote the formation of pollutants, leading to deteriorating air quality, which can have adverse effects on residents' respiratory health.It can also cause discomfort and disrupt daily life, especially for poorly insulated or non-insulated buildings that become stifling or uninhabitable. Outdoor activities may be limited or disrupted, and overcrowded public transportation can become even more uncomfortable.There can also be a rebound effect due to the use of air conditioning. The release of hot air from air conditioners exacerbates the urban heat island effect. | Storm: A few days before the year 2000, the Lothar storm hit France, with winds reaching over 170 km/h in Saint-Brieuc (Côtes-d'Armor) and Solenzara (Corsica) (173 km/h at 22:00). On December 26th, gusts of 169 km/h were recorded in the capital. Thirty people lost their lives in these events, with extensive damage.Storms can make travel difficult or even impossible, and falling objects can occur due to the high density of buildings (relay antennas). Roads become dangerous and impassable (reduced visibility, challenging vehicle control), and accidents can happen quickly. Severe weather conditions such as storms can affect the quality of tap water, so it is necessary to ensure its potability before using it for consumption.In case of material damage or any other harm related to weather conditions, individuals or businesses can contact Météo France to obtain a weather certificate (or insurance certificate):http://services.meteofrance.com/e-boutique/attestations-certificats/certificat-intemperie-detail.htmlRecognized by insurance companies, this paid document details the specific weather conditions that occurred on a particular day, highlighting the remarkable events that happened and could have caused damage, harm, an incident, or an accident. Natural disaster decrees are issued by the government at the request of the City. | Extreme wind: Transportation networks (rail, traffic, river transport) could be damaged or disrupted due to falling objects, power outage for rail, etc. In Paris, energy networks are mainly underground, but outside Paris, energy networks could be damaged by the wind, causing supply disruptions. Buildings, private properties, public heritage, gardens, and woods could also be damaged. If there are significant damages, there can be economic consequences due to the overall cost of repairs.In Paris, due to the urban environment, strong winds can damage roofs, leading to tile falls or chimney collapses. Advertising panels can also be carried away by gusts of wind, and tree branches can be uprooted. A wind is considered dangerous when its speed reaches or exceeds 80 km/h. It is recommended to seek shelter inside a building and not under a tree, and support measures are provided in schools. In the event of strong winds or heavy rain, the City may take the following measures:• Prohibit public access to all Parisian green spaces, including cemeteries.• Disseminate messages calling for caution to the population through the City of Paris website, variable message boards (PMVs), and social media platforms. | Heavy precipitation: Managing Risks of Intense Rainfall: Enhancing Resilience and InfrastructureHeavy rains, caused by soil sealing, can overwhelm the drainage system and flood roads or basements, making pedestrian and vehicular traffic difficult. They can also disrupt certain railway lines in Île-de-France and the Parisian metro. In August 2022, torrential rains hit the city. The weather station at the Eiffel Tower recorded gusts of wind reaching up to 104 km/h. Within less than an hour, 26 mm of rain fell, according to the Montsouris weather station. | Extreme heat: During heatwaves, the population in Paris, including vulnerable groups like homeless people, the elderly, outdoor workers, and children, is directly impacted in various settings. The risks associated with heatwaves include public health issues, economic impacts, sanitary concerns, increasing water demand, and water stress. Additionally, certain facilities face challenges, such as water eutrophication, degradation of electric or telecommunication facilities, and power cuts due to the fragility of the electric network. Biodiversity in gardens and woods may also be affected.The constant rise in temperature in Paris will result in extreme heat, with temperatures increasing by an average of 2°C. This can have significant consequences for watercourses, impacting the biological and chemical quality of the water, including higher concentrations of pollutants and increased turbidity. The urban vegetation will experience the urban heat island effect, and evapotranspiration from vegetation and soils will become limited.Notably, the heatwave of 2003 caused around 15,000 excess deaths in France, including nearly 1,100 in Paris. Subsequent heatwaves in June 2017 and 2022 also had severe impacts, with 580 additional deaths in 2017 and 22 days above 30°C in 2022 in Paris. The summer 2022 report by Santé Publique France recorded a 21% increase in excess mortality in the Île-de-France region from July 11 to July 21, with 2,082 visits to emergency rooms and 285 SOS Médecins interventions due to extreme heat.When the average of maximum and minimum temperatures over 3 days exceeds the alert thresholds, the department is considered to be experiencing a heatwave for the entire period of exceedance. Paris has established 4 levels of the Heatwave Plan based on Météo France's vigilance levels. These plans aim to address risks for the health of Parisians and the city identified in the MIE \'Paris à 50°C\' report published in 2023. Risks include heatstroke, dehydration, respiratory and cardiac issues, and deteriorating air quality. Vulnerable and less affluent individuals may face amplified socio-economic inequalities, especially in non-insulated housing, and have difficulty accessing cool areas during extreme heat. The mission also focuses on energy risks related to increased demand and security risks, such as high fire risks and overload of medical centers. | River flooding: During a major flood, similar to the one in 1910, power cuts would affect electricity networks and have widespread consequences on various infrastructures, especially transportation. Heating, sanitation, and waste collection services would also be impacted. Although telecommunication, gas, and water networks are relatively less vulnerable, buildings would still be affected.In the Île-de-France region, approximately 450,000 homes, 100,000 establishments, and 830,000 people are at risk of exposure to a centennial flood (Institut Paris Région, 2018). About 90% of flood-prone zones are urbanized, and around 60% of housing surfaces in the region face high to very high hazard levels, with submersion heights exceeding 1 meter. Buildings' vulnerability is linked to factors like disruptions in energy supply (excluding gas), resulting in heating issues, material damage (e.g., flooded basements), and potential structural destabilization.In recent years, Paris experienced 2 major floods in 2016 (the Seine reached 6.10 meters) and in 2018 (5.84 meters), leading to nearly 2 weeks of flood warnings, caused by rainwater accumulation on saturated and impermeable soils (swollen watercourses). The consequences of such floods in a densely populated city are significant, including flooding of metro stations and disruptions to underground transport (e.g., RER C's central section remained closed for weeks after the 2016 flood). The District Heating Company of Paris which uses steam produced with Seine water, is also sensitive to flooding (shutdown of 9 steam sections during the 2016 flood, leaving almost 10,000 homes without hot water). Additionally, over 107,000 homes in Paris are situated in flood-prone areas, and the Seine's banks host important activities, such as the Louvre Museum, Ministries of Economy and Finance, Gare d'Austerlitz, and Georges Pompidou Hospital. Such a flood would cause considerable damage to cultural heritage, requiring extensive drying and restoration efforts for artwork, collections, archives, and museum reserves. Surface infrastructure like riverbanks, quays, bridges, and historic foundations would also weaken, leading to structural instability and short-term negative impacts on tourism. In economic terms, a centennial flood like the 1910 event could result in losses of up to 60 billion euros, with 430,000 jobs directly at risk. | Water stress: Hydric stress occurs when water demand exceeds available resources in Paris. Despite stable water consumption and diverse supply sources, climate change's effects raise concerns about water shortages beyond 2050. Parisians may face water usage restrictions during significant droughts, leading to rationing and reduced water consumption. Hydrological drought is expected to intensify in the Seine basin, with projected river flow reductions between 10% and 30% by the end of the century. Reduced water quantity results in higher pollutant concentrations, endangering the aquatic ecosystem. Tensions may arise from increased water needs and scarcity, impacting urban cooling, energy, and agricultural demands. Significant hydric stress could threaten Parisian flora, fauna, and soil's infiltration capacity, leading to floods or landslides.Water management impacts informations publicly available at:https://www.apc-paris.com/article-rubrique/secheresse-a-paris#:~:text=La%20s%C3%A9cheresse%20hydrologique%20devrait%20elle,%C3%A9tiage%20(minimums)%20encore%20davantagehttps://www.apc-paris.com/actualite/changement-climatique-a-paris-quels-impacts-sur-leauhttps://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2023/02/22/note-d-enjeu-resilience-de-paris-au-risque-de-rarefaction-de-l-eau-n9sz.pdf | Snow and ice: see winter emergency plan at : https://www.paris.fr/pages/plan-grand-froid-episodes-de-neige-5471#le-plan-grand-froid | Increased water demand: see EDP safety watersupplying plan | Mass movement: Not occuring in Paris | Extreme cold: Not occuring in Paris | Oceanic events: Not occuring in Paris | Soil degradation/erosion: Not occuring in Paris | Loss of green space/green cover: Not occuring in Paris | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Not occuring in Paris | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Not occuring in Paris

Other: Many areas : renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, forestry, energy renovation of buildings, etc. - Carbon cooperative: Paris has made the decision to establish a carbon offset operator as part of its efforts to accelerate the ecological transition. This initiative aims to support individuals, businesses, and local authorities seeking to offset their greenhouse gas emissions by financing environmentally beneficial projects. The operator takes the form of a cooperative, bringing together various stakeholders such as companies, experts, NGOs, and project developers, all working towards the common objective of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. 

To encompass a wide range of sectors, the operator will utilize multiple financing tools including a low-carbon label, energy saving certificates, and crowdfunding. These resources will be directed towards initiatives in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, forestry, energy-efficient building renovations, and more. 

For instance, the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, which aim to be carbon-neutral, attracted 600 000 € of compensation, as Paris 2024 has opted to finance projects in France through the Low Carbon Label.
(https://press.paris2024.org/news/paris-2024-presents-the-results-of-its-actions-to-make-the-games-more-sustainable-36aef-7578a.html) 

In order to match the offsetting required to balance the part of the Parisian footprint currently deemed incompressible by 2050, disposing of a local operator and of local offsetting projects will be a pivotal financial mechanisms.

For more information, see the Cooperative Carbone's website.
(https://coopcarbone-parismetropole.fr/les-projets/)

Urban systems may be affected, resulting in tensions on non-potable water networks, reduced soil water infiltration (leading to floods and inundations), decreased potable water production, and potential risks to fauna and flora. In the summer of 2020, restrictions were imposed in Paris and its surroundings, and Eau de Paris had to reduce withdrawals from the Yonne and Seine-et-Marne sources for drinking water production, compensating through other supply points. On August 2, 2022, Paris issued a drought vigilance alert. This marks the first level of drought alert, urging individuals and professionals to conserve water (with 4 levels of drought severity: vigilance, alert, reinforced alert, and crisis). When drought is confirmed, municipal services take measures to moderate water consumption: watering of parks and green spaces is done outside the hottest hours of the day to reduce water evaporation, floor and equipment washing is limited, and some ornamental fountains in closed circuits are closed. | Biodiversity loss: Nearly 2,800 wild species, both animals (dragonflies, ladybugs, crayfish, eels, pikes, frogs, newts, peregrine falcons, tawny owls, foxes, martens, red squirrels, hedgehogs, and 11 species of bats) and plants (orchids, ferns, mosses, as well as cultivated plants and trees), have been observed in Paris in recent years (observations between 2010 and 2020). The City has 500 parks and gardens, 200,000 avenue trees, the Seine, and canals.This regional biodiversity is present but very fragile and mostly declining (due to multiple pressures), and Paris has lost 73% of its sparrows between 2003 and 2016 due to intensive agriculture, habitat fragmentation, lack of breeding sites, and soil artificialization. Strong winds can rapidly exacerbate the fire's spread from one building to another and can make firefighting challenging for firefighters. Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning can trigger fires when they strike areas where vegetation or buildings are particularly dry. | Heat stress: Thermal stress refers to the impact of extreme weather conditions, particularly heat, on the human body. When temperatures increase significantly, it can have considerable effects on the health and well-being of the population. Thermal stress increases health risks. High temperatures and stable weather conditions promote the formation of pollutants, leading to deteriorating air quality, which can have adverse effects on residents' respiratory health.It can also cause discomfort and disrupt daily life, especially for poorly insulated or non-insulated buildings that become stifling or uninhabitable. Outdoor activities may be limited or disrupted, and overcrowded public transportation can become even more uncomfortable.There can also be a rebound effect due to the use of air conditioning. The release of hot air from air conditioners exacerbates the urban heat island effect. | Storm: A few days before the year 2000, the Lothar storm hit France, with winds reaching over 170 km/h in Saint-Brieuc (Côtes-d'Armor) and Solenzara (Corsica) (173 km/h at 22:00). On December 26th, gusts of 169 km/h were recorded in the capital. Thirty people lost their lives in these events, with extensive damage.Storms can make travel difficult or even impossible, and falling objects can occur due to the high density of buildings (relay antennas). Roads become dangerous and impassable (reduced visibility, challenging vehicle control), and accidents can happen quickly. Buildings, private properties, public heritage, gardens, and woods could also be damaged. If there are significant damages, there can be economic consequences due to the overall cost of repairs.In Paris, due to the urban environment, strong winds can damage roofs, leading to tile falls or chimney collapses. Advertising panels can also be carried away by gusts of wind, and tree branches can be uprooted. A wind is considered dangerous when its speed reaches or exceeds 80 km/h. It is recommended to seek shelter inside a building and not under a tree, and support measures are provided in schools. Hydrological drought is expected to intensify in the Seine basin, with projected river flow reductions between 10% and 30% by the end of the century. Other: Patronage fund - Paris 2050 Fund: The City of Paris benefits from occasional patronage on a project to project basis. The Paris 2024 fund, created for the Olympics, established solid partnerships, potentially interested for patronage opportunity beyond 2024 in order to contribute to the investments needed for the betterment of Paris and its ecological planning in order to become a low carbon and resilient territory.

The Council of Paris therefore approved in October 2024 the principle of creating a patronage fund titled 'Paris 2050'. 
(https://a06-v7.apps.paris.fr/a06/jsp/site/plugins/solr/modules/ods/DoDownload.jsp?id_document=176945&items_per_page=20&sort_name=&sort_order=&terms=dotation%202050&query=dotation%202050)

First and foremost, Paris 2050 will be a distributive and participatory fund, aiming to promote and develop public policies led by the City of Paris and thus finance, in compliance with the City's Ethical Charter for Patronage and Sponsorship, innovative projects pursuing a general interest, particularly in the ecological transition and in the fields of sport, culture, social, education, heritage, and philanthropy. These projects may be implemented by City departments or by any non-profit organization in the Paris region for initiatives supported by the City.

Its governance will be ensured by a Board of Directors comprising three committees composed of four representatives each: a committee representing the City of Paris, a committee of patrons, and a committee of qualified individuals.

The Board of Directors will be assisted by an Investment Committee, which will provide opinions and recommendations on investment policy and may propose studies and expertise. Finally, in order to maintain a certain flexibility of action, the Mayor of Paris will only approve the most structural projects [which will concern only the Parisian community]: projects exceeding one million euros, or an amount lower than requested by at least two members of the City's college of representatives.

The organization and operation of the fund are detailed in the draft statutes annexed to this resolution and will be supplemented in internal regulations to be adopted subsequently by the fund's board of directors.

The Low Emission District, created and coordinated by the Planning Office of the Subsecretariat of Planning and Monitoring of Results of the Secretariat of Finance and Planning, is aligned with the Municipal Decree \'Green and Healthy Streets\' (Decree Rio no. 46.081/2019) and with the Sustainable Development and Climate Action Plan (PDS) of the City of Rio. In 2021 the District was established by Complementary Law No. 229/2021. In the City's Strategic Plan for the years between 2021 and 2024, the Low Emission District-DBE is established as one of the strategic goals. As provided for in Complementary Law No. 229/2021, the DBE was regulated by Rio Decree No. 51047/2022. The District, with an area of ​​2.34 km², is located in the Administrative Region of the Center of Rio de Janeiro, which includes the neighborhoods of Centro and Lapa, which together has a population of approximately 32,758 residents, according to the 2012 sense. The floating population in the area must still be considered. The DBE delimitation considers an area with strong centrality, high concentration of services, commerce and companies, intense flow of pedestrians and vehicles. Also noteworthy in this area are factors such as: the existence of non-polluting modes of transport, such as VLT and Metro, its location between two transport hubs (Central do Brasil and Praça Quinze), and the existence of historic areas and several pedestrian routes with high traffic, where the benefits of the project can reach a large number of people. In this way, the project and its implementation have great potential to bring both environmental and socio-economic benefits, and could be a great example that encourages new solutions to promote resilience and urban quality in the center, generating a healthier urban environment for people who live in or transit through the region. Central, and indirect benefits such as reducing health problems related to air pollution, increasing occupancy in the Central area (commercial and residential) and stimulating the clean energy market. To date, Air Quality and GHG monitoring plans, a communication plan, have been developed, some sections of cycle paths have been implemented, a preliminary study has been prepared for the urban requalification of an avenue in the DBE, and studies are underway to outline transition strategies for zero-emission freight transport.

Land-Use - Mapping of the Municipality's Vegetal Cover within the scope of the Continuous Vegetation Cover Monitoring Program (PMCV)
: The Municipality of Rio de Janeiro, by promoting the extensive alteration of natural spaces and not prioritizing the implementation of open/green spaces, compromises the provision of a range of environmental services, such as the preservation of water resources, maintenance of slope stability, cooling of intra-urban heat and conservation of urban green areas that promote well-being and social interaction. In this context, environmental monitoring activities are increasingly relevant and are extremely important for planning and managing the territory in favor of sustainable cities and the search for environmental justice. Monitoring vegetation cover provides information on the factors that influence the state of conservation, preservation, degradation and environmental recovery of the studied area. It also subsidizes planning and control and assists in the definition of public environmental policies. The Atlantic Forest biome, protected by Law No. 11,428/2006 (Atlantic Forest Law) and by different categories of Conservation Units, is under pressure from the process of expansion of the urban fabric of the city of Rio de Janeiro, becoming increasingly fragmented, presenting an unequal spatial distribution between the neighborhoods of the different planning areas, causing the loss of biodiversity and the population's quality of life. Through the systematic, continuous and broad collection of data relating to the municipality's vegetation cover, the Vegetation Cover Continuous Monitoring Program seeks to generate spatial information and environmental indices that allow the creation of a spatio-temporal database that highlights changes related to the city's vegetation cover. The generated database allows municipal bodies to have a safe and accurate management tool for taking decisions in the areas of inspection, environmental licensing, biodiversity conservation, environmental restoration and adaptation to climate change. The database containing the cadastral values ​​of each mapped physiognomy on a detailed scale is available from a Web GIS that can be consulted at https://www.data.rio/app/sig-floresta. Vegetation cover mapping provides support for achieving activities and goals related to the city's mitigation and adaptation to extreme climate events, such as: Classification of new green areas as protected areas; Maintenance and improvement of a database with updated information on environmental action and recovery programs in the city of Rio de Janeiro; Diagnosis of priority areas for reforestation and; Control of the factors that drive the advancement of the urban network over the Atlantic Forest. PMCV guidelines are i) Use of geotechnologies to support data acquisition and processing; ii) Construction of indicators and indices to support planning and management of vegetation cover; iii) Mapping and Classification of the municipality’s green areas according to their phytophysiognomies; iv) Periodic identification of the species composition and plant structure of the communities and ecosystems present in the municipality; v) Spatio-temporal analysis of green areas to better understand the process of land use and occupation and; vi) Monitoring public policies for protection, conservation, restoration and compensation related to vegetation cover. Some of the PMCV's specific objectives are: i) Systematize information regarding the characteristics of the city's vegetation cover; ii) Monitor the dynamics of landscape transformation in terms of the city's vegetation cover and; iii) Subsidize government mitigation and adaptation actions in the city related to maintaining the ecological balance of ecosystems associated with the Atlantic Forest Biome in the City. Finally, the products of PMCV are related to mapping, classification, quantification, spatial and temporal assessment, and recording and dissemination of data relating to the municipality's vegetation cover. These products allow the application of a series of actions such as defining priority areas for conservation and recovery of the Atlantic Forest; proposal to implement green corridors; carrying out tree inventory studies; estimation of carbon stocks in Rio's ecosystems; land use and occupation planning and the dynamics of landscape transformation; calculation of green area indices (m2/inhabitant) in different municipal areas; preparation of studies to create Conservation Units and management plans for these territories and; spatial analyzes aimed at licensing and environmental inspection.

Nature-Based Solutions - ReflorestaRio Menos Carbono - More forest and biodiversity in the City of Rio de Janeiro. 
: The city of Rio de Janeiro intends to resume its global leadership in the search for environmental sustainability and resilience, following the path of neutrality of carbon emissions and towards a green and inclusive recovery, including promoting the protection of ecosystems and sustainable management of forests, reversing soil degradation, loss of biodiversity, and carrying out adequate management of reforested areas for the formation of green corridors.
Within this perspective, the “ReflorestaRio minus Carbono” program seeks a more green, with our forests contributing to the coolness of the city on the heat islands, contributing to the reduction of landslides and floods, richer in fauna and flora, protecting the waters and providing a better quality of life for Carioca.
Aiming to remodel the program for the next 10 years, in Carbon Neutralization Strategy, follows the proposal for “ReflorestaRio minus Carbon”, proposing to increase the scale of the current reforestation program, so that at the end of the 10-year period, the Secretariat will plant more than 3 million seedlings and recover more than 1,000 hectares (= 10 million m²) of reforestation in the Atlantic Forest biome.
This planting is expected to capture carbon 29,940.9 tCO2e - estimated sequestration for the year 2035, which includes the analysis of the last 20 years of the project, removing atmospheric carbon and mitigating GHG emissions.

project_info: Renewable energy - Decarbonizing energy grid: Decarbonizing Mumbai's energy grid and building energy-efficient and climate resilient infrastructure. The city will work to decarbonize the energy grid, increase proportion of renewable energy and improve climate-resilient buildings in Mumbai. This priority directly aligns with the Paris Agreement. To tackle Mumbai's energy sector emissions, the approach addresses both the supply side - increasing RE- and the demand side - improving energy efficiency (EE). The impact of this action will reduce the overall carbon emissions and heat effects, enabling good health for all residents of the city. Achieving this priority implies increasing the availability of RE mix-energy generation, improving energy efficiency in new and existing infrastructure, promoting green buildings, integrating passive design strategies for thermal comfort in all affordable housing projects and ensuring equity in energy access.
