climate_hazard: Water stress: The drinking water supply situation in the Metropolitan Region is critical. In this region, the effects of a decrease in water availability, due to megadrought and climate change, and a high and growing demand for water for domestic use converge. The current margin between availability and requirements of drinking water is narrow and the minimum ecological flows that should flow through these channels are being compromised. The growth of the city and water demand, together with projections of decreased rainfall and the consequent water availability (e.g., Bozkurt et al., 2018), will only narrow this margin further, further decreasing the levels of water security in this area, which concentrates the largest number of inhabitants in the country. | Urban flooding: Flooding is characterized by physically affecting the infrastructure, generating direct damage and affecting its integrity. Service cuts stand out due to flooding and erosion, dragging of material, with consequences on water quality, network services (electricity, telecommunications) and problems in regional mobility systems. The agri-food sector can be affected by river flooding in floodplains, after intense rains. Considering that the industrial zones of the RM are located in areas prone to flooding due to being in low-lying areas, it is expected that flooding and interruption of the operation of industrial plants will occur. | Loss of green space/green cover: The south-western area of ââthe RM has the highest probability of fires and is the area with the highest risk of loss of greenery in native forests. | Drought: Drought acts over a wide temporal range, stressing water storage systems for human consumption, industrial consumption, irrigation and others. This produces a series of concatenated impacts. Agri-food systems can be affected by scarcity and large-scale desertification processes. The electricity supply may also suffer consequences, since the drought acts on a broader spatial scale than just the RM. In this way, the supply of energy from hydroelectric plants can be reduced and affect the functioning of multiple infrastructures, services and productive sectors. Drought and the consequent water shortage can trigger socio-environmental conflicts around water rights and the use of the resource. The above directly affects the productive sectors that depend on the resource (industry, mining, agriculture). The Impacts of the water situation, within the framework of the drought that affects the south-central area of ââChile, has led the state to seek mechanisms in its regulation and prioritization. Thus, it is possible to observe an accelerated growth of water scarcity decrees. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Forest fires have impacts on various time scales. In the long term, they can affect the water supply as a result of soil erosion and loss of the vegetative layer. This can cause sedimentation of reservoirs for human consumption and irrigation, generating shortages. By themselves, or in combination with prolonged droughts, they can trigger large-scale desertification processes, affecting the productivity of agri-food systems, with indirect impacts on trade and supply. Large fires, which have increased in recent years in the RM, generate fragmentation of protected natural areas of high value for biodiversity and provision of ecosystem services. On the other hand, in the short term, fires can affect network services (electricity, telecommunications), tourism, airports and generate an overload in emergency services. In the case of forest fires in the RM, it is possible to see that CONAF data shows that 99% are due to human causes. | Mass movement: Mass removal tends to have localized impacts. This threat is related to extreme rain events at altitude and flooding as a result of the same. Similar to the previous threat, mass removal can affect drinking water supply services by contaminating the supply with sediment overload. Transportation and mobility systems may be affected by specific outages, affecting the movement of goods and people and general accessibility. The above can have indirect impacts on the provision of emergency services (health, firefighters, police). | Extreme heat: The heat wave is a regional-scale threat that can produce immediate and cumulative impacts over time. Regarding immediate impacts, the heat wave produces an increase in energy demand due to the use of air conditioning and/or refrigeration systems. The above can cause network overload and service interruption with a series of concatenated impacts on sectors and systems that depend on electrical energy to function. In turn, the heat wave can affect crops, disrupting the agri-food value chain. Regarding the cumulative effects, the role that increasing temperatures play in regional ecosystems has already been discussed, which are key in the provision of ecosystem services, many of them linked to adaptation to climate change, and conservation of biodiversity.
project_info: Public and green spaces - Pocket Forests Program - stage 1 and 2: The Pocket Forests program aims to contribute to the reforestation of the RMS to improve the conditions of the ecosystem and reduce the negative externalities of urbanization, including environmental pollution, urban heat islands and extreme heat, as an effect of climate change. For the above, the program contemplates the design and execution of 33 pocket forests (high-density urban forests) with the miyawaki technique that are conceived as climate refuges. The program has 3 components: 1) Implementation of forests, with citizen participation, maintenance for two years and monitoring of environmental variables such as humidity, temperature, capture of particulate matter and Co2, noise, etc., through sensors; 2) Forest Management with a Governance Model for each neighborhood where the forests are installed, forming teams of managers in order to leave installed competencies that contribute to the sustainability of the initiative; 3) Environmental education and citizen participation based on strategies that include activities at an informative, consultative, binding and co-management level, in addition to providing basic environmental knowledge and practical tools for the care and protection of species, in order to leave competencies installed in the users and direct and indirect beneficiaries of the investment. In this first stage, the implementation of 33 pocket forests in 33 communes of the 52 that the Metropolitan Region has, will be financed, for a total amount of MM$ 4,687 (for 33 forests in stage 1). For the second stage, it is intended to seek financing to implement 9 pocket forests, for an amount of MM$1,300.

project_info: Water management - Modular wetland for the treatment of household gray water and its reuse in the maintenance of green spaces and other applications: The Modular Wetland for gray water is a modular constructed wetland system that helps family groups have a new source of water, to mitigate the impact on the use of drinking water in the maintenance of green spaces, both home and community. This automated system has a nature-based solution to treat and reuse gray water generated from washing machines with high water consumption, and other possible sources within the home. Unlike conventional treatment plants found on the market, this system is modular, easy to use, ergonomic, has a potential lower cost than conventional treatment systems for homes, and is environmentally friendly, since it imitates the purification function and ecosystem of natural wetlands.

project_info: Health systems and services - Code Red: Extreme Heat and High Temperatures Protocol: The Code Red is a protocol that seeks to install and make visible the risk of extreme heat both for citizens and in public services that are called to generate actions to confront it. The first version was launched on December 14, 2022 and will be updated year after year to make it increasingly robust. This is the result of the work carried out with the Extreme Heat task force in which institutions both at the regional and central levels participate: Metropolitan Regional Government of Santiago, Presidential Delegation, Regional Directorate of ONEMI, Meteorological Directorate of Chile, Regional Ministerial Secretariat of Health, Regional Ministerial Secretariat of Social Development and Family, Regional Ministerial Secretariat of Labor and Social Welfare and Regional Ministerial Secretariat of Education. Coverage: The protocol extends to the entire Metropolitan Region. Activation of the protocol alerts is carried out based on the following table: · Green Alert - Early Preventive: it will be activated when the predicted temperature is equal to or greater than 33°C. · Yellow Alert: it will be activated when the predicted temperature is equal to or greater than 34°C. · Red Alert: it will be activated when the predicted temperature is equal to or greater than 35°. activate its associated networks.The code is associated with risk communication through campaigns on social networks and the press with the following recommendations:• Drink plenty of water.• Eat foods such as fruits and vegetables.• Wear a hat or cap, UV glasses and breathable clothing.• Do not expose yourself to the sun, and if you do, use appropriate sunscreen.• Do not drink alcohol.• Take a shower with cold water.• Put cold cloths on your neck and forearms.• Keep your home colder than the outside by prioritizing ventilation. crossed before A/C. • Avoid physical activity between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. Currently the cost has not been sized, so far only management measures are applied without resources for projects.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Philadelphia is an old city with old infrastructure and climate change is amplifying existing vulnerabilities. As is the case elsewhere, existing vulnerable communities tend to be low-income, people with minority status, immigrants, indigenous populations, those with existing health conditions, and the young and elderly. Inland flooding (also called urban flooding, pluvial flooding, or flash flooding) is exacerbated by Philadelphia's history of capping over the rivers and creeks to incorporate them into the drainage network. These underground creeks are now part of the stormwater drainage system which is undersized and challenged to maintain levels of service due to the dense urban development that increases impervious surfaces and a climate that includes intense convective storms. Climate projections and observations indicate that precipitation events will become more intense in a changing climate, particularly the most extreme storms. Global climate model projections downscaled for Philadelphia indicate that the average annual precipitation will increase from 44 inches to 49 inches under a moderate emissions scenario RCP45 and to nearly 50 inches under a high emissions scenario RCP85 by the end of the century. Given that extreme storms are increasing in intensity any neighborhood and many sectors are vulnerable to inland flooding when the amount of rain falling in one location cannot be accommodated by the drainage network which can cause localized flooding of streets and properties and basement backups. Although inland flooding is experienced across the city, specific neighborhood—and the vulnerable populations that reside within them—including Northern Liberties, Germantown, South Philadelphia and businesses along Columbus Boulevard are at greater risk. Urban flooding and a lack of capacity in a stormwater system can lead to basement backups which can expose residents to pathogens from diluted sewer water. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise will increase flooding risk along Philadelphia's tidal rivers, which includes the entire coast of the Delaware River and tidal tributaries (e.g. Darby-Cobbs creek and Schuylkill river). Coastal flooding in Philadelphia threatens communities, waterfront industry and important municipal assets along the coast, including the port, Navy Yard, wastewater and drinking water treatment plants and the Philadelphia International Airport. There are also acute but particularly damaging extreme events with storm surge that will reach farther inland and have greater flood depths as sea levels rise. Using a scenario of 4 feet of sea level rise, more than 30 city-owned facilities would be highly or moderately vulnerable to coastal flooding. Future scenarios that include storm surge would place hundreds more facilities at risk. The long-term, chronic flooding associated with sea level rise is caused by higher baseline water levels that change flood frequencies and permanently inundate new parts of the city. Models of future storm surge and sea level rise for Philadelphia, demonstrate the risk for flooding in parts of the city that have not experienced it in the past. Residents in these communities may be less prepared for coastal flooding as they were not previously exposed to storm surge. Coastal floods can devastate low-lying communities and the vulnerable populations that reside there. The Eastwick neighborhood, a marginalized/minority community that has suffered from a history of environmental injustices, is exposed to coastal flooding as well as a host of other environmental hazards, such as toxins from a superfund sites. Their risk is increasing due to climate change, especially because of the compounding impact of coastal and riverine flooding. In addition to surface flooding, sea level rise also threatens Philadelphia's water quality and source water supply. If sea levels rise high enough, the salt front (the zone where saline water from the ocean meets freshwater from the river) could move far enough north to reach the Baxter Drinking Water Treatment plant intake, threatening the drinking water supply for Philadelphia. Water quality issues and flood events also put Philadelphia's natural resources and native species at risk, such as Philadelphia's freshwater tidal wetlands and sensitive fish populations. | Extreme heat: Current science projects the number of days over 95°F will increase from fewer than 5 annually to nearly 30 days per year by 2100 under a moderate emissions scenario (RCP4.5) and over 65 days under a high emissions scenario (RCP8.5). This will result in higher incidents of heat health events (eg. heat stroke) for residents and visitors and could impact infrastructure and municipal services. The urban heat island effect exacerbates heat issues in the city and disproportionately impacts vulnerable populations exposing equity issues. Average surface temperature data shows some neighborhoods in Philly can be up to 29°F hotter than others, with hotter neighborhoods tending to have more low-income residents and residents of color. A 2025 heat vulnerability survey provided new insights into extreme heat impacts. Results indicate that seniors, a particularly vulnerable population, had less tree cover near their homes and fewer of them had access to air conditioning compared to non-seniors. Nearly half of respondents said they have AC, but it is too expensive to operate or is unreliable. When asked if residents used their AC even if it meant sacrificing food or other essential items, 31% answered yes. Nearly half of respondents said they had an underlying health condition that increased their vulnerability to heat and 15% said they or a family member had been hospitalized due to heat-related illness. \nThe City developed a Heat Vulnerability Index to identify residents most at-risk from high heat, looking at the overlap between census tracts that have the highest heat exposure and social sensitivity using socio-demographic and health indicators. At-risk health groups, including the elderly, low-income populations, and children, will face greater risks. Increased temperatures also worsen air quality, impacting those with respiratory diseases like asthma. Philadelphia's childhood asthma rate is already three times higher than the national average. Over 24% of Philadelphia's population lives below the poverty line, more than 12% of the population is aged 65 years or older, and seven 7% is under 5. Extreme heat can also affect city services and infrastructure. City departments indicated that hotter days may require construction activities (eg, street paving and repairs) to shift to night hours, which may require longer curing times. Source water quality could degrade and drinking water treatment processes could also be impacted by increasing temperatures. | River flooding: Philadelphia sits towards the bottom of the 12,800 square mile Delaware watershed so riverine flooding is serious threat to the City. Even if it hasn't rained in Philadelphia, riverine flooding can occur if there are intense precipitation events in other parts of the watershed. Climate projections and observations indicate that precipitation events will become more intense, particularly the most extreme storms. Downscaled climate models for Philadelphia indicate that the average annual precipitation will increase from ~44 inches to 49-50 inches under a moderate (RCP4.5) and high (RCP8.5) emissions scenario by the end of the century. \nGiven that extreme storms are increasing in intensity, any low-lying neighborhood along the banks of Philadelphia's rivers or creeks is vulnerable to riverine flooding, but some of Philadelphia's most marginalized communities are located in the floodplain. One example is Eastwick, a low-income primarily Black environmental justice community that has experienced historic and systemic discrimination. Eastwick is extremely vulnerable to riverine flooding, and experienced catastrophic flooding several times in the past 25 years, including Hurricane Floyd in 1999, an unnamed storm in 2004, Hurricane Irene in 2011 and tropical storm Isaias in 2020. In 2021, remnants from Hurricane Ida caused extensive riverine flooding in Philadelphia particularly in the Manayunk neighborhood and center city adjacent to the Schuylkill river. Some residents had to be evacuated, major roadways were flooded disrupting traffic and damaging infrastructure, and drinking water infrastructure was damaged and required capital investments to rebuild. An assessment of unmet needs estimated that damage from Ida were $1.3 billion. Thirteen city-owned historic properties are also within the current 100-year floodplain (areas with a 1% chance of flooding in any given year). Seasonal projections indicate significant increases in winter precipitation through the 21st century. This will stress Philadelphia's road and transit networks many of which date back more than a century, as well as the City's municipal budget to deal with increased storms. Vulnerable populations often do not have flood insurance, e.g., low-income residents and/or renters who may not know their flood risk and therefore have a higher risk of having their lives disrupted and a lack of funds to repair their homes after riverine flooding.
project_info: Other: Flood mitigation for the Eastwick neighborhood, an environmental justice community - Eastwick Place-Based Resilience Strategy: Eastwick is an environmental justice community in Southwest Philadelphia that is vulnerable to multiple sources of flooding, including riverine (historically the source of catastrophic flooding), tidal flooding, and coastal storm surge. With sea level rise, nuisance flooding may also occur in parts of Eastwick. A multi-pronged flood resilience strategy is needed to holistically address current and future flood risk in Eastwick. Residents have been waiting a long time for action to address flooding. Over the years, many partners have come developed various ideas and concepts on how to mitigate flooding in Eastwick. These ideas are in different phases of feasibility and include options like a levee on Cobbs Creek, nature-based solutions, voluntary buyouts, a land swap/relocation plan, and reconstruction of current homes on higher foundations.\nThe Office of Sustainability (OOS) has received funding through FEMA's Flood Mitigation Assistance Program to develop a community driven Flood Resilience Strategy. The Flood Resilience Strategy aims to bring these ideas and partners into one dedicated planning process with Eastwick residents steering decision making on how to move forward. Through engagement of community and agency stakeholders, technical feasibility analysis, and an options evaluation, the project will identify a community-supported preferred comprehensive flood resilience strategy, which will likely include multiple components that work together, and an implementation roadmap for Eastwick. With this roadmap, the project team intends to develop at least one funding application for the implementation of one or a combination of flood resilience measures.\nWhile a long-term strategy is being developed, OOS has secured funding to design and construct an interim flood barrier to provide near-term relief from riverine flooding.

project_info: Transport - Lower South Infrastructure Improvement Plan: The Mayor's Fund for Philadelphia, in collaboration with the City of Philadelphia's Office ofTransportation, Infrastructure, and Sustainability (OTIS) and the Office of Sustainability (OOS), has issueda Request for Information (RFI) on behalf of the larger Lower South InfrastructureResilience Collaborative to solicit statements of interest, capabilities, and Rough Order ofMagnitude (ROM) cost estimates from Respondents interested in developing a LowerSouth Infrastructure Improvement Plan. The RFI is intended to inform the development of aforthcoming Request for Proposals (RFP), specifying a specific scope of work for this analysis, andsubsequent contract with a consulting firm, or team of firms, to support the development of a LowerSouth Infrastructure Improvement Plan. The Infrastructure Improvement Plan will focus on mobility but also ensure that resiliency is considered. This Plan is intended to balance two objectives 1) establish a set of solutions and coordinated actions to deliver a multi-model transportation system that catalyzes inclusive growth and development in the Lower South area, which includes the expansion of the Philadelphia International Airport, the Port of Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Navy Yard, the Philadelphia Sports Complex and the former PES Refinery, which is being transformed into the Bellwether District, a 1300-acre campus for e-commerce, life sciences, and logistics and 2) ensure these investments are resilient and holistically preparing for existing and expected impacts of climate change. While the exact total project cost and total investment costs are unclear at this point, it is estimated that this plan will help preserve and protect an estimated $2 billion in economic investments in this region of the City. climate_hazard: Other coastal events: The San Francisco shoreline is relatively developed with seawalls and harder urban edges that are more at risk from coastal flooding than tidal inundation. The southern shoreline of the city is more natural and tidal wetland resources are at risk from rising sea level. Inundation of facilities, causing water damage to structures and contents. Along the bay shoreline, inundation may close roadways and cause damage to nearby structures; wave action can damage waterfront facilities. With sea level rise, the number and intensity of these inundations are likely to increase. | Heavy precipitation: Stormwater ponding occurs when runoff during heavy rains is too great to be captured and carried by the stormwater system. The stormwater system may also be disrupted when debris blocks inlets or pipes and low-lying areas may be flooded. Stormwater ponding can create a pollution problem during heavy rain storms as floodwaters carry debris, chemicals, trash, and other pollutants that have collected on streets. This disrupts the normal operation of city's waste management and transportation systems, along with posing sanitation risks. Because the City has a combine sewer and storm drain system rainfall runoff can have consequences on both infrastructure and public health. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): In 2018, a wildfire in Butte County coincided with the westward “Diablo Winds” and funneled wildfire smoke south and west through the delta into the San Francisco Bay. A high-pressure system off the coast blocked San Francisco's normal ocean breezes and trapped the wildfire smoke in the Bay Area. San Francisco's AQI was over 150 for 12 straight days, peaking at 228. This wildfire smoke emergency caused significant disruption as schools were canceled. It is likely that the wildfire smoke emergency impacts were not evenly distributed as residents with access to air filtration were less exposed to wildfire smoke. | Drought: Apart from impacting food production, crop yields, damage to wildlife habitat, drought also has a social and economic impact, including economic and physical hardship and increased stress on residents of a drought-stricken areas for water supply and other healthcare services. In San Francisco, the primary impact of drought is reduced availability of water for residential and commercial use. Sourcing water from the Hetch-Hetchy Reservoir across drought-stricken California and with limited and/or unpredictable changes in rainfall for direct capture, San Francisco has already grappled with this hazard. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Flooding from sea level rise will damage building and roads in the coastal neighborhoods of the city. Flooding also represents a risk to major transportation hubs infrastructure in the region. Coastal flooding can have a long-term effect on major industrial and commercial activities along the coastal areas of the city as well as damage urban forestry and local natural biodiversity. Coastal flooding also increases the risk of shoreline erosion, undermining or damaging nearby facilities. | Extreme heat: A main concern is that people are much less prepared for and acclimatized to heat waves in otherwise mild city climates. During a heat wave, rates of emergency department visitation and hospitalization increase, as well as heat-related deaths. In addition, many housing units do not in San Francisco metropolitan area have access to air conditioning or other cooling mechanisms. Heat waves overwhelm the work of hospitals and other health providers. The elderly, the very young, and those with chronic health problems are most at risk when extreme heat occurs. Severe heat waves lead to increase in electricity demand for cooling and the city's electric reliability may be more vulnerable. | Other: Urban Heat Islands: Urban heat islands may be 5 to 8 degrees Celsius warmer than surrounding areas experiencing the same weather systems. Impervious ground and roof surfaces limit natural cooling that takes place when plants and soil release water vapor into the air, a problem compounded by lack of shade. This increases energy demand for cooling and impacts health: Heat waves are more dangerous for people when the body cannot cool off at night. Heat-related illness and death also increase the need for better emergency response management and capacity-building. | Water stress: Increasing pressures on water supplies from extended periods of drought, population growth, regulatory challenges, and the many uncertainties brought about by climate change are threatening water security. The city's public utilities commission has been able to diversify sources of the city's water supply to protect residents from potential disruptions in water supply from emergencies or natural disaster; however, climate change's exacerbation of drought conditions makes water stress continue to be an issue affecting residents, particularly those in vulnerable populations who may have reduced access to water supply. | Other: Salt water Intrusion: Salt water intrusion will likely cause damage to underground infrastructure, such as pipes and foundations. Rising coastal water levels will affect San Francisco's waste water treatment systems and slow drainage of runoff to the bay, as some of the waste treatment plants lack the capacity to fully handle storm flows increasing the risk of potential spillage of sewage into the Bay. Saltwater intrusion into the city's treatment facilities will also alter the biotic conditions necessary for the breakdown of waste material. Additionally, saltwater intrusion poses a particular concern for the Bayview-Hunters Point district (which predominantly houses low-income and minority residents), where residential areas adjoin a Superfund cleanup site at a former naval shipyard. The Superfund site is heavily contaminated with a number of hazardous substances, including but not limited to heavy metals, polychlorinated biphenyls, and radionuclides. Saltwater intrusion and rising groundwater levels could create a new exposure pathway for residents if intrusion causes groundwater to rise and interact with hazardous contaminants in soil.
project_info: Other: Infrastructure Improvements - SFO Storm Drain Pump Stations Improvements: Storm Drain Pump Stations Improvements at SFO Airport to adapt to salt water intrusion due to sea level rise. Stormwater ponding can create a pollution problem during heavy rain storms as floodwaters carry debris, chemicals, trash, and other pollutants that have collected on streets. project_info: Other: Infrastructure improvement - Seawall Earthquake Safety Program: Seawall Earthquake Safety Program. San Francisco's Embarcadero Seawall was constructed more than a century ago and is the foundation of over three miles of waterfront stretching from Fisherman's Wharf to Mission Creek. Today, the Seawall provides flood protection to downtown neighborhoods. The Seawall requires significant improvements to survive the next major earthquake and to address increasing flood risk from sea level rise and climate change. Improvements under consideration include: a) strengthening the ground below the seawall, b) improving the ground landslide of the seawall, c) constructing a new seawall, d) strengthening or replacing bulkhead walls and wharves, and e) relocating or replacing critical utilities. An estimated $5 billion may be needed to stabilize the entire Seawall and infrastructure, and adapt to sea level rise. The $500 million Phase 1 will address the most immediate life safety and high-priority upgrades.\n\nhttps://onesanfrancisco.org/resiliency/seawall-earthquake-safety-and-disaster-prevention-program

project_info: Other: Infrastructure Improvement - Heron's Head Park Shoreline Restoration: Heron's Head Park Shoreline Restoration. One of San Francisco's ecological landmarks, Heron's Head Park is a 22-acre open space and thriving wildlife habitat located in the City's Southeast Sector. The existing shoreline on the south side of the park is experiencing severe erosion and consequently discharges sediment into the Bay. The proposed project would stabilize the shoreline, improve habitat and biodiversity, and include sea level rise adaptation, as possible. Planning and design are fully funded with prior appropriations, and staff will seek funds for construction.

The vulnerability factors that affect each sector and that affect the most exposed populations: -Transport: Stopping thresholds, Number of people transported per line and Type of asphalting;-Supply: Volume of water passage and Overload situation thresholds.-Energy: Regions with underground cabling become vulnerable to the effects of flooding-Social Infrastructure: Number of students served; Ability to convert into temporary shelters; Ability to care for patients, monitor waterborne diseases. -Cultural heritage: Presence of collection and assessment of value; Mitigation infrastructure present; Age of construction;-Economy: Location of shopping centers and sub-centers; Location of industrial district;-Environmental: Absorption capacity and number of trees. | Extreme heat: The Climate Risk Analysis carried out for SÃ£o Paulo indicates that there will be, in the 2030-2040 horizon, an increase in the average temperature, an increase in the number of hot nights, a decrease in the number of cold nights and an increase in heat wave events, with the formation of heat islands in densely populated areas, which act as a potentiator of impacts related to temperature extremes. Human health: High temperatures aggravate atmospheric pollution produced by fixed or mobile sources (mainly industries or combustion-powered vehicles), potentially causing respiratory and cardiovascular problems, especially in children and the elderly, and increasing the demand for care in hospitals, with the population's vulnerability to heat waves being greater in the North and East regions of the municipality. The study also indicates that the impacts on the health of the most sensitive population, such as the elderly (over 65 years old), must be considered, since the population's aging rate is increasing. Therefore, consequences related to morbidity and mortality deserve special attention. In this sense, adaptation actions must prioritize the well-being of this population. Other: Establishment of a carbon neutral implementation system based on citizen, business, and public cooperation - Project to strengthen the carbon neutral support system based on citizen, industry, and public cooperation: This project has the strength of being promoted through three-axis cooperation of “administration (public) company (industry) citizen (society)”.

It does not stop at simply establishing policy, but expands reduction performance through an implementation system in which citizens, companies, and institutions all participate.

1. Operation of the Changwon City Carbon Neutral Support Center
1) Core role: A hub that oversees and coordinates carbon neutral policies in the region
2) Main functions: Supporting the establishment and evaluation of carbon neutrality basic plans and implementation plans, linking policies between national and local governments and overseeing reporting on international response systems (CDP, GCoM, etc.), establishing cooperation channels with private companies, civil society, academia, etc.
3) Performance goals: Strengthening administrative consistency, enhancing policy enforcement, and building public trust Secure

2. Support for the transition to carbon neutrality of small and medium-sized businesses in Changwon
1) Target: Small and medium-sized enterprises located in Changwon-si
2) Support method: Providing carbon emission diagnosis and consulting, supporting replacement of high-efficiency facilities and introduction of greenhouse gas reduction technology, strengthening capacity to respond to carbon regulations through training and workshops
3) Expected effects: Reduction of emissions in the industrial sector, improvement of corporate competitiveness (strengthening ESG management and export response), creation of green jobs

3. Changwon City's carbon-neutral platform operation and activation of citizen participation
1) Platform function: Online/offline integrated governance window where citizens and companies can participate
2) Disclosure of greenhouse gas inventory and policy performance, citizen carbon footprint calculation and practice certification function, sharing of participation cases of companies and institutions
3) Activity campaign to activate citizen participation, citizen supporters, practical challenges in daily life, distribution of climate education content
4) Expected effect: Transforming citizens into active actors rather than passive subjects Transition

4. Changwon City's practical carbon-neutral living lab operation
1) Living Lab: A field-centered participation model where citizens, companies, researchers, and the public directly experiment and verify in real-life environments
2) Operation examples: Reduction of disposable products (pilot project for disposable gloves at gas stations, etc.), production and distribution of waste banner recycling pouches, life energy saving, and resource circulation Campaign
3) Expected effects: Creating reduction results that can be felt in the lives of citizens, adjusting and disseminating policies and technologies to suit the field

As a result, Changwon City will build an integrated local model that can respond to national climate policy goals and international reporting systems (CDP, GCoM, etc.).

Extreme heat: With the increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events such as heatwaves, cold spells, and heavy rainfall, the number of climate-vulnerable populations—such as the elderly, children, low-income groups, outdoor workers, and residents in vulnerable facilities or locations—is also rising.
These groups are disproportionately exposed to escalating climate risks, which can directly impact their health and livelihoods, thereby exacerbating existing social inequalities.
In this context, targeted protection measures and focused management for vulnerable populations are essential. | Urban flooding: Flood damage caused by urban inundation is particularly severe in areas with a high concentration of semi-basement (banjiha) and aging homes in central Seoul.
Districts such as Gwanak-gu, Dongjak-gu, and Yeongdeungpo-gu have shown especially high levels of vulnerability.
Flooding in these areas poses serious threats to livelihoods, including home inundation and the displacement of residents. | Extreme cold: Cold waves pose significant health risks to vulnerable populations, including residents of jjokbang (tiny room housing) communities and people experiencing homelessness.
In addition, heavy snowfall can severely disrupt urban transportation systems, causing broader negative impacts on the city.

climate_hazard:
Extreme heat: There were multiple heatwaves in 2019 and 2020 each with five or more days over 35 degrees Celsius. Between 2021 and 2024, there were multiple waves again with more than three days over 35 degrees Celsius, with the most notable in March 2021, being 5 days over 37 degrees Celsius which coincided with the March long weekend and several international festivals (e.g WOMADelaide and Fringe Festival). 

The increase in the incidence of heatwaves and extreme heat is expected to adversely impact the health safety and wellbeing of vulnerable members of the community. These include members of the community who are already vulnerable due to poor mental or physical health the elderly those who are isolated by a lack of mobility or transport options and or are highly dependent on particular facilities or support. Increased heatwaves and extreme heat will also influence Adelaide's amenity and attraction as a place to live do business and visit. 

On Thursday 24 January 2019 the Adelaide CBD recorded an all-time capital city high of 46.6 degrees Celsius and a new record was set for highest minimum temperature. As of April 2020, Adelaide had experienced 10 days over 40 degrees over the summer period which is already greater than the projections of days over 40 degrees for 2030. Visitation and corresponding commercial and retail activity to outdoor activity centres is likely to reduce during extreme climate events such as heatwaves thereby impacting on local businesses and the economy. Conversely visitation to indoor environments may increase as people seek out or retreat to protected areas to socialise and shop. Participation in events celebrations and activities will also be impacted. Continuity of services may be affected due to disruptions to electricity services. 

The number of days 40 degrees Celsius and over in Adelaide is projected to increase from an average of 11 days per year historically to 52 by 2050. Guide to climate projections for risk assessment and planning in South Australia 2022: https://data.environment.sa.gov.au/Content/Publications/Guide%20to%20climate%20projections%20for%20risk%20assessment%20and%20planning%20in%20South%20Australia%202022.pdf 

Extreme heat poses risk to City of Adelaide's assets and reduces their lifespan. | Heat stress: An overall warming both day and night across all seasons is predicted for our region with a high likelihood of an increase in frequency and duration of heat waves / extreme heat. Since the 1970s the number of days 35 degrees and over has already increased by 40 in Eastern Adelaide (https://australiainstitute.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/P666-Heatwatch-Adelaide-WEB-.pdf). 

The Adelaide region has a historical average of 131 days per year over 35 degrees with current data indicating climate change predictions of a maximum of 196 days by 2030 224 days by 2050 and 233-265 days by 2090. Adelaide has a historical average of 11 days per year over 40 degrees with current data indicating climate change predictions of a maximum of 3 days by 2030 52 days by 2050 and 42-107 days by 2090 (https://data.environment.sa.gov.au/Content/Publications/Guide%20to%20climate%20projections%20for%20risk%20assessment%20and%20planning%20in%20South%20Australia%202022.pdf). 

Observed average days over 35 and 40 degrees from 2012-2021 surpassed the predictions above for 2030. The impact of this is financial pressure on vulnerable communities due to a higher need to cool homes. The increase in heat combined with a decrease in overall rain results in a drying which also requires community to water more or leave gardens to dry out. Similar pressures affect our business community. The result for the CoA is a need to influence urban design developments approved improving urban design and retrofitting and increase greening and water availability for this. 

Climate stressors (eg. extreme temperatures, flooding, storms, bushfire smoke) will disproportionately impact vulnerable communities (eg. homeless, campers, students, elderly, disabled, low-income, CALD), leading to increased demand for emergency response, evacuation, and post-event support services, especially related to Code Red and Code Blue activations. This will strain Council's human and financial resources. | Drought: Climate change will impact the condition of natural landscapes and green spaces such as parks due to warmer and drier conditions and climate extremes such as heatwave. Remnant native vegetation may experience declining condition as a result of drying plant loss decreased germination introduction of disease and may also be damaged by bushfire. Existing biodiversity threats including pest plants and animals may become greater as pest plants and animals are often opportunistic and have a greater ability to respond to disturbance than native species. The effect will vary for open and green spaces across the Region depending on their access to irrigation. On private land individuals may choose to design a garden more suited to dry conditions or simply not water a garden which will in turn increase the heat experienced. 

Average annual rainfall is projected to decrease by 310 by 2050. The greatest decline is projected for Spring rainfall (https://data.environment.sa.gov.au/Content/Publications/Guide%20to%20climate%20projections%20for%20risk%20assessment%20and%20planning%20in%20South%20Australia%202022.pdf). 

Extreme heat, water scarcity and increasing aridity will severely degrade and devalue natural assets (eg. trees, wetlands, WSUD, gardens) in open spaces and streetscapes. This will increase the likelihood of limb drop and mass die-off (eg. tree species, fruit bats), while reducing flood management function, urban cooling, amenity and recreational value. This will affect the City's reputation and the parklands UNESCO World Heritage bid, and prematurely devalue Council investments. 
 | Urban flooding: Stormwater management infrastructure will be impacted by climate change due to increasing rainfall intensity which will place it under increasing pressure particularly where infrastructure is ageing or designed to standards inconsistent with projected climate change and higher density landscapes. Rainfall in 2022 was higher than average across Adelaide and was the wettest year since 2016: http://www.bom.gov.au/climate/current/annual/sa/adelaide.shtml. 

The intensity of heavy rainfall events is projected to increase by at least 10 by 2050 https://www.resilienteast.com/impacts.
More frequent and intense rainfall events may exceed existing stormwater capacity, leading to more widespread flash flooding. This will damage transport links (roads, paths, public transport, bridges), public and private buildings, and parklands. It will affect vulnerable people, housing and outdoor events. Mapped flood risk catchments include the River Torrens (Adelaide Oval, golf course, rowing clubs), First to Fifth Creeks (east parklands, lower Adelaide University, Adelaide Botanic HS, Wine Centre, Botanic Gardens and Park, Zoo), and Brownhill and Keswick Creeks (southern parklands, around South Terrace east of King William). Downstream impacts on private property may also be significant if flood defences fail.
project_info: Water management - Karrawirra Parri / River Torrens wetlands: The purpose of the project is to implement a Karrawirra Parri Restoration / River Torrens Restoration and Nature Space that: •Contributes to improving water quality and ecological health in Karrawirra Parri (Torrens River) and Torrens Lake. • Enhances biodiversity in Karrawirra Parri and Torrens Lake. • Increases social, cultural, tourism and recreational activities, particularly with respect to connection to nature and local biodiversity. • Improves amenity of the Torrens Lake. The project outcomes are: 1. To improve water quality, increase biodiversity and provide habitat through the reintroduction of aquatic vegetation and innovative wetland/waterway design. 2. To create a high-quality community space of Kaurna significance that enhances recreational and tourism opportunities through the interaction of people, nature, the river, and culture. 3. Demonstrate innovative approaches to managing water quality and urban waterway renewal.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Higher levels of CO2 in the atmosphere can increase the impact of other hazards - stronger storms, increased ocean acidification, increased number of heavy rain storms. Higher levels of carbon dioxide, higher temperatures, and more precipitation change the quantity, spatial distribution, and seasonal timing of aeroallergens, as well as the intensity of humans' allergic reactions to these substances. Higher levels of carbon dioxide decrease the carbonate ion concentration in the water, making it difficult for marine life to grow healthy shells. As a result, these species have slower growth, thinner shells, and their mortality rates rise. Broadly defined, ocean acidification is caused by the release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere from burning fossil fuels (cars, buses, homes, industries) and when the carbon dioxide mixes with water, it becomes more acidic. All ocean acidification vulnerabilities will be exacerbated by increases in atmospheric CO2. The Gulf of Maine, in particular, may have a higher susceptibility to ocean acidification because of its relatively low pH and colder waters, which more readily absorb carbon dioxide. Increases in CO2 also mean more high heat days that will stress populations that lack air conditioning. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Storms and storm surges present the potential for extreme damage to public and private infrastructure and property, threat to life, and potential for serious injuries. Based on a 2012 buildout of the Back Cove area, a Portland neighborhood, the study suggested that Portland could see $447 million to $3.68 billion in damage to Back Cove real estate from a 100-year storm with 1.6 feet of sea level rise and 5.9 feet of sea level rise above MHHW, respectively. Damage to buildings from floods, as well as high winds in heavy storms, are expected to increase household financial burden due to climate change. Residents have expressed concern that extreme weather and flooding are already beginning to drive up the costs for buildings to operate effectively. Some food processing facilities are also at risk to storm damage, such as Portland's H.P. Hood facility, which could pose a slight risk to the supply chain. Five of eleven supermarkets in Portland and South Portland show vulnerability to sea level rise and storm surge. | Urban flooding: Higher levels of flooding have already been experienced in Portland, especially on roads like Marginal Way. As flooding continues, there is also the potential for loss of important privately owned marine infrastructure and impacts to commercial activity and marine tourism.High-risk properties are also more likely to be put on the market with each passing year, and the study notes the trend in which the purchase price continues to decline as fewer people want to buy high-risk properties. While wealthier homeowners, businesses, or neighborhoods may have more cumulative value to lose, those with more limited financial means risk losing a much larger portion of their wealth. Lower income homeowners become forced to weigh the tradeoff between costly flood-proofing investments and defaulting on loans. Financial burden will also be worsened for high-risk-home owners due to higher insurance costs and/or costly retrofits. Flooding can also limit our ability to access resources that ensure health and wellbeing on a day-to-day basis—whether that's healthy food, childcare, routine health services, a sustainable income, or a sense of community and support. Already the Friends of Casco Bay have documented a rise in the acidity of Casco Bay over the past 15 years. If the financial health of the cities were to decrease as exposure to chronic flooding increases, the cities may face more limited options for financing resilience investments, a vicious circle that could leave the cities increasingly vulnerable to flood risk. | Storm: Surrounded by water, Portland has already experienced substantial flooding on essential roads during severe storm events in recent years. Sea level rise and storm surge are expected to increasingly inundate roads in Portland, and most critically portions of I-295, a key corridor for travel in and out of the city. Storm surge inundation models suggest that I-295 directly south of exit 8 will likely be the first bottleneck area due to flooding with a category 1 hurricane. A category 2 hurricane could impact the same location on I-295, as well as cut off connections between Portland and South Portland by affecting the I-295 bridge, Casco Bay Bridge, Veteran's Memorial Bridge, and the Congress Street (ME-22) bridge, all crossing the Fore River. Marine terminals, along with railroad corridors along Commercial Street and Turner Island will likely experience regular flooding by 3.9 feet of sea level rise.The sewer and stormwater systems in Portland shows vulnerability to storms and sea level rise in areas along the waterfronts, including Back Cove and the Fore River. Lyme disease, which is spread by black-legged ticks or deer ticks, is the primary and most common vector-borne disease in Maine as of 2019. Symptoms for Lyme disease in humans usually include a fever, headache, fatigue, and a skin rash called erythema migrans. If left untreated, the infection can spread, resulting in chronic joint pain and neurological dysfunction.Changes in the climate, including warmer winters, higher humidity, and more precipitation, impact the breeding and survival rates of ticks and mosquitoes, as well as the reproductive rate of the pathogens. We expect in the future: impairment of human health, in particular of sensitive groups such as the elderly or weakened persons and children; performance degradation at work; increase in cooling energy requirements; degradation of soil, water and air quality; impairment of biodiversity (heat stress).

The Citizen-Science project '3-2-1-heiss!' in Zurich is a pilot project conducted in summer 2024 to investigate heat hotspots and cool places in the urban district Kreis 4. Seniors equipped with temperature sensors measured temperatures during their walks and daily activities, noting locations of strong heat discomfort and places that offer cooling. The project addressed the increasing urban heat island effect intensified by climate change, which is a significant health burden, especially for vulnerable groups like seniors.
In a concluding event, participants and city representatives exchanged experiences, discussed which public places are most affected by heat, and jointly selected the most pleasant local spot—Bullingerplatz was notably appreciated for its coolness despite relatively high temperatures due to features like a fountain and reduced traffic. The collected data and insights feed into Zurich's future urban heat mitigation efforts.
The project was funded by the Stadtgrün program, which focuses on research and pilot projects for heat reduction, climate improvement, and increasing biodiversity. It was carried out in cooperation with Catta, Sensirion, and NOA.

Since high material assets and infrastructure are often located underground, major damage would have occurred even if the water had been shallow. 
In July 2021, the expected precipitation for the whole month occurred in only four days, causing the Sihl and Limmat rivers and Lake Zürich to fill up to alarming levels. The expected increase in heavy precipitation events and floods can lead to landslides, erosion and flooding. This affects in particular buildings on slopes and along watercourses where damage to the building may be caused.

More material must be purchased. | Drought: So far the city of Zurich has not experienced significant impacts due periods of drought. Longer and more intense droughts are expected in the future for the entire greater Zurich area, especially in the summer. Possible impact on drinking water quality with negative impact on human health. Stress for the local flora and fauna, thus increasing the need for maintenance and irrigation of open spaces. Soil settlement, which can cause damage to the building material. Energy production or water for firefighting. Harvest losses on farms in the city and the risk of forest fires can increase. | Heat stress: Hazard: Heat / Thermal Stress

Vulnerable populations: 
Elderly (75+, especially 80+):
- Reduced cardiovascular capacity → higher risk of heart/circulatory failure.
- Documented peak in heat-related mortality (e.g. 1,402 deaths in summer 2003 → 5.6% of all summer deaths).
- In 2023: 542 heat deaths, almost all among >75 years old.
Infants / young children (<6 years):
- Limited thermoregulation → more sensitive to high temperatures and dehydration.
People with chronic illness (esp. cardiovascular, pulmonary):
- Higher morbidity and mortality in heat.
Workers (indoor & outdoor):
- Productivity losses of 3-12% during heatwaves; at 30 °C and 50% humidity, physical productivity drops ~15% per °C increase.
- Night heat stress reduces recovery between work shifts.
Students / young adults:
- Studies show 10-15% reduced cognitive capacity (reaction, memory) without cooling.

Sectors affected:
Healthcare sector:
- Higher admissions for cardiovascular/circulatory collapse and dehydration.
Labor/education:
- Falling productivity, performance losses in schools/universities.
Social care/elderly homes:
- High criticality → need for targeted adaptation (shading, ventilation, cooling).

Information and heat warning systems
In order to protect the health of the population during hot spells, the existing information and heat warning systems have been further developed specifically for hot summer days. New findings are being incorporated into the training programs for employees in retirement and care facilities. For employees who are already severely affected by the heat, suitable measures are being implemented, e.g. appropriate clothing, protective material, adaptation of work processes and times, sufficient drinks. Measures to prevent reduced productivity due to heat are planned.

A cooling strategy for the city
With increasing heat stress, more cooling is needed in living and working spaces. The city is responding to this by developing a cooling strategy. The cooling demand is to be reduced through summer heat insulation and other construction and operational measures. Excess heat is also to be used, for example through seasonal storage in the ground. It is important that non-usable excess heat is not discharged into the outside air wherever possible. | Other: Air quality: Higher ozone concentration in areas near streets during hot and sunny days.

Elderly (75+, especially 80+):
- Reduced cardiovascular capacity → higher risk of heart/circulatory failure.
- Documented peak in heat-related mortality (e.g. 1,402 deaths in summer 2003 → 5.6% of all summer deaths).
- In 2023: 542 heat deaths, almost all among >75 years old.
Infants / young children (<6 years):
- Limited thermoregulation → more sensitive to high temperatures and dehydration.
People with chronic illness (esp. cardiovascular, pulmonary):
- Higher morbidity and mortality in heat.
Workers (indoor & outdoor):
- Productivity losses of 3-12% during heatwaves; at 30 °C and 50% humidity, physical productivity drops ~15% per °C increase.
- Night heat stress reduces recovery between work shifts.
Students / young adults:
- Studies show 10-15% reduced cognitive capacity (reaction, memory) without cooling.

Healthcare sector:
- Higher admissions for cardiovascular/circulatory collapse and dehydration.
Labor/education:
- Falling productivity, performance losses in schools/universities.
Social care/elderly homes:
- High criticality → need for targeted adaptation (shading, ventilation, cooling).

In order to protect the health of the population during hot spells, the existing information and heat warning systems have been further developed specifically for hot summer days. These events all increase river and water table levels, leading to overland or groundwater flooding. Although these floods may last only a few days, the flood impacts on people and communities can remain for months to years. Some of the more significant impacts of floods include injuries and the risk of fatalities, power outages, dislocation of residents from their homes and communities, service disruptions, stormwater backups and basement flooding, costly damage to buildings and infrastructure, and long term changes to rivers including erosion and reduced river bank stability. 
The City of Calgary has been addressing the risk of river flooding since the major flood of 2013, through mitigation actions such as upstream water management, river bank engineering, riparian restoration, redesign of storm-water outfalls, construction of berms, flood gates in high-risk areas, and lot-level protection. | Other: Higher Average Temperatures: Increased annual temperatures, a longer season of cooling degree days (CDD), and higher extreme warm temperatures impact air conditioning needs and costs for buildings to maintain thermal comfort. While there may be less energy expended for heating in a warming climate, increased cooling needs should be considered. Warmer air temperatures can increase the concentration of ground-level ozone, which can trigger or worsen a variety of cardiovascular and respiratory health problems including bronchitis, emphysema, and asthma. 
With higher average temperatures, this can create ideal conditions for pest and disease outbreaks. This can directly impact people's health as new diseases migrate further north, as has already been seen with Lyme disease, Zika, and the West Nile virus. Outdoor workers and those who enjoy outdoor activities will be most at risk. Growth of invasive species, such as the pine beetle, can wipe out entire forests, with potential impacts to the food chain and local wildlife, as well as negative impacts on forestry and tourism. 
Pine beetle killed trees can lead to extreme risk of forest fires, which have affected Alberta and BC communities already. | Drought: The consequences of a multi-year drought are far reaching. In addition to the impact on local agriculture and other water intensive businesses, droughts affect the health of plants, wildlife, wetlands, forests, parks, open spaces, recreational facilities and private yards. Drying out of forests increases the risk of wildfires, which impact both local air quality and even water quality if they occur upstream of the source of Calgary's water supply. Trees and plants also become more susceptible to pest and disease outbreaks (e.g. pine beetles) since lack of water can stress trees, limiting their ability to react to these attacks. Calgary has recently completed a Drought Resilience Plan and provides support for provincial drought management planning efforts. 

Alberta has a large farming and ranching community, and multi-year droughts could impact income of these families, and possibly lead to migration of rural people to the cities. Water restrictions in 2024 led to a better understanding of the wider impacts of a drought that reduces city water supply. | Extreme heat: Climate change will significantly impact the frequency, duration, and intensity of heat waves in Calgary. This may increase heat-related illnesses and fatalities, especially for outdoor workers, people with health conditions, children and seniors. Heat waves can also result in increased electricity demand for cooling, which can lead to brownouts during periods of peak demand, further increasing health risks. Source water quality can be decreased, and decreasing quality/warmer receiving water body for treated effluent will require higher treatment needs. | Extreme wind: Consequences of high winds include exposing City populations to injury and fatality risk from building collapse, downed powerlines, damaged trees, and compromised transportation corridors (for example signal loss or damaged streets as a result of mobilized debris and increased likelihood of traffic accidents due to lost road signal infrastructure). Populations would also be impacted by stranding or displacement compromised living or working conditions, exposed landfill material in public spaces, and psychological effects. Wind gusts would damage building envelopes as well as mobilize debris, trees and construction site materials. Loss of urban tree canopy would be widespread, recreation and historical sites would be damaged, and water bodies would see increased sediment load from dust and deposition. City infrastructure may be damaged including bus shelters, signals, street signs, street and lamps. Critical infrastructure would experience interruptions, possibly outages. Tall buildings may see damage to foundations and structure. Damaged or compromised streets and pathways would cause congestion, parks, open spaces and trails would be temporarily closed or restricted, special events would be cancelled, and access to community programs would be reduced or lost. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Calgary is less exposed to physical damage from local wildfires due to the limited amount of forest in close proximity to the city. However, Calgary is on the fringe of the Canadian prairie which can become very dry. Calgary has experienced multiple grass fires, such as those on Nose Hill Park, and some communities in Calgary adjacent to urban forests and grassland areas have an elevated risk to wildfires. Although the physical risk due to wildfire is low within most areas of the City, there is the potential to experience increased wildfire smoke and poor air quality days, due to the higher number of wildfire days expected and the prevailing westerly wind direction. In 2023, Calgarians experienced 513 hours of poor air quality due to wildfire smoke. This prolonged exposure to smoke was a record for Calgary, putting health and well-being of Calgarians at risk. As future climate conditions increase the projected number of wildfire spread days for the region, there is likely to be an increase in poor air quality due to smoke in the Calgary CDP Page 6 of 46 region. Wildfire smoke and poor air quality have had significant impacts on Calgarians' health, well-being, and enjoyment of outdoor activities in the recent past. 
Wildfires upstream along the Elbow and Bow Rivers could also impact drinking water supply and quality for years after a fire due to wildfire's tendency to destroy natural features that assist in protecting water sources from runoff contamination (chemicals, erosion and turbidity). A Wildfire Hazard Assessment was completed and a Wildfire Task Force was in place, specifically to manage risk to our drinking water due to wildfire in the source watershed. | Storm: The increasing frequency and intensity of severe storms (hail, lightning) cause costly damage to private and public infrastructure and impact service delivery including electricity provision. Physical health and safety concerns also must be considered, as hail, lightning and heavy rain can contribute to injuries as well as property and vehicle damage. 
Hail damage accounts for many insurance claims for damage to households and automobiles each year. Hail causes damage to personal property primarily vehicles, building envelopes and items stored outdoors. The June 2020 hail storm in Calgary led to $1.3 billion in insurable losses.

Far from being just an environmental disaster, they have profound and unequal consequences for populations. The impacts of these events impact both biodiversity and natural resources and compromise health, the economy and social well-being. In the face of climate change, all these impacts are exacerbated, given population growth, land use and occupation and the increased flammability of natural environments.
The economic impacts are vast and multifaceted. For rural and indigenous populations, who often depend directly from the forest for their subsistence, the loss of natural resources is devastating. The destruction of crops, pastures and areas of sustainable extraction of natural resources threatens food security and sources of income.
The agricultural sector also suffers massive losses. Plantation fires, animal deaths and soil degradation compromise long-term production. Tourism, another important source of income in natural areas, is drastically affected by the destruction of landscapes, negatively impacting the local economy.
For cities, the effects are also serious. The need to evacuate risk areas puts a strain on shelters and emergency services. The destruction of infrastructure such as power lines, roads and telecommunications disrupts essential services and hampers emergency response and subsequent recovery. The smoke, loaded with fine particles and toxic gases such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide, can travel for long periods of time. distances. People exposed can develop respiratory and cardiovascular problems, such as asthma, bronchitis and heart attacks. Children, the elderly and people with pre-existing illnesses are particularly susceptible to these effects, placing a burden on the health system.
Social vulnerability is a determining factor in the distribution of the impacts of fires. Low-income communities, which often live in areas of greater risk and with less resilient housing, feel the consequences first.
In short, forest fires catalyze a silent humanitarian crisis, exposing social inequalities. Its consequences reinforce the importance of robust public prevention and mitigation policies, which consider the vulnerability and specific needs of the most affected populations. | Mass movement: Marginalized/minority communities and low-income families are those that most live in hillside and open hillside areas with a high risk of landslides, with many houses built without adequate infrastructure. Many times they are not in other places to reside or take temporary shelter and choose to remain in these risk areas. 

Agriculture and Forestry may lose cultivation areas and suffer damage due to burial. There is an increase in demand from public administration and defense/social that overloads the alert and rescue system and monitoring of risk areas. Preservation is exposed to the greatest risk of ecosystem degradation and loss of biodiversity.
project_info: Transport - Mobility Observatory: Urban Mobility Observatory (new website and tools): since 2013, Belo Horizonte has had an Urban Mobility Observatory, based on indicators to evaluate the results of the Belo Horizonte Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan and a group of 64 stakeholders (including social movements, universities, technical associations, public institutions from other sectors, etc.). The current website (www.bhtrans.gov.br/observatorio) has some sections to disseminate information (library, indicator pages) and to stimulate discussion (critical opinions) about the problems and solutions of urban mobility. The content of this project is to improve this website with new tools such as a digital library with browser, information sheets on good practices, a platform to receive ideas from civil society based on maps and a digital edition of the Urban Mobility Balance, an annual report with the result of key indicators. The group of indicators used by the Observatory includes environmental issues, such as global and local emissions, and is very useful for also evaluating the effectiveness of PREGEE - Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction Plan.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Solar Schools: The Solar Schools Project is being developed within the scope of the COMPASSO UFMG Program, through a partnership established between the University and the City of Belo Horizonte, with the aim of developing methods and solutions for municipal areas most vulnerable to climate change. The project aims to research the dynamics of electricity use in standard buildings in the municipal education network, propose actions to improve energy efficiency in accordance with national regulations and prepare the installation of a solar photovoltaic generator system interconnected to the local utility's electrical grid. Since September 2018, the Solar Schools project has been accelerated by the Urban-LEDS II Project and, since the end of 2019, it has been part of this project's LEDS Lab initiative, both funded by the European Commission and implemented by ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability in partnership with UN-Habitat. In this context, Belo Horizonte was selected to receive direct support from a consortium of specialized consultancies contracted by ICLEI and composed of Mitsidi Projetos, I Care & Consult, Markup Consultores and Hill Consulting with the aim of implementing a pilot photovoltaic energy and/or energy efficiency project based on occupancy and electricity use analysis at the Herbert José de Souza Municipal School (EMHJS), in the northern region, as the first step towards implementing the Solar Schools Project. Recently, the consortium of LEDS Lab consultancies concluded the series of webinars on climate finance, aimed at members. Furthermore, mitigation measures were proposed based on analyzes carried out by UFMG and the initiative's consultancy, which consider energy efficiency actions and renewable energy generation. Two measures were selected for presenting technical, financial and environmental feasibility, with a view to implementing them at EMHJ, namely: installation of a photovoltaic (PV) solar energy generation system; efficiency of internal lighting, considering the exchange of lamps and luminaires with the aim of meeting standards, improving visual comfort and saving energy. These two mitigation measures will involve the development of a basic project for each, that is, they will be studied, budgeted and detailed in order to effectively guide their execution. Part of these actions will be implemented with the seed capital made available by the Urban-LEDSII project (EUR 15,000 or R$ 73,253.00), and part will be applied to obtain financing from other sources. Recently, the consultancy submitted the Solar Schools project to the PAR-PROCEL call, but was not, however, among the finalists. In the proposal presented, the total costs of the project were considered, i.e., a scenario in which all energy efficiency measures were met and the photovoltaic solar energy generation system was fully installed at EMHJS. Furthermore, replication of the project was considered in two new buildings in the municipal public education network. project_info: Transport - Electric Mobility: This project is coordinated by BHTRANS and accelerated, since September 2018, by the Urban LEDS II Project (implemented by ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability in partnership with UN-Habitat with funding from the European Commission and executed in Belo Horizonte in partnership with the City Hall, through the Special Projects Management of the Municipal Secretariat for the Environment), aimed at the electrification of the city's collective public transport fleet. capital. Its vision is as follows: \'In 2021, Belo Horizonte will have a fleet of at least 25 electric buses operating in its conventional service, with the aim of improving air quality, reducing noise pollution and reducing greenhouse gas emissions\'. To this end, technical, economic, commercial and political risks were mapped and risk mitigation actions are being studied. Alternatives for financing vehicles or batteries (imported components of greater value) are also being studied, but are still a challenge to be overcome. The pilot project includes a fleet of vehicles consisting of 3 minibuses, 17 standard buses and 5 articulated buses. The minibuses will be allocated to the Vilas e Favelas system (villages and favelas) and on lines that circulate on roads with restrictions on the operation of larger vehicles. They can also be allocated to the complementary service. Conventional and standard vehicles represent the vast majority of the municipal fleet, distributed across circular, diametric, radial and feeder lines. The use of articulated vehicles is concentrated in the trunk system and they travel on exclusive routes or with preferential treatment for public transport. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving air quality and reducing noise pollution are among the opportunities and impacts of the project, as well as increasing the service of the public transport system, with the possibility of implementing this same technology in other areas. of the city.

project_info: Other: Climatic Refuges - Climatic Refuges: The structure is part of the Centro de Todo Mundo program - which envisages the requalification of the central region of the city - and will function as an “urban oasis”, an “island of green” in the hypercenter. With a tree as its central element, the refuge will feature a structure designed using passive cooling techniques, containing a set of permeable floors (lawn and covering of micro drainage axes). In this way, it will contribute to the correct infiltration of rainwater in the area, avoiding accumulation and, consequently, flooding. \nThe space also has other structures, such as a bench under the tree, a lounger and a drinking fountain. This way, citizens will be able to use the refuge not only to shelter from the sun and reduce the feeling of heat, but also to rest and hydrate. In total, the climate refuge will occupy an area of ​​25.61 square meters. \nThe drinking fountain has advanced technology, with three spouts different categories, aimed at adults, children and pets. It also has misting stations, with sprinklers to dissipate a refreshing mist so that residents can relieve themselves from the heat. Just press one of the buttons and wait for the steam to release.
