Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): In Baltimore, coastal tidal flooding usually occurs as a result of storm events, such as nor'easters or hurricanes. As an additional concern, flood maps indicate that some areas of tidal flooding are also affected by high-velocity flooding. High-velocity flooding, where floodwaters can move faster than five feet per second, can exacerbate flood damage. Tropical storms and hurricanes are very intense, low-pressure wind systems that form over tropical or subtropical waters and can cause coastal flooding. Baltimore has experienced 13 coastal hazard events from 1997 to2017. These events are likely to be more frequent and intense in the future. Due to the concentration of transportation, warehousing, wastewater treatment, electricity & gas supply infrastructure, and arts, cultural, historic, and recreational facilities along the city's waterfront areas, these sectors are most vulnerable to flooding impacts. In Baltimore, 32.35 miles of local roadway would be underwater in a 500-year event with the projected additional 5-foot sea level rise. (Excerpt from DP3) | Extreme heat: Heatwaves are characterized by prolonged extreme high-temperature days. According to the National Climate Assessment, regional climate model simulations suggest that Maryland could experience more than twice as many days per year over 95°F by mid-century — with an estimated 15 additional days above 95°F each year. During Baltimore's hottest and most humid days, elderly residents living in neighborhoods with little tree cover are at a greater risk of suffering from heat-related impacts than are most other residents. Resident income, in addition to resident age, may play a factor in an individual's ability to cope with extreme heat. For instance, when comparing the distribution of poverty throughout Baltimore's neighborhoods along with the location of low tree canopy areas, it becomes clear that areas with lower tree coverage are typically neighborhoods where residents have lower income. While it is more likely that lower income residents will not have air conditioning, those who do may experience rising electricity costs as a result of the higher energy use required to cool their homes. Extreme heat can lead to power outages due to the increase demand on the electrical power supply infrastructure. During extreme heat events, people rely on air conditioning, thus increasing the power demand. Government facilities, especially those categorized as essential that do not have emergency back-up power are at-risk. These facilities must remain operational for the City to be considered resilient. Baltimore's exposure to extreme heat is extensive and fatalities due to heat exposure occur each summer. Aside from local characteristics, which may lessen the intensity of an extreme heat event, extreme heat impacts all areas of the City. Certain urban systems or building types are highly sensitive to the impacts associated with high heat. Infrastructure systems are quite sensitive to extreme heat. Energy systems will be taxed, which will have additional impacts on other systems and structures. Understanding this, certain facilities, including hospitals, emergency shelters, and schools, are likely to endure increased financial burdens as normal operating conditions must be maintained under more demanding circumstances. Additionally, impacts on critical facilities may be exacerbated by damage to transportation systems.(Excerpt from DP3) | River flooding: Flooding occurs when rivers, creeks, streams, ditches, or other hydrological features receive too much water. Three categories of food are common in the State of Maryland: flash, riverine, and coastal. In Baltimore, major flooding events are the result of riverine flooding along the stream tributaries of the Patapsco River — including the Gwynns Falls and the Jones Falls, as well as their own tributaries — or from tidal flooding in the Northwest Harbor and Middle Branch of the Patapsco River. Most of Baltimore's recorded foods have been the result of either flash flooding during sudden, short-lived rainstorms, or localized flooding due to poor drainage and stormwater management. Baltimore has experienced 72 flood events in the period from 1996 through 2017, seeing an average of 3.27 events annually. In Baltimore, 6.4 percent of the City's total area is currently designated as a high-risk flood zone while 3 percent is within the coastal floodplain. More frequent and extreme precipitation events could make these conditions a common hazard, and the impacts from sea-level rise and land subsidence will likely intensify future losses.A flooding vulnerability assessment estimates the number of structures that are within the regulated 100-year floodplain and thus susceptible to 100-year flooding. There are about 2,941 facilities with an estimated value of $2,659,994,010 within the City's 100-year floodplains. (Economic loss estimates do not include calculations for contents and inventory.) Additionally, as many as 2,000 people would be displaced by a 100-year tidal flood. As many as 3,027 properties, with an estimated value of $1,861,554,433, are within the 500-year floodplain (Table 33). Due to the concentration of transportation, warehousing, manufacturing, waste water treatment, electricity & gas supply infrastructure, and arts, cultural, historic, and recreational facilities along the city's waterfront areas, these sectors are most vulnerable to flooding impacts.(Excerpt from DP3) | Drought: The entire population of Baltimore City (591,489 people) is vulnerable to drought events. 
Drought conditions can affect people's health and safety, including health problems related 
to low water flows and poor water quality and health problems related to dust. Droughts also 
can lead to loss of human life (NDMC 2013). Other possible impacts on health from drought 
include effects on air quality; diminished living conditions related to energy, air quality, and 
sanitation and hygiene; compromised food and nutrition; and increased incidence of illness 
and disease. Health implications of drought are numerous and can include readily available 
access to drinking water | Extreme cold: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), populations most at risk 
from extreme cold and heat events include the following: (1) older adults, who are less able to 
withstand temperatures extremes due to their age, health conditions, and limited mobility to 
access shelters; (2) infants and children up to age 4; (3) individuals with chronic medical 
conditions (e.g., heart disease, high blood pressure); (4) individuals experiencing economic 
hardships that cannot afford proper heating and cooling; and (5) the general public who may 
overexert themselves during work or exercise during extreme heat events or experience 
hypothermia during extreme cold events. | Storm: There are 591,489 people who are exposed to severe storm hazards in Baltimore City. District 11 has the highest population with over 48 thousand vulnerable to severe storm hazards. The population groups that may have a higher vulnerability due to 
economic and social factors, such are: Persons over the age of 65; those under the age of 5; 
7-55 non-English speaking; and those with disabilities. These populations may have a higher 
overall vulnerability to severe storm events than the general population. | Mass movement: Landslides, sinkholes, and urban karst are three contributing factors in soil movement impacting Baltimore City. Generally, soil movement events are isolated incidents and impact the populations within the immediate area of the event. To estimate population exposure to the soil movement hazard, the steep slope >30% grade boundaries was used. Based on the spatial analysis, there are an estimated 25,424 residents living in the landslide (steep slope >30% grade) hazard area, or 4.3 percent of Baltimore City's total population.

Risk and vulnerability are dependent upon the population density, critical infrastructure, and mitigation actions and plans implemented within these coastal communities. The metropolitan areas of Baltimore, such as downtown Baltimore, are most vulnerable to coastal storm events due to its high population density and critical infrastructure near the bay.

project_info: Other: Community-Led Resilience Support - Resiliency Hub Program: We are currently working with 18 Resiliency Hubs, each with identified Resiliency Hub Leaders that serve as main points of contact with the City. Resiliency Hubs are located in some of the most vulnerable neighborhoods in Baltimore and are a key component of our larger Community Resiliency Planning efforts. Resiliency Hubs are non-profit community organizations, including churches and faith-based organizations, in under-resourced neighborhoods across Baltimore that agree to partner with the city to provide essential resources and community support during times of crisis and emergency, particularly during natural hazard events. They agree to be a trusted community location where vulnerable neighbors can access reliable power for their essential devices, continue to give and receive information as emergency situations develop, store medications sensitive to temperature, and safely congregate until sufficient emergency recovery services arrive, among other things. Resiliency Hubs receive support from the city in many forms including high-quality emergency supplies, energy efficiency improvements to their building, back-up power capabilities (solar and solar storage), emergency response training, connections to grant funding opportunities, and focused support and communications from the Office of Emergency Management, Health Department, and Office of Sustainability. We recently secured $7million+ to convert 16 Hubs t solar energy and install solar backup generators. We are currently working with partners and applying for grants to finance rooftop solar and battery storage projects for Hub use. Additionally, we have and will continue to offer Hub stakeholder convenings and trainings. We would also like to secure a sustainable funding stream to support a small grants program to assist Resiliency Hubs in funding the resources and programs they offer to strengthen community resilience and support their communities during emergencies.

Other: Public health: Many Cincinnati residents experience poor outdoor air quality which contributes to adverse health conditions, including asthma and lung disease. As Cincinnati's climate changes, there could be many changes that affect our daily health. Air quality deteriorates as hotter weather causes more pollutants—ozone and fine particles—which exacerbates respiratory conditions like asthma and chronic obtrusive pulmonary disease. As air pollution increases, so do negative cardiovascular outcomes like heart attacks and deep vein clots. As extreme temperatures become the new normal, Cincinnati could see heat-related deaths increase by 70-120% by the 2080s. Outdoor workers and individuals living without homes are vulnerable due to prolonged exposure to sweltering and polluted air. Children and elderly populations are especially vulnerable to the negative public health implications of climate change because of their weakened immune systems. Additionally, the rise of heavy downpours and floods due to climate change will lead to more sewer overflows and wet basements. These events can cause mold to grow in homes and businesses, and transport disease-causing bacteria, viruses, and parasites. Human health and social work activities will be impacted by an increase in number of patients. | Extreme cold: Extreme winter conditions have caused shortages of resources and the temporary shutdown of businesses, which can harm the economy of Cincinnati. Roads are also increasingly dangerous, and more accidents can occur. Extreme winter conditions can cause an increased health risk to many vulnerable populations. As energy prices rise, low-income households and other vulnerable populations may be faced with the loss of heating due to utility disconnects. During episodes of extreme cold, children and elders are more susceptible to frostbite. Outdoor workers and homeless individuals are also at serious risk of hypothermia and frostbite due to prolonged exposure. All these impacts will likely worsen as extreme winter conditions worsen in both quantity and strength. Exposed sectors include construction (due to increased damage to the built environment from snow and ice) and human health and social work dealing with the impacts discussed above. | Mass movement: Cincinnati has a high risk for landslides due to both the geography of the area as well as the development of land. The city and surrounding area have one of the highest per-capita costs due to landslides in the U.S., especially since 2011. The city is especially susceptible to landslides along streams and valleys, because these areas have primarily silt and clay soils that result in bedrock failure. These failures primarily occur in areas dominated by shale, such as the Kope Formation and the Miamitown Shale. Hazard risk also increases in areas of development, where the land is disturbed due to construction and other activities. Landslides in recent years have increased due to increased rainfall and the hilly nature of the city. Columbia Parkway has been subject to multiple landslides in the last several years alone, which have resulted in road closures and structural damage costing millions of dollars. As landslides become more common, Cincinnati will continue to see damage to infrastructure and housing in residential areas, which increases risks to citizens and harms the strength of our economy. Low-income households will bear a greater proportion of income loss covering landslide-related damage to their property. Areas with higher risks of landslide slides (due to development and geography) are considered vulnerable marginalized communities. | Drought: One of the chronic threats to agriculture from climate change in the Greater Cincinnati Area is crop loss. Rise in average temperatures will lead to longer frost-free seasons and other conditions that can increase crop yield (such as higher concentrations of atmospheric CO2), but this heat will also lead to severe drought and pest issues. Across the state of Ohio, summer drought severity is projected to increase by 50% by 2050. Lower, more erratic water levels and rising temperatures will cause inland Greater Cincinnati counties such as Butler and Warren to experience the worst droughts in the area. Hotter summers will create more high-risk working conditions for farmers, and cause crop ranges to migrate north (particularly for corn and soy, resulting in major economic output losses). Wetter springs, more flooding, and effects to quality of agricultural water resources will create more production unpredictability and lead to crop losses if farms are not prepared for severe events. Due to persistent drought, the price of local food could increase and negatively impact low-income households. | Urban flooding: Cincinnati has seen almost a 40% increase in the amount of precipitation falling in very heavy rain events since the 1950s, and it is predicted that this trend could cause the Ohio River to surge by 25% in the next 30 years. Major storm events can cause major damage, ranging from sewer backups, to landslides, to flash flooding. Hardscapes and gray infrastructure with aging or limited capacity have amplified the effects of extreme storms. The excess water that runs off of hardscapes and gray infrastructure during heavy storms creates overland flooding, sewer backups, and sewer overflows. Urban flooding events pollute our recreational and potable water supplies, and they have had a direct effect on hillside instability, resulting in more frequent landslides. Vulnerable populations include marginalized neighborhoods with inequitable tree canopy coverage and inadequate greenspace to absorb and slow excess water during extreme storms. project_info: Renewable energy - Renewable Energy on City Facilities: The City completed solar installations totaling over 1 MW on nine of its facilities. The City is currently in the design phase for a solar and battery project. Solar serves as a budget hedge and protects the City from increases in transmission costs by its utility. Future projects will likely include a variety of funding sources and will help the City achieve its goal of 100% clean energy for City facilities by 2035 by installing solar on another batch of properties.

project_info: Buildings - City Facilities Upgrade: The City has established a 100% renewable energy for all its facilities by 2035. To achieve that goal, the City must electrify its buildings and maximize their efficiency. Unfortunately, Cincinnati like many older cities has an aging building stock and an enormously deferred maintenance backlog. The City is using funds from the Energy Efficiency Community Block Grant to conduct building audits and develop an upgrade plan moving forward. The initial phase of the upgrade project would focus on buildings with a high EUI. The project would seek to upgrade an initial group of buildings through electrification, efficiency and controls upgrades, and renewables and storage.

As energy prices rise, low-income households and other vulnerable populations may be faced with the loss of heating due to utility disconnects. project_info: Renewable energy - Little Miami Wastewater Treatment Plant Anaerobic Digester: The Metropolitan Sewer District is constructing an anaerobic digestion facility at the Little Miami Wastewater Treatment Plant. The facility will process waste solids from the Little Miami, Polk Run, and Sycamore Creek treatment plants on the east side of Hamilton County. These solids are currently being landfilled. It will produce biogas, which is primarily methane, which will be reused onsite as a renewable energy source to run other plant operations. This will reduce our carbon footprint.

Heavy precipitation: While Cape Town is projected to receive less annual rainfall into the future, storm events due to cut-off low systems are projected to remain at approximately the same as current levels. Cut-off low systems can bring particularly damaging winds and heavy rains. Storm events due to mid-latitude cyclones are projected to decrease into the future due to the southward shift of these weather systems. However, flooding in Cape Town is primarily driven by high vulnerability due to poor drainage, high water tables, the presence of wetlands, and informality and sub-standard housing. This is expected to remain into the future and worsen as increasingly marginal land is informally occupied. Outdoor workers are restricted from working during a rain storm due to unsafe working conditions and potential for contracting illness. A rain storm could halt the construction process due to unsafe working conditions, resulting in major financial losses and timeline extensions. This is true for contracted City of Cape Town construction companies, which could also impact public operations if the project involves large-scale infrastructure such as roads, bridges etc.

During 2024, more than 45 000 people located in informal areas and from low-income households were displaced and approximately 16 000 informal / formal structures impacted due to heavy precipitation. Additionally, 42 high- risk areas prone to water table rise, storm water over flow and river/flash floods were identified and mainly included areas of informality. | Storm: Extra tropical storms can bring damaging winds and heavy rains that increases flooding in areas of high vulnerability due to poor drainage, high water tables, the presence of wetlands, and informality and sub-standard housing. These storms consequently impact people living in informal settlements or backyards, infrastructure or buildings in flood prone areas/close to watercourses and can cause service delivery disruption such as increased pressure on disaster relief systems, challenges to stormwater systems in urban settlements, possible flooding of roads and disruption of traffic flows for commuters. Damaging winds can pose risks due to trees and power lines being damaged. Damage to power lines can cause isolated areas of the city to be without electricity for days, depending on the severity of the damage. Stronger winds can also cause damages to buildings or houses and will have an impact on certain economic sectors, such as the harbour, which is already not able to operate for a number of days a year due to high wind speeds.

During 2024, 33 098 storm related incidents were reported and responded to mainly across low-income households and people living in high-risk areas.

The cost of repairing or replacing public infrastructure damaged or destroyed by storm surge is a challenge, especially in areas where repeated impacts occur. | Extreme wind: Stronger winds, especially those associated with severe storms, pose risks due to trees and power lines being damaged. Damage to power lines can cause isolated areas of the city to be without electricity for days, depending on the severity of the damage. Stronger winds will have an impact on certain economic sectors, as this will affect the harbour, which is already not able to operate for a number of days a year due to high wind speeds. project_info:
Landscape and Jurisdictional Approaches - Development of Catchment Stormwater Masterplans in Cape Town to Improve Understanding of Flood Risk and Develop a Portfolio of Flood Alleviation Measures: Development of catchment stormwater masterplans (including specialist studies, stakeholder engagement, hydrology and hydraulic modeling) in 21 drainage catchments City-wide, with the aim of: 

1. Improving understanding of flood risk under different land-use, climate and rainfall scenarios (including the location and extent of flooding, frequency and severity including damage costs). 
2. Scoping flood alleviation measures in the catchments (including nature-based, green infrastructure and sustainable urban drainage solutions), including estimating the implementation costs. 
3. Quantifying the direct flood alleviation benefits and additional co-benefits of the proposed measures. 
4. Developing and applying a methodology to undertake a cost benefit analysis of the flood alleviation measures to support prioritizing investment needs and mobilizing finance for further project preparation and implementation.

Land-Use - Coastal Resilience: This proposed programme consists of two phases 

•Phase one consists of two key components, as follows: 1. An updated sea-level rise and extreme wave run-up model for the City of Cape Town consisting of a city-wide assessment of sea-level rise, extreme wave run-up levels, and coastal erosion risk for the present day, mid-future (2050) and far future (2100) periods, taking into account the latest global and local scientific data and updated IPCC climate change scenarios as per AR6. 2. Detailed fine-scale extreme wave run-up models and coastal erosion lines that consider local biophysical factors influential to hazard exposure for the determination of high risk zones for the present day, mid-future and far future periods, taking into account the latest global and local scientific data and updated IPCC climate change scenarios as per AR6. 

•Phase 2 consists of three key components, as follows: 1. Development of a pipeline of coastal resilience infrastructure projects, including both green infrastructure, “grey” infrastructure, and a hybrid approach combining both green and “grey” infrastructure, in response to the results of phase one. 2. A high level technical and financial feasibility assessment for the above pipeline. 3. A business case for investment in coastal resilience infrastructure projects for both the City of Cape Town (to use its own budget) and potential external investors. 

Note: The development of the pipeline of projects must take into account principles of restorative justice in the context of addressing the legacy of apartheid spatial planning through sustainable and risk averse coastal development in areas of need. This aspect is of critical importance to the Cape Flats region of the False Bay coastline, which has been underserviced and under-invested compared to other parts of Cape Town's coastline. 

Due to the value of coastal real estate and the high demand of living along the coastline and benefiting from its resources, coastal mixed-use development is seen as a conduit from which to achieve socio-economic upliftment for coastal communities. Such development does however require that coastal risks are considered to ensure that this development is risk averse and ultimately sustainable over the long term.

project_info:
Nature-Based Solutions - Liveable Urban Waterways Programme: The Liveable Urban Waterway Programme (LUW) is a strategic and transversal programme developed by the City of Cape Town in response to the Climate Change Strategy, Water Strategy, Resilience Strategy and Environment Strategy. The programme is rehabilitating various waterways across the city, using water sensitive design, nature-based, and green infrastructure approaches, thereby achieving many benefits for society, the environment and the economy. A number of projects are in planning, development or implementation, and are being implemented by different departments. These are testing different rehabilitation and water sensitive design approaches to demonstrate the shared benefits that nature-based solutions and green infrastructure can provide. 

Projects include: 
1. Sand Langevlei Canals. 
2. Keyser River. 
3. Spaanshemat and Prinskasteel Rivers. 
4. Grootboschkloof River. 
5. Westlake River and Kirstenhof Wetlands. 
6. Vygekraal River. 
7. Asanda Wetland Park. 
8. Upper Kuils River. 
9. Upper Elsieskraal River. 
10. Various waterways in the Diep/Sand catchment. 
11. Various waterways in the Zeekoe catchment. 
12. Adderley Street Canals and Fountain.

 These projects have been designed in collaboration with communities, and to date five co-design workshops and a further 17 community engagements have been undertaken. A project pipeline is in development that has 45 identified projects that could be included under the Liveable Urban Waterway Programme. Work is underway to develop a business case for the investment, package the projects ready for financing and future implementation.

Because people working outdoors often work in physically taxing professions, their elevated respiration rates ensure that they inhale larger amounts of pollution, further increasing their vulnerability to its effects. People experiencing homelessness also live on the frontlines of poor air quality, particularly those who stay in encampments. This underlying exposure is compounded further, as many homeless individuals reside in areas that already have higher ambient pollution levels, such as under bridges and along heavily trafficked roadways. Lastly, children are particularly at risk from poor air quality, as they have smaller lungs and breathe a larger volume of air than adults, relative to their body mass. Among children, air pollution is linked to a wide array of adverse health impacts, including preterm birth, infant mortality, asthma, respiratory illness, and mental health issues. Wildfire smoke is particularly dangerous for children; researchers have concluded that it is approximately 10 times more harmful for the respiratory health of children than PM2.5 from other sources. Clevelanders believe the community systems most vulnerable to poor air quality are public health and safety, ecosystems/environmental health, and community/cultural systems. Northeast Ohio bears a considerable health burden from air pollution, and poor air quality days, like what Cleveland experienced on June 28-29, 2023, further burdens public health infrastructure. Emergency room for respiratory illnesses can double in the days following exposure to wildfire smoke. Prolonged episodes may place a serious strain public health systems; one study estimates that a seven-day pollution event could overwhelm intensive care units. Air pollution is likewise harmful for ecosystem health. Plants and animals suffer from air pollution. project_info: Public and green spaces - Restoring and Maintaining Cleveland's Urban Forest: The Cleveland Tree Plan was developed in 2015 by the City of Cleveland in partnership with four non-profits and many additional stakeholders. One of the key tenets of this plan is to treat trees as infrastructure that needs to be invested in. It's clear that the City of Cleveland cannot do this alone, so we are looking for the private sector to step up as well. The Cleveland Tree Coalition recently announced a goal of 50,000 trees by 2020, and 30% canopy by 2040 (the City currently has 19% canopy). The total cost of project represents an estimate of funding needed to get from 19% to 30% tree canopy by 2040. In 2019, former Mayor Jackson announced a $10 million commitment ($1M/year over 10 years) to support tree planting and maintenance efforts in the City. An updated Urban Tree Canopy Assessment was completed in 2019 to identify current tree canopy. As of 2019, canopy coverage was 17.9%, down from 19% reported in 2015. The City of Cleveland is currently working to identify neighborhoods with lowest tree canopy as targets for future planting efforts.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Dallas is subject to periodic flooding. Flooding causes property damage in low-lying areas prone to flooding, and is increasingly in areas not previously identified as being flood prone. Severe flooding and flash flooding can result in mortality. Climate change will result in increased intensity and frequency of high-intensity rainfall events that can cause flooding. Dallas has invested in improvements to levees/ pumping systems and some local drainage systems to reduce the impacts of flooding; however, the City is now working to address the older local neighborhood drainage systems that remain vulnerable due to aging infrastructure, and capacity to reflect current land use. Specific risks or hazards from flooding include damaged roads and buildings, fatalities, and damage to our public infrastructure like bridges and utilities that serve millions of people in our metroplex. Flooding can also pollute our drinking water by causing sewage overflows and hazardous waste runoff. | Infectious disease: As the ongoing challenge with vector diseases and its many variants indicates that all outdoor activities, and in particular those in public health, social services, and homeless populations carry the highest potential risk of exposure. At particular risk, are those community members who do not have insurance, or health benefits so that they have to remain working, even if potentially sick, and those, like first responders who have a greater risk of exposure to infected individuals. As conditions warm, diseases from warmer climates may become more prevalent in Dallas. Without cold winter weather, insects such as mosquitos will be more common and diseases carried by insects and other diseases will impact the community. Some of the specific risks to our community include west Nile virus, Lyme disease, diarrhea, intestinal infections, respiratory diseases, and ehrlichiosis. | River flooding: The main stem of the Trinity River flows through Dallas. Along the Trinity River system upstream of Dallas, there are four large reservoirs used for water supply and flood control. In 2015, the localized areas of the Main Stem received about half of the average annual rainfall (16.9 inches) in a month, with up to 30 inches occurring in the headwaters of the watershed, causing the upstream flood storage capacity to be simultaneously exceeded at all four reservoirs. This resulted in both localized flooding near the reservoirs, and uncontrolled discharge and flooding within the Trinity River floodway for an extended period. Dallas has an extensive levee system that protects a majority of the city population, and the central business district from this type of flooding. However, the outlying areas not protected by levees, and areas served by aging infrastructure remain vulnerable to local and riverine flood threat. Specific risks or hazards from river flooding include damaged roads and buildings, fatalities, and damage to our public infrastructure like bridges and utilities that serve millions of people in our metroplex. Car accidents can be caused due to people driving through flood areas. Flooding can also pollute our drinking water by causing sewage overflows and hazardous waste runoff. | Heat stress: Climate predictions in the 4th National Climate Assessment predict that that Dallas will see a drastic increase in the number days above 100 F. There are also long-term predictions that extreme summer temperatures may reach 120◦ F, with an increase of 30 to 60 “extreme heat days (temperatures over 100◦ F). In extreme heat, many outdoor operations become limited. Water supply, and transportation infrastructure is under stress, and the health of the community, particularly the elderly and infants, is threatened. Summers in Dallas often have extreme heat warning days. The hazards of this on our community includes risk of heat stroke, heat exhaustion, death, dehydration, higher costs of energy for air conditioning, higher energy use, crop failure or damage. In August 2024, the City of Dallas is participating in an urban heat island mapping study with the National oceanic and atmospheric administration to identify the hottest part of the city and address them through urban planning, tree planning, and other measures. | Drought: Dallas is located in the South-central Great Plains Region of North America, as defined in Chapter 23 of the 4th National Climate Assessment (NCA4) (2018), a 1,500 page two-part congressionally mandated report by the U.S. Global Change Research Program (USGCRP). Droughts are historically common and can be severe. Water resources are critical for the health and prosperity of the City. As droughts become more frequent and more severe, the City must adapt and change to deal with the conditions. The City operates under a continuing Drought Contingency Plan, along with Long Range Water Supply Plan, and Water Conservation Plan to help mitigate extreme impacts. Both of these documents include future climatic conditions into the modeling used to develop the plan actions. Specific consequences of droughts to our community can include dry vegetation, low water levels in our lakes, rivers, and reservoirs, crop failure, increased water prices, and damage to our ecosystem. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Dallas is subject to periodic droughts. During these events the danger of wildfire increases, especially near open areas with dense vegetation. Dallas has Wildfire Plans as part of the FEMA All-Hazards Planning; primary impacts are anticipated to be for homes and businesses in grasslands, and forested areas, particularly at margins between natural areas containing fuel, and urbanized areas. Fires are hazardous to our community because they can lead to more destructive fires because of low humidity and high winds. These types of fires can be harder to contain and control, and the risk of crop and community destruction is higher.
project_info: Renewable energy - Community Solar: The City of Dallas is continuing to explore ways to support community solar initiatives that will decrease the energy burden among low- and moderate-income households. In 2020, the city received a National Community Solar Partnership Technical Assistance Grant from the U.S. Department of Energy that recommended developing a solar farm on city-owned property. A follow-on plan to assess feasibility and provide initial conceptual planning for placing community solar on City property is underway to inform potential City efforts moving forward.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Dallas is subject to periodic flooding. Flooding causes property damage in low-lying areas prone to flooding, and is increasingly in areas not previously identified as being flood prone. Severe flooding and flash flooding can result in mortality. Climate change will result in increased intensity and frequency of high-intensity rainfall events that can cause flooding. Dallas has invested in improvements to levees/ pumping systems and some local drainage systems to reduce the impacts of flooding; however, the City is now working to address the older local neighborhood drainage systems that remain vulnerable due to aging infrastructure, and capacity to reflect current land use. Specific risks or hazards from flooding include damaged roads and buildings, fatalities, and damage to our public infrastructure like bridges and utilities that serve millions of people in our metroplex. Flooding can also pollute our drinking water by causing sewage overflows and hazardous waste runoff. | Infectious disease: As the ongoing challenge with vector diseases and its many variants indicates that all outdoor activities, and in particular those in public health, social services, and homeless populations carry the highest potential risk of exposure. At particular risk, are those community members who do not have insurance, or health benefits so that they have to remain working, even if potentially sick, and those, like first responders who have a greater risk of exposure to infected individuals. As conditions warm, diseases from warmer climates may become more prevalent in Dallas. Without cold winter weather, insects such as mosquitos will be more common and diseases carried by insects and other diseases will impact the community. Some of the specific risks to our community include west Nile virus, Lyme disease, diarrhea, intestinal infections, respiratory diseases, and ehrlichiosis. | River flooding: The main stem of the Trinity River flows through Dallas. Along the Trinity River system upstream of Dallas, there are four large reservoirs used for water supply and flood control. In 2015, the localized areas of the Main Stem received about half of the average annual rainfall (16.9 inches) in a month, with up to 30 inches occurring in the headwaters of the watershed, causing the upstream flood storage capacity to be simultaneously exceeded at all four reservoirs. This resulted in both localized flooding near the reservoirs, and uncontrolled discharge and flooding within the Trinity River floodway for an extended period. Dallas has an extensive levee system that protects a majority of the city population, and the central business district from this type of flooding. However, the outlying areas not protected by levees, and areas served by aging infrastructure remain vulnerable to local and riverine flood threat. Specific risks or hazards from river flooding include damaged roads and buildings, fatalities, and damage to our public infrastructure like bridges and utilities that serve millions of people in our metroplex. Car accidents can be caused due to people driving through flood areas. Flooding can also pollute our drinking water by causing sewage overflows and hazardous waste runoff. | Heat stress: Climate predictions in the 4th National Climate Assessment predict that that Dallas will see a drastic increase in the number days above 100 F. There are also long-term predictions that extreme summer temperatures may reach 120◦ F, with an increase of 30 to 60 “extreme heat days (temperatures over 100◦ F). In extreme heat, many outdoor operations become limited. Water supply, and transportation infrastructure is under stress, and the health of the community, particularly the elderly and infants, is threatened. Summers in Dallas often have extreme heat warning days. The hazards of this on our community includes risk of heat stroke, heat exhaustion, death, dehydration, higher costs of energy for air conditioning, higher energy use, crop failure or damage. In August 2024, the City of Dallas is participating in an urban heat island mapping study with the National oceanic and atmospheric administration to identify the hottest part of the city and address them through urban planning, tree planning, and other measures. | Drought: Dallas is located in the South-central Great Plains Region of North America, as defined in Chapter 23 of the 4th National Climate Assessment (NCA4) (2018), a 1,500 page two-part congressionally mandated report by the U.S. Global Change Research Program (USGCRP). Droughts are historically common and can be severe. Water resources are critical for the health and prosperity of the City. As droughts become more frequent and more severe, the City must adapt and change to deal with the conditions. The City operates under a continuing Drought Contingency Plan, along with Long Range Water Supply Plan, and Water Conservation Plan to help mitigate extreme impacts. Both of these documents include future climatic conditions into the modeling used to develop the plan actions. Specific consequences of droughts to our community can include dry vegetation, low water levels in our lakes, rivers, and reservoirs, crop failure, increased water prices, and damage to our ecosystem. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Dallas is subject to periodic droughts. During these events the danger of wildfire increases, especially near open areas with dense vegetation. Dallas has Wildfire Plans as part of the FEMA All-Hazards Planning; primary impacts are anticipated to be for homes and businesses in grasslands, and forested areas, particularly at margins between natural areas containing fuel, and urbanized areas. Fires are hazardous to our community because they can lead to more destructive fires because of low humidity and high winds. These types of fires can be harder to contain and control, and the risk of crop and community destruction is higher.
project_info: Water management - Water Conservation Five Year Work Plan: Large scale water supply, storage, pumping, pipelines and system enhancement measures. Storm: Between 1995 and 2021, the City of Detroit experienced a total of 43 thunderstorms, 4 lightning strikes, 5 tornadoes, 32 hail events, and 5 instances of extreme heat, according to the National Center for Environmental Information. This amounts to an average of approximately 3.42 weather-related incidents per year during that period. Extreme summer weather poses a significant risk to Detroit's most vulnerable populations, who are increasingly concentrated in the city and face greater exposure to power outages and infrastructure failures, with limited resources available for protection and response.
 | Urban flooding: Detroit has experienced multiple successive flood disasters since 2014. In the latest flooding disaster in 2021, several roads and highways became impassable due to flooding. Significant basement sewer backups including in freeways. This resulted in a lot of debris set out on the curbside - leaving several communities to facilitate their own debris removal plans. | Extreme cold: The heightened vulnerability of older adults to hypothermia is well documented. Although individuals aged 60 and over make up only about 20% of the U.S. population, they account for more than half of the approximately 700 annual deaths caused by cold exposure. Infants and very young children are also at high risk. Additionally, data show that males are more likely than females to die from cold exposure across nearly all age groups.For the past 26 years, Detroit has experienced 17 extremely cold temperature events
and 55 winter weather events for an average of 2.9 events per year. Based on this
history, the likelihood that Detroit will experience extreme winter weather in any given
year is high. Although the number of reported deaths is 21, the National Centers For
Environmental Information admits that the actual number of deaths caused from
severe winter weather is higher because of underreporting.

climate_hazard: Heavy precipitation: Durban has had about five high intensity storm events over the past few years, of which the April 2022 was the most widespread and impactful. High costs and lots of lives (just over 450 in that one storm alone). In 2024, there have been two significant storm events taking the lives of 8 and 9 people respectively. | Extreme heat: Heat stress and extreme heat is becoming more of a risk in urban centres in eThekwini Municipality, particularly in informal settlements which do not have insulation in roofs nor cooling infrastructure. | Drought: During the El Nino event of 2015, southern Africa experienced a crippling drought and this caused high food prices. Whilst Durban was less impacted than the central parts of South Africa, there were water restrictions in place. In the most recent El Nino event (2023), Durban was cushioned by the high rainfall received the previous 2 - 3 years, so dams were full enough to withstand the dry conditions experienced between Jan - Jun 2024. With the global system expected to swing back to neutral or La nina, we are not expecting water supply issues. | Storm: During the equinox of 2007 the Durban coastal strip was severely impacted by a coastal storm with high storm surge causing lots of damage to public infrastructure and sea front housing. We have not had a repeat of that storm since, but the potential remains.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Ekurhuleni experiences localized flooding. The City has the most incidence of flooding in the Gauteng province. Areas of particular susceptibility are Tembisa, parts of Kempton Park, Kliptown, Katlehong, Tokoza, Vosloorus, Tsakane and Nigel. The degree of flooding varies from roads washed away, broken bridges, dam bursting, inundated houses and the blockage of drainage systems. These flooding incidents often result in the displacement of both formal and informal households. The impact of floods across the City of Ekurhuleni has been visible through flooding of housing in low-lying areas, road infrastructure which in some parts have been submerged in water. This is expected to increase in future and will affect not only infrastructural assets but also people through possible flooding of settlements. Flooding also affects the City's ability to deliver services such as water and power to some areas. The Disaster and Emergency Services Department leads the City in coordinating action around this and ensuring that communities are educated about what to do in an event of flash flooding. | Extreme heat: Most parts of Ekurhuleni experience strong to very strong heat stress, especially in densely built city quarters such as Tembisa, and in open sun-exposed areas. The Urban Heat Assessment work has revealed the following: • Ekurhuleni experiences a strong urban heat island effect, urban neighbourhoods being warmer than nearby rural areas by 3-4°C at night, in some areas rising to 6°C. • The highest urban heat island intensities are found in densely built townships, such as Katlehong and Tembisa, the patterns clearly demonstrating that city neighbourhoods face sharp disparities in heat intensity.• Within neighbourhoods, large disparities in heat exposure also exist in green residential areas, on a heatwave day, daytime heat stress levels range from 'limited' in the shade of trees to 'strong' at open and unshaded locations; densely built settlements that are devoid of green vegetation experience heat stress levels ranging from 'moderate' in the shade of buildings to 'very strong' at open locations• The community-based heat monitoring campaign demonstrates that low-cost dwellings may face extreme temperatures. Light-weight constructions built around a wooden frame and involving corrugated iron sheets are particularly prone to overheating, indoor temperatures in such dwellings being higher by up to 15°C compared to more robust buildings constructed with bricks and concrete• Currently most of Johannesburg sees less than 20 hot nights per year (nights with temperatures greater than 20 degrees), under medium or high climate scenarios poorer neighbourhoods will see 80 - 120 of such nights. The health impacts of these are severe and include increased mortality. • The indoor heat assessment campaign that was carried out confirmed the impact of building material and structures on heat exposure. These campaigns showed that temperatures in poorer communities (shacks and townships) can vary by up to 8 degrees when comparing to more affluent communities (under a moderate hot spell in Feb 2022). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Ekurhuleni has a high likelihood of occurrence of wildfires in most parts on the City. The risk of wildfires is likely to increase by up to 50 per cent with climate change thus resulting in a 10 to 50 per cent rise in the frequency of days with a very high to extreme risk of bushfire. The fire season is expected to be extended in most regions of the City. | Drought: Ekurhuleni is sitting at a low-medium drought tendency. Ekurhuleni's drought vulnerability factors relate to rainfall variability which are unpredictable, aging water infrastructure and maintenance challenges which exacerbate water scarcity and the increasing population which puts pressure on already strained water resources. Climate change is expected to increase the likelihood and severity of droughts in the region; this is supported by the below assessments.

project_info: Buildings - PACE Financing for Energy Efficiency Refurbishment: The City implements a PACE program—Property Assessed Clean Energy program—to finance energy efficiency improvements and renewable energy in buildings. The loan is attached to the property, not the individual or company. Governments or private lenders provide financing to building owners, which helps pay for the upfront costs. Loans are paid back by increasing property taxes by a set rate for an agreed-upon term. Property owners begin saving on energy costs while paying for improvements, often resulting in net gains even with increased property tax.The PACE program is accompanied by an Energy Performance Labeling (EPL) program for some privately owned buildings, which requires public disclosure of energy performance and adherence to minimum standards. The EPL program creates the enabling environment for PACE by putting in place the systems to measure and track energy performance, which make it easy to identify comprehensive energy efficiency improvements that are cost-effective and appropriate to individual buildings.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Green municipal buildings.: This measure proposes that the City commits to building green for all new municipal buildings, as well as retrofitting existing buildings to be more energy and water efficient through a refurbishment programme and generates renewable electricity with solar photovoltaic (PV) panels on rooftops of municipal buildings. It would build on work already done as part of the Green Building Framework for City-owned Buildings (CoE & Makone, 2019) which summarises the baseline energy status of City-owned buildings, outlines green measure decision-making tools, and presents a marketing strategy for implementation. In addition, discussions are also underway separately with COE and the Gauteng Infrastructure Financing Agency (GIFA) concerning possible IFC support for COE's alternative waste treatment technology project for which project preparation is being supported by GIFA.

project_info: Water management - Combined heat and power (CHP) from wastewater biogas (i.e. sludge beneficiation): This measure proposes that ERWAT expand capture of biogas from wastewater treatment plants and uses it to generate electricity and heat in CHP system. Biogas is a by-product of anaerobic digestion treatment of sewage sludge. Biogas is currently captured at the Welgedacht wastewater treatment plant. The GCAP considers that 75% of future wastewater treatment capacity is equipped to generate combined heat and power from biogas. This could include, for example, converting biogas from Welgedacht to energy, as well as capturing and converting biogas from Waterval, Olifantsfontein, Carl Grundlingh, Vlakplaats and Hartebeestfontein treatment plants. Initial conversations have been held with the IFC to look at funding pathways for this.

climate_hazard:
Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The coastal strip of Fortaleza is made up of highly anthropized stretches, causing considerable vulnerability to extreme events caused by ocean masses. In the coastal area of ââFortaleza, 162 events called sea hangovers were identified, with 95 of these events being recorded since the 1980s, when there was greater urbanization of the Fortaleza coast. With the landfills on part of the coast and the installation of groynes, impacts are expected to be reduced, however, a new calculation is necessary to verify the effectiveness of the measures. The impacts of coastal flooding include erosion of dunes and beaches, damage to urban structures and the potential for flooding. Considering that it is in the neighborhoods with an interface to the sea, Aldeota, Meireles, Centro, among others, where the largest job offers are currently located and also where banks and other institutions linked to the financial market, a direct impact on the city's development can be inferred. Furthermore, part of the city's economy depends on services related to tourism, hotels, entertainment and gastronomy, whose location is also on the seafront. The main risk seen in relation to infrastructure concerns the destruction of urban infrastructure located on the seafront, as well as the emergence of sewage, also in neighborhoods located on the coast, due to marine intrusion, which is the invasion of seawater through underground routes. The impacts related to human health would be directly related to the emergence of effluents to the surface, the transport of solid waste to the interior of the city and the salinization of supply sources, both wells and the regular supply network. The main impact of rising sea levels on the water supply and resources system would be due to widespread salinization due to the advance of the wedge saline. Likewise, protected areas represented by mangrove vegetation and located close to river mouths could be decimated, with a tendency for invasive species of both flora and fauna to become established. | Heavy precipitation: High sensitivity to extreme rainfall occurs in neighborhoods with high density and low HDI, including a high presence of vulnerable people who are most affected by extreme rainfall and its impacts. The ability of drainage systems to withstand increased precipitation interferes with the movement of vehicles, people and products. Measures have been taken to improve urban drainage and reduce flooding in areas with low HDI, but the increase in the risk of intense and extreme rainfall can still have direct impacts on the city's development, both in terms of transport infrastructure, rainwater drainage galleries and also sanitary sewage, as well as through the provision of resources. financial resources necessary for works and repairs necessary to adapt to a new climate context. Among the main health impacts, waterborne diseases stand out, whose vectors proliferate through undrained water in certain urban areas, and transmitted by solid waste, which can be carried by rain. There is also a risk of contamination of supply sources due to the aforementioned context regarding the rainwater drainage capacity and the intersection of these with clandestine sewage connections. Possible impacts on green areas and conservation units in Fortaleza can be inferred in the event of an increase in rainy periods and rainfall intensity, since the environments are adapted to current conditions with little rainfall during the year. In addition to the death of some plant species due to water saturation, there is still a risk that invasive species that are more adapted to swampy or flooded environments will begin to occupy these spaces requiring adaptation throughout the directly associated ecosystem. Civil Defense is the municipal body that would need the most support, as it responds to incidents in Fortaleza during heavy rains, including removing families affected by the rains to safe locations, the solidarity shelter process, such as referral to Social Rent. | Drought: In the context of Fortaleza, for the IVCC analysis, meteorological drought, hydrological drought and socioeconomic drought were considered. The threat of drought to the people of Fortaleza occurs because the main source of water supply is the CastanhÃ£o Dam, located in the interior of the CearÃ¡ territory, where there are frequent occurrences of droughts. However, Fortaleza's supply has not been impacted by this phenomenon for many decades, since the State Water Resources Policy prioritizes and has guaranteed the uninterrupted supply of Fortaleza and its metropolitan region.
Furthermore, the city depends on production of some foods carried out in other municipalities in CearÃ¡ and droughts have the potential to affect the productive sector, the supply of food and its related services. Transport and housing sectors may also be affected if water shortages encourage migration from other municipalities to Fortaleza, as well as the water supply and energy sectors which, in this context, may suffer overload. Waste management (including waste recycling) - Metropolitan Green Points: Metropolitan Green Points (MVP) are spaces where waste is received, collected, and sent for recovery in a circular economy dynamic, promoting the connection between community, nature, and territory. Based on the waste management model of the Barcelona Metropolitan Area through its experience and technical support.

The Guadalajara Metropolitan Area has 9 PVMs distributed and strategically located in the metropolitan municipalities. In each of them, recoverable waste is received for its correct disposal and activities to raise awareness about responsible consumption.

The PVMs are part of the Metro Resilience Guadalajara (MRG) or Resilient Metropolis action, due to its adaptation to Spanish, it brings together community, local and international efforts, to strengthen governance in order to respond, adapt and prosper in the face of challenges urban areas in the Metropolitan Areas of Guadalajara (AMG) and Barcelona (AMB).

It is an international cooperation action with a duration of 3 years (2022-2025), which is possible thanks to the financing of the European Union and the Partnership for Sustainable Cities program.

It is possible to learn more about it at: https://metropoliresiliente.imeplan.mx/nnEl additional financing would allow for a greater number of Metropolitan Green Points to expand their benefits and co-benefits.

Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Building Electrification and Greening Fund: Develop a financial and technical assistance program that helps residents, particularly low-income, to pursue climate action. Many actions in the City's carbon neutral plan require incentivization or financial assistance. Additionally, in order to ensure all city residents can move towards more environmentally friendly technologies and appliances, low-income residents especially need assistance. To move towards carbon neutrality in an equitable fashion the City needs to develop a funding mechanism to provide grants, loans, and other assistance so residents can harden their homes to protect them from storms, ensure better building envelope, improve their air conditioning, replace natural gas appliances with electric, install solar and storage, and install electric vehicle chargers. Costs are estimated for a multi-year effort. 

In April 2024, the City developed a project scope for the EPA Climate Pollution Reduction Grant to fund the “City of Miami Climate Ready Housing Program Suite.” The suite consists of three existing programs, Keep Safe Miami, the Homeowner Preservation Program, and Miami Cools which are all geared towards improving energy efficiency for low-income residents. The City requested $36,880,459 for this project but was not awarded funding.

project_info: Buildings - Miami Cools: In 2025, the City, in partnership with C40 Cities and The Miami Foundation, launched the Heat Sensors in Homes project which deployed heat sensors inside and outside of approximately 75 resident homes in Miami's climate justice communities during the 2025 Heat Season to compile indoor and outdoor heat and humidity data and will gather resident feedback on lived experiences that will help the City understand unhealthy indoor and outdoor temperatures that residents encounter and the building types where they reside. Analysis of this information will help inform the City of Miami when implementing potential future cooling strategies for households through a Miami Cools program. Based on early data, the City anticipates that a program subsidizing a range of cooling solutions will be needed for the 2026 Extreme Heat Season. project_info: Jurisdictional REDD Program - Restaura Recife: UCNs do Recife ecosystem restoration program. The idea is to implement strategies and actions to restore biodiversity in the UCNs of the City of Recife that are already listed in the approved and published Management Plans. The UN declared this decade as the decade of ecosystem restoration. The city of Recife can make a great contribution to the restoration of biodiversity since there are 25 Nature Conservation Units-UCN in its territory. These UCNs are home to Atlantic Forest and Mangrove ecosystems, in addition to having many floodable habitats that are essential for the city's water regulation. The positive relationship between biodiversity and carbon sequestration has already been duly documented in the scientific literature. Therefore, restoring the biodiversity of these UCNs can significantly contribute to carbon sequestration and the adaptation of the city of Recife to the effects of the climate crisis. In study carried out by the team from the Secretariat of Environment and Sustainability, an estimated cost of 14 million reais to implement a broad restoration program with the execution of the actions foreseen in the management plans. It is important to highlight that this initiative is innovative. Few cities have plans to restore biodiversity in their territories. Furthermore, the initiative is innovative due to its socio-environmental impact. The implementation of a biodiversity restoration program will generate jobs of a type not yet seen in the region: green jobs. In partnership with the community, thousands of direct and indirect jobs can be created with a reduced environmental footprint and the potential to neutralize emissions.
