project_info: Transport - NAMA DOTS for Perpetual Help, Economic and Creative District of Medellín: Urban planning and intervention initiative with mitigation criteria oriented to transportation development (NAMA TOD). The NAMA DOTS initiative for Perpetual Help, Economic and Creative District of Medellín, seeks to contribute to the construction of a compact city and generate environmental and urban conditions that promote habitat and human well-being. Furthermore, the area to be intervened, as a district, seeks to promote the development of the creative and low-carbon economy for the city. The pre-feasibility analysis was developed with the aim of conceptually, functionally and spatially designing the structure of the public open space of Perpetuo Socorro, enhancing its DNA status (Orange Development Area), through the development of concrete projects in the public sphere that allow the transformation of this future Ecodistrict into a well-connected destination, with sustainable mobility, biodiverse, dense and highly mixed, which becomes an urban, cultural and creative place, ideal for living, working and recreating, contributing to the national low-carbon development strategy. The Perpetuo Socorre neighborhood, where this project will be developed, has been populated by companies that recognize this potential and have begun to turn it into a creative territory, giving it transformative leadership and entrepreneurial spirit, which has made it the guarantor of its recognition and appointment as ECONOMIC AND DISTRICT PERPETUAL SOCORRO CREATIVE and ORANGE DEVELOPMENT AREA (ADN- the first in the country), proposing it as the epicenter of the creative ecosystem of Medellín. The Perpetuo Socorro project is to be recognized as a collective space that promotes human mobility and neighborhood dynamics around public space. Inhabitants, users and visitors will be able to enjoy the space between traditional uses and new uses creatives. This will be possible by mixing services, shops and housing at walking distances and connected to the diversity of the collective mobility system. The project for the District, then, consists of a set of interventions on open public space focused on prioritizing pedestrian and bicycle mobility and the reintegration of nature. Accompanied by other complementary interventions aimed at promoting the arrival of initiatives and talents and integration with mobility. In this transversal, comprehensive initiative, which envisions a total transformation of Perpetual Help, the bets that coincide with the strategies prioritized by the Partial Plan have been prioritized, with accompanying the initiatives already existing in the neighborhood and with the vision of reconnecting the ecological network, articulating the stations of the collective transport systems, cycle routes, bicycle parking lots, facilities and pre-existing public spaces in a mix, which It promises to be the catalyst recipe for the transformation necessary for an example of a more sustainable city, with much fewer emissions, a sensible reduction in the carbon footprint while being sufficiently mixed and compact to attract businesses, talents and inhabitants.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Climate change is expected to bring more variability and extremes especially around precipitation. Monsoon rain has been less reliable than in past years. 2024 was the 7th driest and hottest monsoon season on record, with 0.74 inches of monsoon rain recorded at Sky Harbor International Airport (https://www.azfamily.com/2024/10/02/monsoon-2024-was-hottest-record-phoenix/ ). Precipitation for the Phoenix region can either be uncharacteristically dry or be high-intensity and duration rain events. When a high amount of rain occurs in a short period of time or when the soil is already saturated, flood risk increases. Flood Risk is addressed, partly, in the joint Maricopa County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan (MJHMP) (https://www.maricopa.gov/1760/Hazard-Mitigation ). Several City actions included in the MJHMP including, in part: 1) Review building permits for compliance with Floodplain Ordinance and NFIP regulations, 2) inclusion of the General Plan policies that protect the natural flow regime of washes, designate areas for Open Space and Preserves, and when possible support the use of green stormwater infrastructure/low impact development, 3) Storm Drain Capital Improvement Program - Constructions of drainage facilities to mitigate flooding hazard to residents, 4) Coordination of review and approval of development projects located within flood hazard areas, 5) Provide information to sources of hazard mitigation educational materials, 6) Address extreme heat through regional programs to network, 7) The “Take a Hike do it Right” Outreach Program educating hikers on trail selection and hiking safety to avoid heat related illnesses, 8) Provide shade coverage at all City bus stops to shelter riders from extreme heat, 9) Increase frequency of bus routes around vulnerable communities to minimize exposure to extreme heat, 10) Maintain and execute the Drought Response Plan, 11) Maintain and execute a water use awareness outreach program, 12) Revise and ratify the General Plan every ten year, 13) Update and adopt revised building codes, 14) Continue to ensure zoning stipulations are met before construction permits are issued, and zoning is compatible with zoning ordinances, 15) Design and construct Rio Salado Oeste in Salt River, including low flow channel improvements and riparian/xeririparian vegetation to improve flow conveyance and increase native vegetation/habitat. | Drought: Phoenix has a certified 100-year supply of water. Phoenix and partners have been working on mitigating the effects of the possible shortage with actions like the Drought Contingency Plan. Some Phoenix residents have difficulties affording utility bills, including water. The City's Water Services Department (WSD)has a Water Equity initiative established to assist residents with reliable access to clean water (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices.html). The shortage of water on the Colorado River, prolonged drought, and climate change, has promoted Phoenix to declare a Stage 1 Water Alert and activated its Drought Management Plan. (Drought | City of Phoenix). For the Stage 1 Water Alert, Phoenix asks for community cooperation in implementing voluntary water conservation measures. The Mayor's “Save Water Pledge” was made permanent in May 2025 and underscores the City's commitment to sustainability and water resiliency in the face of ongoing drought and climate challenges (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/supply-conservation/save-water/mayor-pledge.html). WSD offers residential turf replacement incentive programs that started in 2024 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/water-services-news/3259.html). The City is promoting the use of Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI). The GSI Handbook released in November 2024 educates residents on how to capture and use stormwater for water conservation and ecosystem support. In March 2024, the City Council passed a large water user ordinance that places additional water conversation requirements on large water-use projects. These users must submit a water conservation plan approved by WSD as part of their proposed development. Phoenix adopted the Sustainable Desert City Development Policy in early 2024. Phoenix has developed a list of stipulations to consider for all rezoning cases related to water conservation and has been applying the stipulations since January 2024. The City Council approved the rehabilitation of the Cave Creek Water Reclamation Plant (CCWRP) in October 2023 to use advanced water purification technologies to treat wastewater to potable standards. Phoenix also executed a system conservation agreement with the Bureau of Reclamation and Central Arizona Project to implement the Lower Conservation and Efficiency Program. This agreement will make available 50,000 acre-feet of Phoenix's Colorado River entitlement in exchange for compensation. | Heat stress: Heat is included in actions in the Maricopa County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan. Phoenix typically has over 100 days annually that exceed 100 ⁰F. According to the World Climate Research Program, by 2060, that number is expected to rise to 132 days per year and by 2100, Phoenix will see an estimated 163 days per year that exceed 100 ⁰F. Data collected by the Maricopa County Department of Public Health identify these groups as those that experience disproportionately high rates of heat-related mortality and morbidity: people experiencing homelessness, drug use, older residents, men, those living with inadequate or no air conditioning, people who work outdoors and people with certain physical or mental health conditions. Heat stress represents a significant climate risk, with 337 heat-related deaths reported in Phoenix during 2024, (https://www.maricopa.gov/ArchiveCenter/ViewFile/Item/5934). 58% of the Maricopa County heat-associated deaths in 2024 were associated with drugs and/or alcohol, and 49% were experiencing homelessness. Phoenix is part of the regional Heat Relief Network with over 200 organizations that provide heat mitigation, cooling centers, water distribution, and outreach (https://azmag.gov/Programs/Heat-Relief-Network). In 2025, Phoenix operates the only 24/7 heat respite center for overnight heat relief in the state, with three additional libraries serving as cooling centers during extended hours until 10 pm, May 1 through September 30 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/heat-news/city-of-phoenix-opens-heat-relief-locations-to-keep-residents-sa.html). Extreme heat puts extra pressure on our electric grid by increasing peak demand. It increases cooling costs for residents during the summer that can challenge households on a limited budgets to pay for these increased costs. The Phoenix City Council passed a new ordinance that requires contractors who work with the City to enact heat safety protections for outdoor workers in March 2024, which took effect in May 2024 (https://nationalcosh.org/news/press-releases/2024-03-phoenix-heat-ordinance). The new rule requires those contractors to have a heat safety plan that provides free cool water to employees, shade and air conditioning access, hydration breaks, and training. Additionally, the Governor of Arizona signed Executive Order 2025-09 establishing a Workplace Heat Safety Task Force for the state. | Urban flooding: Some areas in Phoenix are vulnerable to occasional flooding. Higher than average precipitation in the 2023 winter season in Arizona led to reservoirs along the Salt and Verde river systems to release water at higher rates and more frequently. These excess flows caused flooding and road closures in the city of Phoenix. Projects to address flooding are part of the voter-approved 2023 general obligation (GO) bond funds. The GO bond includes $8.2M to implement drainage mitigation options to reduce flood impacts in Laveen Village and $19.2M to implement the Hohokam Area Drainage Master Plan, both in the southwest portion of Phoenix. These projects will provide flood protection to existing homes and other structures and reduce roadway safety hazards from storm events. The GO bond also includes $2.5 M to investigate locations to replace deteriorating 30-year-old metal storm drainpipes found throughout the city with new reinforced concrete pipes to reduce road hazards and neighborhood flooding. Phoenix City Code 32A-24 requires on-site stormwater retention for all developments, with limited exceptions. On-site stormwater retention areas must be sufficient to contain the 100-year, 2-hour storm event per the 2013 Phoenix Stormwater Policies and Standards Manual. The City code also requires that developments not increase the 100-year, two-hour peak runoff, change the time of the runoff peak, or increase the total runoff from pre-development values. | Extreme heat: Phoenix typically has 100 days or more that are over 38 degrees Celsius. By 2060, that number is expected to rise to 132 days per year, and by 2100 Phoenix would experience at least 163 days per year, according to the World Climate Research Programme. Extreme heat impacts individuals and families differently but makes it difficult to maintain indoor temperatures that are comfortable and healthy. Vulnerable communities to extreme heat include elderly, low-income households, outdoor workers, and those experiencing homelessness. In 2024, the City created 370 new shelter beds for those experiencing homelessness. An additional 310 shelter beds have opened in 2025, with an additional 70 beds planned to open by the end of 2025 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/homeless-solutions-news/phoenix-opens-new-280-bed-shelter-ahead-of-summer-heat.html, https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/neighborhood-services-news/3277.html). The Phoenix City Council passed a new ordinance that requires contractors who work for the City to enact heat safety protections for outdoor workers in March 2024. This ordinance took effect in May 2024 (https://nationalcosh.org/news/press-releases/2024-03-phoenix-heat-ordinance). The new rule requires those contractors to have a heat safety plan that provides free cool water to employees, shade and air conditioning access, hydration breaks, and training. Phoenix continues to participate in the Maricopa County Heat Relief Network, with numerous facilities participating in 2025, offering cooling centers and hydration stations. In 2025, Phoenix operates the only 24/7 heat respite center for overnight heat relief in the state. Phoenix also has extended hours at three of its libraries serving as cooling centers May 1 through September 30 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/heat-news/city-of-phoenix-opens-heat-relief-locations-to-keep-residents-sa.html). | Infectious disease: The vector-borne diseases (VBD) threat is an emerging climate change concern in Phoenix. New and increased disease risks require community and public service agencies to manage and adapt to these environmental changes. Vector-borne diseases are infections that are spread through the bite of a living organism, such as a mosquito. Mosquito-borne diseases are the most common VBD reported in Maricopa County including Phoenix. Mosquitoes, like other vectors, are sensitive to changes in climate. Rises in average temperature and increased precipitation are expected to broaden the geographic distribution and the abundance of many vectors in the United States. The Maricopa County Environmental Services Office of Vector Control tests for several VBD, including West Nile virus, St. Louis Encephalitis, and Dengue, among others. In 2022, the Maricopa County Department of Public Health reported two cases of locally acquired Dengue, the first in the area unrelated to travel. For information from the Maricopa County Department of Public Health, on West Nile Virus & St. Louis Encephalitis reporting for 2025, please visit https://www.maricopa.gov/4236/Vector-borne-Zoonotic-Reports. Phoenix established the Office of Public Health in October 2022.. The City provides information and resources to residents, businesses, and decision-makers to reduce chances of impacts and to avoid infection. Phoenix works with Maricopa County to address community exposure to VBD through vector control measures such as reducing and removing standing water. The City makes an effort to increase community and employee awareness of VBD, risks, and response plans through public service announcements and direct education and training.
project_info: Water management - Drought Pipeline Project: On April 9, 2020, the City of Phoenix Civic Improvement Corporation (the “Corporation”) issued $290,000,000 Junior Lien Water System Revenue Bonds, Series 2020B (the “Series 2020B Bonds”). The Series 2020B Bonds are designated such based upon the social impacts of sustainable, clean water management as well as the climate adaptation and/or mitigation benefits of the Colorado River Resiliency projects. The Series 2020B Bonds will partially finance the Sustainability Projects. As of May 31, 2025, $286,828,668 of the $290,000,000 bond proceeds Series 2020B Bonds have been spent. The City intends to spend the rest of the Series 2020B bond proceeds in fiscal year 2025-26. The Drought Pipeline is now in service and currently operating to mitigate drought conditions on the Colorado River. The Drought Pipeline Project brings water to north Phoenix to make sure all residents have access to safe, reliable, and clean drinking water during times of shortage on the Colorado River. The project is essential to Phoenix's economic health and vitality, serving up to 400,000 residents. The Water Services Department's construction of the Drought Pipeline was completed in August 2023. The Drought Pipeline interconnects the northern part of the Water System's 543 square mile service area, previously only supplied with Colorado River water, with the southern part of the Water System currently supplied with Salt and Verde River water. The interconnection will ensure the City's ability to provide reliable service to the population in the northern portion of the Water System in the event of reduced availability of Colorado River water, due in part to climate change and the aridification of the Colorado River system basin. The Sustainability Projects has provided new mains, booster pump stations, and pressure-reducing valves that now interconnect the northern and southern transmission and distribution systems so that alternative water supplies can be moved across the entire Water System (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/development-infrastructure/our-infrastructure/drought-pipeline-project.html ). The City is committed to be a leader in sustainability and has established 2050 Environmental Sustainability Goals (“Sustainability Goals”) that articulate the community's desired long-term environmental outcomes that would fulfill the General Plan aspirations of a sustainable desert city. The Sustainability Goals include providing a clean and reliable 100-year supply of water. The Sustainability Goals and other sustainability-related information are available at https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/sustainability.html . The Sustainability Projects are intended to advance the purposes of the Sustainability Goals and to generally comply with the “Green Bond Principles,” “Social Bond Principles” or the “Sustainability Bond Guidelines” promulgated by the International Capital Market Association (“ICMA”) in June 2018. The Series 2020B Bonds will not constitute “exempt facility bonds” issued to finance “qualified green building and sustainable design projects” within the meaning of Section 142(1) of the Code. Impacts from the Sustainability Projects are also aligned with several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (“UN SDGs”). By reference to the ICMA “Green and Social Bonds: A High-Level Mapping to the Sustainable Development Goals” (June 2019), the Sustainability Project primarily aims to address goals 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and 13 (Climate Action). To see the full disclosure, please visit https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/06-30-2024%20Sustainability%20Bonds.pdf?appId=aemshell

project_info: Transport - Zero Emissions Bus Fleet: The Phoenix City Council voted to transition the City's heavy-duty bus fleet to zero-emission models by 2040 as part of the Climate Action Plan and Transportation Electrification Action Plan goals, with a contract approval to begin procurement of $230 million. project_info: Transport - City Facility Vehicle Electrification Stations: The Mayor and City Council approved a proposed General Obligation (GO) Bond program of $500 million (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/budget/general-obligation-bond.html ) with recommendations presented to and approved by the City Council in 2022. The GO Bond Program was approved by Phoenix voters on November 7, 2023. These included projects from the Environment and Sustainability Subcommittee (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/budget/general-obligation-bond/environment-sustainability.html ), like City Facility Vehicle Electrification Stations for $1.3 million (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/bondsite/documents/Executive_Committee_Recommendations_to_City_Council.pdf ). These will provide electrification infrastructure at city facilities to support the city's fleet, residents, and employees. The number and type of installations funded by this item are driven by capital needs identified by an ongoing fleet electrification study. Energy and water efficiency and renewable energy upgrades at City facilities have $13.5 million allocated, heat and resiliency are funded with $7.3 million, and City Brownfield redevelopment projects were assigned $3 million. On April 9, 2020, the series 2020B bonds were designated based on the social impacts of the Colorado River Resiliency projects that will fund or partially fund some of the following projects among others: 1) Groundwater Well Projects, 2) Booster Pump Station Rehabilitation, 3) Water Resiliency Program, and 4) Landfill Injection Well.

project_info: Transport - Increase City Fleet Turnover to Reduce Emissions: Transportation is Phoenix's largest category of GHG emissions. The City and the Phoenix community are adding infrastructure and vehicles that use more sustainable fuels, such as electric vehicles (EVs), a zero-emissions electric bus fleet, and a growing number of EV charging stations for the public, City fleet, and City employees. The City is transitioning its fleet to EVs, with a Phoenix Electric Vehicle implementation strategy goal of 200 EVs in the fleet by 2030. There are 100 EVs in the fleet as of summer 2025. The City of Phoenix is committed to green fleet technology related to alternative fuels and new vehicle technology, focusing on low-carbon alternative fuels and electric vehicles. In November 2023, the City received the EV City Award from Plug In America for its efforts identified in the Transportation Electrification Action Plan. “The City of Phoenix is a shining example for cities around the country when it comes to the creation and implementation of an electric vehicle program,” said Joel Levin, Executive Director with Plug in America. The City received the Top Green Fleet Award in August 2023 from the National Association of Fleet Administrators (NAFA). The Top Green Fleet Award recognizes organizations that make a positive fleet environmental impact and implement groundbreaking initiatives. “The City of Phoenix really does it all,” said Rhea Courtney Bozic, NAFA 's Chief Judge of the Green Fleet Awards. “It's clean fuel integration is the best in the country. They have excellent training for staff and a strong organizational commitment to greenhouse gas reduction.”

On-site stormwater retention areas must be sufficient to contain the 100-year, 2-hour storm event per the 2013 Phoenix Stormwater Policies and Standards Manual. The City code also requires that developments not increase the 100-year, two-hour peak runoff, change the time of the runoff peak, or increase the total runoff from pre-development values. | Extreme heat: Phoenix typically has 100 days or more that are over 38 degrees Celsius. By 2060, that number is expected to rise to 132 days per year, and by 2100 Phoenix would experience at least 163 days per year, according to the World Climate Research Programme. Extreme heat impacts individuals and families differently but makes it difficult to maintain indoor temperatures that are comfortable and healthy. Vulnerable communities to extreme heat include elderly, low-income households, outdoor workers, and those experiencing homelessness. In 2024, the City created 370 new shelter beds for those experiencing homelessness. An additional 310 shelter beds have opened in 2025, with an additional 70 beds planned to open by the end of 2025 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/homeless-solutions-news/phoenix-opens-new-280-bed-shelter-ahead-of-summer-heat.html, https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/neighborhood-services-news/3277.html). The Phoenix City Council passed a new ordinance that requires contractors who work for the City to enact heat safety protections for outdoor workers in March 2024. This ordinance took effect in May 2024 (https://nationalcosh.org/news/press-releases/2024-03-phoenix-heat-ordinance). The new rule requires those contractors to have a heat safety plan that provides free cool water to employees, shade and air conditioning access, hydration breaks, and training. Phoenix continues to participate in the Maricopa County Heat Relief Network, with numerous facilities participating in 2025, offering cooling centers and hydration stations. In 2025, Phoenix operates the only 24/7 heat respite center for overnight heat relief in the state. Phoenix also has extended hours at three of its libraries serving as cooling centers May 1 through September 30 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/heat-news/city-of-phoenix-opens-heat-relief-locations-to-keep-residents-sa.html). | Infectious disease: The vector-borne diseases (VBD) threat is an emerging climate change concern in Phoenix. project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Climate Hazard Assessment including vulnerability to contaminated sites and waste facilities: Assessment of vulnerability to contaminated sites and waste facilities from extreme weather events. The City of Phoenix, Office of Environmental Programs, worked with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on a pilot project to understand the risks to communities from exposure to water-and air-borne pollutants during extreme weather events, including extreme heat, floods, and drought. The results of this pilot research will be useful in future development and remedial decision-making. The goal of the project was to develop a clear, transparent, and credible indicator-based method to assess and respond to the impacts of extreme events on pollutants released by waste management operations or the cleanup and restoration of land resources at varying stages of identification, characterization, and regulatory control. The project also developed methods for prioritizing those facilities and sites for future investigation and action. The project included a hazard map with exposure pathways and potentially vulnerable populations in the area, emphasizing a 0.5-mile north and south boundary of the Salt River.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Our anticipated time scale is Current. Our City is experiencing larger rainfall events in greater frequency that create flash flooding. This flooding results in landslides, combined sewer overflows, property (infrastructure) damage, and, in the worst cases, loss of life. Flash flooding combined with aging infrastructure leads to public safety issues wherein roads are not passable to respond to emergencies and cars can be swept away. In 2011, flash flooding on Pittsburgh's Washington Boulevard led to 4 deaths. Increased flooding in our streets can also lead to sewage backing up into residential and commercial basements. This leads to health issues such as exposure to harmful bacteria, respiratory illness from mold spore inhalation, and an increase in mosquitos and cholera exposure due to standing/stagnant water. As rain events become more frequent and more severe, roads that were paved over streams are more prone to flooding, endangering citizens and emergency responders.We are actively combating this issue with major upgrades to our water infrastructure to install separated storm sewer systems under our MS4 permit. In addition, our water utility has instituted a stormwater fee and is working to roll out a Stormwater Management Strategic Plan to identify and remediate our most flood risk communities with green and grey infrastructure upgrades. We also updated our Stormwater Management Ordinance in 2022 to address the increasing rainfall and infrastructure needs for new and redevelopments. Awareness campaigns and flood prevention technologies have also been deployed | Heavy precipitation: Much of the city is adjacent to rivers and streams and their floodplains, and local weather patterns can produce a range of extreme precipitation events. In Pittsburgh the main precipitation related hazard will be in form of more frequent and intense heavy rainfall events, such as microbursts. In the last 20 years Pittsburgh has broken its wettest year on record three times, with the most recent record set in 2018 followed by 2019 . These are events are not outliers, they are becoming the new normal. In the last century, average precipitation in Pennsylvania has increased an average of 10% and is expected to increase an additional 8% by 2050.Increase in rainfall equates to flooding, landslides, and Combined Sewer Overflow for Pittsburgh. As rain events become more frequent and more severe, roads are more prone to flooding, endangering citizens and emergency responders. | Mass movement: Landslides and subsidence incidents regularly affect parts of the city and may only get worse. The city and region have a long history of coal extraction and related erosion, putting many areas at risk for subsidence and sink holes in addition to the landslide risk to Pittsburgh's fragile hillsides. These risks are exacerbated by extreme weather events such as heavy rainfall. In fact, 900 structures within the city limits are considered to be in areas “very hazardous to landslides”, and all of Allegheny County is classified as a “high incidence” area for landslides.39,54 In recent years, landslides have occurred in the neighborhoods of Oakland, Greenfield, and Perry North.Because the region is expected to continue experiencing increased precipitation due to climate change, areas around Pittsburgh's hillsides with an existing elevated risk of landslides due to topography and development must be prepared for increased number of landslide occurrences. Currently, landslides are not regulated unless they affect a road, pipeline or waterway. In 2022 alone the City of Pittsburgh allocated $14 million for slope remediation to address slides and earth movement across Pittsburgh's many hillsides. Often the amount allocations is not enough to cover unexpected incidents and has put a strain on the City budget, taking allocations away from other services to cover the cost. The infrastructure disruption impacts the fabric of the city including access and puts the lives of our residents and emergency service staff at risk. | Extreme heat: Extreme hot and cold temperatures are expected to have a greater impact on the city in the future. Pittsburgh also experiences an “urban heat island effect,” in which cities with morethermal mass tend to be 1 to 3 degrees warmer than surrounding rural areas. Pittsburgh's aging population and housing infrastructure, including outdated heating and cooling systems, place residents at increased risk of negative health effects stemming from extreme temperatures. | Loss of green space/green cover: Invasive forest pathogens and pests, in particular the emerald ash borer and the asian longhorned beetle, pose a current threat to Pittsburgh's tree canopy. As much as 70% of Pittsburgh's trees could be lost if the Asian Longhorned Beetle were to come to Pittsburgh. The emerald ash borer was first identified in Pittsburgh in 2007 and attacks all ash trees, which make up nine percent of the city's tree canopy. Loss of tree canopy leads to hillside instability and higher landslide susceptibility. A reduction in tree canopy would not only reduce air and water quality benefits but it would also reduce green space available for outdoor recreation and can lead to higher surface temperatures.
project_info: Water management - WaterNow Green Stormwater Infrastructure: The project with the WaterNow Alliance will establish the foundation for a joint program between the City of Pittsburgh and the Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority for strategic, large-scale conversion of vacant lots to green stormwater infrastructure (GSI). The program will help to address flooding and water quality challenges by advancing GSI implementation in areas facing particularly high Combined Sewer Overflows, flood risks and environmental injustices across Pittsburgh. It will improve the climate resiliency of local communities, the quality of human life, and promote healthy natural systems and improved water quality in Pittsburgh's priority watersheds, and hopefully establish a model that can be replicated region-wide.

project_info: Public and green spaces - Riverview Park Invasive Species Management: At 259 acres, Riverview Park is one of the City's largest and most wooded parks, facing a deluge of ecological and environmental threats that will only continue to be exacerbated by climate change. The park is suffering from multiple active landslides, overpopulation of deer which has resulted in a Crazy Snake Worm infestation, furthered destabilized soil, and complete upheaval of a healthy ecosystem. There is a dire need for addressing the presence of invasive plant species such as woody vines threatening the vital tree canopy provided by the park. Funding is needed for exploring deer population management, which could aid in addressing the worm infestation (and thus more stable soil), establishing a crucial understory, and bringing balance to the natural ecosystems of the park. https://www.thenorthsidechronicle.com/2022/11/17/opinion-riverview-park-how-one-parks-ecosystem-and-maybe-its-legacy-is-eroding-away/

project_info: Land-Use - Flooding and Landslide Properties Buyout Program: As the City continues to see more frequent and intense rain events, the issues of flooding and landslides cannot be ignored. The City must design and deploy a sustainable, equitable strategy for removing properties from the most at-risk areas. The FEMA grant we have received ($300,000 grant + $100,000 city match) will use the Saw Mill Run watershed as a pilot for developing policies and programs for how to engage residents in conversations around buyouts, as well as establishing a cost-benefit analysis for decision-making. There is additional funding needed for expanding the resulting program to the rest of the City, including exploring land-use tools such as Transfer of Development Rights or other development regulations for properties in the landslide prone areas of the City.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Rain Gardens in Complementary Green Areas: Porto Alegre is frequently subjected to flooding resulting from heavy rains that compromise the economic, social and environmental development of the affected regions. The city has so-called Complementary Greens, public spaces, located at roundabouts and medians, distributed throughout the territory. The proposal presented seeks to promote, in an innovative way, the use of these spaces for the implementation of rain gardens, using existing public infrastructure as a tool to mitigate the effects caused in times of large volumes of rain. Furthermore, it promotes adaptation, ecological restoration and beautification of roads, given the scarcity of vegetation and high densification of the area, through the planting and maintenance of flora with greater water absorption potential, also enabling the diversification of fauna. These spaces are identified as strategic for the implementation of the project, as they are residual areas, already part of the municipality's strategic environmental public policy actions and with great potential to house nature-based solutions and which represent an important step by the Municipality of Porto Alegre in the construction of a new approach to the management of rainwater in the municipality. climate_hazard: Heat stress: Cities across the Southeast are experiencing more frequent and longer summer heat waves, with increasing overnight low temperatures and extended frost-free seasonality. Data from the National Climatic Data Center (NCDC) shows that temperatures are currently approximately 1° C (1.8° F) above pre-industrial levels, with the last decade being the hottest on record. The last three decades have each been successively warmer than any decade before since recordings started in 1850. Tampa is experiencing increasing overnight low temperatures and extended frost-free seasonality. Tampa currently experiences approximately 73 days each year with 'feels like' temperatures of 100° F and above. By 2053, that number is expected to reach 103 days. Average annual temperatures for Tampa have increased by 2.5° F since records began in 1891.9 The summer of 2022 was the warmest on record for Tampa with an average temperature of 85.7° F. These changes are absorbed into the urban environment, creating thermal impacts, especially as hard and impervious surfaces soak up the heat. Climate change induces ecosystem change, and issues such as water quality are important to monitor. There is a human response to heat as well. Increased temperatures require more air conditioning and can cause risks, particularly for vulnerable populations. Hotter days can have dangerous impacts on public health, including on people's ability to work, to bike, or to walk around their neighborhood, with especially adverse effects on older populations, those with underlying health conditions, and those with special needs. Research has also shown that infectious diseases and non-historic health problems may occur more frequently as climate zones shift. People can become exposed to non-endemic influences, causing unique reactions. Vector borne diseases from mosquitoes is a primary concern, especially in the Tampa region. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) suggests that sea levels will rise by 14 to 18 inches in the Gulf from 2020 to 2050, with flooding to occur more than 10 times as often as is experienced today. The Tampa Bay Climate Science Advisory Panel has concluded that Gulf waters will be anywhere between 1.5 to 5.5 feet above 2020 levels by the year 2100. Many coastal communities are built to the edges without much room to spare. Drainage systems, which rely on ponds and soil for water storage, will be affected by increased groundwater levels. The National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration has recently said that, based on historic trajectories, we can expect 4-8 inches of sea level rise in the next 30 years, with high levels of confidence. This change at the coast will not only affect water entering stormwater systems and overtopping sea walls, but habitats will change, stormwater ponds will become brackish and will not serve their purpose, aquifers will also be affected by salinity, and infrastructure will become impaired, such as roadways and utilities. Increased sea levels will cause flooding at the coast, but will also put pressure on stormwater systems inland. Combined with an expectation of more intense storms, urban areas could see more flooding, especially in low-lying zones | Storm: Warmer coastal waters can create more intense storms for the Gulf region, with heavier and longer-lasting rainfall events. When rainfall is concentrated, or when it lasts longer, total water volumes can overwhelm stormwater systems, leading to increased flood levels and damage. The economic impacts of such storms can be devastating. The costs of Hurricane Ian, for example, which directly hit the Fort Myers Beach area, is projected to have costs of more than $50 billion. 2017 was the costliest year on record, with a figure of near $300 billion. Studies have shown that there is roughly a 30% increased likelihood of major storms in the coming decade. \n\nHurricanes Helene and Milton hit the west coast of Florida within a two-week span. Helene brought historic storm surges to coastal neighborhoods, and Milton brought unprecedented levels of wind and rainfall. 2024 has been the rainiest year on record for Tampa, with 77 inches of rain registered so far. It has put a strain on individuals, businesses, front-line workers, first responders, and government officials. Hurricane Helene's size and Milton's rapid intensification linked to climate change could cost insurers $30-$60 billion.

River flooding: San Jose has three major rivers/creeks with numerous tributaries featuring various levels of flood control mitigation. While flood mitigation features continue to be installed over time, climate change is projected to increase flood volumes by 60 to 80% over the next 50 years. Climate change is also expected to drive earlier snow melt upstream, leading to higher stream flow increases and increased likelihood of flooding. San José's waterways have a history of flooding causing damage to private property and transportation infrastructure. In February 2017, the Coyote Creek flooded large areas of downtown San José causing 11,000 residents to evacuate and $73 million in damages, including extensive damage in residential neighborhoods. During this flood, one sewage pump station was flooded, suspending sanitary sewer service for a day. Most recently, in February 2024, an atmospheric river storm led the City to issue an evacuation order along the Coyote, Los Gatos, Penitencia, and Ross Creeks; additionally, more than 20,000 residents lost power. 
Low-income households are less likely to have the resources to recover from flood damage to their homes. Many unhoused people in San José live along river and creek corridors, and so have to relocate if there is a risk of flooding or face direct flooding impacts like losing their belongings.
Real estate activities are impacted because increased flooding risk can lead to increased home insurance prices. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): San Jose is ringed by zones of Moderate Fire Hazard Severity. As of 2022, approximately 46,000 residents (4% of the total population) live in areas at risk to wildfire and 16,122 structures worth $487 million are in high wildfire risk areas. In addition, all residents are vulnerable to reduced air quality from wildfire smoke. For example: In 2020, the SCU Lightning Complex wildfire led to the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in the East San Jose foothills. Additionally, the skies were orange and Northern California had the worst air quality in the entire world. Wildfires can also disrupt energy distribution, both directly by disrupting transmission lines and indirectly by causing utilities to shut down electricity distribution to avoid generating fire-starting sparks. In San Jose, PG&E began using Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPSs; https://www.pge.com/en_US/residential/outages/public-safety-power-shuttoff/psps-reports.page) during the 2019 fire season to reduce the risk of wildfire by preemptively stopping electricity distribution during high-temperature, high-wind conditions. In the first PSPS event affecting San Jose in 2019, almost 20,000 San Jose customer accounts went without power an average of more than 16 hours. In the second PSPS event affecting San Jose, almost 7,500 customer accounts went without power for an average of more than 40 hours. These accounts included hundreds of residents relying on electrically powered medical equipment and many different critical facilities. Fortunately, the situation was better in 2020, with fewer than 10 electricity customers in San Jose affected by PSPS events.Children and youth, elderly people, and people with health conditions are more vulnerable than others to health impacts from breathing in wildfire smoke.People in marginalized/minority communities and low-income households (who are less likely to live in well-sealed homes with good air filtration), outdoor workers, and people who are unhoused are more likely to be exposed to wildfire smoke.The agriculture and construction sectors have many outdoor workers who are more likely to be exposed to wildfire smoke. | Drought: Santa Clara County has experienced four prolonged periods of drought since 1975. The most severe drought in the last 1,200 years occurred from 2012 -16, during which record high temperatures and low precipitation led to a statewide emergency and water restrictions to limit water use by 20%. From 2020-21, 90% of the Southwest and California was in a severe drought due to high temperatures and very low rainfall in the spring and summer of 2020. Record low snowpack in the Sierra Nevada mountains led to reservoir levels at 34-50% of capacity, prompting Valley Water and water retailers servicing San José to implement water conservation programs and mandatory restrictions.
Droughts are projected to become more severe as average annual temperatures rise and dry spells between precipitation events become longer. The maximum length of a dry spell is projected to increase from 119 days historically to 129 days in mid-century and 134 days in late-century. Average snowpack in the Sierras is projected to decline by 30-60% in mid-century and by over 80% in late-century. Drought, both in the Sierra Nevada mountains and the local region, decreases the availability and quality of water for humans. This includes reduced water levels to fight wildfires. Drought may increase exposure to health hazards including wildfires, dust storms, extreme heat events, land subsidence, increased water pollution, erosion, degraded water quality, reduced water quantity, degradation of watersheds, alteration of ecosystems and loss of habitat. 
Low-income households would be most affected by any increases in rates for water as a response to droughts, as the high cost of living in San Jose means that many low-income families are already struggling to make ends meet.
The agriculture sector would be greatly affected because of the need for crop irrigation.
In addition, habitats in our county have evolved in a relatively mild climate, with large storms and long, intense droughts happening only rarely, so droughts have an impact on conservation as well. The county currently supports several fragile habitats that may be particularly vulnerable to climate extremes; however, precipitation changes will impact all habitats. Examples of potential impacts include species composition changes due to more frequent wildfires and increase in invasive species. Decreases in ecosystem services associated with vegetation change may also result in impacts to adjacent built lands. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise threatens the South San Francisco Bay shoreline, including parts of the City of San José. Roughly 2% (33,000) of county residents live within the current 100-year flood zone, and almost half of that exposed population are at higher risk due to a combination of social vulnerability factors. By 2100, this increases to 4% (86,000) of residents. 
The residential community of Alviso, the San Jose-Santa Clara Regional Wastewater Facility (Facility), several solid waste facilities, a water purification facility and numerous other privately-owned industrial sites, including many of Silicon Valley's 'high-tech' companies, could all be subject to coastal flooding. The area also features extensive wildlife habitat. 
Sea level rise may mobilize contaminants and expose vulnerable populations to metals and petrochemicals. Low-income households are less likely to have the resources to recover from flood damage to their homes. In addition, many of the residents of Alviso belong to marginalized/minority communities and/or have low incomes. | Extreme heat: A limited increase in the number of heat waves is expected by 2050. By 2100, between six and 10 more heat waves can be expected per year. In addition, extreme heat days and especially nights have become more frequent since 1950 and will continue to increase. Increased temperatures manifested as heat waves and sustained high heat days directly harm human health through heat-related illnesses (mild heat stress to fatal heat stroke) and the exacerbation of pre-existing conditions in the medically fragile, chronically ill, and vulnerable. Children and youth, elderly people, and people with vulnerable health are innately more vulnerable to the impacts of heat. Low-income households and people in marginalized/minority communities (who are less likely to have air conditioning), outdoor workers, and people who are unhoused are less able to avoid being exposed to heat during extreme heat events. The agriculture and construction sectors are particularly exposed to extreme heat impacts because many workers in these sectors work outside. Human health and social work activities must respond to increased needs (for example, for cooling centers) during extreme heat events. In 2010, the county had approximately 39,000 outdoor workers whose occupation increased their risk of heat illness, and about 35% of households in the county were estimated to lack air conditioning. Increased heat also intensifies the photochemical reactions that produce smog and ground level ozone and fine particulates (PM2.5), which contribute to and exacerbate respiratory disease in children and adults. Increased heat and carbon dioxide enhance the growth of plants that produce pollen, which are associated with allergies. Increased temperatures add to the heat load of buildings in urban areas and exacerbate existing urban heat islands adding to the risk of high ambient temperatures. Extreme heat can lead to rolling blackouts and power loss across the City, cause infrastructure stress and deterioration as well as a decrease in availability of cooling technologies.

Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfire: 
In the City's Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment the City of San Diego used a conservative approach to plan for a future wildfire risk of equal or greater severity than that of recent decades The City based its wildfire vulnerability assessment on its four current measures of fire risk: the City's brush management zone, a 100 foot and 300foot buffer around the brush management zone, and the fire hazard severity zone. These areas indicate where fuel for potential wildfires exists within the City.

Conservation The vulnerability assessment found conservation areas open space lands and community parks to be highly vulnerable to wildfire as many of these resource areas are located within the very high fire hazard severity zone and are highly sensitive can be destroyed by wildfires Additionally wildfires in open space areas can lead to increased erosion and high volumes of pollutants entering the air and water impacting overall quality and function. 

Transportation assets such as airports bridges and major arterials were found to be highly vulnerable in the City's vulnerability assessment These assets face high exposure and can be damaged by wildfires resulting is limited functionality and/or required replacement Vulnerable communities who have limited mobility access and are located near high wildfire risk areas may also face increased risk if required to evacuate.

Low-income households may have more limited mobility access and may face more difficulty if required to evacuate and seek shelter elsewhere. Vulnerable health populations may be disproportionately impacted by the poor air quality associated with wildfires. 
 | Heavy precipitation: Changes in Precipitation:
According to the City's Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment annual average precipitation projections from CalAdapt and other sources suggest only modest changes in total annual precipitation in the decades ahead but there is expected to be more variability in rainfall from year to year and more intense transitions between droughts and deluges. This is in part due to an expected intensification of atmospheric rivers which are often responsible for extreme precipitation events that punctuate dry spells in Southern California. 

Vulnerable populations: Vulnerable populations including low-income households and marginalized communities will have fewer resources to respond to and recover from flood events For example it may be more difficult for a low-income household to complete necessary repairs following a flood event Additionally marginalized communities who have not historically seen the same level of investment may have aging infrastructure that is less able to handle flood events 

Water supply: Extreme precipitation can cause dam overtopping and may increase sediment load in water held by dams.
Wastewater (sewerage): Wastewater pumpstations could be highly vulnerable to precipitation due to failures of pump stations or generator failure that could affect operations.

Conservation: Flash flooding has the potential to impact habitats. Increased precipitation patterns could encourage the growth of invasive species, which increases the risk of habitat type conversion (especially for sensitive, rare native habitat types such as coastal scrub and maritime chaparral communities) to exotic grasslands. In addition, flooding in watersheds could impact water quality by bringing more nutrients and total dissolved solids into the water supply.

Stormwater: Stormwater assets such as outfalls pipes and channels can be overwhelmed during high volume peak flows Extreme precipitation events that exceed system design may require system upgrades for full functionality.
 | Drought: Manufacturing: During drought conditions, reductions in or interruption of the water supply can result in decreased plant productivity or closure of manufacturing facilities, affect reservoir and groundwater levels, and impact sanitation and hygiene, including increase in disease. Manufacturers often use high volumes of water for many processes and a shortage would require business owners to find alternatives, decrease productivity, or close facilities. Lower water levels at reservoirs not only impact availability of drinking water but also impact recreation and tourism. Many manufacturing processes rely heavily on water. If seeing a decrease in available water supply, manufacturing facilities will ultimately suffer a reduction in productivity and feel the economic impacts of such. This can result in workforce reductions or even plant closures. Additionally, some manufacturing processes rely on clean water to dilute pollutants that they discharge to waste streams and lack of water supply could have negative impacts on City-owned treatment works (these negative impacts could include fire/explosion hazards, corrosive materials, or other materials that disrupt the treatment process).

Water Supply: Droughts cause public health and safety impacts, as well as economic and environmental impacts. Public health and safety impacts are primarily associated with catastrophic wildfire risks and drinking water shortage risks for small water systems in rural areas and private residential wells. Examples of other impacts include costs to homeowners due to loss of residential landscaping, degradation of urban environments due to loss of landscaping, agricultural land fallowing and associated job loss, degradation of fishery habitat, and tree mortality with damage to forest ecosystems.

Human Health and Social Work Activities: Social workers are needed to address the impact of the current drought by aiding those most affected. They help provide individuals and families with basic necessities, such as food and water. This includes providing guidance and counseling for parents and children and making referrals to hospitals for those with critical health conditions. 

Vulnerable populations will face greater difficulty in their ability to pay for increasing water rates. Cost of water will be a greater cost burden to these populations. | Extreme heat: Extreme Heat: In the City's Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment the City used urban heat island index data from CalEPA to project areas that could be exposed to extreme heat. These data were the best available spatial information for heat within the City at the time of the vulnerability assessment. Since then the City has developed an Urban Heat Vulnerability Index (UHVI) that considers heat exposure and socioeconomic vulnerability (i.e. age, pre-existing health conditions) to extreme heat by census tract. The UHVI shows that risk to extreme heat is not evenly distributed across the city with certain census tracts facing disproportionate risk due to lack of green space heat retention due to development patterns or existing health factors such as age or preexisting conditions that increase heat vulnerability. 

Vulnerable populations / health groups: Overall there is a high degree of overlap of areas that have a large Urban Heat Island effect or are high risk under the UHVI with both the City's designated Communities of Concern and more vulnerable populations. Elderly populations, children and youth, pregnant women, and people with pre-existing health conditions are all at higher risk to impacts from extreme heat events. 

Additionally the City's Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment found the Open Space and Environment sector including conservation areas and open space land to be highly vulnerable to heat. Conservation and open spaces areas were found to be highly vulnerable to extreme heat due to increased rates of evaporation resulting in less water conveyance to distribution reservoirs shifts in species ranges and negative impacts to survival rates of sensitive species. 

Human health and social work activities are vulnerable to extreme heat as the climate hazard can lead to health impacts such as cardiovascular failure or respiratory disease. Outdoor workers are particularly vulnerable. 

Projections are for more frequent and longer heat waves higher peak temperatures for hot days and warmer nights.
 | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea Level Rise:
According to the June 2024 updated sea level rise guidance from the California Ocean Protection Council, based upon the 2022 Federal Sea Level Rise Technical report, which is based on the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change report, sea levels in San Diego are likely to rise between 0.8 and 1.3 feet by 2050 and may rise between 1.6 and 6.7 feet by 2100. By elevating storm tide sea level rise makes it easier for waves to surpass natural barriers increasing the relative frequency of flooding along the coast. 

Coastal Erosion: The sandstone bluffs along the San Diego coast are prone to erosion from waves and from storm water runoff. Sea level rise together with increased storm frequency are likely to accelerate beach and other shoreline and cliff erosion. In 2003 the City completed a coastal erosion assessment In 2018 the updated coastal erosion assessment found that while the City has made improvements to pedestrian access and safety along the erosion sites additional sites pose threats to pedestrian access or safety. 

Conservation: Conservation areas could experience damage or significant alteration if exposed to chronic flooding. The changes to ecosystems that come with sea level rise impacts—changes in sediment, nutrient availability, and salinity—could lead to shifts in habitat locations and may cause certain habitats to shrink or disappear.

Stormwater: There are outfalls with elevation that would be chronically inundated or submerged resulting in poor drainage and/or backflow of water. The storm water system may become inundated by floods and higher groundwater levels.

Transportation: Daily inundation could cause structural damage to roads and bridges and cut off access from flooded routes Conservation Sea level rise can cause changes in sediment nutrient availability and salinity leading to shifts or reduction in habitat Coastal bluffs are home to sensitive species that may be impacted by future coastal erosion.

Public Safety: Lifeguard stations face high exposure to sea level rise driven flooding and erosion due to the requirement of their coastal location.

Low Income households: Low-income households will have fewer resources to adapt to sea level rise whether adaptation includes home retrofits increased insurance rates or potential relocation

The project has completed 60% design. The City is requesting funds to support construction.

Water management - El Cerrito and Rolando Park Storm Drain and GI project: The El Cerrito & Rolando Park Storm Drain and Green Infrastructure project is located in the disadvantaged community of Mid-City: Eastern Area within Council District 9, which is located in the Chollas Creek sub-watershed. The project consists of replacing Corrugated Metal Pipe (CMP) storm drains in poor condition at the intersection of College Avenue and University Avenue and in an adjacent residential neighborhood (Rolando Blvd, Vivian St, Vista Grande Dr, Hope St, and Loma Alta Dr). The pipes will be replaced with appropriately sized Reinforced Concrete Pipe (RCP). In addition, a new RCP storm drain will be installed starting at a proposed cleanout in front of 4054 Loma Alta Dr. and terminating at the concrete lined channel west of the Rolando Blvd./Vista Grande Dr. intersection. Also, this project will abandon pipes within private property and realign it to the right-of-way when feasible. The flood resilience improvements will encompass a drainage area of approximately 48 acres. Finally, this project will also target six drainage areas with one of the highest pollutant loads near the College Avenue and University Avenue intersection by capturing runoff and treating a portion of the runoff with Best Management Practices (BMPs). The runoff will be treated by eight (8) Modular Wetland Systems. The green infrastructure improvements encompass a drainage area of approximately 25 acres.

The storm drain infrastructure within the project location is aging, and the area is prone to flooding. The proposed improvements will provide a 100-year level of service and mitigate the flood risk by adequately capturing storm water within the streets. In addition, the project will improve water quality by installing new green infrastructure that will remove pollutants from the captured runoff. This project would support compliance with regulatory requirements, specifically the metals Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) targets for Chollas Creek. Meeting these targets is essential for maintaining environmental health and the sustainability of natural resources. 

This project has completed final design. The City is requesting funds to support construction.

Landscape and Jurisdictional Approaches - Wildfire Operations and Resilience Center: Establish a Wildfire Operations and Resilience Center in the City of San Diego. The facility will centralize key wildfire mitigation programs, serving as the base of operations for the Fuel Treatment Program, Chipping and Vegetation Management Program, Public Education and Community Outreach Program, and Certified Tree Faller Deployment Program. Utilizing modular shipping container structures for rapid deployment, the center will be constructed on City-owned property at the San Diego Fire Department Logistics Division site in Kearny Mesa. 

The facility will include: 
•	Modular container-based structures 
•	Upgraded pavement and drainage 
•	On-site power and lighting systems 
•	Covered vehicle and equipment storage bays 

The project scope includes resurfacing of the site, foundational work, and electrical upgrades necessary to support long-term facility operations. This site will also store and protect equipment procured through prior wildfire preparedness efforts and provide staging space for field crews.

Many of these structures are over 60 years old and require significant reinvestment to meet current seismic and safety standards. Several are classified as high-hazard by the California Division of Safety of Dams.\n\nThe Dam Safety Program addresses these risks through condition assessments, seismic studies, and modernization projects, including the planned replacement of Hodges Dam. These investments are essential to maintain water reliability and ensure public safety.

climate_hazard:
Heat stress: Tel Aviv-Yafo is increasingly experiencing heat stress due to climate change. The coastal location typically moderates temperatures. However, rising sea levels and changes in atmospheric circulation patterns can lead to increased humidity, which intensifies the perceived heat and makes it more difficult for the body to cool down. Additionally, the urban heat island effect, where urban areas are significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas due to human-induced factors, exacerbates heat stress in the city. 
Rising temperatures and humidity levels pose significant health risks to the population, particularly vulnerable groups. 
Vulnerable Populations
•	Elderly: Older adults are particularly susceptible to heat-related illnesses due to age-related physiological changes that impair their ability to regulate body temperature. 
•	Children: Children's bodies are less efficient at regulating temperature, making them more vulnerable to heat stress. 
•	Individuals with chronic health conditions: People with underlying health conditions such as heart disease, respiratory problems, or diabetes are at a higher risk of heat-related complications. 
•	Outdoor workers: Individuals working outdoors, such as construction workers, farmers, and street vendors, are exposed to high temperatures and humidity for extended periods, increasing their risk of heat-related illnesses. 
Heat stress can also significantly impact the functioning of city services. Extreme heat can strain the healthcare system, as demand for emergency medical services increases due to heat-related illnesses. Public transportation systems may face disruptions due to high temperatures and increased demand, affecting mobility and accessibility. The city's energy infrastructure can also be challenged during heatwaves, as demand for electricity for cooling increases. 
 | Heavy precipitation: Intense rain results in flooding, due to river overflow and blockage of the city's drainage system. The overflow of rainwater drains directly into the sea which causes further flooding and water pollution. Rainstorms affect residents, businesses, and living conditions. The location of the city in the floodplains of the Yarkon and Ayalon Rivers makes it a vulnerable spot for flooding, and the proximity of disadvantaged neighborhoods' to the floodplains increase the vulnerability of these populations. Flooding also causes infrastructure and transport-related damages, personal injury and property damages, and is harmful for both disadvantaged population groups and natural ecosystems. | Drought: According to climatic models, the amount of rainfall is expected to decrease and evaporation is expected to rise—consequently, droughts are likely to increase. More intense droughts might cause drinking water and food supply problems and negatively affect biodiversity. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Tel Aviv Yafo is a coastal city' with a relatively long stretch of beach front of 13km. This area is vulnerable to storm surges and the gradual rise of sea level. | Extreme heat: The average temperature in Israel is expected to rise from 0.90 to 1.20 degrees (Co) from the current period (2018) to the end of 2050. Summer is getting longer.Impacts: Heat waves coupled with the humidity in Tel Aviv-Yafo amplify the urban heat island effect. The heat waves make the city's public spaces and streets practically unusable, thus negatively effecting local businesses and urban living. The heatwaves also affect the city's sustainability, water quality, transportation system, biodiversity, telecommunication, and electricity usage. Health impacts result in increased morbidity, higher demand for health services, and increased vulnerability of vulnerable population groups. The overload of air-conditioning on the electricity grid produces frequent power shortages and emits heat to the public realm. | Drought: Climate change directly affects water availability for nature due to rising heat and evaporation, increasing the need for irrigation while natural water sources decline. The type of vegetation also influences water consumption; local plants adapted to a hot, arid climate are less affected by climate change. In recent years, Tel Aviv-Yafo has been making efforts to preserve and integrate local, native vegetation in both public and private spaces. However, over the last decade, the municipality has already had to extend the irrigation season by four months
. In 2024, an extra month of irrigation was added, and the system was effectively operational for 11 months.

Some companies and factories interrupted their activities for days, with costs due to the productivity losses and damage to production infrastructures. The school system was suspended. The impacts were on the public health system and relative service costs, on the industrial processes (more fire due to very hot temperatures and difficulties in the water using for cooling). The heatwaves affect the green of the city, favoring the invasive plants (algae bloom in the rivers) and insects spread out. The human wellbeing was affected, with general discomfort for the people living in the city, transportation and social activities.
