Other: Higher average temperature: Higher average temperatures have an impact on different seasons. They cause a longer summer and a shorter winter, among other things, which in turn have repercussions on various parameters related to climate. 

As a result, the population will be more exposed to ultraviolet rays when practicing outdoor activities over a longer period. It could increase the prevalence of related health problems, such as eye and skin diseases, including cancer. Higher average summer temperatures could also extend allergenic plants' pollen production season, which can result in greater health problems for people who have allergies. In Montréal, the pollen season in late summer (July to October) has the greatest impact on health, particularly due to ragweed. Children, young adults, people with asthma, pale-skinned people, people with compromised immune systems, people who regularly practice outdoor activities and people genetically predisposed to allergies are vulnerable to the impacts of higher average temperatures. 

The effects of higher average temperatures on the built environment are mainly observed in the wintertime. The increased number of freeze-thaw cycles entails an accelerated deterioration of the roadway system (potholes) while accelerating wear on bridges, tunnels and overpasses. It also impacts the growth rate and geographical distribution of some harmful insect species, which may result in more frequent infestations and intensified damage to plants. An increase of a few degrees can generate drastic changes in plant biology, which may alter species' distribution areas and could stimulate the growth of undesirable plant species. The increase in average temperatures is also causing a northward migration of vector borne pathogen animal populations; in recent years, we have observed an increase in the occurrence of Lyme disease and West Nile virus (WNV). 

These effects will occur more or less equally across the entire island of Montréal. 

For more details: https://ville.montreal.qc.ca/pls/portal/docs/PAGE/ENVIRO_FR/MEDIA/DOCUMENTS/2017_PACCAM_2015-2020_REPORT.PDF | Extreme heat: In the past 30 years, heat waves have been responsible for over 400 deaths in the Montréal agglomeration. In Canada, atmospheric pollution is linked to around 15,300 premature deaths every year. The principal impacts of heat waves on vulnerable groups are health problems caused by air pollution, pollen and poor thermoregulation, illnesses caused by contaminated swimming water, increased mortality rate and economic losses. The boroughs of Ville-Marie, Mercier-Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension and Montréal-Nord have especially vulnerable populations: underprivileged people, people living alone, seniors, and people who speak neither French nor English. 

Vegetation is also vulnerable to heat waves, because extreme heat induces shocks, such as water stress, that can lead to illnesses; in turn, these problems increase the need for preventive maintenance and treatment. Heat waves, even brief ones, can diminish the populations of many insects. Extreme temperatures can affect or weaken the agglomeration's infrastructures by impacting roads and arteries. Finally, heat waves often give rise to an increased demand for certain services, such as the use of swimming pools, wading pools and splash pads, and the extension of the business hours of air-conditioned public buildings such as libraries and community centers. 

Industrial, commercial and highly populated areas are prone to forming IUHIs, because a good part of their surface is made up of materials that absorb the sun's rays, the soil is often sealed, and there is little vegetation. Residential buildings in densely populated areas (triplexes, multiplexes and multi-apartment buildings) are often adjoining, and have little or no backyard space. The boroughs and municipalities in the western part of the island are less prone to forming IUHIs, because they have lower density, and the most common type of dwelling is a single-family home surrounded by a yard. Some areas in the central and eastern parts of the island which share these characteristics are also located outside IUHIs, such as certain sections of Rivière-des-Prairies-Pointe-aux-Trembles and Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie. 

For more details: https://ville.montreal.qc.ca/pls/portal/docs/PAGE/ENVIRO_FR/MEDIA/DOCUMENTS/2017_PACCAM_2015-2020_REPORT.PDF 
 | Other: Destructive storms: Destructive storms are associated with a higher number of injuries related to accidental falls, building collapses, falling trees and debris; such incidents can even cause premature death. The principal impacts on vulnerable groups are inconveniences and accidents related to power outages, inconveniences related to service interruptions on above-ground utilities other than electricity (telecommunications), economic losses, accidents other than road accidents (falls, falling debris, electrification and electrocution) and psychological distress. 

The three most vulnerable groups are underprivileged people, people living alone, and seniors. These three factors are often combined. As a result, the areas where people with several of these characteristics live present particularly high social susceptibility, such as Montréal-Nord, Saint-Léonard and Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension 

Strong winds, freezing rain, hail and heavy snowfalls can all result in damages and wear on infrastructures and vegetation, which mainly consist of falling trees and branches, and damages to roofs or other components of the building envelope, and can also be a hazardous for pedestrians. Destructive storms may also cause power outages. The environmental impacts of destructive storms in an urban setting mainly affect the vegetation, particularly in terms of uprooting trees or breaking trunks and branches, which renders them more vulnerable to insects and diseases. Destructive storms increase pressure on service teams providing road maintenance (snow removal and road salting), tree maintenance and first response. 

The vulnerable areas to destructive storms are scattered throughout the island of Montréal, with a light concentration in more densely populated neighborhood's, such as Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension, Le Sud-Ouest and Verdun. 

For more details: https://ville.montreal.qc.ca/pls/portal/docs/PAGE/ENVIRO_FR/MEDIA/DOCUMENTS/2017_PACCAM_2015-2020_REPORT.PDF | Drought: Drought periods are often combined with high heat, which affects the levels of air pollutants. In dry weather, dust and particles, such as pollen, are more easily carried and contribute to poor air quality. Water quality can also be affected in times of serious drought. In very hot weather and drought, pollutants in watercourses are more difficult to dilute due to lower water flow rates. Swimmers are more likely to be contaminated and get sick. Water-borne diseases generally manifest in the form of short-term gastrointestinal trouble. Skin contact with or ingestion of poor-quality water can also cause dermatitis, as well as infections to the eyes, ears and throat. The principal impacts of droughts on vulnerable groups are health problems caused by smog, fine particles and pollen, illnesses caused by contaminated swimming water and economic losses. Many people are vulnerable to the impacts of drought, such as children aged 0 to 15, seniors aged 65 and up, people living alone and underprivileged people. The boroughs of Montréal-Nord, Saint-Léonard and Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension and Montréal-Nord have especially vulnerable populations. 

Droughts in urban settings mainly affect water quality due to a rise in temperature, a decline in dissolved oxygen concentrations, cyanobacteria blooms, eutrophication and an increased concentration of some pollutants. Droughts are also a source of water stress for plants, and may even kill them should the drought be a long one. This stress can also increase trees' vulnerability to pests and pathogens. The operational impacts of drought particularly affect drinking water production and distribution networks. 

The drying of certain types of soils causes damage to the built environment, particularly to home and building foundations, road surfaces and sidewalks. The impacts on the built environment in turn cause economic impacts due to the costs associated with reconstruction work on damaged infrastructures. Clay soils cover a good portion of the Montréal agglomeration's territory, so it's common practice here for buildings and infrastructures to be built on such soils. The Plateau-Mont-Royal and Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension boroughs are prone to settling of foundations, sidewalks and road surfaces. 

For more details: https://ville.montreal.qc.ca/pls/portal/docs/PAGE/ENVIRO_FR/MEDIA/DOCUMENTS/2017_PACCAM_2015-2020_REPORT.PDF | Heavy precipitation: Floods may increase the prevalence of health problems caused by an increase in mold if measures are not taken after the flood which can lead to serious health problems such as asthma and allergic reactions. The prevalence of gastrointestinal disease epidemics and the prevalence of psychological distress are also known impacts on vulnerable populations. Flooding can also cause material losses, which can lead to psychological distress among disaster victims. 

The principal impacts of heavy rainfall on vulnerable groups are health problems caused by the presence of mold, illness caused by the contamination of swimming pool water, vector-borne and zoonotic diseases, psychological distress, gastrointestinal disease caused by sewer backflows and floods, accidents other than road accidents, inconveniences related to the interruption of utilities other than electricity (telecommunication, gas, etc.) and economic losses. The presence of underprivileged people increases social susceptibility, since these individuals are more heavily affected by several impacts of heavy rainfalls. Elderly people are also strongly affected. Since a high proportion of elderly people live alone, and are often underprivileged, they constitute a particularly sensitive group 

Topography is the factor with the greatest influence on physical susceptibility. During heavy rainfall, once the network is saturated, runoff water can no longer enter and instead accumulates in lower points, which can cause flooding. Basements are particularly at risk of being flooded. Factors such as inadequate ground levelling and the presence of a garage entrance with a slope toward the house can result in the flooding of homes. Also, unprotected buildings can suffer from sewer backups. Older neighborhoods, located in the centre of the island and home to a high density of inhabitants, buildings and streets feature areas with water accumulation potential (Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Côte-des-Neiges-Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, Côte-Saint-Luc, Hampstead, Plateau-Mont-Royal, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, Saint-Laurent, Sud-Ouest, Verdun, and Villeray-Saint-Michel-Parc-Extension). The island's west end and part of its east end are less mineralized areas with more vegetation, which helps the soil absorb some of the rainwater, reducing the accumulation of water in basins.

When it grows significantly, it can lead to serious health problems such as asthma and allergic reactions. The prevalence of gastrointestinal disease epidemics when people are in direct contact with flood waters and of psychological distress are also known impacts on vulnerable populations. Flooding can also cause major emotional and material losses, which can lead to psychological problems among disaster victims. 

Any infrastructure or population located within a flood-prone area represents vulnerability for the territory. 5 boroughs of the City of Montréal (Ahuntsic Cartierville, L'Île-Bizard-Sainte-Geneviève, Montréal-Nord, Pierrefonds-Roxboro, Rivières-des-Prairies-Pointe-aux-Trembles) and two related cities (Senneville and Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue) are affected by river flooding. 

The principal impacts on vulnerable groups are health problems caused by the presence of mold, psychological distress, gastrointestinal disease caused by sewer backups and floods, accidents other than road accidents, inconveniences related to the interruption of utilities other than electricity (telecommunication, gas, etc.) and economic losses. Many people are vulnerable to the impacts of river floods, such as women, children aged 0 to 15, seniors aged 65 and up, people living alone and underprivileged people. 

In an urban setting, floods result in damage to the built environment and especially to buildings located in floodplains. In a flood, the sewer systems may saturate more quickly, resulting in backed up sewers in buildings. Heavy floods may weaken overtaxed infrastructures and damage them. Spring floods may also cause damage to underground utilities, which can lead to service outages. Also, floods cause premature erosion and destabilization of riverbanks. Floods in an urban environment can make it more difficult to move around, close sections of roadways and slow down traffic. Lastly, river floods require a major mobilization of the teams responsible for implementing emergency response measures.

project_info: Buildings - Ecological transition program for municipal buildings: This project is two-fold. 1) Improve the energy efficiency of buildings and decarbonize them. 2) Improving the resilience of municipal buildings to present and future climatic hazards. 1) The energy performance and decarbonization project for Montreal buildings, of the City of Montreal, aims to implement the Roadmap towards zero-emission buildings in Montreal as well as the implementation of exemplary practices in buildings owned by the city. The exemplary practices that the city wishes to put in place will serve to demonstrate that achieving carbon neutrality and energy sobriety are possible and that it's even possible to go beyond the requirements of the national codes. As part of the implementation of the Roadmap, regulations will be adopted by the City Council to require that all new construction, public or private, be zero emissions and sober in energy and existing buildings will have to gradually reduce their GHG emissions.To achieve this, the City of Montreal will put in place efforts to: - Accelerate capacity to adopt codes and regulations- set up a community of practice on the Codes with the boroughs - set up a working table with stakeholders (including energy suppliers such as Hydro-Québec and Énergir) - identify and eliminate existing regulatory barriers- provide resources and tools (guides, working methods, software, etc.) at the Permits and Inspection level,- adopt regulations in line with the Codes (construction, energy efficiency and decarbonization strategy) - carry out preliminary work to prepare the regulations that allow the improvement of the codes (regulation on the new zero emission building)- allow the imposition of GHG performance thresholds for the existing building, mandatory declaration of equipment foremissive heating)- strengthen communication capacity (awareness and mobilization)- set up a tool for monitoring and analyzing real data- develop training modules on the new construction code for City staff - set up a one-stop information window (targeting citizens) concerning financial assistance programs for GHG reduction and energy efficiency - carrying out studies on the development of municipal programs oriented towards decarbonization and promoting greater social equity. - set up a citizen assistance office - plan and implement improvements to municipal buildings - etc. The building stock—residential, commercial and institutional—produces approximately 28% of Montreal's GHG emissions. The renovation of the latter and the construction of new low-carbon and less energy-consuming buildings are a necessity and an unprecedented opportunity to reduce GHG emissions and improve the quality of life of citizens. A grant application to the federal Codes Acceleration Fund program (https://natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/buildings/codes-acceleration-fund/24794) has been submitted by the City. The request was revised and a conditional financial assistance of $2 million was granted to the City of Montreal to carry out some of these activities. Other grant other subsidy opportunities are being studied by the City of Montreal, including the Quebec's program Accélérer la Transition Climatique Locale (ATCL - https://www.quebec.ca/gouvernement/politiques-orientations/plan-economie-verte/actions-lutter-contre-changements-climatiques/agir-localement/aide-financiere-organismes-municipaux/accelerer-transition-climatique-locale). 2) This component of the project helps analyze the climate risks of municipal building assets to then plan and carry out the interventions necessary to improve their resilience and more generally, the resilience of the City's territory. These projects are difficult to finance. In the past, applications have been submitted to some programs (e.g. Green and Inclusive Community Buildings - https://www.infrastructure.gc.ca/gicb-bcvi/index-eng.html), but without favorable results . The City is also evaluating the possibility of submitting to the OASIS program (https://www.environnement.gouv.qc.ca/programmes/oasis/index.htm) of the Government of Quebec or to certain financial assistance from the Green Municipal Fund - https ://greenmunicipalfund.ca/funding)

project_info: Renewable energy - District Energy Sharing Network (sector of the Faubourgs): The construction of a District Energy Sharing Network in the Faubourgs sector (Borough of Ville-Marie) is a project that includes the construction of : - a thermal power plant on land or in the facilities of one of the buildings in the sector;- a pipeline for the recovery of thermal waste (VRT) from one or more promising industrial sources - a main network of pipes that transport hot and cold water to meet the heating and cooling needs of the connected buildings; - Energy Transfer Station in connected buildings;- new pipes (or the rehabilitation of existing pipes) between the sector and the St. Lawrence River to include the use of this thermal deposit for hydrothermal purposes;- infrastructure necessary for the recovery of waste water thermal discharges from the sector;- one or more thermal storage systems in order to reduce the power demand of the thermal power plant during peak periods. A pre-feasibility study has confirmed the interest and the high potential for reducing GHGs associated with this project: https://www.ecohabitation.com/media/uploads/2021/11/24/rapport_reseauthermique_faubourgs_2019vf.pdf (FRENCH) The preferred governance model was studied and the recommendation concluded that a semi-public company whose main shareholder is the City of Montreal would be the most suitable. A grant application was filed with the provincial and federal levels of government. A conditional funding promise was granted to the project. Hydro-Québec, the main energy distributor, has also conditionally committed to financially supporting the project.

project_info: Water management - Replacement of sludge treatment and recovery unit: The JR Marcotte waste water plant is the highest municipal GHG emitter on Montreal island. The projet is meant to replace all incinerators within the next ten years by technologies including biomethanization. The project aims to replace the 4 existing multiple hearth incinerators which are a major source of GHG emissions. The alternative to incinerators is to implement 3 technologies: fluidized bed incineration, anaerobic digestion and thermal drying. The sludge from the treatment plant will be treated at 60% by incineration and 40% by anaerobic digestion followed by thermal drying.Anaerobic digestion is a natural biological process of decomposition of sewage sludge by microorganisms which activate under anaerobic conditions, i.e. without oxygen. This process takes place in a closed bioreactor which converts part of the solids in biogas and the remaining solids in digestate. Methane or biogas from this process will be recovered and used to heating the sludge while the surplus will be injected into the natural gas distribution network of a private distributor.Fluidized bed incineration is a proven technology for the high temperature combustion of municipal sludge. The sludge is mixed with a bed of sand which is constantly in motion. This technology is newer than hearth incinerators multiple and operates at higher temperatures. This higher temperature produces less N2O, a powerful GHG that is nearly 300 times greater than the GWP (Global Warming Potential) of CO2. This type of incinerator also makes it possible to reduce the air emissions from existing incinerators. It will also be possible to recover the heat from the hot gases which will be used as an energy source for the production of steam (heating of buildings) and for thermal drying. Thermal drying or thermal stabilization consists in evaporating the water contained in the sludge or in the dehydrated digestates. This process will be powered by heat from fluidized bed incineration and no other external energy input will be required.Phase 1 of the project, the installation and commissioning of an anaerobic digester, will extend from 2024 to 2026. Phase 2, four fluidized bed incinerators and four thermal dryers, will be carried out from 2029 to 2031. And phase 3, four anaerobic digesters, will run from 2031 to 2033. From the point of view of environmental benefits, it is estimated that a reduction of 2,399,970 tonnes of CO2 equivalent over a period of 40 years would be attributable to the project. A grant application to the federal Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program (https://www.infrastructure.gc.ca/plan/icp-pic-INFC-eng.html) has been submitted by the City. This request as been reviewed. Both federal and provincial have conditionally committed to financing a significant portion of the project.

Other: Higher average temperature: Higher average temperatures have an impact on different seasons. They cause a longer summer and a shorter winter, among other things, which in turn have repercussions on various parameters related to climate. 

As a result, the population will be more exposed to ultraviolet rays when practicing outdoor activities over a longer period. It could increase the prevalence of related health problems, such as eye and skin diseases, including cancer. Higher average summer temperatures could also extend allergenic plants' pollen production season, which can result in greater health problems for people who have allergies. In Montréal, the pollen season in late summer (July to October) has the greatest impact on health, particularly due to ragweed. Children, young adults, people with asthma, pale-skinned people, people with compromised immune systems, people who regularly practice outdoor activities and people genetically predisposed to allergies are vulnerable to the impacts of higher average temperatures. 

The effects of higher average temperatures on the built environment are mainly observed in the wintertime. The increased number of freeze-thaw cycles entails an accelerated deterioration of the roadway system (potholes) while accelerating wear on bridges, tunnels and overpasses. It also impacts the growth rate and geographical distribution of some harmful insect species, which may result in more frequent infestations and intensified damage to plants. An increase of a few degrees can generate drastic changes in plant biology, which may alter species' distribution areas and could stimulate the growth of undesirable plant species. The increase in average temperatures is also causing a northward migration of vector borne pathogen animal populations; in recent years, we have observed an increase in the occurrence of Lyme disease and West Nile virus (WNV). 

These effects will occur more or less equally across the entire island of Montréal.

Vegetation is also vulnerable to heat waves, because extreme heat induces shocks, such as water stress, that can lead to illnesses; in turn, these problems increase the need for preventive maintenance and treatment. Heat waves, even brief ones, can diminish the populations of many insects. Extreme temperatures can affect or weaken the agglomeration's infrastructures by impacting roads and arteries. Finally, heat waves often give rise to an increased demand for certain services, such as the use of swimming pools, wading pools and splash pads, and the extension of the business hours of air-conditioned public buildings such as libraries and community centers.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Natural environment acquisition program: This program aims to acquire natural environments that ensure the maintenance of biodiversity, increase the resilience of urban environments and help fight climate change, enriching the quality of life of citizens. and contribute to the city's power of attraction. The availability of undeveloped territory is becoming rarer throughout the Montreal metropolitan area. It is important to acquire and protect vacant sites (also coveted for urban development) in order to achieve the target of 10% protected environments on the territory of the agglomeration. Some funding is available under the Green Infrastructure stream from the Government of Canada, but generally the parameters of the programs are difficult to reconcile with the high cost of acquiring land in urban areas.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Development of the nature park : Écoterritoire de la falaise Saint-Jacques: To counter episodes of extreme temperature, Montreal is creating a new 60 hectare urban nature park. The development of the park will allow the demineralization of a vast vacant site and the creation of 30 hectares of natural environments with high ecological value, in the heart of Montreal. The proposed developments will increase biodiversity by creating diverse and connected environments, associated with the woods of the Saint-Jacques cliff -to manage rainwater by creating a body of water fed by runoff from the Turcot interchange site and the redevelopment of Notre-Dame Street West -create an island of freshness by greening a large area of a highly mineralized space and creating a blue space (pond) -improve air quality through greening; and consolidate the natural environments of the Saint-Jacques cliff. Due to the scale and complexity of the project, the creation of the nature park has the potential to become an exemplary project in terms of greening and adaptation to climate change in an urban context. The project, which was the subject of a request for funding from the Government of Canada's Disaster Mitigation and Adaptation Fund (DMAF) program, recently received a conditional funding promise.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Strengthening the canopy through the urban forest program: The City of Montreal is committed to expanding its canopy, going from 20 to 26% by 2025. In accordance with the 2020-2030 Climate Plan, and in order to achieve this objective, the City intends to plant 500,000 trees by 2030, i.e. 320,000 trees on public property and 180,000 trees on private property. Achieving this ambitious objective results in an intensification of planting efforts. The master plantation plans and the demineralization program are essential means of increasing the rate of plantations. This important program already benefits from certain subsidies including an extraordinary program (PEV subsidy) from the Quebec government, the 2 billion trees program from the federal government. Other funding avenues are also being explored, including ATCL from the Quebec government and the Green Municipal Fund planting program from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.

project_info: Transport - Program for the conversion and renovation of public parking lots towards sustainable and resilient mobility hubs: The parking lot conversion and repair program will allow the City to carry out several projects on the parking lots currently under its management, including: 1- The development of mobility hubs which involves the creation of attractive, safe and comfortable places and which concentrate a range of sustainable mobility services (car and bicycle parking, bike sharing, car sharing, drop-off points, electric charging stations, etc.), services related to mobility and information and orientation services, in a space that fits into the neighborhood and life daily life of its population. The deployment strategy developed in collaboration by the City and AMD provides for the establishment of several mobility hubs to serve the entire Montreal territory from 2024. 2- The eco-responsible conversion of parking lots involves the redevelopment of sites according to specific criteria aimed at greening, rainwater management, sustainable mobility, installation of charging stations for electric vehicles, user-friendliness and management sustainable (e.g.: pricing and pooling). The Montreal Regional Environmental Council has developed a certificate based on a point system and a series of measures which aim to integrate eco-responsibility criteria. This certificate will serve as a guide for the development of parking lots. Several lands have already been targeted for this type of redevelopment. The repair of parking lots involves major structural work of development, renovation, upgrading, improvement, replacement and repair required to ensure the sustainability of parking lots, in compliance with laws and regulations. applicable regulations. The work includes, without limitation, perimeter walls, concrete slab, mechanical and electrical systems, capitalizable work and others. For the conversion to eco-responsible parking spaces, a funding request was submitted in the summer of 2024 to the OASIS program of the Government of Quebec. The City is awaiting a response regarding this grant request.

Other: Higher average temperature: Higher average temperatures have an impact on different seasons. They cause a longer summer and a shorter winter, among other things, which in turn have repercussions on various parameters related to climate. 

As a result, the population will be more exposed to ultraviolet rays when practicing outdoor activities over a longer period. It could increase the prevalence of related health problems, such as eye and skin diseases, including cancer. Higher average summer temperatures could also extend allergenic plants' pollen production season, which can result in greater health problems for people who have allergies. In Montréal, the pollen season in late summer (July to October) has the greatest impact on health, particularly due to ragweed. Children, young adults, people with asthma, pale-skinned people, people with compromised immune systems, people who regularly practice outdoor activities and people genetically predisposed to allergies are vulnerable to the impacts of higher average temperatures. 

The effects of higher average temperatures on the built environment are mainly observed in the wintertime. The increased number of freeze-thaw cycles entails an accelerated deterioration of the roadway system (potholes) while accelerating wear on bridges, tunnels and overpasses. It also impacts the growth rate and geographical distribution of some harmful insect species, which may result in more frequent infestations and intensified damage to plants. An increase of a few degrees can generate drastic changes in plant biology, which may alter species' distribution areas and could stimulate the growth of undesirable plant species. The increase in average temperatures is also causing a northward migration of vector borne pathogen animal populations; in recent years, we have observed an increase in the occurrence of Lyme disease and West Nile virus (WNV). 

These effects will occur more or less equally across the entire island of Montréal.

project_info: Transport - Acquisition and installation of charging stations for electric vehicles: In accordance with its transportation electrification strategy, Montreal wishes to implement a large-scale network of level 2 public charging stations for electric vehicles with the objective of serving its entire territory by 2025. The deployment objective is to reach 2,000 terminals in 2025. To date, nearly 1,400 terminals have been deployed in Montreal. We are therefore continuing the deployment in order to implement 2000 charging stations for electric vehicles by 2025. Financial assistance was received from special funding outside the Quebec government program (PEV agreement), from the federal PIVEZ program. Other applications will possibly be submitted to the PIVEZ program, the Hydro-Québec bors program and the Accelerate local climate transition (ATCL) program of the Quebec government.

It could increase the prevalence of related health problems, such as eye and skin diseases, including cancer. Higher average summer temperatures could also extend allergenic plants' pollen production season, which can result in greater health problems for people who have allergies. In Montréal, the pollen season in late summer (July to October) has the greatest impact on health, particularly due to ragweed. Children, young adults, people with asthma, pale-skinned people, people with compromised immune systems, people who regularly practice outdoor activities and people genetically predisposed to allergies are vulnerable to the impacts of higher average temperatures. 

The effects of higher average temperatures on the built environment are mainly observed in the wintertime. The increased number of freeze-thaw cycles entails an accelerated deterioration of the roadway system (potholes) while accelerating wear on bridges, tunnels and overpasses. It also impacts the growth rate and geographical distribution of some harmful insect species, which may result in more frequent infestations and intensified damage to plants. An increase of a few degrees can generate drastic changes in plant biology, which may alter species' distribution areas and could stimulate the growth of undesirable plant species. The increase in average temperatures is also causing a northward migration of vector borne pathogen animal populations; in recent years, we have observed an increase in the occurrence of Lyme disease and West Nile virus (WNV). 

These effects will occur more or less equally across the entire island of Montréal.

project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - Heat Recovery Valorization (HRV) from the Leachate Treatment Facility - Complexe environnemental Saint-Michel (CESM)
: A potential source of significant heat has been identified, originating from the leachate pretreatment facility — a contaminated liquid derived from the former CESM (complexe environnemental de Saint-Michel) landfill site — pending confirmation by third parties. A preliminary analysis of this resource revealed a high potential, currently estimated at 2.2 MW, equivalent to the heating demand of approximately 750 housing units.
Two major projects currently under development near the CESM have been identified as candidates that could benefit from this heat resource in the short term:

-New Greenhouse: This project plans to use of the Heat Recovery Valorization (HRV) from the leachate.

-Écoquartier Louvain Project: This project plans to implement an urban thermal network (RThU) to supply thermal energy to all buildings within the Écoquartier, which will include approximately 1,000 social and affordable housing units, along with community, institutional, and commercial spaces.

: As part of the ecological transition of the Montréal agglomeration, particular attention is being given to the development of sustainable mobility, especially through the enhancement of the cycling network and the interconnection of mobility hubs. This initiative aligns directly with the objectives of the Climate Plan, which aims to reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicles and promote active and collective modes of transportation.
A government grant has been received to support planning and strategic analysis activities related to this network. This funding enables in-depth studies of current and future needs in active mobility, taking into account territorial dynamics, residential densities, employment hubs, and public transit infrastructure, including REM stations.
The proposed projects include the creation and extension of multifunctional cycling corridors, the redevelopment of strategic areas such as the Canora station surroundings, Saint-Jean Boulevard, and the Île-aux-Tourtes bridge. These interventions aim to improve connectivity between neighborhoods, parks, mobility hubs, and new residential developments, while ensuring universal and safe access.
Special attention is also being given to integrating biodiversity principles and sustainable stormwater management into the design of paths and infrastructure. These elements not only strengthen the resilience of infrastructure to climate change but also enhance the quality of life for residents.
Finally, cross-cutting and pilot projects are being developed to test innovative approaches to mobility, aligned with the specific needs of different territories and the broader GHG reduction goals. These initiatives will help guide future funding applications and structure upcoming interventions within a coherent and sustainable framework.

Promising areas that Singapore has a niche in include clean technology, waste and water technology, urban management and solutions and green ICT. Many global leaders in these fields have chosen to base their R&D and manufacturing operations in Singapore, utilising the talent pool here to grow their operations for the Asia Pacific markets. Such R&D activities are part of an expanding and vibrant cluster in Singapore, and we aim to provide private sector companies with access to a combination of technology, markets, capital and talent.

Under the Research, Innovation, and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plan, the Urban Sustainability and Solutions (USS) domain will further strengthen our capacities in building Singapore as a liveable, resilient, sustainable and economically vibrant city. We will build on our efforts and increase funding support to 3 areas: (i) understanding, mitigating and adapting to climate change, (ii) developing Singapore as a city that promotes citizens health and well-being through built environment interventions and (iii) transforming our built environment to become more sustainable while optimising our limited manpower and resources.

For (i), USS will adopt a multi-pronged approach to prepare Singapore for the impact of climate change. We will invest in research that deepens our understanding of climate change impact, such as understanding sea-level rise, changing weather patterns, and impact on zoonotic disease transmission. We will develop cost-effective solutions to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and increase our use of renewables and low carbon technologies such as green/low-carbon materials for the built environment, low-carbon hydrogen and novel carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) technologies. We will also ensure that we are able to adapt and build resiliency to the impact of climate change by developing solutions to address coastal and marine challenges arising from climate change, to protect our coasts, resources and people against sea levels and temperatures. Given Singapore's strategic location in a region of rich biodiversity, there are also opportunities to conserve and leverage our natural assets to meet sustainability goals. This includes developing multi-functional greenery, accelerating industry's adoption of energy efficiency technologies in buildings and exploring nature-based solutions for climate change mitigation and adaptation.

For (ii) and (iii), USS will also leverage modelling and simulation tools to better model environmental factors and the impact on building and infrastructure health and lifespan, and develop effective technologies/materials to strengthen structural integrity of buildings. USS will also continue to tackle heat stress through infrastructure interventions, and deepen our understanding in managing impact of heat and improving community heat resilience.

The Singapore Government published the Singapore Green Bond Framework (Framework) in June 2022, which lays the foundation for the issuance of green bonds by the Singapore Government under the Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act 2021 (SINGA), and serves as a reference for Statutory Boards' respective green bond frameworks.

The Framework is developed and structured in alignment with the core components and key recommendations of the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Green Bond Principles 2021 and the ASEAN Capital Markets Forum ASEAN Green Bond Standards 2018. The Framework details the Singapore Government's (i) intended use of green bond proceeds, (ii) governance structure to evaluate and select eligible projects, (iii) operational approach to manage green bond proceeds, and (iv) commitment to post-issuance allocation and impact reporting.

Morningstar Sustainalytics, an independent ESG research firm, has completed an external review (Second-Party Opinion) on the green credentials of the Framework, and is of the view that the Framework is credible, impactful and aligns with internationally recognised market principles and standards.

The Singapore Government is updating the Framework to align with the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy, which was released in December 2023.

As at 31 March 2024 (end of Financial Year 2023), the Singapore Government has issued S$5.2 billion sovereign green bonds to finance the expansion of Singapore's electric rail network and green our transportation system.

More information on the Singapore Green Bond Framework and Second-Party Opinion can be found at https://go.gov.sg/greenbonds.'

Other: Decarbonization Master Plan with the identified projects - Sustainable Cali Decarbonization Master Plan: The Sustainable Cali Master Plan is a comprehensive public policy instrument designed to promote environmental action in the city of Santiago de Cali. This plan not only works as a local climate action tool, but also positions the city in the global fight against climate change.

In terms of climate change mitigation, the Cali Decarbonization Plan was structured, in which ten macroprojects with the potential to reduce Greenhouse Gases (GHG) were identified in three strategic sectors: transportation, energy and waste management. This will allow the city to make significant progress in reducing GHG emissions in three time horizons: 2030, 2040 and 2050.

In general terms, it is estimated that, through the implementation of the proposed macroprojects, the GHG emissions of Cali will be reduced by 67% by 2050. The Decarbonization Plan not only operates as a local climate roadmap, but also positions Cali as a key actor for the fulfillment of Colombia's climate commitments, including the goal of 51% emissions reduction by 2030 established in the Long Term Strategy (E2050), as well as compliance with the Paris Agreement through the correct execution of its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

project_info: Transport - Inclusive Transport Transformation in Accra: A national transport policy in 2007, identified exponential growth in rural-urban migration trends and also diagnosed the growth in annual increases in vehicle ownership of about 8 percent as a result of a growing national economy which will eventually lead to a worsening of vehicular traffic congestion in major urban centres of Ghana especially Accra. Public transport operations in Accra is structured along the following modes:•70% Tro-tros (mini buses)•15% Taxis•15% Large busesEven though 70 percent of persons trips are by some form of public transport (distributed across the modes indicated above), it has been estimated that public transport only engages 30 percent of road space in Accra with private modes occupying 70 percent of road space even though they (private modes) carry only 30 percent of travels into the City. In an effort to address the urban transport problems and also take advantage of the growing densities of population and economic activities in Accra, a Ghana Urban Transport Project was proposed with the following objectives:1.Improve mobility in areas of participating Metropolitan/Municipal/District Assemblies (MMDAs), through a combination of traffic engineering measures, management improvements, regulation of the public transport industry, and implementation of Bus Rapid Transport (BRT) system; and2.Promote a shift to more environmentally-sustainable transport modes and lower transport-related GHG emissions along the pilot BRT corridor in Accra. The measures of success for these objectives are:1.Reduction in average travel time for bus passengers2.Increase in average travel speed for all traffic3.Increase in productivity of bus service (passenger share of large buses)4.Reduction in CO2 emissions along the BRT pilot corridor in AccraProject deliverables were categorised under the following components1.Institutional development,2.Traffic engineering, management and safety,3.Development of a BRT system,4.Integration of urban development and transport planning; and 5.Project outcome monitoringThe development and implementation of a BRT project as an objective and sub-component of the Ghana Urban Transport Project was designed to represent the rallying point for all other objectives of the Ghana Urban Transport Project in terms of the following:1.Efficient and cost-effective means of moving people rather than vehicular traffic2.Influencing the urban form to prevent further sprawl development3.Redesigning road infrastructure in favour of sustainable travel options and modes4.Improving air quality and other environmental factors5.Building local capacity for transportation and mobility planning. In the context of project performance with the implementation of the Ghana Urban Transport Project, the objectives of components 2, 3 and 4 were not met and this informed the results of an Independent Evaluation Group of the World Bank to rate the Ghana Urban Transport Project as unsatisfactory.However, there were some success stories on the Institutional development component in setting up Urban Passenger Transport Units at the city-level which have now been transformed into Departments of Transport with functions supported by a legislative instrument of the Local Governance Act 2016, Act 693 of Ghana. Also in order to consolidate some institutional development gains of the GUTP, all the local administrative authorities of the Greater Accra Metropolitan Area have come together to form the Greater Accra Passenger Transport Executive (GAPTE) to manage cross-jurisdictional passenger transport services. At the city level, legislative reforms have been undertaken to enable the city-administration to do both quantity and quality regulation of passenger transport services. project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - CO-producing Nature-based solutions and restored Ecosystems: transdisciplinary neXus for Urban Sustainability: The EU-funded CONEXUS project will co-produce, structure and promote access to contextualised knowledge by co-creating Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) to support the restoration of urban ecosystems. Cities in Europe and Latin America share urgent global-local challenges to integrate practical actions with strategies to achieve greater inclusion, biodiversity, climate change adaptation and environmental quality. CONEXUS brings together community, private, public and research partners to experiment with novel co-production methods to deliver NBS innovations in 'Life-Lab' pilots, using a place-based approach to solve problems together with citizens (in São Paulo, Bogotá, Santiago, Buenos Aires, Lisbon, Barcelona and Turin). The combined palette of socio-cultural, ecological and governance contexts presents the opportunity to move forward faster together, and to inform changes in urban policy and practice.https://www.eu-conexus.eu/en/

Public and green spaces - MARTIM MONIZ Urban Regeneration Project: The Martim Moniz project is a flagship urban regeneration initiative in Lisbon that integrates climate adaptation and mitigation goals. It includes: 
• Increase of green cover and shaded areas to counter urban heat island effects 
• Expansion of pedestrian zones to promote active mobility 
• Reduction of vehicular traffic and emissions in the square 
• Reuse of water for irrigation and cleaning purposes 
These measures contribute to Lisbon's Climate Action Plan goals for resilience, biodiversity, water efficiency, and decarbonization.

project_info: Other: - Sensor Network: The monitoring of environmental parameters, air quality, noise, traffic and weather conditions aims to map the city in real time or near real time, in terms of these indicators, in the form of 'sensing as a service'. The entire network monitors suspended particles (PM2.5 and PM10), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), ozone (O3), equivalent continuous sound level (LAeq), atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, wind, precipitation, temperature, global radiation, ultraviolet radiation and hourly traffic volume (VTH), although not all parameters are monitored at all locations. Monitoring covers the period from 2 January 2025 to 31 December 2027.

Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The coastal flooding events in Venice are increasing in frequency and intensity in the last years, mainly due to phenomena such as the increase in the average sea level on a global scale (eustatism) and the subsidence of the lagoon soil. The 12 November 2019 happened an extraordinary high tide of +187 cm a.s.l.By calculating the average sea level, the Tide Forecast and Reporting Center (Centro Previsioni e Segnalazioni Maree) of the Municipality of Venice demonstrated how the level has progressively risen over the decades and is currently about 31 cm higher than that verified at the beginning of the last century. It also has highlighted the correlation between the rise in the average sea level and the high tides that occurred in Venice in the period from 1972 to 2021.The tide in Venice that exceeds 80 cm a.s.l. (commonly referred to as \'acqua alta\') is a problem for transport and pedestrian ways in the lowest points of the city. When tide exceeds 100 cm a.s.l., approximately 5% of the public land is flooded. At an altitude of +110 cm a.s.l., about 15% of the city is affected by flooding (\'very high tide\'). When +140 cm a.s.l. is reached (\'exceptional high tide\'), 55% of the city is flooded.The vulnerability of the different areas of the city to the phenomenon of high water varies according to the morphological aspects, to the position with respect to natural and artificial barriers but, above all, according to the altitudes at the local level of the territory.In the urban context the flooding causes damage to roads, to the historical and cultural heritage, to public, commercial and productive activities and buildings, with significant impacts in urban economy. Since 2020, Mose Barrier are protecting the lagoon from high tides > 100 cm above the mean sea level. | Extreme heat: The Venetian territory has been affected by increasing heat waves over the last 20 years, which have increased in terms of frequency, intensity and duration. Heat waves are events linked to the recording of extreme temperatures both in terms of intensity and frequency and residence time. Analysing ARPAV data, we can confirm that the average temperature in the Municipality of Venice is constantly growing, as are the tropical days (days with temperature over 25°C) and nights (over 20°C). All this leads to urban contexts with increasingly poor thermal comfort and greater risks to human health and the environment.Urban \'heat island\' phenomena reduce the quality of life and human well-being, create inconvenience for activities related to education, art and culture and economic activities, produce an increase in energy costs for the cooling of buildings.Morphological factors (both artificial and natural) of the urban environment and the territory allow us to identify the areas of the municipal area of Venice most subject to the events described above: the effect of heat waves is more impactful in areas of the city characterized by a high density of buildings and a high presence of industrial and commercial activities, an absence of green and shaded areas, therefore with a prevalence of the extension of artificial surfaces compared to natural ones. | Urban flooding: Recent ARPAV (Environmental agency for Veneto Region) reports show an increasingly irregular trend in rainfall, with a general increase in frequency of short and high intensity rains. This factor could lead to a increase in the risk of urban flooding.In the last decade (2010-2020) is recorded an annual cumulative average precipitation level decreasing compared to the previous one, but at the same time we can find an upward trend in precipitation quantities (increase in number of days with heavy rainfall: precipitation equal to or greater than 20 mm).Urban areas are exposed to hydraulic instability mainly due to unregulated use of the soil, with a consequent decrease in the environmental resilience against extreme rainfall and intense meteorological events. The increase in waterproof surfaces and the progressive impoverishment of the drainage network, no longer suitable for the management and disposal of water also due to the new ones urban settlements, have made the management of the consortium network problematic, causing extensive and frequent flooding.Therefore, also cleaning and maintenance of the hydrographic network is essential to avoid the risk of flooding. It is high the number of natural and artificial watercourses draining into the Venice lagoon that represent a potential source of risk in relation to floods.Vulnerability to floodings occurs mainly in industrial, commercial, infrastructural areas and in areas with intensive and complex urbanization; areas with a reduction in the soil permeability. The occurrence of these events leads to damages to property and infrastructures, art and culture, as well as relating to the social situation (e.g. education). The possibility of danger to population's health also must be considered.

Public and green spaces - Conservation measures for SACs (Special Areas of Conservation): Conservation measures for SACs (Special Areas of Conservation) refer to interventions aimed at protecting and maintaining the conservation status of habitats and species within these protected areas. SACs are part of the Natura 2000 network, a European network of protected areas created to ensure biodiversity by conserving natural habitats and species of community interest.

Examples of conservation measures in SACs include:

Habitat management and maintenance: Actions aimed at preserving the natural characteristics of a habitat, such as preventing the spread of invasive species, controlling weeds, or managing grazing areas.

Ecological restoration: Interventions to restore degraded ecosystems, improve soil or water quality, and recreate natural habitats that have been altered or destroyed.

Biodiversity monitoring: Continuous monitoring of species and habitats to assess their conservation status and identify potential problems or threats.

Fauna protection interventions: Projects to protect vulnerable or endangered animal species, such as creating ecological corridors, protecting breeding areas, or regulating human activities.

Control of human activities: Regulating and managing human activities within SACs to reduce the impact on flora and fauna, such as controlling tourism, fishing, or agricultural activities.

climate_hazard: River flooding: River flooding has caused $3.1 billion in property damage to the Mid-South region between 2007 and 2017 and from 1996 to 2023, there were 442 reported flooding events in the Memphis Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA). When the Mississippi River rises, is pushes excess water into the region's smaller creeks and rivers causing widespread flooding. Flooding has direct and indirect impacts on health and safety. If high velocity waters over-top the waterway, they can sweep people into the flood or carry heavy debris into populated areas causing injury or fatality. When riverine flooding inundates roadways, emergency services vehicles may not be able to reach their service areas in a timely manner, if at all. Health service providers with facilities in the floodplain may need to evacuate patients, often with negative impacts on patient care. During the May 2011 floods, the Mid-South Health and Rehab Center had to evacuate 146 patients. Other institutions that are in the floodplain may face similar challenges. During the May 2011 floods, the Millington Minimum Security Federal Prison was flooded and prisoners were transported to another site. All manner of residential facilities in the floodplain may experience this type of disruption during flood events. Physical health problems, such as respiration issues, stem from molding building materials left in inundated homes after the waters subside. Roadways become impassable due to standing water, or can be washed out due to the high velocity floodwaters. Riverine flooding can also erode the soil base for roads, railroads, and pipelines, causing them to destabilize and collapse. Navigable waterways and ports are also at risk during riverine flooding events. When the water level exceeds the height of dams and locks it isn't safe for barges to move along the river. This affects the movement of coal, building materials, and agricultural products. The entire Midwest depends on the Mississippi River for freight transportation, and 60% of U.S. grain exports are shipped on the Mississippi River. When industrial sites flood, they can release contaminated materials or soils into waterways, which has deteriorated water quality in several tributaries. From 2001 to 2011, over 4,700 acres of built space has expanded within the 500-year floodplain. Within the MSA, 58% of all census block groups and 52% of Low-Income Disadvantage Community (LIDAC) block groups are located within 100 ft of a 2022 FEMA flood hazard zone. | Extreme wind: The Mid-South region experienced an average of 8.4 wind events per year between 1956 and 2018. Evidence suggests that wind events are also becoming more frequent. For the ten year period between 2007 and 2017, 223 wind events were recorded, averaging 20.2 events per year with $17.8 million in wind damage occurring in that period. Between 2019 and 2022, 52% of block groups within the City of Memphis experienced longer disruption times than the average American, with 82% of these block groups designated as Low-Income and Disadvantaged Communities (LIDAC). Customers lose power 3 times a year, on average, due to wind events. Strong winds can dislodge trees from the ground, toppling them onto people, cars, buildings, and transportation routes. This can be a direct cause of injury. Additionally, the fallen trees or branches can trap people in cars, block building egress routes, and obstruct roadways. Weather Degradation
Rocks in contact with the atmosphere undergo physical and chemical changes that alter their mechanical and mineralogical properties. Easily observable are processes that lead to the progressive fragmentation of rock, the swelling of clayey lithologies, the alteration of minerals, or the dissolution of evaporitic rocks by water.
Gravity
Rock fragments produced by slope weathering processes are moved from their position by the force of gravity. This can overcome frictional forces if the slope of the slope equals or exceeds the so-called detachment slope, while the fragments accumulate downward when the slope of the deposit is equal to or less than the so-called accumulation slope. Modeling processes tend to bring the slopes into equilibrium conditions (regularized slope), close to the detachment slope, where gravity alone cannot cause debris evacuation and further fragmentation processes are thus prevented.
Washout
The term washout refers to geomorphological processes linked to the direct action of rainfall on the ground, both during impact and flow.
Landslides
Landslides represent the most intense and severe manifestations of slope degradation and the main causes of geological risk when they directly or indirectly affect residential areas and infrastructure.
The hydrogeological risk issue in the city of Palermo is linked to the presence of highly disturbed mountain slopes close to residential areas, the exceeding of critical rainfall levels along the slopes, and the hydrometric levels of the watercourses of the minor hydrographic network and rainwater disposal system, including the city sewer system.
The abandonment of piedmont lands, illegal construction, deforestation and forest fires, the lack of maintenance of slopes and watercourses, and the alteration of the natural dynamics of watercourses have undoubtedly aggravated the instability and increased the exposure to risk of the already fragile territory. The combination of these factors is at the root of phenomena such as rockfall, debris flows, and flooding of residential areas or city streets.

The project is a mid-term to long term project that will have mixed use development, residential opportunities , industrial opportunities and other civic uses. The project looks at changing the fabric of society.At this juncture we cannot quantify the approximate number of opportunities that will be created but a lot of part time and full time jobs will be created during construction and once operational.The property is located on the south western side of the CBD and is located 7km away from the city. project_info: Water management - unknown: Purpose of the project is to sensitize schools and surrounding areas about the use of alternative technologies that are cleaner, safer and environmentally friendly to adapt towards climate change and adaptation by using infrastructure that has minimal impact on the environment. The project aims to provide at least 10 Pietermaritzburg schools with solar panels (renewable energy infrastructure) and water harvesting (JOJO) tanks to store rain water which can be used by the schools for gardening and sanitation purposes. The project also aims to encourage communities to employ green building designs/ models for schools and household use.Project Objectives • To purchase and install solar panels and JOJO tanks for water harvesting in 10 schools.• To encourage the use of cleaner technologies as energy sources.• To educate learners, teachers and communities to use clean, safe and environmental friendly technologies.• To educate learners about climate change and adaptation hence the promotion of the use of resources with no negative impacts on the environment.• To encourage use of alternative technologies to acquire both water and energy services in schools and surrounding communities.Project Activities• Purchase and install solar panels (hybrid solar system)• Purchase and install water harvesting tanks (JOJO tanks) • Facilitate education and training for learners about energy renewable options that are more sustainable and wiser water management practices.

project_info: Water management - flood risk and vulnerability assessment: The impact of climate change tends to be unevenly distributed affecting mostly vulnerable communities; which can be further exacerbated by poor response planning. Recent flooding events experienced in April 2022 demonstrates the vulnerabilities of communities to the increased, rapid flooding events. More flooding has further occurred in November 2022, where Msunduzi River burst its banks communities in wards 11, 16, 21, 22 and 23 were affected. Roads and bridges were left submerged, and some homes destroyed in low-lying areas. \n \nAs a result, the Msunduzi Municipality intends to undertake and develop a Detailed Flood Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for all wards within the Municipality, that will highlight high risk areas; to inform planning, disaster management and resource allocation. Floods are a natural phenomenon but can also be exacerbated by anthropogenic activities. The project will be undertaken to increase resilience and preparedness against extreme climate change events.

The regions of City Halls-Bairro do SubÃºrbio/Ilhas, Cajazeiras, Cabula/Tancredo Neves and Pau da Lima concentrate significant portions of the population with very high vulnerability to this type of occurrence, which indicates less capacity to adapt and recover from the impacts of floods, which can result in human losses, economic damage and psychological trauma.

project_info: Renewable energy - Solar Park: The project is the construction of a photovoltaic energy generating system (a Solar Farm) through the installation of solar panels in Canabrava Park and on the roofs of BRT Stations, generating an installed power of 5MW, for use by the City Hall in public lighting and energy consumption in municipal public buildings. The system will be operated under a Onerous Concession or PPP regime, in order to supply a significant part of the energy demand of the Municipal Public Administration, through demand guarantee and energy management and subsequent reversion of the asset to the City Hall, at the end of the concession period (build-operate-transfer). With this Solar Farm pilot project, the City Hall aims to create a business model that is, at the same time, attractive to the market and with appropriate counterparts to the public interest, comprising the following premises of socioeconomic benefits:•The creation of value, through the generation of assets energy furniture;•The gradual replacement of the municipal administration's energy matrix with energy from clean and renewable sources;•The neutralization of Salvador's carbon and consequent enabling of the municipality to issue processes of green bonds, incentivized infrastructure debentures, national and international green certification programs and financing lines for specific programs for activities of environmental interest; and•The use of energy generated as a commodity in the implementation of programs to promote economic development and entrepreneurial activity (PMAMC, 2020).

•	Develop guidelines for replication and integration of the system into municipal solid waste management, promoting sustainable practices aligned with the circular economy and climate mitigation.

climate_hazard:
Urban flooding: Flooding is one of the biggest climate hazards that the City of Indianapolis faces and is expected to see an increase in severity over the coming decades. The city's infrastructure is aging, and in the event of a 100-year flood event as much as $3.6 billion in damage is estimated. More than $7 billion of property resides in the floodplain, including several schools, emergency response facilities, and bridges.

Vulnerable populations most at risk:
- Population over 65 years of age as older populations are more likely to have pre-existing medical conditions or compromised mobility, which reduces their ability to evacuate areas at risk of flood in a timely manner.
- Communities experiencing poverty as having limited income may make it difficult to suddenly evacuate and shelter during a flood or tolerate missing days of work. Additionally, research shows that low-income people are more likely to be overlooked during the emergency response period following a disaster.
- Population with limited English proficiency since language barriers can limit a person's ability to effectively act during emergencies and make it harder to follow directions and interact with agencies, limiting the amount of support available.
- Non-white populations tend to be particularly vulnerable to disasters and floods. This is due to language differences, housing patterns, variations in the quality of housing, community isolation, and cultural barriers.
- People living with disabilities are subject to a series of health complications that are often significantly heightened due to environmental conditions. Limited mobility can significantly delay or prevent effective evacuation and the flooding can disrupt one's ability to get medical treatment.
- Renters tend to experience more income burden on housing costs and rental homes are not typically well-maintained.
- Homeless people are the most exposed as they lack the resources to find protection during times of floods. | Extreme heat: Hotter summers will make it increasingly difficult for the community to meet ozone standards, requiring stricter environmental controls and discouraging business expansion. Hotter summers will also result in increased education costs. Currently, Indianapolis Public Schools sends children with asthma to air-conditioned schools. Schools without air conditioning will need to find ways to provide a comfortable learning environment. Children, older adults, those with underlying health issues, and anyone working outdoors are at a greater risk. In addition, increases in pollution levels reduce crop yields and also decrease the visibility, both of which have economic and quality of life impacts. A heatwave in 2000 resulted in one death. In 2017, there was a heat wave in Marion County that included multiple days with heat indices of approximately 100 degrees.

Extreme heat also increases the demand for cooling, which means higher energy prices for community members and more stress on the electric grid - potentially leading to brownouts or blackouts if supply can't keep up. 

First responders and emergency rooms are also stressed during heatwaves as staff has to respond to an increase in ambulance runs and patients suffering from heat-related illness. Social service organizations like park facilities, libraries, and community centers face a similar stress as more community members may seek their services or facility for refuge during extreme heat. | Drought: Though Central Indiana has reliable sources of water, current water use patterns paired with increasing temperatures and reduced precipitation could lead to severe drought conditions within the next 5 to 10 years. In 2012, Indianapolis had a drought that lasted 45 days which caused significant losses to agricultural producers. | Snow and ice: Some type of severe winter weather is expected every winter; however, the severity, frequency and duration of winter weather events varies each year and is difficult to predict. These events affect everyone, but are particularly harsh on specific populations, like the homeless. Those who are unable to afford adequate housing or heat are at extreme risk because long exposure to the cold, snow, and ice causes harmful health
repercussions. Also, lower-wage workers with less flexible work hours may suffer financially from road closures and public transportation delays. Local emergency services personnel have capabilities and plans in place to help vulnerable populations during severe winter weather events. Historically, this has included efforts such as directly engaging homeless people to move to shelters and transporting people with
underlying health issues to receive care. There is also a risk of water main breaks in addition to the damage done to public infrastructure by the freeze-thaw cycle. | Other: Decreased air quality: Increased heat waves in intensity and duration typically produce air quality stagnation which increases PM2.5 and ozone levels. Public health faces greater jeopardy not only from the heat but also the deterioration of air quality associated with it. Children, pregnant women, and the elderly are particularly vulnerable to unhealthy air quality.

Indianapolis has higher than the national average rates of asthma, pediatric asthma, and COPD.

Additionally lower income people are more likely to use public transit, which requires waiting outside at bus stops. This population and any household without a vehicle are therefore more vulnerable to unhealthy air quality.

Outdoor workers, including city workers, are another vulnerable population who often are not protected from air pollutants during their daily activities. Homeless people face a similar vulnerability.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Improving waste systems in Indianapolis: Indianapolis has an outdated solid waste infrastructure and fee system. Indianapolis is without a universal recycling system and has no commercial-scale organics composting providers. 

In early 2024, the Indianapolis Department of Public Works released a series of requests for proposal for the disposal and processing of solid waste for the 279,000 households it services. These processes include traditional trash, diversion of recyclable materials in an improved recycling system, and investigation of the disposal and processing of organic material. As of October 1, 2024, these contracts are being negotiated with selected vendors. 

RFPs for the collection and hauling of these same materials will be released in late 2024. These procurement processes aim to align with Thrive Indianapolis's goals of providing universal residential curbside recycling to all Indianapolis residents and offering subscription curbside composting to all Indianapolis residents. 

Office of Sustainability is assisting DPW in these efforts and assisting in developing grant applications for EPA's Recycling Education and Outreach and Solid Waste Infrastructure for Recycling grant applications to fund the advancement of this work.

Buildings - Energy efficiency upgrades for community-benefit buildings: As part of Thriving Buildings, the Office of Sustainability is planning four energy efficiency sub-programs. 

1. Energy Efficiency Conservation Block Grant (DOE): hire an Energy Manager, conduct energy audits of municipal buildings, and implement cost-saving and emissions-lowering retrofits

2. Energy Future Grant (DOE): competitive grant, will fund Indiana Innovation Hub, an energy efficiency partnership including seven Indiana cities and two non-profits, goal to share a variety of knowledge and policy resources, and built environment professionals can be trained and retained in Indiana

3. Thriving Nonprofits: In partnership with IFF, offer 5-10 nonprofits tutorials on energy efficiency and building management, supply technical assistance for implementing retrofits, and guide NPOs through the process. Project has applied for funding from McKinney Family Foundation, currently in consideration with MFF

4. Heat Pump cohort: partnership with Environmental Resilience Institute to provide local building owners technical assistance on heat pumps, and connect organizations with contractor/vendors to convert buildings to heat pumps, currently in consideration with ERI for McKinney Climate Fellow to assist in program execution
