Goals related to the Food Action Plan will include:

- stakeholder engagement
- promoting sustainable agriculture
- reducing food waste
- improving access to healthy food
- supporting local food businesses
- advocating for supportive policies

Benefits of a food action plan for sustainability include:

- environmental benefits (reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved soil health, increased biodiversity, and water conservation)
- social benefits (increased food security, improved nutrition)
- economic benefits (new business opportunities, reduced costs associated with food waste)

Nature-Based Solutions - School Gardening Programming: The city would like to support the expansion of school gardening programming in elementary and middle schools, with the primary purpose of providing students with hands-on learning experiences and fostering a connection to nature and healthy food systems. This will include building garden infrastructure, a full-time staff member to run the program and fees for consultants.

Potential outcomes that we can see this programming offering include:

- Students being actively involved in the entire gardening process, from planning, planting, and caring for plants to harvesting
- Using the garden as a living laboratory to teach concepts across various subjects, including science (plant life cycles, ecology), math (measurement, counting), language arts (journaling, descriptive writing), social studies (history of agriculture, cultural significance of plants), and art (observational drawing, design).
- Students learning about the environment, the importance of sustainable practices, and the role of pollinators and other creatures in the ecosystem
- Students more likely to try and enjoy fruits and vegetables they have grown themselves, leading to improved attitudes towards healthier eating habits
- Students understand where their food comes from, how it grows, and the effort involved in producing it.
- Providing opportunities for physical exercise through gardening activities
- Students develop a sense of responsibility for plants and organisms

project_info: Renewable energy - Utility scale geothermal: This project will explore the innovative use of City Right-of-Way, including under City streets, for the development of utility-scale geothermal distribution systems. The project would pilot a district geothermal system in a dense urban environment using City facilities, primarily four facilities in a historic district in Old Town, Alexandria, Virginia. We have determined these investments would result in a minimum 5% reduction in our peak loads for the impacted facilities. The City is exploring multiple options, including installing systems below the existing utilities, utilizing about 2104 linear street feet, 168 bores at an approximate depth of 471'.\nWe anticipate running the geothermal loop along Cameron Street, to N. Pitt Street, to Prince Street and back up N. Royal Street to connect at Cameron Street. It would cross King Street, a major commercial street.

project_info: Transport - DASH Zero-Emission Bus Fleet Replacement: DASH is pursuing a transition (depending on cost feasibility, range progress, and reliability) from clean diesel to a 100%electric bus fleet over the next 15 years. DASH has purchased 14 100% electric buses over the last two years, including sixreplacement buses that were funded by the Virginia VW Environmental Mitigation Trust. DASH is the first transit agency inNorthern Virginia to deploy electric buses. The City and DASH have completed the first phase of a Zero Emission BusImplementation Study which will provide a detailed, strategic roadmap to transition the entire fleet by approximately FY 2037.The second phase of this study is expected to be completed by late 2022.For FY 2023, DASH has 15 buses that will have reached the end of their useful life and are eligible for replacement; however,due to funding constraints, DASH is only requesting 8 clean diesel replacement buses. DASH and City staff are working to applyfor federal funding which could fund the cost differential for these eight buses to be 100% electric as well as the purchase of upto 7 additional 100% electric replacement buses/trolleys and the associated charging infrastructure.Funding is the most significant constraint on the pace of transition. Since the up-front cost of an electric bus is nearly twice thatof a clean diesel, these buses will require a higher up-front capital investment. Significant state, federal, or regional grantsupport will need to be identified and secured to fully fund electrification of the DASH bus fleet in the next 15 years. While it ispossible that some of the increased up-front investment may be recovered through lower lifecycle maintenance costs, thiscannot yet be accurately determined.https://media.alexandriava.gov/content/budget/FY23ProposedCIPCompleteDocument.pdf

climate_hazard: Water stress: Loss of snowpack and retreat of glaciers threatens to reduce river levels during summer months, with wide ranging impacts to salmon, hydroelectric dams, forest ecosystems, etc. This impacts electricity capacity and costs, traditional subsistence patterns reliant on salmon, and much more | Heavy precipitation: The increasing frequency of short duration/high intensity rainfall events has already posed challenges to the storm water system capacity temporarily at times, resulting in landslides, street and surface flooding and high sediment loads washing into the Bay and potential over flow at the central sewage treatment plant.A new storm water main is currently in construction in downtown which should alleviate some of the episodic urban flooding. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Although the risk of wildfire itself within Tacoma is low due to urbanization and corresponding reduced tree canopy, the effects of wildfires in Washington's Cascade Range and further afield in Oregon, California, British Columbia, etc. are very much felt on an episodic basis within the City. Specifically, wildfire smoke reduces air quality to hazardous levels on a nearly yearly basis, typically during mid-to-late summer. Wildfire smoke is known to have adverse health effects for all populations, but particularly on those vulnerable population groups highlighted above. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Tacoma has not experienced serious impacts related to SLR yet but has had erosion from a long history of wind storms and king tides. USGS is currently working on modelling future impacts of storms and run-up to couple with the recent updated SLR projections. According to that recent science, by 2080, there is a 95% probability of 1.1' SLR, 50% probability of 1.8' SLR and a 1% probability of 3.5' of SLR. In 2150, there is a 50% probability of 4.2' of SLR.Tacoma has over 33 miles of shoreline and several industrial businesses and a major port in its tide flats area. Coastal flooding or inundation will have serious impacts on environmental, economic and social systems. There are some residences along the shoreline and many businesses that will be impacted. The tide flats is a major employment and transportation nexus, both locally and regionally. National railroad and highways pass though low lying areas. The regional sewage treatment plant (owned and operated by the City of Tacoma) is located on the Puyallup River, which is expected to have increased chances of flooding in the future. It flows into Commencement Bay where tide and sea level rise impacts can complicate the chances of flooding. All City residents and many in the County depend on the operation of the plant. A flood wall was built in 2010, before current local SLR projections were available, but should afford some level of protection for several years. Among the groups likely most impacted by sea level rise and associated habitat and fisheries loss will be the Puyallup tribe, whose ancestral lands since time immemorial are the Tacoma tideflats and surrounding areas. Salmon have profound and ongoing cultural importance to the tribe and are also a source of subsistence and commercial fishing, and inundation of crucial juvenile salmon rearing habitat associated with sea level rise threatens to severely impact salmon abundance. | Extreme heat: We have not experienced considerable impacts so far but the Tacoma Climate Change Resilience Study notes the following potentials:PUBLIC HEALTHClimate change impacts, particularly extreme heat events, pose a considerable threat to human health. In the last decade, more Americans died from extreme heat than from any other weather-related cause. Anticipated health impacts from climate change include increased rates of the following [37]:- Heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion and stroke.- Air quality-related respiratory illnesses such as asthma and allergies due to wildfire smoke, ozone, and increased allergen production.- Extreme weather-related physical and mental health injuries.- Some infectious diseases transmitted by food, water, and insects, such as West Nile Virus and fungal diseases.LAW and ORDERA recent study by an economist in Cambridge suggests that rising temperatures will lead to an increase in criminal activity in the United States [39]. The reason for this relationship is unknown—it may be that when temperatures are warmer, there are more opportunities to commit crime due to open windows and more potential victims who are outside and interacting with one another. Another theory is that temperature has a direct effect on human aggression; studies have found that subjects make more aggressive choices when they are in a hot room. Regardless of the cause, this relationship warrants careful consideration of how governments deploy police and other resources to combat future crime in the context of a changing climate.COMMUNITY and CULTUREBoth nighttime and daytime temperatures are excepted to increase and many homes in the Pacific Northwest do not have air conditioning. Warmer weather can interfere with sleep quality and duration which negatively affects human energy levels, attention spans and moods. If daytime temperatures are also higher than normal, the effects are often compounded. People may tend to stay at home or in their neighborhoods rather than get out and attend community and cultural events.---Vulnerable groups are likely to experience these impacts disproportionately, affecting health and economic outcomes and decreasing capacity for adapting to additional future impacts.
project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Soft shore armoring for Commencement Bay: The City seeks funding to repair aging and damaged hard shore armoring infrastructure with more habitat-friendly soft shore armoring along Commencement Bay. A Master Plan for this work has been funded and is in the early stages.

Vulnerable populations often live in areas with poor infrastructure, leaving them more susceptible to property damage, health risks from contaminated water, and displacement. Those with limited financial resources may struggle to recover from flood impacts, while elderly residents and individuals with mobility issues may find evacuation and access to emergency services challenging.

Impacts on Sectors:

project_info: Renewable energy - Solar at the Butterworth Landfill: Over 10 years ago, the City of Grand Rapids began exploring installing solar panels on the Butterworth Landfill, which is a 190-acre Superfund site where cleanup was completed in 2000. Due to the protective cap that was installed and cannot be disturbed, ground mounted solar panels, an open field or a paved parking lot are the only viable beneficial reuses of the property. In 2013, the EPA completed a solar reuse assessment and found that the Butterworth Landfill is well-suited for solar power generation due to the relatively flat, open and unobstructed surface of the site as well as plenty of sun exposure and close proximity to necessary electricity infrastructure. In that assessment, the EPA determined that 63 acres were viable for solar installation. The City entered into a contract with a solar developer in 2015 for an approximately 2.5 megawatt DC array in the southwest corner of the landfill that was intended to go over or under the river and supply the City's Water Resource Recovery Facility (WRRF). The developer ultimately went bankrupt and the project fell through. In the last year, the City has revitalized its efforts to develop the site and has developed a multi-project approach. The City first plans to develop the optimal amount of solar-powered electricity at the site behind-the-meter to the City-owned and operated Primary Circuit (PC). The City will maximize direct benefits to the Grand Rapids community through emissions reductions, air pollution reduction, affordability, electrification, jobs, etc. and demonstrate innovative approaches to the deployment of solar in conjunction with interpretive/educational uses. The City intends to deploy up to a 2MW solar array to support the Primary Circuit. The City has already initiated and completed the RFI/RFQ phase of this component and has 10 qualified solar developers participating in workshopping of next steps toward a formal RFP in late Spring/early Summer. In addition, the City's Engineering Department is currently at 30% design for the PC extension required to connect the array. Michigan currently has no enabling legislation for privately developed community solar. However, the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) approved the Solar Gardens Sunrise program within Consumers Energy's (CE) Voluntary Green Pricing program; The Community Solar component of this project is designed to provide 3,520MWh of solar electricity annually to low income and disadvantaged communities within the city of Grand Rapids via a 5MW array with a 30-year life expectancy. This component of the project is estimated to cost $14.7 million, with $12.5 million accounting for capital costs associated with constructing 5MW of solar. The remaining amount of requested funding for this component supports hiring a full time solar specialist (this person will manage all three measures of the grant), a subaward with a qualified non-profit that will manage household participation in the program, a subaward with community partners to create and facilitate a Solar Justice Team, funding for the development of a Grand Rapids-based solar career development program, and enrollment costs for 30 people to participate in the training program. The third component of the project is installation of an 8MW solar array that would serve the City's district energy/steam district. The persistent challenge across the globe in electrifying steam/district energy systems has been twofold. First, the capital costs of reinvesting in and retrofitting existing plants can be challenging. The second - and perhaps greater - challenge is the fuel cost differential between traditional natural gas and electricity, which can be 6x-10x. Fortunately, Vicinity has made a commitment to investments on the former, while this public-private PV partnership can help to address the latter. Vicinity Energy (Vicinity) owns and operates the district energy system in Grand Rapids and serves approximately 120 buildings in the downtown core. It operates under a franchise tariff with the City of Grand Rapids as its regulating authority. The system provides gas-fueled steam heating for over 10 million square feet of space, including residential buildings, hospitals, colleges/ universities, municipal and commercial office buildings, the arena, convention center, hotels, churches, non-profits, restaurants, and retail facilities.

This scenario begins with freezing rain, coating power lines, roads, sidewalks, and trees with ice, followed by blizzard conditions lasting over 60 hours, reminiscent of the February 1978 storm. Impacts of freeze-thaw cycles include:
Infrastructure stress: Expansion and contraction of moisture in asphalt, concrete, and clay soils accelerates damage to roads, sidewalks, and underground utilities, leading to more frequent pipe breakages, cracked foundations, and degraded transportation networks.

Public safety risks: Ice formation from sudden thaws followed by refreezing increases the risk of slips, falls, and traffic accidents.

Service disruptions: Freeze-thaw cycles can overwhelm drainage systems, cause localized flooding, and damage residential properties such as basements and sewer lines.

Impacts on vulnerable populations:

Elderly residents and people with disabilities face greater risks of injury from icy sidewalks and uneven surfaces caused by freeze-thaw damage.

Houseless residents and those without adequate shelter are more exposed to dangerous cold snaps and icy conditions that follow thaws, increasing health risks such as hypothermia or frostbite.

Low-income households may be disproportionately affected by home damage (e.g., cracked foundations, sewer back-ups) since they have fewer financial resources for repairs or to relocate during service disruptions.

Frontline outdoor workers (e.g., maintenance, construction, utility crews) experience higher exposure to unsafe conditions, physical strain, and mental stress during unpredictable freeze-thaw events.

Water management - Water Network Expansion Project: As part of the City of Regina's long-term growth strategy, the Water Master Plan (WMP) identified critical infrastructure upgrades necessary to support the city's expanding water distribution needs over the next 25 years. To ensure sustainable growth and reliable water service during emergencies, the WMP outlines a comprehensive 25-year capital upgrade plan, including a recommendation to implement the Water Network Expansion Project, formerly known as the Eastern Pressure Solution.

The Water Network Expansion Project aims to enhance Regina's water distribution system by building critical infrastructure that supports both current and future population growth. This project includes the construction of:

A new water pumping station.
Two 42.5-megalitre (ML) water storage reservoirs.
An 8.4-kilometer water supply main.
These upgrades will improve the city's capacity to meet daily water demands, handle emergency situations like facility shutdowns and firefighting, and ensure reliable water service for a population of up to 310,000 people. Moreover, the design of the new facilities includes future expansion capacity, enabling the system to support a population growth of up to 500,000 people.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Residential Home Retrofits Rebate: The Energy and Sustainability Framework (ESF) identifies retrofitting buildings as a significant opportunity to achieve reductions in energy consumption and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while also creating local jobs. As of 2022, approximately 61,000 residential homes will require retrofits for Regina to reach its goals of becoming 100 per cent renewable and net-zero by 2050. The speed and intensity of those retrofits are important due to the compounding and lasting effects of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.Cities across Canada are facing the same challenge in terms of needing to complete retrofits at scale. To assist homeowners improve their home energy efficiency, the federal government created the Greener Homes Grant. The Grant provides funds for home evaluations and retrofits, to a total of $5,600. To encourage retrofits in Regina, Administration recommends launching a residential retrofit rebate program (Retrofit Rebate Program) that matches the funding for work covered and rebated by the federal Greener Homes Grant. Funding approved in the 2022 Budget will enable the initial implementation of the Program, with funding for subsequent years requested through the 2023-2024 budget process.Not only do more efficient homes support long-term climate objectives but retrofit investments also create economic and financial benefits. Encouraging and accelerating action on home retrofits will create new demand for jobs — for energy auditors, retrofit contractors, and the next-generation of skilled workers — and an increased demand for energy efficient equipment and low-carbon materials will grow the green building product supply chain in Canada. Link: https://www.regina.ca/export/sites/Regina.ca/about-regina/renewable-regina/.galleries/pdfs/Big-Move-1.pdf

Transport - EV Bus purchases, Transit facility upgrades, EV Charging Stations: The switch to Low-emissions vehicles is one of the seven 'Big Moves' identified in the Energy & Sustainability Framework that will make Regina renewable by 2050. Regina, like many Canadian cities, is heavily reliant on individual automobile trips to get around. The transportation sector makes up 23 per cent of community emissions on a yearly basis. While the city cannot avoid all vehicle trips, there are viable alternatives to gasolinefueled vehicles. The technology continues to evolve for battery electric vehicles while prices decrease. Other technologies such as hydrogen vehicles are in rapid development. Both solutions require new infrastructure to support their widespread adoption. Other benefits of low-emissions vehicles are that they are more efficient than gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles, so they use less energy overall, and the ongoing operation and maintenance costs tend to be lower. The City of Regina is budgetting the purchase of at least 7 EV busses in 2023 ($8.5M), with plans to continue to expand the EV fleet moving forward as busses reach the end of their lifecycles. The City is budgetting electrification upgrades to its transit facility infrastructure ($40M) as well as the installation of additional EV chargers throughout the City throughout 2023 ($750K) and 2024 (750K).

project_info: Transport - Transit Enhancements & Pedestrian Connectivity: The Transit Master Plan is one the City's main strategic priorities identified by Council. Passed in 2022, the plan identifies key actions to improve transit and expand mobility options for residents, employees and visitors in Regina. Pedestrian connectivity is a key component of the plan and in order to make transit a transportation mode of choice, an additional $10M investment in pedestrian connectivity is required to help support an accessible and sustainable community. This project will connect sidewalks and pathways to and from transit bus stops. It will be completed by the Roadways & Transportation department on behalf of Transit & Fleet.The investment in pedestrian connectivity will address a number of accessibility issues, for example, a significant number of the City's transit stops have no sidewalks, or limited access to sidewalks, which creates transit challenges, especially for those residents with accessibility issues. In addition to pedestrian connectivity, there are a number of operational and infrastructure areas that require investment if the City is to achieve the opportunities identified in the Transit Master Plan. These projects include $7.5M in upgrades to 11th avenue to support downtown transit development and efficiency, $1.5M investments in a transit mobile system, and $5M (over five years) for customer service and shelter improvements. Transit is in the process of scoping other work that may also be required; including the option to purchase additional EV busses not included in the City's submission to the Zero Emissions Transportation Fund. The transit enhancements and pedestrian connectivity projects directly align with the City's Transit Master Plan; Energy and Sustainability Framework; as well as the federal government's Active Transportation Strategy. \n\nhttps://www.regina.ca/transportation-roads-parking/driving/road-maintenance-construction/

Other: winter storm: A worst-case scenario for a severe winter storm, such as a large system covering agricultural zones, would disproportionately impact vulnerable populations and key sectors. This scenario begins with freezing rain, coating power lines, roads, sidewalks, and trees with ice, followed by blizzard conditions lasting over 60 hours, reminiscent of the February 1978 storm. Vulnerable populations, such as the elderly, those with limited mobility, and rural residents, would face heightened risks. Widespread power outages, exacerbated by frozen and damaged utility lines, would leave many without heat, leading to increased instances of hypothermia, carbon monoxide poisoning from improper heating sources, and fatalities from hazardous road conditions. Rural populations could be especially affected, lacking accessible alternatives for heating, transportation, and medical support.

Social impacts would include short-term disruptions to quality of life and damage to localized culturally significant objects. Vulnerable populations might struggle to access basic services or stay connected to community support, intensifying social isolation.

Critical infrastructure would be severely disrupted, potentially requiring multi-municipal, provincial, and federal responses to restore power, clear roads, and manage emergency services. The inability to repair infrastructure due to the ongoing storm conditions would prolong the suffering of vulnerable populations. The agricultural sector would experience devastating losses, particularly for livestock producers, as seen in the 1998 ice storm, which led to major losses of livestock and poultry. In urban areas, ice-covered tree limbs falling on power lines would compound outages, further delaying recovery efforts.

Economically, the storm could lead to long-term regional damages, including the collapse of aging buildings under snow accumulation and disruptions in critical infrastructure that last more than two years. Vulnerable sectors such as agriculture and small businesses reliant on power and transportation would be severely affected.

Environmentally, the storm would result in both immediate and delayed impacts, with damage to vegetation and trees taking years to recover, particularly in rural areas where recovery resources are more limited. This scenario begins with freezing rain, coating power lines, roads, sidewalks, and trees with ice, followed by blizzard conditions lasting over 60 hours, reminiscent of the February 1978 storm. Vulnerable populations, such as the elderly, those with limited mobility, and rural residents, would face heightened risks. Widespread power outages, exacerbated by frozen and damaged utility lines, would leave many without heat, leading to increased instances of hypothermia, carbon monoxide poisoning from improper heating sources, and fatalities from hazardous road conditions. Rural populations could be especially affected, lacking accessible alternatives for heating, transportation, and medical support.

Social impacts would include short-term disruptions to quality of life and damage to localized culturally significant objects. Vulnerable populations might struggle to access basic services or stay connected to community support, intensifying social isolation.

Critical infrastructure would be severely disrupted, potentially requiring multi-municipal, provincial, and federal responses to restore power, clear roads, and manage emergency services. The inability to repair infrastructure due to the ongoing storm conditions would prolong the suffering of vulnerable populations. The agricultural sector would experience devastating losses, particularly for livestock producers, as seen in the 1998 ice storm, which led to major losses of livestock and poultry. In urban areas, ice-covered tree limbs falling on power lines would compound outages, further delaying recovery efforts.

Economically, the storm could lead to long-term regional damages, including the collapse of aging buildings under snow accumulation and disruptions in critical infrastructure that last more than two years. Vulnerable sectors such as agriculture and small businesses reliant on power and transportation would be severely affected.

Environmentally, the storm would result in both immediate and delayed impacts, with damage to vegetation and trees taking years to recover, particularly in rural areas where recovery resources are more limited. These impacts underscore the need for emergency preparedness plans tailored to the needs of vulnerable populations and sectors.

However, Regina's efforts were below the regional average relative to Land Use Planning and Flood Risk Assessment. In reference to Regina's Land Use Planning policies, the city reported that mechanisms exist through which developers can apply to create developments on floodplains. Such developments may require floodproofing measures, but development on floodplains is not explicitly prohibited in Regina, in contrast to what is mandated in some other Canadian jurisdictions. While the overall number of freeze-thaw days is projected to decline, these events are expected to occur at more irregular times of year or outside the traditional winter season, creating additional risks.

Impacts of freeze-thaw cycles include:
Infrastructure stress: Expansion and contraction of moisture in asphalt, concrete, and clay soils accelerates damage to roads, sidewalks, and underground utilities, leading to more frequent pipe breakages, cracked foundations, and degraded transportation networks.

Public safety risks: Ice formation from sudden thaws followed by refreezing increases the risk of slips, falls, and traffic accidents.

Service disruptions: Freeze-thaw cycles can overwhelm drainage systems, cause localized flooding, and damage residential properties such as basements and sewer lines.

Impacts on vulnerable populations:

Elderly residents and people with disabilities face greater risks of injury from icy sidewalks and uneven surfaces caused by freeze-thaw damage.

Houseless residents and those without adequate shelter are more exposed to dangerous cold snaps and icy conditions that follow thaws, increasing health risks such as hypothermia or frostbite.

Low-income households may be disproportionately affected by home damage (e.g., cracked foundations, sewer back-ups) since they have fewer financial resources for repairs or to relocate during service disruptions.

Frontline outdoor workers (e.g., maintenance, construction, utility crews) experience higher exposure to unsafe conditions, physical strain, and mental stress during unpredictable freeze-thaw events.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Food and Yard Waste Program: By investing in the infrastructure for a green cart service for 65,000 households, the City has the opportunity to set the foundation for a long-term organic waste diversion program. Currently, over 50 per cent of what Regina residents send to the landfill each year is compostable. Diverting this material will reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, extend the life of the landfill and contribute to Regina's Community Priority of conservation, stewardship and environmental sustainability. Once the residential program is in place, the City would then look at non-residential diversion. After a successful pilot, City Council has approved a citywide curbside food and yard waste service to be rolled out in fall 2023. This new service is part of the City's long-term solid waste management plan, Waste Plan ReginaOpens in new window, to send less waste to the landfill and reach the 65 per cent residential diversion target.The City used data and feedback from our pilot participants to build a food and yard waste service specific to the needs of Regina residents. The city-wide service will save landfill space, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and the material collected will be processed to create a useable product.Here's a look at what residents can expect coming in 2023:A 240-litre green cart will be used to collect the material - this is two-thirds the size of the blue carts that residents have todayAll food scraps, including meat, bones, dairy and greases, yard waste and soiled paper (paper towel, cardboard and tissues) can go into the green cartwhich will divert roughly 50 per cent of the waste that is currently going into the garbage in ReginaResidents can use compostable bagsGreen carts will be collected weekly between April and October and biweekly between November and March; garbage will be collected biweekly year-round.\n\nhttps://www.regina.ca/home-property/recycling-garbage/food-yard-waste/

Buildings - Renewable Upgrades to Municipal Facilities: This funding is for a program to align city facilities with Council's commitment to being a 100% renewable city by 2050 and the recently adopted Energy and Sustainability Framework. A significant portion of the organization's greenhouse gas emissions is attributed to the facilities portfolio. Utility consumption in facilities represents a significant portion of the department operating budget and with escalating utility costs, inflation, carbon pricing and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions there is a need to upgrade facilities to lower the utility consumption to meet the renewable target. Facility upgrades can include infrastructure systems, mechanical and electrical systems, building envelope assemblies, alternative sources of energy and upgrades based on the recommendations from the Energy Monitoring & Optimization Infrastructure project being completed in 2021 and 2022. A roadmap and implementation plan being developed in 2022 will provide further detail and the initial target facilities for investment.Retrofitting buildings is one of the seven 'Big Moves' identified in the Energy & Sustainability Framework that will make Regina renewable by 2050. Retrofitting municipal facilities presents a significant opportunity to achieve reductions in energy consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and energy costs for municipal operations. Retrofitting municipal buildings also positions the City as a leader and models the actions being asked of the community. Energy use in buildings accounts for 69 per cent of GHG emissions in Regina. To reach net-zero in Regina, all existing buildings in the community will need to be retrofitted to be more energy-efficient. Facility upgrades can include infrastructure systems, mechanical and electrical systems, building envelope assemblies, alternative sources of energy and upgrades based on the recommendations from the Energy Monitoring & Optimization Infrastructure project being completed in 2021 and 2022. A roadmap and implementation plan will be in place by the end of 2022 to prioritize investment to maximize impact.This project aligns with the federal government's 2030 Emission Reduction Plan and the provincial government's Prairie Resilience: A Made-in-Saskatchewan Climate Change Strategy.

Buildings - Energy Monitoring and Management System: A corporate energy monitoring and management system is required to centralize and modernize the tracking of energy use, utility costs, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. At present, utility data is stored across multiple departments and platforms, while facility GHG emissions are calculated manually in spreadsheets—an approach that is time-intensive, increases the risk of errors, and slows both real-time and long-term decision-making.

The City's previous monitoring software, which was connected to roughly 50 sites, now requires replacement. This presents an opportunity to implement a more integrated, corporate-wide solution that can deliver real-time energy data and forecasts, automate GHG tracking, and streamline utility data management.

Such a system could reduce annual utility costs by 10% or more by enabling staff to act quickly on real-time data, prevent billing errors, and verify energy savings from efficiency projects (e.g., LED lighting upgrades, building retrofits). The system should also feature a web-based dashboard capable of aggregating solar photovoltaic production data from City-owned sites, providing a comprehensive view of renewable energy generation alongside utility consumption.

Extreme heat: The Fifth National Climate Assessment projects that Knox County will experience 20-80 more extreme heat days by 2050 compared to a 1991-2020 baseline. Knoxville's HMP expects that this hazard will impact 50-100% of the county, cause minor injuries, damage or destroy more than 10% of property, and shut down critical facilities for at least a day.

NOAA has shown that heat is one of the leading weather-related killers in the United States. Those at greatest risk for heat-related illness (such as stroke) include infants and children, people 65 years of age and older, people with chronic medical conditions, and pregnant people. Also at risk are those who work or participate in strenuous physical activities outside, those who lack adequate shelter, and lower-income households who may not use air conditioning. 

Extreme heat events can have severe impacts on natural ecosystems, agriculture, power infrastructure, water supply, and public health. When prolonged, extreme heat can deteriorate infrastructure such as pavement, railroads, and transmission lines.
 | Urban flooding: Knoxville has approximately 6,700 acres in flood zones, extending into populated areas that can experience property damage during flood events. There were 44 floods reported in Knox County between 2013-2023. Modeling from Oak Ridge National Laboratory suggests that the HUC 12 watersheds intersecting Knox County will experience an increase in the annual number of very heavy precipitation days (precipitation greater than 0.8 inches) compared to the historical average. 

Although future precipitation patterns are very difficult to predict, a general increase in global temperatures is expected to increase the frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events because of increased evaporation and the ability of warmer air to hold more moisture. The combination of heavy rain, development in flood-prone areas, and impermeable infrastructure is likely to increase the scale, intensity, duration, and damage of floods. | Storm: Severe storms occur frequently in the City of Knoxville, especially from May-August. The region experiences approximately 30-50 thunderstorm days per year. The HMP area experienced 212 severe thunderstorms with winds exceeding 58mph between 1993-2017, causing nearly $3.5m in property and crop damages.

Storms in the Knoxville area are most commonly accompanied by high wind, lightning, and hail. Most storm events cause downed trees and power lines, causing disruptions in normal daily operations that often require debris removal and other associated costs. Common types of damages were structural damages caused by falling limbs and debris, roof damages, overturned vehicles and light structures, and downed power poles resulting in some loss of electric service. In addition, clearance of the
debris left behind can be costly and is generally not reported in damage estimates in NCDC.

WIND: The planning area is in FEMA's Wind Zone III, where winds can reach 160-200 mph. On average, over 4 wind events occur in the planning area every year. High winds can cause significant property and crop damage, threaten public safety, and have adverse economic impacts from business closures and power loss.

LIGHTNING: The planning area is in a region that received 4-8 lighting strikes per km2 per year, but most do not result in damages. The NCDC reports only 2 lightning events from 1995-2017.

HAIL: The NCDC reports 128 hail events in the planning area from 1962-2017 (averaging one event every two years). 28 of those events were of 'destructive magnitude' with hail exceeding 1.75' in diameter and property damage exceeding $51,000.

climate_hazard:
Snow and ice: Heavy snowfall, ice storms, and an increase in winter precipitation has resulted in damage to built and natural infrastructure. Heavy, wet snow causes roofs to collapse, more frequent freeze-thaw cycles has caused damage to roads and agricultural crops, and an increase in winter rain has resulted in homes and businesses flooding. Increased freezing rains events may damage power lines and trees, increase hazardous road accidents, and increase the use of salt which may impact water resources. 

The impacts of winter weather extremes are felt acutely by those who are unhoused or with unstable housing who may struggle to find shelter during winter storms; low-income households who may struggle to afford the repairs resulting from damage to their property or pay high heating bills; and the elderly, those with underlying health conditions, and those who need mobility supports who may struggle to safely travel in winter conditions and access the supports they need. In Greater Sudbury, there is an overrepresentation of Indigenous individuals experiencing homelessness. The main reason for losing housing is due to not having enough income. In Greater Sudbury nearly 21,000 people or 12.8 percent of the population live in poverty, and according to the 2016 census, the average individual income of women in Greater Sudbury is approximately 65% of that of males.

Changes in winter weather can increase demand on public services including snow and ice removal, road repair, plumbing, and utilities. For example, ice storms can cause significant damage to utility lines and heavy snow, rain, and freeze-thaw cycles can damage water pipes leading to a large financial cost in repairs and gaps in service. Our tourism and culture industry can also be impacted due to changes in winter activities and less travel to, and within, the City due to poor conditions and damaged infrastructure. 

 | Extreme heat: Those who are unhoused or experience housing instability are at risk of heat-related illness due to prolonged exposure to extreme heat and limited access to shelter, water, and food. This furthermore places stress on community groups, non-profits, government agencies, and healthcare workers who perform outreach and provide resources and support to those at-risk. In Greater Sudbury, there is an overrepresentation of Indigenous individuals experiencing homelessness. The main reason for losing housing is due to not having enough income. Children and the elderly are also particularly at risk of heat-related illness due to their physiology which impacts their ability to regulate temperature. In addition to extreme heat days, the increasing number of warm days and decreasing number of cold days will adversely impact air quality which can result in respiratory symptoms among vulnerable populations and sectors. These symptoms can be exacerbated in people with pre-existing health conditions.

In addition, extreme heat and drought have resulted in observed shifts in growing seasons, generating concern for the City's agricultural industry, and farmers, whose livelihoods depend on the health of their crops. Extreme heat can also impact sectors such as construction, roadwork, forestry, and the hospitality and service industry as employees are at-risk of experiencing high heat levels and subsequent health impacts such as dehydration and heat stress. 

 | Drought: Drought can lead to lower water levels in lakes, streams, and rivers, groundwater, and reduced soil moisture. This can impact our drinking water supply, harm fish and wildlife populations, cause shifts in the growth pattern of plants, increase the risk of wildfires, and reduce air quality from wildfires happening locally and in other parts of the province and country. 

Reduced water levels and changes to fish and wildlife populations can negatively impact those who practice subsistence living, those who rely on well water, tourism and recreation industries, as well as hydroelectric power generation. Drought can limit crop yields and harm livestock, which impacts the agricultural industry and the livelihoods of farmers. Those with prolonged exposure to reduced air quality, such as those living unhoused and those working outdoors, are at risk of the health impacts of particulate matter in wildfire smoke and heat-related illness. 
 | Extreme cold: Low-income groups are more at risk of extreme cold due to high heating costs. 
Outdoor workers and those experiencing homelessness have increased exposure to extreme cold and resulting health impacts such as hypothermia, frostbite and windburn. 
Colder winter temperatures will increase freezing rain events and road ice, reducing travel conditions and increasing the risk for power outages. 
These impacts can result in an increased demand on healthcare and social work services and heating systems.
 | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Air quality issues, Increased incidence and prevalence of disease and illness, Increased risk to already vulnerable populations, Increased mental health concerns (become more anxious, worried, etc. when smoke from forest fires affect us), Others at risk include children due to their developing respiratory systems and those with underlying health conditions. | Urban flooding: Damage to private property, closed businesses.
Increased rain events in the summer may lead to urban flooding especially in basements in low-lying areas.
Increased frequency and intensity of rainfall may flood roads in low-lying areas.
Increased incidences of flooding leading to displacement of residents
 | Other: Invasive Species: An increased presence of invasive species due to changes in temperature and precipitation can threaten native species populations, can cause a loss of biodiversity, and can impact the availability of local food sources (forest and freshwater food), and threaten human health. Those who work outdoors, rely on local food sources, and native species of plants and animals for cultural and ceremonial purposes can be particularly impacted. For example, this can include those who work in forestry, conservation, local food production, as well as Indigenous peoples. 
The spread of invasive species and these subsequent impacts to the natural environment can impact agricultural, forestry, conservation, tourism and recreation, and land-use planning sectors. 
 | Infectious disease: Changes in precipitation and hotter summers are leading to increased algal blooms and water-borne disease which can be harmful to aquatic ecosystems and human health. Children are more susceptible to water-borne disease because they are more likely to spend time swimming and accidentally swallow water. Additionally, the elderly and people with underlying illnesses or compromised immune systems have increased risk to illness from water-borne bacteria, and those who are pregnant are more susceptible to water-borne disease because of immune system changes. Those with limited access to safe drinking water such as the unhoused are also more at risk of being exposed to water-borne bacteria. The use of an individual private well can also increase exposure to water-borne disease since testing and treatment is the responsibility of the owner. 
The arts, entertainment and recreation, and tourism sectors can be impacted by the closure of public beaches and water access points.

Hotter summer temperatures also make the Greater Sudbury area a suitable breeding ground for ticks which can carry and spread diseases like lyme disease, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, and Powassan virus disease. Those who work outdoors, particularly near areas with vegetation like tall grass, shrubs, and trees, have increased exposure to ticks and tick-borne diseases. According to Public Health and Districts, 4 cases of lyme disease was reported in 2024. 

In 2024, there were 103 cases of food- and water-borne illness reported, with salmonellosis being the most frequently reported. According to Public Health Sudbury & Districts, “while anyone can become infected with salmonella bacteria, young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems are more likely to have serious complications from the infection” (Snapshot of infectious disease data, 2024, p. 30). Additionally, females reported a higher rate of this food-borne illness than males. 
 | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Tornado warnings where residents are unsure of what to do and are unprepared.
Increased damage or injuries.
Vulnerable populations affected by damage to property when they can't afford to fix it.
More storms, lightning, tornadoes may increase property damage.
More storms, lightning and tornadoes may impact electricity line and power outages.

Vulnerable populations like older adults, those with vulnerable health and disabilities may be more impacted by spring/summer storms due to the potential for power outages (impacting those who need constant electric supply for health or heating/cooling needs). Outdoor workers may be affected if caught by a surprise summer storm and unable to quickly find shelter, and low-income residents may live in homes that are less structurally equipped to deal with major rain or wind events and be without resources to recover if their homes or properties are damaged. Winter storms may become stronger and more intense as the average temperatures increase; they may or may not become more frequent, though. The strength and additional snow that comes with more powerful winter storms could affect older adults, those with disabilities, and those without a vehicle who may find it more difficult to connect to essential services during periods of snow. | River flooding: Since the city was founded in 1864, Fort Collins has experienced many devastating floods. However, according to the 2022 Larimer County Community Health Survey, conducted by the Health District of Northern Larimer County, more than 50% of residents do not consider flooding to be a problem for the Fort Collins area. Previous floods have been caused by snowmelt and overflows from the various rivers and creeks in the areas, strengthening summer storms and increased heavy rainfall, and development that has encroached on drainage areas. project_info: Transport - West Elizabeth Bus Rapid Transit Corridor: As shared in section 9.2, Fort Collins is expanding the West Elizabeth Street Bus Rapid Transit corridor to provide better access to and more frequent service for one of the most heavily trafficked corridors in the city. The West Elizabeth Corridor will be an accessible and reliable multimodal transportation corridor with an emphasis on connecting Colorado State University's Foothills and Main Campuses, the Mason Express Bus Rapid Transit (MAX), and the Downtown and South Transit Centers. The project will also improve existing business access and ensure access to future infill and redevelopment areas to accommodate the growing number and diversity of people using the corridor. A key feature of the corridor is the goal for 100% electric buses, including electric charging infrastructure along the route for bus charging. Additionally, the plan incorporates improvements to sidewalks, bicycling pathways, and intersections to enhance the safety and multi-modal nature of this three-mile corridor. 30% design was completed in 2022, with 100% design scheduled for completion in 2025. The team has secured partial funding though federal grants and other sources, and continues to work with their partners on additional opportunities. For more details about the project, please see the City's website: https://www.fcgov.com/westelizabeth/

project_info: Buildings - Adopting and Implementing Building Performance Standards: As mentioned in section 9.2, Fort Collins is part of the National Building Performance Standards coalition, which is a group of state and local governments working to create policies that will improve performance and efficiency in existing buildings. Within Fort Collins, the goal is to implement building performance standards for commercial and multi-family buildings. A community task force, technical committee and equity committer are contributing to develop the policy and supporting resources needed to deploys a successful BPS that is specific to our building stock. Staff originally proposed BPS to council in April 2024 and continue to have active community conversations around targets and launching a program. Funding will be required to support building owners who need to undertake upgrades to meet the standards when they go into effect. The total cost of the project is based on annual estimates through 2040.

project_info: Transport - Active Modes Plan Implementation: High-Priority/Readiness Projects: As shared previously in Fort Collins' Active Modes Plan (section 8.2), the City has a goal of increasing trips using active modes of transportation (walking, biking, rolling, micro-mobility) to 50% of all trips taken. Do accomplish this, the City will focus on shifting shorter trips under 3 miles to using active modes by providing better connections between pedestrian and biking networks, increasing protections and safe access to infrastructure, and improving the quality of sidewalks, intersections, and crossings. The Active Modes planning team has prioritized projects into high-priority/high-readiness projects (for implementation in the next 5-years), medium-priority/readiness projects (for implementation in 5-10 years), and low-priority/readiness projects (for implementation beyond 10-years). The collection of projects shared for funding here include those in the high-priority/readiness list, which, when implemented, will have immediate safety and accessibility impacts that will support active mode shifts in the near-term, 5-year timeframe (see pages 68-70 of the Active Modes Full Plan for specific cost details; https://www.fcgov.com/fcmoves/active-modes-plan). These projects include pedestrian infrastructure improvements like intersection redesigns and signal operations, and bicycle improvements such as creating separated bike lanes and improving signage and signals. To-date, approximately $1.7 million of funding has been secured for upcoming projects, with $.5 million additional awaiting approval (the slight discrepancy between remaining funds needed compared to the total project cost less funding secured is due to differences between the opinions of probable cost used to estimate the total cost of high priority/readiness projects and changes in project scope in design and escalating construction costs).

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Epic Homes Loan Program: Fort Collins launched a version of an on-bill financing program in 2013 and redesigned it in 2018 when the City was awarded a grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies to improve and revamp the idea. Extreme heat: Extreme heat is a priority hazard identified in Lakewood's Climate Hazard and Social Vulnerability Study and is projected to lead to longer, hotter summers and more frequent extreme heat days in the coming decades. Rising nighttime temperatures will further intensify heat stress, particularly in areas most affected by the urban heat island effect, where paved surfaces and a lack of green space trap heat, making it harder for temperatures to cool down overnight. When nighttime cooling is limited, both people and infrastructure experience prolonged exposure to heat, increasing health risks and straining energy systems as air conditioning demand rises. Extreme heat events pose serious health risks, especially for older adults, young children, outdoor workers and individuals facing social isolation. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can lead to heat exhaustion, heat stroke and other heat-related illnesses, which can become life threatening if not addressed quickly. People without access to air conditioning or stable housing face greater challenges, as they have limited ways to escape the heat. Extreme heat can also affect buildings and infrastructure, causing roofs and facades to crack, warp or curl, leading to costly damages to homes and businesses.

Jefferson County has hundreds of square miles of parks and open space which provide habitat for species that are vulnerable to extreme temperatures. Increasing temperatures may cause species to shift habitats in elevation and latitude and extended periods of extreme heat can stress both flora and fauna species. Warmer temperatures can also lead to earlier snowmelt affecting insect and wildlife life cycles as well as seed production and germination. | Urban flooding: Flooding is considered a moderate but growing risk for Lakewood, with climate change expected to bring slight increases in precipitation and runoff over the coming decades. While overall annual precipitation is projected to rise slightly, spring rainfall is expected to increase more quickly than in other seasons. Additionally, the number of heavy rainfall days — when more than one inch of rain falls in a single day — is also projected to increase. This could lead to more frequent localized flooding, particularly in areas where stormwater drainage systems may struggle to keep up. Over time, annual runoff is expected to rise, which could place additional pressure on urban infrastructure, roads and waterways.

The City of Lakewood has 212 improved parcels, 269 buildings with an estimated loss of 74,482,466 within the 1% annual chance flood. Of the buildings in the 1% annual flood area, 138 are considered residential, exposing an estimated 388 residents to flooding. Lakewood is among the cities with the greatest potential losses in the County from flooding the 1% annual flood chance. There are an additional 297 parcels, 309 buildings located in the 0.2% annual chance flood hazard area, with estimated loss of 40,745,542. There are 290 residential buildings in the 0.2% annual flood area and an estimated 686 residents potentially exposed. There are 22 critical facilities in the 1% annual chance flood zone, 14 of which are bridges, and there are seven additional critical facilities in the 0.2% annual chance flood zone. 

Certain populations are especially vulnerable to flooding, including residents with mobility challenges, individuals experiencing homelessness, outdoor workers, and residents experiencing social isolation, who may face greater challenges in evacuating or recovering from flood-related damage. Additionally, homes, businesses and critical infrastructure in flood-prone areas are at higher risk of water damage and disruption. | Drought: The geographic extent rating for drought is extensive. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor records for Jefferson County, in the 1,096-week period from 2000 through January 4, 2021, the county spent 645 weeks (60% of the time) in some level of drought, defined as Abnormally Dry (D0) or worse conditions. Approximately 36% of the time, or 393 weeks, was spent in Moderate Drought (D1) or worse conditions. Drought impacts in Jefferson County can be wide-reaching: economic, environmental, and societal. The most significant impacts associated with drought are those related to water intensive activities such as wildfire protection, commerce, tourism/recreation, municipal usage, and wildlife preservation. Although the agricultural industry in the County is limited, it is expected to experience crop losses and livestock feeding expenses and deaths. Jefferson County will see an increase in dry fuels, beetle kill, associated wildfires, and some loss of tourism/recreation revenue. Water supply issues for municipal, industrial, and domestic needs will be a concern for the entire County. Lawn and tree impacts in suburban areas could result from water restrictions. Vulnerability increases with consecutive winters of below-average snowpack. Drought conditions can also cause soil to compact and not absorb water well, potentially making an area more susceptible to flooding. It also increases the wildfire hazard and even landslide hazard. The impacts of drought on vulnerable populations include agricultural and recreation/tourism sector job loss, secondary economic losses to local businesses and public recreational resources, increased cost to local and state government for large-scale water acquisition and delivery, and water rationing and water wells running dry for individuals and families. Other public health issues can include impaired drinking water quality, increased incidence of mosquito-borne illness, an increase in wildlife-human confrontations and respiratory complications because of declined air quality in times of drought. | Extreme cold: While extreme cold events are expected to become less frequent in Lakewood, they will still pose significant risks to vulnerable populations when they do occur. Climate projections suggest a declining likelihood of extreme cold, along with lower wind speeds, which may reduce the impact of wind chill. However, the destabilization of the polar jet stream adds uncertainty to these trends. As the Arctic warms faster than other regions, the reduced temperature difference can weaken and disrupt the jet stream, leading to sudden, prolonged periods of extreme cold in mid-latitude areas like Lakewood.

Even as winters become milder overall, the potential for unexpected and intense cold snaps remains a concern. Certain groups, including outdoor workers, residents experiencing homelessness, children and older adults, are especially at risk when temperatures drop, particularly if they do not have access to adequate shelter. While most local buildings and infrastructure are designed to withstand cold conditions, severe cold events can still cause frozen and burst pipes, road hazards and increased demand on energy systems. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfires are considered a moderate but growing climate risk for Lakewood, as warmer and drier conditions are expected to increase the likelihood of fire activity in and around the city. With more extremely hot days and a slight increase in the number of dry days each year, vegetation could become more prone to ignition, elevating wildfire risks. While fires have traditionally been more common in rural and forested areas, climate change is making urban and suburban communities more vulnerable, particularly those near parks, open spaces and the wildland-urban interface. Residential property types have the greatest number of parcels at risk of wildfire, in addition there are 4,654 residents exposed to wildfire risk, a majority of which (1,988) are located in the low and moderate-risk areas. The City of Lakewood has a total of 36 critical facilities at risk to wildfire, most of which are within the lowest to moderate wildfire risk areas. More recently, all populations in Lakewood have been exposed to wildfire smoke from not only within the region, but also the western United States and Canada, which has severely impacted the air quality index several days each year. 

Certain areas and populations face greater wildfire risks than others. Residents living near Bear Creek, Green Mountain, Crown Hill Park and the Rooney Valley are especially vulnerable due to their proximity to fire-prone landscapes. Additionally, older adults, individuals with respiratory conditions and those sensitive to smoke exposure may experience health impacts from wildfire smoke, even if fires do not directly threaten their homes. Homes and businesses may also face power outages from utility shutdowns, a precaution sometimes taken during periods of extreme fire danger. Parks and natural areas are also at risk of damage from wildfires. | Other: Hailstorms: Hailstorms pose one of the most significant climate risks for Lakewood, and they have caused widespread property damage and rising insurance costs in recent years. Some insurance providers have even reduced their presence in Colorado due to the increasing financial burden of severe hailstorms. However, projections for key climate indicators suggest that the frequency and severity of hailstorms are unlikely to increase significantly, though there is uncertainty in forecasting hailstorms, as complex interactions between several climate variables drive hail formation. While future storms may resemble historical events in intensity, the financial impact of hail damage could continue to rise due to expanding development and increasing repair costs. 

Although hailstorms themselves may not worsen, many local systems remain highly vulnerable to their effects. Outdoor workers, residents without shelter, pedestrians, and cyclists face direct risks of injury, particularly during fast-moving storms. Homes without hail-resistant roofing, as well as farms, parks and recreational spaces, are also highly susceptible to damage. The aftermath of a severe hailstorm can disrupt local businesses, delay public services and strain emergency response resources. Given these risks, strengthening building resilience and increasing public awareness will be key strategies for reducing the impact of future hail events in Lakewood.

project_info: Renewable energy - On-Site Solar for Municipal Facilities: A feasibility study was prepared in 2022 to evaluate the potential for on-site solar generation at several municipal facilities. Extreme heat: Extreme heat is a priority hazard identified in Lakewood's Climate Hazard and Social Vulnerability Study and is projected to lead to longer, hotter summers and more frequent extreme heat days in the coming decades. Rising nighttime temperatures will further intensify heat stress, particularly in areas most affected by the urban heat island effect, where paved surfaces and a lack of green space trap heat, making it harder for temperatures to cool down overnight. When nighttime cooling is limited, both people and infrastructure experience prolonged exposure to heat, increasing health risks and straining energy systems as air conditioning demand rises. Extreme heat events pose serious health risks, especially for older adults, young children, outdoor workers and individuals facing social isolation. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can lead to heat exhaustion, heat stroke and other heat-related illnesses, which can become life threatening if not addressed quickly. People without access to air conditioning or stable housing face greater challenges, as they have limited ways to escape the heat. Extreme heat can also affect buildings and infrastructure, causing roofs and facades to crack, warp or curl, leading to costly damages to homes and businesses.

Jefferson County has hundreds of square miles of parks and open space which provide habitat for species that are vulnerable to extreme temperatures. Increasing temperatures may cause species to shift habitats in elevation and latitude and extended periods of extreme heat can stress both flora and fauna species. Warmer temperatures can also lead to earlier snowmelt affecting insect and wildlife life cycles as well as seed production and germination. | Urban flooding: Flooding is considered a moderate but growing risk for Lakewood, with climate change expected to bring slight increases in precipitation and runoff over the coming decades. While overall annual precipitation is projected to rise slightly, spring rainfall is expected to increase more quickly than in other seasons. Additionally, the number of heavy rainfall days — when more than one inch of rain falls in a single day — is also projected to increase. This could lead to more frequent localized flooding, particularly in areas where stormwater drainage systems may struggle to keep up. Over time, annual runoff is expected to rise, which could place additional pressure on urban infrastructure, roads and waterways.

The City of Lakewood has 212 improved parcels, 269 buildings with an estimated loss of 74,482,466 within the 1% annual chance flood. Of the buildings in the 1% annual flood area, 138 are considered residential, exposing an estimated 388 residents to flooding. Lakewood is among the cities with the greatest potential losses in the County from flooding the 1% annual flood chance. There are an additional 297 parcels, 309 buildings located in the 0.2% annual chance flood hazard area, with estimated loss of 40,745,542. There are 290 residential buildings in the 0.2% annual flood area and an estimated 686 residents potentially exposed. There are 22 critical facilities in the 1% annual chance flood zone, 14 of which are bridges, and there are seven additional critical facilities in the 0.2% annual chance flood zone. 

Certain populations are especially vulnerable to flooding, including residents with mobility challenges, individuals experiencing homelessness, outdoor workers, and residents experiencing social isolation, who may face greater challenges in evacuating or recovering from flood-related damage. Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Coastal flooding in Sunnyvale would disrupt daily life and long-term stability by threatening homes and workplaces in low-lying shoreline areas, cutting off transportation routes, and damaging critical facilities such as the wastewater treatment plant that serve the entire community. Floodwaters would also degrade wetlands and Baylands ecosystems that normally absorb storm surges and protect against erosion, reducing the city's natural defenses and negatively impacting conservation efforts. Real estate would be damaged because of the coastal flooding too, and also arts, support services and waste management. For low-income households and workers in shoreline industries, these impacts translate into higher recovery costs, potential displacement, and loss of income, making them especially vulnerable to lasting economic and social consequences. For any marginalized groups, this would also be devastating, just as for the low income households. | Drought: California has had multiple droughts in the last century, and the drought's have become much more frequent over the years. Annual rainfall is also expected to decrease. This puts communities in Sunnyvale and around at a high risk of wildfires, droughts, and loss of habitats and ecosystems. Though Sunnyvale doesn't have a huge agriculture industry, it does have several parks and other regions which require water and would be affected in the event of a drought. Furthermore, Sunnyvale's community would also be affected by a heavy drought due to possible increases in water prices. Lastly, conservation efforts in order to maintain habitats in the region would also be hampered as a lack of water would end up driving many plants and animals in Sunnyvale to extinction. Manufacturing, accomodation, and food service industries will also be impacted by water restriction enforced during drought. 

Droughts would also impact low-income households as they may not be able to financially bear the burden of more expensive water. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat would hamper conservation efforts because plants and animals unable to endure the heat would end up dying or being forced to migrate out of Sunnyvale. Furthermore, extreme heat and heat wave would end up harming Sunnyvale's community and its residents, especially those who do not have the money to purchase air conditioning units. Some commercial and industrial facilities may not have the proper air conditioning, thereby endangering workers and leading to losses in productivity across all sectors, especially education and human health/social work activities. Any residents who are required to be outdoors during extreme heat periods would be susceptible to heat stress and exhaustion, particularly vulnerable communities like the elderly, youth, and outdoor workers. | Urban flooding: Sunnyvale sits in a relatively flat part of the South Bay, with stormwater flowing through creeks and engineered channels. During intense rainfall or atmospheric rivers, the storm drain system can be overwhelmed, leading to localized street and property flooding. Some areas that are low-lying in northern Sunnyvale and near the major freeway and highway onramps and intersections experience flooding due to the large amounts of impervious surfaces.

Flooding would be devastating for children, the elderly and low-income households as they may not know what to do or may face devastating financial impacts due to this. Furthermore, outdoor workers may lose their job due to flooded workplaces that may no longer be able to employ people. | Soil degradation/erosion: In Sunnyvale, soil degradation is an emerging climate risk closely linked to sea level rise and groundwater rise in low-lying areas such as Moffett Park and the Baylands. Rising groundwater can cause soil salinization, waterlogging, and reduced stability, which threaten building foundations, utilities, and transportation infrastructure. In addition, Sunnyvale's shoreline includes areas of artificial fill and industrial legacy soils; as groundwater rises, contaminants may be mobilized, increasing environmental and public health risks. Degraded soils also reduce the resilience of Bayland ecosystems, undermining their ability to provide natural flood protection. This would directly hamper conservation and real estate activities and would disrupt sewer and waste management systems. | Other forms of climate-induced landscape shift/degradation: Beyond soil salinization, Sunnyvale faces risks of climate-induced landscape shift and erosion in its Baylands and creek corridors. Sea level rise threatens to submerge or fragment tidal marshes, leading to a loss of natural flood buffers and shifts from marsh to open water ecosystems. Stronger storm events can accelerate creek bank erosion and undermine adjacent trails, roads, and utilities. In highly urbanized areas, impervious surfaces and altered runoff patterns intensify scouring and sediment displacement, further destabilizing landscapes. These changes reduce ecosystem services, increase flood risk, and threaten recreational and natural areas that are valued by the community. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Although Sunnyvale is located in the urban core of Silicon Valley and not in the wildland-urban interface, the City is increasingly vulnerable to the impacts of regional wildfires, particularly smoke and poor air quality.
