climate_hazard: Fire weather (risk of wildfires): In 2023, smoke from wildfires in northern Quebec and Ontario blew toward Peterborough. The smoke was low-level in the atmosphere and significantly deteriorated local air quality that produced some of the most polluted air since records began in the city. Many residents with pre-existing health conditions were affected with some individuals being rushed to the hospital because of complications from smoke inhalation. As climate change dries northern forests, larger fires are expected that will result in more extreme smoke conditions for Peterborough. | Extreme heat: The intensity and duration of heat waves are increasing for the city of Peterborough. In 2018, a significant summer heatwave occurred with multiple days of +30C and nighttime lows of +20C. The heat wave put added strain on the Ontario electricity grid from the increased demand for electricity to power air conditioners. Extreme heat also increases the risks of heat-related illnesses of outside workers, the homeless, individuals waiting for public transit, children, and the elderly. The City responded by extending cooling shelters hours to accommodate the city's homeless and at-risk populations without AC to cool down. | Heavy precipitation: The City of Peterborough is experiencing an increase in average rainfall precipitation making the city more prone to localized flooding. There have been multiple events of localized flooding from extreme rainfall over the last 20 years. Extreme rainfall events are projected to heighten for Peterborough due to increasing humid weather conditions in summer months and raising the likelihood that more acute flooding will impact the community in the future. To counteract this risk, the City has put in place measures to help prevent the risk of flooding through the promotion of low impact development (LID) for residential properties. This initiative supports the naturalization of properties to absorb rain and retain the precipitation as long as possible before discharging it into receiving infrastructure. Along with rain gardens, rain barrels have also been encouraged to be adopted by residents to store rainfall as well as utilizing the rain for watering gardens and lawns. In addition to the LID, Green UP, a local community environmental organization has been actively working towards depaving driveways, curbs, and dead-end roads with permeable materials to aid in absorbing rainfall. | Urban flooding: In 2004 the City of Peterborough experienced overland flooding from an extreme rain event that inundated the downtown core with 240 mm of rain. This caused $95 million in damages with an additional $21 million being spent on repairs to public infrastructure such as bridges and roads. The event was so significant that the City of Peterborough developed the Flood Reduction Master Plan in 2005. The events during the flood have become a community-wide touchstone across generations of Peterboroughites, which has catapulted flood reduction as one of the top municipal priorities to mitigate. To prevent downtown flooding, the City constructed the Jackson Creek Flood Diversion Project in 2023 that relieves Jackson Creek, which bisects the downtown core, to support flood control. Additional flood mitigation efforts that have been completed or are being currently undertaken to curb flooding include stormwater scenario modelling, updating the sub-watershed flood maps to identify flood-prone neighbourhoods, annual stormwater sewer monitoring and maintenance, downspout disconnection from sewers, and widening culverts in flood-prone areas to handle increased flows. | Extreme wind: In May 2022, a derecho windstorm impacted Peterborough that caused a 6-day power outage for parts of the city. The City established emergency shelters at arenas to provide 24-hour access for residents to shower, charge devices, and take respite till power was restored. | Snow and ice: In 2025, a severe multi-day ice storm impacted Peterborough, knocking out power for the majority of residents for 3-7 days. Many tree branches came down onto power lines, roofs, and vehicles. Municipal emergency protocols were enacted to support residents without power, including the opening of warming shelters in arenas and providing food. Damages amounting to $6.5 million were reported as a direct result of damages caused by the ice storm in Peterborough.
project_info: Buildings - Community Buildings Retrofit Program: The City is in the midst of retrofitting 11 facilities to reduce GHG emissions by 50% in 10 years and 80% in 20 years. Completed feasibility studies revealed that implementing energy conservation measures would cost up to $72,000,000. Funding is available from the Green Municipal Fund, but it is limited and first-come, first-served basis. The City is looking for an external capital funder to provide grants to realize the GHG reduction potential at facilities, such as community arenas.

climate_hazard: Extreme wind: Although all buildings are susceptible to high winds, the following structures are more likely to suffer damage, making low-income households more vulnerable: mobile homes, homes on crawlspaces, and schools, especially those with large span areas. Additionally, electrical infrastructure, communication lines, antennas, and towers can suffer damage from wind and downed branches/trees. Damages to buildings, roads, and vehicles can also be costly. Businesses interruptions can occur due to power outages. Flights may be delayed or canceled due to severe wind events. | Urban flooding: Ann Arbor is vulnerable to significant flooding due to existing development. Potential annualized loss from flooding is estimated at $47,590 (2017 dollars). GIS analysis was used to determine FEMA special flood hazard areas (A and AE Zones) cover approximately 1.6 square miles of the city (5.7 percent of the city's area). An examination of land parcel data and the digital FIRM (100-year floodplain map), shows 1,211 parcels of land that are either within or touch the FEMA mapped 100-year floodplain (3.7 percent). However, buildings outside of these areas are still at risk. In fact, a significant number of insurance claims are from properties outside of regulatory special flood hazards areas (FEMA 1.0 percent ACF). Recent events in Houston, TX estimated this figure as high as 80 percent. As a result, all current and future buildings, infrastructure, and populations in Ann Arbor are considered at risk to flooding. | Drought: Ann Arbor is considered to be a water-rich community. Drought is expected to have minimal impacts on infrastructure. Green infrastructure, such as green stormwater infrastructure, may incur minor damages during drought occurrences if plants cannot resist drought. Drought can have (and has had) several economic impacts on the city. One of the most pronounced economic impacts is that on agricultural holdings, as water supply is imperative for regional crops and livestock. There is limited agriculture within the Ann Arbor city limits, but a regional drought could have severe impacts to food prices in Ann Arbor which would disproportionately impact low-income-households and may even result in food shortages. Drought resulting in water shortage can also impact businesses (ranging from restaurants to manufacturing) which cannot operate without water. Lastly, in the case of a water shortage, the cost of water may increase (or the city may be forced to buy water from a water-rich area), which would have a more pronounced impact on low-income households and ripple effects in terms of a reduction in the local economic multiplier as money leaves the county. | Extreme heat: Groups particularly vulnerable to extreme heat include: 1) Older adults who do not adjust as quickly to changes in temperature. Older adults are also more likely to be on medications or have chronic illnesses that affect the body's ability to regulate its temperature. 2) Infants and children, who rely on others to keep them cool and hydrated. 3) Outdoor workers, who have more exposure to extreme heat and are more likely to become dehydrated. 4) Low-income populations, who may not have air conditioning available at home. Extreme heat events generally have minimal impact on infrastructure. Power consumption for air-conditioned environments could increase and thus stress utility infrastructure, resulting in blackouts. Ann Arbor currently experiences issues with electrical capacity during high-demand periods, and members of the TAC noted power outages during extreme heat events. In severe cases, heat can cause railroad tracks to expand. This is referred to as a heat kink in the rail line, and can result in disruptions or derailments. Heat can also cause pavement to expand. | Extreme cold: Certain populations, such as the elderly, young children, and low-income households without access to an adequate heat source are considered at a higher risk to the impacts of extreme cold, which could include death. Economic impacts from extreme cold/wind chill include repairs to burst pipes or degraded roads. In some cases, extreme cold may result in business or educational disruptions if people remain inside and cannot get to work, to school, or to the store.
project_info: Buildings - Aging in Place Efficiently: Aging in Place Efficiently partners with qualified older adults to help them remain in their homes for as long as possible. Improvements focus on three areas: comfort, lower energy bills, and home safety. The home improvements offered will depend on the needs of each homeowner. A licensed energy auditor, an occupational therapist, and a social worker will help determine the best options for your home within the available budget. Examples of potential home improvements include: insulation in walls and attics; weatherization; appliance upgrades; grab bars in bathrooms; handrails and ramps; improved lighting. Learn more here: https://www.a2gov.org/sustainability-innovations-home/sustainability-me/for-families-individuals/aging-in-place-efficiently/

project_info: Buildings - Bryant Sustainability Project: Imagine a resident-designed home energy audit that centers people, comfort, safety, and health. Imagine that assessment being piloted in a single low-income neighborhood such that identified needs can be aggregated and bulk discounts and improvements negotiated to help frontline populations immediately improve health, safety, comfort, and reduce energy bills. That's what we aim to do through a partnership with residents in the Bryant neighborhood, the Community Action Network, Bryant Community Center, the City of Ann Arbor, Elevate, home energy auditors, and contractors conducting home repair, weatherization, electrification, and solar installations. Located in the south of Ann Arbor, the Bryant neighborhood is defined as the roughly 260 households that are served by the Bryant Community Center - a community center run by the Community Action Network with support from the City of Ann Arbor. All the houses in the neighborhood were built by the same developer and only two archetypes exist - making extrapolation and comparison of opportunities possible across the neighborhood. The Bryant neighborhood is one of the City's largest low-income neighborhoods. Of the 260 households, about 75% are considered low-income, 50% are owner occupied, and the majority of residents are People of Color. In 2020, the City approached the McKnight Foundation and secured a planning grant to work with residents in the Bryant neighborhood, along with Community Action Network, to co-design a whole home health, safety, comfort, and decarbonization assessment specifically to improve indoor air quality, resident comfort, and to advance the City's goals of achieving a just transition to community-wide carbon neutrality by 2030 (known as A2ZERO). This work began in April 2021 and has already uncovered many opportunities to improve indoor air quality and improve resident safety and health, while also highlighting many of the unique and charming elements of the Bryant neighborhood that are valued by residents. With information highlighted through these initial assessments, Ann Arbor and the project team has obtained around $5 million spread throughout a few grants and is seeking more funds to complete implementation a district geothermal installation that has been designed in collaboration with residents and geothermal experts. The funding to-date is enough to work on around 120 of the 262 homes. The Department of Energy has also awarded Ann Arbor $10 million to install the district geothermal system, but with the Federal budget situation, those funds have yet to be allocated. Michigan's relatively low cost of natural gas and high cost of electricity makes these improvements difficult to complete without external funding, despite the clear benefits to the community and beyond. The data generated by the project around energy efficiency, air quality, public health, work force development, comfort, safety, and more benefits, along with the unique community engagement strategy, can be collected to replicate in other neighborhoods, cities, and regions.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Reduce, Reuse, Return: Establishing a City-Scale Returnable Foodware Program in Ann Arbor: The global crisis of single-use plastics has reached a critical point, with over 8 million tons of plastic entering our oceans each year (United Nations, 2017). Of particular concern is plastic food contact packaging, which not only poses risks to human health through the leaching of harmful chemicals like bisphenols and phthalates, but also contributes to the widespread contamination of our soil and waterways with microplastics (Gore et al., 2024). These tiny plastic particles now permeate ecosystems and even infiltrate the food and water we consume, raising alarm about long-term impacts on public health and the environment (World Health Organization, 2019). This project will demonstrate one meaningful pathway to address these concerns by creating a City-wide returnable foodware container program to be used in Ann Arbor's restaurants, venues, institutions, and public schools - thereby replacing single-use plastics. Designed in collaboration between the Ann Arbor Office of Sustainability and Innovations, the Ecology Center, Perpetual, and local restaurants, grocers, food vendors, and community institutions, this program will demonstrate how to drastically reduce plastic waste while stimulating a more circular economy and healthier natural systems. This will be done by providing at least 150 area restaurants and institutions, including K-12 schools and college campus locations, with reusable food and beverage containers to replace single use plastics, developing and operating a centralized station that washes, dries, and transports these containers, and building the social infrastructure, including business training, community engagement, and public education, to ensure that this initiative achieves the adoption necessary to become the preeminent form of consuming foods and beverages in Ann Arbor. By eliminating six million single-use food and beverage containers during the project timeline - and developing the infrastructure to expand this initiative for years to come - this project will directly address the environmental and human health impacts of plastic pollution within the project area, including concerns associated with microplastics within the Huron River. The Huron River, located within the project area, is the area's primary source of drinking water, and is frequently used by members of the community for recreation, including swimming and kayaking, A 2016 study conducted by the US Geological Survey found that the Huron River had the highest rate of microplastic pollution of any of the 29 Great Lakes tributaries that were tested. With extreme rain events increasing by 37% over the last 30 years in Ann Arbor, marine plastic and microplastic pollution are only expected to increase as heavy rains carry single-use plastics into the area's waterways with increased frequency and severity. Further, this project addresses human health impacts associated with plastic and microplastic pollution, namely the adverse respiratory impacts of fine particle pollution. Of the 24 EPA IRA Disadvantaged Community ID tracts that comprise the project area, all but two are in the top quartile for adult asthma rates, with 15 ranking in the 92nd percentile or higher, making both the environment and people who comprise the community outlined in the project area disparately vulnerable to plastic pollution. project_info: Buildings - Insulate A2: Rental units account for about 55% of the housing stock in Ann Arbor. Many of these units are well-built and maintained, providing tenants - from students to life-long Ann Arborites - the ability to live in comfortable and affordable homes. But this is not always the case. Some buildings and units were constructed in a time before modern building codes and have not been updated, meaning tenants pay high energy bills, live in uncomfortable units, and reside in buildings that produce disproportionately more emissions inside and outside of the building, harming the physical, financial, and mental health of tenants. To address this, the City, the University, and DTE are collaborating on a new incentive program called Insulate A2 to support the installation of insulation in rentals across the City.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Compost Collection Expansion: The City of Ann Arbor is working to expand composting access for multi-family residents by establishing a network of food scrap drop-off sites and promoting curbside collection for smaller multi-family properties already located on existing service routes. The creation of the new food scrap drop-off sites will extend a more convenient way for the roughly 50% of City residents living in multi-family housing to recycle their food scraps. While Ann Arbor has long offered curbside food scrap collection for single-family homes, limited resources have largely prevented the expansion of this service to multifamily housing, aside from a few pilot properties. A comprehensive analysis of the size, type, and location of multi-family housing along with expected generation and participation rates yielded the establishment of a drop-off system to be the most efficient and cost-effective way to extend food scrap collection to multi-family households, especially to those living larger (greater than ten units) properties. Specifically, the establishment of twenty drop-off sites will put 98% of multi-family parcels within one mile of a drop-off location. Smaller properties of less than ten units will be encouraged to obtain a cart from the City for curbside collection. The requested funding will support the purchase of tech-enabled cart enclosures, curbside compost carts in three sizes, and a specialized organic waste truck. The tech-enabled enclosures are key to creating unstaffed drop-off sites, as they will keep the cart locked until accessed by a registered user. Each drop-off site will either house a 64-gallon or 35-gallon cart inside an enclosure, while 96-gallon carts will be provided to smaller multi-family properties eligible for curbside service. The specialized organic waste truck will be equipped to service and wash up to three carts at a time, which is essential for maintaining sanitary, low-maintenance drop-off sites without needing a separate cleaning service. This project addresses a primary source of greenhouse gas emissions by reducing the amount of food waste sent to our local landfill. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that food waste accounts for 58 percent of methane emissions from municipal solid waste landfills. By redirecting food waste to composting, the city addresses this significant source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas. The EPA's Wasted Food Scale indicates that composting is the most environmentally beneficial option for food that cannot be used for human or animal consumption, thereby making this project a key strategy in reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Food Waste Reduction & Composting Educational Campaign: The City of Ann Arbor seeks to develop and provide a robust educational campaign to all residents about the importance of food waste reduction and composting. The over-arching goal of this project is to prevent household food waste from being landfilled. The primary objectives that will allow us to reach this goal include 1) developing a city-wide food waste reduction educational campaign, and 2) providing up to 25% of the city's households with food waste starter kits. A city-wide educational campaign will focus on both food waste reduction as well as the importance of composting. The messaging is intended to pull from resources provided by the NRDC “Save the Food Campaign” regarding proper food storage, meal planning, and how to use food that is about to spoil. We want our residents to think first about reducing how much waste they generate, and then take the most responsible action with any waste that remains. Waste management (including waste recycling) - Cardboard Bailers: In order to increase existing local capacity, decrease contamination, and improve efficiency of collection for the recovery of clean cardboard from the City's commercial recycling customers, the City will purchase cardboard compactors, work with businesses to install them at key collection points and purchase an associated collection truck to serve the compactors and increased demand for recycling collection. This project will reduce waste to landfill and improve collection efficiencies.
The City of Ann Arbor has provided recycling collection to commercial businesses for over 20 years, yet we know we are missing some materials as evidenced in the State of Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy's (EGLE) 2024 Waste Composition study, that found 16.5% of commercial trash is cardboard. Anecdotally, City crews observe unflattened boxes in recycling. Additionally, the City contracted with a local non-profit, The Ecology Center (EC), to provide direct education to our commercial customers. In the first year, EC worked with 9 businesses in 4 shopping centers, while in year 2 they worked with 40 businesses in 13 shopping centers. The businesses were a mix of retail, service, and restaurants, each with 1 to over 50 employees. Prior to engaging each business, EC completed a visual assessment of trash, recycle, and any compost containers. They noted percent full, composition, relative percentage of different materials, specific contaminants, and whether boxes were flattened. Then they engaged with the employees directly including on-site interviews and training followed by 1 or 2 more visual assessments. 

Results show that in year 1 of the contract, 2 of the 4 shopping centers (50%) had cardboard in their trash, and 2 (50%) had unflattened boxes in their recycling. In year 2 of the contract, 6 of the 13 shopping centers (46%) had cardboard in their trash, 3 (23%) did not have enough capacity for their cardboard, and 9 (69%) had unflattened boxes in their dumpsters. It was noted that cardboard in 96-gallon carts was regularly flat. One shopping center had a cardboard baler and there was no contamination noted in their recycling. The diversity of businesses engaged by the Ecology Center is representative of the businesses throughout the city, making their data a good reference for our commercial customers overall. To address issues with capacity, not flattening boxes, and boxes in the trash, the City proposes to install cardboard compactors at 15 strategic locations identified with high need. A truck will be purchased to service the compactors and to add collection capacity to the City's fleet to help meet an increasing demand for service as the city grows and adds more development. This ties to the national recycling strategy by increasing collection and improving materials management infrastructure. A consultant would be hired to manage and report on the grant and develop and implement the cardboard compactor program.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Sub-award infrastructure grants to local non-profits and service organization involved in materials reuse: This project aims to support greater recovery of usable goods during annual student move out events. Specifically, it will provide sub-award infrastructure grants to local non-profits and service organizations involved in materials reuse in order to increase collection. This project will reduce waste to landfill and keep goods in circulation. 

The City of Ann Arbor has a deep and extensive reuse network already in place that serves the county as well as the city. However, as Ann Arbor is a university town, there remains a significant opportunity to recover materials left behind by students and provide them to people in need. Ann Arbor's population is approximately 125,000; about 30% or 37,000 are off-campus students. These students are very transient and produce an estimated additional 1,400 tons of municipal solid waste annually during May and August move-outs. The University of Michigan offers collection for reuse to on-campus residents and collected about 11 tons of materials in Spring 2024. An area non-profit collected 14 tons from off-campus housing for reuse, specifically to furnish homes for those coming out of homelessness. Additionally, the City runs a temporary drop off site for reuse, recycling, and trash that in 2024 diverted 24 tons of material for reuse and recycling. However, there is still a lot of untapped potential, and the City strives to do more with it. 

To determine how to further increase collection and improve material management pathways for materials left behind by students, the City researched 27 universities and towns and spoke with 6 of them about their relevant programs. From this we learned: 1) many and diverse partners are needed, 2) many and diverse material streams can be addressed, and 3) outreach needs to be comprehensive, institutionalized, frequent, and through many channels. With this research, we formed Move Out Ann Arbor (MOAA), a collaborative initiative to improve the recovery and reuse of unwanted materials to the benefit of communities facing adverse disproportionate health, environmental, climate-related, and economic impacts. We met 8 times in 2024 and are building upon the many existing services by creating synergies and connections. Our partners include various departments at the university, property managers, non-profit reuse/service organizations, and waste haulers. 

In addition to the MOAA work of meeting, creating connections, and piloting some management pathways, the City has done extensive engagement to understand the landscape and timing. We have spoken with property managers/landlords, students, the Panhellenic Group, communities of faith, the Inter-Cooperative Council, and area non-profit reuse/service organizations. We have learned that there are already many non-profits in this space with well-aligned goals and services. For example, House N2 Home gathers materials left behind by students to help furnish approximately 400 homes in 2024 for people transitioning from homelessness. Their clients are referred to them from 40 other service organizations. House N2 Home then works with all their clients to ensure their new home reflects their tastes, preferences, and style as much as possible. When the client comes to their new home, House N2 Home has completely furnished it and provided a home cooked meal, dessert, flowers, and a card. These non-profits need additional support to expand and grow their efforts at recovering materials for reuse. For example, House N2 Home has expressed they could do more if they had an additional box truck for pickups and deliveries. We have also learned from property managers/landlords that timing is very important, with a typical 2-week window of opportunity between students leaving and new students moving in. 

To further support the National Recycling Strategy of enhancing policies and programs to support circularity, we propose to have sub-award grants for infrastructure for area non-profits/service organizations to deliver materials left behind by students to adversely impacted communities. Based on our engagement thus far, these non-profits are interested in items like box trucks to transport materials, supplies/containers to collect and transport materials, and leased or purchased containers for material storage or other warehousing. This ties to the National Recycling Strategy by increasing collection and improving materials management infrastructure. A consultant would be hired to manage and report on the grant and would also complete program development and management of the reuse sub-award grants.

climate_hazard: Extreme wind: Although all buildings are susceptible to high winds, the following structures are more likely to suffer damage, making low-income households more vulnerable: mobile homes, homes on crawlspaces, and schools, especially those with large span areas. Additionally, electrical infrastructure, communication lines, antennas, and towers can suffer damage from wind and downed branches/trees. Damages to buildings, roads, and vehicles can also be costly. Businesses interruptions can occur due to power outages. Flights may be delayed or canceled due to severe wind events. | Urban flooding: Ann Arbor is vulnerable to significant flooding due to existing development. Potential annualized loss from flooding is estimated at $47,590 (2017 dollars). GIS analysis was used to determine FEMA special flood hazard areas (A and AE Zones) cover approximately 1.6 square miles of the city (5.7 percent of the city's area). An examination of land parcel data and the digital FIRM (100-year floodplain map), shows 1,211 parcels of land that are either within or touch the FEMA mapped 100-year floodplain (3.7 percent). However, buildings outside of these areas are still at risk. In fact, a significant number of insurance claims are from properties outside of regulatory special flood hazards areas (FEMA 1.0 percent ACF). Recent events in Houston, TX estimated this figure as high as 80 percent. As a result, all current and future buildings, infrastructure, and populations in Ann Arbor are considered at risk to flooding. | Drought: Ann Arbor is considered to be a water-rich community. Drought is expected to have minimal impacts on infrastructure. Green infrastructure, such as green stormwater infrastructure, may incur minor damages during drought occurrences if plants cannot resist drought. Drought can have (and has had) several economic impacts on the city. One of the most pronounced economic impacts is that on agricultural holdings, as water supply is imperative for regional crops and livestock. There is limited agriculture within the Ann Arbor city limits, but a regional drought could have severe impacts to food prices in Ann Arbor which would disproportionately impact low-income-households and may even result in food shortages. Drought resulting in water shortage can also impact businesses (ranging from restaurants to manufacturing) which cannot operate without water. Lastly, in the case of a water shortage, the cost of water may increase (or the city may be forced to buy water from a water-rich area), which would have a more pronounced impact on low-income households and ripple effects in terms of a reduction in the local economic multiplier as money leaves the county. | Extreme heat: Groups particularly vulnerable to extreme heat include: 1) Older adults who do not adjust as quickly to changes in temperature. Older adults are also more likely to be on medications or have chronic illnesses that affect the body's ability to regulate its temperature. 2) Infants and children, who rely on others to keep them cool and hydrated. 3) Outdoor workers, who have more exposure to extreme heat and are more likely to become dehydrated. 4) Low-income populations, who may not have air conditioning available at home. Extreme heat events generally have minimal impact on infrastructure. Power consumption for air-conditioned environments could increase and thus stress utility infrastructure, resulting in blackouts. Ann Arbor currently experiences issues with electrical capacity during high-demand periods, and members of the TAC noted power outages during extreme heat events. In severe cases, heat can cause railroad tracks to expand. This is referred to as a heat kink in the rail line, and can result in disruptions or derailments. Heat can also cause pavement to expand. | Extreme cold: Certain populations, such as the elderly, young children, and low-income households without access to an adequate heat source are considered at a higher risk to the impacts of extreme cold, which could include death. Economic impacts from extreme cold/wind chill include repairs to burst pipes or degraded roads. In some cases, extreme cold may result in business or educational disruptions if people remain inside and cannot get to work, to school, or to the store.
project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - Community Based Social Marketing to Increase Reuse, Rental, Repair, and Other Actions that Keep Goods in Circulation: This project aims to support greater recovery of usable goods during annual student move out events. In order to do this, the City would hire a consultant to perform the 5 phases of community based social marketing with the goal of encouraging all students to participate in the reuse economy when moving into and out of the City. The 5 stages of community based social marketing are selecting behaviors, uncovering barriers and benefits to the behavior, developing strategies to reduce barriers and amplify benefits, piloting strategies, and implementing broadly with evaluation.
The City of Ann Arbor has a deep and extensive reuse network already in place that serves the county as well as the city. However, as Ann Arbor is a university town, there remains a significant opportunity to recover materials left behind by students and provide them to people in need. Ann Arbor's population is approximately 125,000; about 30% or 37,000 are off-campus students. These students are very transient and produce an estimated additional 1,400 tons of municipal solid waste annually during May and August move-outs. The University of Michigan offers collection for reuse to on-campus residents and collected about 11 tons of materials in Spring 2024. An area non-profit collected 14 tons from off-campus housing for reuse, specifically to furnish homes for those coming out of homelessness. Additionally, the City runs a temporary drop off site for reuse, recycling, and trash that in 2024 diverted 24 tons of material for reuse and recycling. However, there is still a lot of untapped potential, and the City strives to do more with it. 

To determine how to further increase collection and improve material management pathways for materials left behind by students, the City researched 27 universities and towns and spoke with 6 of them about their relevant programs. From this we learned: 1) many and diverse partners are needed, 2) many and diverse material streams can be addressed, and 3) outreach needs to be comprehensive, institutionalized, frequent, and through many channels. With this research, we formed Move Out Ann Arbor (MOAA), a collaborative initiative to improve the recovery and reuse of unwanted materials to the benefit of communities facing adverse disproportionate health, environmental, climate-related, and economic impacts. We met 8 times in 2024 and are building upon the many existing services by creating synergies and connections. Our partners include various departments at the university, property managers, non-profit reuse/service organizations, and waste haulers. 

In addition to the MOAA work of meeting, creating connections, and piloting some management pathways, the City has done extensive engagement to understand the landscape and timing. We have spoken with property managers/landlords, students, the Panhellenic Group, communities of faith, the Inter-Cooperative Council, and area non-profit reuse/service organizations. We have learned that there are already many non-profits in this space with well-aligned goals and services. The goal of this project would be to increase student participation in these avenues so that more materials are kept out of the landfill and provided to those who can most use them.

climate_hazard: River flooding: Spring freshet flooding was experienced along the St. John River in 2018 and 2019. River levels reached 5.73 m in 2018 and 5.55 m in 2019. Flood level on the St. John River is considered to be 4.2 m. This event led to the voluntary evacuation of approximately 1,900 people in 2018 and 605 in 2019. Twenty-nine roads were impacted by flooding and isolated several neighbourhoods. Spring freshet flooding will likely become more frequent as precipitation increases and sea levels rise. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The City of Saint John is projected to experience coastal flooding due to sea level rise. ACAP Saint John analyzed three sea level rise/coastal flood scenarios: 1) A 4.6 m HHWLT (Current highest average tide), 2) 5.6 m (20-50% probability in 2050, 50-100% probability in 2100), and 3) 6.8m (1 in 100 year storm in 2100). Sea level rise will affect Multiple roadways, including 36 evacuation routes, 2,264 buildings, 1,734 properties and 32% of the population of Saint John will be affected by the worst case sea level rise scenario in 2100. 6% of the people living in these flood zones are considered low income, and 8% are above the age of 65. | Urban flooding: On the eastern side of the City, flooding is frequently experienced after heavy rainfalls, especially if it is during high tide, which reduces the capacity of storm sewers. With a projected increase in precipitation intensity and sea level rise in Saint John, this issue is likely to continue/worsen. | Water stress: Tropical storms are likely to impact the City annually, the number of storms experienced each year are difficult to predict. Climate change will likely increase the frequency and intensity of tropical storms. Recently the City has seen significant damage to large trees in City parks due to high wind. Ice storms also cause similar impacts, as well as damage to energy distribution systems.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Thunder Bay has seen an increase in hot days and heat waves. climate_hazard: Heat stress: Heat stress exacerbates health conditions and increases the risk of dehydration and other heat-related illnesses. | Urban flooding: Urban flooding disproportionately affects vulnerable populations. These groups, such as low-income communities, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities, often live in areas with inadequate infrastructure and limited resources. When floods occur, they face higher risks of displacement, property damage, and health hazards. Limited access to clean water, food, and medical care exacerbates their vulnerabilities, leading to increased physical and mental health issues. Furthermore, the recovery process is often more challenging for these populations due to limited financial resources and social support networks. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat can have severe impacts on vulnerable populations. It can lead to heat-related illnesses and even fatalities, especially among the elderly, children, and those with pre-existing health conditions. Heatwaves can worsen respiratory and cardiovascular problems, increase hospitalizations, and strain healthcare systems. Vulnerable communities may face limited access to cooling resources, suffer from inadequate housing conditions, and lack sufficient financial means to cope with high energy costs. Overall, extreme heat exacerbates health disparities and poses significant risks to vulnerable populations. | Extreme cold: Climate change affects late freezes on agriculture by altering weather patterns. Rising temperatures can lead to earlier bloom and bud break in plants, making them more vulnerable to late freeze events. Unpredictable and extreme weather patterns increase the frequency and severity of late freezes, causing economic losses for farmers and food shortages. Albany has one of the highest amounts of community garden per sq mile. These community garden increase our community climate resilience and food security. | Drought: As temperatures rise and precipitation patterns shift, cities are at risk of experiencing prolonged periods of water scarcity. This can strain water supplies, leading to restrictions on water usage for residents, businesses, and industries.Drought can have severe impacts on urban ecosystems, including parks, green spaces, and trees, which rely on adequate water availability. Reduced rainfall and water scarcity can also impact agricultural activities within or near the city, affecting local food production and increasing dependence on external sources. | River flooding: Vulnerable communities, such as those with low-income households or inadequate infrastructure, are often hit the hardest, exacerbating existing social and economic disparities. Flooding can contaminate water sources, leading to a lack of clean drinking water and increased health risks. Access to healthcare, food, and essential services may be disrupted, further compromising the well-being of vulnerable populations.

climate_hazard: Infectious disease: A severe outbreak of mosquito-borne illnesses could result in illness, death, and economic loss. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment reported that West Nile virus was first detected in Colorado in 2002 and is linked to stagnant water and drought conditions. The Boulder County Health Department indicates that both Boulder County and the City of Boulder remain at risk for West Nile virus, though the severity of outbreaks may vary yearly based on factors such as weather patterns, mosquito and bird populations, and human immunity. Incidents of the disease have been declining since 2007 but recently have begun rising again. Significant increases in both West Nile virus (WNv) carrying mosquito species and the proportion infected with the WNv have been recorded in the last 5 years. According to the Boulder County Climate Change Preparedness Plan, milder winters and warmer summers could make the county more hospitable to new mosquito species, potentially increasing cases of established mosquito-borne diseases. Additionally, increased precipitation from extreme events could expand mosquito habitats. However, accurately assessing changes in public health risks from vector-borne illnesses due to climate change is complex, as it also requires considering shifts in human behavior related to weather changes. | Urban flooding: The state of Colorado identifies Boulder as having the highest flood risk in the state, given its location at the base of the Rocky Mountains and the presence of 15 major drainageways or creeks. This vulnerability to flash flooding can occur with little or no warning. Over 15% of Boulder's city limits fall within the 100-year floodplain boundaries. Recent efforts to update floodplain modeling suggest that existing mapping approaches may be significantly underestimating the proportion of the community at risk of flooding. Although there is no comprehensive technical assessment on how climate change may affect flooding in Boulder County, research summarized in the Climate Preparedness Plan indicates a trend towards less frequent but more intense rain events. Consequently, while rainy days may become less common, extreme events could become more severe due to increased atmospheric moisture. This means that what is currently considered a 100-year flood might become more frequent, such as a 50-year event, rendering existing design levels and regulatory practices potentially inadequate. Additionally, in Boulder, low-income households are more likely to reside in flood-prone areas. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfire risk is particularly high in wildland-urban interface areas where development is close to fire-prone landscapes. Such fires can lead to significant property and structural losses. Boulder has a history of wildfires, including the Marshall Fire of 2021, the most destructive wildfire in state history. The fire started on December 31, 2021, in the winter, fueled by unusually high spring grass growth, a warm and dry summer and fall, and strong winds reaching 115 mph due to the mountain wave effect. By January 1, 2022, the fire had destroyed approximately 1,084 structures and damaged another 149, surpassing the 2013 Black Forest Fire in terms of destruction. As human development and population increase, and the wildland-urban interface expands, the threat of wildfire and potential losses continue to grow. Climate projections suggest worsening wildfire conditions due to earlier snowmelt and rising summer temperatures. Beyond physical damage, wildfire smoke poses significant health risks, as fine particulate matter can cause temporary reductions in lung function, pulmonary inflammation, and affect the immune system. | Drought: Since 1900, Boulder has experienced eight periods of drought. The most significant impacts of drought in Colorado involve water-intensive activities such as agriculture, wildfire protection, municipal use, commerce, tourism, recreation, and wildlife preservation. Over the past decade, Boulder County has faced 23 drought-related impacts across various categories: agriculture (5), business and industry (1), fire (7), plants and wildlife (6), relief response and restrictions (11), public health (2), tourism and recreation (1), and water supply and quality (8). The City of Boulder primarily relies on snowpack for its water supply, but if future climate trends lead to warmer temperatures, snowpack may become less reliable for water storage, potentially resulting in more severe drought restrictions. | Extreme heat: Since record keeping began in 1895, heat waves in Boulder have become more frequent and intense. This trend of rising temperatures is expected to increase heat-related deaths and illnesses, as extreme heat events can impair the body's temperature regulation and cause direct or indirect health complications. Vulnerable populations—such as the very young, the elderly, individuals with existing medical conditions, and the unhoused—are particularly at risk. Additionally, increased extreme heat days will place greater stress on energy systems to meet cooling demands, with those lacking access to cooling mechanisms or natural shade, particularly low-income households, facing the greatest impacts from rising temperatures. | Extreme wind: Extreme wind acts as a threat multiplier for fires and can cause significant damage on its own. The 2021 Marshall Fire, which occurred under extreme wind conditions, spread rapidly, damaging or destroying over 1,000 homes and businesses. Additionally, two separate wind events in December 2021 led to significant power outages and the loss of a crucial communication antenna used for emergency communications. The winds also caused extensive property damage, including the complete loss of homes in manufactured housing communities. | Other: Insect infestation: From 1996 to 2010, 122,455 acres of forest in Boulder County were affected by the mountain pine beetle (MPB). Current research indicates that warming temperatures and increasing drought conditions are driving MPB populations upward. Warmer temperatures enhance beetle activity, increase stress on affected trees, and accelerate beetle development. These conditions raise the likelihood of MPB populations escalating from endemic to epidemic levels. If favorable climatic conditions persist, MPB populations may spread rapidly across the landscape. Additionally, Boulder is also impacted by the Emerald Ash Borer (EAB), first detected in Colorado in Boulder in September 2013 and later in Longmont in summer 2016. All ash species in Colorado, including green and white ash, are susceptible to EAB, which has already cost municipalities, property owners, nursery operators, and the forest products industry hundreds of millions of dollars. Without pesticide treatment, ash trees will eventually die. In response, Boulder's EAB strategy, developed with input from state and federal agencies, other city foresters, and leading EAB experts, includes measures such as tree planting, pesticide applications, tree removals, biocontrols, wood utilization, and an Urban Forest Strategic Plan. | Other: Air quality: Ozone pollution is a serious hazard for the Denver Metro/North Front Range region and the nine air quality monitors in the region often exceed EPA air quality standards. Poor air quality can have significant social, ecological, and economic impacts. Although impacts to human health are most documented, poor air quality can also have negative effects on vegetation, crops, and forests leading to loss of environmental and economic benefits. Colorado's complex topography and variable weather patterns can significantly impact differences in air quality from point to point. | Snow and ice: Winter storms in Boulder, characterized by strong winds and blizzard conditions, can cause localized power and phone outages, and lead to closures of streets, highways, schools, businesses, and nonessential government operations. These storms can isolate people from essential services in their homes and vehicles and escalate into life-threatening situations if emergency response is hampered by severe conditions. Other issues include the risk of physical overexertion, which may result in heart attacks or strokes, and significant costs associated with snow removal. Additionally, heavy snowfall can contribute to flooding or landslides in the spring if the snowpack melts too rapidly.
project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Renewable and Resilient Electricity System: The partnership agreement between the City of Boulder and Xcel Energy outlines specific strategies and projects that will be undertaken to make the energy grid cleaner and more resilient, make buildings more efficient and less reliant on natural gas, and support community-wide adoption of electric vehicles. The city has been exploring financing solutions to enhance the resilience of the electrical infrastructure through strategic undergrounding. The overhead lines are highly concentrated in areas of the community that are of particular concern for climate event impacts (flood, fire, wind). The city and Xcel have worked collaboratively to plan and execute undergrounding projects in support of city improvements. As a part of the franchise between Xcel Energy and the city, 1% of the gross electric revenues from the City of Boulder is dedicated to burying existing distribution lines that are currently overhead to improve the system's reliability, performance, and aesthetics. These funds currently accrue at an estimated rate of $1.1 million per year. Ineligible expenses, including telecommunications undergrounding, easements, customer service conversion and associated customer related expenses, need to be funded through other funding sources.

Water intrusion into buildings can result in mold contamination that manifests later, leading to indoor air quality problems. Populations living in damp indoor environments experience increased prevalence of asthma and other upper respiratory tract symptoms, such as coughing and wheezing, as well as lower respiratory tract infections such as pneumonia, respiratory syncytial virus, and pneumonia. project_info: Renewable energy - Wastewater effluent heat recovery for district energy: The goal of our LNPK 156 Geothermal Coalition is to analyze and design a 4th generation geothermal district heating system to meet 100 percent of the heating loads of the properties adjacent to the 1.6-mile USDOT RAISE (Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity)-funded rebuild of West Superior Street through LNPK 156. Duluth can be a national example of how innovative design and integration across technologies (transportation, funded by RAISE, and geothermal) can cost effectively accelerate the transition to clean energy and provide communities with resilient heating solutions even in the coldest of climates. The baseline analysis and design will include financial and technical analysis of the use of geothermal heat pumps to recover waste heat from the effluent of the Western Lake Superior Sanitary District (WLSSD) wastewater treatment plant located immediately adjacent to Lincoln Park, as well as development of clear career pathways associated with design, deployment, and operations of the system. Additional analysis will include potential system adds including: 1) Interconnecting the LNPK 156 system and the City of Duluth's district heating system (Duluth Energy System) serving Duluth's Central Business District and the two regional hospitals to further decarbonize the downtown system and provide increased resilience, and financial and environmental sustainability to the broader community, 2) Analysis of incorporating public housing and a community resilience hub into the system (adjacent, but not in the primary footprint), 3) Potential of the system to support snowmelt for the active transportation corridor components and/or newly designed transit stops, and 4) Criteria for expanding support into the adjacent residential area or to assets active in reducing health disparities.

project_info: Renewable energy - Implementation of Renewables Advancing Community Energy Resilience (RACER) award: Form Follows Function (F3): A framework for community-based energy resilience planning in the MidwestTo meet the critical needs of a community during various periods of grid disruption, our project focuses on energy resilience by developing greater understanding of functional needs at different community-scales and deployment potentials of solar PV plus storage, along with distributed micro-resilience resources (DMRRs). The F3 Framework development process is applicable to cold climate communities subject to multiple hazards and will build off of past disasters experienced in northeastern Minnesota. This approach will develop novel community-based research that informs resilient energy improvements, de-risks projects for local partners, and is responsive to, and centered-on, traditionally marginalized communities at greatest risk of negative impacts associated with climate change, disasters, and grid outages. F3 will provide a process to determine where and how City renewable energy investments can provide community benefits and access to clean energy for traditionally-marginalized residents.

Since 1900, the number of days per year with extreme rain has been increasing by 0.2 days per decade on average. However, most of that increase has occurred since 1990. project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Bloomington Green Home Improvement Program: This rebate program represents a successful partnership between the City of Bloomington's Department of Economic and Sustainable Development, CDFI Friendly Bloomington, Clean Energy Credit Union, and Hoosier Hills Credit Union. The revised 2025 BGHIP provides substantial rebates for homeowners completing sustainability projects, helping Bloomington residents finance energy efficiency upgrades, install renewable energy sources, reduce utility bills, and increase the environmental sustainability of their homes. The program offers rebates of 25% of project cost for general population applicants and enhanced 40% rebates for low-income applicants, with maximum amounts varying by project type. Eligible projects include solar panels, battery energy storage systems, level 2 EV chargers, heat pumps, energy-efficient HVAC systems, door and window replacements, and attic insulation. The program advances the City's goals to improve environmental and economic equity while reducing community-wide fossil fuel consumption. More information is available at bloomington.in.gov/sustainability/bghip.\n

project_info: Renewable energy - Low Income Solar Program: The City has successfully implemented programs to expand solar access for low-income residents in the community. Through targeted initiatives, the City provided $250,000 to Habitat for Humanity to install solar systems for ten low-income households in Bloomington, as well as $100,000 and up to 420 pre-purchased solar panels to Bloomington Housing Authority for installation at Walnut Woods Apartments. By the end of 2025, the City will have provided Bloomington Housing Authority an additional $700,000 for solar installations and battery energy storage systems on multi-family housing, single-family housing, community and office buildings. These programs help ensure more affordable upfront housing costs while reducing energy burden for low-income communities, demonstrating the City's commitment to making sustainability more equitable and accessible for Bloomington's most impacted residents.\n

project_info: Water management - Stormwater Grants: The City of Bloomington Utilities (CBU) continues its successful residential stormwater grants program, which invites homeowners interested in building environmentally-friendly features to apply for small grants to improve stormwater management on their properties. The program distributes approximately $70,000 annually in small grants to homeowners to help offset the cost of building green stormwater infrastructure projects. The goal of green stormwater infrastructure is to slow water flow, allowing for enhanced filtration and removal of pollutants before water enters storm drains. Eligible projects include rain gardens, detention/retention pond maintenance or retrofitting, vegetated swales, and driveway culvert replacements. This innovative program has received statewide recognition and continues to receive dedicated funding, demonstrating the City's commitment to sustainable water management practices.\n

project_info: Renewable energy - City of Bloomington Municipal Solar Project: The City of Bloomington has successfully completed its comprehensive municipal solar installation project working with contractors from Energy Systems Group (ESG). Since 2017, the City has deployed solar installations on 33 City buildings, with additional installations completed in 2024. Since municipal solar installations began in 2017, the City has generated more than 16,768,181 kWh of power from solar, totaling 13,770.91 metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions reductions, equivalent to powering 2,165 homes in Bloomington for a year. These municipal solar installations demonstrate the City's leadership in renewable energy adoption and contribute significantly to the City's greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals.\n

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Solar & Energy Efficiency Loan Program: The 2025 SEEL program provides grant funding and technical assistance for nonprofits, community organizations, and small businesses to improve building efficiency and install solar panels or battery storage. Solar and battery grants provide $25,000 to sponsor a solar photovoltaic (PV) panel system installation, $20,000 to sponsor a battery energy storage system (for non-profits only), or a combined $45,000 solar and battery installation (for non-profits only). To date, the SEEL program has helped 54 Bloomington businesses and community organizations to install solar and/or undertake energy efficiency upgrades. The expanded 2025 program now includes battery energy storage systems for nonprofits, allowing organizations to store low-cost solar energy and use it during periods of peak electricity rates. Eligible projects include solar installation, weatherization, lighting, refrigeration, ventilation, cooling, and water heater upgrades. This program advances the City's goals to increase renewable energy sources, decrease CO2 emissions from fossil fuel consumption, and support local organizations across the community.

climate_hazard: Storm: Strong storms combine the hazards of heavy precipitation and extreme winds. These powerful storms can be a hazard to the health and safety of residents, particularly those belonging to vulnerable population groups, and impact buildings and transportation infrastructure. Electrical distribution infrastructure is particularly vulnerable to these storms. In the aftermath of a strong storm vulnerable populations can be without electrical power for days or even weeks. This impact can compound the danger to those with existing health conditions. Those that need home medical equipment powered by electricity will be without that necessary equipment. During such outages people will also be without air conditioning, which can exacerbate many preexisting health conditions, especially if extreme heat follows in the days after the storm passes. | Heavy precipitation: More years with unusually high number of days with rainfall of greater than 1.25” (8 days or more)Strains stormwater sewer system, potentially leads to flash flooding, damages crops, can lead to mold issues in homes | Extreme wind: Extreme wind, especially in the form of a derecho is a threat that people in Iowa City and the surrounding region understand very well, after experiencing a devastating example in August of 2020. Extreme wind can knock out electrical power for days on end, which can be deadly for those who rely on life-saving medial devices. These highly destructive events damage and destroy property, and debris can block roadways for a significant time before heavy equipment can be deployed to clear transportation infrastructure. Impacts include road closures, injures, property damage, and damages to tree canopy. Vulnerable populations are particularly sensitive to this hazard. | River flooding: Spring and summer precipitation and extreme rainfall events are expected to increase substantially over the next 30 years, leading to a higher probability of the Iowa River flooding. Causes road closures, bridge closures, mold in flooded properties, requires extensive and expensive clean-up, can be potentially deadly, causes extensive property damage, creates large amounts of waste, can shut down water and wastewater treatment leading to water supply issues, damages infrastructure. River flooding impacting residences poses an additional burden on vulnerable populations for whom the cost of housing is a burden. Impacting the transportation system by blocking and damaging roads is a major concern for the transportation and storage sector, especially in Iowa City when there are so few routes from the east side of the city to the west side. | Drought: Decreased supply of fresh drinking water, have to pump from deeper wells, potential food supply and local economy issues | Urban flooding: More years with unusually high number of days with rainfall of 1.25” (8 days or more)Strains stormwater sewer system, can lead to mold issues in homes, can close roads, cause infrastructure damage | Extreme heat: Projected higher average temperature and average minimum temperature in hottest 3-day period. Negatively affects elderly and at-risk populations, requires increased energy use for air conditioning. This hazard also negatively impacts the utility sector, as the electrical infrastructure struggles to keep up with increased demand during extreme heat.

Fire weather (risk of wildfires): A longer warm season and drier climate are projected to lead to more damaging and hazardous wildfires and post-fire flood events.
Flagstaff is at a high risk of more frequent and more severe wildfires and medium-high vulnerability to post-fire flooding events. The elderly, children and youth, and those with pre-existing respiratory conditions are especially vulnerable to smoke from wildfires. Additionally, many of Flagstaff's low-income neighborhoods, which are home to a higher percentage of marginalized and minority community members, are partially or wholly within the 500-year floodplain, which floods more often than other areas of the city. In the event of an evacuation, those without homes, adequate transportation, or with limited disposable income are at greater risk of negative consequences. Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Prior to Hurricane Helene, tropical storms were not deemed to be of great risk to the City, however the hazard was shown to be real and highly significant. Destruction from hurricanes and tropical storms can impact many sectors through widespread power outages, damaged and destroyed roads, and physical impacts to natural and human built environments. The impacts described above can disrupt normal operations for the named exposed sectors. Impacts can come from a lack of electricity or fuels leading to closures; lack of access to services and supply chains for community members, businesses, and organizations from disrupted transportation networks; and physical damage to critical infrastructure like energy systems, water systems, waste management facilities and routes, communications networks, medical facilities, and housing. Physical impacts to agricultural lands and forests can have long term impacts for food systems and ecological health with tree loss, soil loss, and soil and water contamination. The disruptions can have cascading effects leading to higher risk situations for vulnerable populations.The elderly and vulnerable health groups face heightened risks due to medical equipment dependence and mobility limitations during evacuations, both of which can be further compromised through power outages and blocked roads. Marginalized and low income communities may lack resources for emergency preparations, temporary relocation, or post-storm recovery and may be located in higher risk locations, like flood plains, leading to increased exposure to risk. | Heavy precipitation: Agriculture: Excessive rainfall can lead to flooding, soil erosion, and crop damage. This can disrupt food production, increase costs for farmers, and impact food prices for consumers.

Transportation and infrastructure: Heavy precipitation can overwhelm drainage systems, causing flooding in urban areas. This can damage roads, bridges, and buildings, leading to costly repairs and disruptions in transportation that impact public safety, businesses and tourism. 

Water Supply: While heavy precipitation can temporarily increase water supplies, it can also lead to water quality issues and pollution if runoff carries contaminants into waterways. Extreme precipitation events can damage or destroy water distribution lines or impact water treatment facilities leading to disruption of potable water supply.

Public Health: Heavy precipitation can create conditions that favor the spread of waterborne diseases, such as E. coli and salmonella. Additionally, flooding can disrupt access to essential services like healthcare and sanitation.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: The Santa Clara County Multijurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan assigned Hazard Risk Scores to major hazards based on probability and impact. Extreme heat ranked in the top five hazards with a score of 1.85. A recent study conducted by Stanford students showed that neighborhoods in the southern part of the City are both subject to higher afternoon temperatures and have relatively high numbers of residents of color compared to other areas in the City. These results suggest a need to focus efforts on mitigating urban heat in the southern part of the City in order to mitigate potential inequitable impacts of extreme heat. Low income individuals, including unhoused individuals, are likely to be highly impacted by extreme heat due to limited resources to mitigate heat in their homes or locales. Extreme heat could impact utilities because of fire risk, potentially causing widespread impacts to multiple industries. Recreation and tourism could also be impacted if residents and visitors choose to stay inside or visit other locales because of heat. Industries that require outdoor work, including construction and environmental \'green jobs\' would also be impacted. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfire received a risk score of 1.95, above extreme heat but below earthquakes and heavy rain. A total of 1,711 people (2.5% of Palo Alto's total population) reside within wildfire hazard areas. 604 properties valued $25 million exist in wildfire hazard areas in Palo Alto, and potable water reservoirs are also vulnerable to wildfires. \n\nVulnerable groups such as elderly or low-income individuals are especially at risk in the case of a wildfire because mobility and financial constraints may limit their ability to evacuate in the case of a fire. Additionally, the impact of smoke and reduced air quality from wildfires disproportionately effects those with asthma or other health conditions and those working outside in these conditions, such as outdoor and frontline workers. Wildfires may also affect recreation- and tourism-related activities as outdoor events would be canceled. | Drought: An event is expected/probable. Experts have confirmed potential for occurrence. Stress to water and food supply due to drought conditions put vulnerable populations such as low-income households and the elderly especially at risk because they may have income or mobility constraints that limit their ability to adapt to changing conditions. Drought also has secondary impacts due to efforts to reduce wildfire risk, such as power outages and utility work to reduce the risk of fires from power lines. Elderly and medically sensitive individuals are also at greater risks from power outages. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level is expected to increase by 36 inches in the next century, and which would impact several key infrastructures including the airport, wastewater treatment facility, highway 101, and utilities by the end of the century. With 36 inches of sea level rise, a high groundwater table could occur at over 7,000 residential parcels, and over 4,000 residential parcels could be flooded during 100-year storm tides. (SLR Vulnerability Assessment). In the shorter term, many areas in Palo Alto are already impacted by high tides and shallow groundwater. Lower income households may have financial constraints that limit their ability to prepare their homes for floods and repair their home or relocate after a flood. City operations, aviation, and transportation industries would be impacted by sea level rise. | Extreme wind: High wind received the same hazard rating as extreme heat (1.85). As many entertainment and recreation activities take place outdoors, those sectors will be impacted by almost any climate-related hazard. Similar to drought and extreme heat, utilities may be affected and in turn affect vulnerable health groups that rely on electricity to maintain their health. | Heavy precipitation: Heavy rain is in the top three hazards (along with drought and earthquake) identified in the Multijurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan. The risk score for heavy rain is 2.05 and heavy rain is considered highly likely to occur. Flooding is considered occasional with a risk score of only 0.65, though heavy rain may lead to river flooding. Low income households, including unhoused individuals, are likely to be impacted by heavy precipitation due to potential property damage and limited ability to make repairs before or after a heavy rain event. Heavy precipitation could impact wastewater treatment as heavy precipitation has previously led to increased need for treatment from rainwater infiltrating the system. It could also impact transportation, food service and hospitality, and tourism-related industries as it could lead to unsafe or damaged roads and residents or visitors would likely choose to stay home during heavy precipitation events.

climate_hazard: Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Impacts on life and property resulting from fire hazards\n | Other forms of climate-induced landscape shift/degradation: As high-intensity rainfall events increase in frequency the risk of inland flooding increases. Secondary impacts associated with flooding include landslides, subsidence, slippage, creep, or sinkholes. Cities with hilly terrain can experience increased risk of these events, and both landslides and liquefaction during earthquakes are more likely and more severe if the ground is wet or saturated when the shaking occurs. Due to Fremont's location and topography, the risk of experiencing landslides is limited to the area east of Mission Boulevard in the hills and to Coyote Hills Regional Park on the shoreline. Areas to the north are mainly at a medium level risk for landslide, however Mission Peak Regional Preserve and Coyote Hills Regional Park are subject to high levels of risk, which may be exacerbated by intense precipitation events, earthquakes, and, along the shoreline, sea level rise. As defined by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), most of Fremont experiences very few landslides, but the hills to the east and Coyote Hills Regional Park are in zones identified as experiencing “few” to “many landslides.” Landslides are considered to be most likely to occur in and around the places where they have previously taken place. A landslide in 1998 at the Mission Peak Regional Preserve indicates that this area is at an increased risk because landslide probability increases where past events have taken place. Fremont is at medium to high risk of experiencing landslide events, with the area east of Mission Boulevard at the highest risk. An event in this area would primarily affect individual residential water service and the local sewer system, as the primary infrastructure in the area are sewer lines and structures. The Alameda County Water District Mission San Jose Treatment Plant, a hazmat facility, is also in the vicinity and at a medium risk for landslide. Disruptions to this facility, the surrounding sewer system and underground supply pipelines could have negative public health consequences if damaged, potentially exposing the public to raw sewage or other hazardous materials. Other regions at risk for landslide include the shoreline of Coyote Hills Regional Park, with the area of risk stretching down across CA-84 to Jarvis Landing. | Urban flooding: Climate change is expected to exacerbate flooding through storms and more intense periods of rainfall. Many of Fremont's citywide assets are vulnerable to flooding based on analysis conducted by FEMA, including essential emergency response, transportation, power and sewer assets. With more extreme precipitation events, the intensity of rainfall-induced flooding events may cause more flooding of vulnerable assets. Flood events expected to have a 0.2 percent chance of occurring in a given year, or a 500-year recurrence interval, based on historical information may occur more often under changing climate conditions. These changing conditions would translate to a shift in the maps of the 100- and 500-year floodplains. According to FEMA flood maps, Fremont has multiple citywide assets located in the 100-year and 500-year floodplains. Note that the citywide assets directly addressed in this report are limited to important facilities as determined by the City. Important direct effects of inland flooding exist for other vital community assets such as business corridors, places of community assembly, and housing, but these are not individually considered here. Inland flooding critically challenges the City of Fremont by putting emergency response facilities, key arterial roads and highways and a considerable portion of the storm sewer system at risk. Fremont has large areas that are at risk of high hazard severity in the event of a wildfire, with increased exposure to the northeast of the city where Kilkare Woods has very high hazard severity levels. According to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) Fire Hazard Severity Zone maps, Fremont has moderate to high wildfire severity zones in many areas of the city, primarily located in the hills and throughout the parks and property on the shoreline. Fire hazard severity is a metric of the potential exposure of wildland and urban properties to wildfire based on vegetation, topography, and dangerous fire characteristics. The extent of these zones will therefore depend on land use change, but the occurrence of fire within these zones may increase due to climate change impacts such as more frequent droughts.Fire risk in Fremont is concentrated in the hills east of Mission Boulevard and along the coast but also extends further into the city, especially between the Baylands and Mission Peak Regional Preserve in South Fremont. Fremont does not have any very high severity fire zones, but is adjacent to a very high fire hazard severity zone to the northeast.Fire Station 4 is the most vulnerable emergency asset due to its locations in a high fire severity zone. Education assets in designated fire severity zones in Fremont include Forest Park Elementary School, Vallejo Mill Elementary, St. Joseph Elementary, Mission San Jose High, Ohlone College and Northwestern Polytechnic University. Niles Elementary is one city block outside the designated fire hazard zone. In addition, Mission San Jose de Guadelupe and the Dominican Sisters property are in a high fire severity zone. Communication assets in high fire severity zones include a GTE cell tower and the Fremont Newark Community College FM antenna, both in the hills. At least three other cell towers are close to high hazard severity areas throughout the city.
