This is especially true in the high severity areas in the western portion of the city. | Drought: Drought occurs over several dry years, depleting reservoirs and groundwater basins without the expected annual recharge from winter precipitation. Climate change is likely to increase the number and severity of future droughts, resulting in drier conditions, and will alter the timing and efficiency of the Bay Area water supply. An increase in temperature and a reduction in snow pack are the two most direct effects of climate change that will result in a drier state with fewer natural water resources than historically have been available. Prolonged periods of drought can reduce water supply for regional crops and livestock feed; increased wildfire hazard; and subsidence. Fire hazard increases where drought conditions are high. Additionally, drought reduces the water supplies available to fight wildfires, leading to larger and more extended fires. While drought does not have any primary impacts in the Bay Area, prolonged periods of drought can cause secondary impacts that can affect the region. Regional and statewide impacts include reduced water supply for urban water supply, crops and livestock feed; increased wildfire hazard; and subsidence. Drought is not localized, but occurs simultaneously across the region, and may extend statewide or across a larger expanse of western states. The impacts of the drought are locally unique, based on local water supply systems, soil conditions, and the typical climate and vegetation land covering. The effects of drought are managed in the Bay Area through the importation of water and the storage of water in reservoirs.The reduction in snowpack does not have direct impacts on Fremont, since there is rarely accumulation of snow. Shortages in precipitation in the Sierra Nevada can have a more pronounced impact on water supply in the region than a drought in the Bay Area itself because of the reliance of the region on water from the Sierra's. Currently, Alameda County Water District receives 40% of the water from the State Water Project; 20% from San Francisco Public Utilities Commission; and 40% from Alameda Creek Watershed Runoff. That means that over 60% of the water is imported to Fremont from beyond the Bay Area. Climate change will have an impact since snowfall accumulation will decrease in the winter. Snow that accumulates will melt earlier in the year with warmer weather throughout California. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea levels are rising as a result of higher atmospheric and oceanic temperatures across the globe. The rate of sea level rise is expected to accelerate throughout the century, threatening coastal resources, but projections are complicated by the potential for a substantial acceleration of glacial ice melt resulting in rapid sea level rise, which is not currently accounted for in many global scenarios. The Bay Area is especially exposed to the impacts of sea level rise because of the large number of assets located on the coast. In Fremont, the assets most at risk from sea level rise include storm drain assets west of I-880, power lines and railways. Sea level rise, and the combined effects of periodic King tides and storm surge, is expected to inundate several exposed assets along the shoreline, first flooding marshlands and eventually threatening property and assets in west Fremont. By mid-century, about 12 inches of sea level rise is projected to permanently inundate the city's marshlands, eroding the city's defense to storm surge and high tides. Assets flooded under these conditions include the Union Pacific railway along the shoreline, five power lines and three storm drains. Exposure levels remain comparable as water levels reach 24 inches, but the number of exposed assets increases as sea level rise reaches 36 inches, which is likely by the end of the century, and possible by mid-century with a five-year extreme tide. With between 24 and 36 inches of sea level rise, flooding of CA-84 could cut off access to the Dumbarton Bridge. I-880 could also begin to flood in South Fremont, near Milpitas, and the number of exposed storm drains increase from four to 48, and exposed buildings increase from two to 32 structures. At 48 inches of sea level rise, likely by the end of the century when combined with average yearly storm surge, water threatens a growing number of power line, rail, sewer and hazmat assets. As these resources and facilities are compromised, public health and safety may be at increased risk. Even with 72 inches of sea level rise, emergency service facilities, schools and community resources are outside the area projected to be impacted, despite the fact that many of these assets are located in the 500-year floodplain. | Extreme heat: The frequency of days over 90 degrees F is expected to increase from a baseline average of once a year between 1970 and 2000 to 37 days per year by end of century. From 1970-2000, Fremont experienced a daily average temperature of about 58.5 degrees F, an average maximum temperature of 69 degrees F and an average minimum temperature of 48 degrees F. According to climate models, future temperature patterns exhibit a clear trend toward warmer average temperatures, and more common high or even extreme temperature events. Under RCP 8.5, daily average temperature is projected to increase between 2.7 degrees F to 3.5 degrees F. By the end of the century, temperature changes are estimated to be substantial, for daily average, minimum and maximum temperatures with the high-end of the range of RCP 8.5 temperature increase projections suggesting increases from 7.7 degrees F to 9.2 degrees F. According to Cal-Adapt, between 1961 and 1990, Fremont averaged six days per year exceeding 90 degrees F. The number of hot days is projected to climb more rapidly after mid-century. Under a medium emissions (RCP 4.5) scenario, Fremont will likely experience an average of fifteen days per year over the 90 degrees F threshold by mid-century (2035-2064) and eighteen days per year by the end of the century (2070-2099). Under a high emissions (RCP 8.5) scenario, Fremont would experience eighteen extreme heat days by mid-century and thirty-one days per year by the end of the century. Higher temperatures will likely increase the magnitude of heat hazards in the city, for instance, heat stroke or exhaustion among local residents, workers and visitors, or raised demand for power during peak periods which could affect the frequency of outages. Extreme heat affects various age groups. However, seniors are more at risk as they may not exhibit signs of dehydration until several hours after dehydration sets in. They may also have limited access to resources like cooling centers. Seniors that live alone and lack air conditioning can face serious limitations mainly due to the ability to physically get to a cooling center. Construction workers will also be heavily affected as they work outdoors and may not have access to air conditioning.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Boise is one of the fastest-warming metropolitan areas in the country (Climate Central, 2023). Boise experiences extremely hot days almost every year, with an average of 34 days over 95 degrees F and 12 days over 100 degrees F from 2002 - 2022. The frequency of days over 95 degrees F has doubled since 1940 - 1960 and the number of days over 100 degrees F is four times what it was in 1940 - 1960 (National Weather Service, 2023). Additionally, impacts on the human body increase when temperatures stay hot overnight, and the number of days with a minimum temperature above 70 degrees F has also been gradually increasing. \nCertain areas of Boise experience higher temperatures than others. The risk of extreme heat impacts is particularly high for areas in the city center and a 2019 study found that August temperatures can differ by up to 7 degrees F across the community, with particularly large discrepancies during the morning and evening hours (CAPA Strategies, 2019). This is due to an urban heat island effect and connected to the distribution of urban tree canopy throughout the community. | River flooding: Boise is at increased risk of river flooding due to weather and precipitation changes anticipated with climate change. Boise has recently experienced a flooding event due to abnormal weather patterns. In 2017, Boise had a large snow event followed by rapid melting that resulted in flooding. The meltwater invaded the sewer collection system, and the excessive water in the sewer lines almost exceeded capacity of our water renewal facilities. There was also localized flooding of homes and businesses and public spaces along the river. A Presidential Disaster Declaration was declared, and total damages were $3,341,767. In 2023, the Greenbelt, a pathway used for recreation, closed due to high flow levels. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfires happen every year in the Boise area (Ada Fire Adapted, 2023 b). The Boise community has been directly impacted by wildfires in the past, including the 2008 Oregon Trail Fire which resulted in one fatality and $1.7 million in damages. \nHousing developments at the wildland-urban interface are at increased risk of fire due to drought and high heat conditions and human caused ignitions. Increased temperatures will lead to longer and more intense wildfire seasons. | Drought: Drought negatively impacts our surface water supply, which can reduce both water quality and quantity. Reduced water quantity results in less water available for surface irrigation through Boise's extensive canal system. Irrigation water from canals has been opened later in the spring and shut off earlier in the fall due to drought, and this has impacted agricultural production. Irrigators in our area also rely on groundwater. A prolonged drought may result in wells drying. Drought also impacts our electricity supply because approximately 50% of our electricity typically comes from hydroelectricity. In low water years, the dams produce less electricity, which means more electricity must come from natural gas and coal plants.

climate_hazard: Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Bushfires present a lower risk to the City of Yarra than to its neighbouring, outer urban municipalities. However, the risk to vulnerable populations is still present, particularly the risk of smoke inhalation to vulnerable health groups, the elderly, and those who work outdoors. As with most climate-related hazards, the risk to low-income households is greater as this group are less able to invest in safeguarding against this risk. | Drought: Severe droughts have been experienced recently and are projected to get worse in the future. Drought presents a challenge to long term water security and food/agriculture production. Water restrictions imposed during periods of drought present challenges for meeting the healthcare needs of vulnerable populations. Construction of the Wonthaggi desalination plant has minimised the risk that water restrictions in response to drought will impact upon vulnerable populations. | Infectious disease: A warming climate presents challenges such as the Southern migration of diseases such as Ross River and Dengue. Populations with existing health conditions are more vulnerable to the impacts of acquiring these diseases. Linguistically diverse communities may face barriers to information about the outbreak or treatment of emerging infectious disease. | Extreme heat: Yarra has already experience severe heatwaves, such as during and around 'Black Saturday.' This is exacerbated being an inner-urban municipality and is expected to get more frequent and more severe. Elderly are most susceptable, as are vulnerable people due to lack of quality housing or finances for appropriate cooling systems (or running of them). The potential extreme and high risk heatwave impacts are associated with an increase in premature deaths and a higher incidence of heat related illnesses and exacerbation of medical conditions and mental and behavioural disorders. From an indirect impact perspective, heatwaves have the potential to reduce the potential for council officers to deliver services to vulnerable communities due to the need to ensure the ongoing health and safety of officers. This has the potential to exacerbate impacts to those most vulnerable. | Urban flooding: The impact of climate change is likely to be more severe for vulnerable groups within the Yarra region. Heavy precipitation and flooding, present a particular risk to vulnerable populations such as low-income households, community members living with disability, indigenous populations, linguistically diverse communities, and vulnerable health groups. These groups are disproportionately affected during emergencies as they may have limited resources to prepare for and recover from disasters, and may have less access to information and communication in the lead up to and during weather events.

climate_hazard: Storm: Land parcels (lots) impacted by Storm Tide Inundation (Storm Surge) predominantly have a low to medium risk rating due to the very short-term nature of any inundation impacts. A 1% STI event has a likelihood rating of unlikely. The number of lots exposed to STI is expected to gradually increase over time.Storms are associated with disruptions in power supply, extreme winds and precipitation. These can impact on the provision of mobile phone services and internet connections leading to disruptions to communication and information distribution as well as delivery of human health and social work activities and retail.Manufacturing is reliant on electricity which is often disrupted by storm damage to distribution networks.Storm impacts on waste management through the disruption of collection services and impacts on waste management facilities. | Heat stress: Vulnerable groups are more likely to suffer health impacts from heat events leading to increased mortality and illness during heatwaves. Our heat strategy identified impacts of heat such as increased incidence of violence and mental health challenges, increased respiratory illness, reduced mobility and reduced access to volunteer support services. | Heavy precipitation: Elderly people are less mobile and less able to avoid flooding. Areas of low socio-economic status and high proportion of english as a second language are subject to high flood risk such as in the suburbs of Berkeley and Warrawong. Several schools are located in high flood risk environments leading to temporary school closures in heavy precipitation conditions. Flooding has lead to damage to local road networks including major access routes such as the Bulli Pass. The primary water quality treatment facility for the region is located on low lying land subject to flooding. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): The number of days with high or extreme fire danger are increasing and the firefighting season is being extended each year. Our LGA contains a large amount of vegetation which increases the risk to the community from bushfires. Areas of high bushfire risk include aged care housing. Low income households have less access to air filtration through air-conditioning, making them more vulnerable to bushfire smoke impacts. Non-english speaking households have less access to information on emergency management due to limited translation services and lack of lived experience of Australian bushfire conditions.Water supply for the region is surrounded by vegetation that is subject to bushfire risk.Several key threatened ecological communities are at risk of impacts from bushfire. Access to Wollongong is limited due to the Illawarra Escarpment, leading to access roads into the area potentially being cut off from bushfire events. The provision of human health and social work activities is dependent on connection to other communities including Sydney to the north.Key communication infrastructure is located in areas subject to bushfire risk. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat events are projected to be more likely in the future due to climate change. Extreme heat is known to affect a wide variety of people across many industries. Known vulnerabilities include the very young, old, immobile or isolated members of the community.

Heavy precipitation: The New Plymouth District is already prone to high rainfall events. These events can lead to a range of hazards including:- Floatation of wastewater pipes by rising groundwater driven by back to back heavy rainfall events.- Increased inflow and infiltration issues with the wastewater network leading to overflow events.- High rainfall intensity can overwhelm stormwater capacity- Drainage and culverts in the transportation network can be overwhelmed- Total road washouts can occur in rural and forested areasIsolated rural communities often with a high proportion of indigenous people can be susceptible to the impacts of heavy precipitation particularly the impacts to the transportation network. Stormwater issues exist in the township of Waitara which is home to many low-income and indigenous families. | Other coastal events: Many of the coastal areas exposed to coastal erosion are of cultural significance to Māori with urupa, marae, wahi tapu, and other areas of significance within the coastal erosion hazard zone.Low-income households living within the coastal erosion zone do not have the money to undertake a managed retreat process and will require financial support from central and local government.Councils own and maintain coastal protection structures which over time will become too expensive to maintain putting private and public assets behind them at risk.Coastal ecosystems and public open spaces are at risk from coastal erosion. Coastal squeeze of native species is another existing risk that is projected to increase in the future.Local roads servicing coastal properties are at risk from coastal erosion and planning will need to occur to re-route areas. In the New Plymouth District our active transport network is reliant on the coastal walkway, which is highly exposed to coastal hazards.Onsite wastewater treatment systems in coastal areas are at risk to erosion. Plans are underway to address this risk. Wastewater outfalls may be at risk from coastal erosion, and several critical wastewater assets lie within the coastal erosion hazard zone.There are historic dump sites that are at risk of being exposed by coastal erosion which would result in environmental harm and possibly public health issues. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Similar to coastal erosion low income households may struggle to adapt to the future extent of coastal flooding, they are less likely to be able to access insurance to cover events, and where required are less likely to be able to undertake a managed retreat without significant government support.Coastal flooding poses risks to several wastewater pump stations within our district.Public open spaces have been impacted by storm surge and coastal flooding events. These events have damaged amenity structures, artworks, and walkways. | Drought: Rural communities dependent on the agricultural sector will be impacted by low river flows which limit freshwater abstraction for agricultural purposes. Rural communities are also not connected to municipal water supply and may be impacted by reduced water availability and quality.Electricity generation from petrochemical and gas-fired systems can be impacted as they are reliant on river flow water for cooling purposes.Municipal water supply is not projected to be as impacted by climate change as it is by population growth. There are existing projects to increase storage capacity resilience. Decreasing river water quality associated with droughts can pose challenges to water treatment.Drought can have negative impacts on plants and trees leading to ecosystem degradation and loss of amenity in parks and open spaces. Dry weather can also lead to higher rates of plant disease and competition with pest species.Lower flows in rivers can result in degradation in freshwater quality leading to negative impacts on freshwater ecosystems. | Soil degradation/erosion: Hill country erosion and landslides triggered by heavy rainfall events pose risks to our rural communities through damaged agricultural infrastructure and transport networks.The main route out of region to the North goes through landslide prone area which can impact connectivity.Forestry in hill country areas can be directly impacted by landslides damaging trees, or by loss of connectivity for maintenance and logging.Landslides have impacted paths and other assets within our parks and open spaces.Hill country erosion and more frequent landslides lead to higher sediment loading in our rivers and streams which has a negative impact on freshwater quality and can have an impact on coastal ecosystems. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Indigenous communities can be disproportionately impacted by storms and ex-tropical cyclones. Many of our coastal communities have a high Māori population. Coastal communities are impacted by ex-tropical cyclones and tornadoes coming off the Tasman Sea. Māori are also significantly impacted by the resulting environmental damage of storms due to their ancestral connection to the land and sea.Low income households can be disproportionately impacted by storm damage. Low income households are less likely to have insurance to cover storm damaged property/assets. They are also less likely to have disposable income to cover storm damage. Low-income households are also more likely to be dependent on public transport which can be impacted by storm damage. Outdoor workers can be disproportionately impacted by storm events due to the nature of their work - and the inability to work during storm events and in the days following. Rural communities can be isolated during storm events which can bring trees down across roads and impact power supplies. Noting that some rural communities are quite resilient and have developed coping strategies.Exotic plantation forests are particularly susceptible to wind damage, which can affect wood quality. Dead wood debris creates a risk of wildfires and of forestry slash entering rivers and streams and damaging bridges or other structures.Fishing expeditions can be cancelled due to extreme sea states.Water supply infrastructure can be exposed to falling trees and debris.Electricity supply can be impacted through damage to powerlines from stong winds and falling trees.Wastewater outfalls can be impacted by extreme sea state during ex-tropical cyclones. Stormwater catchpits and inlets can become blocked with debris during storms and ex-tropical cyclones leading to flooding issues.Kerbside collection and waste facilities can be impacted by strong winds during ex-tropical cyclones. Bins are blown over and litter is scattered impacting environmental quality and potentially public health.Strong winds and extreme sea states/storm surge can impact local transportation routes. This may be damaged and blocked roads or walkways/cycleways. Active transport becomes dangerous or unavailable.Storm damage to the natural environment can have biodiversity implications and reduced amenity in public open spaces. | River flooding: Low-income households in smaller centres and rural communities can be disproportionately impacted by river flooding which can impact transportation, power supply and housing.Rural communities are also affected by the impact on agriculture caused by flooding events.Māori occupy many of the coastal and rural areas prone to flooding damage. Māori are also significantly impacted by the resulting environmental damage of flooding due to their ancestral connection to the land and sea, and the traditional food collection sites (mahinga kai) that can be damaged or unsafe to collect from - this could be sediment inundation on intertidal reefs, or contamination from farm run-off into freshwater and coastal ecosystems.Electricity, gas, and transportation (bridges) infrastructure can be damaged or obstructed by flooding. Flood control schemes can be overwhelmed leading to increasing spillway use and subsequent damage to private property. Stormwater outfalls can be damaged during flooding events.There is a long-term risk to wastewater reticulation in river valleys.Flood insurance for private and public assets/property is a growing risk.
project_info: Transport - Walkway Extension to Waitara: The Walkway Extension to Waitara will link New Plymouth with Waitara via a pedestrian/cycling shared pathway along the coast and inland. This will contribute through increased active transport (lower vehicle use and therefore emissions) and increase resilience through the community having an alternative link between the township and New Plymouth central. https://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/news/104739903/waitara-pleased-to-get-coastal-walkway-extensionThe cost estimates have been refined and now sit at $39.4 million (before inflation adjustments), with the $18 million dollar contribution the project is still short $6.2 million on the Council funding side. Current LTP budget is $28.3M, of which $18 million has been pledged by Waka Kotahi funding, Council's budget is $15.2M Council cost, therefore leaving $6.2 miilion to find. The Airport Company have committed to constructing elements of the shared pathway through the airport area; the security fencing, the matairangi (lookout) the roading changes where the pathway crosses. Value approx. $926k. Other funding opportunities are also being explored. A discussion with Toi foundation is sounding favourable. The additional budget could be found through the 2024 LTP process and potentially through the \'better off funding\' tranche two.

Storm: 1. Impact on vulnerable groups
Coastal low-income groups: Most of them live in old houses with weak disaster resistance, which are susceptible to seawater intrusion and heavy rainwater accumulation, resulting in flooding of their residences, damage to property, and interruption of basic living security. 
Persons with limited mobility, such as the elderly, the weak, the sick, pregnant women, etc. lack the ability to move quickly during emergency evacuation, making it difficult to reach a safe area in time. Their personal safety faces direct threats, and medical care may be interrupted due to disasters. 
2. Impact on the industry
Fisheries: Take the strong typhoon in 1985 as an example. Coastal beach farms were washed away by waves, and a large number of fish, shrimp and crab seedlings were lost. Farmers lost all their annual production results, and the production resumption cycle was long and costly. 
Port shipping industry: The storm surge caused damage to port terminal facilities. Ships were unable to dock and load and unload cargo normally, and transportation operations were interrupted, seriously hampering logistics turnover and the progress of import and export trade. 
Coastal tourism industry: Core attractions and facilities such as trestles may be washed away, and scenic spots need to be temporarily closed, which will directly lead to a decline in ticket revenue, catering and accommodation and other related businesses, and damage to the tourism economy. 
Municipal infrastructure industry: Frequent failures of power supply, water supply, and communication lines due to storm surges have disrupted the normal operation of the city. Subsequent maintenance and restoration require high costs and affect the continuity of people's livelihood services.
Urban flooding: Not evaluated yet

Waste management (including waste recycling) - TPA Terjun Gas Project and Sustainable Closure of TPA Terjun: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KimyXrJo--Sai4CfKvitn_jqSxTp_HTj/view?usp=drive_linknnRencana Sales of Carbon Credits in the Context of Sustainable Closure of TPA Terjun Medan City

1. Background
As waste generation increases in Medan City, the capacity of the Terjun Final Disposal Site (TPA), which has been operating since 1993, is increasingly limited and has the potential to cause environmental impacts in the form of methane gas emissions, leachate pollution and the risk of landslides. For this reason, the Medan City Government has taken the initiative to implement a sustainable landfill closure program by adopting methane gas management technology (landfill gas recovery system) and utilizing carbon trading mechanisms (carbon credits) as an environmentally friendly alternative funding source.
This program is implemented through collaboration between the Medan City Government and international partner Afvalzorg and Multriwell (Netherlands) and PT Sumatra Deli Lestari Indah (SDLi) as local partners. This collaboration is a strategic step in supporting the national target of reducing Green House Gas (GHG) emissions and implementing the Net Zero Emission 2060 policy.

2. Activity Objectives
a) Implement sustainable closure of the Terjun Landfill to reduce environmental and social risks. 
b) Implementing landfill gas capture and combustion technology (Landfill Gas Flaring System) to reduce methane emissions.
c) Obtain funding through the sale of international carbon credits in accordance with the principle approval of the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (KLHK). 
d) Providing landfill land that is safe and can be reused for the public interest.
e) Making this project a model for sustainable landfill management based on a green economy in Indonesia.

3. Scope of Activities
a) Expansion of the TPA Terjun area to a minimum of 4.5 - 6 hectares, forming one TPA body that can be closed in stages.
b) Construction of a gas and leachate management system, including installation of pipelines, flares and monitoring facilities.
c) Implementation of technical, economic, legal and social feasibility studies to support project implementation.
d) Submission and accreditation of carbon credits through international institutions recognized by the government.
) Sale of carbon credits (CO₂) to potential buyers from South Korea, Switzerland and the Netherlands.
f) Implementation of final capping and post-operation land restoration.

4. Funding Mechanism
This activity does not use APBD funds, but is funded through the sale of carbon credits resulting from reducing methane gas emissions from TPA Terjun (around 392,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per year). Initial funding is carried out through pre-financing from prospective carbon buyers, while the sales proceeds are used to finance the construction of the gas closure and management system.
Because it is an unsolicited project and does not use government funds, This project does not require a tender process in accordance with investment cooperation procurement provisions.

5. Implementation Stages
a) Pre-feasibility study (completed).
b) Signing of Letter of Intent (LOI) between Medan City Government and Afvalzorg-Multriwell.
c) Approval of carbon sales principles by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry.
d) Preparation of feasibility study and signing of cooperation MoU.
e) Carbon accreditation process, contract preparation, and implementation of closing construction.
The total estimated implementation time for the initial phase up to the MoU is 6 months, followed by project implementation according to the results of the study eligibility.

6. Expected Benefits
a) Reducing GHG emissions by ±392,000 tonnes of CO₂/year.
b) Improving environmental quality through controlling landfill gas and leachate.
c) Optimizing land for new safe and productive functions.
d) Increasing institutional capacity and green technology in Medan City.
e) Support for sustainable development targets (SDGs), especially goals 11 and the 13th.

1. Background
Processing Waste into Electrical Energy (PSEL) for Medan City is a strategic project of the Medan City Government which aims to reduce the volume of waste while producing environmentally friendly electrical energy through the implementation of waste management technology interventions. This project is a follow-up to the Letter of the Minister of Environment and Forestry No. B.1307/A/RB.01/10/2025 concerning Waste Management Technology Interventions, and is based on various national regulations:
- Law no. 18 of 2008 concerning Waste Management,
- Presidential Decree no. 35 of 2018 concerning the Acceleration of PSEL,
- Presidential Decree no. 109 of 2025 concerning Waste Management Cities Through Renewable Energy, and
- Minister of Environment and Forestry Regulation No. P.16/2021 concerning Waste Management.

2. Location and Characteristics
PSEL is planned to be located at TPA Terjun, Terjun Village, Medan Marelan District. The initial area prepared is ± 4.98 hectares, for the construction of main facilities, utility areas and buffer zones.
PSEL carries the Waste to Energy (WtE) concept, namely converting waste residue into electricity using environmentally friendly technology, including:
- Thermal: incineration, gasification or pyrolysis.
- Non-thermal: biogas and RDF (Refuse Derived Fuel).
Processing capacity is targeted to reach 1,500 tons of waste per day, with the potential The electricity produced is around 31-50 MW depending on system efficiency.

3. Strategic Goals and Benefits
a) Reducing waste generation and extending the life of landfills.
b) Generating renewable electrical energy from local sources.
c) Increasing the efficiency of urban waste management.
d) Realizing a circular economy and creating opportunities green work.
e) Supports the national target of Net Zero Emission 2060.

4. Financing Scheme
Funding is designed through a mixed (hybrid) scheme, namely:
- APBN/APBD for land preparation and basic infrastructure.
- PPP (Government and Business Entity Cooperation) for construction and operations.
- Private investment and CSR for additional support.
- Potential for international green funding (green finance).

5. Implementation Stages
a) 2025-2026: Land acquisition, technical studies and permits. (Currently a Feasibility Study process is being carried out by Waste 4 Change).
b) 2026-2027: Construction of main infrastructure and technology installation.
c) 2027-2028: Operational trials, integration with the PLN network.
d) Post-2028: Full operation and replication to other regions.

6. Conclusion
The Medan City PSEL Project is a concrete form of the Medan City Government's commitment to supporting the national technology and clean energy-based waste management policy.
PSEL is expected to become a symbol of the city green and energy sustainable, while encouraging people's welfare through a clean, efficient and sustainable environment.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Sanitary Landfill Development: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1v-OI_EKH276lcyX477slVWGBnBIOUr8I/view?usp=drive_linknnRencana Sanitary Landfill Development

1. Background
The Terjun TPA located in Medan Marelan District, Terjun Village, has been operating since 1993 and currently has almost full capacity (±90%). Medan City's waste generation reaches ±1,400 tons per day, so additional areas are needed for safer disposal and management. The Medan City Government plans to acquire new land of ±14.44 ha around the existing landfill for the construction of a modern sanitary landfill zone, as a transition solution towards environmentally friendly waste management and a sustainable closure project.

2. Activity Plan
The activity plan for the construction of a sanitary landfill includes:
a) Acquisition of land covering an area of ​​±14.44 Ha for a new landfill area.
b) Soil investigation work (sondir test, drilling, laboratory) for base layer design.
c) Sanitary landfill technical design includes:
- Impermeable base layer (geomembrane and clay)
- Leachate collection and processing system
- Landfill gas capture system
- Operational routes (access and drainage)
- Supporting facilities (office, weighing scale, workshop and temporary storage area)
d) Integration with the old landfill closure plan through installation of a gas system and final arrangement of the landfill.
e) Rehabilitation of the surrounding area and planting vegetation cover.

3. Goals and Benefits
a) Providing environmentally friendly sanitary landfill standard final disposal facilities.
b) Increasing the capacity and efficiency of Medan City waste management.
c) Reducing the risk of leachate pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Heat stress: In Coimbatore's CRCAP, extreme heat and urban heat island effects are treated as a cross-cutting hazard that stresses multiple urban systems simultaneously. A consolidated hotspot analysis shows that, out of 100 wards, two wards face four or more fragile systems under combined heat and flood risk—specifically water supply, wastewater, health, and transport—while nine wards have three vulnerable systems and 22 wards have up to two. These multi-hazard hotspots are prioritised because the same neighbourhoods are dealing with high temperatures, service complaints (like low water pressure or road damage), and limited access to critical facilities, which together erode overall resilience. 
Sector-wise, heat has clear, quantified impacts. In water supply, wards that already face frequent complaints about low pressure, leakages, or limited/no supply overlap with heat hotspots; about 16.22% of the city's population lives in areas exposed to both high land-surface temperatures and water-supply issues, making them highly or extremely vulnerable. Solid waste systems are also heat-sensitive: three micro-composting centres, one resource-recovery centre and one transfer station fall within heat hotspots, and several wards experience both heat, flooding and solid-waste complaints, increasing risks of odour, pests and blocked drains. For health services, nine UPHCs, twelve private hospitals and two fire stations lie within urban-heat hotspot areas, meaning critical emergency and healthcare infrastructure is directly exposed to high temperatures. Together, these findings highlight that heat is not only a public-health threat but also a systems risk that can disrupt water, waste and emergency services in the same vulnerable localities. | Urban flooding: Urban flooding in Coimbatore is a recurring climate hazard that affects low-lying and densely populated neighbourhoods, especially informal and mixed-use settlements with limited drainage capacity. Although only about 2.29% of the population lives in directly flood-prone areas, a much larger share experiences water-logging during short, intense rainfall events caused by undersized drains, silted channels, solid-waste accumulation and rapid urbanisation. Flooding damages homes and belongings, deteriorates indoor air quality, and increases exposure to contaminated water, leading to diarrhoea, skin infections and other waterborne diseases. Low-income households, women, children, the elderly, persons with disabilities and informal workers are disproportionately affected due to mobility constraints, loss of livelihoods, unsafe sanitation access and restricted access to health services.

Flooding also disrupts core urban systems. In water supply, inundation of valve chambers and infiltration into ageing pipelines increases contamination risks and may require temporary shutdowns of supply. Wastewater and stormwater systems experience manhole overflows, sewage backflow and service disruptions when pumping stations are affected. Solid-waste management is significantly impacted, with waste drifting into drains, reduced accessibility for collection vehicles and prolonged unsanitary conditions.

Transport networks face delays, diversions and road safety risks as arterial roads and junctions become waterlogged, particularly affecting two-wheeler users and daily commuters. Health and emergency services face access challenges, while flood-related surges in waterborne and vector-borne diseases increase the service burden. Local businesses—especially small shops, roadside vendors and micro-enterprises—experience reduced customer footfall, damage to stored goods and interruptions to daily operations.

Overall, even if flooding is localised, its cumulative impacts on vulnerable populations, public systems and the city's economy are significant and recurring, underscoring the need for strengthened drainage infrastructure, improved waste management, resilient service delivery and targeted support for at-risk communities.

Urban flooding: A climate-related hazard in Palembang City is urban flooding, where the inundated areas are low-lying areas, if high rainfall is accompanied by tidal river conditions, inundation/flooding will occur, impacting:
- Low-income households: Those living in poverty are more vulnerable to the impacts of flooding due to limited access to resources, financial services, and basic support to overcome the impacts of flooding.
- Women and Children: Women and Children require special attention because they are vulnerable to the impacts of flooding which can rob them of joy, affection, and polite treatment.
- Parents: because their physical limitations can affect their response to social situations including floods.
Also affects sectors that are vulnerable to floods:
- Agriculture: The agricultural sector can be affected by floods, because crops can be damaged and agricultural production disrupted.
- Infrastructure: Infrastructure such as roads, bridges and buildings can be damaged by flooding, thereby affecting mobility and community activities.
- Wholesale and retail trade is part of community economic activities: Floods can disrupt economic activities, causing significant material losses.
- Human Health: Floods can cause the spread of disease and other health problems, especially if flood water is polluted.
- Residential areas: Residential areas can be flooded, causing property loss and disruption to daily life. | Drought: The climate-related danger in Palembang City is drought, especially during the dry season, which impacts:
- Women: Women have an important role in collecting water in slum areas, so lack of water can affect their daily lives.
- Girls: Children, especially girls, are also very vulnerable to the impacts of drought, especially if they do not have access to clean water sufficient. Lack of water can cause health problems and disrupt their daily activities.
The danger of drought impacts vulnerable sectors, namely:
- Agriculture: Drought can cause plants not to get enough water, so that agricultural production is disrupted.

Drought: Based on the analysis results, the Bogor City area has a drought hazard index range of 0.37 - 0.66 which indicates a low to high category. High hazard values are in South Bogor and East Bogor Districts. The analysis results show that the potential for drought is in higher areas or regions because the runoff has the potential to go directly to lower areas. Further validation was also carried out through the use of data from the Regional Apparatus, PODES survey data in 2018 and field validation. Based on the PODES data validation, there is a match in South Bogor District, while validation from OPD shows that there was a drought in Ciluar Village, North Bogor District. There was only one drought in one area in Bogor City in 2018-2019, namely Mulyaharja Village and it was recorded that 1,107 families were affected and the number of losses has not been calculated, especially in the agricultural, health and other sectors that require water. | Urban flooding: The contour of the Bogor City area which is located in a highland area provides the opportunity for flooding with a relatively short duration (potentially resulting in inundation). Flood hazard analysis is carried out through an overlapping process between topographic maps and areas that have experienced flood disasters based on administrative reports based on DIBI BNPB data from 2010 to 2020 or consultation with the Bogor City Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD). Then a baseline map is prepared which shows the flood hazard in current and future conditions based on the output of the CSIRO and MIROC models. Based on the results of the regional analysis, Bogor City has a flood hazard index range of 0.18 - 0.75, which means that flooding in Bogor City is in the range of very low to high values. Areas with high flood hazard are in West Bogor, Central Bogor, North Bogor, Tanah Sareal and several points in Central Bogor. Validation obtained from the Regional Apparatus, DIBI BNPB data and the Bogor City BPBD shows that the results of the analysis carried out are in accordance, except in the northern areas of West Bogor. Further validation was also carried out through the use of Regional Apparatus validation, 2018 PODES survey data and field validation. Based on field validation, the potential for flood areas with high hazard index values also corresponds to the results of flood hazard mapping validation. Bogor City has high hazards in five sub-districts except South Bogor Sub-district. The highest flood hazard is in the areas along the banks of two main rivers, namely Ciliwung in the east such as Baranangsiang Village and Cisadane in the west such as Pasir Jaya Village. These results are in accordance with the records of reported disaster events in Bogor City which show that the southern region has fewer flood reports. Based on the results of the joint validation workshop with OPD on February 18, 2020, the suitability of flood hazard mapping for sub-districts such as Cibadak, Ciparigi, Kedung Badak, and Tanah Baru was also obtained. Based on future flood hazard mapping, there is an increase in the potential for flood hazards in Tanah Sareal District, but there are no significant changes for other sub-districts. The increase in the area of potential flooding is caused by increased rainfall in the future in Tanah Sareal District. | Mass movement: Based on the results of the regional analysis, Bogor City has a landslide hazard index range of 0.18 - 0.64, which means that Bogor City has a potential for landslides from low to high. High hazard values are in East Bogor and South Bogor and areas close to river cliffs or areas with high slopes. Based on validation of DIBI data and the Bogor City Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), the results of the analysis carried out are in accordance. Further validation is carried out through the use of data from the Regional Apparatus, village potential data collection survey data (PODES) in 2018 and validation to the location/field point. The results of the validation of DIBI and BPBD data against the PODES survey also have a match, for example, Cimahpar Village has steep cliffs. This is also in accordance with the results of field validation, especially points with landslide hazard values. Furthermore, in the validation workshop there were landslide areas whose results did not match the analysis results, namely Mulyaharja, Pasir Jaya, Katulampa, and Genteng Villages because these areas experienced landslides in the riverbank area. The results of the future hazard mapping analysis indicate the potential for changes in landslide-prone areas (color changes). Based on the results of the analysis of future conditions, there was a decrease in the area with a high category in the southern region of East Bogor and there is still the potential for landslides because the area has a steep slope profile and a fairly high slope. Areas that experienced an increase in the landslide hazard index include the northern part of East Bogor District and the northern part of South Bogor District. Based on the results of the analysis, the Bogor City area has a tornado hazard index range of 0.62-0.97. Waste management (including waste recycling) - Litter-Free Neighborhood (RT Bebas Sampah): The Waste-Free Neighborhood Program in Bogor City is an initiative supported by various parties, including the Bogor City Environment Agency (DLH), to reduce waste by sorting and managing waste at its source, especially at the neighborhood (RT) level. This program involves education, socialization, and support facilities such as waste sorting facilities, transport carts, and the creation of special trash bins. In addition, this program also promotes economic benefits through the management of organic waste into compost and inorganic waste that can be sold or further processed. 
The objectives of this program are to create a clean and beautiful environment, reduce the volume of waste disposed of, encourage community participation, and provide economic value. 
The activities carried out include conducting outreach activities to the community on the importance of sorting waste from home, providing facilities such as separate bins for organic and inorganic waste, utilizing food or vegetable waste to make compost that is beneficial for plants, managing non-organic waste that has sale value through the Waste Bank Unit (BSU) or selling it to collectors, building awareness and a tradition of good waste management in the neighborhood, and developing recycled products such as ecobricks from plastic or pots from used materials.

Extreme heat: In Davao City, climate-related hazards like extreme heat, heavily affect vulnerable populations and key sectors. Women and girls face health risks during pregnancy and reduced education opportunities in poor households. Children and youth are highly sensitive to heat stress and diseases, with learning disrupted by hot classrooms and disasters. Elderly people are prone to dehydration, heat stroke, and mobility challenges during extreme events. Indigenous Peoples experience threats to food security, livelihoods, and cultural practices due to heat, drought, and biodiversity loss. Marginalized communities in informal settlements face unsafe housing, lack of cooling, and sanitation issues, raising risks of heat stress and disease. Vulnerable health groups struggle with chronic illnesses and limited access to care, while low-income households lack resources for cooling, resilient housing, or recovery, deepening poverty. Outdoor and frontline workers endure direct exposure, heat stress, reduced productivity, and both physical and psychological strain during climate emergencies.

Sectors such as agriculture, forestry, and fishing suffer from lower yields and water scarcity; construction faces productivity and safety issues; trade and food services experience customer decline and food spoilage; education and health systems are strained by heat impacts; and arts and recreation activities are disrupted, affecting livelihoods and community life. | Drought: Drought primarily impacts rural communities, low-income households, and indigenous peoples who rely on rain-fed agriculture and coastal or upland fisheries. Water scarcity affects daily living, reduces agricultural productivity, and threatens food security. Vulnerable health groups, including the elderly and persons with chronic illnesses, are at risk from limited access to potable water. Key sectors exposed to drought include agriculture, forestry, and fishing, which suffer from declining yields and livestock mortality; water supply services, which face reduced availability for domestic and industrial use; and accommodation and food service operations, where water scarcity affects hygiene, food preparation, and overall service continuity. | Urban flooding: Urban flooding presents a major climate-related hazard in Davao City, with 81-90% of the population exposed and a high probability of occurrence. Its current impact is assessed as medium-high, and the intensity is expected to increase in the short term. Vulnerable groups—including women, children, the elderly, Indigenous peoples, low-income households, marginalized communities, outdoor workers, and frontline responders—face the greatest risks. These populations are more likely to live in flood-prone areas, have limited access to resilient infrastructure, and experience heightened health and safety concerns, such as disease outbreaks, disrupted mobility, and reduced access to essential services.

Urban flooding also significantly disrupts key sectors across the city. Essential services such as water supply, electricity, waste management, transportation, education, and health care experience operational delays and increased demand. Economic sectors—including agriculture, fisheries, construction, manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, and accommodation and food services—face productivity losses due to damaged facilities, supply chain interruptions, and unsafe working conditions. These widespread impacts highlight the urgent need for strengthened adaptation measures, resilient infrastructure, and coordinated planning to reduce the city's vulnerability to worsening flood conditions. | River flooding: River flooding affects communities along riverbanks, particularly low-income households and rural populations, leading to displacement, damage to homes, and destruction of crops. Children are unable to attend school during flood events, and the elderly and vulnerable health groups face increased risks of injury and waterborne illnesses. Agriculture and fisheries sectors are heavily impacted, with soil erosion, crop damage, and livestock losses, while transportation, storage, and construction sectors face delays and infrastructure damage. Health services encounter increased patient loads due to illnesses associated with contaminated water and flooding events. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Coastal flooding, including the effects of sea-level rise, disproportionately affects coastal communities, particularly fisherfolk and low-income households. Homes, livelihoods, and fishing grounds are at risk, and frontline workers are exposed to hazards during rescue and recovery operations. The fishing and coastal agriculture sectors face reductions in productivity, while accommodation and food services, transportation, and health sectors experience operational disruptions, property damage, and heightened risks of infectious diseases. | Mass movement: Mass movement events, such as landslides and soil erosion, pose severe threats to upland communities, indigenous peoples, and residents in hazard-prone areas. Children and the elderly are particularly at risk, and frontline workers face danger during rescue and mitigation operations. Agriculture, forestry, mining, and construction sectors are affected through loss of arable land, forest degradation, operational delays, and blocked transportation routes. | Infectious disease: Infectious diseases are exacerbated by climate hazards such as floods, extreme heat, and changing rainfall patterns. Children, the elderly, low-income households, and vulnerable health groups are most affected. Outbreaks of vector-borne and waterborne diseases, including dengue, leptospirosis, and diarrhea, compromise health, reduce school attendance, and disrupt daily activities. Health and social work services face surges in patient loads and staff exhaustion, while education, retail, food service, and accommodation sectors experience productivity losses and service disruptions. | Loss of green space/green cover: loss of green space and green cover has cumulative impacts on urban residents, particularly children, the elderly, and low-income communities. Reduced green areas increase urban heat, exacerbate flood risks, degrade air quality, and limit recreational spaces. Agriculture and forestry sectors face declining soil fertility and biodiversity loss, while construction, accommodation, food services, and arts and recreation sectors are affected through increased heat stress, higher energy costs, and disrupted outdoor activities.

Poor communities are especially exposed to these floods, often situated in flood zones and with fragile houses.Some of the major impacts of a 100-year flooding under an RCP 8.5 scenario are as follows: 
1. Informal settlers that reside in Quezon City are high-risk areas. These settlements, due to their informality, are often not built to code or with flood resistant materials which increases their vulnerability to flood events. In 2021, there are 200,591 informal settler families (ISFs) listed by the Quezon City Government. A great number of these are in flood prone areas. District 1 lists 21,518 ISFs and about 95 % (20,491) are situated where flood depths can be higher than 0.5 meter. All of 61,439 ISFs can experience high flood depths. District 3 has 21,780 ISFs, and 21,039 or about 97% can experience depths higher than 0.5m. District 4 has 42,722 ISFs and 98% (41,955) can experience depths higher than 0.5m. District 5 has 11,060 ISFs listed, and all are in locations prone to floods. District 6 has 42,072 ISFs and all these families are in flood prone areas. 
2. Buildings: A focus on vacant or open spaces that are less prone to flooding from river overflows can be used for the deployment of emergency response services. This is taken as potentially damaging to the building structure or its contents. Most one-story buildings are largely for residential use and are less than four (4) meters high from floor to ceiling. 
3. The distribution of police stations, fire stations, and public facilities within the city are considered to be essential functions that must be preserved and functioning during a disaster. In the event of a 100-year flood, these facilities can provide essential services to community members who had to evacuate before the storm. They can serve as temporary shelters during times of emergency. By identifying the facilities most at risk of flooding, actions can be taken to decrease their vulnerability. A detailed analysis of the flood hazard and risk assessment can be found in the Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) document that is attached herewith. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: In 2024, a series of typhoons (local names Carina, Enteng, and Kristine) and an enhanced Southwest Monsoon left the city internally displacing 22,164 families accounting for 60,948 individuals due to heavy rains and floods over a period of four days. A similar occurrence took place in 2025 with tropical cyclones Crising, Dante, and Emong displacing 10,521 families with 37,373 individuals across 63 barangays. Both having more than 450mm of rain received by the city in the course of 4-6 days. During one day alone on August 30, 2025 the city also received an unprecedented amount of rainfall in 2 hours caused by the Southwest Monsoon peaking at 135.6 mm between 2:00-3:00 pm in the afternoon overwhelming the city's drainage systems. Such extreme weather events show the city's vulnerability where the following are the expected impacts of the hazard in the future for Quezon City: 

1. Very high level of displacement and loss of lives because of storms and floods. It is estimated that a 100-year flood will result in 111 casualties in Quezon City, with floods also leading to accidents and injuries like contusions, fractures and electrocution. 

2. Very high level of post-flood disease outbreaks. Extreme rainfall and the resulting floods may lead to increased transmission of infectious diseases. Systematic failures of healthcare systems could lead to increased fatalities. 

3. High level of threatened access to safe drinking water after flooding. After a flood, many people in Quezon City do not have access to safe drinking water, especially the urban poor. 

4. Medium level of threatened food security. Excessive rainfall could inflict serious damages to agricultural crops. After extreme rainfall, access to food can be limited which could also influence the general condition of the population, including malnutrition and the lack of adequate immunity.

5. Medium level of disruption of traffic. | Drought: Metro Manila has experienced dry conditions in the past El Niño events. Long dry periods can have a serious impact on the availability of water. In 2019, data from PAGASA showed La Mesa dam at a critical level of less than 70 meters, the lowest in 12 years. Low water levels may result in water interruption schedules, leading to barangays experiencing low water pressure to no water at all throughout the summer. The length of the longest dry spell, which is the maximum number of consecutive dry days with daily precipitation under 1 mm, is projected to increase with 7.5 days towards 2050.Water stress is an indicator of competition for water resources: an increase in water stress indicates more competition among users, hitting the urban poor the hardest. For Quezon City, the World Resources Institute indicates that the current low/medium level of water stress will worsen to an extremely high level in 2040.The following are the expected impacts of the hazard in the future for Quezon City: 
1. Very high level of decrease in dam water availability. Long dry spells have caused problems in water availability as dams get depleted. Service interruptions and water rationing measures might be needed more often, impacting poorer communities more. 
2. High level of increase of drought-related health impacts. Particulate matter suspended in the air can irritate lungs, causing chronic respiratory illnesses. 
3. High level of threatened biodiversity because of drought. Prolonged drought may lead to drops in biodiversity - the variety and number of species, possibly leading to more serious consequences, such as ecosystem collapses. 
4. Medium level of drought-related decline in food productions. Increased dry spells and droughts may result in crop damage and reduction in yields affecting the food supply in Quezon City. Decreased food production may have economic implications potentially affecting the poor and marginalized communities. 
5. Medium level of threatened food security. Food security in Quezon City may be threatened due to dependence of food supply from external sources affected by drought. | Extreme heat: Temperatures have risen steadily in the Philippines with an average of 0.1C per decade. Quezon City is developing rapidly with obvious signs of urban sprawl, including their placement of natural vegetation with buildings and other infrastructures. This has inadvertently caused dramatic shifts in the City's microclimate, raising summer temperature in the City by up to 7C. Since 1951, nights and days in Quezon City have become increasingly warm. 

Climate projections suggest continuous warming in the future, with the largest surge in the summer months of March, April, and May. Under a high emissions scenario, the mean temperature in the Philippines could increase by as much as 1.2 - 2.3C until 2050. 

In April to May 2025, Quezon City experienced high heat indices averaging 42-44°C, continuing a trend observed in previous years, this is in accordance with Quezon City's iRiseUp and PAG-ASA's heat index temperatures.

climate_hazard: Heavy precipitation: Intense rainfall can lead to rivers overflowing their banks, causing widespread flooding. The frequency of floods in Makati is attributed to the 16 creeks and canals surrounding the city. During the height of extreme rainfall, households near the waterbodies are prone to flooding. School classes and work in public agencies are also suspended. Some of the streets in the city are unpassable to light vehicles affecting commuters. Food deliveries having difficult time to access flooded streets. Internet connection are slow up to no connection at all disrupting communications. In this regard, the city government in coordination with various national government agencies, neighboring cities, and the barangay done series and continuing collective efforts to conduct weekly waterways clean up drive, rehabilitation of waterways easement, partnership with private sectors through the Adopt-an-Estero/Waterbody program among others. | Urban flooding: Makati has so far only experienced prolonged flooding, with 25 to 30 minutes to recede, during typhoon Ondoy in 2009. Locations that were susceptible to flood have close proximity to Pasig River or other flood-prone areas in neighboring cities. With a business-as-usual scenario, the hazard is expected to worsen based on the 50 to 100 year flood cycle. During urban flooding the following are the impacts to the city, exposure of infrastructures to higher flood level and/or longer duration of flood; Inaccessible roads; Clogging of drainage inlets due to garbage; Disruption in transportation of goods and services; Road obstruction; Heavy traffic; overflowing of waterways/canals, and Increased cases of water-borne diseases. The city continuously maintains and improves it's drainage system to avoid flooding and has made plans for vulnerable areas as envisioned in Disaster Resilient Initiative for Vulnerable Enclaves (DRIVE) sites based on the City's Comprehensive Land Use Plan. | Storm: When a tropical storm and/or a Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) hits the city, we expect the occurrence of flooded streets in low-lying areas, overflowing of waterways/canals, transportation affected due to heavy traffic, unpassable roads, and insufficiency in mass transport, possibility of rain-induced landslides, disruption of electricity and water supply in some areas, huge volume of debris from the after effects of storm and flooding, and suspension of school classes affecting students and the youth. There is loss of biodiversity due to increased plant mortality during storms. Also disruption on the delivery of environmental services. These impacts are lessened through the city's pro-active Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) system such as Early Warning System, Town Watching, Disaster Preparedness and Response, Social aid, among others. | Extreme heat: Certain parts of Metro Manila including Makati City had fluctuating water supply due to El Niño which affected the water supply in Angat Dam. It is expected that there will be an increase in frequency of days experiencing increased temperature of Tmax > 35 degree Celsius. This heat is expected to manifest heat cramps and heat exhaustion to people which could result to heat stroke. Other impacts are the following: Increase in demand of potable water needs; Rapid spoilage rate of perishable goods during heat waves, Increase in mental health issues/stress, Increase cases of heat-related diseases/illnesses, Increase in number of fire incident, Limited outdoor/recreational activities, Increase in GHG emissions due to utilization of mass transport instead of walking or taking bike, among others. The city through the Makati City El Niño South-Oscillation (ENSO) Task Force implements the action plans laid out in the Makati ENSO Contingency Plan. | Extreme wind: When the tropical storm or southwest monsoon (Habagat) hits the city, associated with this is the extreme/severe winds. It can damage or destroy vehicles, buildings, bridges and other outside objects. Certain parts of Metro Manila including Makati City has so far experienced extreme wind with the occurrence of a typhoon based on the Greater Metro Manila Area Risk Analysis Project (GMMA RAP). In which the main objective is to analyze the risk of severe wind due to tropical cyclone. Locations that were susceptible to extreme wind are low-lying areas, have a close proximity to river that surrounds the City. Other impacts are the following: uprooted trees and plants leading to loss of biodiversity, downed communication lines, damage to buildings, vehicles, and other properties, flying risky debris, possibility of power outages, transportation disruptions, and injury or death. These impacts are lessened through the city's pro-active Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) system such as implementation of enhanced Contingency Plans, DRRM Plan, and other disaster preparedness and response mechanisms. | Drought: Certain parts of Metro Manila including Makati City had fluctuating water supply due to El Niño in 2015 and in 2019. This scenario is mostly caused by recorded below threshold value of the Angat Dam. 19 out of 33 barangays in the city is expected to be affected by low water pressure and service interruption due to cut-down of allocation according to Water Concessionaire's advisory. Drought affects low water supply for irrigation which cause decrease in agricultural production from nearby provinces which supplies the food in the city. Other impacts are the following: Increase in demand of potable water needs; Rapid spoilage rate of perishable goods during heat waves, Increase in mental health issues/stress, Increase cases of heat-related diseases/illnesses, Increase in number of fire incident, among others. The city through the Makati City El Niño South-Oscillation (ENSO) Task Force implements the action plans laid out in the Makati ENSO Contingency Plan.

This made it the first-ever green building incentive introduced by local authority in the country. 
For next, it is suggested to replicate above mentioned exercise to other local authoritiries i.e. Majlis Bandaraya Iskandar Puteri (MBIP).

Other: Green Investment Framework - Green Investment Framework For Iskandar Malaysia and Pengerang (JS-SEZ): As the global economy transitions toward sustainability, green investment has become a vital pillar in national and regional development strategies. In Malaysia, the push for low-carbon, climate-resilient growth is gaining momentum, particularly in strategic economic zones. Among these, Iskandar Malaysia and the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ)—including Pengerang—have emerged as key platforms to implement and accelerate green transformation initiatives. This document presents an integrated Strategy and Green Investment Framework to guide sustainable development across these regions. It aligns with national goals such as the Twelfth Malaysia Plan (12MP) and Malaysia's Net Zero 2050 ambition, while responding to global imperatives such as the Paris Agreement and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).Iskandar Malaysia is a key economic corridor in southern Johor, envisioned as a sustainable metropolis of international standing. It has pioneered various green economy policies, most notably the Low Carbon Society Blueprint for Iskandar Malaysia 2025 (LCSBPIM 2025), followed by the LCSBPIM 2030 - Climate Action Plan. These initiatives are backed by regulatory instruments such as the Green Economy Guidelines (GEG).In parallel, Pengerang has gained prominence as part of Malaysia's energy and petrochemical hub through the Pengerang Integrated Petroleum Complex (PIPC). As Johor and Singapore formalize the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), Pengerang is poised to become a green industrial growth node. The JS-SEZ framework outlines strategic sectors such as green economy, digital economy, logistics, and advanced manufacturing as core investment targets. To ensure the SEZ's relevance in a decarbonizing world economy, a well-defined green investment strategy is essential. This requires leveraging existing industrial strengths in Pengerang while embedding green technologies, nature-based solutions (NbS), and sustainable infrastructure within future development plans.

This Strategy and Green Investment Framework aims to:

Provide a coherent roadmap for aligning investments in Iskandar Malaysia and JS-SEZ with green growth objectives.

Facilitate cross-border cooperation with Singapore on environmental innovation and sustainable industry.

Identify priority sectors, incentives, and enablers for green investments.

Propose governance and monitoring mechanisms to ensure accountability and results.

The framework seeks to position Iskandar Malaysia and Pengerang as regional leaders in green economic development, attracting sustainable investment, creating green jobs, and ensuring long-term resilience for communities and ecosystems.

climate_hazard: Snow and ice: Finland is expecting increased winter precipitation, which can in the nearest future seen as higher amounts of snow. The winter temperatures will alternate more around zero celsius, causing several freezing-thawing cycles in the wintertime. This causes dangerous and slippery conditions on the roads, which are difficult to predict. There might not be enough resources to keep the roads in good condition. This can cause a) more injuries to people who fall while walking on slippery surfaces, b) cause car accidents c) prevent help, e.g. ambulance or home nurses getting to their cliants (especially in the more rural areas). | Extreme heat: Mortality in hospitals and elderly homes increase when temperature is above 24C day-round. Children in daycare and schools are exposed to heat in their yards, which do not have enough shading vegetation. Energy demand rises and stresses energy system when cooling is turned on in many households and offices and hospitals. Heat waves can damage agriculture, food production and food poisonings are more possible. We have also identified urban heat island effect in the city center of Lahti. Heat causes stress to ecosystems and water bodies, including groundwater. New invasive alien species or diseases are more likely to spread. Similarly endemic species, such as the European Spruce Bark Beetle, have more favourable conditions to population growth than earlier, causing damage for forestry sector. More irrigation and rain water storages are needed. Strong apposition in lakes can create lack of oxygen in some levels. | Urban flooding: Heavy rains are expected more often and that can create urban floods. Storm water floods damage infrastructure and properties. Floods can also pollute groundwater and surface waters and cause erosion. Management capacity changes and capacity re- sizing will be needed. Traffic congestions and electricity distribution problems are possible due to urban flooding. climate_hazard: Biodiversity loss: Alien species pose a threat to the local ecosystems of Tampere. Even without alien species, some endangered species and their ecosystems might have difficulties to adapt to changing climate. Most vulnerable ecosystems are those that are narrow or separated from the others. Plant diseases and pest insects can significantly damage agricultural production and forests. | Extreme wind: Extreme wind is not expected to become more severe in the close future. However, its impacts will be more serious due to lack of ground frost as trees fall more easily without it. Hence, forest damages and windthrow will be more frequent in the future, causing economic losses for forest and property owners. In addition to forest damage or as a result of it, extreme wind can disturb electricity supply and thus indirectly affect heat and water distribution, telecommunications and other critical functions of the society. | Infectious disease: Infectious diseases can spread via water, air, insects or vector animals such as deer or vole. Examples of situations causing waterborne diseases are a person drinking water that has been contaminated with stormwater in the event of flooding or a child who has accidentally swam in a lake with blue-green algae and swallowed some water. There are other pathogens too, some perhaps still unknown or not met in Finland, who might thrive in the warming waters of Tampere. An example of diseases transmitted by an insect (more specifically tick) are borreliosis and tick-borne encephalitis (TBE). Ticks are spreading higher up north as the average yearly temperatures rise up. They can be brought to the city by a vector animal like deer. It is expected that there will be an increased number of borreliosis and TBE cases in Tampere in the future due to longer growing season. | Drought: Long periods of drought cause groundwater decline. Drought is especially harmful for agriculture and forestry because it causes damage to crops and increases the risk of fire, respectively. Availability of irrigation water is a challenge too. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Risk of forest fires increases as extreme heat and drought are to become more frequent. Forest fires destroy timber and cause economic losses for forest owners. They are burden for rescue services and cause challenges for the resource distribution if they occur at the time with other disasters. Depending on the wind direction and strength, fire gas can spread to nearby surroundings and endanger human health, especially vulnerable health groups' respiratory systems. | Heavy precipitation: Heavy precipitation has impacts on surface water quality, building stock, urban environment and agriculture. Stormwater runoff and sewer network overflows can cause pollution and eutrophication of surface water bodies. In addition, heavy rainfall increases the load to wastewater treatment plant and thus affects its ability to treat wastewater properly, although the networks for wastewater and stormwater are mostly separated from each other in Tampere. Heavy rainfall and especially driving rain may damage old and poor conditioned buildings and require moisture control and other repair measures from the owners. Especially in densely populated areas of Tampere, heavy rainfall and insufficient stormwater management capacity can disturb transportation activities. Heavy rainfall has an impact on agricultural activities which are located in the northern parts of Tampere. lt can result in crop damage and erosion, causing significant economic losses for the farmers. | Urban flooding: Intense rain saturates an urban drainage system, resulting in urban flooding. The impacts of it include erosion, pollution, damages on buildings and infrastructure and sewage overflows. During street flooding transportation infrastructure, electricity distribution and other services and business operations can be directly or indirectly damaged. For example, it might be more difficult for rescue services to reach their destination. The impacts of flooding are most severe in densely built areas, such as the city center. | Extreme heat: Extreme hot temperatures pose a challenge to public health, especially among elderly people and other vulnerable health groups. A significant portion of the elderly are living in the city center of Tampere where the conditions are particularly tricky due to heat island effect. However, the effect is partly reduced by the proximity of two lakes, Näsijärvi and Pyhäjärvi. Also, population living in old or poor conditioned buildings are more exposed to extreme heat than others because they do not have sufficient technology to cool down their apartments. In addition, old apartment buildings that were built before WWII have thick walls that reserve heat.During extreme heat events, demand for cooling and thus energy increases. Extreme heat can also have effects on water supply because of drought and increased need for irrigation. In the agricultural sector extreme heat can cause crop losses and in forestry forest fires. | Snow and ice: Freeze-thaw cycles get quicker as the temperature changes below and above 0 degrees celsius. There will also be more rain in the winter time that can come as snow. This can cause difficulties for vulnerable groups, elderly and those with limited moving abilities, and pressure to good maintenance of the infrastructure, such as sanding and snow ploughing.
project_info: Public and green spaces - Collaboration with local businesses in the theme of adaptation to climate change and re-greening the city: Collaboration with local businesses will increase the possibilities to add private land to ecological networks, which helps in adapting to climate change and preserving biodiversity, and has many health benefits too.
