project_info: Transport - Safe and interesting transportation environment: piloting AI and people together: At the moment, we can calculate Driver Danger Index which describes traffic environment for drivers based on e.g. speed limits and traffic accidents. In this project we want to form a similar index for cyclists and pedestrians. For this, we will identify unsafe spots within city's transportation infrastructure, both in the city centre and suburbans, by utilizing AI recognition and data from traffic monitoring cameras. This way we can get accurate data from cycling and walking safety. The index will be constructed based on cyclist and pedestrian numbers, road conditions and near misses (= ”almost accidents”) recognized by AI.We have already had one pilot before with a service provider. However, it was limited to a small area, so now we wish to expand it to cover the whole road network of Tampere. The project is a part of city's new four year old program Carbon Neutral Actions.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Urban green as a resource for residents to adapt to climate change: City permission has been granted to start preparations for an EU-project to revitalize degraded ecosystems and develop multi-purpose blue-green infrastructure in the city. The goal of Tampere is to continue the development of innovative stormwater systems based on nature, which has already started, and to invest them in the existing urban structure. The aim is also to rehabilitate our city streams so that the natural increase in salmonids can also start in Tampere. strengthens Tampere's position as part of international networks and as a major player in the world. We also share Tampere-based know-how and promote business opportunities for Tampere-based companies both locally and globally.With the project, we will be better able to prepare for the increasing amounts of stormwater as a result of climate change and the condensing city. With effective stormwater solutions, we can protect swimming and fishing grounds from water turbidity and wastewater discharges, even during large discharges. At the same time, we can bring nature into the city and make our city more comfortable. Nature-based stormwater systems support the carbon neutrality goal of our urban strategy and the goals of our stormwater program.

project_info: Other: New governance - Climate Budget: Main idea of the project is to share experience and develop ways of working on climate budget as a tool for transparancy in climate work and planning of climate friendly investments. climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Heat related illnesses and mortality will increase. Especially the elderly and chronically ill are vulnerable to heat. The need for emergency services will increase do to extreme heats. Aged, especially people over 80 years of age, are in a particularly vulnerable position and sensitive to temperature changes. Both warm and cold temperatures are harmful for these groups. Compared to Southern Europe, people in Finland are poorly adjusted to warm weathers. Studies show that the ideal temperature for Finns is around 14 Celsius degrees. Even minor changes in temperatures affect people's health and well-being and effects on mortality appear quickly. Particularly sensitive to temperature changes and extremely hot or cold periods are aging and chronically ill, for example those who suffer from cardiovascular or respiratory diseases. | Urban flooding: Increasing flood risk requires improved management of stormwaters. Stormwater management especially in the inner city but also in other built-up areas. Risks to buildings, disruptions to traffic and possible challenges to emergency services. Several measures have been planned and some have recently been implemented but due to lack of resources this has not progressed within the desired schedule. Risks to waste water management as the treatment plan (one centralised facility) is in the risk of overflowing with stormwaters (not 100 % separated from sewage system). | Storm: Potentially severe damage to crops, forests etc. In rural areas prolonged power outages. In more densely populated areas flooding and e.g. falling trees, flying debris can cause material damage (and potential health threat). Disruptions to traffic. | Other: Increased pollen: Possible increase in the pollen levels was recognized as one of the indirect effects of the climate change. As the carbon dioxide levels increase, the flora has improved reproduction conditions and therefore the levels of pollen are projected to increase. Increased amount of pollen is directly connected with the symptom description of those who suffer from allergies and asthma, and indirectly connected with the risk of developing these symptoms. According to future projections, pollen yield will increase by tens of percent, which could lead to more than half of the population in Europe developing pollen allergies in the near future. In Finland, 15-20 % of citizens suffer from pollen allergies. The possible increase in people suffering from allergies and asthma would burden the health care sector, weaken people's work and functional capacity and cause economically significant effects. | Snow and ice: Increasing amounts of snow (as the amount of precipitation is expected to increase especially during the winter), temperature changes in winter and changes in freeze-thaw cycles. More frequent slippery conditions and deteriorating road conditions, which can result in increase in slips and falls, and in road accidents. Reduction in the ice cover leads to easier marine transport but on the other hand, there will be more ice floes in the future.
project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - KISS Life: As part of a larger, national EU-Life project, we concentrate on nature-based solutions for stormwater management. Besides the actual stormwater infrastructure tasks for indicator testing, social acceptability and general knowledge are also included.

project_info: Transport - Cycling superhighway network: Efficient maintenance of cycle lanes ensures that cycling and walking are always a noteworthy option for most trips - even in the winters. The Baana cycle lanes are wide roads paved with red concrete that lead from the city centre to the north, east and south. Heavy precipitation: Since 2009 we did have several extreme rain events in summer. Before we had this once in a five year. Not only the frequency has rised but also the heavyness of the rain showers and thunder storms. So we have to extend our rules of obliged water storage in new buildings and building ares to a higher level. Especially in the compact areas of the city. | River flooding: Nijmegen has finished the biggest river adaptation project Room for the Waal with a huge dike relocation in the town centre. Now the state government is improving all the dikes at the north side of the river Waal. This has also big impact on the cultural-historical values alongside the dikes and the ecological values in the flood plains. In NIjmegen this is also in conflict with our new housing developmentes in Nijmegen North clos to the dike. | Drought: Degeneration of public green spaces by draught especially for recently planted trees and shrubs and for older trees . We also faced for the first time in 2018 problems with sagging of houses because the clay soil was shrinking. We have now faced several dry years in the last five years. | Heat stress: Over the years more ponds in the city were facing the danger of blue algae and Botulism. Also the new created side channel and one of the lakes in the north face this threat. If the the weather changes (more dry and hot summers) continues then the risk will grow. The need for cooling is rising and that means that we need more green spaces and trees, but the green objects faces drought problems as well. A combined strategy is decided by the municipal council (2023) for creating more green-blue spaces (water storage and cooling spots) and creating more biodiversity. We have a new Tree Plant Programme, a Biodiversity Strategy and a Climate Adaptation Strategy (concept). All three deliver new structure maps. The Tree Structure Maps shows the tree structure alongside streets and cycling high ways and combined with the \'Shadow on streets maps\' we know where we have to plant more trees to secure cool routes for cycling and walking people. The \'Distance to Cool Spots\'maps points out where we need more green cool spaces to meet and play. The Green Structure Maps shows the bigger green areas (parcs, nature areas and small forests) and the ecological routes between. Therefore we hope to strenghten the biodiversity. The Climate Adaptation Maps shows the public and private spaces vulnerable for rain water flooding and heat stress. But also the areas where we have to find the solutions in order to lower the threats by means of taking measures for water storage and cooling.

climate_hazard: Heavy precipitation: Extreme precipitation can lead to urban flooding, reduced accessibility, water intrusion in municipal and private buildings, pollution, and landslides. Children, youth, vulnerable health groups, and the elderly are most at risk as they may have limited physical capabilities during urban floods and with reduced accessibility. The cloudburst plan assessed and set acceptance criteria for objects such as buildings, roads, and critical societal functions. Individuals were not assessed due to significant uncertainty, but it is clear that certain groups of people are more vulnerable to flood events. For railway and road traffic, it has been noted that they may be affected. This falls under the sectors of Sewerage, waste management and remediation activities and Transportation and storage. This, in turn, can affect rescue services. Several pumping stations will have standing water against the pump house. Buildings such as hospitals, nursing homes, police stations, fire stations, schools, and kindergartens have been mapped, which may affect sectors such as public administration and defence; compulsory social security and Human health and social work activities. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Vulnerable groups may face challenges with accessibility during floods due to rising water levels. The city center is located near the sea and is protected as a medieval town, which poses a challenge for conservation. Many buildings in the immidiate vicinity are hotels and restaurants that will be affected by coastal flooding in the city center. | Storm: Extreme weather can cause a number of unwanted events, in addition to posing a direct threat to life and health. Vulnerable health groups are assumed to be more susceptible to disruptions and may be more dependent on municipal services and critical infrastructure such as power supply. Front line workers, such as emergency services, will be operational during a storm and therefore more exposed.\nImportant infrastructure can be damaged during storm, creating disruption for the general public. The electricity sector can be affected if trees fall over power lines. It can also lead to failures in public and private service production. If extreme weather leads to a loss of communication, sectors such as public administration and defence, including compulsory social security, will be affected. Power supply and electronic communications are considered to be the two most critical infrastructures in the municipality. Failures in power supply (long-term) and electronic communications can contribute to a wide range of other undesirable events. Cultural monuments are also at risk with increasing storms. \n | Mass movement: The municipality has conducted an analysis of steep terrain to identify the risk of rockfalls. Additionally, some areas are below the marine limit, with a risk of quick clay landslides. The municipality has not made assessments regarding whether there are any sectors that are particularly affected by mass movement. Furthermore no population group are impacted more than others.

A collaboration agreement between Statkraft and Trondheim Municipality was signed in June 2023. This will be conducted through Citizen Assemblies, involving various stakeholders over a period of two years (2024-2026).

Nyhavna Utvikling AS, a company established by Trondheim Municipality and the Trondheim Harbour Authority, has been tasked with leading this process.\nThe overall development plan aims to transform Nyhavna into a zero-emission neighbourhood, where the energy system will play a crucial role (https://nyhavna.no/byutvikling/helhetlig-plan-for-nyhavna/). Seven boreholes have been drilled, the thermal properties of the bedrock have been tested, and geotechnical investigations have been completed during the last 12-14 months. health, biodiversity, and climate resilience. Despite its potential, current frameworks and policies are not
sufficient for wide implementation. The project addresses this by developing cross-sectoral strategies through
collaboration among researchers, municipalities, government agencies, and other stakeholders.

accounting and certification, and long-term knowledge building. Using methods from systems innovation and cocreation, prototypes of policies and practices will be developed, tested, and refined. Results will be disseminated
via national networks such as Viable Cities and Biochar Sweden.

while strengthening society's resilience through links to local energy systems, agriculture, and climate policy.

Extreme heat: Climate change means that the UK, and the south-east of England in particular, is experiencing hotter & drier summers. The temperature of the hottest days each year are expected to increase more than the average summer temperature increase. As with many other parts of the country impacted by hotter temperatures, Brighton & Hove high temperatures bring an increased impact to human health & wellbeing, and emergency services. The following risks have been identified in the Local Heatwave Plan for Brighton & Hove for 2023: potential increase in adverse outcomes amongst e.g. older people aged 75+; children aged 5 and under; people who live alone and/or are socially isolated; people with long-term health conditions such as cardio-respiratory diseases; people taking certain medications; people who need the assistance of others for their routine activities; people with difficulty adapting their behaviour in warmer weather (for example, due to dementia, mental health issues or alcohol/recreational drug use). Specific populations also at increased risk of exposure to heat due to the context in which they live include: homeless people (whether sleeping rough or in shelters); people resident in specific institutional settings (Care Homes, inpatient psychiatric units); some occupations, workplaces & schools - particularly those involving significant manual exertion, heat generation (e.g. cooking, some manufacturing roles) & in buildings prone to overheating & without air conditioning. Brighton & Hove's urban heat island has been analysed as part of the CRVA and helps understand the variation in exposure to heat across the city, and and the likelihood of 'hotspots' of overheating. High temperatures are an emerging risk for Brighton & Hove's infrastructure. particularly to transport infrastructure, service delivery, passengers, buckling of rail lines, line sag and rail speed restrictions, damage to bridges, pavements and road surfaces. Hot summer weather poses a significant challenge for Brighton & Hove, as many buildings and housing stock across the city are vulnerable to overheating. Higher temperatures can also worsen local air quality, which can exacerbate existing health (respiratory) issues, particularly in areas with significant car traffic. | Soil degradation/erosion: Loss of natural ground and soil, alongside soil degradation, erosion, and compaction is an issue for the city of Brighton & Hove. This includes the loss of soils to built environment / development and infrastructure pressures which leads to and exacerbates surface water flooding and over-heating issues as identified in the Climate Risk Vulnerability Assessment (2023). This is combined with impacts on the City Downland Estate (farmland etc), located in the South Downs National Park, which reduce farm productivity / food growing, causing land damage and biodiversity loss and likely impacts the city's water supply aquifer. These impacts affect the most vulnerable and the most deprived first and more significantly as reflected in the cost of living crisis with food costs escalating (2023 estimates c.£700-800 added to food bills) and the higher use of food banks as seen in the city and beyond. Land uses will be forced to change to adapt. This is addressed in The City Downland Estate Plan: https://www.brighton-hove.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2023-02/7640%20City%20Downland%20Estate%20Plan%20phase4%20FINAL2.pdf. There is a risk to soil erosion from heavy rain events causing major erosion events, especially during the summer when a heavy rain event/storm happens after a period of dry weather. This could lead to the loss of more fertile top soil. | Storm: Increased flooding of sections of the lower promenade along Brighton Seafront has occurred since 2014 from high tides and storm surges. This flooding affects local businesses along the seafront. Work to implement the Brighton Marina to River Adur Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management Scheme ( FCERM) when complete will manage the impact of storm events as well as flood protection work to seafront properties, and go some way to reduce the impact of the hazard in the future. https://ww3.brighton-hove.gov.uk/sites/brighton-hove.gov.uk/files/Newsletter%20No.1%20technical%20version_.doc.pdf Coastal homes and businesses are at risk of damage and there's an increase risk to beach users. The Southern Water, water treatment plant located at Portobello on the Peacehaven coast is at risk of damage due to storm influenced coastal cliff erosion, this could impact sewerage water treatment for the whole City. Lower income households and those without a home are also vulnerable due to higher exposure and lower capacity to cope with property damage. Weather and Health Plan: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1155633/Adverse-weather-health-plan-2023-v2.pdf “Future climate projections estimate that UK winter precipitation will increase significantly, and summer precipitation will decrease significantly. However, the variability in rainfall is also expected to increase, meaning that we can expect to see more intense storms in summer months, driving 'flash' flooding. Unlike the observed and anticipated trend in increasingly intense storm-driven rainfall, there is no observed trend in increasing high winds (maximum gust speeds) since records began in 1969. Winter wind speeds are anticipated to increase between 2050 and 2100, accompanied by an increase in the frequency of winter storms. However, the overall projected increases in wind speeds are small compared to the inter-annual variability observed in recent years , and so the future risk is considered similar to present-day.” | Heavy precipitation: The underlying geology of the City is dominated by the extensive chalk beds & chalk aquifer, which serve to provide the city's water supply. The highly permeable nature of this bedrock contributes to the risk of groundwater flooding. The City has experienced a wide range of flooding events over the last 25 yrs with surface & groundwater flooding being the most notable. Groundwater flooding has historically occurred where the Downs meet with the northern edge of the city. The autumn & winter events of 2000-2001 and February 2014 are the largest recorded events when extreme weather caused flooding across the city. We often cannot capture much data on each smaller occurrence due to reluctance on the part of homeowners to officially report flooding at their home and therefore risk affecting insurance prospects. Brighton & Hove City Council is the Lead Local Flood Authority and as such complies with the national statutory regulation on flood risk & flood risk is taken into account at all stages of the planning process. Flooding events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in the future. The Met Office's projections going forward in a high emission scenario are for: • Winter rainfall increasing by 35%; • Summer rainfall decreasing by 47% • Intense rainfall increasing by 25% with more intense rainfall in the summer. (Despite overall summer drying trends in the future, new data from UKCP Local suggests future increases in the intensity of heavy summer rainfall events. For urban areas particularly, this will impact on the frequency and severity of surface water flooding.) Current strategies in place include: B&H Strategic Flood Risk Assessment; B&H Surface Water Management Plan; B&H Local flood risk management strategy; B&H Marina to River Adur flood and coastal erosion risk management strategy; National Flood Risk Management Strategy; South East River Basin; Catchment Flood Management Plan which includes Brighton & Hove as a flood risk area https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/south-east-river-basin-district-flood-risk-management-plan | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The updated Brighton Marina to River Adur Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management Scheme (FCERM)(2023) includes coastal modelling inclusive of the latest climate change figures including sea level rises. This provides the current understanding of the impact of future coastal flooding. Vulnerable populations include those that live/ work in close proximity to the coastline and those that use coastal roads at risk of damage from coastal cliff erosion such as the A259. The Southern Water, water raising main to the treatment plant located at Portobello on the Peacehaven coast is at risk of loss due to erosion, this could impact sewerage water treatment for the whole City. | Biodiversity loss: Biodiversity loss is detrimental to well-functioning ecosystems and impacts on the overall health of the natural environment and the communities that depend on it. Biodiversity underpins ecosystem services that are essential for both people and nature such as water quality, pollination, commercial and community food growing and air quality. As such, biodiversity loss impacts on all aspects of society including individuals, communities and businesses that are reliant on ecosystem services e.g. agriculture. There is also increasing evidence of the benefits of biodiversity and connection with nature to human health and wellbeing, as well as wider community cohesion and installing a sense of pride. 

The BHCC CRVA and action plan (2023) focuses on biodiversity loss and how to conserve and enhance biodiversity. This is complemented by the City Downland Estate Plan (2023) that provides guidance and a route map on managing the Downland estate through actions to reduce and store carbon through natural processes, enhance wildlife, improve public access and encouraging sustainable, local food production. On a wider scale, the emerging Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) due for publication in Spring 2026, will highlight measures and opportunities for improving nature and habitats across the East Sussex and Brighton & Hove area.

Changes in climate such as hotter and drier summers, alongside changes in water availability and recharge of our chalk aquifer present a significant risk to species and ecosystem services. We are already seeing declines in species populations, local extinctions, species range modifications, impacts on migratory patterns and increases/changes in presence of pests and invasive species. Sea level rise is also a notable emerging risk for Brighton's natural environment. It could lead to saltwater intrusion of Brighton's chalk aquifer, due to hydrological connectivity with the sea. This can have cascading impacts for the natural environment which is reliant on the freshwater provided by the aquifer. In addition, rising sea levels could result in the loss of rare coastal habitats such as the city's iconic shingle coastline.

Sustainable food consumption/production - Greater Brighton: The Future of Food: As part of the development of a Greater Brighton Food Plan we have created investment plans for city region infrastructure, business support and training in alignment with Government Food Strategy and city-region pledges on the Environment. 

Larger projects will require feasibility work and impact assessments before project structuring. The focus is on growth areas and supply chains. Growth opportunities have been identified for smaller projects (quick wins) that may move quickly into implementation phase, depending on local capacity and resourcing. 

The Greater Brighton region has many pre-existing assets that give it the potential to become a leader in local food economy development, including: 
1) An economy and geography with food already at its heart 
2) Proximity to valuable markets 
3) World class knowledge and resources already at its disposal 
4) Local complementary assets to facilitate a local and sustainable food system 

Because food is so integral to so many elements of our lives, investing in food systems approaches has a broad and long-term impact across many areas, including: 
• Tackling the climate crisis and the carbon emissions produced within our food system 
•Reducing inequality and tackling the cost-of-living crisis in the long-term, by creating resilient food systems for everyone, not just funding food banks 
• Increasing wellbeing and social outcomes through bringing people together and community development 
• Improving public health through better access to nutritious food 
• Supporting both the rural and urban economy through supporting SMEs 
• Increasing the quality of the places we live and spend time in 
• Ensuring public sector stability through income generation and local economic growth 

The Greater Brighton: Future of Food systems project has a set of combined strategic objectives: 1) Systems approach to economic growth 2) Local food to local markets 3) Minimum waste, maximum efficiency 4) World-leading experts and skilled communities 5) Maximised social, health, environmental, equity and place outcomes for every £1 spent. 

The following projects have been costed as part of a whole system approach: 
• Dynamic food procurement system - A dynamic food procurement system streamlines the procurement process for local food businesses by connecting them with local suppliers and providing real-time information on availability and pricing. 
• Food hub (depot) - This project is modelling a food depot, whose primary aim is to give local producers a route to local markets, increasing the accessibility of local food, and the sustainability of the food supply in the region. It is modelled as a purpose-led commercial business. 
• Training and support programmes - This modelling looks at potential training and support programmes for businesses around circular economy practices. • Community supported agriculture - A partnership between farmers and consumers in which the responsibilities, financial and other risks are shared. 
• Large scale community composting - Community composting diverts household and/or business food waste to produce compost for use locally. A systems approach means looking at all elements of the system and how they work together, tackling root causes rather than symptoms. It also recognises that all outcomes are also interlinked - we can't reduce the need for food banks without building a more environment friendly system, we can't do that without allowing local SMEs to thrive, and we can't do that without building community power and wealth, and so on. We define the goal as building a local and sustainable food system.

climate_hazard:
Extreme heat: Sunderland's Climate Change Risk Assessment and The Northumbria LRF Community Risk Register lists Adverse Weather, including heat waves and consequent failure of essential services, as a top risk. The frequency of such events is likely to increase in the future, increasing the health risks for people in Sunderland, particularly the vulnerable populations in the city, as well as posing a potential risk to the local economy. Agriculture/Conservation: reduced growth of shoots, resulting in lower crop yields. Higher temperatures reduce yields of desirable crops and increase growth of weeds and pests. Heat increases the risk of drought. Businesses: Heat and humidity can impact employee productivity and therefore labour productivity. Workers not in a controlled climate environment e.g. outdoor workers will be most adversely affected and can suffer from the health implications associated with extreme heat. Summer energy demand: Electricity usage will increase with greater use of air conditioning, which could lead to shortages and price increases. High temperatures can reduce generation efficiency, transmission and cause line sag. Water Supply: Climate change and reduced summer precipitation will increase the likelihood of periods of water scarcity and droughts, which together with demand increases may lead to interruptions of household water supplies and associated health, social and economic impacts, with impacts anticipated to be greater on vulnerable households. Transport: High temperatures can increase thermal loading on bridges and pavements causing expansion, bleeding and rutting. Information and Communication: High temperatures, as well as rapid fluctuations in temperature and humidity, pose challenges particularly to data centres, which need to be kept cool to operate Education: Children are more vulnerable to heat risks, especially young children and those with special needs. Building design of schools is key determinant of heat risks. Health and wellbeing: These events result in increased hospital emissions for heat related conditions including heat stroke. Small children, the elderly, and other groups including people with chronic diseases, low-income populations, pregnant women, and outdoor workers have higher risk for heat-related illness. Global average temperatures in 2024 were around 1.6C above those of the pre-industrial period, breaking the record of 2023 by just over 0.1C, and means the last 10 years are now the 10 warmest years on record. | Storm: Storms disrupt and damage transport infrastructure and roads may become impassable, making it more difficult for travel to school and work and for Council and other services to be carried out. In the case of extreme storms, schools may close, causing disruption to education. Supply chains for businesses within sectors such as manufacturing may also be disrupted.
Damage to buildings, power networks and flooding caused by heavy precipitation results in people needing to find safer temporary accommodation. This particularly affects the elderly who may be more vulnerable when moving from their immediate networks and potentially becoming isolated. Marginalised, minority communities and low-income households typically live in less well-maintained housing, which is more likely to be susceptible to storm damage. If the repair costs after a storm are unaffordable, housing may be unsafe.
Outdoor workers will be unable to work due to safety concerns, potentially resulting in loss of income and are more likely to be injured from flying debris. Transport - City Region Sustainable Transport Settlement (CRSTS): 
The £4.2bn fund is planned to be a 5-year settlement at regional level, for a series of projects a region wishes to deliver and to 'begin the process of bringing their local transport systems up to the standard of the capitals'.

Regionally, £147m capital has been allocated to NECA (excluding Nexus, Highways maintenance, TCF, block funding and other priorities) for the period 2024/25 to 2026/27. 
SCC continues to work with NECA to review and develop local priority schemes submitted as part of the refresh of the North East Transport Plan. 

As of August 2025, 7 Sunderland projects have been indicatively allocated CRSTF grant to deliver a range of strategic transport and active travel schemes including Silksworth A690 cycle route and SSGA to Ryhope Village cycle route. This equates to a total of £30.4m CRSTS funding for the period up to 2026/27. Progress on scheme designs is underway with business cases in development. All CRSTS1 schemes need to be contractually committed by March 2027, with construction of the first scheme -Ryhope Road strategic cycle route - due to commence in Autumn 2025. Additional CRSTS funding is also being invested in station improvements, bus shelter renewal, active travel schemes and EV infrastructure projects.

-	Destination locations

-	Key community and business locations.

Buildings - Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme - Wave 3c and 4: The Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) funds capital energy efficiency and heat decarbonisation projects within public sector non-domestic buildings including central government departments and arm's length bodies in England. PSDS supports the aim of reducing emissions from public sector buildings by 75% by 2037, as set out in the 2021 Net Zero and Heat and Buildings strategies.

After a successful £2.2m bid to decarbonise 8 municipal buildings through PSDS Wave 1, Sunderland City Council submitted a targeted bid to PSDS Wave 3a seeking £792,500 grant support towards £873,473 total project costs to replace old gas boilers and install low carbon heating systems and fabric measures at 2 community sites in the city - Thorney Close Action and Enterprise Centre, and the Rainbow Family Centre in Washington. Unfortunately, this bid was unsuccessful. 

Phase 3c saw a successful bid of £2,070,782 awarded in March 2024, to retrofit:
•	Museum & Winter Gardens (project cost £540,000)
•	eVolve (project cost £665,000)
•	Leechmere (project cost £720,277)
•	Bunny Hill (project cost £538,977)
Works at EVOLVE are now complete and Bunny Hill and Leechmere are expected to be completed August 2025.

SCC also received a successful bid to PSDS 4 in March 2025, focussing on works to decarbonise Bishopwearmouth Crematorium, replacing gas cremators with electric and removing the gas boiler to allow heat exchange from the cremators to heat the building. The project is in the development phase.
Further public sector decarbonisation measures will be supported through ongoing work delivered by the Strategic Energy Advisor (Jacobs) and Boldyn (further discussed in questions 3.1 and 9.1 respectively), as well as continuing to utilise the significant in-house expertise within the Council via the energy services manager. 

The Council has procured two pieces of work which will support development of its next PSDS applications and ongoing decarbonisation of its operational estate - a Strategic Energy Advisor project (through which Jacobs were appointed) and a multi-year project as part of the city's Smart City Joint Venture with Boldyn.

Buildings - Local Energy Advice Demonstrator (LEAD) Project (NEY Net Zero Hub working with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero): A regional bid was successful in August 2023. The LEAD project is coordinating in-person energy advice across the North East region which includes Durham, Gateshead, Newcastle upon Tyne, North Tyneside, Northumberland, South Tyneside and Sunderland. The project aligns to the One Stop Shop for retrofit advice signposting and/or providing retrofit assessments. The project is piloting the use of QR codes to link to retrofit recommendation plans. The project is also providing retrofit awareness training to local community leaders/charities/service providers to support engagement with harder-to-reach residents.

In Sunderland, this is in addition to existing energy advice services such as EST, CAB, & Green Doctors supported through the ECO4 programme. 

Programme extension agreed until end October 2025 for advice and guidance only. NECA setting up Project Board to establish procurement route for a regional support framework.

Buildings - Ofgem Energy Industry Energy Redress Scheme: Round 8 was announced in June 2024. 

Sunderland City Council have forged a £240,000 citywide partnership with Groundwork North East & Cumbria Sunderland and Citizens Advice Sunderland to deliver an OFGEM/REDRESS-funded and Energy Saving Trust (EST) administered energy and retrofit advice programme to assist 3300 households via home visits, community events and telephone advice calls from February 2025 to March 2027. The project, entitled “Energy Savvy”, is delivered by Green Doctors from Groundwork NE&C who liaise directly with SCC Public Health Team and the citywide GP Alliance (GPA) so partner home-visiting health and social prescribers can refer privately owned and rented households with health conditions made worse by living in cold, mouldy and damp conditions. As part of the project Groundwork NE&C Sunderland also provide energy and retrofit advice training to health and social prescribers to ensure the Make Every Call Count (MECC) initiative is maximised. Nature-Based Solutions - Nature, Towns and Cities: In July 2025, Sunderland received project approval from the National Lottery Heritage Fund with £490,000 funding secured (82% of total approved project cost). 
Project delivery is scheduled to take place from August 2025.
The project over the next 3 years will bring organisations across the city together to better connect residents with local greenspaces, and help communities improve their health and wellbeing by making access to nature easier.
Led by SCC in partnership with Durham Wildlife Trust and the voluntary sector, the project will also be supported by other key partners within the city. Plans include a focus on linking community greenspaces, parks, transport routes and the city's coastline and riverbanks, connecting people and creating a sense of pride in the local environment. The project will bring together organisations citywide to work in partnership to increase understanding of the benefits of the natural environment via volunteering opportunities, outdoor activities, training and nature-based social prescribing.
The project will also support communities to consider and prepare sustainable maintenance improvement plans which will allow communities to secure future investment to ensure natural spaces are able to adapt to the changing climate, as well as support vulnerable residents to live comfortably within their communities as the climate continues to change (creating additional shade for heat stress for example).

Further information can be found here including reference to Sunderland's project.
https://naturetownsandcities.org.uk/
https://naturetownsandcities.org.uk/grants/

project_info: Other: Urban Intervention - Integrative Landscapes of Palmas: The “Integrative Landscapes of Palmas” project aims to implement a Linear Park following the edge of Lake Palmas, planned with a focus on local climatic conditions, taking into account the specificities of flora and fauna, as well as the social customs of the population. Developed with an innovative designer, the project seeks to combine environmental preservation with economic exploitation, so that one makes the other viable. In the design of the park, there is a combination of native trees with a system of cycle paths, boulevards and sidewalks accessible to pedestrians, boat moorings and marina, restaurants and halls for social gatherings and cultural events. There is also the provision for the use of rainwater for the operation of the park, from the sustainable watering of gardens to the cleaning of structures and public equipment. The entire conception of the park project had as one of the main objectives the issue of thermal comfort in Palmas. In this way, it is possible to proposed to soften the local temperature, either through afforestation, as well as the installation of structures that reduce the local climate. The project is part of the action plan of the Sustainable Emerging Cities (ICES) initiative and was made possible through a partnership between the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), the Austrian Ministry of Finance (BMF - Bundesministerium für Finanzen) and the municipality of Palmas, through the Palmas Urban Planning Institute (IPUP). Studies were carried out on the economic viability of the project, which foresees the installation of real estate projects, such as apartments and shops, which would finance its installation. Another issue that would facilitate the viability of the park is the forecast for its implementation in stages over a 25-year horizon, leaving time for financial planning for its installation. It is noteworthy that of the total cost to implement the project, estimated at R$ 203,797,634.00, a significant part, around R$ 170,768,927.00, will have to be return to the municipality through various revenues arising from private investments in the area.

project_info: Public and green spaces - Socio-environmental Qualification in the Córrego Machado Area: Land Regularization and Creation of a Linear Park: The project's scope is to qualify the AVU Córrego Machado and its surroundings, historically marked by low-income occupations and irregular subdivisions, deficits in infrastructure and community equipment, as well as environmental degradation of springs, vegetation and the watercourse itself. Its detailed diagnosis will make it possible to classify portions of the territory, in general, into: (i) priority areas for conservation; (ii) priority areas for environmental recovery; (iii) areas destined for regularization and sustainable urbanization with the implementation of leisure, entertainment, education and cultural activities; and (iv) areas destined for reforestation and the creation of biodiversity corridors. For the delivery horizon, the proposal is divided into two axes that will make it possible to leverage the territory in a sustainable, integrated and inclusive, namely: (1) recovery and environmental qualification of Córrego Machado, including the implementation of a linear park; and (2) resolution of land conflicts, enabling the provision of infrastructure and community equipment. The first axis will be developed through the implementation of an Urban Linear Park along the Córrego Machado, guaranteeing the recovery of its riparian forest, springs and perennial protection through the public use of the equipment and services that will be made available in its coverage area. Public sports, leisure and recreation spaces will be provided, as well as cycle paths, safe and accessible sidewalks and a landscaped path along the banks of the stream. The second axis will address the land tenure situation of the territory, providing for the regularization of informal settlements, in possible cases, as well as the relocation of irregular occupations inserted in Permanent Preservation Areas - APPs, risk areas, springs and other environmentally fragile areas or relevant. Resettlement will be carried out, preferably, to units to be made available in the intervention area itself, avoiding disruption of the local social fabric. Still on this axis, in addition to resolving land conflicts, it is intended to reparcel areas, notably the properties located in Jardim Aureny III. The area planned for re-allotment comprises part of Jardim Aureny III (regularized allotment), precisely where the springs and drainage lines are concentrated, which impact roads and around 22 residential blocks and 08 Municipal Public Areas already implemented. This problem is an impediment to the implementation of infrastructure (rain drainage, asphalt, sewage) in this location. The resolution of land demands will enable the provision of infrastructure for the local population, predominantly characterized by low-income families not served by traditional and sustainable urban drainage systems, road connections and paving, sidewalks, cycle paths, sewerage, public lighting and public transport. Furthermore, it is intended to allocate specific areas to implement local community equipment, especially early childhood and elementary education units, basic health units and those focused on public safety and social assistance. The community facilities planned in the intervention area can be fully integrated into the park, enabling their use for environmental education and sustainable urban development actions, contributing to their full appropriation by the population.

project_info: Transport - Public Transport Fleet Renewal\n: Palmas is part of the TUMI (Transformative Urban Mobility Initiative) E-Bus Mission Cities Network program, the TUMI E-Bus Mission which aims to accelerate the transition to electric buses in cities in developing countries. The initiative is financed by the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), through the German Cooperation for Sustainable Development and is being implemented by Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) GmbH together with partners: C40 Cities, The International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), The Institute for Transportation and Development Policy (ITDP), ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability, International Association of Public Transport (UITP) and World Resource Institute (WRI). The program aims to significantly contribute to the creation of sustainable urban transport systems by supporting 20 cities in their transition for the implementation of electric buses and, by the end of 2022, contribute to strengthening capabilities for the electrification of fleets in 100 other cities. Palmas has been participating, through the Municipal Environmental Foundation and the Municipal Secretariat for Security and Urban Mobility, in technical training aimed at the central objective of the program and in the future following the path of transition from the conventional fleet to that of electric buses.

Mapping territories and their voices for
citizen training, community resilience and
water protection in Santo André: This is an environmental education and education project for risk and disaster reduction that has as its general objective: Promote environmental education and awareness actions contributing to
coping and adapting to climate change and its impacts on water
resources in areas vulnerable to flooding and geological risk in the municipality of Santo
André.

Specific objectives
A. Promote an educational approach for local mobilizing audiences (teachers and
health agents) on climate emergency, water security and
21

disaster risk reduction, with Environmental Education as a transversal and
interdisciplinary theme.
B. Carry out socio-environmental training that integrates social cartography and
ducommunication and encourages community resilience and social participation of
young people and adults residents in areas susceptible to disasters with a focus on
addressing the climate emergency, adaptation, promoting
water security and reducing disaster risks.
C. Implement small planting interventions in a participatory manner as a
climate adaptation strategy in schools participating in the project.
D. Produce and make available communication and environmental education materials on the
climate emergency, water security and disaster risk reduction
for dissemination among social actors relevant to the Project.

E. Disseminate the process, results and lessons learned so that it can be replicated

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Innovation, inclusion and technology for the Intelligent and Circular Management of Solid Waste in Caxias do Sul: The project is structured into three interconnected and complementary axes, which act in an integrated manner to promote innovation, efficiency and inclusion in solid waste management:
Axis 1 - Sandbox Caxias
This is an Experimental Model of Public Policy Management. The tests will take place in delimited spaces (SANDBOX, according to Decree no. 22,746/2023), with investments limited by the Legal Framework for Startups (R$ 1,600,000.00). It is worth noting that only initiatives with the potential to solve public problems will be developed, which suggests that the project itself will not lead to future needs, in addition, the solutions tested in SANDBOX do not generate any contracting obligation on the part of the municipality.
It is intended to select and hire at least 08 (eight) startups to test innovative solutions applicable to the management waste in the municipality. Initiatives may include:
- Diagnosis and mapping of the recycling production chain and its actors, formal and informal (associations, collectors, citizens and the private sector).
- Testing technological solutions for collection, sorting and traceability of waste (such as smart containers, sensors and digital platforms).
- New routes for marketing recyclables with traceability, integration with reverse logistics programs and recycling credits.
- Tools for environmental education and population engagement.
The results of these experiments will provide practical evidence to support the implementation of PMGIRS and improve public policies in the municipality of Caxias do Sul.
Axis 2 - Instrumentalization and Intelligent Execution of PMGIRS
This axis aims to operationalize the municipality's Municipal Plan for Integrated Solid Waste Management (PMGIRS), ensuring its effective execution based on data, technology and integration institutional.
Digital monitoring instruments, performance indicators and management tools will be developed to monitor goals, costs, flows and impacts. Based on the solutions tested in the Sandbox, the municipality will be able to adjust practices, routes and plans, making management more efficient and aligned with the circular economy.
This axis also provides technical support for the regulation and application of complementary policies, such as rules for large generators and incentive mechanisms for composting and reverse logistics.
Axis 3 - Strengthening the Recycling Chain
Provides for the professionalization, regularization and structuring of the 11 associations and 1 cooperative affiliated with the municipality, including:
- Legal and environmental regularization;
- Works and physical adaptations (PPCI, Habite-se, structural improvements);
- Acquisition of equipment and PPE;
- Technical and cooperative management training;
- Specialized consultancies for marketing, traceability and integration into the circular economy.
- Support for the implementation of ecopoints and improved logistics to expand the collection and reuse of materials.
Strengthening sorting organizations is the final link that guarantees the effectiveness of the actions of the other two axes, translating innovation and management into concrete results.
The three axes form an integrated system of innovation, social inclusion and institutional strengthening: the Sandbox generates evidence and solutions applicable to waste management and the strengthening of cooperatives; PMGIRS consolidates and systematizes these solutions; and practical application occurs through strengthening the recycling chain, where innovations and improvements translate into social, economic and environmental impact.

The initiative is structured around three main axes:
Axis 1 - Mesh of Sensors and Infrastructure Monitoring
The proposal includes the implementation of an intelligent network of sensors (IoT) for continuous monitoring of meteorological, geotechnical and atmospheric variables, which will be integrated in the future in real time with the Integrated Operations Center (CIOp) and the Smart City Observatory (DataLAB).
- Automatic meteorological stations with digital rain gauges: initial installation of 12 units, with their location being defined based on other studies, with risk analysis carried out by the SGB. The stations will send data on accumulated rain and intensity to the CIOp, supporting preventive alerts and contingency plans.
- Ground movement sensor (seismograph): implementation of 1 unit to record vibrations and movements, to understand phenomena and minimize landslide risks.
- Electronic inclinometers: installation of 10 units on steep slopes with dense occupation and a history of instability. The equipment will monitor soil microdisplacements and send data on rupture trends, and the geotechnical report for the Galópolis neighborhood indicates the installation of this device for occupied areas with high geological risk.
- Water level and flow sensors: 3 monitoring points in the main urban and peri-urban watercourses (Arroio Dal Bó, Tega), allowing the issuance of early warnings of floods and floods, including for other municipalities nearby. downstream.
- Automatic Mobile Station Air Quality and Meteorology Monitoring: reference equipment for analyzing fine particles (MP2.5, PM10), polluting gases (NO, SO, CO, O₂₂₃) and Greenhouse Gases (CO, CH and NO)₂₄₂, as well as meteorological variables (temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation). The station will allow the modeling of pollutant dispersion and the quantification of urban emissions, together with a network of fixed air quality sensors (minimum of 5 sensors) in areas of high urban density and intense traffic, complementing the mobile station.
Axis 2 - Climate Planning and Risk Management
The second axis comprises the development of technical and strategic instruments complementary to the sensor network:
Municipal Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory (GEE)
It will be prepared based on IPCC methodologies (2006, 2019), integrating data collected by sensors and information from the Resilient Green Model Cities Platform. The inventory will provide the baseline for mitigation targets and the preparation of the Local Climate Action Plan. The inventory will be published and updated biennially, with technical support and external financing.
Municipal Risk Reduction Plan (PMRR)
Prepared in compliance with Law No. plan.
Caxias do Sul Climate Action Plan
Will consolidate the results of the Resilient Green Model Cities platform, the Climate Vulnerability Analysis (SGB, 2024), the GHG Inventory and monitoring systems, among other municipal studies. The plan will establish adaptation, mitigation and carbon neutrality goals, aligned with PNA 2025-2035, PNMC, Plano Clima Nacional and ProClima2050 (RS).
Axis 3 - Environmental Education, Transparency and Data Governance
The implementation of the system will be accompanied by actions of community engagement and participatory governance, including:

Workshops and training with communities in risk areas, schools and universities.

Creation of an online public panel with real-time sensor data.

Integration with the Smart City Observatory (DataLAB), strengthening the culture of open data and social involvement in climate policy.

Creation of an intersectoral technical group involving different Municipal Secretariats involved and Civil Defense, responsible for maintenance and interpretation of the data.

Other: Biodiversity conservation and protection - Asa.Delta: The 'Asa.Delta' project is a citizen science initiative that aims to promote the conservation of biodiversity in Guimarães, with a focus on butterflies and birds (Asa.Delta Project wants to protect birds and butterflies in Guimarães - Lab Paisagem). Aligned with the National Strategy for Nature Conservation and Biodiversity 2030 and the National Environmental Education Strategy (ENEA 2020), the project aims to raise awareness and train the community on the importance of biodiversity, involving both the general public and schools, farmers and private companies.
The Landscape Laboratory (LdP), as a research and environmental education center, coordinates the project, which stands out for integrating citizen science as a biodiversity monitoring tool. Through the mobile application developed within the scope of the project, citizens will be able to record sightings of different species, allowing large data collection scale. The application also includes features such as species identification guides and interactive challenges that encourage active community participation.
Several environmental education actions have been planned for schools, in which students will have the opportunity to learn about local biodiversity and participate in practical activities, such as observing butterflies and birds in the schools' green spaces. One of the central activities involves the conceptualization of butterfly beds with species attractive to different types of pollinating insects, using digital tools such as Minecraft. Subsequently, the students, with the support of LdP, will turn the projects into reality, creating these green spaces in their schools.
The project is also aimed at the agricultural sector, encouraging the creation of floral borders, which will act as habitats for pollinators and birds, in addition to encouraging more sustainable agricultural practices. This collaboration with Farmers aims to increase biodiversity in rural areas, preserving species that play essential roles in agricultural ecosystems.
In the private sector, the 'Biodiverse Companies' initiative challenges companies subscribing to the Climate Pact to adopt measures that favor biodiversity, such as planting native species, reducing artificial lighting to protect nocturnal fauna and implementing infrastructure that prevents bird collisions with buildings. The companies' progress and commitments will be closely monitored, ensuring that the implemented actions have a lasting impact.
In addition to direct interventions in schools and companies, Asa.Delta also promotes awareness-raising actions aimed at the community in general, such as bioblitzes, which are participatory species observation and cataloging events (Laboratório da Paisagem (@labpaisagem) • photos and videos from Instagram; Laboratório da Paisagem (@labpaisagem) • photos and videos from Instagram), and gastronomic events that highlight the relationship between biodiversity and sustainable food. These activities seek to connect citizens with nature in a practical and educational way, providing an engaging experience that promotes the protection of ecosystems.
In the end, the project also includes the creation of a digital butterfly garden, where citizens will be able to access detailed information about the butterflies of Guimarães, their life cycle and ecological importance. This educational tool aims to promote a greater understanding and appreciation of local biodiversity, as happened with previous publications created by the Landscape Laboratory (Publications - Lab Paisagem).

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - e-mission 0 (Mission for Climate Neutrality in Schools): Average global temperatures have increased significantly since the industrial revolution. The European Union aims to achieve climate neutrality by 2050, with net-zero GHG emissions. The transition to a climate-neutral society is an urgent challenge, but also an opportunity to build a better future for everyone. Taking into account that schools play a privileged role in disseminating knowledge, raising awareness and promoting behavioral changes, the ability to promote knowledge about environmental neutrality becomes increasingly important. In this sense, the PEGADAS environmental education program aims to contribute to one of the pillars defined by the 2020 Environmental Education Strategy: Decarbonizing society. The project \'e-mission 0\' (Mission for Climate Neutrality in Schools), promoted by the education for sustainability at the Landscape Laboratory, aims to raise awareness of the urgency of actions to adapt to climate change. To this end, the project consisted of four sessions held in a school environment for each enrolled class. In total, 32 sessions were held, involving 143 students from different grades, distributed across 8 classes. During the 1st session, evidence-based information was presented to explain the effects of GHGs on the climate, highlighting the influence of human activities on these processes. They were tolerant of climate change, such as increasing global temperatures, changes in weather patterns and impacts on various areas, including ecosystems, water resources and human health. In addition, good practices were explored to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with an emphasis on sustainable solutions. Finally, discuss the concept of climate neutrality. In the 2nd session, students had the opportunity to visit the Academy of Ginástica de Guimarães, an exemplary building characterized by high energy efficiency and low CO2 emissions. During a visit, equipped with an exploration sheet, participants explored the resources and technologies used in the building. The importance of science and technology in creating innovative solutions to mitigate climate change was highlighted, as well as the advantages of renewable energy in reducing GHG emissions and transitioning to a more sustainable energy model. In addition, energy efficiency strategies were developed. Participants also had the opportunity to understand how the implementation of these strategies is directly linked to the reduction of GHG emissions. In the third session, students were divided into groups to hold an energy efficiency auditorium at the school. During an activity, equipped with a checklist, the groups analyzed and evaluated different aspects of the school, such as lighting, use of electrical equipment, thermal insulation, waste management, among others. It is worth mentioning that the aspects analyzed are maintained in most buildings, which is why a parallel was drawn between the building followed (school) and other buildings, such as individual residences. In the final session, students were encouraged to debate and brainstorm ideas to fill in a grid identifying concrete measures to improve schools' performance in terms of climate neutrality, creating an action plan. In this sense, the students proposed specific actions in three categories: Repair, Action and Installation. These measures covered, for example, the proposal to eliminate failure of equipment and structures, adopt energy practices, implement renewable energy generation systems, effective waste management programs and protect the school's green spaces. The proposed measures were then created into the final works, which were presented to the community educational in the form of posters and digital presentations. https://www.pegadasguimaraes.pt/atividade/e-missao-0/

project_info: Water management - CApt2: CApt2 is a planning project focused on the priority theme Urban Water Cycle and in addition to the cross-cutting themes Digital Transition, Decarbonization and Equity and Social Inclusion. The project aims to develop a participatory local governance model that integrates the different agents responsible for water management and includes citizens as drivers of transformation towards a circular and participatory model. It also aims to contribute to influencing water management policies and the guidance of municipalities for the transition to a circular economy, promoting the creation of synergies between partners and the training and environmental training of all actors in the Urban Water Cycle, including citizens. The final product of the project is the preparation of an Integrated Action Plan that sets out a list of actions and strategies for the sustainable management of water resources in all dimensions of the Urban Water Cycle, applied to the municipality of Guimarães. To this end, a Local Action Planning Group was created through the mobilization and inclusion of different local actors in Guimarães, including various departments and services of the municipality, water management entities, associations, public and private partners and citizens. The main role of the multidisciplinary group was to define and prepare the actions to be included in the Integrated Action Plan, based on a process of co-production and co-creation over several work sessions. An Integrated Action Plan was developed for the municipality of Guimarães, which includes 9 actions scheduled to be implemented in the areas of Water Efficiency, Water Reuse and Environmental Awareness in order to promote the circularity and sustainability of water resources. This project also had an educational component, where 192 students divided into 7 schools worked together to create and implement water saving action plans to be used in their schools. The objective This project was to raise students' awareness about the importance of water and the lack of this resource. At the end of the project, the students better understood how to be sustainable in relation to water, changed some of their own habits and behaviors and drew up good plans to make their school more sustainable.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - RRRCICLO: RRRCICLO is the name of the circular economy strategy of the municipality of Guimarães. This is a production and consumption model based on the reduction, reuse, recovery and recycling of products, materials and resources. Within this strategy, several initiatives have emerged, such as the EcoPontas & PapaChicletes project, by Laboratório da Paisagem in partnership with the Waste Recovery Center, which is an innovative solution that seeks to reduce the agglomeration of cigarette and chewing gum waste in public spaces as well as protecting water lines. In terms of waste, and integrated into RRRCICLO's strategy, Guimarães develops from textile waste, blankets and cloth bags, as well as hangers and cell phone holders for disposable masks. With the aim of reducing textile waste present in residents' common trash, a strategy was adopted to separate and collect textiles, avoiding their disposal in landfills. toilets. Since implementing this strategy, 20 tons of textiles have been collected, transformed into 140 blankets, shared by establishments in the historic center and municipal kennel, and 800 bags, distributed throughout the municipal market. The CARE project, a reusable cup from Guimarães, developed by the municipal company VITRUS, to face the challenge of the necessary reduction in the use of disposable plastic cups in a deposit system where the user can get their money back by returning the cup, also part of this strategy of eliminating the linear economy. Originating from an application by the Urgezes Parish Council and the Landscape Laboratory to the Environmental Fund \'Act local, Think global\' was defined as the motto of the Urgezes Circular, building environmental education and awareness actions; the transformation of a warehouse for the collection and repair of end-of-life products that until now had fallen into disuse; of practical sessions intended for the repair and enhancement of products; the promotion and enhancement of the sale of used products/equipment and the signage and renovation of stores with history in the Parish, dedicated to extending the useful life of equipment. All actions converge towards the general objective of the new Action Plan for the Circular Economy, and RRRCICLO's local strategy, with the reintegration of products into the market and the reduction of waste, contributing to a truly sustainable economic model. Currently, the best-known aspect of the RRRCICLO strategy is the collection and recovery of organic waste. The organic waste collection plan is already being implemented in Guimarães. By 2028, the entire territory will have selective collection of this waste, which corresponds to around 40% of all waste produced. In addition to this collection, the treatment of waste at source is also encouraged with the allocation of domestic compost bins. In terms of green garden waste, small pruning and cleaning of leaves are also included in RRRCICLO, and citizens can schedule the collection of this waste at Guimarães City Hall, or deposit it directly at one of the municipality's ecocenters. Another area of ​​action of this strategy is water resources with the reuse of water from municipal swimming pools which, although not in the initial conditions, and as a result of the treatment they receive, can be used to wash the streets of the Historic Center of Cuiabá. In this way, this ongoing strategy acts on several aspects, from waste to water resources or equipment recovery, to achieve the transition from the linear economy to a circular economy.

project_info: Other: Tagged emissions domains: transport, electricity consumption in buildings, Land use, waste management, consumption of non-electricity energy for thermal uses in buildings & facilities - District C: a zero-carbon commitment: Guimarães has been strategically defining medium and long-term goals for the promotion of urban regeneration, promotion of heritage and genius loci, textile and creative industries, culture and sense of community, with a strong environmental commitment. The city has a long history of engaging citizens in their actions and motivations, mainly linked to culture and the environment. The EU Cities mission and the CoM are examples of Guimarães' commitment to climate neutrality and its support for this pilot. With this pilot, Guimarães wants to take a step forward, strongly connecting citizens and bringing them to the center of change. The city has identified the main emission areas and intends to begin the transition, addressing them in a intersectoral and systemic. Thus, and based on the concepts of climate, culture and community in its governance structure, Guimarães will use District C (a project of discursive reinterpretation of the city, implementing in an experimental social laboratory a model of territorial development based on culture, knowledge and creativity) [8] as a testbed for a set of measures within the scope of a zero carbon commitment. The pilot aims for an integrated approach across the domains of energy, mobility, waste and land use emissions, leveraging behavioral change, social innovation, culture, policy and regulation, green technology, sustainable finance and new business models. The pillar of the pilot is a Citizen Pact in search of neutrality and co-creation strategies, enabling action in all sectors. Within mobility, the city's main emitting sector, non-fossil vehicles and private vehicles will be discouraged, public transport promoted and public space improved. Buildings are responsible for ~36% of CO2 emissions. Energy efficiency and local renewable energy production will be promoted through regulation and policy updates, one-stop shop implementation, access to innovative energy efficiency financial schemes, facilitation of photovoltaic installation and energy renovation in fostered historic buildings. Waste and land use go hand in hand in this pilot, promoting circular economy strategies to value and divert waste, private urban gardens and a green belt as a means of capturing CO2, improving biodiversity and eradicating bio-waste. All actions will involve strong involvement of citizens, local actors and interested parties, bold communication and dissemination activities, without neglecting the importance of financing the actions.

project_info: Other: Citizen Engagement and Governance - Eco Parliament: This activity, divided into several phases, stimulates the democratic and critical spirit of young students in the first, second and third cycle of studies, in the construction of a better school and community for all, with the creation and implementation of projects that respond to the Sustainable Development Goals, established by the United Nations General Assembly, ““opening a solid path for active and responsible citizenship”” as stated by the President of the Portuguese Republic, Professor Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa in his closing speech of the Eco Parliament in 2022. In the 2022/23 edition, we had the participation of eight school groups, with students from the fourth year of schooling to the ninth year, focused on the development of various projects, with emphasis on the treatment of textile waste, promotion of biodiversity, sustainable consumption of energy and water, among others, contributing in various ways to the search for neutrality This project takes on an even greater dimension because it is not just limited to participating students, they extend the work to all students in their schools, local political bodies that help carry out the actions, as well as local companies or associations that, from a governance perspective, involve the entire community. The work carried out disseminates a good practice that experiences, through debate, sustainable development policies with the main agents of environmental change: the young community. The beginning of this project comes with the training of students in two non-formal education sessions. The first is carried out by the United Nations University team at the Operating Unit on Policy-Driven Electronic Governance located in Guimarães, a research center that connects research and public policies in the search for innovation with a focus on transversal sustainable development and active citizenship. The second session, and technical support throughout the project, is under the responsibility of the Landscape Laboratory. The evaluation methodology consists of a discussion between students from different education cycles, from various groups of schools who present, in a simulated parliament, the solutions they have identified for the environmental problems of their own school or municipality, while at the same time seeking to involve their community. This presentation and defense of young people's projects is carried out by them before political power and experts from different sectors, such as universities, private companies and researchers, among others. At an individual level, students find in this project a way to increase discursive skills, the synthesis of knowledge acquired in a school context, the organization of scientific information and the presentation of ideas and solutions in teamwork to identified environmental challenges, which constitutes an added value for the participants. Greentour addresses several innovation actions framed in a transregional cluster model that include:1. methodologies and actions to promote the circular economy in the tourism sector on a transregional scale not previously discussed;2. scientific and methodological innovation with an eco-label to assess environmental impacts from a life cycle perspective caused by tourist activity in a destination, in addition to economic and social variables;3. promote inter-regional cooperation in the SUDOE space between institutions and policy makers, considering the tourism sector's validation of the proposed tools and strategies. It is intended to move towards a new environmental, economic and social model that simultaneously informs the consumer and promotes their commitment to the environment in which the tourist activity takes place. The study of the environmental performance of the tourism sector aims to contribute to environmental awareness and the promotion of sustainable tourism, by reducing the ecological footprint of tourist destinations. The main objective of the environmental tool was to publicize and promote the assessment of environmental performance among tourist establishments (accommodation, restaurants and tourist activity companies). In Guimarães, around 30 tourist establishments became associated partners of the project and completed the online data collection form, with information on consumption of water, energy, maintenance and cleaning products, food and beverages. In the area of ​​environmental awareness, a Cycle of Seminars on Environmental Management in Tourism was programmed and developed at the Landscape Laboratory, aimed at tourist accommodation, restaurants and tourist activity companies, which aimed to train and encourage the adoption of good practices by tourism agents, in order to make their business more sustainable and circular. Also within the scope of the project, a Green Map was produced, which brings together a set of good practices in the areas of nature and biodiversity, green areas and leisure parks, ecological trails, water resources, sustainable mobility, circular economy initiatives, but also marks all trees of public interest, experiences to explore wine tourism, among other activities that you can do in nature. Therefore, for MEASURE 1, the following actions were designed: Action 1.1 - \'Characterization and identification of waste\'In this action, non-recyclable waste from the production circuit of Guimarães and a recovery and/or recycling strategy was outlined through the creation of synergies with research institutions and the local academic environment. Action 1.2 - \'Waste Valorization - Development and Production of the cultivation kit\' In this action, the identified and categorized waste served as a reference for the development of kits for pedagogical use in environmental education actions, mainly aimed at raising awareness about the reuse of resources and recycling of materials, encouraging reflection and the construction of more sustainable communities.Regarding MEASURE 2 - \'\'EDUCATE, RAISE AWARENESS AND EMPOWER\' the following actions were designed: Action 2.1 - \'Development of environmental education actions in the school community\'Environmental education sessions were organized for the school community. project_info: Other: Monitoring the environmental sustainability of sports clubs - Desporto Carbono Zero: Guimarães Desporto Carbono Zero is a pioneering project in Guimarães and at national level.
