project_info: Other: Biodiversity - SEM Invasoras: The “SEM Invasoras” project (i.e., Invasive-Free Project) in Guimarães is an initiative of the Municipality of Guimarães that aims to raise awareness, educate and monitor invasive species in the region. The project arises as part of the municipality's efforts for sustainable development and its expertise in the area of ​​invasive alien species. The main objective of “SEM Invasoras” is to eradicate and control the invasive species Pennisetum villosum, recently introduced in Guimarães, in all green areas where it was detected. These areas are located near densely populated areas, making the removal of P. villosum urgent due to the potential health problems it can cause. Additionally, the project aims to recover these areas through the promotion of native biodiversity, leisure and recreational activities, as well as the health and well-being of citizens. Another invasive species of concern in Guimarães is Fallopia japonica, observed for the first time in 2016 in Serra da Penha, an important natural area in the region. The project also aims to control this invasive species, which can cause structural damage and has high control costs. SEM Invasoras seeks to test and implement innovative control and eradication measures, using physical/mechanical methods instead of chemical methods. It aims to fill the gap in knowledge about the most effective control and eradication techniques, using biodegradable materials that, if successful, can be applied to other locations and invasive species. The project is innovative in the municipal context and can serve as an example of good practices in the management and control of invasive species. It involves a multidisciplinary team made up of biologists, architects and engineers from Guimarães City Council and the Landscape Laboratory. Furthermore, it includes a detailed implementation plan divided into three main actions: control and eradication, monitoring and georeferencing and awareness and education. SEM Invasoras contributes to increasing the natural capital of Guimarães, promotes the conservation of biodiversity, educates the population about invasive species and their ecological impacts and recovers intervened habitats through the planting of native species. It also demonstrates the commitment to continuing control and eradication actions in the municipality. The environmental benefits generated by the project include the conservation of species, improvement of ecosystem services and cultural benefits. The project is aligned with national and European nature and biodiversity conservation objectives. Furthermore, it is intended that the results of the project will be widely disseminated and used by other entities and municipalities interested in the issue of invasive species.Project links: Project Webpage https://labpaisagem.pt/projetos/sem-invasoras/Workshop \'\'Prevention and Control of Invasive Alien Species\'\' open to the community.https://labpaisagem.pt/noticia/duas-dezenas-de-pessoas-ajudaram-a-eliminar-invasoras-na-uf-briteiros-santo-estevao-e-domim/Awareness video raising awareness about the problems associated with the occurrence of invasive exotic species, specifically emphasizing the importance of disseminating the prohibition of their use as ornamental species and the significance of replacing them with other species that have no environmental impact.https://labpaisagem.pt/noticia/sem-invasoras-lanca-video-para-sensibilizar-populacao/

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Circular Ecosystems: Circular Ecosystems is a European project whose main objective is to develop circular economy strategies and action plans to consolidate territorial ecosystems capable of developing systemic solutions that contribute to minimizing the use of resources and accelerating the transition to zero waste, eliminating pollution problems caused by waste.

The development of joint governance models in the circular economy will allow the establishment of common strategies between Spain and Portugal that help to conserve public services ecosystems in the transboundary space, through the efficient use of endogenous resources and minimizing the impact of economic activity on ecosystems, thus avoiding the deterioration of biodiversity.

To this end, an Action Plan for the Circular and Sustainable Economy is established for each of the territories that are part of the project, which will serve as a conceptual framework for the transition to the circular economy. This Action Plan must support the proposals in each territory and will be supported by the review of municipal and regional regulations that may affect the circular economy.

Actions will be developed to be implemented in the form of easily replicable micro-pilot projects that will serve as an impetus for the global Systemic Solution, and in the case of Guimarães the focus will be on the circularity of textile waste. The strategy for the Circular Economy of Guimarães will also be developed and a Guide for Circular Ecological Public Procurement will be developed.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Let's Go Circular: The 'Let's Go Circular' project's main objective is to promote the importance of circularity as a crucial contribution to achieving climate neutrality.

As part of the project, Integrated Action Plans for the Circular Economy in urban areas will be developed. In addition to Guimarães, other cities such as Munich (Germany), which leads the network, Lisbon (Portugal), Malmö (Sweden), Cluj (Romania), Corfu (Greece), Granada (Spain), Riga (Latvia), Oulu (Finland) and Tirana (Albania) are also part of the consortium.

To execute this initiative, the consortium will have a total budget of €849,730.00, where project partners will work together, sharing knowledge and experiences, to create innovative solutions that promote the circular economy in their respective cities.

The Circular Economy is a concept that aims to break with the traditional model of linear production, in which it extracts, produces, uses and discards resources, generating a large environmental impact. In contrast, the circular economy seeks to promote the reuse, recycling and regeneration of materials, reducing waste and minimizing negative effects on the environment.

By participating in the 'Let's Go Circular' project, the Municipality of Guimarães assumes an important role in developing strategies and concrete actions to drive the transition to a circular economy in the region.

The project is scheduled for completion in December 2025. During this period, it is expected that participating cities actively collaborate, exchanging good practices and implementing effective measures to promote the circular economy in their communities.

project_info: Other: air quality - Network of environmental sensors to monitor air quality in Águeda - monitoring and monitoring: The Municipality installed a network of sensors to measure air quality throughout the municipality, covering areas with rural characteristics, urban areas, areas where there is greater road flow and in the various industrial areas. This network of environmental sensors aims to monitor air quality throughout the municipality's area and provide information to the population about air quality, as well as issuing alerts when atmospheric pollution levels occur that exceed the legal limits imposed and that could cause some health problems for citizens. In 2017, the installation of stations to measure air quality began, constituting a municipal network for evaluating various parameters related to this matter. The implementation of the sensor network was completed in 2018, in a total of eight installed and functional locations, as listed below: EB1 of Aguada de Cima, EB Fernando Caldeira, Largo 1º de Maio, Casarão Business Park, EB1 of Macinhata do Vouga, Escola Secundária Marques de Castilho, Randam Motocross Track, Belazaima do Chão Parish Council. This network of stations will have a diversity of sensors in each of the locations. meteorological information, sound pressure and environmental pollutants, to achieve a more comprehensive view of air quality in the municipality. Air quality monitoring sensors enable the collection of data relating to various atmospheric pollutants, continuous monitoring of Suspended Particles (PM2. 5) and (PM10), Carbon Monoxide (CO), Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2), Sulfur Dioxide (SO2), Ozone (O3). allow you to collect data related to parameters such as Air Temperature, Relative Humidity, Wind Speed and Direction, Precipitation, Ultraviolet Radiation (UV) and atmospheric pressure. The noise monitoring sensors are made up of class 1 sound level meters, and allow ambient noise levels to be monitored continuously. These sensors will be located in an urban environment, in mixed and sensitive areas, one of them close to the Agitagueda festival venue and close to roads with a high intensity of car traffic. The stations and sensors are periodically calibrated by the company responsible for their maintenance. This network also makes it possible to provide information, via a Web platform, on the parameters that are monitored and to issue warnings when the programmed parameters reach the defined values ​​to send a warning email. project_info: Water management - Rehabilitation and Enhancement Project of Ribeira da Aguieira and Rio Marnel and Ecogaleria de Agueda (Ribeira do Ameal) - Águeda: The intervention area is located along the section of Ribeira da Aguieira next to Parque da Boiça until the mouth at the confluence with the river Marnel and the river Marnel from Parque da Garganta to the confluence with Ribeira da Aguieira, located in the parish of Valongo do Vouga, municipality of Águeda, making up a total length of approximately 5 km. The Ameal river constitutes a structuring element of the natural morphology and landscape of the city of Águeda, with different naturalized areas and opportunities for recreation and production for the population, influencing urban expansion, simultaneously as a pole of urban attractiveness and an area of strong exposure to the risk of flooding, when extreme phenomena occur, particularly due to the proximity to the river Águeda. The rehabilitation of the present habitats will be carried out simultaneously in these two projects that, although geographically distant, are complementary. Given this context, the project for the recovery and protection of riparian galleries aims, in general, to contribute to the pursuit of a set of objectives at different levels - environmental, hydraulic and socioeconomic - that converge in river rehabilitation processes and which aim to: ⎯ Comply with community and national legislation on cleaning and valorization of water lines (WFD and Water Law), which states that all interventions must be subject to a planning process and defined objectives and measures. that aim to obtain the good status or good ecological potential of water bodies; ⎯ Recover the riverside gallery and the consequent functionality of the riverside natural systems, promoting connectivity with the surrounding areas; ⎯ Promote landscape enhancement and biodiversity of the water environment, together with growing connectivity between natural faunal and floristic communities of riverside corridors; ⎯ Promote riverine, riparian and marshy habitats, creating the necessary conditions for the use of these spaces (and the main bed) by native fauna, particularly for the target species of this project;⎯ Environmental enhancement of plots adjacent to watercourses;⎯ Encourage people to come into contact with nature,⎯ Increase the attractiveness of river spaces, creating and revitalizing places with deep meaning and interest for populations locals and visitors; ⎯ Contribute to the improvement of water lines; ⎯ Promote the safety of people, goods and services operating near waterways;⎯ Waterfronts constitute an opportunity for territorial and environmental rehabilitation, through the promotion of ecosystems and the increase in biodiversity and surrounding spaces. The renaturalization of the riverside landscape and the creation of habitat conditions for flora and fauna make it possible to improve the capacity of hydrological and ecological resilience of the river system and, in the long term, increase the quality of life of the local population, through the renewed public use of these spaces, and increase community involvement as an entity monitoring problems present in the water lines and alerting the competent authorities. The concept of creating a model of the landscape of the river system affected by the watercourse and municipality seems crucial to understanding the complementarity between the continuous and discontinuous perspectives of seeing the hydroecosystem, recreating a model approaching, in a confined space, the Potential Riparian Vegetation (VRP) of Águeda, which corresponds to the climax stage of a series of edapho-hygrophilous riparian vegetation. Concept of utility for planning and territorial ordering, indicates the maximum theoretical evolution of vegetation in a given location and for a given period of time, if there were no human influence on it, whether for the population in general, to the extent which allows them to view and interact with native forests representing the municipality's potential natural vegetation.

project_info: Water management - ECOPATEIRA DE FERMENTELOS - REHABILITATION AND ENHANCEMENT OF MARGIN IN THE PARISH OF FERMENTELOS, ÁGUEDA: Pateira de Fermentelos, considered the largest natural lagoon in the Iberian Peninsula, currently occupies an area of ​​variable surface and depth that can reach 5 km2. It extends across the municipality of Águeda, Aveiro and Oliveira do Bairro. Given its size and importance at an ecological and environmental level, it constitutes a structuring element of the natural morphology and landscape, forming part of the Ria de Aveiro Special Protection Zone (PTZPE0004) and, as such, included in the Natura 2000 Network. It is also classified as SIC and ZEC Ria de Aveiro since 2014 (PTCON0061) and as a Ramsar 2089 site. Given this context, the intervention project aims, in general, to contribute to the pursuit of a set of objectives at different levels - environmental, hydraulic and socioeconomic - that converge in river rehabilitation and valorization processes and that aim to: Provide compliance with community and national legislation on cleaning and valorization of watercourses and wetlands (WFD and Water Law), which states that all interventions must be subject to a planning process and defined objectives and measures aimed at obtaining the good status or good ecological potential of water bodies; Recover the riverside gallery and the consequent functionality of riverside natural systems, promoting connectivity with surrounding areas; Encourage landscape enhancement and biodiversity of the water environment, through water and climate regulation, water purification, counteracting the greenhouse effect and feeding underground natural reservoirs; Promote wetland habitats, in particular, the natural habitats of the Natura 2000 Network - 91E0pt1 - Riparian Amial; 91E0pt3 - Amial Paludoso; and, 3150 - Natural eutrophic lagoons with Magnopotamion or Hydrocharition vegetation, creating the necessary conditions for feeding habitats refuge and reproduction, notably for the target species of this project: Pointed-snouted Frog (Discoglossus galganoi), Water Lizard (Lacerta schreiberi), Red Heron (Ardea purpurea) and Little Bittern (Ixobrychus minutus). Environmental enhancement of plots adjacent to the bank, implementing a contiguous multifunctional space - ecological, social and landscape - through the formalization of the leisure area; Rehabilitation of a marginal pedestrian trail on the edge of the intervention area, under analysis; Encouraging people to get in touch with nature, acting on the premise that interaction with nature has proven results in improving people's health status, both physical and emotional; Increasing the attractiveness of river spaces, creating and revitalizing places with deep meaning and interest for local populations and visitors;Promote the safety of people, goods and services operating close to the intervention area.Waterfronts thus constitute a opportunity for territorial and environmental rehabilitation, through the implementation of roads dedicated to smooth mobility, as well as the promotion of ecosystems and the increase in biodiversity and the valorization and promotion of surrounding spaces. The intervention proposal essentially consists of applying soil stabilization measures and rehabilitation of the riverside gallery and improving existing paths, through the formalization of a pedestrian trail, along the area marginal to Pateira de Fermentelos, where the formalization of a living laboratory and some spaces for recreation (e.g. fishing and bathing) and contemplation (natural amphitheater) is expected. The creation of the EcoPateira de Fermentelos concept appears as an opportunity to reconcile the renaturalization of the wetland with the creation of a place of strong collective identity and the promotion of environmental education.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Lighting Living LAB(LLL): Lighting Living Lab (LLL) - (Lighting Living Lab (lighting-living-lab.pt). It was with this objective that the Municipality of Águeda framed the territory's development model in sustainability commitments in recent years and, in particular, a line leading to competitiveness, innovation and growth, investment in renewable energy and promotion of integrated energy efficiency. One of the Municipality's main initiatives in this matter resided in the development of the Lighting Living Lab Association (LLL), which is made up of several public and private entities, such as the municipality of Aveiro, in addition to the University of Aveiro and several Águeda companies. In recent years, intensive policies and projects have been developed in the field of eco-energy, and lighting (public and private) in areas where we have developed more interventions, in order to promote innovation and product development, and encourage new technologies and applications in lighting. This effort resulted in a series of projects and actions implemented on the ground with a high degree of innovation and demonstrating the ability to create lighting solutions, including public ones, that are competitive in national and international markets, providing greater economic sustainability to producers and greater energy sustainability to the territories where they are installed. Some of these solutions developed/installed: Replacement of several streets and avenues of conventional lamps with LED lamps, installed and programmed to turn on based on a computer application that manages the numinous intensity and the periods in which they are at full output or less. Replacement of existing lamps with lamps (or LEDs) of better quality and greater durability; Replacement of damaged lamps with new ones with more efficient ballasts and progressive replacement of lamps with LEDs; SIGLuzEE Development Project - a software application to support the management of the City Council's public lighting infrastructure; Preparation of an Águeda Lighting Master Plan abroad; Lighting design for IPSS; etc. The Lighting Living Lab project's mission is to promote innovation and the development of research into new technologies and applications in the area of lighting, focusing on the concepts of intelligent lighting and eco-sustainable lighting, with the aim of creating new services, systems, products and business opportunities for its members. The Lighting Living Lab aims to establish itself as an experimentation platform where the key idea is to think outside the box, approaching challenges from different perspectives and involving different areas of knowledge to solve them. via website: https://www.lighting-living-lab.pt/.

project_info: Other: Adaptation to climate change: territorial resilience - Restoration and preservation of wetland ecosystems: implementation of walkways and rehabilitation of habitats: The promotion of natural habitats as a way of mitigating the effects of climate change in wetlands is an excellent practice that has been implemented in the municipality, through direct and indirect intervention from the city hall. Therefore, and in this context, the removal of AIS from aquatic flora is a program that has been developed in the municipality for over 15 years (removal of tons of water hyacinth (Pontederia crassipes) and pine weed (Myriophyllum aquaticum) in the Pateira de Fermentelos lagoon and watercourses affected by these species. More recently, intervention was initiated to restore riparian habitats with the removal of terrestrial AIS (e.g. Acacia ssp., Ailanthus altissima, Robinia pseudoacacia, Arundo donax, among others), and reforestation using native species. In this sense, and to allow the visitation of humid areas by the countless visitors and tourists who annually visit the banks of rivers and the lagoon, the installation of walkways (built in material suitable for the location, with landscape integration) is planned. This project aims to allow the creation of a circular and inclusive route around the Pateira de Fermentelos Lagoon on foot or by bicycle, adapted for use by people in wheelchairs. This project is partially financed, however its execution would benefit in terms of speed of implementation if there were extra-municipal funds to complement that made available by the municipality. It is worth noting that it has already been partially implemented, and that a section already has financing and is in the process of being implemented. The entire structure costs around €2,000,000.00. The execution of a part of this more comprehensive project is currently being carried out, with a cost of around 200,000 euros, with financing co-funded by the PDR2020 program.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Rehabilitation of water lines in Águeda: The broad scope of river rehabilitation in the municipality of Águeda has as its main objective to create conditions to encourage the rapprochement of the population with rivers and streams, through the improvement of existing pedestrian trails and promoting greater contact with nature and appreciation of natural heritage. In this context, these projects are part of various conservation and rehabilitation measures for the river network and riverside areas, provided for in the Water Law (Law no. It will be necessary to act in order to promote the stabilization of points of river erosion, carry out the cutting and cleaning of vegetation on the bed and banks necessary, contain exotic and invasive vegetation, removal of debris and trees from the bed, ecological valorization of the river corridor and improvement of pedestrian trails throughout the intervention areas under study. The municipality of Águeda has more than 1,500km of water lines (temporary and permanent). Rivers and streams constitute a structuring element of the natural morphology and landscape of the municipality of Águeda, with different naturalized areas and opportunities for recreation and production for the population, influencing urban expansion, simultaneously as a pole of urban attractiveness and an area of strong exposure to the risk of floods, when extreme phenomena occur, particularly due to proximity to the Águeda river. Given this context, projects for the rehabilitation, valorization and protection of riparian galleries aim, in general, to contribute to the pursuit of a set of objectives at different levels - environmental, hydraulic and socioeconomic - that converge in river rehabilitation processes and which aim to:⎯ Comply with community and national legislation on cleaning and valorization of water lines (DQA and Water Law)⎯ Recover the riverside gallery and the consequent functionality of riverside natural systems, promoting connectivity with the surrounding areas⎯ Promote landscape enhancement and biodiversity of the water environment, along with growing connectivity between natural faunal and floristic communities in the corridors riverside habitats⎯ Promote riverine habitats, riparian and marshland habitats, creating the necessary conditions for the use of these spaces (and the main bed) by native fauna, particularly for the species targeted by this project: orange-bellied newt (Lissitriton boscaii), otter (Lutra lutra) and bay cow (Lucanus cervus), ash bluebird (Laeosopis roboris); Common Verdemã (Cobitis paludica)⎯ Environmental valorization of plots adjacent to stretches of waterline⎯ Rehabilitation of pre-existing pedestrian trails and agricultural paths, bordering the sections of watercourses⎯ Encourage people to come into contact with nature, acting on the premise that interaction with nature has proven results in improving people's health status, both physical and emotional⎯ Increase the attractiveness of river spaces, creating and revitalizing places with deep meaning and interest for local populations and visitors⎯ Contribute to the improvement of watercourses through the promotion of water activities social entrepreneurship⎯ Promote the safety of people, goods and services operating next to watercourses⎯ Waterfronts thus constitute an opportunity for territorial and environmental rehabilitation, through the promotion of ecosystems and the increase in biodiversity and the valorization and promotion of surrounding spaces. project_info: Water management - Improvement of water resources: removal of species of aquatic invasive exotic flora (AIS).: The promotion of natural habitats as a way of mitigating the effects of climate change in humid areas is an excellent practice that has been implemented in the municipality, through the direct and indirect intervention of the city hall. Therefore, and in this context, the removal of ISS from aquatic flora is a program that has been developed in the municipality for over 15 years (removal of tons of water hyacinth (Eicchornia crassipes) and pine weed (Myriophyllum aquaticum) in the Pateira de Fermentelos lagoon and waterways affected by these species. The acquisition in 2006 of a vessel suitable for carrying out this function improved the semi-lentic ecosystem of the Pateira de Fermentelos lagoon, by removing tons of plant biomass from invasive allochthonous species. Operation is possible by a specialized employee. The daily cost of an operator is around €95.00, the cost of operating the harvester is around €100.00, values ​​used when the machinery is loaned for use to other entities that request it, which must be maneuvered by the specialized operator, thus collaborating with the improvement of aquatic habitats in various parts of the country. Operating the harvester therefore costs around R$70,000.00 annually. In addition to the operation of the harvester, invasive control must include a manual removal component in places where the vessel cannot reach. The acquisition of other equipment to facilitate removal operations is also necessary (e.g. containment barriers). The machine also occasionally requires more intense maintenance operations to extend the useful life of the equipment.

Urban flooding: Flooding in Braga represents a significant risk for the entire population, but has a particularly severe impact on the most vulnerable communities, such as low-income families and people with disabilities. These groups often reside in flood-prone areas where housing conditions are inadequate. During flood events, these populations may face loss of material assets, displacement and limited access to essential services such as health and education.

Furthermore, floods can worsen public health problems, as contaminated water can cause water-borne diseases. Psychological stress resulting from the loss of homes and family environments is another critical impact, which can affect people's mental health and well-being. The lack of financial resources makes recovery difficult, as many of these families do not have insurance to cover the damage.

For the elderly and people with reduced mobility, floods pose an additional risk. Evacuation can be complicated, and access to safe shelter can be limited, increasing your vulnerability during and after flood events. Braga's Climate Action Plan prioritizes the creation of response strategies that consider these specific needs, such as improving drainage infrastructure in vulnerable areas and implementing early warning systems to inform about imminent floods. | Mass movement: Tilt movements, such as landslides, significantly affect communities that inhabit mountainous areas or slopes, many of which are inhabited by low-income populations. These families often live in precarious conditions, with limited access to information about geological hazards, making them more susceptible to losing their homes and livelihoods due to landslides.

Impacts include the destruction of homes, which can lead to forced displacement, in addition to risks to personal safety, as landslides can occur suddenly and without warning. For children, this can result in disruptions to education as schools can be damaged or destroyed. The psychological consequences are also significant, as the trauma associated with landslide events can impact the emotional well-being of affected families.

The most vulnerable communities also face challenges recovering after such events, as a lack of financial resources and government support can make it difficult to rebuild homes and regain stability. Braga's Climate Action Plan includes awareness measures about geological risks and mitigation strategies, such as the rehabilitation of slopes and the implementation of containment infrastructure. | Extreme heat: Heat waves have a particular impact on the elderly, who are more susceptible to heat-related illnesses. The highs Temperatures can lead to dehydration, exhaustion and even serious conditions such as heat stroke. For this population, access to health services is critical, and they often face barriers that make it difficult to seek care during periods of extreme heat.

Additionally, many older adults live alone, which increases vulnerability as they may not have immediate support to help them deal with the effects of heat. The lack of air conditioning in their homes can further worsen the situation, leading to an indoor environment that offers no relief from high temperatures. Loneliness and social isolation, common among older people, can also be exacerbated during heat waves, as outdoor activities become less safe.

Economic impacts are equally relevant, as healthcare costs increase in medical emergency situations. Braga's Climate Action Plan prioritizes actions that aim to protect the elderly during heat waves, such as creation of social support programs that guarantee regular visits to these populations and the installation of refrigeration areas in accessible locations. | Extreme wind: Extreme phenomena, such as strong winds and storms, can cause significant damage to the entire population of Braga, but the most vulnerable communities, including those in social housing or with inadequate housing structures, are the most affected. During severe weather events, these populations are more likely to lose their homes and face difficulties accessing safe shelters.
Additionally, disruption to essential services such as electricity, water and emergency services can have serious consequences, especially for elderly and disabled people who rely on medical devices and support for their daily needs. The psychological stress and trauma generated by the loss of property and the destruction of the family environment can affect the mental health of vulnerable populations, leading to an increase in cases of anxiety and depression.
Disaster recovery is also more challenging for these communities, as they often lack financial resources and access to adequate government assistance. The Braga Climate Action Plan includes preparedness and response measures that consider the specific needs of these populations, such as the creation of reception centers and early warning systems that inform about the approach of extreme weather phenomena.

Water scarcity can lead to reduced harvests, affecting food security and the local economy. Low-income families already struggling may be forced to cut back on essential spending, such as food and healthcare, to cope. loss of income.
Drinking water becomes a scarce good, increasing competition for water resources and raising prices. This can force households to turn to untreated water sources, leading to public health problems and waterborne illnesses. For children and the elderly, the effects of droughts can be even more severe, with dehydration and malnutrition becoming greater concerns.
In addition, forced migration can occur in search of better living conditions, destabilizing communities and families. Braga's Climate Action Plan includes strategies for sustainable water management and the promotion of resilient agricultural practices, ensuring that vulnerable populations have access to resources and support during periods of drought.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Artificial Intelligence Platform for Municipal Energy Optimization: The Municipality of Braga intends to develop an AI platform that monitors and optimizes the energy consumption of municipal buildings and the public network in real time. Using IoT (Internet of Things) sensors, the platform collects data on energy consumption, weather patterns, and building occupancy, allowing automatic adjustments in the use of heating, ventilation, air conditioning, lighting and other energy systems.

project_info: Water management - Updating the rainwater register and integrating the urban water cycle: Supplying a growing municipal population with quality water, alongside growing urbanization, is one of the challenges facing the Municipality of Braga. These growing needs for quality water for different purposes - agricultural, industrial and urban consumption - occur in a scenario of uncertainty dominated by climate change, which, by causing changes in precipitation patterns, could make the desired water supply even more difficult. In this context, we are witnessing a paradigm shift regarding water management in urban areas, promoting the transition from a model based on supply management to a new model based on demand management. In this new model, the fundamental commitment is to efficiency in the use of water, but at the same time with the promotion of alternative sources of water, such as waste reuse and the use of rainwater, for purposes compatible with its quality, and in order to promote the sustainability of the Urban Water Cycle. In this project, the Municipality of Braga intends to use a model capable of describing the Urban Water Cycle in a systemic, holistic way, considering the precipitation-runoff and water supply-wastewater (and rainwater) sanitation sub-systems, so that for a specific urban river basin, scenarios aimed at promoting the use of alternative water sources, such as the use of rainwater, and to evaluate its significance in terms of sustainability indicators (such as reduction of fresh water, reduction of wastewater production and reduction of surface runoff of rainwater). In the first phase, the Municipality of Braga needs to prepare the infrastructure register by surveying all the devices that complete the water supply and wastewater systems. With the systematized information it will be It is possible to build a tool to support effective and sustainable decision-making, and the operationalization of maintenance, operation and network expansion tasks. Finally, it is an indispensable basis for defining strategies for the urban water cycle, which is the main concern of network managers.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Rising average temperatures and an increased incidence of extreme heat events could impact public health in the City by increasing the risk of heat illness and heat stroke, particularly among vulnerable populations like seniors, low-income and unhoused residents, and those with underlying health conditions. The increased frequency of warm nights does not allow buildings to cool down overnight, worsening the City's urban heat island effect, and exposing people to longer durations of dangerous heat levels which will increase the risk of mortality. A warming climate could also affect air quality in the City and County as hotter temperatures increase the formation of ground-level ozone, a respiratory irritant that is a component of smog. Children, pregnant women, outdoor workers, unhoused residents, older residents or those with underlying respiratory health conditions like asthma (a condition that disproportionately affects BIPOC communities) are particularly vulnerable to such air pollution. Hotter and longer extreme heat events will affect the health and safety of outdoor workers, even among workers who are acclimatized to such temperatures. This could reduce productivity and prompt workplace changes since State regulation requires employers to provide shade/cooling to employees when outdoor temperatures exceed 80°F; more high-heat days would necessitate more frequent provision of shade/cooling. Temperature changes will impact energy usage in the City. With rising average temperatures and more frequent, longer heat waves will come increased demand for air conditioning. This demand will also stretch further into the evening and nighttime due to increased overnight lows. This additional sustained electricity demand for cooling, especially in late afternoon and early evening when solar production falls, can stress the grid and lead to brownouts. Low-income residents and residents who are cost-burdened by rent will be disproportionately affected by higher utility bills from increased use and possibly increased electricity rates caused by the necessary grid upgrades. Vulnerable populations that have a greater reliance on consistent power due to their health conditions will be more severely impacted by power outages. Many vulnerable and low-income residents may not have access to air conditioning. In these cases, they are more directly impacted by the increased temperatures and may require access public transit to public cooling centers. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): The increased probability of wildfire in the City and the projected increase in area burned within the City could result in significant impacts to ecology in open space, the destruction of property, and loss of life. The City is surrounded by open space that is prone to wildfire. The US Department of Agriculture's Forest Service shows that populated areas in the City are, on average, more likely to experience wildfires than 33% of other communities in the County. Populated areas in Simi Valley, Saticoy, Santa Paula, Moorpark, Fillmore, Ojai, and Piru showed higher average wildfire likelihood. Climate change-related increases in wildfire probability and burn area would have clear impacts on the safety of residents in the event of wildfire and have already led to increased fire insurance rates. Areas on the periphery and outer edges of the City generally have a higher probability of wildfire, with less-developed areas in the Simi Hills to the east and the Santa Monica Mountains to the south most likely to experience wildfires. As one moves away from the periphery and toward the urban core of the City, wildfire burn probability decreases. Vulnerable populations are determined by specific indicators including limited English, people of color, those without a car, and those in poverty. These populations are less equipped to withstand wildfire due to limited financial resources, higher rates of being uninsured and without access to a vehicle to evacuate, and/or other factors that make them more sensitive such as higher rates of physical or mental disabilities or respiratory conditions. Particular attention to fire hardening of homes in these areas is recommended. Wildfires occurring in other areas of Ventura and Los Angeles Counties have the potential to adversely impact the City by exposing residents and workers to smoke and other air pollutants. Children and pregnant women, unhoused residents, people with underlying respiratory conditions, outdoor workers, residents who are uninsured, and low-income communities are particularly vulnerable and may not have adequate access to healthcare. Wildfires can strip land of vegetation, increasing the potentials for non-native invasive species to populate open space, for debris flow hazards like landslides, and for erosion of exposed soils. | Drought: Drought occurring throughout California and the western U.S. has already had significant impacts on water resources. The City's water supply is almost exclusively imported via the State Water Project, which originates in the Sierra Nevada Mountains north of Sacramento. Reduced precipitation paired with warmer temperatures reduce the snowpack, which serves as a reservoir by storing water for use throughout the spring and summer. A significantly reduced annual Sierra snowpack since 2011 coupled with the driest three years on record (2020, 2021 and 2022) and the driest ever spring in 2022 led to extremely low water levels in the primary reservoir, Lake Oroville, that serves the State Water Project. Consequently, the State reduced its allocation of water to the Metropolitan Water District (MWD) in 2022 which resulted in a local water shortage emergency and impacted the MWD service area throughout southern California. The City was forced to limit outdoor irrigation to one day per week and pass other restrictions in an attempt to meet a mandated volumetric reduction of 50% in total water use. Future reductions in the Sierra snowpack are anticipated to occur with climate change. The City will need to plan for alternative supplementary water supplies and adopt strategies to reduce water demand from its residents and businesses. Although the City does not receive its potable water from local supplies, local drought impacts water use through increased demand for irrigation. Extended periods of diminished local precipitation will impact natural fauna and flora, landscape vegetation, and the City's tree canopy. Lower rates of groundwater recharge affect the possible use of groundwater to supplement water imports in the future. Residents with on-site wells might experience greater difficulty pumping groundwater from increasingly lower depths.

Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Cambridge is vulnerable to coastal flooding including sea-level rise and other climate impacts exacerbated by this. For example, the Fresh Water Pond Reservoir is vulnerable to salt water intrusion from storm surge should the downstream Amelia Earhart Dam be compromised. The impact of this would impact many residents in Cambridge, disrupt critical services, and cause economic impacts. | Urban flooding: Several neighborhoods in Cambridge are more vulnerable to urban flooding than others. The City is currently undergoing storm water infrastructure upgrades. As an example please see the linked Preparedness Plan: https://www.cambridgema.gov/CDD/Projects/Climate/~/media/A3977AB1B6AB47D7BEE02AE4D0B1410B.ashx | Heavy precipitation: Heavy precipitation would have significant impacts on Cambridge's vulnerable populations through urban flooding, river flooding, and possible freshwater contamination. Several neighborhoods, such as Area 4 and Alewife, have already experienced repeated flooding over the years. Over three time periods (today, 2030 and 2070), the area of the City projected to flood increases from 13% to 18% by 2030 and 23% by 2070. That is, the additional 2.5 inches of rainfall expected in a 2070 100-year 24- hour storm would flood an area almost twice the size of what would be flooded today. Water damage to buildings and infrastructure. Blockage of roads and transit. Flooding of subways, disruption of bus routes and roads, electric substation flooding, flooding of buildings with contaminated water, possible drinking water supply disruption | Extreme heat: Temperatures are expected to rise through 2070 and beyond. This assessment projects that the number of days over 90 degrees F will nearly triple by 2030 from the current annual average of 11 days and that there may be 4 to 6 times more days by 2070. This trend will be experienced both as increasing average or “new normal” temperatures and as more extreme, less predictable heat events. It is very likely that Cambridge will experience heat waves of greater frequency and duration and that this shift will have implications for both human health and the built environment. Northern cities are less adapted to extreme heat because of little historical need to do so. The duration and intensity of heat waves have significant implications for public health - especially for vulnerable populations that do not have access to sufficient cooling options. Each passing day of extreme heat decreases a person's ability to cope with the heat stress. This is especially threatening for the very young, the elderly, and those with existing health challenges like cardiovascular, circulatory, and respiratory conditions. Increased mortality and morbidity, and possible effects on electricity distribution are expected. Additionally, there are water quality concerns associated with extreme heat such as algal blooms, toxic algae, and dissolved oxygen. | River flooding: Cambridge sits between the Charles River and the Alewife Brook which during heavy precipitation events can exceed their banks. The Alewife neighborhood is particularly vulnerable to river flooding and there has been significant development of the site in recent years. The Alewife Brook extends all the way from the Mystic River to Fresh Pond in Cambridge, which is an important source of freshwater for the City. With increased extreme weather events such as flooding and storm surge it is not out of the realm of possibilities that floodwaters reach Fresh Pond and contaminate this vital source of water for the City.

cityname: City of West Palm Beach, FL
climate_hazard:
Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: From 1996 to 2016, Palm Beach County has endured over $33 billion dollars in estimated losses from tropical systems. Due to rising ocean temperatures, hurricanes are expected to increase in severity and intensity. Considering West Palm Beach's proximity to the Atlantic Ocean, these increased storms put the City at great risk for the disruption of transportation and local economic interests. This could also strain emergency management services should there be a dramatic storm stretching the need for emergency response units.

Emergency was declared for the State of Florida during Hurricane Irma on 09.10.2017, Hurricane Ian on 09.24.2022, and Tropical Storm Nicole on 11.07.2022. According to the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Ian caused an estimated $112.9 billion worth of total damage in the United States. In Palm Beach County, damages occurred mostly due to storm surges, tornados, and beach erosion. | Extreme wind: Wind is a threat to property and life associated with other climatic events, including hurricanes, tropical storms, hail events, and tornadoes. It impacts the ability to carry out basic services including emergency medical care, water treatment, supply and sewerage, and interrupts transportation and power systems. Economic impacts stem from the interruption of basic government services and property damage. Vulnerable populations include those in substandard housing or without the ability to evacuate to safer structures, and they are at higher risk of injury or death from extreme wind events. There is also a threat to frontline workers who assess and clean up directly after these wind events. | Other: Air Pollution: A variety of factors can increase a person's or population's vulnerability to climate change-related health impacts, including age, underlying conditions, socioeconomic status, communities of color, and geographic location. For the purposes of the City's assessment, the CDC's SVI was used to identify populations that might have special needs in the event of a public health emergency. It is important to note that geographic proximity is only one of several barriers to medical care for vulnerable populations, others could include cost, transportation, social access, and communication. 
In 2022 Palm Beach County Air Quality Index reported 323 good and 42 moderate days. In 2023 report shows 260 Good and 104 Moderate Days, in 2024 257 good and 109 moderate days. . https://www.epa.gov/outdoor-air-quality-data/air-quality-index-report | Urban flooding: Represented as rainfall induced flooding in the climate resilience assessment, urban flooding represents a significant risk to areas of the city that also have a higher overall social vulnerability. In the 15 areas of the City with at least 146 homes vulnerable and at-risk, four also have more than 27% of the families living below the poverty line. In regards to economic impact, it was estimated that 43% of the city's annual sales volume and 36% of the city's jobs/employees are highly vulnerable to rainfall induced flooding. Several neighborhood areas and key corridors have potential for roads and properties becoming isolated or inaccessible during flood events. Generally, the more built up, urban areas of the city with decreased permeability and stormwater runoff capacity have increased flood risk, compared to the western areas surrounding wetlands and other natural areas. About 25 percent of all residential properties in the City are highly vulnerable and at-risk to rainfall-induced flooding. | Water stress: The average annual and average monthly pollutant loading for the City was estimated as part of the City's 2017 Draft Stormwater Master Plan. The study results indicated that the City's eastern portion has the highest pollutant loads, likely due to the lack of water quality treatment in these highly urbanized and historical sections of the City. Nutrient loading and increased heat contribute to harmful algal blooms, which can have a potential impact on potable water treatment and also cause health concerns for vulnerable populations if they come in direct contact with the water outdoors. This impacts recreation as well, leading to economic losses. Additionally, there are vulnerabilities to contamination from wastewater and other chemical and microbiological contaminants that may impact potable water treatment. The proportion of the population exposed namely reflects the minor health-sensitive populations that would be impacted by algal issues in the water supply or come into direct contact with contaminated recreational waters, as potable treatment would protect the majority of the population from adverse effects of water pollution. | Other coastal events: Storm surge is expected to increase due to warming ocean temperatures that will bring more intense tropical systems and intracoastal flooding. Erosion associated with storm surge also poses a threat to roadways/railways, and commercial and residential properties. Regarding economic impacts, about 11% of the City's annual sales volume and 15% of the City's jobs have medium to high vulnerability and risk to storm surge. In this area, populations with limited access to transportation may be more vulnerable due to fewer options for evacuation before a storm surge event. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Despite not having any direct ocean coastline, West Palm Beach is already seeing some 'sunny day flooding' in the event of King Tides, which happen mostly during the fall equinox, where water from the Intracoastal Waterway intrudes storm water drains and affects roadways and commercial and residential properties. This is expected to increase as sea levels rise in the future. While the overall total number of vulnerable properties in the assessment was low, the impacts of persistent inundation and increased frequency and severity of future tidal flooding could have high consequences for residential neighborhoods, commercial corridors, and transportation and mobility. However, it is important to note that West Palm Beach does have a higher elevation than some of the cities to the south, which does give the City more time to prepare for sea level rise. (see page 48 of the resiliency assessment for more information). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): According to FDACS, PBC is a moderate risk for wildfires. From 2017 to 2022, there were 75 wildfires throughout Palm Beach County, although most of these wildfires have been outside city limits. The built system group highlighted issues such as property damage, supply shortages, and poor water quality. Additionally, flood damage to transportation networks—including roads and bike lanes—can limit mobility and emergency access, further isolating vulnerable communities. climate_hazard:
River flooding: Being on the confluence of the Rivers Ouse and Foss York is well known for flooding from those rivers with approximately 7200 homes and businesses at risk. Many areas in the City benefit from flood defences constructed following flooding in 1978 Since then additional defences have been built to protect other areas of the city These defences have been designed for a 1 Annual Exceedance Probability AEP or 1 in 100 year event however predictions indicate that the country will experience warmer wetter winters and hotter drier summers resulting in more extreme rainfall events As a result flooding of greater magnitude and frequency from all sources is expected and the current standard of protection has now fallen to 2 AEP or 1 in 50Transport Road closures affecting evacuation and response from emergency servicesProperty During the 2000 floods 3000 residents had to be evacuated from their homeBusiness Loss of telephone services to 50000 customers Insurers paid out over 70m in payments following the floodsFull details of the impact from the 2015 floods are reported in the York Flood Inquiry https://www.york.gov.uk/downloads/file/1444/york-flood-inquiry-main-report-2-18mb-pdf- Evacuations from homes can have an exacerbated effect on the elderly, vulnerable health groups, and low-income households. Research has shown that lower-income households are most exposed to the financial consequences of a flood when it occurs. Research by AgeUK has shown that people who rely on medical equipment, such as oxygen or dialysis machines, can be severely impacted by flooding. Disruption to care services during flood events can also impact both elderly and vulnerable health groups. York's 2015 Flood Inquiry heard that some older and more vulnerable people without extended support found it difficult to cope with the upheaval of being evacuated or living in temporary accommodation. Many of York Businesses, as highlighted in the sectors most exposed category, were affected by flooding. Some flooded businesses remained closed for many months; some went out of business as a consequence of the flooding. Small business owners are particularly financially affected by flooding, with large financial implications caused by floods. | Extreme heat: The high temperatures observed recently represent risks to risks to health and wellbeing from high temperatures, particularly amongst the vulnerable; risks to productivity due to overheating in places of work; financial markets; risks food security and risks to infrastructure. Extreme heat has the potential to exacerbate health outcomes for populations such as children, the elderly and are vulnerable health groups due to the effects of heat stress. Moreover, heatwaves and extreme heat may also impact food security, further impacting vulnerable populations, including low-income households. Another concern within the risk to building fabrics is unusually high heat. July 2022 saw temperatures of nearly 40°C in York and has raised questions about the threat of fires due to the increased dryness during the summer months. Much of York's building stock was not designed to accommodate such temperatures (which could impact vulnerable groups such as the elderly in care homes), nor to deal with the increased threat of fires.High temperatures can also impact building foundations which can lead to subsidence, especially if the building is constructed on clay soil, which represents much of York's soilscape. Much of the land around York is classified as grade 2 or 3 conditions suitable for high quality arable crops (such as wheat, barley, oilseed rape etc.) and horticultural crops, making the impact of extreme heat to crops and soil a threat for socio-economic health and food security. This will impact York's residents and the agricultural sector in York whose arable crops will be at risk, causing financial impact. Urban flooding: Extreme rainfall events and insufficient stormwater drainage have led to frequent urban flooding in Vijayawada, primarily driven by overflow from the Krishna River and Budameru rivulet. The city's main flood vulnerabilities include low-lying wards near these water bodies, where unauthorized settlements and inadequate drainage systems intensify waterlogging, especially during the retreating monsoon and reservoir releases. Historical records show increasing flood depths and expanding affected areas during high-return period rainfall events, with several notable flood-prone wards accounting for a significant portion of the city's area and population.

VMC faces ongoing challenges in managing stormwater and waste disposal, as silt accumulation and limited drain coverage hinder proper runoff, worsening flood impacts. Nearly 35% (21.71 sq. km.) of the city's area and 31% (0.37 million) of its population reside in zones most susceptible to flooding, underscoring the urgent need for improved infrastructure and urban planning interventions.

Flooding and water stagnation disrupt mobility, economic activities, and basic urban services in the city, while also heightening the risk of vector-borne diseases due to stagnant water. Irregular and intense rainfall events strain water management, stormwater systems, wastewater treatment, and other essential urban infrastructure—leading to outages, contamination, and reduced service delivery. The urban poor are disproportionately affected, with 42% of the city's slum population (0.12 million people out of 0.29 million) particularly vulnerable due to dilapidated housing and limited capacity to cope with service breakdowns.

Refer to Section 5.3.2 in the attached Vijayawada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan | Heat stress: Vijayawada is experiencing a rising trend in both maximum and minimum surface air temperatures, with extreme heat events recorded in recent years. Heat-stress and impact analysis of satellite imagery shows that several city areas consistently exhibit land surface temperatures above the mean (33 degrees Celsius), indicating they are hotspots. This increase in heat conditions leads to thermal discomfort, reduced productivity, a rise in heat-related illnesses, and especially affects vulnerable groups like slum dwellers and outdoor workers. Overlay studies indicate that 75% of the city's slum population (i.e., 0.22 million people out of 0.29 million) is likely to be affected by high temperatures.

Higher temperatures also impact urban services, including increasing water demand, challenging the capacity of water supply infrastructure, accelerating waste decomposition, compromising worker health and waste management systems, damaging road surfaces, and increasing energy demand for cooling. 

Refer to Section 5.3.1 in the attached Vijayawada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Vijayawada, located 70 km from the coast, is highly vulnerable to cyclones, having experienced 33 cyclonic disturbances within 150 km of the city between 1877 and 2013. Severe cyclonic events, such as those in 1977 and 1990, brought extremely high wind speeds and significant impacts to the city. UNDP study on Vijayawada city disaster management plan estimates that the entire city could experience severe cyclonic storms with wind speeds exceeding 89 km/h every 50 to 100 years, with the majority of wards at risk from storms reaching up to 151 km/h. Slum populations are especially at risk due to their often temporary housing structures.

Cyclones pose a serious threat to urban infrastructure, frequently overwhelming stormwater systems and causing waterlogging, supply disruptions, infrastructure damage, and increased exposure to flood and health risks.

Refer to Section 5.3.4 in the attached Vijayawada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan. | Other: Landslide: Vijayawada's terrain consists of rocky hills and extensive plains, with landslides occurring mainly due to prolonged rainfall and destabilizing construction activities on hill slopes. Population growth has driven unauthorized settlements into these hazard-prone foothill areas, intensifying vulnerability. UNDP studies show that 2% of the city falls under high landslide susceptibility and 3% under medium, with select pockets exposed to landslide hazards. Around 25% of the total population (0.29 million people) and 30% of slum residents (~0.09 million people) are at risk, as 15 city wards are prone to landslides.

Landslides disrupt urban infrastructure and services by damaging water and wastewater pipelines, contaminating water sources, blocking drainage, and blocking transportation networks. Slums in the foothills are particularly affected, with casualties and property damage recorded; mitigation efforts, such as relocation and improved rainfall and water-level monitoring, are essential to reduce risk.

Refer to Section 5.3.3 in the attached Vijayawada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

Other: Community Based Organization Support - Resilience Hubs: Resilience Hubs have become a key community of practice of the Urban Sustainability Directors' Network (USDN), of which New Bedford is an active member. Resilience is the ability of people and communities to anticipate and adapt to or thrive amidst changing climate conditions and other hazard events. Resilience Hubs operate through three very different conditions: everyday; disruption; and recovery. At its core, the Resilience Hub serves as a central point to design and implement a strategy to address everyday stressors that are the root causes of vulnerability, and to help the community thrive. In addition, the Resilience Hub can deliver preparedness messaging to the communities that the Hub serves, and trusted community leaders can disseminate information and facilitate community cohesion before a disruption. Ideally, residents, businesses, and organizations will collectively manage the Hub including both internal and external communications. During a severe weather event or other disruptions, a Resilience Hub can be the central point for gathering, assessing impact, assembling information, accessing resources, and spearheading non-governmental response. Resilience Hubs can play a critical role in post-disruption recovery and ongoing communications needs. For resilient communications, the site can remain a central point for gathering, sharing information, and accessing resources. Hubs can also provide space for additional experts, aid organizations, volunteers, and support networks to gather and better understand and help meet community needs.
Resilience Hubs are built out around five Foundational Areas:
•	Services and programs - Outside times of disruption and recovery, providing services and programs that build relationships, promote community preparedness, promote life and job skills and entrepreneurial opportunities, and improve residents' health and well-being.
•	Communications - Ensuring the ability to communicate within and outside the service area year-round and especially during emergency disruptions and throughout recovery.
•	Building and Landscapes - Strengthening the resilience of the facility to ensure that it meets operational goals in all conditions and provides shelter during disruptions and recovery.
•	Power - Ensuring reliable backup power to the facility during a hazard while also improving the cost-effectiveness and sustainability of operations in all three operating modes.
•	Operations - Ensuring trained personnel and processes are in place to operate the facility in all three modes. 
 Resilience Hubs, like the communities they serve, are unique and no two are completely alike. New Bedford completed Resilience Hub feasibility and energy efficiency evaluations with two CBOs in 2019 through funding from the Funders' Network and the Island Foundation of Southeastern Massachusetts, and with technical assistance from USDN and American Microgrid Solutions (AMS). Two of these Hubs are in progress with a third in conceptual stages.

Extreme heat: The elderly and individuals with pre-existing health conditions are expected to be vurnerable populations under extreme heat. 
Health-related risks such as dehydration, heatstroke, reduced appetite, and general physical strain can have severe consequences for these groups, especially those already affected by illness or frailty.
Consequently, the human health and social care sectors are especially exposed under extreme heat conditions. There will be an increased need for targeted preparedness and response measures within healthcare and social work activities to protect at-risk individuals and maintain service continuity during heatwaves.

Agriculture:
Extreme heat increases evaporation from the soil, resulting in a dryer soil. This can lead to damage in crops, as well as potentially having an impact on different types of habitats. Moreover, extreme heat can make it harder for resident species to spread, while it could ease the spread of new and invasive species. Furthermore, a greater emission of CO2 and methane can occur when extreme heat leads to a drying up of wetlands in the open land. 

Consevation: 
Ecosystems may suffer from drought, habitat loss, and heat stress on plants and animals, increased risk of wildfires, disruption of ecological processes | Heavy precipitation: The drainage of rainwater from urban areas occurs either through the sewer system, at streams or through a combination of these possibilities. Under normal conditions, this works without problems. Elsinore municipality, like other municipalities, has problems handling rainwater during extreme rainfall. This can result in areas being flooded and that some homeowners in extreme cases experience water entering the house. The reason is usually either that the sewers cannot keep up, or that large amounts of rainwater cannot be accommodated in the water streams. 

Repairing damage after flooding can be financially challenging, particularly for low-income households including elderly. Viewed through an intersectional lens, these impacts may disproportionately affect marginalized and minority communities, who often have fewer resources to prevent or recover from such climate-related events.

Besides having an impact on housing and infrastructure, the overflow of sewage- and rainwater can have a negative impact on the water quality of the municipality's watercourses, the beach water and Øresund, and the ecosystem and biodiversity in Øresund.

At extreme rainfall, which gives extensive floods, Elsinore Municipality's emergency plan applies. The emergency plan describes how to handle the flood, including how personnel are distributed where pumps are requested, which roads must be blocked etc.

The wet winters and dry summers can lead to floods and draughts, respectively, which can emit CO2 and methane from the soil, thus leading to further global warming. And also cause negetives effects on crop growth. | Storm: The coast is at risk of being eroded by rising water levels, which will affect the environment both on land and in the water, especially the coastal settlements. 

Repairing damage after a storm or flood can be financially challenging, particularly for low-income households, indcluding elderly. Viewed through an intersectional lens, these impacts may disproportionately affect marginalized and minority communities, who often have fewer resources to prevent or recover from such climate-related events.

In November 2011 and December 2013 the coast of North Zealand suffered from coastal floods due to storm surge. Coastal areas were damaged, among others a local hotel, residential areas, roads and harbours. Areas with solid structure coastal protection were severely damaged. In the future, storm surge is expected to occur more frequently and therefor increasingly affect build-up areas near the coast.
 | Extreme wind: Extreme winds can contribute to storm surges and coastal flooding, which are described separately. Along with rising sea levels during storms, we are experiencing increased sand transport along the coast and accelerated coastal erosion. If extreme wind triggers secondary climate hazards, it can result in severe damage and significant financial costs, particularly for vulnerable populations, such as low-income households, marginalized communities and elderly.

Extreme winds can cause substantial damage to buildings, trees, and other unsecured objects. This can be problematic in terms of damage to the power grid, power outages, and impacts on infrastructure, for example, due to fallen trees. Heat stress: In Beşiktaş Municipality, heat stress due to rising temperatures and frequent heatwaves has significant impacts on both vulnerable populations and key economic sectors.

Impacts on Vulnerable Populations:
Elderly People and Those with Health Conditions: Elderly residents and individuals with chronic illnesses, such as heart disease and respiratory conditions, are particularly vulnerable to heat stress. High temperatures can worsen their health conditions, leading to increased risks of heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and even mortality. Beşiktaş, being an urban area, often experiences the 'urban heat island' effect, where temperatures are even higher due to dense buildings and limited green spaces, further exacerbating the problem.

Low-Income Households: Households with limited financial resources often lack access to cooling systems like air conditioning or proper ventilation. These residents are more likely to experience heat-related health problems during heatwaves, as they may not be able to afford adequate cooling or may live in poorly insulated homes that retain heat.

Children and Outdoor Workers: Children, especially young ones, are more sensitive to extreme heat, which can affect their health and outdoor activities. Similarly, outdoor workers, such as construction workers or street vendors, are at high risk of heat stress due to prolonged exposure to high temperatures without proper shade or hydration.

Impacts on Economic Sectors:
Healthcare Sector: Heatwaves lead to an increased number of hospital admissions due to heat-related illnesses, putting additional pressure on the local healthcare services. This rise in demand can strain the capacity of hospitals and clinics, affecting their ability to provide adequate care for all patients.

Tourism and Retail Sectors: The tourism sector, which is important for Beşiktaş, may face challenges during extreme heat events as tourists might avoid outdoor attractions, such as parks, historic sites, and markets, leading to reduced visitor numbers and lower revenue. These people may face the risk of damage to their homes or temporary displacement due to flooding. Tourism Sector: The coastal areas of Beşiktaş are an important attraction for tourism. However, coastal flooding and sea level rise can negatively affect beaches, coastal walking paths, and seaside restaurants and cafes. Renewable energy - Sustainable Energy Transition: Integration of Renewable Systems like Solar and Wind for Residential and Tertiary Buildings in Beşiktaş.: Project description:

The 'Renewable Energy Integration for Residential and Commercial Buildings' project is a major initiative by Beşiktaş Municipality aimed at reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and fostering sustainable energy use. This project focuses on integrating solar and wind energy systems into residential and tertiary buildings, with the goal of reducing dependence on fossil fuels and increasing the share of renewable energy by 2030.

The project targets a total GHG reduction of 275,896.3 tCO2e by 2030. This will be achieved by installing renewable energy technologies such as solar panels and wind turbines across residential and commercial buildings, contributing to both local and national climate goals. The systems installed will generate clean energy, reduce the overall carbon footprint of the district, and shift energy production towards renewables.

Implementation Phases:

Feasibility Studies and Planning:
In the initial phase, detailed feasibility studies will be conducted for each building to assess its potential for solar and wind energy. Factors such as solar exposure, wind potential, and building structure will be considered in this process.

Installation of Renewable Systems:
Once planning is complete, solar panels and wind turbines will be installed on rooftops and in suitable areas. These systems will be optimized for energy generation and storage, allowing buildings to meet a portion of their energy needs with renewable sources.

Energy Monitoring:
After installation, energy production will be continuously monitored to ensure the systems' efficiency. Performance metrics such as energy savings, GHG emission reductions, and renewable energy generation will be tracked regularly.

Grid Integration:
Excess energy produced by the systems will be fed back into the local grid, allowing building owners to sell surplus energy. This will provide an additional source of revenue and help to promote local energy security.

Expected Outcomes:

GHG Emissions Reduction:
The project is expected to reduce GHG emissions by 275,896.3 tCO2e by 2030, a significant contribution to Beşiktaş's climate targets.

Increase in Renewable Energy Generation:
By integrating solar and wind energy systems, the project will substantially increase the district's capacity for renewable energy generation, reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

Energy Security and Independence:
Local energy production will decrease the district's dependency on external energy sources, providing greater resilience to energy price fluctuations and disruptions.

Economic Benefits:
Building owners will benefit from long-term energy savings and additional revenue from selling excess energy. The project will also create local jobs in the installation and maintenance of renewable energy systems.

Public Engagement:
The visibility of renewable energy systems on residential and commercial buildings will help raise public awareness about clean energy and encourage more widespread adoption of sustainable practices throughout the district.

Transport - 'Expansion of Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure for Sustainable Transportation in Beşiktaş': Project description: Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging Infrastructure Expansion

Beşiktaş Municipality is committed to supporting the growing adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) by expanding its EV charging infrastructure. The project will involve the installation of new EV charging points across key public areas, including parking lots, municipal buildings, and other high-traffic locations. This expansion will provide greater convenience for EV owners and encourage the broader adoption of electric transportation in Beşiktaş.

The municipality's objective is to mitigate transportation-related greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, contributing to the city's climate goals and improving local air quality. By making EV charging stations more accessible, the municipality aims to reduce reliance on fossil-fueled vehicles and support the transition towards clean energy in transportation. The project will also include provisions for renewable energy-powered charging stations to maximize environmental benefits.

Key elements of the project:

Installation of EV charging stations in public spaces, including parking areas and municipal facilities.
Incentivizing the use of electric vehicles by improving charging access and reliability.
Contribution to local air quality improvements and a reduction in Beşiktaş's carbon footprint.
Expected Outcomes:

Significant reductions in CO2 emissions related to transportation.
Enhanced convenience for EV owners, encouraging more widespread adoption of electric vehicles.
Improved air quality due to decreased fossil fuel vehicle usage.

These systems will be installed across various locations in the district, continuously collecting data to inform necessary measures and actions. - Environmental Monitoring Systems (for Air Quality, Atmospheric Conditions, and Noise Levels) in Beşiktaş: The 'Environmental Monitoring System for Beşiktaş' project aims to establish a comprehensive network of environmental monitoring stations across the district to track and assess key environmental indicators, including air quality, atmospheric conditions, and noise levels. This project is critical for improving public health and safety, while also contributing to Beşiktaş's broader sustainability goals. By continuously gathering and analyzing real-time data from multiple locations, Beşiktaş Municipality will be able to monitor environmental factors and take necessary actions to mitigate risks posed by pollution and climate change.

The monitoring system will provide detailed data on pollutants like PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and ozone (O3), along with meteorological data such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure. Additionally, noise pollution levels will be recorded to identify areas that need regulatory attention or noise reduction initiatives. The data collected will be accessible to the public through an online platform, ensuring transparency and community engagement in environmental issues.

Implementation Phases:

Feasibility Studies and Planning: In the first phase, a detailed study will be conducted to identify the optimal locations for the installation of environmental monitoring stations. Areas with higher pollution risks or population density will be prioritized to ensure effective coverage.

Installation of Monitoring Stations: Once the planning phase is completed, the monitoring stations will be installed at key locations throughout Beşiktaş, including public areas, parks, and busy urban zones. These stations will be equipped with advanced sensors to capture a wide range of environmental data.

Data Collection and Monitoring: After installation, the system will begin collecting continuous data on air quality, atmospheric conditions, and noise levels. This data will be analyzed in real-time to detect any concerning trends, allowing for early warnings and prompt responses to environmental risks.

Public Access and Reporting: The municipality will develop an online platform where residents can view real-time environmental data from the monitoring stations. Regular reports will be generated to provide insights on pollution levels, weather conditions, and potential health risks.
