Water management - 
Gray water reuse strategy
: Considering the experience that Independencia has with the gray water treatment plants in the Nueva Zealand, Balmaceda and Antu Hulien schools, in addition to the one installed in the Environmental Practices Center, the municipality formulated the project 'Gray water reuse strategy'. This project seeks to use gray water from nine public and five private buildings to irrigate 30,000 m² of public sidewalks, applying a treatment that will allow 44,000 m³/year of gray water to be reused. To do this, Fixed Film Treatment System technology will be used, which uses filters and macrophyte plants to reduce the organic load of the water, making it suitable for urban irrigation. In addition, it is intended that this project be financed with funds at the regional level. It should be noted that this project was presented at the CDP Business Round and at the Research and Innovation Symposium of the ICLEI World Congress 2024.

project_info: Public and green spaces - Ecological Corridors\n: The development of a network of ecological corridors is proposed that connects the green areas of Independencia with the natural landmarks of the Metropolitan Region. This project combines urban biological corridors and planting with the Miyawaki method, intervening on sidewalks and sidewalk areas on trunk, collector and service streets. The corridors will be composed of nuclei of native vegetation with accelerated growth, regenerating degraded soils and promoting biodiversity. The soil will be protected with organic mulch to prevent erosion and improve moisture retention. This initiative has already been implemented in three streets and two avenues, covering a total of 150,000 square meters with regional funds.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Energy Evaluation Cesfam Dr. Agustín Cruz Melo\n: The Municipality of Independencia was awarded, through a competition by the Energy Sustainability Agency of the Ministry of Energy, the technical assistance of Ecological, a company that has collaborated in gray water treatment projects, for the project “Comprehensive Energy Improvement, Cesfam Dr. Agustín Melo”. This building corresponds to a Family Health Center that serves the population of Independencia and an important part of the population of the northern area of ​​the Metropolitan Region. The assistance includes an energy diagnosis with Cesfam officials and patients, as well as the formulation of a project that contemplates the improvement of the thermal envelope of the building (insulation of walls and roofs, installation of windows with thermopanel, green infrastructure and a modification of the main access), the incorporation of photovoltaic solar energy (cleaning of roofing, installation of solar panels and electrical standardization of the building) and air conditioning (multi-split air conditioning equipment, electrical connections and panels). This project is intended to be submitted to regional funds, which are not yet secured, so it is also available to receive international financing.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Replacement of public lighting to LED technology: There are three projects that seek to increase the replacement of lighting to LED technology in the commune of Independencia. These correspond to the projects: “IMPROVEMENT OF PEDESTRIAN LIGHTING NEIGHBORHOOD UNIT 9” (31 LED luminaires), “IMPROVEMENT OF LIGHTING NEIGHBORHOOD UNIT N° 3, HIPÓDROMO AND VENECIA STREETS, COMMUNE OF INDEPENDENCIA” (100 LED luminaires), and “ENVIRONMENT LIGHTING HERITAGE AREA_MARURI, RIVERA, COLÓN” (149 LED luminaires). These projects are sectorized and contemplate intervention in specific streets and sectors of the commune. Of the three mentioned, the first already has financing, while the remaining two are in the process of applying for regional funds. However, the municipality is open to receiving international financing for the execution of these projects.

Renewable energy - Implementation of photovoltaic panels in homes: Thanks to the financing granted by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Planning, 16 homes and families in the commune of Independencia were benefited through the Family Asset Protection Program, accessing the implementation of photovoltaic panels for on-grid generation. project_info:
Land-Use - Urban Nursery and Garden Program: At the Center for Environmental Practices, an urban and community garden program is developed aimed at strengthening the green infrastructure of the commune in a socially and environmentally responsible manner. This space allows people from the commune to be trained in values ​​linked to the dignity of work, while they are guided in the search for employment, promoting job insertion and personal development.

Through orchards and the installation of greenhouses for local vegetative reproduction, access to agroecological production of organic fruits and vegetables is encouraged, encouraging local production and strengthening community economic development schemes. The participation of women and older adults is prioritized, contributing to food security and the empowerment of key sectors of the population.

The program also promotes the cultivation of medicinal herbs and the rescue of knowledge ancestral knowledge about herbalism and native species, promoting their use within the community and strengthening local identity. In addition, a group of volunteers meets weekly to work on the care of orchards and the application of cultivation techniques, transforming these spaces into meeting points, collective learning and citizen participation.

These initiatives consolidate an inclusive and sustainable environmental management model, where education, community work and agroecological production are integrated to improve the quality of life of the inhabitants of Independencia.

Other: Environmental Education Program - Independence Environmental Education Program: The commune's Environmental Education Program seeks to strengthen the awareness and sustainable action of the community through training and workshops in waste management, energy efficiency, climate resilience and responsible use of water.

Activities are carried out aimed at homes, educational centers, businesses and industrial associations, addressing waste classification, reduction at its source, recycling, reuse and correct implementation of the REP Law, with emphasis on environmental and health impacts and social aspects of inadequate waste management.

In the energy field, energy efficiency practices and the use of Non-Conventional Renewable Energy (NCRE) are promoted, including solutions from the Center for Environmental Practices. The Tu Energía program of ENEL Chile stands out, which benefits 30 homes in the commune with private financing of 35 million Chilean pesos, being the only program with an external contribution.

For climate resilience, the community and students are trained in protection strategies against precipitation and windstorms, teaching practical actions to reduce risks in homes, schools and critical infrastructure.

Finally, the responsible use of water is promoted through talks and workshops on savings, gray water reuse and efficient irrigation techniques, complemented by dissemination campaigns on social networks to motivate sustainable habits throughout the community. commune.

It should be noted that, outside of the Your Energy program, all these initiatives are developed with municipal planning and financing, without additional costs for the community.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Implementation of organic waste dehydration technology in housing complexes: An organic waste recycling system will be piloted, where the treatment and reuse is proposed in the same rooms of the housing complex by enabling an Organic Green Point, which is capable of transforming the organic waste generated, daily, into organic fertilizer and condensation water, usable in green areas. A preliminary study determined that the sector has an estimated generation potential of 380 kilos per day. It is important to highlight that the Organic Green point will incorporate specialized technology that has not been implemented in Chile, being pioneers in local organic management. This technology consists of a dehydrating machine that divides and collects the organic fraction and liquid, both of which can be used to strengthen green areas. For compliance with the PLADECO in its guideline 4.2.1. Promote the reduction, separation and recycling of household solid waste (this Program is financed with the cleaning fee), and seeks to test models that allow us to advance to being a Zero Waste commune, since this Neighborhood Unit would contemplate a complete management plan for organic and inorganic waste.

project_info: Transport - Renewal of Providencia's electric vehicle fleet: Acquisition of 11 electric vehicles, positioning the communal electric vehicle fleet and activating a progressive replacement process over time. It is based as one of the mobility goals in the Local Energy Strategy annexed to PLADECO (Specifically action A7 of Electromobility), in the Sustainable Mobility Report, the Smart Cities action lines and in PLADECO in guideline 4 of Sustainable Commune, with the objective of promoting energy efficiency in the commune and reducing the environmental impact of municipal activities. Electric vehicles have a series of social and environmental benefits, positioning Providencia as a sustainable commune, since they reduce noise, do not emit pollutants and the current market meets comfort standards referring to the minimum needs of the municipal fleet. In addition, its operation is aligned with the new standards maximum speed (50 km/h) and the Live Streets public space programs and innovation lines. Given the positioning of markets and after-sales services, incorporating maintenance and insurance, medium-load gamma models are projected, such as the Z.E. line. of Renault Kangoo. Additionally, the renewal of charging points is included.

project_info: Water management - Water efficiency in municipal establishments with high water consumption: Implementation of pressure regulation systems for the drinking water supply system of the 12 educational establishments in Providencia, achieving average savings of 40% of water consumption. This technology allows the water pressure to be regulated according to the schedule and specific use, also being able to identify the existence of leaks and any type of water loss. Currently, there are important problems of inefficiency and misuse of water, added to the economic deficit in the educational field, which is why savings initiatives promote better economic and environmental management. Pressure regulation generates concrete, verifiable and immediate results. The savings potential is variable depending on the infrastructure of each establishment, but there are cases reported in the RM where savings reach 78% of total consumption. On average per school They project savings of over 10,000 m3/year, equivalent to 4 Olympic swimming pools. It is important to consider that the savings in water consumption cushion the costs associated with investment.

Extreme heat: - Projected to see an increase in extreme heat days from an average of 3 days up to 24 days by 2050 and 47 days by 2080. 
- Number of tropical nights is expected to increase to 21 by 2050 and 41 by 2080. 
- Average minimum temperatures are expected to increase by 4.4-5.4°C by 2080.

Extreme heat is associated with human health impacts, heat related morbidity, and mortality. Exposure to extreme heat can also exacerbate pre-existing health conditions that affect the circulatory, respiratory, and cerebrovascular system, putting those individuals at greater risk of adverse effects. | Extreme wind: - Increase in accidental morbidity and mortality associated with flooding events.
- Indirect health impacts related to storm events due to impacts to infrastructure and service delivery. | Heavy precipitation: - More intense rain storms: Large-scale rainfalls and wind storms are projected to happen more frequently.
- Increased flood risk.
- Increase in accidental morbidity and mortality associated with flooding events.
- Indirect health impacts related to storm events due to impacts to infrastructure and service delivery.
- Heavy rainfall and flooding is strongly associated with water-related illness outbreaks for individuals who drink from private wells.
- Potential for increased exposure to mould, impacting individuals with underlying respiratory issues | Extreme cold: The frequency of extreme cold is projected to decrease, however the intensity of extreme cold events and storms is projected to increase as a result of climate change, therefore remaining a concern for the affected populations. 

Exposure to extreme cold can cause hypothermia and frostbite and exacerbate circulatory conditions, similar to those impacted by extreme heat.

Urban flooding: Impacts experienced to date include business interruptions, damage to residential homes, destruction of natural areas (impact to conservation sector), evacuation of long-term care facilities (vulnerable population), utility supplies (utility sector), prevention of emergency services and disruption in road network (transportation sector). | Infectious disease: The rise in vector-borne illness can (in part) be attributed to rising temperatures and precipitation that lead to wetter and hotter environments promoting ideal environments for vector breeding seasons, prolonging typical transmission periods. For example, a higher prevalence of mosquitoes can promote the transmission of West Nile Virus and tick prevalence can increase the chances of Lyme disease transmission. It is expected that this hazard is almost certain to occur within the City of Mississauga moving forward. | Heavy precipitation: Impacts experienced to date include business interruptions, damage to residential homes and increases in the value of buildings and cost of reconstruction. Average annual economic costs, assuming current climate conditions, following stormwater flooding and freezing rain events are valued at $32 and $9 Millon per year respectively (Insurance Bureau of Canada). Future anticipated impacts include community level flooding, increased stress on the built environment and natural systems, disruptions to the road network and transportation systems, prevention of emergency service access and egress. Critical infrastructure such as the electrical distribution system may be impacted by downed power lines and tree branches interacting with above ground electrical wiring leading to blackouts. Increased prevalence of vector-borne diseases such as West Nile Virus due to wetter conditions, as well as surface run-off to water bodies leading to increased contaminant concentrations in surface water is anticipated. | Extreme cold: Extreme cold temperatures can lead to greater frost depth (affecting below grade infrastructure), causing freezing in near-surface pipes that service building structures of all types. Projected increases in magnitude and probability of extreme cold days will continue to impact below grade infrastructure material. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Smoke risk increases reflect a trend towards warmer and drier conditions within the broader Ontario region from where wildfire smoke can migrate to the City of Mississauga. | Extreme wind: High winds can lead to infrastructure, property damage and urban forestry damages causing fallen branches to interfere with electrical wires which can result in power outages. Unknown changes in the future intensity of high wind events makes it difficult to quantify the level of impact this hazard will have on the City of Mississauga. However, future probability levels suggest that these conditions will continue in the future. | River flooding: Riverine flooding can lead to property damage to buildings and assets and disruption to public road network and transportation systems, delaying emergency service access and egress to these areas. Depending on the severity of the flooding, residents or occupants may require evacuation. Areas adjacent to the Credit River and Cooksville Creek are particularly vulnerable to riverine flooding within the City. | Snow and ice: Winter storms that include heavy snowfall can lead to energy disruptions and power outages, where the weight of the snow can lead to the collapse of electrical wires or break tree branches causing them to fall into and interfere with the wires. Extreme snowfall could exceed the municipality's capability to clear it, causing temporary delays in the regular transport of goods and services, disruptions in the transportation network due to road closures and blockages. This could result in delayed emergency response times. Projected increases in heavy snow intensity will continue or generate higher severity impacts to the energy, transport, and infrastructural (residential) sectors within the City, as well as services such as waste management and school closures. | Extreme heat: Extreme hot temperatures and or heat waves could give rise to public health issues such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Vulnerable populations who may not have access to cool spaces for heat relief could be at an increased exposure to this hazard. Extreme heat events have the potential to increase society's energy demand due to the necessity for cooling needs. A higher demand could lead to energy shortages or a blackout event depending on the energy infrastructure system itself and the severity and duration of the high temperature event. Heat waves and extreme hot temperatures are expected to intensify, the severity of which is projected to impact the City in the future. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Mississauga is not located along a coastline that would experience flooding due to sea level rise, however the south portion of the city along the Lake Ontario shoreline could be subject to lakeshore flooding (fluvial). Coastal flooding (or shoreline flooding) can lead to property damage to buildings and assets located within flood prone areas and disruption to public road network, transportation and emergency service access and egress to these areas. Depending on the severity of the flooding, residents or occupants may require evacuation. This hazard has not significantly impacted the City and projected severity of future impacts is expected to be low. | Storm: Changes in precipitation could place stress on stormwater infrastructure, leading to localized flooding. Stormwater flooding can damage personal property (including basements in low-lying areas) and interfere with critical infrastructure. It may also disrupt the road network and transportation systems, preventing emergency service access and egress. Runoff resulting from the increased presence of water moving over the land area can contain pesticides, waste sewage or other hazardous materials exposing people to illnesses and pathogens resulting in contaminated food and water source. | Drought: Changes in seasonal temperature will lead to ecosystem impacts, shifting eco-regions for flora and fauna communities, and can lead to the increased spread of invasive species, as well as local extinctions. Decreased summer precipitation will increase the probability of summer drought, leading to increasingly higher tree mortality, affecting urban forest cover, and poor soil quality. These effects can also impact water availability, critical to agricultural production. The magnitude of future impacts is expected to be high suggesting that changes in seasonal temperatures may provide much more severe drought conditions which will continue to not only magnify ecosystem-related impacts, but public health and safety.

climate_hazard:
Heavy precipitation: Heavy precipitation events are increasing in frequency and intensity, leading to localized flooding that strains stormwater and drainage infrastructure. Flooding disrupts transportation networks and damages buildings, particularly in low-lying or high-density areas.

Vulnerable populations most affected include homeless residents, people without access to transportation, and those living in socially vulnerable or densely populated neighborhoods. These groups face greater challenges in sheltering in place or accessing community shelters during flood events, highlighting the need to plan for adequate shelter capacity and accessibility.
 | Urban flooding: More frequent and intense heavy rain events increase the risk of flash and surface flooding, which disrupts transportation, damages buildings, and overwhelms stormwater and sewer systems, risking, especially, socially vulnerable populations, particularly in high-density census tracts. They face greater risks due to limited financial capacity to recover from damages and increased reliance on community services, shelters, and county resources. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Hurricanes do reach the mid-Atlantic states, and have reached the City of Takoma Park. The impacts include heavy rain and wind that can have damaging effects. It is expected the frequency of hurricanes reaching this region will increase. Vulnerable populations such as elderly and low-income residents may have limited fiscal capacity to respond to the emergency costs and property damages associated with hurricanes, cyclones, and other extreme weather events. The sectors most exposed include the energy, transportation, water supply, buildings and housing, communications and ICT, food systems depending on the severity of events. | Extreme heat: Heat waves are expected to be hotter and last longer. According to downscaled climate change projections developed by DC, in the past, the average heatwave in the area lasted just under 5 days. In the future, the average length is expected to be around 6 days by the 2020s, 8 to 9.5 days by mid-century, and 9.5 days to 12 by the 2080s. Vulnerable populations including the elderly, homeless residents, low income residents and those with medical conditions are most at risk for heat stroke and other heat related health conditions, due to exposure and limited mobility. Heat waves will impact the following sectors in Takoma Park: the energy sector and its infrastructure, as peak demand for cooling may strain the distribution system; the transportation sector as existing roads and rail lines were not designed for temperature extremes; the local economy and livelihoods in some areas more exposed to heat will also be impacted as less people is able to work and there is a decrease in productivity; health services as there will be more ER visits. | Drought: Increasing frequency and severity of drought, compounded by rising extreme heat days, poses risks to multiple sectors in Montgomery County. Water supply systems, agriculture, and public health are most affected, with prolonged drought reducing water availability, stressing crops, and increasing health risks during heatwaves.

Vulnerable populations most exposed include low-income households, outdoor workers, the elderly, and those with pre-existing health conditions, who face higher risks from limited water access, lost income, and heat-related illnesses.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: The years 2014-2024 make up 6 of the 10 hottest years on record for the state of North Carolina. The impact of extreme heat can lead to a combination of impacts on vulnerable populations and sectors, including health and financial challenges. These impacts are commonly felt hardest among the vulnerable groups and sectors listed above (children and youth, elderly, marginalized/minority communities, low-income households, vulnerable health groups, outdoor workers, frontline workers). We estimate that the total population at risk to extreme heat to be approximately 50%. In FY2026, we are developing with Orange County and other partners a heat action plan. This work will help us pinpoint these impacts down to the neighborhood and household levels by partnering with community-based organizations who know these communities best. | Urban flooding: 2020 was the second wettest year on record in North Carolina and Chapel Hill experienced above-average precipitation. Historically, significant flooding has occurred in low-lying commercial, residential and natural areas located within the Lower Booker Creek Subwatershed area. This area includes housing where marginalized/minority communities, low-income households, and elderly live. We have also experienced flood events downtown and in areas adjacent to our three largest creek systems. We estimate that the total population at risk to urban flooding--whether it be nuisance flooding or a more significant event--to be approximately 21%. In FY2026, we will continue to work on ways of pinpointing these impacts down to the neighborhood and household levels by partnering with community-based organizations who know these communities best. | Drought: With heavier than normal rainfall in 2020, the levels in our water reservoirs were high and have remained stable. However, our area experienced severe drought within the last 10-20 years, where water levels in our reservoirs were dangerously low. For this reason, our local water and sewer authority (OWASA) updated a long-term water supply plan that accounts for future risk, including climate change. We also have interlocal water sharing agreements and conservations regulations for drought conditions. In FY2026, we will continue to work on ways of pinpointing these impacts down to the neighborhood and household levels by partnering with OWASA who is studying water burden.

project_info:
Water management - Stormwater Infiltration Project: https://www.manhattanbeach.gov/departments/public-works/engineering-division/subsurface-infiltration-drainage-project

• Sited along a popular beach in the City of Manhattan Beach
• Designed to meet wet and dry weather Santa Monica Bay Beaches Bacteria TMDL.
• Will capture, pretreat and infiltrate dry and wet weather runoff from ~1500-acre drainage area tributary to the high priority 28thStreet storm drain outfall on the beach.
• Full scale version of successful concept piloted by the award-winning Hermosa Strand Infiltration Trench.
• Key project elements: diversion structure, subsurface pretreatment system for trash, debris and sediment, followed by subsurface infiltration below the beach. Gravity flow.
• Native dune habitat restoration along the length of the project to remove invasive ice plant and replant with native plant community.
Benefits:
• Improved recreational water quality and surfer/swimmer health through 100% reduction of fecal indicator bacteria in captured stormwater
• Up to to 570 acre-feet stormwater capture during 90th% rain year
• Elimination of land-based litter conveyed through MS4
• 2-acres of native dune habitat restoration
• Infiltration of fresh stormwatermay assist in reducing intrusion of shallow saline groundwater due to sea level rise thus protecting subsurface infrastructure from corrosion
• Improved flood management with 4.6 acre-feet of offline storage at the outfall to alleviate tailwater effects on the tidally-influenced storm drain outfall
• Leverages local funding and partnership with The Bay Foundation and Santa Monica Bay National Estuary Program.

climate_hazard: Mass movement: As greater climate change effects are felt, Evanston is receiving and plans to receive greater numbers of climate refugees. Accommodating greater numbers of people who will need shelter and resources will be a challenge. This also puts a strain on government administrative support services and social workers, with the increase in population. | Heat stress: Year after year, we are seeing an increase in days over 90 degrees. This has significant stressor on unhoused community members, those that do not have air conditioning in the home, and outdoor physical jobs. This issue also further underlines the need for an increased clean energy workforce as our region struggles to accommodate the demand for energy efficient and renewable HVAC technology. | Other: Poor air quality: Air quality is shaped by pollution from vehicle emissions, industrial activity, smoke, and building energy utilization. Low air quality can increase risk of, or exacerbate, a variety of health conditions, including asthma, lung cancer, and cardiovascular disease. In 2023 and 2025 Evanston experienced extreme air pollution due to Canadian wildfires. Over three days in July 2025, Chicagoland area was named the worst air quality in the world, and people were advised to stay indoors. However, this is impossible for frontline workers and unhoused community members. | Heavy precipitation: The region has experienced significant increases in rainfall volume and intensity. Of the 6 most rainy Mays 4 have occurred since 2004 with 2019 and 2018 accounting for the top two in terms of inches of rainfall in the 148 years of recorded rainfall history for the region. In 2023, Cook County experienced the 2nd highest level of rainfall in 1 day (7 inches), which resulted in flooding. Buildings and streets were flooded, the Chicago river flow had to be reversed (a historic incident), and rain posed a significant threat to unhoused community members and those with unstable housing who were exposed to the elements. Because Evanston relies upon a regional stormwater utility to treat storm and sewer water Evanston is limited in our mitigation options and strategies. Nearby water control structures were forced to relieve the urban flooding by reversing sewage runoff into Lake Michigan and local beaches were closed due to the presence of E.coli in Lake Michigan. In the future the City anticipates that more intense precipitation will continue to overwhelm the regional system and lead to an increase in overland/surface flooding throughout the City, causing harm to community members that are dependent on public spaces. | Extreme cold: At least twice in the past 9 years, including February - March, 2019, the region experience devastatingly cold temperatures as a part of the now reoccurring Polar Vortex. Climate Change has been blamed for changed the way in which the cold polar air is \'sucked\' down to lower latitudes leading to the extremely cold temperatures which can last for a few days. This extreme cold can kill animals, plants and humans. It impacts our built infrastructure in many ways including freezing and breaking built systems, causing power outages and damaging infrastructure. It can also lead to strain on City crews and utility companies that have to work increased hours to ensure vital services are kept online. It can cause social breakdowns by closing work places, schools and other services that may keep people at home. As with extreme heat, extreme cold impacts frontline workers in the community who cannot afford to stay inside and avoid the cold weather, and are forced to be outside to ensure that the community is safe and taken care of, and that they are earning wages. Those who cannot drive or don't live close to public transportation are forced to walk or bike to their destinations, and be exposed to risks of hypothermia and frostbite. Low-income and unhoused community members are most at risk, with unstable utility and living situations. These situations also put admin service providers, such as Evanston Public Works employees and snow/ice removal contractors, at risk

project_info: Buildings - Green Homes Pilot Project: The City is starting with properties that are most vulnerable to our anticipated climate hazards as well as other vulnerability factors like aged buildings, occupants on fixed incomes or with existing medical conditions that may be exacerbated by their physical living environment. The program focuses on upgrading those properties first to ensure those communities, the ones most in need and likely to benefit from lower utility bills, cleaner indoor air quality and stronger resistance to flooding and extreme heat, are not left out of a more mainstream program. The City has hired an external partner to co-design and then implement the program. The City acts as an adviser and co-implementer in the project but does not administer the funds or enroll participants.

Water management - Button Rock Forest Stewardship Plan: The City has been thinning the forest around Button Rock Preserve since 2004. The last time the City conducted any prescribed burning at Button Rock Preserve was in 2010 to burn slash piles. In March of 2024, the City conducted a slash pile burn and has plans to conduct more burns in the future to improve forest conditions. Since 2004, over 1,200 - 1,300 acres have been thinned to reduce wildfire risk. Mitigating fire risk around Button Rock Preserve is an important strategy for ensuring the City has an adequate water supply, especially in times of drought. The budget ranges between $75,000 - $100,000 annually. Recent wildfire mitigation funding has increased. Numerous local agencies, including Longmont, have collaborated to form the St. Vrain Forest Partnership Initiative to do a cross-jurisdictional mitigation project. 

To continue this work, the City will need to renew and continue $100,000 per year of funding to be effective and protect our water supply. At this point, there is no guarantee that we can continue funding at that level for 2026 and beyond.

Extreme cold: In Longmont, an extreme cold day is any day where the minimum temperature falls below 10.9 degrees Fahrenheit. This is based on the 95th percentile calculation of observed historical data by Colorado State University since 1900. Over the past 50 years, the number of days per year that fall below that value has followed an overall downtrend from about 40 days per year to about 20 days per year. This data was reported in the City's climate risk and vulnerability map. In 2022 Wind Chill Watches and Warnings forced city of Longmont and HOPE staff to increase staff and resources to support existing shelters for unhoused populations. Local low temperatures of -25 to -40 required over 70 - 100 unhoused to be sheltered for 4 days/nights. City of Boulder opened an emergency shelter at the East Boulder Rec Center sheltering an additional 80.

Extreme cold and winter storms are combined so extreme cold and snow are rated the same. | Extreme wind: The National Climatic Data Center's 2013 Annual Summaries indicates that based on state-level tornado data from 1991 to 2010, Colorado ranks 6th for frequency of tornados. The National Climatic Data Center documents 10 incidents of tornadoes and 7 funnel clouds in Boulder County between January 1, 1950, and December 30, 2012. Information on these events is detailed below: September 17, 1953, 3:00 p.m.—Magnitude F1, property damage of $3,000 May 12, 1955, 4:30 p.m.—Magnitude F1, property damage of $3,000 May 17, 1978, 3:45 p.m.—Magnitude F1, property damage of $3,000 April 30, 1980, 11:00 a.m.—Magnitude F1, no property damage October 15, 1980, 6:22 p.m.—Magnitude F2, property damage of $25,000 (roof at Vo-Tech on East Arapahoe) June 5, 1988, 3:25 p.m.—Magnitude F2, property damage of $250,000 June 1, 1990, 5:03 p.m.—Magnitude F0, no property damage June 6, 1995, 4:45 p.m.—Funnel cloud (3 miles south of Lafayette) June 17, 1995, 5:50 p.m.—Funnel cloud (Broomfield) June 20, 1995, 1:47 p.m.—Funnel cloud (4 miles west of city of Boulder) June 16, 1996, 4:15 p.m.—Magnitude F1 (Pinecliff), no property damage July 12, 1996, 7:40 p.m.—Magnitude F0 (Broomfield), no property damage June 6, 1997, 1:15 p.m.—Magnitude F1, no property damage (Other sources indicate a home was damaged in the vicinity of Baseline Reservoir during this event.) May 22, 2008 11:00 am - 3 funnel clouds (Longmont, Erie, and Superior) June 8, 2009, 1:00 p.m. - Funnel cloud (Lafayette) June 9, 2009, 4:35 p.m. - Funnel cloud (Broomfield) June 5, 2015, 6:59 p.m. - Tornado F1 - F3 (Longmont Berthoud), 25 homes damaged | Infectious disease: Vulnerable populations: Children are especially susceptible to Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome, a complication of shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection that can lead to kidney failure. E. coli infections are known to increase in frequency with increased temperature and heat waves. Many older adults and those with underlying health conditions may be more susceptible to severe disease from vectorborne (e.g., West Nile Virus) and waterborne diseases (e.g., cryptosporidiosis) that will increase in frequency due to climate change. Low-income and marginalized populations often live in locations that are prone to climate hazards such as flooding and extreme heat, while also bearing a higher burden of underlying health conditions. Taken together, these populations will be vulnerable to both increased frequency and intensity of climate-related diseases. Vulnerable sectors: Workers in the agriculture sector will be impacted by increased exposure to vectors (e.g., mosquitos and ticks) that expand their geographic range, and potentially introduce new vectorborne diseases into the U.S. (e.g., malaria, dengue). Water supply can be impacted as heavy precipitation and storms can lead to increased runoff into freshwater (e.g., lakes, streams), leading to contamination with parasites and bacteria found in animal and/or human excrement (e.g., crypto, shigella, giardia). Climate related hazards such as flooding and wildfire, may impact conservation efforts by forcing relocation of certain species and changing their natural range; this may expose animals to new vector species and diseases. Human health will be impacted by direct hazards (e.g., flooding, extreme heat) as well as secondary hazards, such as the spread of viral respiratory illnesses in emergency shelters and other congregate settings. 90-100% of the population exposed to the hazard, but level of exposure and which pathogens individuals are exposed to may vary based on where they live and their behaviors.

Boulder County is currently in near-normal precipitation levels, however streamflow has been about 50% of normal this past Spring and Summer. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfires are a common and naturally occurring phenomenon in forested areas and can benefit forest health in many respects. But the climate change trend which is leading to hotter, more widespread, and destructive fires can make it more difficult for the environment to recover, and lead to increased flood runoff or other secondary/cascading hazards. This can severely impact water quality and watershed health for years after a fire. Wildfires occurring in the region can also cause poor outdoor air quality. Tourism, the accommodation and food services industry (e.g. hotels and restaurants), and retail are major components of Boulder County's economy, and Longmont's as well. Wildland fires can, for example, lead to significant tourism reductions due to health and safety concerns, causing lost revenues from lack of visitation, stays in hotels, spending on restaurants and other commerce sources, and more. According to the Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control, 20 of the largest wildfires have occurred in the past 20 years, with 4 out of the top 5 largest wildfires occurring in the last 3 years (2018 and 2020). https://dfpc.colorado.gov/wildfire-information-center/historical-wildfire-information On December 30, 2021 the Marshall Fire began in unincorporated Boulder County. A flood event would most likely result from a heavy rainstorm that stalls over any of the creek basins with increased risk if it stalled over the Fourmile burn area. project_info:
Nature-Based Solutions - Constructed Wetlands
: The project involves the development of a 30,997 square meter constructed wetland in Barangay Sorosoro, Batangas City—home to the largest number of piggery raisers in the locality. The wetland will serve as a natural wastewater treatment facility designed to filter and reduce pollutant loads from piggery and domestic effluents before they reach the Calumpang River.

Through a combination of sedimentation, filtration, and biological uptake by wetland vegetation, the system will significantly lower biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), nutrients, and suspended solids from wastewater. This initiative complements the city's ongoing regulatory measures such as the mandatory use of septic tanks and biogas digesters, thereby strengthening efforts for the rehabilitation and conservation of the Calumpang River.

The constructed wetland will also provide co-benefits, including habitat creation for local biodiversity, improved water quality for downstream communities, and support for Batangas City's climate change adaptation and mitigation goals.

Buildings - Marine Aquatic Resources of Verde Island (MARVI)
: The Marine Aquatic Resources of Verde Island is an educational exhibit that will be located at Bahay Kaalaman, dedicated to showcase the extraordinary marine biodiversity and ecological value of the Verde Island Passage (VIP) — known globally as the 'Center of the Center of Marine Shorefish Biodiversity.'
This museum is envisioned to be the first LGU initiated internationally accredited marine museum featuring in engaging space where students, educators, researchers, and community members can explore the diverse aquatic life and marine ecosystems that thrive around Verde Island. The exhibit aims to foster environmental awareness, marine conservation values, and a sense of pride and stewardship among local stakeholders.
Key features of MARVI include:
1.	Stories and practices of local communities, emphasizing traditional fishing knowledge and sustainable marine resource use
2.	Visual displays and infographics on coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, and fish species found in the Verde Island.
3.	Specimens and models of marine organisms, including shells, preserved species, and replicas.
4.	Multimedia presentations on the importance of marine protected areas and the threats of overfishing, pollution, and climate change.
5.	Interactive exhibits such as touchscreen panels, videos, and augmented reality tools.

The MARVI is designed to make marine learning more accessible, the exhibit will allow visitors to explore the vibrant underwater ecosystems of Verde Island without having to travel there. This will also promote awareness on conservation, sustainable practices, and the vital role of local communities in protecting this globally significant marine corridor. Through the MARVI, the rich marine aquatic resources of Verde Island will be celebrated, understood, and protected for future generations.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Batangas City Calumpang River\nRehabilitation and Development Masterplan: The Calumpang River Rehabilitation and Development Masterplan is a comprehensive framework aimed at restoring the river's ecological health, reducing pollution, and promoting sustainable use of its resources. Urban flooding: Bacolod's flooding issues are a complex problem, such as clogged waterways, aging flood control systems, and rapid urbanization that outpaces infrastructure development. Here are some if the impacts experienced by the vulnerable populations and sectors:

Social and Human Impacts

Displacement and Disruption: Flooding frequently displaces Informal Settler families (ISF's), forcing them to evacuate to temporary shelters like schools and community centers. This disrupts daily life, especially for those in low-lying and coastal areas.

Health Risks: Floodwaters contaminated with garbage, sewage, and other pollutants pose a serious threat to public health which leads to outbreaks of waterborne diseases and create breeding grounds for disease-carrying insects.

Loss of Life and Property: Severe flooding in some parts of the City leads to the tragic loss of lives. Additionally, it causes significant damage to homes and personal belongings, resulting in financial hardship and emotional distress for affected families.

Disruption of Services: Essential public services, including transportation, communication, and access to schools and hospitals, are often disrupted or completely paralyzed during and after a flood.

Economic Impacts

Damage to Businesses and Infrastructure: Flooding inundates commercial hubs, including major streets and business establishments, causing temporary closures and significant financial losses. Infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and power and telecommunications networks can be damaged, leading to long-term economic consequences.

Paralyzed Mobility: Submerged roads and public transport systems make it difficult for people and goods to move around the city, impacting both the local economy and daily life










 | Drought: Drought, especially during the summer months, has significant effects on the vulnerable sectors in Bacolod City. The impacts are most pronounced in the areas of water supply, agriculture, and public safety.

Water Supply Shortage

Decreased Water Sources: Water sources, including rivers, bulk water suppliers, and deep wells, experience a significant decrease in volume. This has a direct impact on the city's water availability, which in the past has fallen below the required daily consumption thus the
deployment of water trucks and tankers to deliver water to the most affected barangays were done to ensure residents have access to potable water for their daily needs.

Crop and Livestock Losses: The drought during summer months in the City causes widespread damage to crops like rice, corn, and sugarcane. This in turn can lead to higher prices for agricultural products in the city's markets.

Health Concerns: The limited water supply and high temperatures can lead to various health issues, including dehydration and heatstroke among the vulnerable sectors. The lack of water for sanitation can also contribute to a higher risk of diseases endangering the population.
 | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Typhoons pose a significant threat to vulnerable groups in Bacolod City, with effects that exacerbate existing social and economic inequalities. The impact is felt across various aspects of their lives, from immediate physical dangers to long-term challenges in recovery and resilience.

Socioeconomic and Livelihood Impacts

Poverty and Economic Disruption: Typhoons disproportionately affect the urban poor, many of whom live in informal settlements in high-risk areas like coastal zones and river easements.

Loss of Livelihoods: Vulnerable groups often depend on jobs that are highly susceptible to weather disruptions, such as farming and fishing.

Health and Housing

Inadequate Shelter and Displacement: The destruction of houses leaves families displaced, often seeking temporary refuge in crowded evacuation centers which can lead to unsanitary conditions and an increased risk of disease transmission. 

Health Risks: Poor sanitation and a lack of clean water during and after a typhoon can lead to outbreaks of waterborne diseases like leptospirosis and other illnesses. 

All in all, the effects of typhoons on vulnerable groups in Bacolod City are multi-faceted and deeply rooted in socioeconomic factors which
go beyond the immediate physical damage to include the long-term erosion of livelihoods, health, and a family's ability to achieve long-term stability and security. | Other coastal events: Storm surges have devastating effects on vulnerable groups of the City of Bacolod. These groups, which include low-income communities, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and those living in informal coastal settlements, are particularly susceptible to the immediate and long-term impacts of storm surges. Some of the devastating effects include the following:

Immediate Dangers and Fatalities: The rapid and massive rise in water levels can lead to drowning, electrocution from downed power lines, and physical trauma from debris. Vulnerable individuals, such as the elderly, those with mobility issues, or those lacking transportation, are often unable to evacuate in time, placing them at an extremely high risk of injury or death.

Property and Housing Destruction: Vulnerable communities in Bacolod City often living low-lying coastal areas in fragile or poorly constructed housing. Storm surges can easily inundate or completely destroy these homes, leading to widespread displacement and homelessness. 

Loss of Livelihoods: Coastal communities frequently rely on livelihoods tied to the sea, such as fishing, tourism, and small-scale trade. Storm surges can destroy fishing boats, equipment, and coastal businesses, leading to a total loss of income.

Water management - Project RIVER-Smart:
Restoration Initiative Valuing Ecosystem Recovery through Smart Tracing of Pollution Pathways and Behavioral Change Initiative


: The Project RIVER-Smart: Restoration Initiative Valuing Ecosystem Recovery through Smart Tracing of Pollution Pathways and Behavioral Change Initiative demonstrates a strategic response to the increasing threats posed by non-conforming fecal coliform levels in Cagayan de Oro City's urban river systems. In 2024, water quality monitoring for fecal coliform of these rivers resulted in a range of 318 to 18,946 MPN/100 mL, which exceeds the 50 MPN/100 mL standard for a Class A river. Thus, Project RIVER-Smart aims to improve the water quality of the Cagayan de Oro River Basin and its adjacent rivers, thereby contributing to the city's goal of providing clean and safe water for humans and the environment.
As a rapidly urbanizing city and the next metropolitan center in the country, Cagayan de Oro faces significant environmental pressures, including water pollution from untreated discharges, challenges in solid waste management, informal settlements along water bodies, inadequate enforcement of sanitation laws and regulations, agricultural runoff from upstream areas, and increasing demand of water supply. These issues challenge the city government and hinder households and communities from enjoying a future with accessible, clean, and safe water, while also providing tourists with well-deserved recreational activities and enabling businesses to maximize investment opportunities. Given these challenges, the scholar emphasizes that restoring and improving water quality is crucial for maintaining ecological integrity, promoting public health, and ensuring the city's economic resilience.
Project RIVER-Smart is a must-see initiative by the City Government of Cagayan de Oro demonstrating how the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2030 strategies can be translated into on-the-ground actions for improved environmental quality. It aligns with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR)'s nationwide coordinated water resource management strategic framework. Additionally, it supports the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 6, which aims to ensure universal access to safe, affordable, and sustainable water and sanitation for all.
The project focuses on five (5) outputs: (1) Reviewed and updated local policy strengthening the septage and sewerage management program; (2) Improved household participation, a behavioral change initiative for sustainable water use and wastewater management at the community levels; Outputs (3) and (4) Internet of Thing (IoT)-based water quality monitoring and data analysis with predictive analytics for informed decision-making; and (5) Forged partnership with academic institutions for project- based learning and internship program, and other key stakeholders. Some identified project risks, including institutional, operational, and environmental, could affect implementation if not adequately addressed.
Given budgetary constraints and the urgency of action, Project RIVER-Smart strategically prioritizes the Cagayan de Oro River Basin as the initial focus area due to its critical ecological and socio-economic importance to the city and Region. The project will run over the next three years, from August 2025 to June 2028, with an estimated total project cost of PHP 9,268,600.00. This will lay the foundation for Project RIVER-Smart, ensuring an enhanced policy framework and community readiness before launching the technology-based component of the project.
Moreover, the scholar aims for this project to equip the city government with data-driven decision-making for more effective resource allocation in targeted ecosystem restoration initiatives.

Urban flooding: Extreme rainfall events and limited stormwater carrying capacity have led to recurrent urban flooding in Kakinada, particularly in low-lying wards and areas adjacent to drains, canals, and coastal water bodies. The city's flood vulnerability is heightened by inadequate drainage networks, encroachments along natural waterways, and tidal inflows during cyclonic conditions. GIS-based flood mapping in the CRCAP shows that several wards—especially in the central, northern, and eastern parts of the city—experience frequent inundation during high-intensity rainfall, with road corridors, slum settlements, and commercial zones repeatedly affected.
Historical patterns indicate increasing instances of localized flooding and prolonged water stagnation, especially during extreme rainfall associated with depressions and cyclones in the Bay of Bengal. Poor solid waste disposal and silted drains further obstruct runoff, exacerbating flood depth and duration. These disruptions affect mobility, economic productivity, and access to essential services, while stagnant water increases the risk of vector-borne diseases.
It is estimated that 9.5% (~17,920) of the total slum population reside in areas with frequent inundation and face heightened vulnerability during rainfall events. Constant exposure to flooding can lead to property damage, health hazards, and displacement. Poor drainage and inadequate infrastructure exacerbate the impact, affecting access to essential services. These communities may struggle with sanitation issues, waterborne diseases, and socio-economic challenges.
Strengthening stormwater infrastructure, improving waste management, and protecting natural drainage channels are therefore critical priorities for Kakinada.
Refer to Sections 5.3.2 of the Kakinada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan. | Extreme heat: Kakinada is experiencing a rising trend in both maximum and minimum air temperatures, alongside a clear increase in land surface temperatures (LST). Historic climate data (1991-2021) shows warming across seasons, while satellite assessments indicate that daytime LST increased from 39.4°C in 2015 to 42.1°C in 2021, with minimum LST rising from 27°C to 28°C in the same period. The highest LST of 42.1°C was recorded at the city's dumpsite, emphasising the intensifying heat island effect.
LST hotspot analysis for 2018-2022 shows that 40.6% (12.87 sq. km.) of Kakinada's area exceeds the mean temperature of 33.5°C, exposing 50.8% of the city's population (2.54 lakh people) to elevated heat stress. Vulnerable groups includes slum residents, households in kutcha or semi-permanent structures, elderly persons, children, women, and outdoor workers are impacted due to limited access to cooling, inadequate housing ventilation, and prolonged exposure to direct heat.

Ward-level patterns reveal that:
- Ward 13 faces extreme temperatures due to the dumpsite and Anchorage port, where industrial activity, heavy vehicle movement, and storage godowns generate substantial heat.
- Ward 10 records high LST due to heat emitted from industrial units and machinery.
- Wards 19 and 20 experience elevated surface temperatures owing to salt farms, whose reflective, vegetation-free surfaces absorb and release heat rapidly.
Heat stress contributes to thermal discomfort, reduced productivity, and increased incidence of heat-related illnesses such as dehydration, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke. Outdoor workers—including sanitation workers, waste handlers, port labourers, construction workers, and street vendors face sustained exposure during peak heat hours. High temperatures also strain basic services by increasing water demand, accelerating septic conditions in drains, reducing waste-handling efficiency, damaging road surfaces, and driving up household energy needs for cooling, further burdening low-income families.
Refer to Sections 5.3.1 of the Kakinada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: Kakinada's coastal location makes it highly vulnerable to strong winds, storm surges, and cyclones. Between 1890 and 2018, the city experienced 22 cyclones, including 7 very severe events with wind speeds of 44-50 m/s. Notable cyclones such as Nilam (2012), Lehar (2013), Hudhud (2014), Phethai (2018) and Fani (2019) caused heavy rainfall, infrastructure damage, and service disruptions. Wards 9-26, along with areas like Dummulapeta, Parlovpeta, Dairyfarm Centre, Yetimoga, and Mahalakshmi Nagar, are identified as highly vulnerable due to their coastal proximity.
Cyclones severely impact low-income households, particularly fisherfolk, whose homes face structural damage and whose livelihoods halt completely during storms. Storm surges cause saltwater intrusion, affecting drinking water and agricultural land. Flooding from overwhelmed drains leads to mobility issues, contamination of water sources, and disruptions to essential services, affecting vulnerable communities with limited coping capacity.
Refer to Sections 5.3.1 of the Kakinada Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

project_info: Transport - Electric Vehicle Strategy: The strategy seeks to deliver sufficient charge points to meet current demand, and will be reviewed in mid-2025 dependent on the levels of uptake of Battery-powered Electric Vehicles both locally and by commuters and tourists. This is considered a proportionate and realistic way of approaching the issue given the relatively low level of car ownership in Blackpool, the desire to achieve mode shift, and the background level of deprivation in the town. The project has secured £1,708,000 capital funding from the national LEVI scheme. It is part of the local transport plan funding delivery phase with an expected roll out of the full scheme commencing March 2025.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Fast Followers: Blackpool's ambition is that within a decade, its economy will be rejuvenated and its carbon footprint minimised. It is planning a series of renewable-powered, efficient, 'edge' data centres which will underpin a new innovation economy. These data centres will be liquid cooled and their excess heat will feed into a new heat network providing a lower carbon heat source to homes and businesses across the town. The Council is looking at innovative business models to share risks among the different stakeholders and ultimately attract investment to accelerate heat generator connections.

climate_hazard: River flooding: Increases in the amount of rainfall in the winter are predicted to increase the area of severe flood risk in Cambridge from the River Cam. Intense rainfall in short periods could lead to flash flooding, with recent experience of flooding in other regions suggesting that rainfall exceeding the local drainage capacity can be as a great a risk as rivers bursting their banks. A predicted increase of 65% in river flows will mean more areas of Cambridge will be at risk of flooding from rivers and those affected could double.\n\nData from the 2021 Level 1 Strategic Flood Risk Assessment notes that 646 properties in the Cambridge area (includes villages outside the administrative boundary of Cambridge) were estimated at risk of flooding during a 1% annual probability river flood (taking into account current flood defences) rising to 942 properties in 2110 (note this document is currently being updated) | Urban flooding: Cambridge is in the top 2% of settlements at risk of surface water flooding in England with around 11,000 properties at risk across Cambridge. Climate change is likely to increase this number as the latest predictions are for a 40% increase in rainfall for the region. Surface water flooding has already had an impact and businesses in the city. Our local hospital, which is a regional healthcare centre, has experienced flooding of its basement following a cloudburst event, which led to the cancellation of all operations. | Extreme heat: Increased summer temperatures could lead to summer heat waves and vulnerable populations in the city are at risk of over-heating and heat-related illnesses. The whole of the city is exposed to extreme heat given the urban nature of Cambridge and the 'heat island effect' although to varying degrees. In July 2019, the highest temperature on record in the UK was recorded at the Botanic Gardens in Cambridge at 38.7ºC. This was exceeded in number of places in July 2022, and a new UK record temperature was confirmed at 40.3 ºC in Coningsby, Lincolnshire. | Water stress: Cambridge sources its water from an aquifer and as a result of low rainfall recharge rates in the aquifer are low. Research carried out by Cambridge Water as part of its Water Resources Management Plan update suggests that without action, the long term sustainability of Cambridge's water supplies will come under pressure from 2031. Cambridge Water's Water Resources Management Plan WRMP24 (March 2025 and available at https://www.cambridge-water.co.uk/media/zadnmcfe/cam-water-resources-management-plan-2024-final.pdf), provides an update on the current situation. In response to this risk the Council has introduced water efficiency standards for all new development in the city and has an officer in place to provide advice to residents facing water poverty. Further work is underway with Government's Water Scarcity Group to develop an approach to water offsetting for new developments. As part of this approach, developers would need to deliver a certain level of water efficiency on-site and then additional water offset would be delivered for example through the retrofit of existing properties. Other projects underway include a water transfer pipeline from Grafham Water and the development of a new Fens Reservoir by Anglian Water and Cambridge Water to supply the area (see https://fensreservoir.co.uk/)
project_info:
Renewable energy - District Heating Scheme: We are working with the University of Cambridge, city centre colleges and Anglia Ruskin University to produce a business case for this project which aims to create a renewable heat network in the city centre by 2030. Both CCC and UoC have many difficult to decarbonise buildings within Cambridge's historic city centre, such as the Guildhall, the Corn Exchange and this project could supply renewable heating and hot water around the city centre providing a solution to decarbonising these buildings, meeting the Council's net zero target. The project has already received £97k and £272,500 Government funding from the Heat Network Delivery Unit (HNDU) in 2022 and 2024. In addition to the grant, additional funding from the group now means that a budget of c£1,000,000 has been made available to fund the feasibility study. To support this energy transition, we have developed technical guidance to help owners and developers prepare to integrate their buildings into the heat network. Updates will follow as the project progresses.

In 2024, we and our partners signed a memorandum of agreement to formalise our commitment to the next stage of the project's detailed development - preferred design and business case.

climate_hazard: Extreme wind: Vulnerable populations: The elderly and children are more likely to suffer from injury due to extreme wind. Marginalised/minority communities are more likely to live in poverty and therefore may lack access to safe housing or may struggle to access services or information that could provide assistance, restricting their ability to prepare and recover - this also applies to low income households. Vulnerable health groups are likely to have existing health conditions or have mobility issues, therefore would be more vulnerable to injury from extreme wind, or other physical impacts. Outdoor workers would experience direct exposure to extreme wind, creating a dangerous work environment, where work may need to be postponed. Frontline workers would have to manage an increase in demand for services.Sectors: Agriculture may be impacted by delivery issues due to road closure from debris. Forestry is negatively affected as extreme winds damage tree stock, and it limits windows for peatland restoration works. Energy supply can be impacted through damage to wind energy assets and other infrastructure, power cuts can arise from damage to powerlines, and energy supply sourcing can be disrupted - this also impacts information and communication systems. Transport may be disrupted due to road closure from debris and an increase in accidents may occur. Water supply may be lost due to extreme winds and raw water quality could be reduced, as a result of debris. Corrosion and decay of plant materials, for water and sewerage systems, is also a risk. Extreme winds increase the risk of injuries and fatalities in construction, so activities may need to be postponed. Service buildings and assets can be damaged, disrupting education. Commercial and private properties could also be damaged. Extreme wind poses a risk to the homeless community, and increases risk of injuries, alongside causing delivery issues, and disrupting health and social care delivery. | Infectious disease: Changes in the climatic trends and extreme events can lead to changes in vector ecology. Wetter and hotter conditions can create conditions which are more viable habitats for species which spread disease (e.g., Ticks leading to Lyme disease). Additionally, these conditions could also see non-native species becoming much more prevalent bringing with them diseases which can be transmitted to humans (e.g., mosquitos). Depending on the type of disease different groups of society will be impacted. However, those most vulnerable include children and youth, the elderly and vulnerable health groups this is due to them being more biophysically susceptible to diseases. Those working outdoors are at more increased risk of being exposed/bitten by insects, and frontline workers will be more exposed to those already exposed to the disease. Therefore, the sectors exposed would be those that provide care to those impacted such as human health and social work activities. Additionally flooding can result in the increased risk of parasites (e.g., cryptosporidium) which can contaminate water supplies and result in negative impact on human health. Extreme temperatures can result in increase in odour and vermin at treatment facilities resulting in increased spread of diseases. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Vulnerable population: Outdoor workers would be vulnerable to wildfires as they would be significantly exposed to increased air pollution if working nearby a wildfire. Frontline workers would also have to manage an increase in demand for services, whilst putting their own health at risk in wildfire areas. Fishing will also be impacted from poor water quality arising from burnt materials entering the water stream. Wildfires may pose risks to transportation due to smoke and poor air quality reducing visibility. Regional electricity transmission may also fail as a result, with key electrical equipment damaged, which would also affect information and communication. Water supply, sewerage and waste management would also be impacted by wildfires as water sources may be cut off or polluted, and pipes damaged. Education may be disrupted by wildfires if communities need to evacuate. | Mass movement: Vulnerable population: Outdoor workers would experience direct exposure to mass movement events, creating a dangerous work environment, where work may need to be postponed. Frontline workers would have to work through extreme cold and may also be unable to wear appropriate clothing or access heating facilities. Extreme cold also increases the risk of freeze thaw, resulting in ground movements that can impact water supply, sewerage, and waste management activities. Pipes in homes also may burst or freeze, cutting off water supply - this also relates to real estate activities. Transportation may be affected by icy/snow covered roads, being potentially dangerous for road users. For education facilities, there would be a reduction in thermal comfort, disrupting education and wellbeing. Accommodation and food service activities may see a reduction in income due to less visitors leaving their homes. Extreme cold poses a risk to human health and can increase demand for social work activities. | Other: Humidity: Vulnerable populations: The elderly and children are more likely to suffer from humidity related illness due their heightened susceptibility to overheating and heat stress - this also applies to outdoor workers, alongside general discomfort. Marginalised/minority communities are more likely to live in poverty and therefore may live in poor condition housing that is more susceptible to mould and mildew growth - this also applies to low income households. Construction, real estate and human health are all affected by increased mould and mildew growth in homes and buildings, which triggers asthma and allergies, but in severe cases also weakens ceilings or walls, undermining the structural integrity of buildings. Marginalised/minority communities are more likely to live in poverty and therefore may struggle to afford higher food or water prices that could arise from drought - this also applies to low-income households. Extreme heat may also increase daily and peak demand for water, increasing pressure on water supply and waste management. Construction workers would be at risk from exposure to heat and construction processes may halt due to extreme temperatures. Transportation may be affected by an increase in road users (due to tourism and changes in active travel usage) and the potential for road surface melting. For accommodation and education facilities, there would be a reduction in thermal comfort, disrupting education and wellbeing. Risks to human health and an increased demand for social work activities. Playgrounds may experience overheating and there would be an increase in public safety concerns. | Heavy precipitation: Vulnerable population: The elderly are at risk as they are biophysically more susceptible to flooding - as are children, less likely to be able to access services - which is further reduced with flooding impacting road infrastructure, may live in single level dwellings, or be on a low income - reducing their ability to respond and recover. Children are also at risk of mental health issues after events, and their education can be disrupted due to school closures. Marginalised/minority communities are more likely to live in poverty, hence may struggle to access services or information that could provide assistance, restricting their ability to prepare and recover - this also applies to low-income households. Vulnerable health groups are likely to have existing health conditions or a lower ability for their bodies to cope with diseases, or have mobility issues. Outdoor workers may be unable to undertake their jobs due to accessibility issues. Frontline workers would have to manage an increase in demand, an increase in health issues associated with lack of and / or poor-quality water, and physical injuries from flooding.Sectors: Agricultural crops and forestry may be damaged if soils become water-logged. These sectors could also be impacted by an increase in pests, pathogens and invasive species. Energy supply and information and communications are at risk from infrastructure damage, flooding and failure. Transportation can be impacted if drains are overwhelmed or if there is damage to retaining walls. Public transport can be disrupted, and road accidents more likely. Flooding can disrupt water supply, overwhelm culverts, and impact water quality. It can also impact sewerage and waste management as sewers are overwhelmed and flooding delays bin collections. Construction is affected as works become dangerous and need to be postponed. Flooding could result in the closure of recreation services and other businesses, which would lead to insurance claims; as would flooding of real estate. Vulnerable assets may also flood, disrupting healthcare and education. Human health and social work could be affected by sewer flooding, damaged council housing, changes in vector ecology, increased service response time, and an increased risk of injury. There is also an increased risk to the homeless community, and a heightened risk to mental health after exposure to the event. | Storm: Extreme weather is becoming more frequent within Kirklees and this has an impact on vulnerable populations due to the potential damage of infrastructure, homes and utilities. Storm events may also cause damage to vulnerable assets/assets where vulnerable members of the community rely on for food, safety, services. This can be through damage to buildings caused by storms, disruptions to vital services and sectors. project_info: Transport - City Region Sustainable Transport Settlements: Increasing EV uptake by giving advice to residents and businesses on converting to EV's. Offer the opportunity to try electric vehicles before buying in a 'non-sales' environment. Allowing residents and businesses to assess the suitability and practicality of EV use. Delivery via a building premises is the first option but proving cost prohibitive currently, alternatively delivered via a car club approach with vehicles placed directly into district centres and neighbourhoods (funded trials). Seeks to use innovative approaches to tackling the issue of providing residential charging facilities in areas of dense terraced housing where little off street parking exists. Working with CPO's to arranged fixed term trials of their infrastructure solutions to evaluate more methodically •\tLooking at infrastructure such as: Gullies, Lamppost, Pop-Up, Charge Arm, Build outs, Subterranean.

project_info: Transport - Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Pilot: Kirklees Council is working with the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, Calderdale Council, Wakefield Council, Leeds City Council and City of Bradford Council on a proposal for the delivery of local electric vehicle infrastructure across the West Yorkshire region, including Kirklees. This pilot project will deliver fast chargers for the public to use and will use innovative procurement methods. As a partnership, the proposal is looking to attract £1.5 million of funding, which the partner authorities will match fund (for a total investment of £3 million). The project supports the transition to EV use in the region, with a particular focus on provision for those without off-street parking. It will provide an improvement in accessible EV charging provision that would not otherwise be met by current or planned EV chargepoint infrastructure. It is hoped that the project will increase consumer confidence in transitioning to EVs across the region, ensuring increased uptake.

project_info: Renewable energy - Heat Decarbonisation Plans: Creating Heat Decarbonisation Plans (HDP's) for buildings would be an essential part of the drive to meet the Council's own district-wide Net Zero target of 2038 plus the wider Leeds City Region West Yorkshire Combined Authority's Net Zero target, with an associated carbon budget, of which the Council is a signatory. This is complemented by the region's 'Energy Strategy and Delivery Plan', which will help the Council prioritise interventions and projects to deliver carbon and energy savings. In particular, the PSDS/LCSF funding streams would help resource the delivery of projects and provide the skills and knowledge for future projects to reduce the Council's own emissions, to reach our Net Zero targets and align with our Action Plan, arising from the Council's Climate Emergency Declaration back in 2019.The Council is currently in the early stages of engagement with a number of organisations that are currently offering potential assistance with developing HDP's. This includes obtaining proposals for consultancy support and site feasibility studies. We are currently going through a process of data sourcing/acquisition and energy audit/assessment to provide a foundation for this work and have applied for government funding (LCSF Phase 3 and 4). HDP's were completed for 14 Council sites on 31/03/23 through LCSF Phase 3. The Council was not successful in the application for LCSF Phase 4 funding. In 2024/25 the Council has been successful in accessing c.£100k of funding from the WYCA NZRA to continue the programme to develop council site HDP's and feasibility studies for all the key council sites.

project_info: Buildings - Huddersfield District Energy Network: Huddersfield District Energy Network (HDEN)- Development of a municipal heat network opportunity providing heat and power from the town's Energy from Waste (EfW) facility to premises in Huddersfield town centre. The Heat Network will play an important part in reducing the carbon emissions from the district's main town. Crucially, this will be primarily through the decarbonisation of heat, which is a much more challenging area of the energy industry to decarbonise relative to electricity. As the infrastructure of the network itself is likely to outlast several sources of heat, it is also considered a key enabling technology for future low carbon heat sources. The Council approved the Outline Business Case for the HDEN in September 2022.
