project_info: Renewable energy - Heat Decarbonisation Schemes: The Council is in the process of developing a pipeline of preparatory work in anticipation of further Government and Local Combined Authority schemes which we expect to be forthcoming and to be ready for anticipated challenging timescales. We plan to use developed decarbonisation plans as prototypes so that plans for all buildings in those building types covered can be developed in anticipation of future funding where the lessons learnt can be applied. In addition, the benefits will be maximised by the sharing of knowledge, for our own team and further teams from across the council, allowing them to be 'upskilled' in the realm of heat decarbonisation. It is intended that the schemes applied for will deliver excellent value for money by being a 'success story' that would bring multiple teams together by fostering collaboration and cooperation over potential new projects arising from the grant funding. Using the experience and skills gained, there would be an increased likelihood of further decarbonisation projects across the council's building portfolio, leading an expected improvement in the success rate and outcomes of funding bids.The buildings identified cover a representative range of public sector building types which are relatively poor-or-average-performing relative to their typical archetype. The buildings identified also represent the geography of the district to ensure as diverse a range of areas as possible; the sites chosen include council sites from across the wider towns and villages of the district. The potential for flagship decarbonisation schemes across the district allows us to take all our communities with us on this journey to decarbonisation, thereby maximising socioeconomic benefits too, as an opportunity for education and development, and as a form of infrastructure investment by breathing new life into old buildings, to ensure no community is left behind.The project cost (£2.5 million) is purely an estimate at this stage, subject to the next funding scheme's application conditions and funding requirements. The authority has been successful in accessing c.£100k of funding to continue the programme to develop council site HDP's and feasibility studies for all the key council sites which will allow us to apply for further funding in the future to continue this work.

Other: Extreme weather events: Extreme weather significantly impacts vulnerable groups and sectors of a city including but not limited to energy, transport, agriculture, water supply and waste management. Dundee City Council's CRVA noted that each of these sectors will 'likely' be impacted in some way or another at varying levels of intensity. For example, extreme weather events such as droughts, floods or storms impact food security; in the energy sector, extreme weather events disrupt service provision; transport systems face disruptions in the form floods and high winds; the supply of clean water can be compromised; and waste management faces challenges with damaged facilities, or the collection and disposal of waste. The impact to such a vast number of sectors undoubtably affects entire populations, where vulnerable population groups are generally more susceptible to climate hazards. | Urban flooding: The high deprivation area or the areas with high Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD) areas in Dundee are also at higher risk of urban flooding. Similar to river flooding urban flooding has serious adverse consequences for human health, the environment, cultural heritage or economic activity in its area. The property in the area are at risk of severe damage and any damage to the property will have big impact of finance, health and mental wellbeing of the community. The roads, community facilities, utilities, the transport network are at risk of urban flooding. The damage to these services and facilities will reduce community's ability to respond and recover from the flooding. Urban flooding also brings risk of infection and spread of disease, contamination to drinking water etc and impacts the vulnerable communities the most. 

Flooding can damage cultural heritage assets such as historic buildings. It may also cause temporary closures of attractions to the public for safety reasons, and longer-term closures if more extensive repairs are needed.

Flooding can impact businesses directly by causing damage to assets and increasing insurance costs. Flooding can indirectly impact businesses by preventing staff, customers and supplies from reaching the businesses.

In addition, climate change may increase the risk of contamination of drinking water through increased runoff and flooding events that overwhelm current water treatment approaches. Risks to health from contact with bathing water (sea, lakes and rivers) and harmful algal blooms may also increase with climate change.

There is a risk of short-term disruption and closure to education if parts of the city are flooded. Some damage may also cause longer-term closure or loss of facilities, impacting on the educational experience. Playing fields could be particularly at risk. Disruption of education has known impacts on children's development. 

Further risks to delivery of health and social care, critical care services, and transport infrastructure disruption. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Since 2009 Councils in Scotland have had a duty to work towards a co-ordinated flood risk management plan to reduce the overall risk of flooding from whatever source. Studies have demonstrated that large areas of Broughty Ferry in Dundee are at significant risk. During a 1 in 200 year event, extreme water levels in the Firth of Tay would exceed the height of the existing defences and cause flooding in the areas of Long Lane and Brook Street. The estimated costs to residents, businesses and infrastructure would be in the region of £97 million with 450 properties at risk. With the new Riverside and Broughty Ferry flood protection scheme this risk has been reduced. 

Sea level and coastal erosion can cause risks to property and assets on the coast if not properly protected. This is also linked with coastal flooding.

Coastal flooding and erosion can cause damage to and permanent loss of land as well as temporary closures of access routes. All these could potentially impact businesses located near the coast. | Storm: Recent storm events such as Storm Arwen in November 2021 had a very damaging impact in Dundee's transport network and trees. Most of the public parks were badly damaged as trees fell and it took several days to clear the paths, roads and railways. Current storm events have showed that outdoor workers, people living in city outskirts, emergency workers and regular commuters were impacted the most by storm. It also exposed the vulnerability of critical infrastructure such as electricity lines and gas networks as many households in neighbouring local authority areas were left without power supply for several days. The elderly, disabled and sick people were at real risk to their health and wellbeing as heating and power were unavailable. Although Dundee's power disruption didn't last for several days or weeks as in neighbouring local authorities, there were several hours of power cuts and many private and public properties in the city were damaged. 

Increased heavy precipitation and storms, including high winds, can cause direct and indirect damage to the building fabric of historically and culturally important buildings. Water ingress and damage to facades are likely. These impacts are likely to be costly and repairs made difficult due to the protected nature of the buildings. 

Storms can have both a direct and an indirect impact on social care delivery. Direct impacts include damage to buildings or facilities. Indirect impacts include wider disruption, i.e. staff commuting or deliveries being prevented or delayed.

Storms including high winds and flash flooding cause disruption to transport or damage to transport infrastructure. | River flooding: The Cycle 1 Tay Estuary and Montrose Basin Local Flood Risk Management Plan 2016 has identified key impacts on vulnerable population. The Cycle 2 Tay Estuary and Montrose Basin (TEAMB) Local Flood Risk Management Plan (LFRMP) has not been published yet as of 2023. The Tay river flooding has serious adverse consequences for human health, the environment, cultural heritage or economic activity in Tay Estuary and Montrose Basin area. The property in the area is at risk of severe damage and any damage to the property will have big impact of finance, health and mental wellbeing of the community. A lot of SMEs in this area are dependant on tourist revenues, any damage to their business can have lasting impact on their business, finance and daily lives. There are railway lines and emergency services are in the flood risk area. The community facilities, utilities, the transport network, designated sites and agricultural land are at risk of river flooding. The damage to these services and facilities will reduce community's ability to respond and recover from the flooding. | Water stress: Water stress in Dundee and across Scotland is becoming an increasingly pressing issue due to climate change, which is driving longer dry spells and more erratic rainfall patterns. This, combined with rising water demand, is straining local water systems. In Dundee, where water use is already high, the impacts could include reduced water availability for households, agriculture, and industry, as well as ecological damage to rivers and aquatic life. These pressures not only threaten public health and economic activity but also risk exacerbating existing social inequalities if not managed equitably.

Future water restrictions would impact businesses, especially those that are water intensive. Production of goods could be slowed or in the worst-case scenario, temporarily closed. | Other: Air Quality: Climate Change is likely to have a negative impact on air quality both directly and indirectly, as higher temperatures are likely to create atmospheric conditions favouring ozone formation. This causes risks to both air quality and health. | Extreme heat: In Dundee, rising temperatures and more frequent heatwaves pose risks to public health, especially in urban areas where the built environment can amplify heat exposure. Research shows that even modest increases in temperature can lead to higher mortality rates, particularly from cardiovascular and respiratory conditions. Vulnerable populations—those with limited adaptive capacity—are disproportionately affected, and without targeted interventions, heat stress could exacerbate existing health and social inequalities. In addition, climate change may increase the risk of contamination of drinking water through increased runoff and flooding events that overwhelm current water treatment approaches. Risks to health from contact with bathing water (sea, lakes and rivers) and harmful algal blooms may also increase with climate change.

Very high temperatures can cause school closures and risk of heat-related illness to children, vulnerable adults (vulnerable to heat) or staff, especially in buildings prone to overheating. 

High temperatures can impact staff and productivity in many ways and cause wider disruption to transport or other infrastructure services that may delay or prevent staff from reaching their place of work. High temperatures can also bring restrictions to working such as longer breaks or breaks during the hottest part of the day. Lack of energy in high temperatures can reduce productivity, especially in physical roles.

Projected increases in summer extreme heat events and higher average temperatures may result in the need for businesses to install cooling or increase cooling capacity. This will have an associated financial cost to the business, for both installation and running.

Historic artefacts often need to be kept within specific temperatures to prevent deterioration. This range is often between 16℃ and 18℃ (though not always). Increasing summer temperatures are likely to make maintaining these temperatures within buildings more difficult. Additionally, warmer winters and increased winter precipitation may increase humidity, also negatively impacting upon these artefacts.

Dundee as a city sees significant winter tourism due to its proximity to areas which focus on winter activities such as skiing at Glenshee. Reduction in cold days and snowfall is likely to reduce the desirability of the region as a destination for winter sports. | Drought: Drought is emerging as a low but potential climate-related threat in Dundee, where changing weather patterns and rising water demand are increasing the risk of water scarcity. Historically perceived as a water-rich region, Scotland is now facing longer dry spells and reduced rainfall, which strain ecosystems, agriculture, and infrastructure. In Dundee, drought could disrupt local water supplies, impact industries such as farming, and degrade nearby wetlands and biodiversity. The East coast, including Dundee, is particularly vulnerable due to its reliance on agriculture and private water supplies

There is an increased risk to infrastructure from drought, as drought may cause severe drying and cracking of the ground. Subsidence may then occur, threatening subterranean water infrastructure located in these areas. | Extreme cold: Low temperatures in Dundee pose significant risks to public health, particularly during prolonged cold spells. Although the climate is generally temperate, cold-related mortality remains a concern, especially among vulnerable groups. Research shows that extreme cold increases the risk of death from respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Cold weather also exacerbates existing health inequalities, particularly in deprived areas, and can lead to increased energy costs, reduced mobility, and isolation—factors that compound vulnerability.

Beyond health impacts, low temperatures can also affect critical infrastructure. Digital networks, including telecommunications systems, may suffer disruptions due to cold-induced damage, while subterranean assets are at risk from freeze-thaw cycles that can compromise their integrity. Transport infrastructure is similarly vulnerable; frost and snow not only hinder mobility in the short term but can also accelerate long-term wear and reduce asset lifespan. Despite projections of fewer extreme cold events in the future, the residual impacts of low temperatures remain a significant concern for urban resilience and service continuity in Dundee.

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Delivery: The Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategies (Scotland) Order 2022 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/sdsi/2022/9780111053935) puts an obligation on the Council to prepare and publish its first Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy (LHEES) and its first LHEES delivery plan on or before 31 December 2023. The LHEES is the long-term plan for the decarbonisation of heat and tackling fuel poverty. The analysis includes identification of heat network opportunity areas and heat network zones; identification of the most suitable low and zero carbon technologies for heat decarbonisation of on-gas properties; identification of measures to improve fabric efficiency of buildings and removing poor fabric energy efficiency as the cause of fuel poverty. In Dundee the LHEES is integrated with Local Area Energy Plan. The Local Authority's LHEES was formally adopted in April of 2024 and the accompanying Delivery Plan was approved at Committee in November 2024.

Other: All climate related community projects are eligible - Dundee Climate Fund: The Dundee Climate Fund has been set up to support community-led climate change projects. It's based on a model called Community Choices where citizens will decide how to spend a budget that supports the delivery of the City's Climate Action Plan. The Dundee Climate Fund started with a total of £750,000; where £250,000 is revenue and £500,000 is capital funding. The Dundee Climate Fund is split into a number of funding rounds over a period of four years and is designed to raise awareness of Climate Change while supporting communities to identify and vote on local projects aimed at delivering on the following themes: 

Energy: reducing consumption, promoting energy efficiency, use of renewables

Transport: encouraging active travel, decarbonising transport, Waste: reducing waste, recycling, reusing resources

Resilience: improving greenspaces, biodiversity, local food growing and, 

Community Engagement: increasing public awareness, engaging communities and young people in Climate Change. 


The fund has already completed two successful rounds of funding and delivery, with the latest round awarding £326,255 to 10 projects across the city. Dundee Climate Fund opened its third round (3.0) with approximately £106,000 available.

Round 3.0 received 22 applications, resulting in 6 awarded projects and 3,092 public votes, with winners to be announced shortly. Additionally, there is potential to reclaim underspent funds, which could be reallocated to support an outstanding Round 3 project.

project_info: Renewable energy - Dundee Caird Park Heat Network Extension: Dundee City Council has completed a feasibility study that looked into extension of existing Heat Network in Caird Park which runs on ground source heat pump and back-up gas fired CHP . The study has concluded that there is an opportunity to improve the performance of an existing Heat Network by utilising the existing spare capacity in the Caird Park energy centre. This can be achieved by extending the existing heat network across the golf course to connect to a cluster of large buildings. Extending the Network could require ~2,385 m of additional heat network distribution pipework, resulting in an overall linear heat density (LDH) of 3.36 MWh/m.yr. The project has potential to reduce up to 98 % of current emission (around 1500 tCO2e / year). The project is part of an ambition to develop a city-wide heat network to supply low carbon heat.

project_info: Other: Energy Systems - Delivery of the Local Area Energy Plan: Dundee City Council is collaborating with partners through Regional Energy Systems Optimization Planning (RESOP) project (https://www.ssen.co.uk/news-views/2020/2020-ssen-partners-with-dundee-city-council-resop-project/) to develop a Local Area Energy Plan. The plan is Dundee's whole-system approach to decarbonising all components of the local energy system in line with the city's ambition of becoming Net Zero by 2045 or sooner. The aim of the LAEP work is to carry out analysis of technical potential for renewable energy generation; waste and low carbon heat sources; future buildings (domestic and non-domestic) heat and electricity demand mapping and forecasting; analysing and forecasting transport (public, private and heavy goods vehicle) electrification, uptake and charging infrastructure roll-out; and carry out Heat Network analysis. Dundee's LAEP is unique in a sense that it is developed in parallel to statutory LHEES and is being visualised in WebGIS tool called LAEP+. The integration with LHEES means the LAEP is imbedded within statutory plan, has stringent data, has a transparent public engagement approach and a robust monitoring plan. The LAEP identifies the scenarios required for the city to reach net zero.\n\nA copy of the plan can be found here: https://www.dundeecity.gov.uk/reports/agendas/ceb230924.pdf

Transport - Eden Active Travel Connections: The Eden Active Travel Connections project in Dundee is a planned initiative to improve access to the upcoming Eden Project site, located at the former gasworks on East Dock Street. The core aim is to promote active travel—such as walking, cycling, and wheeling—as the main way for visitors to reach the Eden Project. This aligns with broader sustainability and urban regeneration goals, ensuring the development is not just a destination but a well-connected part of the city's transport network.

Dundee City Council is working in partnership with the Eden Project to re-develop a former gasworks site at the eastern edge of Dundee City Centre into a world-class visitor attraction, expected to receive over 500,000 visitors per year and create hundreds of jobs. Anticipated to open in 2030, the Eden Project Dundee will be a transformative development for the city, serving as a beacon for regeneration and green tourism, and combining exhibits, performances, learning, play, immersive experiences, world-class horticulture, live music, art and food, beverage and retail spaces.

The Eden Project Dundee site is located north of East Dock Street, approximately a mile east of Dundee City Centre. Both Eden and Dundee City Council aspire to promote sustainable transport as the main mode choice to the site, and car parking on-site will be limited to disabled bays. Walking, wheeling or cycling will form an important part of most people's journey to the site, but connections for these active travel modes are currently limited. 

The project proposes a network of new and improved routes that will connect the Eden Project to key parts of Dundee. To overcome barriers like the busy East Dock Street and nearby railway, the plan includes infrastructure such as a potential new pedestrian and cycle bridge, which would improve direct access between Eden and the Dundee waterfront area. The emphasis is on creating routes that are not only safe and direct, but also comfortable, attractive, and accessible for people of all ages and abilities.

Beyond transport, the project also plays a role in place-making and urban design. It seeks to improve the overall look, feel, and function of the areas surrounding Eden by making them more walkable and better connected. These enhancements are expected to benefit not just Eden visitors, but also local residents and businesses. In doing so, the project helps to integrate the Eden Project into the wider fabric of Dundee's cityscape, contributing to long-term regeneration and sustainable development.

Transport - Dundee Sustainable Transport Corridors: The Dundee Sustainable Transport Corridors initiative is a far-reaching plan by Dundee City Council to improve transport sustainability, promote active travel (walking, cycling), strengthen public transport, reduce carbon emissions, and better connect communities across the city. 

The Dundee Sustainable Transport Corridors (DSTC) project aims to improve Lochee Road and Arbroath Road. The plan is to build better infrastructure to encourage people to travel in more sustainable ways. These improvements will help the community by making it easier to get around, help protect the environment and improve people's health.

Arbroath Road and Lochee Road have been chosen as key corridors due to their potential to encourage sustainable travel. The area supports a large population, has high bus use, and has existing transport infrastructure.

The DSTC project will improve travel in Dundee by making buses and active travel (like walking and cycling) a priority. This plan follows the goals of the Dundee Sustainable Transport Delivery Plan and other national and regional policies.

Other: Public Engagement and Awareness Raising - Dundee Climate Action - Engaging Vulnerable Communities: A mobile engagement hub is being developed as a multipurpose, mobile event space to raise awareness of key environmental and sustainability issues—such as flooding, biodiversity, air quality, and sustainable lifestyle choices—tailored to local neighbourhoods in Dundee. The hub will prioritise community outreach, accessibility, and inclusivity, aiming to understand local needs and provide support, advice, and expert-led sessions. It will focus on reaching all members of the public, especially marginalised groups such as low-income households, refugees and asylum seekers, with information available in multiple languages.
The project includes a dedicated schools programme involving students and teachers in the design and delivery of fun, interactive learning activities, alongside training for educators. It will also engage with local businesses and begin building a trusted, recognisable brand as a reliable source of information. Dundee City Council is leading the project in partnership with Voluntary Action, Eden Project, Dundee Science Centre, and the University of Dundee's School of Accounting.

The funding will be used to cover staff time, the purchase and design of the mobile event space and materials, subsidies, and will be spread over five years for the proposed duration of this project.

Efforts focus specifically on developing clean energy policy and action plan for sustainable energy for the Nakuru County.

Heavy precipitation: The municipality of SÃ£o Leopoldo grew and prospered on the banks of the Rio dos Sinos, occupying a large part of its floodplains and its relationship with this river and its hydrological and climatological cycles significantly marked the history of the population. The city is affected by cycles of water scarcity at certain times of the year, and on the other hand, it suffers from torrential rains that cause flooding at other times. This new climatological regime with large rainfall gives us the false impression that we are not experiencing a state of water scarcity, however, the drought occurs not due to the reduction in rainfall, but rather, due to the irregularity that appears. Among the cities in the Vale dos Sinos region, SÃ£o Leopoldo is the only municipality in which the river cuts through densely populated areas that historically suffer from devastating floods. For this reason, a flood protection system was built in the past. composed of a set of dikes, macro drainage channels and a pumping system that protect a large part of the central region of the city, 4 neighborhoods in the southwest zone and 5 neighborhoods in the north zone. This important system allowed the municipality to grow and currently, its perfect functioning, as well as its modernization, constitutes an important adaptation action to the effects of climate change. The Professor of Climatology at the Department of Geography at UFRGS, Francisco Eliseu Aquino, warns about the impacts of climate change in Rio Grande do Sul that "Within the scenario of global environmental and climatic changes, the increase in temperature in South America has contributed to the formation of more intense rain, consequently, storms, and also heat waves, droughts and cold waves. The State has always had the four seasons of the year well defined. What we observe is that the intensity of these phenomena is increased and, of course, the sequence of these events become important. The State is expected to suffer over the next five decades from these climate increases.' Between 1961 and 2006 the average temperature in Rio Grande do Sul rose from 18.6 ÂºC to 19.1 ÂºC, which corroborates the increase in extreme events decade after decade. Between 2010 and 2018, around 11 extreme heat events were recorded, while the last 5 decades have recorded an average of 4 events every ten years. According to the Adapta Brasil Platform, there is a projection of an increase in relative air humidity. | Water stress: Among the trends for Rio Grande do Sul, one is a significant change in the precipitation regime, with prolonged periods of drought, interspersed with others of large volumes of rain in a short space of time. The water deficit during periods of scarce precipitation and the problems caused by intense precipitation (floods, flooding, landslides and erosion) have negative impacts on both urban and rural areas.â In the last eight years (2003 to 2010), the Civil Defense of Rio Grande do Sul recorded the occurrence of extreme weather events related to lack or excess of rain, with some type of loss, in 458 municipalities in the State, which represents more than 90% of the total number of municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul. Of the municipalities affected, 20 recorded only events related to excessive rainfall (flooding, flooding, flash floods and/or flooding), 262 events associated with lack of rainfall (drought and/or depletion of water resources), and 176 (around 40% of the total municipalities affected) presented at least one occurrence of each type. Water scarcity will require sanitation operators to invest in their water supply systems, considering water capture alternatives and reviewing water treatment and transport parameters. Pumping systems, in particular, need to be reviewed in order to meet consumption needs in light of new operating conditions, such as, for example, the level pump suction. On the other hand, it is urgent to invest in programs that promote the reduction of physical losses and energy efficiency as a way of mitigating impacts and adapting cities to climate change, making them more resilient. At the same time that operational conditions are changing, requiring investments in infrastructure, it is urgent to universalize access to drinking water and sewage treatment as an impact mitigation strategy. The occurrence of water-borne diseases is increased by extreme heat events and water scarcity, causing an increase in deaths resulting from the combination of these two factors. Also according to MCTI's Adapta Brasil Platform, the water stress impact index currently 0.47 for the municipality tends to increase to 0.67 from 2030, configuring a high impact index. The main factor influencing the index is the population exposed to the volume of water available in the basin. | Heat stress: The city experiences alternating waves of intense cold and periods of extreme heat, in natural cycles. But the intensification of these extreme events is becoming more and more present. The summer of 2018/2019 was recorded as one of the hottest summers in the climate history of Rio Grande do Sul (official maximum in 56 years). In addition to this, we have all the social and environmental implications of this situation and the care that must be taken during periods of extreme heat, with public health, for example, especially with elderly people or people with fragile health, dehydration, opportunistic diseases and also risks linked to UV radiation levels that are very high in extreme heat, on the other hand, reduced performance at work, greater energy and financial expenditure on thermal comfort, risk of fires. In addition to directly impacting agricultural production, the economy and the availability of resources. | River flooding: The increase in heavy rainfall rainfall over the last decade, according to indicators shown on the adapta Brasil platform, a data source that guides climate adaptation actions in the municipality, culminated in the great flood of 2024. The flood hit SÃ£o Leopoldo between April and May 2024 and was one of the biggest in the city's history and caused severe damage throughout the region. The event was caused by extremely intense rains that fell over the Rio dos Sinos basin, causing the river and its tributaries to overflow. Although the city had a flood protection system â such as pump houses and dikes â, the volume of water was much higher than the capacity of these structures, which led to the flooding of several neighborhoods.
More than 180,000 people were directly or indirectly affected by the flood. Approximately 34 thousand homes suffered flooding, many of which were completely taken over by water. Public services were interrupted, schools and health facilities were closed or destroyed, and several families were left homeless or displaced. The city hall declared a state of public calamity, and a large part of the urban infrastructure was damaged, including squares, streets and public buildings.

The causes of the flood are mainly linked to the abnormal volume of rain and insufficient containment barriers. In some points, dikes were overcome or compromised, and drainage pumps had to be turned off when they reached their operational limits.

After the disaster, the municipality began a series of emergency and reconstruction actions. Public areas were cleaned, debris was removed, roads were restored and damage was surveyed. In addition, the city council began investing in works to raise dikes, reinforce flood defenses and improve the drainage system. Projects to support affected families and companies were also implemented. The city has an urban drainage plan and the restructuring of the protection system against floods is under review and under analysis by all municipalities in the river basin due to the regional nature of these initiatives.

The 2024 flood left profound marks on SÃ£o Leopoldo, both from a material and social point of view, and reinforced the urgency of prevention, climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure actions in the region.

In addition to the proposal for shared management and sanitation plans aimed at meeting treatment demands, we intend to integrate several initiatives and actions to make management more effective, including the protection and prevention of extreme weather events due to the effects of global warming.

Heavy precipitation: The municipality of SÃ£o Leopoldo grew and prospered on the banks of the Rio dos Sinos, occupying a large part of its floodplains and its relationship with this river and its hydrological and climatological cycles significantly marked the history of the population. The city is affected by cycles of water scarcity at certain times of the year, and on the other hand, it suffers from torrential rains that cause flooding at other times. This new climatological regime with large rainfall gives us the false impression that we are not experiencing a state of water scarcity, however, the drought occurs not due to the reduction in rainfall, but rather, due to the irregularity that appears. Among the cities in the Vale dos Sinos region, SÃ£o Leopoldo is the only municipality in which the river cuts through densely populated areas that historically suffer from devastating floods. For this reason, a flood protection system was built in the past. composed of a set of dikes, macro drainage channels and a pumping system that protect a large part of the central region of the city, 4 neighborhoods in the southwest zone and 5 neighborhoods in the north zone. This important system allowed the municipality to grow and currently, its perfect functioning, as well as its modernization, constitutes an important adaptation action to the effects of climate change. The Professor of Climatology at the Department of Geography at UFRGS, Francisco Eliseu Aquino, warns about the impacts of climate change in Rio Grande do Sul that "Within the scenario of global environmental and climatic changes, the increase in temperature in South America has contributed to the formation of more intense rain, consequently, storms, and also heat waves, droughts and cold waves. The State has always had the four seasons of the year well defined. What we observe is that the intensity of these phenomena is increased and, of course, the sequence of these events become important. The State is expected to suffer over the next five decades from these climate increases.' Between 1961 and 2006 the average temperature in Rio Grande do Sul rose from 18.6 ÂºC to 19.1 ÂºC, which corroborates the increase in extreme events decade after decade. Between 2010 and 2018, around 11 extreme heat events were recorded, while the last 5 decades have recorded an average of 4 events every ten years. According to the Adapta Brasil Platform, there is a projection of an increase in relative air humidity. | Water stress: Among the trends for Rio Grande do Sul, one is a significant change in the precipitation regime, with prolonged periods of drought, interspersed with others of large volumes of rain in a short space of time. The water deficit during periods of scarce precipitation and the problems caused by intense precipitation (floods, flooding, landslides and erosion) have negative impacts on both urban and rural areas.â In the last eight years (2003 to 2010), the Civil Defense of Rio Grande do Sul recorded the occurrence of extreme weather events related to lack or excess of rain, with some type of loss, in 458 municipalities in the State, which represents more than 90% of the total number of municipalities in Rio Grande do Sul. Of the municipalities affected, 20 recorded only events related to excessive rainfall (flooding, flooding, flash floods and/or flooding), 262 events associated with lack of rainfall (drought and/or depletion of water resources), and 176 (around 40% of the total municipalities affected) presented at least one occurrence of each type. Water scarcity will require sanitation operators to invest in their water supply systems, considering water capture alternatives and reviewing water treatment and transport parameters. Pumping systems, in particular, need to be reviewed in order to meet consumption needs in light of new operating conditions, such as, for example, the level pump suction. On the other hand, it is urgent to invest in programs that promote the reduction of physical losses and energy efficiency as a way of mitigating impacts and adapting cities to climate change, making them more resilient. At the same time that operational conditions are changing, requiring investments in infrastructure, it is urgent to universalize access to drinking water and sewage treatment as an impact mitigation strategy. The occurrence of water-borne diseases is increased by extreme heat events and water scarcity, causing an increase in deaths resulting from the combination of these two factors. Also according to MCTI's Adapta Brasil Platform, the water stress impact index currently 0.47 for the municipality tends to increase to 0.67 from 2030, configuring a high impact index. The main factor influencing the index is the population exposed to the volume of water available in the basin. | Heat stress: The city experiences alternating waves of intense cold and periods of extreme heat, in natural cycles. But the intensification of these extreme events is becoming more and more present. The summer of 2018/2019 was recorded as one of the hottest summers in the climate history of Rio Grande do Sul (official maximum in 56 years). In addition to this, we have all the social and environmental implications of this situation and the care that must be taken during periods of extreme heat, with public health, for example, especially with elderly people or people with fragile health, dehydration, opportunistic diseases and also risks linked to UV radiation levels that are very high in extreme heat, on the other hand, reduced performance at work, greater energy and financial expenditure on thermal comfort, risk of fires. In addition to directly impacting agricultural production, the economy and the availability of resources. | River flooding: The increase in heavy rainfall rainfall over the last decade, according to indicators shown on the adapta Brasil platform, a data source that guides climate adaptation actions in the municipality, culminated in the great flood of 2024. The flood hit SÃ£o Leopoldo between April and May 2024 and was one of the biggest in the city's history and caused severe damage throughout the region. The event was caused by extremely intense rains that fell over the Rio dos Sinos basin, causing the river and its tributaries to overflow. Although the city had a flood protection system â such as pump houses and dikes â, the volume of water was much higher than the capacity of these structures, which led to the flooding of several neighborhoods.
More than 180,000 people were directly or indirectly affected by the flood. Approximately 34 thousand homes suffered flooding, many of which were completely taken over by water. Public services were interrupted, schools and health facilities were closed or destroyed, and several families were left homeless or displaced. The city hall declared a state of public calamity, and a large part of the urban infrastructure was damaged, including squares, streets and public buildings.

The causes of the flood are mainly linked to the abnormal volume of rain and insufficient containment barriers. In some points, dikes were overcome or compromised, and drainage pumps had to be turned off when they reached their operational limits.

After the disaster, the municipality began a series of emergency and reconstruction actions. Public areas were cleaned, debris was removed, roads were restored and damage was surveyed. In addition, the city council began investing in works to raise dikes, reinforce flood defenses and improve the drainage system. Projects to support affected families and companies were also implemented. The city has an urban drainage plan and the restructuring of the protection system against floods is under review and under analysis by all municipalities in the river basin due to the regional nature of these initiatives.

The 2024 flood left profound marks on SÃ£o Leopoldo, both from a material and social point of view, and reinforced the urgency of prevention, climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure actions in the region.

Other: Other, please specify - Sobral Green and Blue Infrastructure System (IVA): The Green and Blue Infrastructure (IVA) proposal, the structuring project of the Sobral Master Plan Review, envisages urban resilience actions through the creation of an interconnected and multifunctional system of green areas and urban waters that integrate the use of technologies inspired by natural processes with existing urban infrastructures.

The IVA was selected to form the group of projects that were mentored by the World Resources Institute (WRI), through the Nature-Based Solutions Accelerator (SBNs) program in cities, providing surveys that made it possible to estimate the budget and its impacts on the population (in)directly impacted by the intervention.

Regarding the reduction of
disaster risks, the proposal includes actions aimed at the infiltration and runoff of rainwater,
such as detention basins, rain garden systems, rainwater beds and bioswales,
siltation of water bodies, with a view to reducing the probability of floods and flooding.

The main benefits of these actions consist of the social inclusion of the local population, promoting the enjoyment of qualified public spaces and a better relationship between residents and the Riacho.

As for the potential positive impacts of implementing the Green and Blue Infrastructure System, we have: within the scope of the Pilot Project, based on urban afforestation, the renaturalization of the body water resources and the recovery of riparian forests, an estimated reduction of 51,360.60 tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2eq). In financial terms, the Project will be able to avoid, in total, R$ 6,441,421.28 by 2050 due to the capture of carbon in the atmosphere.

In total, according to data from the Municipal Health Department (SMS) from 2023, 85,234 inhabitants could be impacted directly or indirectly by the implementation of the Project, of which 44,680 are women and 11,594 are children in the range ages 0 to 9 years old.

ICMS also contributes to achieving the goals of the Agenda2030 by relating its interventions to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 02 - Zero Hunger and Sustainable Agriculture; 06 - Drinking Water and
Sanitation; 11 - Sustainable Cities and Communities; 13 - Action against Global Climate Change; 14 - Life in Water; and 15 - Terrestrial Life.

project_info:
Buildings - Sustainable public buildings - water: The sustainable municipal buildings project is linked to water consumption; its main objective is to reduce and optimize water consumption in municipal facilities, such as government buildings, parks, stadiums and other spaces managed by municipal entities. The purpose is to promote sustainable and efficient practices in the use of water, minimizing waste and maximizing the conservation of this vital resource. Project proposal (summary):The project will focus on implementing a series of measures and technologies that promote responsible water consumption in municipal facilities. Below is a summary of some of the proposals that could be included in the project:
1. Rainwater collection and reuse: Rainwater harvesting systems will be installed on the roofs of municipal buildings. This water will be collected, treated and reused to garden watering, cleaning and other non-potable needs.
2. Improvements in the efficiency of irrigation systems: Smart irrigation technologies, such as humidity sensors and automatic programmers, will be implemented to optimize water use in green areas and municipal gardens.
3. Installation of water-saving devices: Taps and sanitary devices will be replaced with more efficient models that reduce water consumption without compromising the quality of service.
4. Awareness and education: Awareness campaigns will be carried out aimed at municipal employees and citizens to promote responsible practices in the use of water, providing information about the importance of conserving this resource and advice to reduce its consumption.
5. Monitoring and management of water consumption: A system will be implemented to monitor and control water consumption in municipal facilities, with the aim of identifying usage patterns, detecting leaks. and take corrective action in real time.

Renewable energy - Solar panels in municipal public buildings; Neighbor Care Center: The installation of solar panels in municipal public buildings in Peñalolén, or anywhere else, can be a very beneficial option. Peñalolén is a commune in the Metropolitan Region of Chile, and the implementation of solar panels in its municipal public buildings could have the following specific benefits:
1. Taking advantage of the sunny climate: Chile has an excellent solar resource due to its geographical location. Peñalolén, being in the Metropolitan Region, also has a high potential for solar energy generation. Solar panels on public buildings would take advantage of the abundant sun and enable significant generation of clean, renewable energy.
2. Reduction in energy costs: The implementation of solar panels in Peñalolén's municipal public buildings could reduce energy costs in the long term. By generating electricity through the sun, the municipality can reduce its dependence on the conventional electrical grid and potentially save on electricity bills.
3. Example and leadership: The installation of solar panels in the municipal public buildings of Peñalolén would send a strong message about the municipality's commitment to sustainability and the use of renewable energy. Municipal leadership in the adoption of solar energy can inspire other sectors, businesses and residents to follow suit and consider installing solar panels on their own properties.
4. Contribution to emissions reduction: By generating electricity from a clean and renewable source, solar panels help reduce greenhouse gas emissions and the municipality's carbon footprint. This is especially important to address climate change and work towards a more sustainable city.5. Energy resilience: The installation of Solar panels on municipal public buildings can strengthen the energy resilience of Peñalolén. During emergency situations or power outages, solar panels allow buildings to continue functioning and providing essential services thanks to the local generation of electricity. It is relevant to highlight that in Peñalolén, through the agreement made with Google Environmental Sight, we can obtain the solar potential of the buildings, so we are advanced in viability and we would need to evaluate the availability of the roof of each of the premises through a technical organization. And based on that, have an adequate financial plan assuming the installation and maintenance costs.

project_info: Water management - Water efficiency green areas of Peñalolén: Peñalolén is a commune that has worked hard to increase and maintain green areas in its territory. This work has brought with it innumerable associated benefits, which impact the quality of life of all its inhabitants. Parallel to this, conserving these green areas brings with it great challenges. Due to the social characteristics of the commune and the needs of the citizens, unfortunately there are large losses of water in these areas. Some due to theft, others due to carelessness and a large percentage due to leaks that are impossible to identify, are part of the causes of this problem. For this reason, the aim is to install a control system in alliance with the company (TECPA) that allows controlling the volume of water used in each green area. With this, it is hoped to improve the service and protect this privileged resource.

Reduction in energy costs: The implementation of solar panels in Peñalolén's municipal public buildings could reduce energy costs in the long term. By generating electricity Through the sun, the municipality can reduce its dependence on the conventional electrical grid and potentially save on electricity bills.3. project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Strengthening inclusive recycling program: This program helps to dignify and make official the work of grassroots recyclers in the community, people who manage to support their families thanks to this work. Their work consists of recovering and recycling waste from the homes of the commune, revaluing it and incorporating it into the chain of use and providing it with adequate management (they group, treat, repair and sell these products to generate their salary.). For this reason, strengthening and improving the conditions and tools of this program would not only make it more effective and efficient, but would also help improve the work quality of recyclers and increase their opportunities. In addition to this, they contribute to more people generating responsible habits with respect to waste, reducing the amount of waste that goes to landfills and the associated GHGs. It is necessary to provide better conditions to recyclers, thus improving their work quality.

project_info: Water management - Care and protection of the underground water network: Groundwater is the most abundant source of fresh water in the commune, reaching 97% of unfrozen fresh water. It corresponds to 30.28% of the global available physical water reserve. These are an important part of the water cycle and the basis of water security. project_info: Renewable energy - Communal energy management. Solar schools: The aim is to complete the work carried out in 6 public schools in the commune, replicating this initiative in the rest of the municipal schools and ideally encouraging private schools to invest in photovoltaic solar panels, solar thermal panels, heat pumps and LED energy. Then be replicated in all public areas of the commune (municipal and health buildings). Finally and over time, it seeks to bring this business and technical model to the residential area. With this, children from the most vulnerable communities in the commune can benefit, accessing technologies that are out of their reach.

Solar panels on public buildings would take advantage of the abundant sun and enable significant generation of clean, renewable energy.2. Reduction in energy costs: The implementation of solar panels in Peñalolén's municipal public buildings could reduce energy costs in the long term. project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Home Composting Program: In Chile each person generates 1.2 kg of waste per day, with around 58% organic. Currently, the recovery rate achieved by this waste is only 1%, therefore strategies are sought that favor the circularity of this waste so that it is not disposed of in landfills, thus reducing the environmental problems associated with it. \nWith this, Peñalolén has promoted the Municipal Composting Program, which includes the delivery of composting and vermicomposting kits for the sustainable management of organic waste on a household scale, in addition to a support and training plan to ensure the traceability of the initiative. \nTo improve the data, scalability and replicability of the initiative, continuous improvements are sought, such as generating an automation system that allows data to be obtained in real time.

Other: Citizen participation and climate empowerment - Climate Democracy Accelerator: It is an initiative of the People Powered organization that seeks, through local governments, to strengthen citizen participation, including marginalized communities, in the formulation, design and implementation of climate policies.

The central purpose is to promote a just climate transition through participatory methods, ensuring that decisions on mitigation, adaptation, clean energy, transportation, land use, etc., respond to the real needs of people, not just experts. or authorities.

Collaborative work is established, through mentoring, online courses and live sessions, to design a project that promotes the initial objectives, through citizen participation methodologies.

The proposal for a 'Community Environmental Initiatives Competition' was designed, where 3 work areas were established; Responsible pet ownership Protection of biodiversity and sustainable management of waste and gardens. The population is invited to apply for environmental projects, where they participate for a financing of up to $920,000 Chilean pesos (the total project fund is $3,000,000, the idea is that there are multiple initiatives) for the implementation of their initiative, this through accompaniment and monitoring by professionals from the municipality.

project_info: Renewable energy - Community Scale Solar PV and Storage: Description: One or multiple grid‐connected, ground‐mounted utility‐scale solar photovoltaic (PV) fields located within the Town boundaries that feed renewable electricity into the local grid. The total installed capacity modelled in the CEIP is 12MW, installed in 2021. Ownership of the facility is local, returning revenues into the community.Objective: Generates clean electricity locally in order to offset the rising electrical demand caused by electrification as the community's building stock and vehicle fleet transitions away from fossil fuels (fuel oil, gasoline, diesel), while at the same time reducing demand on the regional electrical grid. Combined with a gradual increase in local battery storage, this supports the integration of locally‐generated renewable electricity into the grid.Rationale: As a town with relatively high population density for Nova Scotia standards, the community of Bridgewater has limited vacant land on which to deploy wind turbines, currently the largest source of renewable electricity in the province. Due to the proximity of homes and businesses, solar is therefore the preferred large‐scale source of renewable electricity. With a significant, and growing, electrical base load due to its commercial, institutional and industrial facilities, the local grid has room to absorb locally‐generatedrenewable electricity, and sufficient land parcels exist to deploy one or more large array.

project_info: Renewable energy - District Energy System: Description: A district heating system that supplies heat and cooling to the downtown core of Bridgewater. The system modeled in the CEIP sources its energy from 50% sustainable biomass (through a CHP application) and 50% from geothermal/river water heat pump. The system connects commercial, institutional, and industrial facilities, and is gradually expanded over a number of years.Objective: Generates clean, highly efficient heating and cooling energy in order to offset the rising electrical demand caused by electrification as the community's building stock transitions away from fossil fuels, while at the same time reducing demand on the regional electrical grid.Rationale: Energy systems planning is becoming critical to practical and responsible neighbourhood design or redesign. For Bridgewater this means the development of district energy system in the downtown core. Already, the Town has been approached by developers interested in providing district energy services for the community. In 2016, due to a regulatory vacuum governing district energy systems, the Town amended its Land Use By‐Law (Sections 8.2.4 and 8.1.1) to allow “sustainable energy systems that provide direct heat and/or power to a permitted institutional use” in anticipation of such an application at a local educational facility that would eventually expand to provide district energy services. While the development is still in the pre‐application stage, the Town has been proactive in defining what “sustainable energy systems” means, including, among other actions, by commissioning a study by the Mersey Tobeatic Research Institute on the feasibility of supplying locally‐harvested sustainable biomass to the community for the purpose of large‐scale district energy generation.

Loss of green space/green cover: More than two thirds of the Metropolis's land is respectively occupied by natural spaces (forests, rivers, wetlands, etc.) and agricultural spaces. Urban spaces represent a final third of the territory (29%), and are located mainly along the banks of the Seine and on the northern and eastern plateaus of the Metropolis. 

More than half of this urbanized area is dedicated to residential spaces, 23% to major facilities and road infrastructure, and 21% to economic activities. This land use has been evolving for several decades. Between 1999 and 2023, it is estimated that nearly 2.8% of the territory has been urbanized, resulting in the consumption of more than 1,883 hectares of natural, agricultural and forest areas. These figures demonstrate both the diversity of land use in the Metropolis and significant âurban sprawlâ. This galloping urbanization makes the territory more vulnerable to climate change and contributes to amplifying its effects and consequences (urban heat islands, floods, erosion of biodiversity, fires, drought, etc.). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): The combination of droughts and heatwaves increases the risk of forest and vegetation fires as happened in 2019 in a coniferous forest in the commune of Petit-Couronne. This event highlighted in particular the absence of measures to manage the risk of forest fires on a national scale (firebreak strips or forest roads for firefighters, for example). This phenomenon was also particularly notable in 2022 in France and Normandy. Even if the territory of the Rouen Normandy Metropolis was spared, numerous vegetation fires broke out near the territory (more than 800 hectares burned in the Eure department, 20 hectares in the commune of Montigny). In the future, the territory will become more sensitive and vulnerable to this risk. | Heat stress: At the scale of the Rouen Normandy MÃ©tropole, the MÃ©tÃ©o-France station in Rouen-Boos shows a trend towards a statistically significant increase in air temperature of 2.2Â°C over the period from 1970 to 2020. 

By 2100, climate projections at the scale of the Rouen Normandy MÃ©tropole indicate an increase in average annual air temperatures between  2Â°C (RCP 2.6) at  4Â°C (RCP 8.5) and surface waters of around 2Â°C on average over the entire Seine basin.

The number of hot days (> 25Â°C) is expected to increase on average, between 20 and 40 days in 2050 (RCP 2.6 and 8.5) by 2050, and between 20 and 40 days (RCP 2.6) up to more than 60 days in 2100 for an RCP 8.5 scenario. The average number of tropical nights is also expected to increase from 2 nights (RCP 2.6) to 14 nights (RCP 8.5) on average per year. | Heavy precipitation: In the territory of the Rouen Metropolis, the effect of runoff resulting from heavy rains is aggravated by urbanization and soil erosion. On June 4, 2022, flash floods were caused by torrential rain and led to a death in Rouen.

In the future, climate projections show that episodes of heavy precipitation should be more frequent, increasing the risk of runoff flooding and the resulting consequences. | Urban flooding: An inventory of the main historical floods recorded was carried out by the Seine-Aval Public Interest Group using archives. This work has shown that flooding and submersion are not exceptional episodes. These are classified into 4 types: fluvial, maritime, fluvio-maritime and under the effect of runoff aggravated by urbanization and the movement of the soil and the rise of the water table. 
In addition, per capita costs can also
be relatively high, particularly in
municipalities located on the outskirts of urban centers or rural areas to the north and east of Duclair and Rouen. On the scale of the Rouen Normandy Metropolis, the effects of climate change on water resources are multiple: increase in atmospheric temperature leading to warming of water in rivers, reduction in the average annual flow of the Seine and rivers, drop in the average annual recharge and the level of groundwater, rise in sea level, etc. These changes will have repercussions on the level of the Seine and its tributaries, and the groundwater (chalk tablecloth) from which the samples are taken. This would result in greater and more frequent restrictions, consequently generating conflicts of use between industry, drinking water supply and agricultural activities. In addition, under the effect of the increase in episodes of extreme precipitation and the phenomenon of blocking of flows by the rise in the level marine, the metropolitan area's vulnerability to flood risk could increase, exposing a larger share of the population. All municipalities in the Rouen Normandy Metropolis are subject to the risk of flooding, in one or more forms: overflowing of watercourses, flooding by runoff, flooding by rising water tables. Finally, the warming of water and the reduction in flows of the Seine and rivers will affect water quality, as well as aquatic environments and life.
 | Water stress: The local IPCC has noted the following impacts of water stress on the territory's forests: â¢ the maintenance of native species depends on the evolution of climate change and forest management â¢ a change in forest landscapes â¢ a change in practices in terms of forest management for adaptation â¢ a social consensus to be recreated on the role of the forest and the prioritization of its functions | Biodiversity loss: Biodiversity is particularly rich in the Rouen Normandy Metropolis for an urban territory. In 2023, there were 5,658 species recorded. Animals represent the majority (70%), followed by plants (29%). The most threatened species are those which are restricted to cool environments and which thrive in the northern regions of France and Europe. The Seine is home to around 40 species of freshwater fish, and the presence of migrants is an indicator of water quality. However, Atlantic salmon and European eels are in decline, due to the increase in water temperature on the one hand, then the presence of dams, the destruction of spawning grounds (reproductive zones), or even because flow rates are changing. 
The territory also has 16 species of amphibians, 55% of which are threatened. In particular the spotted pelodyte or the natterjack toad, two rare species, which are losing their habitat, or the common frog, a species today in sharp decline due to increasing temperatures. 9 species of reptiles are also recorded. The Peliad viper, once common, is now in sharp decline due to global warming.
Plants are divided into two groups. On the one hand âthe vascular floraâ that is to say with vessels circulating the sap. In the Metropolis, there are 909 native species, 27% of which are threatened with extinction. Among them, the Rouen violet, the intermediate iberis and the Neustria biscutelle which are found nowhere else. On the other hand, non-vascular plants, grouped under the name of bryophytes in the broad sense. The best known are foams. 
 | Extreme cold: The longest and most severe cold waves occurred before the 2000s.
In Rouen, there has already been a significant reduction in days of cold and frost (minimum daily temperature less than or equal to 0Â°C) of 23 occurrences on average between 1971 and 2020, with an average trend ranging from 58 days to 35 days. Likewise, the number of days of severe frost (minimum less than -5Â°C) declines markedly between the period 1971-1990 for which 155 cases are recorded, and the current period 2001-2020 with 97 cases recorded. Finally, very cold weather (minimum below -10Â°C) is becoming rarer in the region and the Rouen region is no exception. Between 1971 and 1990, a total of 22 cases were observed while only 6 occurrences were noted from 2001 to 2020, with a last appearance in February 2012 (-12.1Â°C on February 12). In general, the trend in cold waves tends to decrease
but with significant interannual variability as evidenced by the year 2010 which was also particularly snowy in Normandy.

Climate projections also show a reduction in the number of days of frost until 2050 in connection with continued warming. From 2050, this trend varies depending on the scenarios considered. This phenomenon could still occur in an optimistic scenario (RCP 2.6), while it would show a further decline of around 19 days and 27 days on average by 2071-2100 respectively for the median (RCP 4.5) and pessimistic (RCP 8.5) scenarios. By 2100, very cold phenomena (minimum temperature below -10Â°C) should no longer occur (or exceptionally), extreme cold (minimum temperature below -5Â°C) would also become very rare (between 0 and 4 days in Rouen). Cold days (minimum temperature less than or equal to 0Â°C) would also be reduced, both in a scenario of low greenhouse gas emissions (RCP 2.6: 32 days in Rouen) and even more in a scenario of high emissions (RCP 8.5: 14 days in Rouen).

project_info: Landscape and Jurisdictional Approaches - Ecological Recovery and Transition Contract: By Prime Minister's Circular No. 6231/SG of November 20, 2020, the French State displays its ambition to contract with each territory a short, medium and long-term ecological recovery and transition project in the areas which correspond to its needs and the objectives of the State's territorialized policies. This ambition is materialized by the implementation of a unique contractual tool, the Recovery and Ecological Transition Contract (CRTE). The Metropolis is very committed to the subject of ecological and social transition through its PCAET, its Ecological Transition Contract, its COP21 approach and this commitment must be strengthened in the months and years to come with all of its partners and stakeholders in the territory, including the municipalities. Also, the conclusion of a CRTE, and its operational variation per share until 2026, makes it possible to establish a first framework clarifying the various financial interventions of the State in the short term as part of the recovery and to prepare its support in the coming years. Furthermore, the reflections undertaken within the framework of the Seine Axis have made it possible to identify strong common issues of ecological transition between the Le Havre and Rouen territories, which can respond to the problem of CRTE. Also, a joint contract between Le Havre Seine Métropole and the Rouen Normandy Métropole and the State was carried out and covers the following issues: - developing clean and efficient public transport and facilitating travel in the territory; - accelerating the energy transition of the territory; - restoring ecological functionalities to anchor the attractiveness of the territory; - promoting a circular economy and land sobriety; - strengthening social and territorial cohesion; - strengthening territorial attractiveness thanks to wealth heritage and an ambition shared cultural;- ​​lead transformations of the industrial-port landscape for a qualitative city-port interface.

climate_hazard: River flooding: Impacts of river floods are similar to Flash/surface floods; however, river floods cause considerable erosion and sedimentation which causes instability in river banks, and requires clean-ups when occurring in developed areas. Also, when the river level exceeds that of streets, water flows into the combined sewer system and mixed sewage backs up into residential basements. The unprecedented rainfall events have caused severe damage to city infrastructure and businesses and homes. The St. Joseph River crested at a history 12.7 feet in February of 2019. The city suffered flood damage to five pedestrian trails and its water filtration systems North Pumping Station in Leeper Park. The waste water treatment plant was inundated and had to shut down, with collected sewage bypassing the plant and directly discharged to the river. The city already has spent about $157,400 to remove flood debris, stabilize the river's banks, and repair pumps and electrical systems. The impact of that single river flooding event led to the damage of nearly 2,000 homes across the region. Residents of Northshore Triangle neighborhood were hit hard from a river flooding event in 2018. New measures have been implemented with the support of new and or deepened partnerships with private engineering firms and federal assistance. Backwater gates for example were attached to the end of stormwater outfall pipes, preventing the river from backing up into sewer pipes when river levels increase ($100,000).South Bend partnered with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for the installation of real-time river gauges for remote viewing of floodway mapping ($222,000). The city has adopted two new approaches for communicating river flooding events with the public. During flooding events Public Works takes over the city's homepage to communicate with the public using maps, and information regarding preparation of resources. The department also recently joined NextDoor, the app that notifies subscribing residents by email and text, with plans to use it to quickly provide flood information to people. Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment provides projections of future conditions for St. Joseph County. https://ag.purdue.edu/indianaclimate/indiana-climate-report | Extreme heat: According to the Notre Dame Urban Adaptation Assessment South Bend, IN is at a higher risk to increased extreme heat. While it is not uncommon for the temperature to exceed 37°C in the summer statewide annual average temperatures have increased by 1.2°F since 1895, and are projected to continue rising. Excessive heat and humidity negatively affects air quality, and increases the occurrence of heat-related health issues like dehydration or heat stroke, which particularly affects the elderly, children, those with chronic health conditions, and those without air conditioning in homes - these four groups make up a relatively large proportion of South Bend's population. Residents who live without air conditioning may also find themselves seeking alternative cooling locations for relief. The City and other partners are responsible for costs of cooling centers and shelters. Those that are without a vehicle are exposed to being outdoors waiting on public transportation thus are also seen as a vulnerable population as it relates to extreme heat. The cost of cooling homes and businesses will also increase considerably as it takes more and more energy to maintain a comfortable indoor climate. Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment provides projections of future conditions for St. Joseph County. https://ag.purdue.edu/indianaclimate/indiana-climate-report | Snow and ice: Heavy snow is very common in the winter, which can hinder citizens' mobility and require significant public resources. However, residents of South Bend, and public systems, are well-adapted to heavy snows. Snow is influenced by weather systems as well as the hydrology of nearby Lake Michigan. Heavy snowfall is projected to be incrementally replaced with rain as regional temperatures continue to rise. Indiana winters are unpredictable. The entire city of South Bend is affected by heavy snow causing a myriad of issues especially for commuters. Road closures from heavy snow are common as well as power loss due to downed lines from heavy snowfall on adjacent trees. Power outages for the region has in the past swelled to nearly 20,000 homes in the Michiana region as in the storm of November 2018. School closures impact the 18,110 students resulting in loss of school days. The School Board has however initiated e-learning days so that students are able to continue their learning and work from home during climate events. Our disabled population under 65 is a little over 12,000 residents with the elderly population over the age of 65 being approximately 13,000 residents. These individuals are at a greater risk of immobility and access when heavy snowfall occurs. Transpo buses may abandon or detour some routes. South Bends local businesses slow down in sales during heavy snowfall as well. Predictions show much more of a mix of rain and snow in future winters. This has its own risks. Destructive flooding in February 2018 was caused by rapid increase in temperature melting 18+ inches of snow already on the ground, which saturated the ground, followed by a moderately heavy rainstorm which was unable to be absorbed. Swings in precipitation also negatively impact revenue from in-town and nearby snow sports such as ice skating, cross country skiing, tubing, and downhill skiing. Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment provides projections of future conditions for St. Joseph County. https://ag.purdue.edu/indianaclimate/indiana-climate-report | Urban flooding: Because South Bend has a combined sewer system and the water table of the region is rather high, streets and sewers can become overwhelmed by heavy rainfall which causes flooding, particularly in low-lying residential areas. In addition to extensive damage to public and private property, this can also become a health hazard because of increased indoor mold, increased unprocessed sewage discharged to St. Joseph River or basements, and increased populations of waterborne pests like mosquitoes. Floods after heavy rains in 2015 washed out numerous public streets, collapsed basements, and required multiple rescue operations, requiring financial and personnel resources to be diverted from basic public services. We expect the hazards experienced in the past to inform priority needs for the City's Long Term Control Plan. Although not in direct response to flooding but water quality, the City's Long term Control plan aims to reduce combined sewer overflows by quantity and frequency. As a result, the Long Term Control plan will address the health and wellness needs of vulnerable populations and resources/businesses that serve them in addition to providing some remediation in relation to flooding. The city is committed to a Long Term Control Plan and use of green stormwater infrastructure and smart cities technology that will minimize sewage discharge that may also indirectly mitigate flooding. Indiana Climate Change Impacts Assessment provides projections of future conditions for St. Joseph County. https://ag.purdue.edu/indianaclimate/indiana-climate-report | Heavy precipitation: Increased rain events are expected to affect already vulnerable populations. Precipitation has increased by 15 percent over the past century. Severe rain events saturate the ground causing tree, building and infrastructure damage. Heavy rain events also can negatively impact water resources through increasing agricultural runoff as well as river floods and flash floods. Future projections show occurrence of downpours to be uneven throughout the year but also are expected to be more frequent. This uneven distribution alters water quantity and its availability for farmers as well as overburdening the city's combined stormwater/sewer system. project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Urban Tree Canopy: The City has established a goal for 40% urban tree canopy coverage by 2050, which equates to the planting of at least 100,000 trees. As part of this effort, the City has also established an urban tree canopy fund. The City is exploring the development of a urban tree canopy campaign to increase tree canopy in the westside and southside of the City. In 2023, City was awarded a $1.8 million grant from the USDA that will support the development of a tree nursery and the scaling of tree canopy expansion throughout the city. The City also established a separate fund for tree projects funded from local grants to support forestry needs that are traditionally not supported through department budgets.

The County's Resilient Environment Department announced a two-year countywide planning effort in 2022 focused on building community resilience to the impacts of climate change predicted over the next half-century, with a primary focus on flood and heat mitigation. This effort is being undertaken with the collective support of municipal and business leaders who meet annually to discuss the resilience needs of the Broward community, the impacts of sea-level rise, more intense rainfall and clean energy initiatives needed to reduce the overall extent of climate change. This project is overseen by the County's Chief Resilience Officer and was designed to address flood mitigation needs across the Broward landscape, with a focus on water management infrastructure, transportation systems, critical infrastructure, basin-level redevelopment and land use. Recommendations are expected to include new water management strategies, expanded surface water storage, additional green infrastructure, infrastructure hardening and relocation, as well as redevelopment strategies. The project also seeks to address the impact of rising urban temperatures through priority use of green infrastructure, such as additional green space and bioswales for improved stormwater management and treatment. Plan development is supported by a steering committee consisting of diverse private sector and community representatives, with extensive participation of local municipalities, water managers, agency partners and public input. Upon completion, the plan is expected to provide the basis for a multi-decade resilient infrastructure and redevelopment plan to serve all of Broward County. Updates on the planning process and opportunities to participate will be posted on the Broward County website.
