project_info: Other: Air Quality - Air Quality Framework: The WMCA is in the process of developing a regional Air Quality Framework, understanding the actions that need to be taken to radically improve public health, and environmental, outcomes for people and places across the region. A high-level options paper has already been produced, indicating a potential 122 interventions that could be taken at a local, regional and national level to improve air quality in the West Midlands. Alongside the development of the Air Quality Framework, which is nearing completion, the WMCA has been successful in securing £1.4 million from DEFRA and DLUHC to support delivery of some Framework options in relation to sensor network, data presentation and behaviour change. Using this funding, in January 2025 the WMCA launched a region-wide sensor network, with 90 sensors monitoring PM2.5. The network is aiding in providing greater spatial resolution on air pollutant concentrations, helping WMCA and local authorities to gain a greater understanding of air quality within the region, at the same time providing the public with easily accessible information on concentrations through a public-facing data platform. The WMCA has also ran 7 behaviour change campaigns on air quality, with a range of trials put in place to test what worked, and which best suited the regional needs, before we look to scale these up. The WMCA also ran a small grant funded programme for the local community to improve air quality and awareness and developed an air quality literacy programme. At the time of writing (2025), the AQ literacy has been completed by over 90 people. The WMCA has an air quality lead to deliver the programme and the Defra funding. This funding will be an excellent start in delivering improved air quality for the region, but further funding will be required to ensure the ambitious air quality targets that will be outlined in the air quality framework, are met.

project_info: Other: Strategy and action planning - Five Year Plans: The WMCA's first Five Year Plan for achieving net zero by 2041 was adopted in 2021. The first plan set out targets for 15 intervention areas which would be required in order to achieve net zero emissions.\nThe WMCA is currently undergoing the development of its second Five Year Plan. As part of this, a review was carried out of the first plan, identifying areas where a different approach is required in light of the lessons learned over the past five years. In particular, the second plan will emphasise ways in which the WMCA can champion a place-based approach to decarbonisation, and in doing so maximise the wider co-benefits. The pathways and scenarios modelled in the second plan will also be more focused on the programmes already funded for local and combined authority delivery in order to highlight the funding shortfall to government to lobby for greater devolution.\n

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Energy Innovation Zones: Five Energy Innovation Zones developed in the region aim to fast-track new clean energy technologies and smarter infrastructure. The resulting energy innovation projects are creating opportunities for smart homes, energy efficiency, retrofit and combined heat and power solutions; microgeneration, storage and flexibility services; smart charging, fuel cells and vehicle to grid technologies, as well as identifying ways to achieve industrial decarbonisation. The Black Country initiative, supported by UKRI and the local partnerships, will move the region's industrial areas towards zero carbon by creating local energy hubs, where Black Country manufacturing technology will be showcased. Investment opportunities lie in design, planning, construction and operation of the energy hubs. Birmingham's TEP, at Tyseley, is a private / public partnership developed by Webster and Horsfall's 300 year old manufacturing business, in partnership with University of Birmingham, and shapes infrastructure for renewable heat and power, energy storage, clean transport fuels in combination with advanced waste processing. climate_hazard: Extreme wind: The West Midlands is likely to experience strong gale force winds over the course of a year. In 2020, 2021 and 2022 we have seen disruption to the transport network and some localised property damage from storms Ciara, Dennis and more recently Storm Eunice. Storm Eunice caused localised property damage, falling trees, the temporary closure of school and over 15,000 homes left without power in the West Midlands. In future, with greater extremes in prospect, it is likely that incidences of severe winds will increase in magnitude. This poses challenges to the transport sector, and to those in sub-standard housing. It can also pose a threat to the energy and telecommunication network. This can have negative consequences for emergency response and public health outcomes. It is worth noting that periods of high wind often occur alongside periods on heavy rain and therefore further compound identified risks. | Extreme heat: The 2003 heatwave served as a warning of what is likely to become more frequent in the West Midlands with unmitigated climate change. The West Midlands had an estimated 90-130 excess deaths during this period. Being a largely urban area, heat waves are amplified by the urban heat island (UHI) effect which in 2003 pushed average temperatures 3C higher than the neighbouring rural areas. It is suggested that the UHI contributed up to 52% of heat related mortality. During the 2003 heatwave, ambulance call outs in Birmingham increased by a third. Globally, average temperatures are 1C higher than in 1850, and if we continue to emit greenhouse gases at today's rate, that could be 5C by the end of the century. Under a high emission scenario, we could reach 4C as soon as 2065. Research using median estimates for increased temperatures, in conjunction with the effect of the UHI, and population projections, predict heat related mortality will rise by 53% in the 2020s and 209% in the 2080s compared with the 2003 heatwave. According to the 2018 UK Climate Projections, annual temperatures in the West Midlands are expected to rise between approximately 1.2C by the 2050s and between 1.3 and 2.4C by the 2080s from a 1981-2000 baseline; as a result extreme heat will occur more regularly.In July 2021 the Met Office issued its first ever 'Extreme Heat Warning' for the West Midlands for a heatwave that covered the Midlands region. In July 2022 the Met Office issued a 'Red Extreme Heat Warning' for the West Midlands. A note accompanying the alert warned of health effects on vulnerable people as well as heat exhaustion and sunburn for the wider population. During the July 2022 extreme heatwave, the West Midlands also experienced wildfires. Increased water scarcity will also cause higher demand and raise water prices, affecting access for lower income households. This is likely to push many of those living under a current 'moderate risk' into a higher risk category. In the West Midlands, in winter, rainfall is expected to increase by approximately 6% by the 2050s and by between 9% to 14% by the 2080s from a 1981-2000 baseline, depending on global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Rapid rainfall can lead to damaging surface flooding. Flooding poses a risk to many aspects of society and infrastructure, including housing, schools, health infrastructure, transport infrastructure and waste services. A recent case study, economic analysis of the 2023 flash floods found that July 2023 was the UK's sixth wettest July on record, with an average rainfall of 120.4mm across England. Roads were flooded across the WMCA area, with Birmingham suffering particularly badly. Businesses were reported to suffer from flooding during this period. The July 2023 flooding event resulted in 80 properties being flooded, with associated property damages. Whilst this was the largest cost of this event (2.5m), there were also economic (societal) impacts from the projected impacts of flooding on mental health (0.26m).\n\nThe WMCA are working with the University of Birmingham to develop its understanding of the lived experiences of urban flooding felt by the most vulnerable communities and wards in the region. This should enable to the WMCA to build its evidence base

project_info: Renewable energy - Investment Zones: In March 2023, the Government launched an Investment Zone programme across eight Combined Authority areas in England, including the West Midlands. This initiative aims to bolster priority sectors through additional funding, business rates growth retention, and tax incentives to stimulate private sector investment. The WMCA has designated its Investment Zone to support advanced manufacturing, with a focus on electric vehicles, battery technology, digital, green industries, sustainable construction and healthtech. Additionally, the WMIZ supply chain transition programme aids businesses in shifting to these new emerging green industries, further supporting the region's net-zero goals. The WMIZ's commitment to green sectors is evident, with two of the three Investment Zone sites being dedicated to developing green industries, engineering, and technology, (Wolverhampton's Green Innovation Corridor and Coventry and Warwick Gigapark) driving forward the green agenda, economic growth, job creation and skill development in these key sectors that would contribute to greater climate security in the future.\nThe West Midlands Investment Zone seeks to transform our regional economy, creating 30,000 jobs, catalyzing £5.5 billion in private sector investment, with £1.5bn business rate growth retained for reinvestment into sites and wider economic growth across the region. climate_hazard: Drought: In the George Municipality, the impacts of drought are evident across multiple sectors, with particularly severe effects on vulnerable population groups. Water supply challenges during droughts lead to stringent restrictions, impacting households that rely solely on municipal water sources. Drought exacerbates the financial strain on low-income households by leading to increased water costs and restrictions, which are particularly burdensome for those earning less than R 4,000 per month. Many of these households lack the means to access alternatives such as bottled water or rainwater harvesting systems, leaving them vulnerable to water shortages. With 54.1% of residents living in poverty, the rise in living costs due to drought pushes these households further into economic hardship, intensifying food insecurity and reducing spending on other essentials. Additionally, the economic downturn caused by drought, coupled with loadshedding and broader recessionary pressures, has led to increased unemployment, particularly among low-skilled workers. The agricultural sector, which contributes around 3.1% to the George GDP, faces significant stress due to prolonged drought conditions. Reduced water availability and rising input costs, such as fertilizer influenced by the Russian/Ukraine conflict, threaten crop yields and livestock productivity. Sewage and waste management systems are also strained by drought conditions, with reduced water availability affecting waste treatment efficiency which may adversely impact the operation of sewage infrastructure. Low-income and marginalized communities, who may already have limited sanitation facilities, face increased health risks from inadequate waste management. This situation exacerbates the existing vulnerabilities of these populations, particularly those already dealing with poor living conditions. George Municipality has 10,175 registered patients in the area that receive antiretroviral therapy. The number of registered patients undergoing TB treatment grew by 14.9% per cent, from 1 162 in 2020/21 to 1 335 in 2021/22. Maintaining adequate sanitation is therefore crucial for maintaining health and preventing infections. Poor sanitation can lead to increased exposure to waterborne diseases, which is particularly dangerous for those with compromised immune systems. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Wildfires are a common occurrence in South Africa and often cause significant damage. The worst wildfires to date occurred in June 2017, impacting parts of the Garden Route in the Southern Cape. The George Municipality has also faced severe wildfire events, highlighting its vulnerability to fires as a climate hazard. In the Outeniqua Mountains around George, wildfires from late October to early November 2018 were the largest in recorded history, burning about 80,000 hectares, killing eight people, and leaving many homeless. The dangers of fighting fires in these remote areas were further emphasized by the death of a helicopter pilot. These fires followed the Knysna fires of 2017. The George Municipality is in the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hotspot for the fynbos biome. This fire-adapted ecosystem depends on fire for seed germination and flowering. However, the increasing frequency and intensity of wildfires, worsened by climate change, threaten to exceed the biome's ability to recover, causing economic damage. Over 70% of the Cape Floral Region has already been lost to land use changes, with climate change adding more stress. Species like Proteas are at risk, affecting industries related to wildflower harvesting and exports. Rising temperatures and reduced rainfall are likely to increase wildfire frequency in the region. Although the fynbos vegetation is adapted to fire, the aftermath poses serious risks to local wildlife and ecosystems. For instance, nectarivorous birds like the Orange-breasted Sunbird and Cape Sugarbird are affected by the loss of their food sources. After the Outeniqua fires, many young, Orange-breasted Sunbirds were found in poor condition, likely displaced from their habitats. | Urban flooding: In June 2011, The George Municipality recieved 120 mm of rainfall in 24 hours. In Septermber 2015, 63 mm of rainfall was received. From 22-24 November 2021, George received 149 mm of rainfall. Of this, the most disruptive rainfall was experienced on 22 November, where 105 mm of rain was recorded within 2 hours. The damage from flooding in 2021 alone was R238 Million. Increased intensity of extreme flooding events has been idientified as a climate change impact that affects and will continue to affect the region. | Biodiversity loss: Wildfires, increased rainfall intensities and frequency, and rising coastal storm surges and sea levels are major climate hazards that have caused, and continue to cause, significant biodiversity loss in the George Municipality. Wildfires, which have become more frequent and intense, disrupt local ecosystems and wildlife habitats. The destruction of vegetation not only affects plant species but also impacts the animals dependent on those plants for food and shelter. For example, fires in the Outeniqua Mountains have led to the loss of critical habitats for nectarivorous birds such as the Orange-breasted Sunbird and Cape Sugarbird, which rely on specific flowering plants that are damaged or destroyed by fire. These changes disrupt ecological balance and reduce biodiversity in affected areas. Increased rainfall intensities and frequency have led to severe erosion along watercourses. Residential dwellings in these areas are experiencing ongoing erosion, prompting the need for hard infrastructure stabilization measures. Such interventions, while mitigating immediate erosion risks, often exacerbate ecological damage by disrupting natural sediment transport and water flow patterns, which are crucial for maintaining diverse aquatic and riparian habitats. Similarly, along the coastline of George, increased coastal storm surges and sea level rise have caused significant coastal erosion. Primary dunes, which play a vital role in coastal ecosystems by providing habitat for various plant and animal species, have been transformed into hard infrastructure such as gabion and sand walls. These defensive measures, while intended to protect against further erosion and flooding, alter the natural coastal processes and degrade habitats. The loss of primary dunes affects the plant species adapted to these environments and disrupts the ecosystems that support a variety of coastal wildlife. Additionally, the growing trend of using boreholes for water supply, especially during droughts, has exacerbated the strain on local water resources. Borehole extraction depletes groundwater levels and can lead to the degradation of wetland areas, which are critical for maintaining biodiversity. Wetlands support a diverse range of plant and animal species and is important for water filtration and flood regulation. The overuse of boreholes during periods of low rainfall reduces the availability of water for these ecosystems but can also lead to land subsidence and changes in groundwater fl | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Coastal flooding due to sea level rise and increased storm surges is becoming increasingly severe along the Western Cape's coastline, particularly in low-lying areas of George such as Herolds Bay and Wilderness. These coastal urban areas have been experiencing significant impacts from rising sea levels, storm surges and extreme weather events, leading to widespread damage and safety concerns. In Herolds Bay, recent storm surges have resulted in roads being submerged and properties along the beachfront sustaining damage. The waves during these events have been powerful enough to impact infrastructure and force closures of affected areas. Similarly, Wilderness has faced extreme conditions, including tragic incidents such as the loss of a life due to the strong waves and storm conditions. The beaches in George, including Wilderness, have been closed multiple times as a precaution against the hazardous conditions brought on by these coastal storms. In South Africa, sea level has increased at a rate of around 3 mm year−1 in recent decades, which is consistent with estimates of GSLR over the same period. A recent study provides projections of mean sea level change for the 21st century (2007-2100) for tide gauges at eight locations along South Africa's coastline. Trends and projections for Wilderness is not available; however, data from the gauge stations in Mossel Bay and Knysna provide indicative measurements for Wilderness, which projects sea level rise (relative to 1986-2005) of approximately 0.65 m (0.25-0.8 m) for RCP2.6 or approximately 0.85 m (0.5-1.25 m) for RCP8.5. These increases are approximately 7%-14% higher than projections of GMSL.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - HOME COMPOSTING PLANT: The generation of solid waste represents an important environmental problem due to its impact on climate change. Each year, approximately 11.2 billion tons of solid waste are collected in the world, and the degradation of the proportion of organic waste contributes approximately 5% of global Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions (UN, 2023), mainly through methane gas. This gas has a climate warming potential 81 times greater than carbon dioxide during the 20 years after its release into the atmosphere (IPCC, 2021). For this reason, taking methane mitigation measures is one of the most efficient ways to stop climate warming. In the municipality of Lautaro, the final disposal of solid waste is carried out at the Monte Verde Los Ángeles landfill, which receives an annual generation of 3,774 tons/year. This The landfill is located more than 100 km from Lautaro, so the municipality needs to look for new alternatives for treatment or final disposal of waste in order to reduce the amount of waste to be disposed of and reduce transportation costs. In relation to the financial background in Chile, household waste management is the responsibility of municipalities, which can be financed through internal and external resources. Internal resources include the Municipal Common Fund and Permanent Own Income, while external resources cover concessions and public-private alliances, shared urban financing, non-reimbursable international cooperation and government transfers. There are also competitive funds created by laws and international financing organizations available, such as the Regional Development Fund. There is a financing process through the National System of Investments, but it usually takes longer than other organizations and is not recommended in the case of Lautaro since it is expected to reduce transportation costs in the short term (CCAP, 2023). Based on an analysis of technological alternatives for the management of organic waste, such as composting plants and anaerobic biodigesters, a composting plant is recommended and described, with the capacity to treat 7,928 tons per year (TPA) of green and brown waste, considering the heterogeneity of organic waste, by-product markets and the costs associated with each cost/benefit to see which technological alternative had the highest NPV. The result was that the forced aeration system option with membrane maturation requires a smaller constructed surface area of both slab and shed, which considerably reduces initial costs, in addition to the time required for the complete composting cycle, improving profitability. This alternative projects a treatment of 10.34 tons per day (TPD) of fresh organic food waste, with a volumetric ratio of 1.00:2.17 between green and brown waste. The plant requires a total area of ​​3,914 m2 and a total investment of $1,574 MM5 CLP.

According to initial assessments, the flood affected more than 700 households, with property damage estimated to exceed 3.5 million Baht. | Storm: Between late August and early September 2019, Yasothon Town Municipality was affected by two consecutive storms. This resulted in damage to the homes of vulnerable populations, such as households with elderly members, individuals with health conditions, low-income families, and outdoor workers. Many of these homes were already in poor condition, and the damage caused increased the financial burden on these households, as they needed to repair their damaged homes. | Heavy precipitation: Heavy rainfall in Yasothon Town Municipality has already caused significant impacts on vulnerable groups such as the elderly, vulnerable health groups, and low-income households. The elderly and individuals with health conditions were unable to move or take shelter quickly, while low-income households, often living in poorly constructed homes, lacked the resources to repair the damage. This resulted in considerable property damage due to flooding and an increased financial burden for recovery. Additionally, these households experienced a reduction in income due to work stoppages or limited employment opportunities.\nThe waste and wastewater management sector were also severely affected. The flooding caused water to accumulate, disrupting waste management and sewage systems, and making it difficult to manage waste and treat sewage as usual properly.
project_info:
Transport - Trams for Happiness: Sustainable Urban Transport in Yasothon: 1. Problems or situations that require this project
1.1 Yasothon Municipality has 8 schools within the municipality, including 2 kindergarten schools, with approximately 8,000 to 10,000 students. Most of these schools are located along major roads in the city, causing significant traffic congestion, especially in front of the schools. This issue is most apparent during peak hours (morning: 07:00 - 08:30, afternoon: 15:00 - 16:30).
1.2 Most people use private cars to commute to work and drop off or pick up their children, and there are also many songthaews from neighboring districts that park to drop off and wait for students. This is because there is no mass transit system, and public transportation services are insufficient. This leads to the emission of greenhouse gases from transportation in the city.
1.3 The number of accidents occurring in front of schools and within the Yasothon Municipality is increasing, showing a rising trend.

2. Objectives of this project (within the implementation period)
2.1 To develop a sustainable transportation model using environmentally friendly trams, suitable as an alternative for students commuting to school, parents dropping off or picking up children, and for public transportation within Yasothon Municipality.
2.2 To study the feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and public opinion regarding the establishment of an environmentally friendly tram-based public transport system in Yasothon Municipality.

3. Expected benefits from this project and measurement methods
3.1 Economic Benefits: Parents who use the tram service for student transportation will be able to reduce travel costs by at least 5%. This will be measured through surveys using questionnaires.
3.2 Social Benefits: 70% of users will experience reduced travel time to their destinations, and the road accident rate will decrease. This will be measured using statistical data from relevant agencies and random interviews with at least 100 users.
3.3 Environmental Benefits: The level of air pollution from traffic will remain within standard limits. This will be measured by air quality monitoring data from relevant agencies. Additionally, greenhouse gas emissions will be reduced compared to before the introduction of trams. This will be measured through calculation formulas and random interviews with at least 50 car users within Yasothon Municipality, conducted daily.

Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Yasothon Towards a Smart City with Smart Poles: Smart Pole Installation Project
Project Goal:
- Install 23 smart poles at strategic locations across the city to enhance traffic management, improve safety, and reduce energy consumption.
- Establish 1 integrated control center that allows collaboration between relevant agencies to monitor and manage the smart poles, gather real-time data, and optimize urban services.

Expected Results of the Smart Pole Installation Project:
Enhanced Urban Safety:
- Improved lighting in key areas reduces accidents and crime rates.
- Better monitoring and response capabilities through integrated security systems.
Optimized Traffic Management: 
- Smart poles with traffic sensors improve flow and reduce congestion.
- Real-time traffic updates available to residents.
Energy Efficiency and Cost Savings: 
Reduction in electricity usage by up to 20% through smart lighting systems.
- Lower municipal energy costs and environmental impact.
Environmental Benefits:
- Decrease in CO2 emissions due to energy-efficient technologies.
- Improved air quality monitoring through environmental sensors on the poles.
Improved Public Services: 
-Real-time data collection and communication improve city planning and emergency response.
- Free or low-cost public Wi-Fi access enhances digital inclusion.
Interagency Collaboration:
- Centralized control center fosters coordination between agencies, leading to more effective urban management.

Urban flooding: Households and businesses flooding, loss of income due to flooding and reduced transport methods. Cost of carrying out post-flooding work. There is an increased risk to all infrastructure from surface water flooding. The impact is assessed to be high as flooding is known to affect Perth and Kinross currently, and climate change is expected to increase the frequency and severity. Damage and disruption to infrastructure may have an outsize impact on rural communities. Based on flood projection data from SEPA, this is the major source of flooding in Perth and Kinross, so surface water flooding is likely to have an increased impact. Conversely, risk projections from river flooding are more mixed; railway lines and stations are more exposed, but other infrastructure such as energy and water may be less exposed. In Scotland, key infrastructure is exposed to both types of flooding. This includes water sites, power stations, and rail lines (and others). Flooding may have an impact in rural areas of Perth and Kinross, particularly in areas that are not well-connected. For example, a train line or road being flooded may have an outsize impact if that is the only major transport connection to a village. There are associated effects such as difficulties for health services in accessing remote regions if transport infrastructure is affected. Flooding can severely disrupt businesses in both the short and long term. Flooding may mandate businesses closing for repairs, and may make it difficult for them to get insurance. Flooding can damage cultural heritage such as historic buildings. It may also require attractions to be closed to the public if they require repairs. | River flooding: 2/3 years ago with increasing rain fall Perth and Kinross was exposed large amounts of flooding in certain areas. Almondbank, Perth, and other areas. This has resulted in large capital investment in flood defences in certain areas. Works including; building up lands, creating flood plains and numerous pumping stations set up across Perth and Kinross area. 

The increased likelihood of storms due to climate change has resulted in increased damage to bridges and pipelines, with high river flows thought to be contributing to this. Several key bridges in Perth and Kinross that connect large sections of the population have been identified as high scour risk.

Furthermore, warmer temperatures may be accelerating weathering-related deterioration for embankments. Risks to infrastructure services from river flooding such as railway lines and stations. | Extreme wind: Overall, wind speed is expected to increase slightly in the winter and decrease slightly in the summer so the risks posed by high winds may be lower due to climate change. However, the likelihood of storms and gusts is uncertain.

Storm (wind) events have caused significant damage in Perth & Kinross over the last five years, with some rural communities losing electricity for over a week, as well as risks to transport, nature, forestry and physical damage | Extreme heat: Risks to business from reduced employee productivity due to infrastructure disruption and higher temperatures in working environments. Risks to health and social care delivery from higher temperatures - Social Care Staff may be affected by higher summer temperatures. Buildings and equipment could also overheat. Due to the health impacts described in risk HCB8, more pressure may be placed on health care during heatwaves. Risks from summer household energy demand for summer cooling. Risks to prison services from high temperatures - Heat related illness for inmates and staff, need to move prisoners if temperatures in some areas of the prisons become too high. Extreme heat: The assessment focused on analyzing indicators such as air temperature trends, future scenarios, land surface temperature (LST), and heat wave patterns. Air temperature trends were studied using IMD data, while LST was assessed through satellite imagery. The LST analysis varied based on land use, infrastructure, and human activities. During the day, LST ranged from 29.5°C to 49.4°C, and at night, it ranged from 28.4°C to 30.6°C, revealing potential hotspots.

A trend analysis of LST was plotted, highlighting high-risk areas with median temperatures exceeding 42°C, showing an upward trend annually.

Bhavnagar has experienced an increase in heat wave events, leading to significant health impacts. There is a clear link between heat waves and heatstroke-related illnesses and deaths.

The city's most vulnerable areas, with high LST, include wards like 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13 Chitra-Fulsar-Nari, Kumbharwada, Vadva-B, North Krushnanagar-Ruva, Kaliyabid-Sisdsar-Adhewada, South Sardarnagar-Adhewada, Gogha Circle-Akwada, and industrial areas. Extreme heat may affect water and energy demands. According to Gujarat SAPCC, heat wave events increased by 4 between 1951 and 2019, with projections of 10-40 more events by 2070. This rise in heat waves may have serious public health consequences.

The elderly, children, women, differently-abled individuals, the uneducated, and the poor are most at risk during extreme heat. Those living in slums face poor living conditions, limited cooling options, and restricted healthcare access. In Bhavnagar, 0.28 million people (0.13 million females, 0.15 million males) are vulnerable, making up 34.8% of the total population, including 31,000 children, 15,000 elderly, 12,000 people with special needs, and 69,000 illiterate individuals. Among income groups, 28,000 slum dwellers and 220 street vendors working in designated zones are especially vulnerable. Additionally, those working at dumpsites and material recovery facilities (MRF) are exposed to hazardous conditions due to accelerated decomposition and open dumping.

Refer to section 4.3.2.1 (pg. 76 to 80) in the attached Bhavnagar Climate Resilient City Action Plan. | Urban flooding: Rise in extreme rainfall events and insufficient stormwater drainage leads to urban flooding. Vulnerable populations, such as the urban poor, are the most impacted due to poor living conditions and limited resources. The flood risk is assessed by analysing rainfall trends, spatial analysis of waterlogged areas, and ward-level analysis of water-borne diseases, revealing areas most affected by flooding. Issues such as heavy siltation in stormwater drains and improper waste and sewage disposal exacerbate flooding, impacting health, mobility, and economic productivity.

Some of the areas severely affected by waterlogging include Kumbharwada, Karchaliya Para, Bortalav and North Sardarnagar-Tarsamiya. The city is experiencing a rise in urban flooding hazards due to intense rainfall occurrences. Residents within a 250 m radius of 27 waterlogged areas or flood points face elevated risks and are susceptible to severe health hazards.

Population Groups Vulnerable to Urban Flooding: Children, elderly, women, and those with special needs are most impacted by urban flooding. Limited access to health facilities, emergency services, and urban services during floods mainly affect these groups. They also suffer from a lack of inclusive infrastructure and access to information. Urban poor living in compromised housing conditions and with limited access to health centres are susceptible to disease outbreaks. Approximately, 3.5% of the city's total area and 6.2% of the city's population i.e., 50,000 (24,000 females, 26,000 males - including 5,000 children; 3,000 elders; 2,000 people with special needs; 12,000 illiterate people) are vulnerable to urban flooding. Vulnerable population by income group includes 24,000 people living in slums and 30 street side vendors sitting in designated vending zones. Urban flooding renders public infrastructure, such as roads, inaccessible; impacting the daily livelihood of street side vendors and slum dwellers.

Heat stress: The median LST of 30.07°C in May 2023, the hottest month of the year, was considered as the threshold to identify LST hotspots in the city. It is observed that the newly developing areas, mostly on the eastern side of Thamirabarani River, with open and barren land parcels witness high LST during the day followed by areas with highly dense developments in the four zones of the city. 
Newly developing areas in Wards 17, 18, 38, 39, 50, 51, 54, and 55 of Tirunelveli, Palayamkottai and Melapalayam zones, i.e., surrounding areas of Sivathipatti Road, KTC Nagar, Thirumal Nagar, Tuckerammalpuram, Anna Hajira College, Pettai Rail Nagar and Suthamalli, Rani Anna College and Palayapettai etc., and densely developed residential and commercial areas in and around old town areas of the 4 zones and areas like Pettai, SIDCO industrial estate, Tirunelveli junction and bus stands are found to experience heat stress due to higher LSTs during summer months. As is evident from the land-use pattern of Tirunelveli city, the residential and commercial development and accumulation of built-up area is concentrated in specific locations across the city while a significant part of the city area is still undeveloped, part of which is being used as agricultural lands. 

High surface temperatures can cause thermal discomfort, impact productivity, increase heat related morbidities such as heat exhaustion and heatstroke. Heat related morbidities can lead to health risks for vulnerable population in a city such as the elderly, children, differently abled and people with pre-existing health conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular diseases who are often prone to non-exertional heat stress leading to heat exhaustion or heat stroke. On the other hand, exertional heat stress is common among hard-working labourers with continuous heat exposure, and low-income group or slum-dwelling people with poor living and workplace conditions, and lack of affordable cooling options. 

51.27% of the total city area is identified as hotspot areas which recorded LST more than the median LST of 30.07°C. This impacts about 340,086 people (61.33%) of Tirunelveli city's total population including 33,477 children and 38,785 people living in slum locations. Details of the assessment can be found in Section 5.3.2.1 of Tirunelveli Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan. | Urban flooding: Tirunelveli city is vulnerable to urban flooding risks during extreme rainfall events in the city which causes water stagnation in low-lying areas and other vulnerable locations across the city. The city is also prone to riverine flooding in Thamirabharani river flowing through city due to extreme rainfall in the watershed areas of Thamirabarani river basin and due to heavy discharge from the Manimuthar, Papanasam and Gadana dams in the upper catchment areas that contribute significantly to water flow in the river. The key factors contributing to urban flooding in Tirunelveli are poor maintenance and inadequacy of existing stormwater drainage network, heavy siltation due to unauthorised solid waste and sewage disposal, encroachment of stormwater and irrigation drains and watershed areas of waterbodies in the city.

The urban flooding risk assessment includes spatial mapping and analysis of flood vulnerable locations identified across the city through field assessments and inputs from discussion with city officials. The wards with population living in low-lying areas along the riverbanks and irrigation canals flowing through the city and wards with more than 30% of the area covered under flood buffer zones are considered as the most flood vulnerable areas/wards in the city.

Urban flooding impacts the livelihood of low-income population in the city, causes health risks and significantly disrupts the daily life of the city population. The vulnerable population groups such as the elderly, children, differently abled, and slum dwellers especially face severe impacts of urban flooding due to disruptions in their accessibility to urban services such as water supply, public transport etc. Further, households in slum locations have poor living conditions and face higher risks of epidemic due to water stagnation caused by heavy rainfall. 

15.58% of the total city area and 39.65% of total city population are vulnerable to urban flooding in Tirunelveli. Around 31 wards in the city face substantial risk of urban flooding impacting a population of 219,872 people (39.65% of total population) including 21,643 children and 22,403 people living in slum locations. Details of the assessment can be found in Section 5.3.2.2 of Tirunelveli Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

Urban flooding: For the flood risk assessment of Eskişehir's Tepebaşı district, the findings of the Sakarya Basin Flood Management Plan (2018) were utilized. According to the results of the hydrodynamic modeling, it was determined that numerous residential areas located along both sides of the stream corridor, as well as the Eskişehir Military Airport, would be affected by flooding. The primary source of this flooding is identified as the Sarısu Stream.

Furthermore, a one-dimensional model of the section of Çatakçı Stream running through Gökdere Neighborhood within the district showed that the water level exceeds the channel capacity. Based on this finding, it was recommended to implement channel improvements capable of conveying a 500-year return period flood discharge. This measure, scheduled for the 2019-2023 implementation period, was assigned a very low priority.

The Risk and Vulnerability Assessment, which examines the district's exposure to climate change-related hazards, was revisited during a workshop attended by 32 participants. As part of this assessment, sectors such as critical infrastructure and the built environment, transportation, agriculture, waste management, water resources, public health, industry, and disaster management were analyzed.

The hazards considered in the study included heatwaves, cold spells, extreme precipitation, storms, hail, drought, and both floods and flash floods. Participants concluded that Tepebaşı is most susceptible to extreme precipitation and flooding, drought, and heatwaves. They also emphasized that, under the growing impacts of climate change, the agriculture and livestock sector and the water sector are expected to be the most affected by climate-related disasters.
 | Drought: Due to the ongoing climate crisis, Eskişehir, which has a continental climate, is experiencing noticeable increases in temperature and decreases in precipitation, creating risks that could lead to water scarcity in the coming years. Water stress is significantly increasing the vulnerability of various populations and sectors. One of the most affected is agriculture and livestock farming. Located in Türkiye's Central Anatolia Region, the Tepebaşı district of Eskişehir plays a vital role in meeting both regional and national needs in these sectors. The district encompasses more than 500,000 decares of agricultural land and is home to over 1.4 million livestock, including both small and large ruminants.

In addition to the high likelihood of water-crisis-induced vulnerabilities in agriculture and livestock, water access is a critical concern for low-income residents, children, and the elderly. The city's primary water source, Kalabak, is showing alarming signs of drought that have been exacerbated by the impacts of climate change.

Another sector facing significant challenges is industry. In manufacturing, where water use is unavoidable, any reduction in supply places additional stress on all water-dependent industries.

One of the most critical sectors is healthcare. Any water-related stress in this sector could result in highly adverse consequences, affecting both public health and the capacity of healthcare facilities to operate effectively.

climate_hazard: Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): The Whitby shoreline is about 12 km long and extends from Lakeridge Road to Boundary Road within the Town limit and consists of residential homes, boat homes, municipal roads, water sanitary storm sewer infrastructures, personal watercraft, a waterfront trail network, parkland, beach, bluff (high & low) and some sections with coastal wetland. Coastal flooding occurs with changes in lake water levels in Lake Ontario and due to storm surges and waves. Water flow into Lake Ontario is primarily from inflow from Lake Erie, with minor contributions from surface runoff and groundwater discharge into the lake. The water level of Lake Ontario was near the 100-year high water mark in 2017, which resulted in severe erosion along the Whitby shoreline. The residential neighborhoods along the Whitby waterfront including, Whitby Harbor, Eastbourne Beach and Crystal Beach are susceptible to similar damages in the future and need an informed risk assessment of existing public and private lands and infrastructure to help with mitigation planning and related prioritization. In 2021, the Town carried out Whitby Coastal Flood Hazard Risk Assessment and Municipal Class Environmental Assessment for the assessment of the coastal flood hazard risk including erosion hazard assessment along the Whitby shoreline. The study provides an evaluation of alternative solutions to the flood and erosion issues, as well as finalizes the preliminary design for the preferred alternative for mitigation of potential damages. Based on the study the residential neighborhoods along the Whitby waterfront that have the highest risk are Whitby Harbor, Eastbourne Beach and Crystal Beach. Additionally, increasing precipitation is causing a rise in Great Lake Water levels which is leading to coastal erosion and flooding along the Whitby shoreline. It is anticipated that the lake levels will start to fluctuate as more extreme precipitation followed by dry days is predicted through the Durham's climate change model. | Snow and ice: The Town of Whitby's 2024 Climate Emergency Response Plan Phase 1: Resilience (CERP) had engagement objectives that involved residents, external stakeholders and technical advisors to inform the plan. For this purpose, the Town partnered with ISeeChange (ISC), an online climate engagement platform that enables community members to share their experiences of climate and social vulnerability through photos and narratives. This helped in documenting the residents' preferred adaptation actions, their local climate change concerns, and their decision-making criteria for the plan. The record-breaking snowstorm on January 17, 2022, allowed for real-time contributions to ISeeChange and allowed the Town to collect data about the community's readiness for and resilience to high-snow-total events. From this event, 12 posts mentioned increased irregularity and increased severity of winter storm events. Relatedly, four posts discussed the prioritization of sidewalk clearing for major bus and pedestrian transit routes and around large apartment complexes where community members may rely more heavily on walking as their main form of transportation. In addition, community members also mentioned the neighbourly support they experienced from their community during this storm event, describing sharing tools (e.g. snowblowers) and providing assistance to residents unable to clear their driveway. In the presence of climate change, there is a risk of longer winters and colder temperatures with quick intense snowfall outside of the lake effect. This would result in increased impacts on aging infrastructure and road capacity within the Town of Whitby. Ice accumulations, combined with gusty winds (from 40 km/h to 70 km/h) have strong potential to result in power outages due to fallen trees and power lines, with the continued threat of flooding. These types of storms will continue to occur, even more frequently, and result in greater damages to both private and public property. In the future, under the Durham Community Climate Adaptation Plan, it is expected that there will be a medium risk for infrastructure failure leading to power outages (due to ice accretion and trees falling on lines), increase in invasive species (increase in local pests), and more fluctuation of winter climates resulting in more rain during the winter months (leading to increase threat of flooding). | Heavy precipitation: CERP Phase 1 focuses on climate hazards which were identified by reviewing climate modelling and engaging with advisory groups and the public. Increased heat and risk of heatwaves, as well as increased flooding from precipitation, were identified as the highest priority hazards with measurable spatial variability across the town. The total annual precipitation is expected to increase, as are the maximum one-day and three-day precipitation amounts in storm events. The number of consecutive dry days is projected to increase slightly, leading to a slight increase in droughts in spite of the increased total annual precipitation. The Durham Region's Future Climate (2040 - 2049) also predicts wetter annual conditions with 50% increase in the one day maximum rainfall, 100% increase in days with more than 25 mm of rain, 72% more rain in July and 79% more in August, 217% more rain and 75% less snow in February. Extreme rainfall that results in overwhelmed drainage infrastructure poses the risk of overland flooding. Flooding of underground electrical vaults or surface-mounted electrical equipment can lead to failure and electrical outages. Increasing rainfall intensities and violent storms will challenge existing infrastructure and potentially cause severe flooding in urban areas. These events could threaten the health and well-being of citizens and the community. | Extreme wind: In the Town of Whitby, there has been significant damage to tree branches and limbs on trails and major arterial streets, conservation lands and downtown areas from extreme wind. As a result, this can have accessibility impacts on sidewalks, powerlines and public services. Back in 2018, severe windstorms were felt in Whitby which caused loose objects to be overturned, older buildings to be more susceptible to damage, branches and top heavy trees to snap, and impacted streetlights and powerlines. Additionally, in May of 2019, the Central Lake Ontario Conservation Authority issued a flood warning and had heavy concerns about the wind forecast which saw winds from 30-40km/h and gusts up to 80km/h. With high water levels and significant winds there were impacts to low-lying and flood prone areas due to storm surge and wave uprush. The Durham Community Climate Adaptation Plan of 2016, expects that by 2040-2049, there will be more extreme weather events with high winds and heavy rain which will impact municipalities in Durham Region. This will continue to cause power outages, infrastructure damages, infectious borne diseases, road failure through subsoil failure, pavement structure failure, and increase chronic and acute exposure for public health air quality.While Whitby's CERP Phase 1: Resilience was being finalized, in May 2022 a powerful windstorm called a derecho moved across Ontario, causing at least 11 deaths and resulting in untold damages, such as Whitby. The derecho event resulted in power losses for days together and extensive tree losses in Whitby. While it is difficult to directly correlate the derecho with climate change, the storm is a stark reminder that climate risks can take many forms. Derechos are not directly addressed in CERP, but many of the measures identified will increase Whitby's resilience against windstorms and risks that are location-specific, such as flooding. In particular, this approach reduces the impact of compounding hazards, for example, when wind storms are combined with floods. | Drought: The Town of Whitby's 2024 Climate Emergency Response Plan (CERP) Phase 1: Resilience details a future climate scenario as RCP 8.5 scenario to model the data for Whitby. The model predicts total annual precipitation is expected to increase, as are the maximum one-day and three-day precipitation amounts in storm events. The number of consecutive dry days is projected to increase slightly, leading to a slight increase in droughts in spite of the increased total annual precipitation. As a result, there are raised concerns regarding groundwater properly recharging due to lack of precipitation in extreme events and morbidity of trees and plant life. This has serious consequences for elderly, children, and vulnerable populations who would be severely impacted by heat waves. For instance, back in 2016, drought conditions were parching the countryside in Durham and transforming the green landscape to dry land. This impacted people across all demographics, and resulted in Town events (e.g. Ribfest) being almost unbearably hot. Additionally, this can impact crops and give high cost to local farmers who are trying to sustain their own business and local communities. Furthermore, drought conditions can place high stress on any newly planted trees, as they lack the sufficient water supply to establish solid growth. In the future, the extreme heat will continue to impact outside workers, reduce asset life, accelerate challenges of ageing infrastructure, vegetation management and growing seasons, transmission and disruption outages, social disruption, health related death and illness, buckling of pavement and bridges, softening of asphalt, and impacts to water supply in the Town of Whitby. | Extreme heat: Climate hazards were identified by reviewing climate modelling and engaging with advisory groups and the public to develop the Town of Whitby's 2022 Climate Emergency Response Plan Phase (CERP) 1: Resilience. As identified in CERP, Whitby is set to see an increase in the number of heat events increased from approx. two days per year above 35 degrees until 2040 and over13 days by 2071 under an RCP 8.5 climate projection scenario. It is expected that this will increase the number of high heat events, add stress to the electricity grid, decrease air quality and impact the growing conditions of plants. Furthermore, increased heat and risk of heatwaves, as well as increased flooding from precipitation, were identified as the highest priority hazards with measurable spatial variability across the Town. Heatwaves, and in particular, extended periods with hot nights, have serious health consequences for at-risk people. project_info: Transport - Whitby Active Transportation Plan - Implementation Phase: The Town of Whitby has completed an Active Transportation Plan (ATP) which involves significant public and stakeholder consultation, in 2021. The purpose of the ATP is to build upon the Town of Whitby Cycling and Leisure Trails Plan (2010) and Town of Whitby Transportation Master Plan (2010) and to develop a comprehensive forward looking plan that contributes to increased transportation options and outlines the Town's short, medium and long term Active Transportation strategy for walking, cycling, and other forms of active transportation.The ATP will evaluate options and identify opportunities and make recommendations for connectivity, safety, convenience, maintenance, accessibility, and encouraging, promoting, creating, and improving facilities and events for non-motorized transportation for the purpose of improving community health through physical activity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and alleviating traffic congestion. The plan for implementation of Active Transportation facilities, user support and encouragement activities as highlighted in ATP are currently underway.

project_info: Buildings - Whitby Sports Complex: Whitby is one of the fastest growing communities in Canada with populations set to double by 2040. The new Sports Complex will help meet both the immediate and future recreational needs of our growing community.The vision for the Complex is to create a multi-purpose gathering space for inclusive sport and community programming - a place for residents of all ages and abilities to connect, play and get active.The need for a new sports facility was identified in the Town's Culture, Parks, Recreation and Open Space Strategic Master Plan as well as the Sports Facility Strategy that was developed based on significant community engagement.This new complex will include:•A twin-pad arena •Indoor aquatics centre •Leisure pool•Wellness Studio/Multi-Purpose Space•Indoor walking track•Meeting rooms, arts and cultural space•Landscaping, parking and pedestrian connectivityThe Complex will integrate design criteria to achieve LEED Gold and Zero Carbon Building standards. This will make it the first municipally owned facility to carry both certifications. This approach ensures that climate resiliency, carbon reduction, and environmental sustainability are achieved.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Corporate Waste Management Strategy: A Corporate Waste Management Strategy is being developed by the Town in 2023 to support the recommendations within the Zero Carbon Whitby Framework to target zero waste by 2040 and aligns with the goals of the Corporate Sustainability Plan. Flooding has been a significant issue with increased precipitation in the Town of Whitby and has lead to significant damages to homes and commercial properties, increased the risk of transportation on roads, aging infrastructure, animal habitat, etc. For example, in 2017, a major road in downtown Whitby was closed due to flooding in the area (Brock Street South/Waste Street) and residents were urged to stay away from bluffs and urged to use caution near the waterfront. Furthermore, in the Durham Community Climate Adaptation Plan (DCCAP), it has been projected that the occurrence of flooding will only increase in local municipalities of Durham, including Whitby. For example, in 2019, Central Lake Ontario Conservation Authority (CLOCA) issued a flood warning for the Lake Ontario shoreline in the Town of Whitby as a storm brought 15-35 mm of rain to the area. In addition, the Canadian National Railway and Metrolinx rail bridges over Lynde Creek restrict flow , resulting in upstream flooding during storm events in the West Lynde/Michael Boulevard neighbourhood in Whitby. Moreover, the residential neighbourhood around Pringle Creek Bridge, Brock Street South and the upstream area are prone to flooding due to the narrow width of the creek under the bridge. Thus, new climate resilience standards must be included in DCCAP and other plans to mitigate these risks. Otherwise in the future, increased precipitation will result in increased river flooding leaving a high risk for stormwater facilities, roads and transportation, sanitary services, erosion, pollution, electrical services, communications services, social services, EMS, police, public use of flood plains, damage to private assets, social disruption, and business disruption. | Extreme cold: Despite winter temperature generally increasing, it is anticipated that Whitby will experience greater fluctuations in extreme weather including extreme winter events such as large snowfall, ice storms and extreme cold. These events are very disruptive to the community as they can close down transportation systems, impact those who do not have access to adequate shelter and heating, increase demand on the energy system and can damage trees and the natural environment. The Region of Durham has conducted a detailed assessment of climate change impacts based on an analysis of several climate models downscaled and corrected for the region (Table A2.1: Consolidated Projections (2000-2009 and 2040-2049 data) of the Durham Community Climate Adaptation Plan, page 87). The 2020 summary of these models tells a story of a warmer, wetter, and wilder Whitby in the future. The future climate scenario used in this model is the RCP 8.5 scenario, a worst-case scenario. Under this scenario, the annual mean temperature in Whitby is expected to rise and will be accompanied by an increase in the number of extreme heat days. The number of extreme cold days will decrease, as will the number of potential ice days and the number of freeze-thaw cycles per year. Less snow and ice cover will reduce opportunities for traditional outdoor winter recreation activities affecting seasonal jobs.
project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Iroquois Park Sports Complex - Deep Energy Retrofits: The Town of Whitby is looking to upgrade the equipment in the Iroquois Park Sports Complex to achieve deep retrofits and lead the pathway to a zero carbon building. Iroquois Park Sports Complex is a sports arena that has six (6) ice pads, two (2) swimming pools and is one of the largest consumers of natural gas in the Towns' corporate buildings portfolio. This would include energy efficiency upgrades for existing equipment, installation of ground source heat pumps and solar PV systems. This would help in eliminating the use of natural gas in the building.

The water level of Lake Ontario was near the 100-year high water mark in 2017, which resulted in severe erosion along the Whitby shoreline. Buildings - Citizen monitoring program for air quality, temperature and other environmental indicators: Cerro Navia faces high levels of atmospheric pollution and urban heat island phenomena that affect the health of the population, especially children, older adults and people with respiratory diseases. 

Currently, the official data from the MACAM system of the Ministry of the Environment is at a metropolitan scale and does not capture the internal variability of the commune. 

This limits the ability of the community and the municipality to identify critical areas and make timely decisions. Given that there is a lack of local monitoring and the absence of territorialized information for education, risk prevention and the design of local environmental measures
lack of decentralized local monitoring.

To this end, this project proposes to initially install and implement a pilot network of 3 community air quality and temperature sensors, generating local data in real time to strengthen environmental education and territorial management in the face of pollution and climate change.

To achieve this, 3 low-cost sensors will be installed that measure PM2.5, PM10, temperature and humidity in strategic points of the commune. The data will be integrated into an open and visible digital platform in real time.

This is based on the acquisition of equipment, installation in municipal/neighborhood headquarters, training of citizen monitors and community dissemination. So that the community has its own environmental information, increasing awareness about air quality and health, and strengthening local decision-making.

This project seeks to be innovative when today at a communal scale there are no tools to measure local meteorological information, given that currently the logic of MACAM is to have metropolitan monitoring, strengthening citizen science and directly linking the community with monitoring environmental.

project_info:
Water management - Community Gray Water Treatment Network with decentralized monitoring: This project seeks to generate a community gray water treatment network in at least 5 social offices and municipal offices

This occurs in the context of the high consumption of potable water for irrigation and non-potable uses in municipal offices and social offices, and inefficient discharge/consumption of gray water, contributing to the depletion of water resources, higher costs and environmental footprint.

Also There is an absence of local systems for the capture, treatment and reuse of gray water in communal infrastructure that could be reused and generate more efficient and strategic use of the water resource.

This is why we seek to design, implement and evaluate a pilot network of small gray water treatment plants in municipal offices and social headquarters, interconnected to a centralized monitoring system, to reuse treated water in irrigation and cleaning. non-potable, reducing the consumption of drinking water and incorporating permanent environmental education, thus being able to be used for the irrigation of green areas, irrigation of orchards, washing of exterior floors and discharges that allow the saving of drinking water and other uses that do not consider human consumption. At the same time, it will allow the reduction of the local water footprint, with actions and data for communal scaling in the reduction of emissions
	
The project seeks to have small modular plants (pretreatment, biofilter/compact constructed wetland, disinfection), and centralized telemetry for real-time monitoring.

Installing collection systems in sinks/showers/non-sewer evacuations (according to regulations), separate pipes, modular plants by site, and sensors (flow, turbidity, pH, residual chlorine, level) that report to a municipal dashboard. Training for operators and community workshops.

This will allow an interconnected network of micro-plants with remote monitoring applied to municipal infrastructures and social headquarters; emphasis on community education and local reuse governance.

project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - “Circular Transformation: Valorization of Organic Waste into Energy and Fertilizers through Biodigestion and the larva of the Black soldier fly”: The commune generates large quantities of organic waste from free fairs and other sources, which in many cases end up in landfills. Currently, through the Food Bank, part of the organic waste from donations is valued to be used in composting, of which the vast majority still cannot be valued
In this sense, there is a lack of local and efficient recovery systems to convert this waste into useful resources, combined with the limitation of space and costs associated with the final disposal of the waste. 
This is why this project seeks to implement a pilot system for the valorization of organic waste through biodigestion and bioconversion with black soldier fly (MSN) larvae, generating energy, fertilizers and permanent environmental education for students, neighbors and municipal officials, contributing to the reduction of waste and the dissemination of sustainable practices in the commune, in which the Pilot is sought to be in the Environmental Educational Center of the municipality taking advantage of the existing facilities, and the vermicomposting work and existing garden.

Which is sought to install a pilot biodigester and an MSN larvae breeding module to process organic waste from free fairs and the Bank of Food.
Classifying waste, feeding the larvae, operating the biodigester and monitoring the production of biogas and fertilizers; implementing workshops and educational material.

This will reduce and valorize the waste that reaches landfills and reduce the polluting gases coming from them, also through workshops we seek to generate environmental awareness in the community

Finally, strategic alliances are expected to be able to give monitoring of this project and training thanks to the collaboration with Entomo Circular who is a pioneer in this initiative using biomanagers from the use of black soldier fly larvae.

Sustainable food consumption/production - Autonomous Modular Eco-Irrigation for Urban Crops: Modular Eco-Irrigation is an autonomous and scalable vertical cultivation system that allows sustainable food production in small spaces. It runs on solar energy through photovoltaic panels that power an automatic irrigation system controlled by humidity sensors and monitored via Bluetooth. This ensures that the plants receive the exact amount of water at the right time, optimizing the water resource and avoiding excessive irrigation.

The module can operate with two types of substrates:

Dry pruning chips: for the cultivation of edible mushrooms.

Coconut fiber dry organic compost: for short-cycle vegetables with low space requirements.

This project was born under the problems of climate change, water scarcity and the growing demand for food, which has made it urgent to look for alternative farming systems. Modular Eco-Irrigation responds to this need by integrating renewable energy, automation and circular economy. Its compact and vertical design makes it possible to take advantage of small spaces, favoring urban agriculture and food sovereignty. Furthermore, the use of organic waste as a substrate contributes to sustainable waste management and the reduction of emissions associated with food transportation.

Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Fires have a significant impact on the health and well-being of different age groups, especially the elderly, children, young people and people with pre-existing illnesses.

Elderly people are particularly vulnerable, as smoke can worsen respiratory diseases such as asthma and COPD, as well as increasing the risk of cardiovascular complications and infections.

Children face similar risks, with exposure to smoke can affect their lung development and make them more susceptible to irritation respiratory problems and allergies, resulting in asthma attacks and other health problems.

Young people are also affected. Poor air quality can limit your ability to participate in sports and outdoor activities, which harms both your physical and mental health. Furthermore, the stress and anxiety generated by the environmental situation can impact their psychological well-being.

Finally, people with pre-existing illnesses experience exacerbation of their symptoms, and may face an increase in hospital admissions due to respiratory crises and other complications.

In addition to direct impacts, fires can cause indirect effects, such as deteriorating quality of life and increasing social inequalities, especially affecting the most vulnerable groups. Therefore, protection and awareness of these risks are essential to mitigate the negative effects of fires.

After cleaning the corrals and milking parlors, cattle waste, rich in nutrients that could be used in the property's plantations, is released into waterways without treatment, becoming a potential polluter of water and soil. Untreated manure attracts flies, insects and can transmit diseases to animals and people. As an alternative technology available on the market and at an affordable cost for family farmers, one can consider the manure pit for liquid cattle waste - known as a manure pit or manure bin for cattle waste (tank). excavated and impermeable used for fermentation of waste). To remove biofertilizer from manure and carry out fertigation of pastures and plantations, you can use the slurry distributor. The equipment is coupled to an agricultural tractor to pump the material from the tank and release it onto pastures. According to information from Emater technicians at the Guanhães office, producers are interested in implementing the manure pit on their property. However, they report two difficulties: the first difficulty is renting the equipment to dig the manure pit due to the high cost charged on the market. The second difficulty is how to remove this material from the manure pit and distribute it elsewhere on the property and after a period of 60 days, due to the lack of equipment, remove the liquid material from the manure pit to distribute to the property's plantations.

This facility will manage and process organic waste from municipal solid waste and livestock manure from the Muar district using Anaerobic Digestion technology to produce biogas, organic fertilizer and upcycled materials.
: Project Scope,
Material Recovery Facility (MRF), Carrying out separation and processing of MSW and chicken manure into several main compositions such as organic waste, upcycled materials and inert waste
Anaerobic digestion plant (AD), the process of decomposing organic matter without the presence of oxygen, instead using natural bacteria/microbes in the digester to produce biogas.
Biogas plant, this biogas can be used as fuel and can be upgraded to methane gas.
Wastewater treatment plant, a treatment system for digestate to ensure that hazardous parameters contained in the wastewater are treated and stabilized. The solid material (sludge cake) will be improved into biofertilizer while the treated liquid will be reused.

Heat stress: Extreme events such as heatwaves,
will likely increase in the future threatening the health of people in Blackburn with Darwen. The borough already sees higher than average rates of
illnesses that are particularly susceptible e.g. high rates of cardiovascular disease and diabetes susceptible to heatwaves. High levels of deprivation make the borough more vulnerable. | Urban flooding: Blackburn with Darwen Borough has experienced major flood incidents especially throughout the summer of 2012. In June 2020 the Blackburn Flood Risk Area was affected by flash flooding of roads and property, including 44 residential and 14 business properties on Whalley New Road, Blackburn. In June 2023, Darwen Market was flooded due to heavy rainfall. The flood hazard and risk maps show that in the Blackburn Flood Risk Area 12,217 people live in areas at risk from flooding from surface water of which 97 are in areas of high risk. Also shown to be in areas at risk of flooding from surface water are 2,159 non-residential properties, including community centres, hospitals, schools, colleges, retail parks and public utilities e.g. the Darwen Wastewater Treatment Works south of the M65, 1,458km of roads, including parts of the A666, A674, A6077, A6078 and M65, 5.1km of railway, 4,732ha of agricultural land, areas of environmental designated sites, listed buildings, parks and gardens and water abstraction points. | Extreme cold: The Joint Strategic Needs Assessment (JSNA) for the borough helps us understand population make up, how healthy it is, and the assets available to help people stay healthy.
The JSNA Overview 2023 outlines the impact of cold housing on health, which is exacerbated by low temperatures. As well as being a major contributor to excess winter deaths, cold housing adds to the burden of circulatory and respiratory disease, colds and flu, exacerbates chronic conditions such as rheumatism and arthritis, and has a negative effect upon mental health. An estimated 10873 households in BwD (17.6%) were classed as being in 'fuel poverty' in 2022. This compares to 13.2% of households in England and 15.3% in the North West. Fuel poverty in England is measured using the low income, low energy efficiency (LILEE) indicator. Under this indicator, a household is deemed fuel poor if living in a property with an fuel poverty energy efficiency rating of band D or below and, after fuel bills are paid, their residual income is below the official poverty line.
Issues of damp and mould in homes, caused by cold housing, can be a public health risk, increasing the likelihood of a person experiencing respiratory problems such as infections, allergies or asthma. A survey of borough residents in 2021, found that 20% experienced both mould and condensation in their homes during the winter months. A higher proportion of those who rent reported this, compared to home owners. The survey also found that 87% of residents could keep their homes warm in winter but 11% could only heat some rooms. A greater proportion of residents who rent could not heat their homes, compared to owners. Of those who could not keep their homes warm, the main reason was cost. As the survey was undertaken before the significant increase in heating costs, the results are likely to underestimate the current picture.
We are addressing these issues through CHiL (Cosy Homes in Lancashire), finding grants to help low-income households improve home energy efficiency and make their home affordable to heat, and through the Affordable Warmth Forum. Led by BwD Health Living the Forum's objectives are to address fuel poverty collaboratively, involving residents with lived experience, sharing information from National Energy Action, improving relationships with residents, and supporting the Council's Poverty Strategy and Cost of Living work. The Care Network's Safe and Warm Homes programme provides home energy advice. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Moorland in the borough was drained in the past and so is at risk of wildfire during periods of drought when it dries out quickly. Fires may be started accidentally (e.g. discarded cigarette) or deliberately. Attending incidents puts fire service workers lives at risk, It puts properties on the edge of the moorland at risk and reduces air quality for residents, numbers dependent on wind direction. Fire destroys biodiversity and leaves the peat soils vulnerable to erosion. Large parts of the areas vulnerable to fire are used for water catchment. Eroding peat can affect water quality, which requires the water company to put additional resource in to cleaning up the contamination. Fire reduces grazing for sheep and affects cover for game birds.

A Public Space Protection Order banning the building or lighting any kind of fire or barbeque, lighting fireworks or setting off sky lanterns has been introduced to try to reduce the incidence of accidental fires.

Re-wetting the moor is the favoured solution to reduce fire risk and improve biodiversity. A local landowner is already in the process of restoring his area of moorland, Lancashire Peat Partnership has secured funds through the Nature for Climate Fund to extend the area of restoration and the Council has commissioned a restoration plan for the section of moor in its ownership. This work is expected to reduce the incidence and severity of future outbreaks of fire on the moors. A Landscape Recovery partnership - West Pennine More - has been established to bring all interested parties together to work collaboratively The Council is a member of the Partnership.
project_info:
Renewable energy - Solar farm feasibility: Early in 2024 the Council began to explore options to increase the amount of solar energy generation in the borough. The exercise was driven by a Climate Emergency Action Plan (CEAP) objective to reduce reliance on grid electricity by exploiting the borough's renewable energy potential, so reducing emissions and costs, and helping to achieve the Council's ambition to be carbon neutral by 2030

A feasibility study of ground-based solar arrays on selected Council-owned land was undertaken. APSE Energy reviewed 8 sites in Council ownership, inside and outside the borough, for their potential for solar farm development. Three locations were deemed to have potential and Outline Business Cases were developed for each. Approval is currently being sought to take one of these sites to full economic business case. The site has the potential to take a 2MW array with or without storage, which could meet the electricity demand of the Council's 3 leisure centres or the additional demand arising from a shift to low carbon technologies, such as heat pumps, for the Council's highest energy using buildings. This could mean a reduction of 352 tonnes CO2e.

The full feasibility assessment will be completed this year with project development in 2025/26, assuming economic feasibility is demonstrated and project finance can be raised.
