cityname: Hammersmith and Fulham London Borough Council
climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Much of the borough lies less than five metres above sea level. The borough is particularly prone to surface-water flooding due to the limited capacity of London's Victorian sewer network, and the extent of hard surfacing in the borough. 1,500 homes in the borough are known to have flooded following extreme rainfall in July 2021. Flooding poses an immediate risk of injury and death, with greater risks to people with less adaptive capacity such as infants and those with mobility or mental health conditions. However, the main health impacts are to mental health. A UK Health Security Agency study found that those directly affected by flooding were 6 times more likely to experience mental health conditions such as PTSD, depression and anxiety. Those with existing mental health conditions or who have risk factors such as a family history of mental health conditions are at heightened risk of new or compounded mental health conditions. Greater risks are posed to those who are less likely to receive or be able to respond to flood warnings due to communication barriers; these include older people, those with language or cultural barriers, and people with mental health conditions. Flood damage to homes results in high costs for occupants. Low-income households and those who are more socially isolated, with fewer networks to draw upon, are likely to face greater difficulties both preparing for and recovering after flooding impacts. This interacts with housing tenure and type; lower-income households are more likely to rent rather than own their properties, limiting the options to invest in measures to protect the property. They may be more likely to live in basement flats which are prone to flooding. Another group severely impacted by disruption to their housing are those who have health or social care services delivered to them at home. As sewers become overwhelmed, a key infrastructure risk during surface water flooding is the surcharging of sewage above ground, including into homes, with resulting health risks. Flooding poses risks to the normal operation of any services and businesses reliant on transport as roads can become impassable, increases likelihood of potholes, and disrupts continuation of built environment and construction activities. Flooding can also disrupt non-road transport such as inundating underground stations and lines. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat is expected to have particularly negative health impacts on older people and those with underlying health conditions, with up to an estimated 21 fatalities and 107 casualties in Hammersmith & Fulham in the event of a 2-week heatwave, based on borough-scaled estimates in the London Risk Register. Older people are at the highest risk of death during extreme heat; during the 2022 UK heatwaves 95% of excess deaths (2,839) were among those aged 65+ (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-mortality-monitoring-reports/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-2022). Extreme heat can exacerbate underlying health conditions including heart and lung conditions, diabetes, and renal insufficiency. Exposure to extreme heat impacts can be exacerbated in those less able to adapt their behaviour, including people with mobility issues, Alzheimers, mental health conditions, and the very young. Impacts are likely to be worst in the private rented sector as this has the most energy-inefficient housing, with households on lower incomes more likely to rent. Numerous council estates are also situated within areas of historically high temperatures. Socioeconomic factors above such as underlying health conditions, low income, and tenancy status are unevenly distributed between communities and likely to be higher risk among some minority communities. A changing climate will impact on community facilities and services, causing disruption to services due to extreme weather and closure of buildings and facilities due to overheating and flooding. Vulnerable residents such as the elderly and children who frequently use educational, cultural, or community facilities may become more isolated if services are inaccessible due to extreme weather. Extreme heat poses a risk of system failures and compound risks locally. An example is knock-on impacts between transport disruption (such as softening road surfaces and buckling rails), power outages and IT failure, and increased demand on health services from vulnerable people leading to crises in delivery of health services. Extreme heat makes the delivery of services such as education and waste collection more challenging due to overheated buildings, equipment failure, and risks to staff. Further challenges to infrastructure include failures in water pumping systems, failing lifts in high-rise homes, offices and underground stations. Extreme heat and drought also pose risks to local biodiversity and green infrastructure. | Drought: London faces a steeply rising water deficit, projected to reach 400m litres per year by 2040. Over 25% of London's water supply is from high-risk sources, and distribution networks have an almost 25% leakage rate. When droughts emerge the impacts occur quickly, affecting health, business operations, infrastructure and amenities; the cost to London during droughts is over £330m per day. The risks are not evenly distributed, with those worst affected frequently in lower socio-economic status groups. In the instance of severe drought, supply restrictions and low water pressure may result. This can lead to a lack of water available to occupants of high rise homes and offices in particular. Occupants of these homes may be more likely to be low-income as many of the taller dwellings in the borough are social housing. Health impacts from reduced availability of water are likely to be worst among those who are more physically at risk including older people, very young children, and those with underlying health conditions. Services and business can be severely disrupted by reductions in water supply. Food and health services are particularly reliant on access to water, and services to more vulnerable groups such as education, childcare and on-site social care may be unsafe to continue without continued water access. As human needs for water are prioritised, there is likely to be die-off of planting, with impacts for local biodiversity and ecosystem services.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Much of the borough lies less than five metres above sea level. The borough is particularly prone to surface-water flooding due to the limited capacity of London's Victorian sewer network, and the extent of hard surfacing in the borough. 1,500 homes in the borough are known to have flooded following extreme rainfall in July 2021. Flooding poses an immediate risk of injury and death, with greater risks to people with less adaptive capacity such as infants and those with mobility or mental health conditions. However, the main health impacts are to mental health. A UK Health Security Agency study found that those directly affected by flooding were 6 times more likely to experience mental health conditions such as PTSD, depression and anxiety. Those with existing mental health conditions or who have risk factors such as a family history of mental health conditions are at heightened risk of new or compounded mental health conditions. Greater risks are posed to those who are less likely to receive or be able to respond to flood warnings due to communication barriers; these include older people, those with language or cultural barriers, and people with mental health conditions. Flood damage to homes results in high costs for occupants. Low-income households and those who are more socially isolated, with fewer networks to draw upon, are likely to face greater difficulties both preparing for and recovering after flooding impacts. This interacts with housing tenure and type; lower-income households are more likely to rent rather than own their properties, limiting the options to invest in measures to protect the property. They may be more likely to live in basement flats which are prone to flooding. Another group severely impacted by disruption to their housing are those who have health or social care services delivered to them at home. As sewers become overwhelmed, a key infrastructure risk during surface water flooding is the surcharging of sewage above ground, including into homes, with resulting health risks. Flooding poses risks to the normal operation of any services and businesses reliant on transport as roads can become impassable, increases likelihood of potholes, and disrupts continuation of built environment and construction activities. Flooding can also disrupt non-road transport such as inundating underground stations and lines. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat is expected to have particularly negative health impacts on older people and those with underlying health conditions, with up to an estimated 21 fatalities and 107 casualties in Hammersmith & Fulham in the event of a 2-week heatwave, based on borough-scaled estimates in the London Risk Register. Older people are at the highest risk of death during extreme heat; during the 2022 UK heatwaves 95% of excess deaths (2,839) were among those aged 65+ (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/heat-mortality-monitoring-reports/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-2022). Extreme heat can exacerbate underlying health conditions including heart and lung conditions, diabetes, and renal insufficiency. Exposure to extreme heat impacts can be exacerbated in those less able to adapt their behaviour, including people with mobility issues, Alzheimers, mental health conditions, and the very young. Impacts are likely to be worst in the private rented sector as this has the most energy-inefficient housing, with households on lower incomes more likely to rent. Numerous council estates are also situated within areas of historically high temperatures. Socioeconomic factors above such as underlying health conditions, low income, and tenancy status are unevenly distributed between communities and likely to be higher risk among some minority communities. A changing climate will impact on community facilities and services, causing disruption to services due to extreme weather and closure of buildings and facilities due to overheating and flooding. Vulnerable residents such as the elderly and children who frequently use educational, cultural, or community facilities may become more isolated if services are inaccessible due to extreme weather. Extreme heat poses a risk of system failures and compound risks locally. An example is knock-on impacts between transport disruption (such as softening road surfaces and buckling rails), power outages and IT failure, and increased demand on health services from vulnerable people leading to crises in delivery of health services. Extreme heat makes the delivery of services such as education and waste collection more challenging due to overheated buildings, equipment failure, and risks to staff. Further challenges to infrastructure include failures in water pumping systems, failing lifts in high-rise homes, offices and underground stations. Extreme heat and drought also pose risks to local biodiversity and green infrastructure. | Drought: London faces a steeply rising water deficit, projected to reach 400m litres per year by 2040. Over 25% of London's water supply is from high-risk sources, and distribution networks have an almost 25% leakage rate. When droughts emerge the impacts occur quickly, affecting health, business operations, infrastructure and amenities; the cost to London during droughts is over £330m per day. The risks are not evenly distributed, with those worst affected frequently in lower socio-economic status groups. In the instance of severe drought, supply restrictions and low water pressure may result. This can lead to a lack of water available to occupants of high rise homes and offices in particular. Occupants of these homes may be more likely to be low-income as many of the taller dwellings in the borough are social housing. Health impacts from reduced availability of water are likely to be worst among those who are more physically at risk including older people, very young children, and those with underlying health conditions. Services and business can be severely disrupted by reductions in water supply. Food and health services are particularly reliant on access to water, and services to more vulnerable groups such as education, childcare and on-site social care may be unsafe to continue without continued water access. As human needs for water are prioritised, there is likely to be die-off of planting, with impacts for local biodiversity and ecosystem services.

project_info:
Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - H&F Healthy Homes - Able to Pay Retrofit Service: We are expanding H&F Healthy Homes to include a retrofit support service for 'able to pay' homes in the borough. The service should provide residents with an end-to-end retrofit customer journey, offering expert support at every stage—from initial assessment (whole house survey), project coordination to project completion and evaluation, signposting quality suppliers and financing options, and maximising energy cost and carbon savings to residents. The key components of this service are summarised:
• Clear information on the role of domestic clean energy technologies in the net zero transition, including whole house/ flat retrofit plans, signposted support for vulnerable and fuel-poor households, and referrals to financial support and trusted installers. It should cover all building and tenure types.
• Advice on accessing funding and finance, including UK Government, energy company and private funding schemes. 
• Advice on finding and managing good quality installers, including links to government accreditation schemes such as Microgeneration Certification Scheme and TrustMark, and a retrofit co-ordinator to help residents manage works to a good quality. 
• Accelerate the deployment of low carbon heat; given the essential role of low carbon heating systems in net zero, the service should improve resident awareness and trust in these technologies.

climate_hazard: Heat stress: Via increased heat stress as an implication of climate change, vulnerable populations face the harshest health and energy impacts. For example, children and youth may face difficulty recreating and learning outdoors, low-income households may face higher utility bills related to A/C that, if unable to be paid, may threaten energy security, and outdoor workers as well as elderly populations may be at an increased risk for heatstroke and other related health issues. Additionally, vulnerable sectors, such as agriculture, electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply, and arts, entertainment and recreation are most impacted. Agricultural yields are threatened due to drought and heat scorching, electricity and other utility access is limited and strained during high-heat days, and outdoor arts, entertainment, and recreation are compromised to avoid heat-related illnesses. The City of West Lafayette recognizes that, as an urban area, heat stress-related risks are amplified without the implementation of adequate adaptation and mitigation actions. | Heavy precipitation: Via heavy precipitation as an implication of climate change, vulnerable populations face the harshest impacts. For example, marginalized/minority communities and low-income households may have an increased risk to flooding that may negatively impact the places in which they live, work, and travel, and outdoor workers may experience heavy precipitation events that threaten their safety during the workday. Additionally, the sectors of agriculture, professional, scientific and technical activities, human health and social work activities, and arts, entertainment, and recreation may be disrupted during and after a heavy precipitation event as resources may not be available to ensure operations can operate successfully. | Increased water demand: Via increased water demand as an implication of climate change and rapid urbanization, vulnerable populations face the harshest impacts. For example, low-income households may experience higher water bills that threaten water security. Additionally, agriculture, manufacturing, and water supply are the sectors most exposed to the hazard as all depend on a stable water source. | Storm: Via storms as an implication of climate change, vulnerable populations face the harshest impacts. For example, marginalized/minority communities may not have access to accessible materials warning about how to prepare for a storm, low-income households may not reside in a property that is well-equipped to withstand storms, and outdoor workers may be exposed to hazardous storm conditions that threaten their safety. Additionally, vulnerable sectors, such as agriculture, forestry, human health and social work activities, arts, entertainment and recreation, and professional, scientific and technical activities, are impacted as crops may not produce adequate yields, trees may cause damage to infrastructure, transportation access and energy security may be at risk in human health-related situations, and certain outdoor activities may be cancelled during and after storm events. | River flooding: Via river flooding as an implication of climate change, vulnerable populations face the harshest impacts. For example, marginalized/minority communities and low-income households residing alongside the river at non-ideal elevations may have an increased risk to river flooding that may negatively impact the places in which they live, work, and travel. Additionally, the sectors of agriculture and arts, entertainment, and recreation are impacted as crops may not produce adequate yields and outdoor activities may be cancelled during heavy rain events that lead to river flooding.

Infectious disease: Lyme disease is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. Generally, blacklegged ticks first need to feed on infected wild animals, such as birds and rodents, and then attach and feed on humans for at least 24 hours to transmit the bacteria. Blacklegged ticks are usually found in wooded or forested areas, in leaf litter or on shrubs and tall grass in some parts of Canada. Those who golf, hunt, camp, fish and hike are at greater risk as well as those who work in wooded areas (leading walks, researchers/scientists, forestry maintenance activities, trail maintenance, etc.). In 2019, the majority of Halton was identified as a risk area for Lyme disease, based on tick surveillance. Tick surveillance (dragging in the spring and fall) is carried out by Halton Region staff and results are posted on https://www.halton.ca/For-Residents/Immunizations-Preventable-Disease/Diseases-Infections/Lyme-Disease
Ticks tend to be active in warmer weather, from the spring to the fall. Ticks can also be active on mild winter days if there isn't much snow. With climate change temperatures are expected to be warmer in the region, including milder winters, increasing the length of time that ticks are active each year and also the potential risk of transmission. 

Impacts: Negative health impacts | Other: Water Quality (algal bloom): The threshold was 'an algal bloom at Burlington public beaches.' 

Impacts: restricted access or closure of beach and water-based recreation activities (access is free and especially important to those who don't have access to pools, whether backyard or can't afford to pay for access to a public pool especially on heat alert days when access to cooling activities is important); stress on aquatic habitat resulting in impairment or loss of ecosystem services; impacts to municipal water treatment processes (considered but determined not to be a factor as Halton has a very detailed Harmful Algal Bloom response plan).

People and pets who were unknowingly exposed to the blue green algae could experience health symptoms requiring medical attention. | Heavy precipitation: Three climate hazards relate to heavy precipitation (wet conditions, stormwater flooding and creek flooding). On Aug. 4, 2014, 191 mm (two months of rain) fell in parts of Burlington over eight hours. The City's Emergency Operations Centre was activated and opened two evacuation centres for residents who were flooded and didn't have another place to stay. Over 3,000 homes reported flooding resulting in $90 million in insured claims. The City and Halton Region introduced programs for residents to increase flood resiliency costing the City over $567 and the Region over $2.5M since 2014; partnered with the Intact Centre on Climate Adaptation and in 2017 and launched the Home Flood Protection Program (50-100% subsidy at different times) helping homeowners identify flood risks and support preventative maintenance activities. Conservation Halton is updating regulatory mapping including floodplain mapping. On July 15, 2024, the City of Burlington received 74 mm of rainfall, with peak 1-hour rainfall intensity equal to a 1:100-year storm event. For the five days before July 15, Burlington had about 95 mm of rain, saturating soils and increasing the volume of runoff managed by creek and stormwater systems. Over 1,600 homes in Burlington experienced flooding within their basements due to sanitary sewer backups or overland flow entering through building openings. During the extreme rainfall, large volumes of stormwater infiltrated the wastewater system, causing the sewers to surcharge. Halton Region identified approximately 875 homes that faced some degree of wastewater backup into basements. Some impacts to vulnerable populations in Burlington include higher worry and stress than non-flooded residents with continued worrying years after the flood when it rained; residents forced to take days off work due to flooding to deal with clean-up, insurance, etc. but not everyone has the luxury of paid time off; physical health impacts like exacerbated asthma and not everyone has health insurance; those who can't afford or are not eligible for flood insurance are further impacted with financial costs for replacement of lost items; those who live in basement units are especially vulnerable as they need to find new accommodations and replace their belongings. Kids who access parks or sportsfields were impacted due to flooded fields. Those without personal vehicles are particularly impacted by detours to get around flooded areas; power outages result in spoiled food.
 | Extreme heat: In mid-July 2013, five days of hot, muggy weather with temperatures feeling like 40 degrees Celsius resulted in heat warnings across much of southern Ontario including Burlington. The City offered some relief from the heat with extended pool hours and by moving some summer camps inside air-conditioned buildings. A heat wave in the early fall 2017 broke heat records in eastern Canada, resulting in the cancellation of a marathon in Montreal and the early closure of the Halton Children's Water Festival on one of the days. An added complication with this fall heat wave was that some landlords had already turned the heat on in buildings in Toronto. A number of heat and extended heat warnings were issued the summers of 2018-2020. The first heat warning of 2020 was issued in late May with additional heat warnings issued throughout the summer. In 2020, under COVID-19, Central Arena Auditorium was opened from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. for one-hour increments with physical distancing protocols. July 2020 included heat warnings on July 2, 18 and 26 and an extended heat warning between July 4 and 11. On Nov. 10, 2020, records were broken across eight Ontario communities. On that day in November, Burlington registered 24 degrees Celsius with a humidex of 27 degrees Celsius at 3:15 p.m. In addition, Montreal and Toronto set the longest stretch above 15 degrees Celsius in November. August 2021 saw extended heat with humidex readings in the 40s and cooling centres open at Burlington Public Library branches. On August 26, the humidex readings in Burlington ranged between 40C and 43C for five hours. By August 25, Toronto (about 60 km east of Burlington) already experienced 24 days over 30C in 2021. Summer 2022 saw heat waves with humidex daytime readings of 38C in May and 44C in June and nighttime readings of 31C in July. In addition to heat, the summers of 2023 and 2025 brought new conditions - wildfire smoke - to Burlington. Cooling centre locations are now also used during poor air quality days. Impacts include: negative health outcomes; increased heat stress for animals and livestock; impacts to building mechanical systems; reduction in labour supply and labour productivity; decline in use of outdoor recreation; temporary closure of buildings without air conditioning; etc. | Snow and ice: We identified two climate hazards related to this: freezing rain and heavy snowfall. Mid-Dec 2013 - 30 cm storm followed by freezing rain on Dec. 21. Many of the 7,500 Burlington Hydro (BH) customers who lost power had it restored within a day. Residents north of Highway 5/Dundas St. and into Lowville, Kilbride and Cedar Springs experienced more extensive damage with trees and power lines down due to the weight of the ice making many of the roads inaccessible resulting in a longer power outage. With 1,550 homes still without power the evening of Dec. 22, the City opened three warming stations. The City qualified for the Ice Storm Assistance Program receiving over $2 million in claims. March 12, 2014 - a major snowstorm prompted early closures and cancellation of March Break programs. Apr. 15, 2018 - an ice storm impacted 6,038 BH customers (nine percent), mainly due to downed wires and trees taking just over nine hours to restore power to 90 percent of affected customers. This storm also cost the City over $25,000 in forestry related clean-up costs less than two weeks after another storm event (due to high winds) impacted 5,673 hydro customers and cost the City over $82,000 in forestry related clean-up costs. Jan. 19, 2019 - A major snowstorm hit Burlington and especially Hamilton where about 40 cm of snow fell coupled with cold temperatures and wind gusts. Dec. 1, 2019 - freezing rain and wind gusts impacted 17,768 BH customers (26 percent) due to falling tree limbs taking just over five hours to restore power to 90 percent of customers. Jan. 16-17, 2022 - a blizzard with about 40 cm of snow fell in Burlington resulting in school closures on Jan. 17 and 18 due to the snow and ongoing clean up. This was followed by a special weather statement for above freezing temperatures followed by a cold front resulting in icy/slippery surfaces on Jan. 19. Impacts: In addition to the major events reported by BH when power is out for an extended period, there are also days when ice results in facility closures including schools. project_info: Buildings - Appleby Ice Centre Decarbonization: The existing ice plant is currently being replaced with a new, higher efficiency ice plant capable of heat recovery. In the second phase of the project, which is currently unfunded, thermal storage tanks will be installed to store recovered heat from the ice plant along with back up electric boilers and a water-to-water modular heat pump. Heat exchangers and hydronic piping will be added through out the building to bring recovered heat to heating loads including, domestic hot water, dehumidification, and space heating. This project will essentially remove the use of fossil fuel in the older half of the building, with a similar project happening in the mid 2030's for the newer half of the building.

project_info: Buildings - Fire Station 7 - Energy Retrofit: This deep energy retrofit project involves comprehensive upgrades to improve the building's energy efficiency and sustainability. Key measures include increasing attic insulation, replacing all existing glazing with high-performance alternatives, and implementing air sealing around the building envelope. Following a shingle replacement, photovoltaic panels will be installed on the roof to offset the facility's electricity consumption. The domestic hot water system will be electrified, and the current forced-air furnace HVAC system will be replaced with a high-efficiency dedicated outdoor air system (DOAS) featuring demand-controlled ventilation, heat recovery, and an air-source variable refrigerant flow (VRF) system.

Infectious disease: Lyme disease is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. Generally, blacklegged ticks first need to feed on infected wild animals, such as birds and rodents, and then attach and feed on humans for at least 24 hours to transmit the bacteria. Blacklegged ticks are usually found in wooded or forested areas, in leaf litter or on shrubs and tall grass in some parts of Canada. Those who golf, hunt, camp, fish and hike are at greater risk as well as those who work in wooded areas (leading walks, researchers/scientists, forestry maintenance activities, trail maintenance, etc.). In 2019, the majority of Halton was identified as a risk area for Lyme disease, based on tick surveillance. Tick surveillance (dragging in the spring and fall) is carried out by Halton Region staff and results are posted on https://www.halton.ca/For-Residents/Immunizations-Preventable-Disease/Diseases-Infections/Lyme-Disease
Ticks tend to be active in warmer weather, from the spring to the fall. Ticks can also be active on mild winter days if there isn't much snow. With climate change temperatures are expected to be warmer in the region, including milder winters, increasing the length of time that ticks are active each year and also the potential risk of transmission.

climate_hazard:
Extreme heat: With climate change, the frequency and severity of extreme heat events in Sakarya province are increasing. Prolonged heat waves, particularly in urban centers, exacerbate the heat island effect, exacerbating health risks. The groups most affected by this situation are children whose thermoregulation systems are not fully developed, women who are more sensitive to heat due to pregnancy or hormonal reasons, elderly individuals struggling with chronic diseases, and outdoor workers, such as agricultural and construction workers, who are forced to work outdoors for long periods. Extreme temperatures can cause serious health problems such as heat stroke and respiratory and circulatory disorders in these groups.

The agriculture and forestry sectors, which play a significant role in Sakarya's economy, are also directly affected by extreme heat. Plant growth is negatively affected, yields are lost, and milk yields and animal health in livestock are at risk. The risk of heat-related drought and fire in forests is increasing, while the sudden increase in electricity demand strains grid systems and threatens energy supply security. Similarly, increased evaporation is depleting water resources, increasing pressure on water supply infrastructure. Therefore, the risk of extreme heat in Sakarya is a priority climate threat for both human health and critical infrastructure and economic sectors. | Drought: Drought is a significant climate hazard that has become increasingly prevalent in Sakarya province in recent years. Changes in rainfall patterns and rising temperatures are leading to a decrease in soil moisture and a significant reduction in water resources. This has particularly serious impacts on vulnerable groups with limited access to clean water. Vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, women, and individuals with chronic illnesses are at higher risk during drought periods due to inadequate sanitation, water scarcity, and waterborne diseases.

Sakarya's rural economy, based on agriculture and forestry, is directly affected by drought. Decreased soil moisture leads to significant yield losses in crop production, and the increased need for irrigation further strains water resources. Livestock farming is also negatively impacted by the decline in forage production and difficulties accessing water. Drought stresses forest ecosystems, increasing the risk of fires. It also puts pressure on drinking water and agricultural irrigation infrastructure due to the depletion of groundwater and surface water reserves. Therefore, drought stands out as a critical climate risk in Sakarya, threatening both the ecosystem and socioeconomic structure. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Rising temperatures, decreasing humidity, and windy weather conditions associated with climate change create favorable conditions for forest fires in Sakarya province. These meteorological conditions, defined as 'fire weather,' increase both the risk of forest fires and their rate of spread. This danger poses a serious threat, particularly to local communities living near rural and forested areas, indigenous people living in close proximity to nature, and individuals whose livelihoods depend on forest ecosystems. Fires directly jeopardize the habitats, health, and cultural heritage of these groups.

Sakarya's vital forest assets are under significant threat under fire weather conditions. Extended dry periods and heat waves disrupt the forests' moisture balance, increasing their vulnerability to fire. Forest fires not only lead to ecosystem destruction, but also to the loss of carbon sinks, the decline in biodiversity, and serious damage to the natural balance. Furthermore, the costs of firefighting and the loss of forest products negatively impact the regional economy. Therefore, fire weather conditions should be considered as a priority climate risk for the forestry sector in Sakarya. | River flooding: Sakarya ili, başta Sakarya Nehri olmak üzere birçok akarsu ve dereye ev sahipliği yapması nedeniyle nehir taşkınlarına karşı hassas bir bölgedir. İklim değişikliğine bağlı olarak artan şiddetli yağışlar ve düzensiz yağış rejimi, özellikle nehir yataklarına yakın alanlarda ani ve geniş çaplı taşkınlara yol açmaktadır. Bu durum, özellikle su kaynaklarına ve doğal ortamlara yakın alanlarda yaşayan yerel toplulukları (indigenous people) tehdit etmektedir. Taşkınlar, bu grupların yaşam alanlarını ve geçim kaynaklarını doğrudan etkileyerek barınma, sağlık ve altyapıya erişim gibi temel haklarını tehdit eder.

Nehir taşkınları; tarım alanlarında ürün kayıplarına, sulama altyapısında tahribata ve içme suyu kaynaklarında kirlilik riskine yol açmaktadır. Kanalizasyon sistemleri taşkın sırasında taşarak halk sağlığı açısından ciddi tehlikeler oluşturabilir. İnşaat ve ulaşım altyapısında hasar meydana gelirken, yolların kapanması ve köprülerin zarar görmesi lojistik süreçleri aksatabilir. Ayrıca konaklama ve yeme-içme hizmetleri gibi turizmle ilişkili sektörler de bu afetlerden olumsuz etkilenmektedir. Artan bulaşıcı hastalık riski, taşkınların insan sağlığı üzerindeki dolaylı etkilerini de artırmaktadır. Bu nedenle nehir taşkını, Sakarya'da çok sektörlü etkiler doğuran önemli bir iklimsel risktir.
project_info: Buildings - Energy-Efficient Building Renovation through Recycled Insulation Materials: The municipality plans to implement on-site retrofitting of buildings without external insulation by introducing recycled insulation materials produced from local waste streams. This initiative aims to improve thermal performance, reduce energy consumption, and increase overall energy efficiency in the building sector. The project will be carried out in stages, ensuring a scalable and sustainable approach that contributes to climate action and resource efficiency.

climate_hazard: Extreme heat: Extreme heat has unequal impacts across the region. Individuals with low incomes are more likely to live in areas with less tree cover and more impervious surfaces compared to wealthier individuals and may also have less access to air conditioning. These conditions make areas hotter and can result in higher energy costs to cool residences. In addition, outdoor workers and the unhoused are exposed to the worst of the hazard. Youth and the elderly as well as vulnerable health groups are more adversely impacted by the heat. Historic events, such as redlining, have also created a racialized pattern of access to cooler areas. Black, Indigenous, and communities of color in the Twin Cities typically have lower access to green space and live in hotter areas than white people. | Extreme cold: Those who spend long periods of time outdoors in the cold may be at increased risk as well as those who have difficulty regulating their body temperature, especially vulnerable health groups. Individuals with low incomes may be more exposed to cold due to high energy costs to heat homes. | Drought: Minnesota is known for its extreme seasonal differences, and precipitation varies significantly from year to year. Flooding, drought and recharge changes are current challenges, and climate change serves as a risk multiplier. The region's water service providers, watersheds, regulators, and users need to adjust practices, behaviors, and develop coordinated approaches that address risks posed by climate change to water and water infrastructure. For instance, about 30% of the groundwater delivered to homes and businesses by water suppliers in the region is used outdoors primarily for lawn and landscape irrigation. During periods of high temperatures and drought these uses tend to increase, when water sources are likely to be stressed, potentially leading to excessive aquifer drawdown, well interference issues, and impacts to surface waters and surrounding ecosystems. These high-demand periods also result in increased energy usage and additional water treatment, infrastructure, and associated costs to meet demands. However, by investing in and implementing efficient water use and conservation programs and practices, non-essential water use can be lessened or eliminated, with water sources and connected ecosystems becoming more resilient to climate stresses. (from the Met Council's draft 2050 Water Policy Plan) | Urban flooding: From an asset management perspective, the financial implications of inaction are well researched and documented. A 2024 Joint Economic Committee (.gov) report estimates “the total annual economic burden of flooding in the U.S. to be between $179.8 billion and $496.0 billion”, making flooding the costliest and most common type of natural disaster in the US. Localized flooding has the potential to impact local and regional infrastructure, services, and public safety. Joint Economic Committee (.gov) also reports “On average every dollar invested in flood protection can save $5-8 in damages with some estimates showing that projects protecting water and waste treatment plants can produce $31 in returns per $1 invested.” In rural areas, crop damage and delay of planting, as well as impact on infrastructure conditions (ditches and culverts) are serious effects of flooding. | Heavy precipitation: Extreme rainfall trends put a strain on stormwater infrastructure and other surface water conveyance or retention efforts. Given the fact that much of the stormwater infrastructure within the Twin Cities metro was designed to convey surface water based on technical standards and rainfall estimations adopted in 1960, the increasingly short, intense rainfalls present a challenge for communities and for the Metropolitan Council. Other types of precipitation, such as hail and snow, also impact the seven-county region. In August 2023, a hailstorm in the Twin Cities resulted in $1.1 billion in damage and was one of the costliest storms in the nation that year. Such precipitation events put financial strain on low-income communities and expose outdoor and frontline workers, such as transit employees, to volatile working conditions. | Other: Poor Air Quality: Poor air quality and pollution disproportionately affects vulnerable populations, including children, older adults, people with preexisting health conditions, and low-income communities. These groups often face higher exposure levels due to proximity to highways, industrial facilities, or other sources of emissions, as well as limited access to healthcare and resources to mitigate impacts. Poor air quality exacerbates respiratory and cardiovascular diseases such as asthma, COPD, and heart disease, leading to increased hospital visits, missed work and school days, and higher healthcare costs. Certain sectors, particularly healthcare and social services, experience heightened strain as they respond to pollution-related illnesses, while the labor force can be impacted through reduced productivity and workforce participation. In addition, the transportation and industrial sectors are both major contributors to air pollution and are directly affected by regulatory changes aimed at improving air quality. Addressing these disparities requires targeted interventions that reduce emissions while prioritizing the health and resilience of those most at risk.

project_info: Water management - Flood Control and River Improvement of Pagsanga-an River in Ormoc City: The pre-feasibility study can be accessed below: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1QWEcLX4Ris1ZAeKctAqbq5q6ofnB35rO/view?usp=drivesdkThe need for Flood Control and River Improvement in Ormoc City, brought up after the number of disastrous events that hits the area. Ormoc City, with its geographical and topographical location, is prone to natural hazards. Pagsanga-an River is one of the major river basins in Ormoc City. It has a total catchment area of about 481 sq.m. and length of waterway of about 56 km.Two schemes are considered for this project, specifically for the Lower Pagsanga-an River: Scheme 1: Resettlement and Scheme 2: River Widening. Scheme I is considered to relocate about 8.5 hectares of the community within Brgy. San Juan. This zone is considered to be a catch basin and a low-lying area, and this resettlement procedure aims to prevent further damages to the life and property. Another proposed scheme is the river widening of the lower Pagsanga-an River to increase its capacity, widen the choke point due to the bridge downstream and immediately drain the flood waters. This should be coupled with proper drainage system of the above-mentioned bypass road to decrease the accumulation rate of excess flows within the community during calamities.The total investment cost required for Scheme I is ₱1,151,480,424.29 and for Scheme II is ₱794,466,959.82

project_info: Transport - Solid Waste Management Facility and Renewable Energy Production: The pre-feasibility study can be accessed below: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1n2vuzrzhaKWvxgItuv1RuramRHwQ3YNZ/view?usp=drivesdkThe main objective of the project is to improve the services and access of the constituents of Ormoc City to an integrated waste management facility that aims to achieve waste reduction, waste minimization, and resource recovery by developing a waste to energy facility to increase power supply thereby providing good quality of life.Phase 1 of the Project is geared towards improvement of collection services and SWM facilities to cope with the increasing waste generation due to the growing population, business establishments, and trade while keeping the environment clean and healthy within the City of Ormoc. This include the construction of a new cell of the sanitary landfill complete with lining system, leachate piping, gas venting, waste treatment ponds, equipment yard, administrative building, guardhouse, and other essential facilities as required under RA 9003.It also includes procurement of additional equipment for garbage collection, composting, and recycling equipment. Eight dump trucks must be acquired by 2030 to cover the remaining barangays which are not covered by current garbage collection. The equipment for materials recovery facility (MRF) includes among others a single line conveyor which will be used for further segregation of waste upon arrival at the area. Composting bins will also be acquired.At this time, the Project design is still largely noncommittal on what WTE system to adopt. The options presented consist of: A Landfill Gas Collector with Electric Generator, Biomass Combustion Technology and the Biomass Gasification/Pyrolysis. There is however, still a mass of legal, technical and financial challenges to the latter two technologies.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Composting of organic waste: Creates a composting plant for the disposal of organic waste from the city's largest generators (restaurants and hotels) and the use of material from pruning and raking leaves from urban trees. 60% of urban solid waste is organic. They are currently sent to a landfill 60 km away from the city. The objective of this project is the construction and operation of a local composting system that removes at least 50% of this volume from conventional collection. Furthermore, the large volume of branches and leaves resulting from conductive and sanitary pruning of urban afforestation, as well as the leaves collected by sweeping public roads would be used in this process to balance the Carbon/nitrogen ratio in the composting process using the \'UFSC Method\'. The compost produced will be used in urban landscaping. The collaboration of large generators will result in reduction of your expenses with solid waste (in application of the new legal framework for sanitation) in addition to the return on marketing. The result of the savings generated by the project will be estimated by indicators and the \'saved\' values ​​must be reverted to the Municipal Environmental Fund for application in environmental actions.

climate_hazard: River flooding: There are a number of key rivers across the district liable to flooding. The major river catchments in South Gloucestershire are the Little Avon, River Frome, the River Avon, and their tributaries; Ladden Brook, Bradley Brook, Folly Brook, Hortham Brook, Patchway Brook, Stoke Brook, Henbury Trym, River Boyd and Siston Brook. These watercourses are managed by the Environment Agency although riparian responsibilities still apply. The settlements identified as most at risk of fluvial flooding are Hanham, Swineford, Emersons Green, Chipping Sodbury and Yate. | Extreme cold: Those with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory conditions as well as the elderly and young children under 5 are at increased risk from extremes of cold - fuel poverty in the district currently stands at 9% (9,439 households) this is just under the UK average but with the rapid increase in the cost of living this is likely to increase sharply. | Extreme heat: Those with pre-existing respiratory or cardiovascular disease and those with renal conditions or diabetes are at higher risk from extremes of heat. We also have an aging population in this district in particular and therefore the likelihood is an increasing pressure on health and social care services across the district. Those who live in poorly insulated housing particularly in denser urban areas in the district are at increased risk along with outdoor workers for example those in the agricultural sector, water supply sector and waste management industries where extremes of heat may lead to a requirement to change shift patterns. Extreme heat leading to dryer conditions this summer has lead to grazing animals needing to be fed supplementary food a cost to livestock managers. | Increased water demand: Increasing predicted population growth in terms of new housing and also increase in extreme heat events and reduced summer time precipitation are likely to lead to increased water demand across the district. For example this summer (2025) horticulture, trees and forestry has required supplementary water. Increasing costs of water services can impact particularly on certain vulnerable groups with pre-existing health conditions. | Urban flooding: Flooding and storms have impacted on transport infrastructure (rail, bus, road and cycling and walking) but this has tended to be localised and not across the network or large areas as yet. More frequent stormy conditions causing tree falls ( combined with ash die back disease making more trees vulnerable to collapse). Based on the Risk of Flooding from Surface Water mapping, South Gloucestershire has approximately 6,900 residential properties and 800 non-residential properties at risk of flooding during a 1 in 100-year (1% AEP) event. This is predicted to increase to approximately 13,900 residential and 1,200 non-residential properties as a result of the impact of climate change (based on the 45% climate change uplift - see Section 3.9.1). | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): This relates specifically to risks from coastal flooding along the Severn Estuary and the low-lying communities along this coastline. Over the longer term there is a risk to the delivery of essential services, impacts on housing and businesses in the effected areas. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): The summer of 2025 has been extremely hot in the UK, and this follows other hot summers such as 2022. This has greatly increased the risk of field fires, including localised ones within South Gloucestershire. | Biodiversity loss: Increased tick populations and increased risk for people from Lymes disease. Crop productivity impacted by reduced pollinators and increased flooding and drought. Lower productivity leading to lower food production and higher food costs- may adversely impact lower income groups and food related businesses such as orchards and honey and supply chains. Species loss of loved species such as cuckoos can cause mental health issues. | Soil degradation/erosion: Degraded soils and other climate hazards impacting food productivity and supply chains. Soils with high agro-chemical (loads) pesticides and fertiliser will impact biodiversity especially in drought conditions (see row 8 above). Sediment run-off from development sites impacts water catchments and biodiversity where Construction and Environmental Management Plans (CEMPS) fail to be adequate and/or there is exceptional flooding. Sustainable grazing levels are impacted by drought and flooding and overgrazing in these conditions can lead soil degradation and erosion impacting productivity and biodiversity and animal welfare (see row 8).

project_info: Energy efficiency (including public lighting) - Decarbonisation of council owned premises includes corporate buildings and schools (117): The Council has re-assessed the costs in 2024 of carried out in 2022 to decarbonise the corporate estate and the non-corporate Council owned estate which consists of 70 primary schools across the area (some primary schools previously owned by the Council have become academies). The report sets out the cost to decarbonise the estate and is currently being updated to the latest figures circa £84 million. The next step will be to consider funding options to deliver including public works loan funding but will include breaking down the report into priority buildings requiring retrofit measures.

climate_hazard: Urban flooding: Sandwell is a heavily urbanised borough with unequal distribution of sustainable drainage systems. The river Tame flows through the borough, as well as a number of underground diverted streams and an extensive canal network that runs through high population areas. While flooding events related to these rivers and canals are infrequent, a combination of poor natural drainage, heavy urbanisation and lack of preparedness mean many areas are at risk of flood events in a changing climate. | Increased water demand: Water quality in West Midlands aquifers is generally poor, and much of the water used for consumption comes from other areas surrounding the Borough. Increased demand during heatwaves and other events is likely to put strain on water infrastructure, meaning an increase in hosepipe bans and other water restriction measures. | Extreme heat: Heat stress will disproportionately impact on our poorest residents, marginalised groups, and those most medically vulnerable. Sandwell has a high proportion of deprived and marginalised communities, and resources and messaging will be difficult to distribute to these communities in times of need. As recent times have shown, the borough is not equipped to deal with prolonged heat, and the poorest residents often live in ill equipped and poorly insulated homes that are impacted most. Furthermore, as an industrial-heavy borough, Sandwell has many residents that would feel the biggest impacts in their workplaces, with high heat industries and the construction sector being most widely affected. | Loss of green space/green cover: Green space is extremely valuable to residents' health, wellbeing, nature connectedness, and protection from climate hazards. However, as a heavily urbanised area with a shortage of good quality housing, green space is always under threat. Sandwell also does not have a good even spread of accessible green space in the borough, with some areas having much better access than others - often in wealthier communities. With increasing pressure on green spaces, and the effects of a changing climate, there is a risk of this provision being reduced, through land use changes and loss of growing space - residents are at risk of losing valuable green infrastructure and the benefits it provides. | Heavy precipitation: Increased and heavy precipitation events can have drastic effects on urbanised populations. Drainage and sewerage systems are ill equipped in the borough to deal with significant downpours, leading to localised flooding and displacement of people and communities. Financial damages associated with costs from flood damage will impact businesses and communities, particularly those in low income households. An increase of flood events may also lead to damages to health assets, impacting on the public's access to health and social care services.

climate_hazard: Extreme wind: High winds also pose a risk to infrastructure reliant upon overhead lines, such as some national train lines from Victoria Station. | Extreme heat: The UN Committee on Climate Change UK Risk Assessment from 2017 states that heatwaves in the UK on the scale experienced in 2003 are expected to become the norm in summer by the 2040s. Even if global temperature increases are limited to 2°C or less, there are projected to be high magnitude impacts for the UK. The number of heat-related deaths in the UK are projected to increase by around 250% by the 2050s (median estimate), due to climate change, population growth and ageing, from a current annual baseline of around 2,000 heat-related deaths per year. Focusing on London, climate projections show that London will experience warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers. As a city, London is particularly vulnerable to heatwaves due to the Urban Heat Island effect. This is a phenomenon which describes the increased temperature of urban spaces compared to rural ones, which can mean a 10˚C difference between London and its surroundings. This is due to the fact the urban landscapes absorb and trap heat more than others (e.g. through buildings, roads). The type of building stock can contribute to enhancing heat, especially with less insulated buildings which is often the case in inner London, including in Westminster (with many buildings predating the 20th century). During the summer heatwave of 2003, differences of up to 10°C between city and rural temperatures were measured in London, with the highest levels of heat recorded in the central London boroughs. In 2003, 600 (mainly elderly) people died in the London heatwave. London had the highest number of deaths in the country but not the highest temperatures. In 2016, there were three extreme heat days with temperatures over 30C.Westminster will be heavily impacted by any increases in the duration, intensity and frequency of heatwaves. For instance, in July 2018, Westminster Council activated the Severe Weather Emergency Protocol to launch an emergency response to support people sleeping rough in the borough during a heatwave when temperatures reached as high as 35 degrees Celsius. This action is likely to be required more often as hot summers become more frequent. | Urban flooding: Surface water flooding occurs when intense rainfall is unable to soak into the ground or enter drainage systems, because of blockages, or breakages in water pipes or where the drainage capacity has been exceeded. Due to the highly built-up nature of Westminster and its limited drainage capacity, surface water flooding is the most likely cause of flooding within Westminster. Predicted increased frequency and intensity of rainfall in the future may increase the risk of flooding, which will be compounded by increased urban intensification and few surfaces able to slow down or absorb rainfall. Westminster will need to ensure sustainable flood risk management measures are in place to improve resistance and increase resilience to flood risk.Current guidance from the Environment Agency suggests that extreme rainfall intensity is likely to increase by between 20% and 40% over the next 100 years, which will increase the risk of surface flooding in Westminster. The Westminster Initial Assessments study has considered the impact of climate change on surface water flood risk. This has been assessed for a 20% and 40% increase in peak rainfall intensity and for the next 100 years. The study shows that in the event of a 1 in 100 rainfall taking place, some parts of Westminster could be flooded to a depth of more than 1.5 metres.Parts of north Westminster recently experienced the effects of major surface flooding. On 12 July 2021, three inches of rain fell across parts of London in 90 minutes, causing severe surface and sewer flooding, evacuations and property damage. Investigations are ongoing into the failure of surface water flood defences which had recently been installed. Further information can be found here: https://committees.westminster.gov.uk/documents/s43811/Appendix%20B%20-%20Section%2019%20Interim%20Flood%20Report.pdf | Drought: Following three consecutive and unprecedented dry winters London is in a severe drought (level 4) situation. Emergency drought orders are in place with millions of properties with severe water supply restrictions and low water pressure (impacting supply to properties at high levels and tower blocks). Increase of illnesses due to reduced use of water impacting on hygiene levels, increased casualties and potentially fatalities. Mental wellbeing impacts communities and public outrage leads to some disorder issues. | River flooding: Climate change is predicted to have a major impact on future flood risk. Westminster sits on the north bank of the Tidal River Thames and is therefore potentially susceptible to both tidal and fluvial flooding. Current guidance from the Environment Agency suggests that extreme rainfall intensity is likely to increase by between 20% and 40% over the next 100 years, which will increase the risk of flooding to Westminster from the River Thames. At present, Westminster has 4.7km of tidal Thames frontage, all of which has good protection against flooding by the Embankment wall. The Thames Barrier (downstream at Woolwich), and the associated Thames Tidal Flood Defences provide a 1 in 1000 year standard of protection (a 0.1% annual probability of failure) up to the year 2030.However, were the Thames flood defences to fail completely, this would result in extensive damage along Westminster's north bank, with some areas inundated within 30 minutes. Flood Zone 3 is the area most at risk from flooding were the Thames flood defences to fail. This area comprises a substantial part of Westminster (14%) including Pimlico and Millbank, which contain well established residential communities and associated services, including shops and schools, and Victoria and Whitehall, which have a more commercial and governmental mixed use character respectively. We have not calculated exactly how much damage would be caused in Westminster by a breach of the Thames flood barriers. However, we can infer the level of damage from the last major flooding events in Westminster, when on January 6th 1928, a tidal surge, at high tide, came up the River Thames Estuary, resulting in the flood defence walls and embankments of the time being overtopped. This resulted in 14 fatalities in Westminster, most of which occurred in basement dwellings in Millbank.Environment Agency data shows the Thames Barrier has been closed 200 times to prevent flooding in its history up to 2021, with over 50 of the closures in the winter of 2013/14. Due to the predicted rise in sea level and increase in peak river flows as a result of climate change, closure of the barrier is likely to become more common. The Environment Agency has indicated that if the barrier is closed 50 times a year on average or more, new tidal flood defences for the Thames Estuary will need to be put in place.

The number of heat-related deaths in the UK are projected to increase by around 250% by the 2050s (median estimate), due to climate change, population growth and ageing, from a current annual baseline of around 2,000 heat-related deaths per year. Focusing on London, climate projections show that London will experience warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers. As a city, London is particularly vulnerable to heatwaves due to the Urban Heat Island effect. This is a phenomenon which describes the increased temperature of urban spaces compared to rural ones, which can mean a 10˚C difference between London and its surroundings. This is due to the fact the urban landscapes absorb and trap heat more than others (e.g. through buildings, roads). The type of building stock can contribute to enhancing heat, especially with less insulated buildings which is often the case in inner London, including in Westminster (with many buildings predating the 20th century). During the summer heatwave of 2003, differences of up to 10°C between city and rural temperatures were measured in London, with the highest levels of heat recorded in the central London boroughs. In 2003, 600 (mainly elderly) people died in the London heatwave. London had the highest number of deaths in the country but not the highest temperatures. In 2016, there were three extreme heat days with temperatures over 30C.Westminster will be heavily impacted by any increases in the duration, intensity and frequency of heatwaves. For instance, in July 2018, Westminster Council activated the Severe Weather Emergency Protocol to launch an emergency response to support people sleeping rough in the borough during a heatwave when temperatures reached as high as 35 degrees Celsius. This action is likely to be required more often as hot summers become more frequent. | Urban flooding: Surface water flooding occurs when intense rainfall is unable to soak into the ground or enter drainage systems, because of blockages, or breakages in water pipes or where the drainage capacity has been exceeded. Due to the highly built-up nature of Westminster and its limited drainage capacity, surface water flooding is the most likely cause of flooding within Westminster. Predicted increased frequency and intensity of rainfall in the future may increase the risk of flooding, which will be compounded by increased urban intensification and few surfaces able to slow down or absorb rainfall. Westminster will need to ensure sustainable flood risk management measures are in place to improve resistance and increase resilience to flood risk.Current guidance from the Environment Agency suggests that extreme rainfall intensity is likely to increase by between 20% and 40% over the next 100 years, which will increase the risk of surface flooding in Westminster. The Westminster Initial Assessments study has considered the impact of climate change on surface water flood risk. This has been assessed for a 20% and 40% increase in peak rainfall intensity and for the next 100 years. The study shows that in the event of a 1 in 100 rainfall taking place, some parts of Westminster could be flooded to a depth of more than 1.5 metres.Parts of north Westminster recently experienced the effects of major surface flooding. On 12 July 2021, three inches of rain fell across parts of London in 90 minutes, causing severe surface and sewer flooding, evacuations and property damage. Investigations are ongoing into the failure of surface water flood defences which had recently been installed. Further information can be found here: https://committees.westminster.gov.uk/documents/s43811/Appendix%20B%20-%20Section%2019%20Interim%20Flood%20Report.pdf | Drought: Following three consecutive and unprecedented dry winters London is in a severe drought (level 4) situation. Emergency drought orders are in place with millions of properties with severe water supply restrictions and low water pressure (impacting supply to properties at high levels and tower blocks). Increase of illnesses due to reduced use of water impacting on hygiene levels, increased casualties and potentially fatalities. Mental wellbeing impacts communities and public outrage leads to some disorder issues. | River flooding: Climate change is predicted to have a major impact on future flood risk. Westminster sits on the north bank of the Tidal River Thames and is therefore potentially susceptible to both tidal and fluvial flooding. Current guidance from the Environment Agency suggests that extreme rainfall intensity is likely to increase by between 20% and 40% over the next 100 years, which will increase the risk of flooding to Westminster from the River Thames. At present, Westminster has 4.7km of tidal Thames frontage, all of which has good protection against flooding by the Embankment wall. The Thames Barrier (downstream at Woolwich), and the associated Thames Tidal Flood Defences provide a 1 in 1000 year standard of protection (a 0.1% annual probability of failure) up to the year 2030.However, were the Thames flood defences to fail completely, this would result in extensive damage along Westminster's north bank, with some areas inundated within 30 minutes. Flood Zone 3 is the area most at risk from flooding were the Thames flood defences to fail. This area comprises a substantial part of Westminster (14%) including Pimlico and Millbank, which contain well established residential communities and associated services, including shops and schools, and Victoria and Whitehall, which have a more commercial and governmental mixed use character respectively. We have not calculated exactly how much damage would be caused in Westminster by a breach of the Thames flood barriers. However, we can infer the level of damage from the last major flooding events in Westminster, when on January 6th 1928, a tidal surge, at high tide, came up the River Thames Estuary, resulting in the flood defence walls and embankments of the time being overtopped. This resulted in 14 fatalities in Westminster, most of which occurred in basement dwellings in Millbank.Environment Agency data shows the Thames Barrier has been closed 200 times to prevent flooding in its history up to 2021, with over 50 of the closures in the winter of 2013/14. Due to the predicted rise in sea level and increase in peak river flows as a result of climate change, closure of the barrier is likely to become more common. The Environment Agency has indicated that if the barrier is closed 50 times a year on average or more, new tidal flood defences for the Thames Estuary will need to be put in place.

climate_hazard: Fire weather (risk of wildfires): While the City of Nanaimo has not experienced any significant wildfires within the City boundary the City has been impacted by wildfire smoke from other wildfires nearby. \n Those with a history of asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD), lung cancer or heart problems may be more impacted by poor air quality. Poor air quality can also adversely impact seniors, pregnant women and young children. Outdoor workers are also more impacted by poor air quality by being exposed to the air for a longer period of time then those that are able to seek shelter indoors. During the 2018 wildfire season, and to a lesser extent in 2020 and 2021, much of the backcountry trails around Nanaimo were closed to mitigate wildfire risk. In June 2023 a wildfire blocked highway access to the West Coast of Vancouver Island effectively cutting off the communities of Port Alberni, Tofino and Ucluelet from the rest of the island. Another wildfire occurred in 2025 in a similar area, this time resulting in evacuations and a local statement of emergency being declared. As the City relies on outdoor recreation tourism this impacted the City's tourism and residents' quality of life. Logging operations were also halted during wildfire season impacting the City's forestry based economy. | Heat stress: From June 25 to July 1, 2021, British Columbia experienced a record heat wave that included temperatures that were five times higher than previous all-time records. This event, referred to as the 'heat dome' resulted in 619 heat related deaths in BC, 55 of which where on Vancouver Island. The impacts of the heat dome were greatest among the elderly, those that live alone, are low income and live in poor housing conditions or socially or materially deprived neighborhoods. Sixty- seven percent of those killed in BC during the heat dome were 70 years old or older. More than half of those who died (56%) lived alone, and most of those lacked cooling systems. The City's Climate Change Resiliency Strategy (2020) recognizes the impact of extreme heat on vulnerable population groups and includes the development of an Extreme Heat Response Strategy that includes information on cooling spaces that can serve community members during heat waves as a priority action. The City has since developed a draft Extreme Weather Strategy and has identified and mapped populations vulnerable to extreme heat to further support the strategy. | Storm: In December, 2018 a windstorm left over 150,000 people on Vancouver Island without power, threated the security of the City's water supply, and caused a debris jam above the City's water supply damn that nearly resulted in flooding. This event led to the City activating its' Emergency Operations Centre. The loss of power in the cold winter months had the greatest health impacts on seniors, those with existing health conditions, and those without a secondary heat source. A similar windstorm occurred in December of 2024, also resulting in power outages and road closures due to downed powerlines. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Nanaimo is a coastal City with a number of lower lying areas and infrastructure vulnerable to sea level rise. Nanaimo is located on the traditional territory of Snuneymuxw First Nation and borders three different Snuneymuxw land reserves, all of which are along the ocean. Two of these reserves are located within the Nanaimo River Estuary and are prone to flooding. These areas have experienced an increase in flood events due to the combined impacts of rising sea levels, winter storms and increased winter rainfall events. The City's Sea Level Rise Study identified a few key areas of the City vulnerable to storm surge and coastal flooding, these areas included the City's downtown core and Duke Point Industrial Park along with the Departure Bay and Protection Island neighbourhoods. The Duke Point Industrial area includes one of the City's two ferry terminal connections to the mainland of BC, which would be inaccessible in a coastal flooding event. City Plan includes a Sea Level Rise DPA to protect future development from sea level rise and storm surges. The Sea Level Rise Study recommends the City complete a Sea Level Rise Management Plan (SLRMP) to better understand coastal flooding risk and impacts in vulnerable area and identify viable solutions- the development of the SLRMP is currently underway. | Drought: The City's Climate Change Resiliency Strategy notes, \'despite increases in the intensity and frequency of rain, the frequency and length of dry spells (or days without rain) in summer months will steadily increase.\' Summer drought leads to crop failure, impacting local agriculture, lower river water levels and decreased water quality, harming the salmon stock and heat stress and drought has resulted in the death of native tree species such as the Western Red Cedar. The Western Red Cedar has historically been an common tree species in the Pacific Northwest and plays a prominent role in Indigenous history and culture and the local economy (forestry and building). Due to increasing dry hot summers Western Red Cedars are starting to die in the summer and have not been resilient to our changing climate. City urban forestry and Parks Staff are no longer recommending planting Western Red Cedars in our region.
project_info: Buildings - Sea Level Rise Strategy: The City has secured funding from the Provincial Emergency Management and Climate Readiness - Disaster Resilience Innovation Fund (DRIF) to complete a Sea Level Rise Management Plan. We are awaiting word on additional funding to include a communication strategy and erosion management plan within the project.
