Biodiversity loss: Climate change risks to Natural Environment and Assets has been identified as high for the CCR including; High Risk: Risks to terrestrial species and habitats from changing climatic conditions and extreme events, including temperature change, water scarcity, wildfire, flooding, wind, and altered hydrology (including water scarcity, flooding and saline intrusion); Risks to terrestrial species and habitats from pests, pathogens and invasive species, Risk to soils from changing climatic conditions, including seasonal aridity and wetness. Risks and opportunities for natural carbon stores, carbon sequestration from changing climatic conditions, including temperature change and water scarcity Risks to and opportunities for agricultural and forestry productivity from extreme events and changing climatic conditions (including temperature change, water scarcity, wildfire, flooding, coastal erosion, wind and saline intrustion). Risks to agriculture from pests, pathogens and invasive species Risks to forestry from pests, pathogens and invasive species Risks to freshwater species and habitats from changing climatic conditions and extreme events, including higher water temperatures, flooding, water scarcity and phenological shifts. Risks to freshwater species and habitats from pests, pathogens and invasive species Risks to marine species, habitats and fisheries from changing climatic conditions, including ocean acidification and higher water temperatures. Risks to marine species and habitats from pests, pathogens and invasive species Risks and opportunities to coastal species and habitats due to coastal flooding, erosion and climate factors. Risks from climate change are species-specific and may lead to changes in species population numbers, timing of life cycle events, species movement and distribution. These can also be affected by habitat availability, wildfires, other climate drivers and interdependencies between species, habitats and ecosystems. | Storm: Risk from storms has been identified as a high risk for the region across infrastructure and natural and environmental assets, including soil, agricultural and forestry productivity and carbon sequestration. In addition, risk to fresh and marine flora and fauna. In 2022, Wales has experienced such high winds and storms that schools and businesses have had to close temporarily. Warnings have been issued about travel and residents urged to stay indoors where possible. These extreme storms have resulted in temporary loss of power to homes and businesses, loss of clean water infrastructure and communication. CCRA3 identifies the role of severe weather, identifying an adaptation planning gap in response to drought, the effects of storms, lightning and high winds. CCRA3 also identifies the need to take climate risks into account related to the types of changes to transport, infrastructure and land use that are required to meet the Net Zero emissions target. | River flooding: Fluvial flood risk has been identified as high for many areas of public service delivery including Business and Industry; Health, Communities and the Built Environment; Infrastructure; Natural Environment and Assets; 
CCRA3 Technical Report outlines how future river and surface water climate change impacts are a major high level risk and that, despite progress with flood defences, risks are not being managed effectively with an adaptation shortfall which will further require government intervention. 
The assessment suggests:• Risks to people, communities and buildings include mortality, physical and mental health impacts, damage to property, financial implications of cleaning up or moving and disruption in terms of access to employment, education, health services and wider facilities.• Climate change will increase the number of properties at risk of flooding from all sources, and these could be in areas that have not previously been at risk of flooding.• Flood risk will be exacerbated and locked in unless building within the flood plain is avoided and properties developed in flood risk areas incorporate appropriate resilience measures and sustainable drainage systems designed for the lifespan of the development. The assessment suggests that although considerable advances have been made regarding the strategic management of flood risk at national and local levels, the risk magnitude remains high now and in the future in Wales, with more action needed due to the scale of the risk. Key areas of challenge relate to continued development on the flood plain, the management of surface water flooding via SuDS, the low take up of Property Flood Resilience (PFR), and the lack of UK-wide standards.
Fluvial flooding has impacted many communities across CCR in 2024 and 2025 including most recently in June 2025, flash flooding impacting vulnerable communities in Bridgend https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2klpjp34mo and in 2024 impacting homes and businesses in Pontypridd https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgj7qvj097po. NRW are coordinating 'catchment' response to address fluvial flooding and engaging all public bodies that operate within a catchment boundary. This regional approach is necessary to ensure that upstream actions don't have negative impacts further downstream. 
 | Extreme heat: As climate shifts result in more extreme weather patterns, there is a higher risk of extreme heat affecting the population within CCR. High risk to workforce and vulnerable populations was identified as impacting service delivery across multiple service areas from waste management to social and care services and the built environment. Over the past five years, there have been 25 days with temperatures of more than 30C (86F) in Wales - compared with four in the previous decade and the hottest day of the year now is nearly a degree - about 0.8C higher - than it was a few decades ago.UKCP18 projections for the UK show increases in average summer temperatures and the number of hot days and heatwaves events. The UKCCRA Technical report projects; • That climate change is likely to increase heat-related mortality, heat stroke and heat exhaustion indoors. In Wales, heat-related deaths could increase from a baseline of 2.4 per 100,000 people per year now to 6.5 per 100,000 by the 2050s, i.e. over a doubling of risk (central estimates). • The assessment of current evidence indicates that climate change related risks to health and wellbeing from heat may be higher than previously understood at the time of CCRA2. The 2018 and 2019 heatwaves in parts of the UK revealed a lack of planning in current systems.• Interactions between risks from high temperatures through combined exposures from air pollution, drought and wildfires are increasingly being recognised as significant.• A major policy gap across all the UK nations is the lack of inclusion of measures to prevent overheating in Building Regulations and other housing policy. Response to the risk can result from:• Public health activities that encourage behavioural change for high risk groups e.g. Public Health Wales early warning approach for extreme weather events.• Improving design through building regulations and standards for new buildings and increasing incentives for retrofitting. • Planning guidance for enhancing green space and urban cooling measures, including nature-based solutions.• PHW have provided some insight into high temperature response through their work on winter health and wellbeing published in 2019. In 2025, the met office is predicting the UK is more likely to experience a hotter-than-normal summer with an increased chance for heatwaves in 2025. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): A large part of the boundary of the CCR is coastal, with two coastal cities (Cardiff and Newport) and a major town (Barry) being located directly on the coast. All of these areas are currently exposed to coastal flooding risk which was identified as a high risk in the CCR Risk Register. 

The Climate Change Commission Risk Assessment (3) for Wales sets out the risk of coastal flooding across five themes;• Natural Environment & Assets • Infrastructure • Health Communities & the Built Environment• Business & Industry • International Dimensions. Welsh Government has recently published planning guidance TAN 15 which sets out: Development, flooding and coastal erosion and a new Flood Map for Planning introduce important changes to the way flooding and coastal erosion risks are considered in the development and planning process. Flood risk in Wales is increasing as a result of climate change. Serious flooding events are becoming more frequent and some areas currently at little risk will become vulnerable to flooding as our climate continues to change. As the National Strategy for Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management in Wales recognises, the planning system can help communities be more resilient to the effects of climate change by locating development in areas away from risk of flooding. Improved knowledge of the places which will be at risk in the future can help keep people safe, by preventing the damage and disruption to homes, workplaces and infrastructure that flooding can cause. TAN 15 provides planning advice that informs local development plans and decisions on planning applications in areas at risk of flooding and coastal erosion. It will be used by the Welsh Government, local planning authorities and developers to direct development away from areas at risk of flooding and coastal erosion. The formal adoption of TAN 15 has been postponed until June 2023 to allow for further review and consultation. Fluvial flooding has impacted many communities across CCR in 2024 and 2025 including most recently in June 2025, flash flooding impacting vulnerable communities in Bridgend https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2klpjp34mo and in 2024 impacting homes and businesses in Pontypridd https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgj7qvj097po. NRW are coordinating 'catchment' response to address fluvial flooding and engaging all public bodies that operate within a catchment boundary. This regional approach is necessary to ensure that upstream actions don't have negative impacts further downstream. 
 | Extreme heat: As climate shifts result in more extreme weather patterns, there is a higher risk of extreme heat affecting the population within CCR. High risk to workforce and vulnerable populations was identified as impacting service delivery across multiple service areas from waste management to social and care services and the built environment. Over the past five years, there have been 25 days with temperatures of more than 30C (86F) in Wales - compared with four in the previous decade and the hottest day of the year now is nearly a degree - about 0.8C higher - than it was a few decades ago.UKCP18 projections for the UK show increases in average summer temperatures and the number of hot days and heatwaves events. The UKCCRA Technical report projects; • That climate change is likely to increase heat-related mortality, heat stroke and heat exhaustion indoors. In Wales, heat-related deaths could increase from a baseline of 2.4 per 100,000 people per year now to 6.5 per 100,000 by the 2050s, i.e. over a doubling of risk (central estimates). • The assessment of current evidence indicates that climate change related risks to health and wellbeing from heat may be higher than previously understood at the time of CCRA2. The 2018 and 2019 heatwaves in parts of the UK revealed a lack of planning in current systems.• Interactions between risks from high temperatures through combined exposures from air pollution, drought and wildfires are increasingly being recognised as significant.• A major policy gap across all the UK nations is the lack of inclusion of measures to prevent overheating in Building Regulations and other housing policy. Response to the risk can result from:• Public health activities that encourage behavioural change for high risk groups e.g. Public Health Wales early warning approach for extreme weather events.• Improving design through building regulations and standards for new buildings and increasing incentives for retrofitting. • Planning guidance for enhancing green space and urban cooling measures, including nature-based solutions.• PHW have provided some insight into high temperature response through their work on winter health and wellbeing published in 2019. In 2025, the met office is predicting the UK is more likely to experience a hotter-than-normal summer with an increased chance for heatwaves in 2025. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): A large part of the boundary of the CCR is coastal, with two coastal cities (Cardiff and Newport) and a major town (Barry) being located directly on the coast. The Climate Change Commission Risk Assessment (3) for Wales sets out the risk of coastal flooding across five themes;• Natural Environment & Assets • Infrastructure • Health Communities & the Built Environment• Business & Industry • International Dimensions. Welsh Government has recently published planning guidance TAN 15 which sets out: Development, flooding and coastal erosion and a new Flood Map for Planning introduce important changes to the way flooding and coastal erosion risks are considered in the development and planning process. Flood risk in Wales is increasing as a result of climate change. Serious flooding events are becoming more frequent and some areas currently at little risk will become vulnerable to flooding as our climate continues to change. As the National Strategy for Flood and Coastal Erosion Risk Management in Wales recognises, the planning system can help communities be more resilient to the effects of climate change by locating development in areas away from risk of flooding. Improved knowledge of the places which will be at risk in the future can help keep people safe, by preventing the damage and disruption to homes, workplaces and infrastructure that flooding can cause. TAN 15 provides planning advice that informs local development plans and decisions on planning applications in areas at risk of flooding and coastal erosion. It will be used by the Welsh Government, local planning authorities and developers to direct development away from areas at risk of flooding and coastal erosion. The formal adoption of TAN 15 has been postponed until June 2023 to allow for further review and consultation. Public Health Wales's health impact assessment of climate change is a strategic and comprehensive appraisal of the potential implications of climate change on population health in Wales. It aims to inform and enhance adaptation planning across health and social care and the wider public sector.

To support health and social care organisations undertake adaptation planning in practice, a publicly available health and social care climate adaptation toolkit has been developed. https://www.gov.wales/health-and-social-care-climate-adaptation-toolkit

Cwm Taf Morgannwg (CTM) climate change risk assessment (covering three Local Authority areas; Bridgend, Merthyr and Rhondda Cynon Taf) in line with the Cwm Taf Health board boundary, has identified the stability and management of this post-industrial heritage as a key climate change risk. (https://www.ourcwmtaf.wales/climate-change-risk-assessment).
The risk assessment considered 11 priority risks, with the primary risk being around post-industrial landscapes, closely followed by climate resilient communities.

CTM's unique post-industrial landscape is likely to be increasingly vulnerable to multiple risks resulting from a changed climate. This includes cumulative risks on specific places and assets across the area: from ground subsidence; changes in hydrology; slope stability; altering levels of minewater; soil water content; shrinkage and heave of soils; potential dispersed pollution from industrial sites; historic landfill and tips; surface water, river and ground water flooding, and impacts on housing condition; transport networks including railway track and road surfaces, and buried infrastructure (electrical cables, sewage and gas and water pipelines). For CTM, due to its industrial legacy, ground movement, sink holes and impacts of mine workings should be of major concern. The highest levels of poverty and deprivation in CTM are frequently co-located with the most challenging physical post-industrial landscapes. Climate risks in CTM are a socioeconomic issue and addressing these risks, at scale, should be viewed as a social justice issue, and not solely as an operational issue.

project_info: Buildings - Domestic Retrofit Ecoflex: CCR has committed to a carbon neutral economy and has embraced a range of initiatives to inform the wider Energy Vision for the region. With support from the Welsh Government Energy Service, it has been possible to quantify the scale and impact of tackling a domestic retrofit programme. The Baseline Energy Assessment sets out the current energy use and generation in the region:• CCR has the lowest number of renewable heat installations with just 0.2% of homes having a heat pump or biomass boiler;• 90% of homes are connected to the gas network, the highest of any Welsh region and above the GB average;• approximately 27,000 homes (4%) are currently fuelled by oil, LPG, coal or other solid fuels;• the average EPC rating is D and the region has the highest average energy efficiency ratings in Wales, with 75% of homes rated as EPC band D or above.Achieving our energy vision for Cardiff Capital Region to meet 51% reduction in domestic emissions.The energy vision scenario modelling assumes a significant shift away from business as usual by 2035. The assumptions of the modelled future vision include: • 154,000 homes improved from EPC band G, F and E to D, C and B;• over 140,000 heat pumps installed;• 42,000 suitable houses accurately fitted with internal or external wall insulation;• over 185,000 other insulation measures in homes;• 112,000 homes currently heated by fossil fuels to move to low carbon heating;• replacing heating systems in oil, LPG and solid fuel heated homes prioritised;• no new gas connections for homes from 2025.The number of homes in the EPC bands A-C needs to increase by 280,822 homes by 2035. The region is currently at 6% 4,000 homes in the most energy efficient banding, so clearly there is some considerable way to go.The CCR energy modelling data assumes a certain level of BAU retrofit happening over the next 14 years, which will support 23k jobs and deliver 4.8bn investment, with 1.7bn GVA. However if we enhance this retrofit programme with a deliberate and targeted investment, levering in the ECO funding, then the region could be looking at an extra 12,000 jobs and at least 2.7bn extra investment and an additional 0.62bn GVA. This activity would be on installing energy efficiency measures such as wall insulation, roof and floor insulation and new double-glazing and low carbon domestic heat measures.

The program involves sustainable management of village forests to increase forest cover, strengthen ecosystem functions, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions from land degradation. A key component of the program is carbon stock certification, which includes biomass inventory, forest area mapping, carbon verification, and registration with official carbon institutions. Certified carbon stocks allow villages to generate carbon credits, which can serve as additional funding for local development, including infrastructure, community economic empowerment, and environmental conservation. Through this program, Sumbawa Regency not only contributes to climate change mitigation but also strengthens the capacity of villages to manage natural resources sustainably and inclusively.

Heavy precipitation: The spring and fall seasons, also known as shoulder seasons, are anticipated to become warmer and wetter, receiving a 26% and 8% increase in precipitation, respectively.

- Large puddles can form, increasing the risk of vehicles hydroplaning and impacting mobility for those on foot, bicycles, and other active transportation. Bus stop access can be affected. 

- If Selkirk begins to receive heavy rainfall events in the spring months, when the threat of Red River flooding is higher, rainfall amounts could exceed the capacity of the storm sewer, resulting in increased sewer backups into residential properties. - Heavy rains can flood argricultural fields located in the city boundaries. 

- Can result in cultural and entertainment events being cancelled.

- damage to exposed buildings, both residential and industrial

- Exposed buildings include seniors' residences, which pose evacuation challenges due to reduced mobility and greater health care needs

- The dryness associated with drought can lead to an increase in fires and the associated impacts. 

- Agriculture will be impacted by a reduction in water available for irrigation. 

- Drought impacts the water available for hydroelectric power generation, potentially increasing rates, which will impact lower-income households and the elderly on fixed incomes.

- Drought can impact water available for construction and industrial processes, recreation activities (pools). 

- Water shortages can lead to community instability.

-People displaced by flood waters will put pressure on local alternative accommodations, such as hotels and rentals. 

- Flooding can result in cultural and entertainment events being cancelled.

- Damage results in increased insurance claims and premiums. | Extreme cold: Although winters are predicted to get warmer overall, the City of Selkirk is still at risk of increased cold snaps, or polar vortex outbreaks. 

The impacts of this are as follows: 

- Increased stress placed on furnaces and heating systems in buildings, resulting in decreased life span and urgent repair requirements. 

- Increased stress on snow removal equipment, resulting in higher maintenance requirements. 

- Threatened reliability of fire hydrants; if water accumulates and freezes during a polar vortex outbreak, it may leave the hydrant temporarily unusable or cause long-term damage.

- Transit users are exposed to low temperatures when waiting for service, which will impact the elderly and people from lower-income households, who tend to use transit at higher rates.

- Ice accumulation on sidewalks and roads increases slip and motor vehicle accident hazards. 

- Increased breakdown of the City's fleet vehicles.

- Fire truck equipment experiences issues due to freezing temperatures.

- Elderly population unable to access services due to icy/cold conditions. 

- School may be cancelled, impacting children, youth, and low-income households who can't source childcare and must miss work. | Extreme wind: Increased wind intensity is expected year-round. The primary risk will be to falling trees and the associated damage to infrastructure. Some soecific potential impacts are as follows: 
- Disrupted power supply due to fallen trees on power lines. This will disproportionately impact lower income households who may not be able to access generators. The elderly and vulnerable will be more succeptible to heat and cold associated with the loss of air conditioning and heating.
- Outdoor workers risk being hit with debris during wind events.
- Wind will blow around solid waste, which will require additional collection activities to retrieved.
- Wind may impact transit service and visibility on roads. 
- Damage caused by wind can result in increased insurance claims and premiums. 
- Wind can result in cultural and entertainment events being cancelled. 
- High winds can damage material stockpiles at manufacturing facilities. 
- Damage to the urban canopy. | Extreme heat: Heatwaves and an increase in the number of extremely hot days are already impacting Selkirk, and adaptation measures are already being pursued. Specific impacts of extreme heat are as follows:
 
- Negative heat stress-related health impacts on the public, especially the elderly, low-income households, and those with vulnerable health, result in strain on health services. 

- Heat waves heighten the risk of grass and urban fires.

- Air conditioning systems may not be able to maintain an acceptable level of service. 

- Outdoor, frontline, and construction workers can experience heat stress while performing their regular duties.

- Increased water demand can increase the risk of water shortage, as well as power outages due to electric grid overload, due to air conditioner usage or excessive wire sagging due to heat and expansion. 

- Public events such as outdoor sporting events may be cancelled.

- Public services such as the pool may reach capacity. 

- Heat is associated with increased aggression and violence, which can strain law enforcement and emergency services.

 - Increased incidence of disease and illness. 

- Agricultural crops, natural areas, and green assets such as trees can experience heat stress, damage, and death. | Snow and ice: Selkirk is projected to have shorter, warmer, and wetter winters. The potential impacts of snow and ice are as follows: 

- Heavier snow will be more difficult for people to remove, which is an increased hazard for the elderly and those with vulnerable health. 

- Heavier snow will be more difficult for the City equipment to remove, shortening their operational life. 

- Lower-income houses won't be able to access snow clearing support. 

- Freezing rain will result in icy roadways and sidewalks, which will cause safety issues for all residents, particularly those with mobility limitations. 

- Power disruptions due to downed power lines.
 
- Disrupted solid waste pick-up.

- Closure of civic buildings and services.
 
- Reduced accessibility for emergency vehicles responding to emergencies.

- Selkirk is a regional health care hub, so people not being able to get to work at hospitals and other health care facilities has a regional impact.

- Increased motor vehicle accidents put pressure on the health care system. 

- Transit service can be disrupted by excess snow and ice, which will more greatly impact youth and those from lower-income households. 

- School can be cancelled due to excess snow and ice, impacting children and those from lower-income households who cannot find childcare and must miss work. 

- Disruption of regular home-based social and health care services, which disproportionately impacts the elderly and those with physical and cognitive limitations. 

- An increase in motor vehicle accidents results in increased insurance claims and elevated premiums. 

- Outdoor workers will be exposed to more slipping hazards. 

- Can result in cultural and entertainment events being cancelled.

project_info: Transport - Town of Superior Beneficial Electrification Plan Implementation: The Town of Superior completed a first-of-its-kind Beneficial Electrification Plan that combines two priority energy topics: EV adoption and building electrification. The primary objective of this plan is to develop a roadmap that includes practical, short-term strategies to advance EV adoption and building electrification in the municipal, residential, and commercial sectors - for both new, and existing development. Integrating EV and building electrification allows the Town of Superior to approach decarbonization from a holistic perspective. The advancement of EV adoption and building electrification both require consideration of grid impacts and electric infrastructure supply needs, general education and supporting resources for residents and businesses. An additional important benefit of an integrated approach is the opportunity to streamline coordination with Town staff and community stakeholders, as there is significant overlap between EV and building electrification stakeholders (e.g., Town staff, building and development community, residents, businesses). This will ensure that Superior's decarbonization efforts are right sized for their community capacity. Plan implementation included launching a residential electrification communications campaign and a four-part event series with neighboring cities Louisville and Lafayette, supported by Xcel Energy's Partners in Energy called 1-2-3 Electrify! The communities presented information related to each step of electrification, with an associated in-person event. For the facilities electrification identified in our Beneficial Electrification Plan, the Town selected a consultant to conduct an ASHRAE Level III Audit of the Superior Community Center, to identify funding sources for implementation and to create an electrification roadmap in 2024. In fall 2024, we will additionally work on engaging our Planning and Building department to see how we can best support the development piece of this work. . link: https://www.superiorcolorado.gov/home/showpublisheddocument/22525/638320277473470000

climate_hazard: Extreme cold: Extreme cold can impact low-income households and vulnerable health groups as access to warming centres are disproportionately affected by power outages and facility closures. Blocked roads and icy conditions increase mobility difficulty for marginalized and health vulnerable groups, especially with higher elevations. An extreme weather event during the Winter Holiday break of 2021 led to challenges in getting warming centers set up because staff were off on vacation and public facilities were closed. Extreme cold events have also led to power outages at major grocery stores and widespread crop losses which led to short-term food and supply shortages, as well as higher costs. In January 2024, an extreme weather event caused transit delays, bridge closures, and bus route cancellations. This hazard can impact the human health sector as winter storms can cause power outages and facility closures and facilities are used as warming centres. | Urban flooding: The October 2024 catastrophic atmospheric river weather event, bringing 340mm of rain in a three-day period, resulted in a declared state of local emergency, evacuations and significant damage to infrastructure and property. Urban flooding can impact the human health, sewerage, and transportation sectors and increase risks for vulnerable health groups, low-income households, and frontline/outdoor workers. Urban flooding can exacerbate inequities between vulnerable population groups; through property damage, mobility issues and increased clean-up costs, affecting low-income households disproportionately. | Extreme heat: The disastrous 2021 heat dome was the deadliest weather event in Canadian history with 619 confirmed heat-related deaths in British Columbia. This event impacted vulnerable health groups, the elderly, and outdoor and frontline workers. Higher summer temperatures can result in inflated costs to water, electricity, and food and can impact agriculture, recreation, and conservation activities. These indirect impacts disproportionately affect low-income populations. Extreme heat directly impacts health and social work activities as this sector responds to this emergency. The BC Coroners Service prepared a report to review the circumstances around these deaths and identify actions to improve public safety and prevent future deaths. See: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/birth-adoption-death-marriage-and-divorce/deaths/coroners-service/death-review-panel/extreme_heat_death_review_panel_report.pdf | Drought: Periods of drought can impact conservation, food security, water supply, human health, recreation and other sectors. Local ecosystems are currently showing signs of prolonged drier, hotter summers and a significant loss of trees, leading to impacts on resident's comfort as well as impacts to the natural area. During a drought period, water and grocery prices can increase while access to clean drinking water and freshwater stores decrease. Drought impacts can affect a range of vulnerable populations, especially low-income households who may face disproportionate price increases, vulnerable health groups and outdoor/frontline workers who may be at increased risk due to associated conditions (extreme heat/drought). | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Air quality is impacted from wildfires near our municipality and from wildfires hundreds of kilometers away. Wildfires are becoming more severe and frequent, with a longer season and dry summers. The 2024 B.C. fire season started early in the year due to overwintering fires from the 2023 seasons. Smoke from forest fires leads to health risks for immunocompromised and vulnerable populations, outdoor/frontline workers, groups that cannot seek clean air shelters, and low-income households, who may not have access to air conditioning or air purification systems at home. Wildfire can impact the public health, transportation, recreation, insurance rates and electricity/gas sectors, as this hazard threatens infrastructure and homes in the wildland urban interface and can increase the risk of landslides in the rainy season. Wildfire and wildfire preparation impacts the work and activities of many residents and workers in the District. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Coastal flooding can disproportionately impact vulnerable populations, marginalized and low-income members of the community, due to the potential displacement of people experiencing housing insecurity and members of the community with precarious housing. Damages to infrastructure and housing, mobility and effects on health can leave lasting effects on vulnerable populations. The 2024 atmospheric river storm surge caused coastal flooding, leading to a state of emergency and evacuations, including six kayakers who were particularly vulnerable during the event. Coastal flooding events, including king tides, can impact infrastructure, human health, real estate, conservation, transportation, recreation and other sectors, as storm surges and sea level rise threaten existing transportation networks, infrastructure, and access to respond to emergencies. Archaeological site and parkland exposure to coastal flooding and erosion was identified as a significant risk of increased tidal and wave action under sea level rise. | River flooding: Intense storms are causing increasingly frequent flooding in the District's rivers, dams, and creeks. Extreme flooding events can lead to increased debris flow, injury and death. Flooding exacerbates existing health inequities and increases vulnerabilities to at risk populations: low-income households can lack the means and opportunity to take protective health measures like affording extra medication or planning for evacuation. Previous flooding in the District has impacted the human health sector, including healthcare delivery systems. In 2024, 340mm of massive rainfall caused overflow of creeks, flooding streets, houses and businesses. Six homes were evacuated, and a state of local emergency was declared. River and creek flooding impacts real estate activities, construction, transportation and storage, and recreation sectors as growing water levels can limit the functionality of these sectors. | Storm: Storms in the District are becoming more frequent and extreme. In 2024, an atmospheric river event produced 340mm of rainfall over 3 days, leading to a declared state of local emergency, flooding and evacuations. Trees (specifically transplants and young saplings) are more susceptible to pests and diseases and therefore more likely to be impacted by windstorms and rain events in the fall which can often lead to power disruptions. In B.C., falling trees and branches are the primary cause of power outages. B.C. has three times more trees per kilometer of power line than anywhere else in North America. In 2024 over 1.4 million B.C. Hydro customers (Provincial utility) experienced weather-related power outages, the most in recorded history. The combination of trees and extreme weather account for nearly 60 per cent of all outages. Storm-related power outages have more than tripled in recent years, causing energy services prices to increase significantly to combat increased vegetation management, affecting low income and vulnerable populations disproportionately. Power outages can affect human health, mobility and real estate sectors. The District predicts an increase in the intensity and frequency of extreme storm events. | Heavy precipitation: Due to the District's geography between the Coast Mountains and the Pacific Ocean, heavy precipitation events are common. However, extreme precipitation events in the District are becoming more intense and frequent due to moderate winters, loss of vegetation, new developments and greater flow rates. Heavy precipitation can cause traffic disruption, flooding, drainage and sewer problems, landslides and can cause issues with water contamination, affecting water supply, sewage, waste management, conservation, construction, transportation and human health. Water contamination disproportionately affects vulnerable and low-income populations at risk, for example immunocompromised and elderly populations. The 2024 atmospheric river event caused flooding, landslides and piling of large debris that storm drains could not manage.

Fire weather (risk of wildfires): Increased air pollution due to vegetation fires can cause respiratory diseases and aggravate health conditions, thereby overburdening public and private health services. 
Workers who fight and mitigate the effects of fires are directly affected by the dangerous nature of their work.
Agricultural and forestry sectors may suffer direct losses due to the spread of fire. | Heavy precipitation: Heavy rains can cause isolated flooding due to the city's topography, but they increase the risk of mass movements. This affects the infrastructure and safety of communities, especially in informal settlements and also in historic settlements resulting from population movements in the municipality due to similar events.
The agriculture and construction sectors may suffer material damage and interruption of activities. | Mass movement: In the case of the city of Ouro Preto, mass movements mainly affect marginalized communities, but a large part of the population lives in areas of geological risk, posing a potential threat to the lives of people of all income levels and to historical heritage. The consequences extend to the loss of homes and livelihoods, overloading and disruption of the transportation system, and increased public spending. Previous events were responsible for the creation of settlements and social movements. | Biodiversity loss: The loss of biodiversity can lead to a decrease in the availability of natural resources essential for subsistence, affecting domestic food production. In addition, some endemic species that perform unique ecosystem functions may disappear, affecting research, environmental education, and potentially air quality. | Heat stress: Because it is a high-altitude location with a naturally milder climate, heat events affect vulnerable health groups by aggravating cardiovascular conditions, dehydration, and heatstroke. The consequences extend to water stress for agricultural activities and public supply, in addition to the potential overload of public and private health systems. | Water stress: Although it is a risk for the entire population, it disproportionately affects marginalized communities and low-income families because they have less access to resources and infrastructure to mitigate the effects of water scarcity, which can result in health and food security problems.
It has consequences for public water supply and sewage treatment systems and mining, which require large volumes of water.
The city's intense tourist activity is directly affected by water scarcity through the operating conditions of the hotel and service sectors.

In addition, Sanggau Regency also has high rainfall, which triggers landslides. The follow-up to this problem is to find solutions with the right steps to reduce the impact of landslides, as an effort to mitigate landslide disasters. One step in trying to reduce the impact of landslides is to find out the distribution of landslide-prone areas by conducting spatial mapping (Amatya et al., 2021; Rahmad et al., 2018). Mapping in this study was carried out using the scoring and weighting method (Yassar et al., 2020; Kinanti et al., 2022). Mapping of landslide-prone areas in Sanggau Regency can help the government and community in responding to the impact of disasters through preventive measures in areas with a high vulnerability category. Landslides occur due to the inability of the soil to support the load of the soil above it. This is due to the addition of soil weight on the slope surface and the reduction in the binding capacity of soil particles (Irvan et al., 2019). The movement of soil on the slope towards the bottom of the hillside is caused by gravity (Muhardi & Wahyudi, 2020). Landslides are one of the geomorphological processes that occur on the earth's surface, especially on the relief surfaces of hills and mountains with steep slopes. Two factors that generally cause landslides are natural and human factors (Fransiska et al., 2017; Muhardi & Wahyudi, 2019). Natural factors originating from nature include high rainfall, steep slope conditions, lack of rock density, and others (Dani et al., 2022). Human factors originate from human behavior including the creation of bare forests, the presence of settlements in areas with steep and sloping slopes, and inappropriate use of land, thus increasing the risk in landslide-prone areas. | Drought: The following are the effects of drought that can occur during the dry season:1. Waste management (including waste recycling) - Landfill Leachate Pond Rehabilitation: The objectives of the Pondok Keumuning Landfill Leachate Pond Rehabilitation are:

• Leachate Stabilization:
Leachate ponds also play a role in stabilizing leachate, reducing fluctuations in leachate characteristics such as pH and organic content. This is important to ensure the effectiveness of subsequent treatment processes.

• Organic Material Removal:
One of the main functions of leachate ponds is to reduce the level of organic matter in leachate. Biological treatment processes, such as the use of decomposing bacteria, are often used to remove this organic matter.

• Sedimentation:
Leachate ponds also serve as a settling area for solid particles dissolved in leachate. This sedimentation process helps reduce leachate turbidity and facilitates subsequent treatment processes.

• Biological Treatment:
Some leachate ponds use biological processes, such as trickling filters, to decompose organic matter in leachate with the help of microorganisms.

Overall, leachate ponds in landfills are an important component in waste management to protect the environment from the negative impacts of leachate.

climate_hazard:
Biodiversity loss: The presence of biodiversity & high quality natural and conserved lands serves as a significant tool for resilience against climate hazards throughout the east central Florida region. Loss of biodiversity is detrimental to crop and stock health and resilience in agricultural, fishing, and forestry sectors. Additionally, loss of biodiversity typically goes hand in hand with loss of green and open spaces and degradation of ecosystem services, which is damaging to all members of society but particularly children and elderly who may be more sensitive to air quality and environmental conditions. It also compounds with marginalized communities who have historically faced environmental injustice and greater rates of pollution. 
This hurts conservation efforts and recreation and agri/eco-tourism industries that rely on vibrant ecosystems to prosper, as well as impacting job opportunities for outdoor workers across sectors. | Drought: Drought affects the sector of agriculture and the ability for farm workers/owners to grow and harvest a healthy crop. However, drought affects almost all vulnerable populations and the population at large in some way. Vulnerable populations are impacted as many already have lower access to other resources which is realized in a more severe compound effect with drought.
Drought, along with high water use in the residential and commercial sectors among the region's growing population, can lead to water stress. With water stress comes the higher likelihood of sinkholes and associated property/infrastructure damage. Water stress as well as damages can be costly not in only upfront cost but through other expenses that go into mitigating the effects of water stress in already financially-burdened communities such as those with predominantly low-income households. Water stress poses a significant issue for agriculture which relies on a significant supply of water for irrigation. | Hurricanes, cyclones, and/or typhoons: With rising ocean temperatures, hurricanes are increasing in frequency and intensity. Hurricanes bring with them high speed winds and inland and coastal flooding that can adversely impact the region's economy, natural and built environment, and people's health and well-being. These hazards can be most impactful in young children, the elderly, pregnant women, and vulnerable health population segments who may have difficulty getting out of harms way. Additionally, these hazards also present a significant economic burden to those individuals whose work has been interrupted by these hazards and to those households struggling to meet the affordability of air conditioning and cooling demands and home improvements and repairs. Moreover, hurricanes and flooding can destroy energy (and other utility) infrastructures, further impacting homes and critical infrastructure such as hospitals that rely on a constant energy supply to function. Hurricanes can wreak havoc on homes, buildings, roads, and the landscape as a whole. Frontline workers are put at risk in rescue and recovery efforts. | Fire weather (risk of wildfires): The sectors vulnerable to wildfire have experienced large monetary losses between the years of 1960-2020. Aside from monetary losses, loss of life during these events has also been substantial according to the risk assessment. As the climate warms, conditions in dry brush, crop fields, and grasslands become drier making conditions for a wildfire more ideal especially along the interface /wildfire breaks with more developed areas. Populations with vulnerable health such as children, the elderly, and the immunocompromised can be affected with respiratory issues due to the air pollution generated in proximity of fire. Outdoor workers have livelihoods that rely on the health of these environments, so wildfires can pose a major threat to their livelihood as well as personal health. Furthermore, when smoke mixes with humidity it creates visibility concerns and impacts roadways where deaths have unfortunately occurred. | Extreme heat: In terms of heat, the region has historically and regularly seen heat indices above 90°F and humidity at high levels. These extreme temperatures are expected to continue to increase, with the greatest rise in heat indices with values of 100-105°F. Depending on future global greenhouse gas emissions, heat indices above 100°F could quadruple by the mid-century and beyond. One of the most significant temperature changes will be experienced in nighttime/lowest-day temperatures. Records show that the region has experienced an average of 20-30 more nights of about 75°F per year. And projections indicate that with an RCP 4.5 scenario, this could increase to as much as 50 or more nights for most places between 2035 and 2065 and to about 100 nights per year with an RCP 8.5 scenario. The region is home to one of Florida's counties with the highest heat stress/heat-related hospitalizations, which makes this hazard relevant to our community's well-being. With a changing climate, industries like agriculture and forestry can be altered due to unsuitable growing conditions for flora and living conditions for fauna. A hotter region will see increased demand for electricity and air conditioning supply, and may see a decrease in residents and visitors as the temperature becomes increasingly intolerable. 
Extreme heat poses a threat to all populations and sectors, but again is most dangerous for health-sensitive groups such as children, the elderly, and the immunocompromised. Marginalized communities and low-income households may experience greater burden due to the expense of air conditioning and cooling measures. Additionally, outdoor workers face extreme risk of heat-related illnesses and injuries. | Other: 100-year flood and flash flood: With climate change, flood events are becoming increasingly common. Urban and suburban infrastructure, many of which are built in floodplains or to aged/insufficient standards, are struggling to cope with the quantities of water. Flooding is consistently one of the main issues we hear our counties and communities dealing with. Flood events can affect all populations, but low income and marginalized households are at particular risk as they may not be able to afford flood insurance or mitigation measures such as raising their house, or have anywhere to evacuate to. Frontline workers face risk during deployment. Flooded streets can become contaminated and unsafe to go through, requiring clean up efforts. Both inland and coastal communities can be affected by flooding, and this affects many sectors such as utilities that may be damaged, sewage that may be contaminated, flooded roads blocking transportation, commutes to work, and rescue efforts. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Sea level rise poses a significant threat to people living and working in the region's coastal areas. Although a relatively small proportion of total land area is in medium to high threat zones, these areas will see stark impacts should this level of sea-level rise occur without mitigation. Areas adjacent to the shoreline have higher risk because they contain more people, higher vulnerability areas, and more lifeline infrastructure. Particularly of note are the region's coastal military installations such as Kennedy Space Center, where coastal flooding and SLR can threaten the ability of installations to carry out their mission. Coastal real estate can be a very profitable industry, so coastal flooding is a threat to the industry as well as inhabitants. Particularly elderly or vulnerable health groups who might not be able to evacuate their residences are at risk. Frontline workers such as emergency services providing rescue and recovery during flooding are also at risk. | Storm: Thunderstorms can produce large, damaging hail, which causes nearly $1 billion in damage to property and crops annually. Straight-line winds, which in extreme cases have the potential to exceed 100 miles per hour, are responsible for most thunderstorm wind damage. One type of straight-line wind, the downburst, can cause damage equivalent to a strong tornado and can be extremely dangerous to aviation. Thunderstorms are also capable of producing tornados and heavy rain that can lead to flash flooding. Thunderstorms may cause electricity losses, which can be problematic for elderly and vulnerable health populations who may rely on it for critical medical support. This issue may be exacerbated in marginalized or low income communities especially in more rural areas that don't have the most reliable connection and it takes a while to restore power to. Critical public infrastructure and healthcare industries also suffer from power losses, and frontline workers who have to respond during storms are endangered by lightning and potentially dangerous road conditions. Extreme rainfall, wind, lightning, and hail associated with severe storms pose damage to real estate/property, infrastructure, and all modes of transportation.
project_info:
Waste management (including waste recycling) - Central Florida Waste to Energy Initiative (CFWEI): A Coalition representing the Orlando-Kissimmee-Sanford Metropolitan Statistical Area (Orlando MSA) is leading the pioneering Central Florida Waste-to-Energy Initiative (CFWEI), poised to revolutionize biosolid management, mitigate environmental risks, and foster sustainable energy generation. Currently, biosolids generated by wastewater treatment facilities pose significant environmental challenges, being directed towards landfills or land application. In response, the CFWEI Board, composed of representatives of the CPRG Coalition members named in this proposal, is spearheading a strategic public-private partnership (P3) aimed at maximizing resource utilization and minimizing environmental impact. 

 

Through collaboration with a third-party private entity, the CFWEI aims to capture methane gas from biosolids generated by the region's wastewater treatment facilities and convert it into Renewable Natural Gas (RNG) through well-established anaerobic digestion technology. This RNG will be seamlessly integrated into the natural gas pipeline and utilized as compressed natural gas (CNG) for transportation purposes throughout the region, including the fueling of the biosolids transport fleet. 

 

Moreover, the innovative Super Critical Water Oxidation (SCWO) process will be employed to address contaminants such as PFAS in the residual digested solids, concurrently generating clean gas expansion power. Through the SCWO process, PFAS chemicals are destroyed and biosolids are rendered an inert solid with less than 30% of their initial volume remaining to be incinerated, land applied, or directed to landfills. While SCWO technology is being successfully used to eliminate organic matter in variety of waste-related applications, this proposal represents its first practical application in the wastewater treatment sector. 

 

By leveraging waste resources for energy production, the CFWEI not only addresses pressing environmental challenges but also establishes a sustainable model for resource management. The revenue generated from the sale of RNG and associated Renewable Identification Number (RIN) credits, as well as an additional energy revenue stream from gas expansion power, will be shared among the participating jurisdictions of the CPRG Coalition. This comprehensive approach to Waste-to-Energy reduces greenhouse gas emissions, mitigates harmful biosolid contaminants, and creates multiple revenue streams, creating a multi-faceted approach to energy generation and revenue generation, positioning the region as a trailblazer in sustainable energy innovation.

The CRVA identifies increasing summer temperatures, more frequent extreme heat days, and higher cooling demand as emerging risks that can strain emergency response capacity and increase operating costs for critical facilities | River flooding: The CRVA identifies significant exposure when the East River is in flood stage due to ice jams, extreme rainfall, or high tide levels in the Northumberland Strait. Flooding can back up into critical riverside areas, affecting recreational facilities like Glasgow Square, interrupting shoreline services, and reducing access for emergency vehicles. Long-term risks increase with sea-level rise and more intense storms, requiring ongoing monitoring and potential future flood-mapping and mitigation planning. | Extreme wind: The CRVA identifies a significant long-term increase in extreme wind gusts (5%-40%) under projected warming scenarios. High winds can cause treefall, damage building envelopes, accelerate roof deterioration, and disrupt transportation and emergency access routes. Critical community facilities face increased risk of power outages and higher maintenance costs. For emergency response buildings and Resiliency Hubs, the CRVA notes growing pressures from outages and increased cooling and shelter demands during storm events. | Drought: The CRVA identifies an increased frequency and duration of drought periods, reduced summer water flows in streams and lakes, and greater risk of vegetation dry-out and fire weather conditions. Drought can reduce available water for municipal supply, increase stress on natural areas, and elevate wildfire risk. The CRVA notes potential operational impacts on wastewater treatment performance and reduced water availability for ecosystem health. Combined heat + drought conditions also increase pressure on public health and emergency services.

Extreme heat: In a low emission scenario, the Kansas City area will experience an average annual temperature increase of 2.78° F. Heat-related illnesses and potential mortality will increase due to the higher temperatures. Increased demand for AC will result in higher energy bills. This will negatively affect lower-income populations, who are more at risk from changing financial circumstances. This will increase the energy burden on this vulnerable population. Under a high emissions scenario, the number of days annually above 105°F is projected to increase from .7 to 6.3 by 2050 and 21.9 by 2100. Urban heat will be exacerbated by these evolving heat conditions, negatively impacting neighborhoods with less tree canopy coverage and heat-absorbing impervious surfaces. Finally, increased crime is projected due to increased temperatures, impacting law and order services. | Urban flooding: Based on the RCP 2.6 climate model scenarios, the Kansas City area will experience an average precipitation change of 2.2 inches yearly. Under a low emissions scenario, Prairie Village has minimal risk of flooding over the next 30 years. There may be risks such as mold in basements, decreased crop yield, and the need for increased planning for stormwater and floodplain management. This will negatively affect low-income households that do not have the expendable income to waterproof their homes. 

As Prairie Village feels the effects of a changing environment, events of all kinds will affect more properties within the community. There are 673 properties in Prairie Village that have a greater than 26% chance of being severely affected by flooding over the next 30 years. Increasing frequency and severity of flooding under climate change is predicted to increase the number of properties exposed to flooding by 11% and average annual losses by at least 26% by 2050 under RCP 4.5, presenting significant costs to property owners and insurers. In addition to the damage to properties, flooding can cut off access to utilities, emergency services, and transportation and may impact the overall economic well-being of an area. In an RCP 4.5 scenario, Prairie Village has a minor risk of flooding over the next 30 years, which means flooding will likely impact the community's day-to-day life. This is based on the level of risk the properties face rather than the proportion of properties with risk.

Given that Prairie Village already has identified stormwater infrastructure as an issue, this can create a high impact risk from sewer system overflow or backup. Rain events occurring back-to-back (storm-stacking) are likely to increase and will contribute to the prevalence of severe flooding in the region. In a high-emission scenario, risks will be much more prevalent, impacting the housing quality. 

The energy sector may be affected as electrical equipment could get flooded, but ultimately, it has a low magnitude of future impact. Transportation could become a high risk due to the increased frequency of flooded roads, the need to replace roads and bridges, and limited access to emergency services due to flooded areas. Finally, high precipitation patterns could negatively impact agriculture due to the impact on the local food supply. | Drought: Regional vulnerabilities to drought stem from moderate precipitation amounts and relatively short growing seasons (compared to other parts of Kansas), relatively high evaporation rates, deep soils, poor groundwater, reliance on surface water, and historical occurrences. Drought will continue to impact the Kansas City region, most notably in the agricultural sector and areas with high drought susceptibility. As the Midwest has already experienced, there will be increasing instances of damage to crop quality and yields. The effects of low crop yields will percolate into the local economy. According to NASA, the current likelihood of a megadrought lasting more than three decades is 12%. If greenhouse gas emissions stop increasing in the mid-21st century, under RCP 4.5, there is an 80% likelihood of a megadrought increases to reach more than 60%. These types of conditions will lead to an increase in water treatment costs. Given the interconnectivity of the water department and Evergy, there will be concerns about power stability when the water supply becomes limited. There is also potential for water line damage and repairs due to drought stress. 

Increased costs will directly impact low income residents due to higher AC demand and water rates (including irrigation costs for farmers). In terms of biodiversity, there will be a higher chance of fires, biodiversity loss, wildlife encroachment, increased stress on endangered species, and loss of wetlands. 

Public health has a high magnitude impact as drought can lead to air quality concerns due to increasing ozone, smoke, and dust. There may be instances of loss of human life due to heat stress and increased respiratory ailments. As insect carrier populations change, there may be an increase in human diseases, insect infestation, and plant diseases. Oftentimes, vulnerable populations such as the elderly and homeless who are more susceptible to illness will be the most impacted.

Nature-Based Solutions - Urban Environmental Services Valuation Program: Payment for environmental services (PSA) has been consolidating itself over the years as an important ecological preservation strategy. In Itabirito, the PVSA (Environmental Services Valorization Program) is a compensation of both a financial and pecuniary nature given to those who provide some type of environmental service generally related to the preservation and maintenance of the environment. However, most of the efforts developed in this field are linked to the preservation and recovery of rural areas, such as springs and vegetation on the slopes of watercourses. 

However, this same mechanism also presents itself as a promising tool in urban areas, such as the drainage management of cities that present proposals for improving infiltration when they temporarily accumulate and slowly dissipate precipitated water. In other words, these measures aim to bring the urban environment closer to natural hydrological conditions, providing improved infiltration and evapotranspiration. In this way, the volume and peak flow rates of surface runoff that will go to the urban drainage system are reduced. Furthermore, it is possible to increase the retention of rainwater that supplies the water table. Examples can be considered: Flood buffer reservoirs; Individual reservoirs: Residential-scale rainwater drainage system with a device that works by directing rainwater from roofs and impervious floors to a micro reservoir. Rainwater is collected by gutters and goes down a pipe to the reservoir; Biological structural compensatory techniques: When compensatory techniques are based on bioretention, they are also capable of improving water quality and mitigating diffuse pollution that would reach urban rivers and rivers; Green roofs: Entire roof or roof, flat or inclined, properly waterproofed and with a drainage system for excess rainwater runoff, which includes in its composition a layer of soil or substrate and another layer of vegetation. Permeable and porous pavements: These are pavements that have free spaces in their structure through which water can drain, infiltrating the soil or being transported through an auxiliary drainage system in addition to constructed wetlands, which consist of flooded spaces with the presence of aquatic plants, called macrophytes, such as cattails, water hyacinth, papyrus, elephant grass, among others, which can be used for the natural treatment of effluents. (sewers). The treatment is carried out by the ecosystem formed between the roots of the plants and the community of microorganisms that form in the water body. It is highly recommended for places without resources, such as poor communities or spaces with a large area, such as the Itabirito Ecological Park, with the advantages of low cost, increased of local biodiversity, improvement of the microclimate. 

In this context, PVSA Urbano explores the possibility of applying PSA in the urban sphere, aiming to understand how already consolidated practices of this type of mechanism can be used in urban environments. The importance of promoting the provision of environmental services in urban areas through the application of compensatory methods and devices is highlighted. Based on the fact that rainwater from the entire drainage network of a municipality is generally interconnected with urban rivers and streams, it was concluded that it is natural that the preservation of these water courses has to take into account all local water dynamics, and that urban waters are interconnected in a larger context to the water basin of the Strategic Territorial Unit (UTE) Rio Itabirito, which is located in the Upper Rio das Velhas and has an area of 541.58 km2. It is made up of the municipalities of Itabirito, Ouro Preto and Rio Acima. The municipality with the largest population size is Itabirito, which accounts for 90.1% of the total. The main watercourses are the Itabirito River, Ribeirão Mata Porcos, Ribeirão do Silva, Córrego do Mango and Ribeirão Bação. Rio das Velhas has 73 km within the area delimited for the Territorial Unit. The waters of the Itabirito River flow into the Rio das Velhas, contributing significantly to the supply of the population of the Metropolitan Region of Belo Horizonte. UTE Rio Itabirito has four Conservation Units partially inserted in its territory, totaling approximately 9,586.49 ha of protected areas, which represents 17.47% of the total area. The entire area is part of the Iron Quadrangle, which qualifies it as a priority area for conservation. It was understood that payment for environmental services applied in urban areas can bring a series of benefits both in a local context and in a larger context of the basin, also considered within the context of the PSA and aimed at minimize damage caused to the environment.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Linear Park: Linear parks (or greenways) can be defined as parks in which one dimension is much larger than the other, they are normally located around watercourses, such as rivers or streams, and in some cases they can be located between two neighboring cities, as is the case with the park that will cover the cities of Itabirito and Ouro Preto, creating a green belt. Investment in this type of infrastructure has become more frequent, especially in cities that are interested in rehabilitating their rivers. Due to its large size, it can bring many direct and indirect benefits, including social and economic ones. In Brazil, some cities have invested in this type of urban improvement. From the point of view of sponge cities, their main benefit is the control of floods and runoff and the recovery of degraded bodies of water. Other important advantages are: connection of green areas; recovery of water bodies or old lines infrastructure; recovery of ecosystems and biodiversity; valorization of surrounding areas; serves as a leisure space for society; reduction of the heat island effect in large urban centers. It plays an important role as a recreation space and for the development of various ecological activities of environmental education and more sustainable production. For its success, it is essential that a management, operation and maintenance plan for the park is implemented, with special attention to cleaning and safety. Lighting is a crucial item that is directly linked to the safety and use of the park by the population. Efficient public lighting projects with low operating costs (for example, using LED lamps and photovoltaic panels). The construction of micro mobility infrastructure (bikes and scooters) is also a very important item. We highlight the main specific socio-environmental characteristics of the areas in which they will be implemented, highlighting some of the its elements, such as: • Drainage network; • Flood control reservoir; • Channels for rainwater drainage; • Energy dissipators for high slopes; • Plumbing; • Conservation of biodiversity and natural resources; • Formation of ecological corridors; • Increase in green areas; • Improvement of the urban microclimate and the capture of dust and gases; • Promotion of environmental awareness; • Encourages outdoor sports and sustainable transport; • Prevention of illegal occupation; • Significant reduction in potentially polluting activities in these areas; • Integration and harmonization of the natural and urban environment; • Real estate appreciation in the investment region. The multifunctional character of these spaces is currently part of the work on how the landscape comes, more and more, interacting with the planning of public open spaces in an integral system of natural resources, continuous and with ecological integrity. In view of the growing number of people seeking recreation in this type of landscape, the provision of these spaces also fulfills a civic function. In this way, the linear park has great potential for recovering the permeability of soils on the banks of watercourses, avoiding irregular occupation of permanent preservation areas, in addition to promoting leisure and social areas for greater interaction between local society, the wooded area that creates islands with a cool climate, attracting the population, but should not be considered as a return to the original natural landscape that was devastated, but rather as a strategy for maintaining ecological processes that directly affect the proper functioning of ecosystems, adding in itself a great potential for connectivity and cohesion in the city. at different levels, community relationships that can range from just landscaping to the inclusion of leisure sports activities and connection with nature, generating new social behaviors and revaluation of the environment environment.

Public and green spaces - Parque Urbano Oásis de Barcarena Project: Barcarena is located in the Tropical Zone, the sunniest and hottest area on the planet. The humid equatorial climate of the Amazon has high temperatures and air humidity above 90% throughout the year. Urban areas have a high population density in more than 50 informal settlements with inadequate or precarious housing conditions. 65.13% of the population depends on the Bolsa Família Program.
Due to its location, the city is already naturally hot. However, meteorological data demonstrate that both maximum and minimum temperatures in Barcarena increased by 1°C between 2023 and 2024. These associated factors increase heat-related health risks, decrease economic productivity and compromise quality of life. In the last 2 years, visits for dehydration, migraines, strokes and heart attacks have increased in the city's Basic Health Units.
The main objective of the project is to transform a conservation area in a conservation area accessible to the population. The Urban Park will directly benefit 74 thousand people who live around the area and indirectly people who live in other areas of the city or tourists. The area is a green island located in the city center, with easy access via public transport.
The main asset of the area is the native forest with dense vegetation. In this sense, the project foresees the removal of trees only for the construction of bathrooms, guardhouses, and environmental education centers. Trails, benches, toys and exercise equipment will be installed under the trees to maximize the passive cooling provided by them.
The project will include water management practices such as rainwater harvesting and irrigation systems to support the growth and maintenance of green areas, a shaded space for climate education activities, ramps and bathrooms for people with disabilities, spaces for breastfeeding and child care.

project_info: Transport - THE PROVISION OF SAFE & FRIENDLY PEDESTRIAN WALKWAYS AND BICYCLE LANES TO PROMOTE ACTIVE MOBILITY: Segamat city intends to lead the way in reducing municipality greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and adapting to local impacts of climate change. Segamat city is committed towards this goal with a target of 50% reduction in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 relative to the base year 2010 emissions level. Sustainable transport emphasizing on green commuting can improve Segamat's citizens' health and save money on fuel and parking. The increasing vehicle ownership rate is directly proportional to the increasing number of vehicles on the road, which in turn increase carbon emission. In the context of Segamat city, promoting walking and cycling as an alternative to short car trips is seen as one of the important strategies to decelerate the increase in car use and help reduce CO2 emissions. Hence, Segamat Municipal Council should further provide pedestrian and bicycle paths that are comfortable and safe in Segamat city. The pedestrian and bicycle paths can be shared and must be separated from the motorised vehicle to prevent the hazardThe facilities for walking and cycling such as bicycle parking, shelters, and safety bollards, must be systematically shaped in a way to make them attractive and accessible. Currently, Segamat Municipal Council has successfully provided pedestrian and bicycle paths near the Segamat city, however, at several areas, the continuity of the pedestrian and bicycle paths are disconnected and needs to be improved.This project is aimed towards promoting active green mobility in Segamat Municipality through the provision of comprehensive pedestrian walkways and bicycle lanes networks connected to the public transport system. The objectives of this project includes:•The construction of networks of pedestrian walkways and bicycles lanes that connects residents in housing areas to places of work, education institutions, recreational places and social spots to improve and nudge the public to participate in the SGR programme: Segamat Green Riders and increase acceptance that the relevant infrastructure inculcates a green and healthy lifestyle (our co-benefit strategy).•Installation of relevant amenities for the pedestrian walkways and bicycle networks in order to attract more pedestrian and cyclists to use the infrastructure for health benefits and reduce travel expenses at the same time.•Connecting the convenient walkways and cycling lanes with the public transport system in order to provide seamless first and last mile connectivity.•The introduction of “micro mobility” transport as a culture and lifestyle aimed towards attracting more users from public transport hubs to place of work, education institutions and recreational spots.•The project will also include tree planting programmes embedding some nature based solutions (e.g. shade, green spaces near water surfaces, evapotranspiration, enhancing wind flows) along pedestrian and cycling networks to increase comfort of user and at the same time sequester future carbon emissions.•Park and Ride facilities with EV Charging infrastructure within the networks will be aimed towards encouraging the usage of electric vehicles.RATIONALE:This project has been proposed in the Segamat District Local Plan (Replacement) 2030 and contributes to the district's targets. Part 6.0 of the urban design in the Segamat District Local Plan (replacement) 2030It is also identified as one of the High Impact Projects in the Segamat District Local Plan (Replacement) 2030. Theme 2: Green Commuting & Logistics in Segamat CAP 2030 is being mainstreamed accordingly and is a long-term bankable project and a good example of how Segamat is localizing and mainstreaming the SDGs at city and district levels as well as benefiting the vulnerable groups. We are scaling our implementation efforts to provide tangible outcomes for our citizens that can be measured and monitoring.

Stakeholders in this SD consist of four main sectors namely Government Agencies (G), Academia (U), Society (C) and Business (I). With close and joint cooperation between these 4 main sectors, the Sustainable Development agenda can be achieved, especially the Johor Green Deal, so that Johor can attract more foreign investors who really put the Sustainable Development agenda in their business model. GUCI 2024 which will take place for 2 days at Sunway Hotel will feature lectures and forums related to SD, ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) for SME (Small and Medium Enterprises), SDG (Sustainable Development Goals) for PBT (Local Authorities), ESD (Education for Sustainable Development) for the community and academia on the first day, while on the second day, two parallel workshops will be held. The first workshop is for SMEs to understand in depth each indicator in ESG so that SMEs can produce an ESG report (ESD disclosure). This ESG report is important for SMEs to become suppliers to large companies listed in Bursa Malaysia (ESG mandatory) and obtain green loans (green financing). SMEs that have an ESG report will have an advantage to compete in the future business world that increasingly requires compliance with Sustainable Development. The second workshop involved local authorities to plan and produce project papers and programs related to Sustainable Development Goals in their respective local authorities involving various GUCI sectors. The GUCI 2024 seminar also features an exhibition and a competition of SD projects involving the collaboration of various sectors. The GUCI 2024 exhibition can highlight leaders in Sustainable Development projects in the state of Johor to further increase cooperation between Sustainable Development stakeholders.
