River flooding: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
•	Low-income households: Poor families often live in floodplains, with houses built from less durable materials (bamboo, wood, unreinforced brick). When floods occur, their homes are often easily destroyed or severely damaged, resulting in prolonged recovery times.
•	Women, children, the elderly, and ethnic minorities: These groups face greater health and safety risks during evacuation and displacement. They also have less access to emergency information, finance, and healthcare services.
•	Rural and mountainous communities: In districts like Minh Hóa and Tuyên Hóa, floods isolate villages due to damaged roads and washed-away bridges, cutting off access to schools, hospitals, and markets.
•	Coastal communities: Floodwaters combined with storm surges increase risk for those in low-lying communes along the Nhật Lệ and Kiến Giang rivers.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture and Livelihoods
•	Crop losses: Rice paddies, maize, and vegetable fields are submerged, leading to yield reductions and food insecurity. For example, the 2010 flood inundated ~9,000 ha of agricultural land.
•	Livestock and aquaculture: Poultry, pigs, cattle, and aquaculture ponds are washed away, causing direct livelihood losses and long-term food supply disruptions.
•	Forestry: River floods damage plantations and increase soil erosion, while in forested areas, they can trigger landslides that affect nearby communities.
Housing and Infrastructure
•	Residential damage: Tens of thousands of houses are inundated during major floods (e.g., ~188,600 houses flooded in the October 2010 event). Many poor households lack insurance or resources to rebuild.
•	Transport: Roads and bridges across the Gianh and Kiến Giang rivers are frequently cut off, hindering disaster response and economic activity.
•	Public facilities: Schools and health centers in flood-prone areas are damaged or forced to close temporarily, disrupting education and healthcare.
Water, Sanitation, and Health
•	Contaminated water sources: Flooding pollutes wells and surface water, causing outbreaks of diarrhea, dengue, and other waterborne diseases.
•	Sanitation breakdown: Latrines overflow, spreading waste and increasing infection risks.
•	Public health emergencies: The elderly and chronically ill face higher mortality and morbidity due to limited access to care during floods.
 | Storm: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
•	Coastal and low-lying communities: Residents of communes along the Nhật Lệ estuary and coastal plain are highly exposed to strong winds, storm surge, and tidal flooding. Their houses—often built with weak materials—are easily damaged or destroyed.
•	Poor households: Families lacking storm-resistant housing face disproportionate losses. Without savings or insurance, they struggle to rebuild and may fall deeper into poverty after each storm event.
•	Women, children, and the elderly: These groups face heightened evacuation challenges, limited access to shelters, and increased risks of injury or health problems during and after storms.
•	Remote mountainous populations: In districts like Minh Hóa and Tuyên Hóa, storms trigger landslides and flash floods that isolate villages, disrupt transport, and cut off access to education and healthcare.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Housing and Infrastructure
•	Housing damage: High winds blow off roofs, collapse weak structures, and flood thousands of homes. For example, Typhoon Doksuri (2017) destroyed or damaged nearly 95,000 houses in Quang Binh.
•	Transport and electricity: Roads, bridges, and coastal dykes are damaged, isolating communities. Storms often bring down power lines, leading to prolonged blackouts.
•	Public facilities: Schools and clinics in storm paths are heavily affected, forcing closures and disrupting essential services.
Agriculture and Livelihoods
•	Crop damage: Strong winds and inundation flatten rice and maize fields, damage plantations, and reduce harvests. Saltwater intrusion from storm surges worsens soil salinity, reducing productivity.
•	Livestock and aquaculture: Poultry, cattle, and fishponds are often lost during storm surges or flash flooding, destroying household income sources.
•	Forestry: Windthrow damages protective forests and plantations, while slope failures cause erosion and downstream sedimentation.
Coastal and Marine Systems
•	Fisheries: Fishing boats are sunk or damaged, affecting the livelihoods of coastal households. Storm surges damage aquaculture cages and coastal infrastructure.
•	Coastal protection: Mangroves, dunes, and sea dykes are degraded, reducing natural defense capacity against future events.
Water, Sanitation, and Health
•	Water contamination: Heavy rainfall and surge pollute surface water and wells, increasing outbreaks of diarrhea, dengue, and skin diseases.
 | Heavy precipitation: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
•	Low-income and rural households: Poor families living in low-lying floodplains experience repeated inundation of houses and assets. Inadequate drainage and weak housing structures make them highly exposed.
•	Children, the elderly, and women: These groups face mobility challenges during evacuations and are more prone to health risks such as respiratory diseases, waterborne infections, and malnutrition linked to disrupted food supplies.
•	Remote mountainous communities: In districts such as Minh Hóa, Tuyên Hóa, and Bố Trạch, prolonged heavy rain triggers landslides and flash floods that isolate villages and disrupt access to schools, hospitals, and markets.
•	Urban poor: In Đồng Hới City, heavy downpours overwhelm drainage systems, flooding streets and informal settlements, with disproportionate impacts on low-income groups.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Housing and Infrastructure
•	Urban flooding: Heavy rain overwhelms drainage networks in Đồng Hới, leading to traffic disruption, property damage, and increased urban flood risk.
•	Transport: Roads, bridges, and rural paths are washed out or blocked by landslides, isolating communities.
•	Public facilities: Schools and clinics are forced to close when inundated, disrupting education and healthcare.
Agriculture and Livelihoods
•	Crop losses: Prolonged heavy rain waterlogs rice fields, reduces yields of maize, vegetables, and other cash crops, and promotes pest and disease outbreaks.
•	Livestock and aquaculture: Flooded barns and ponds cause livestock mortality and fish escapes, directly affecting livelihoods.
•	Soil degradation: Continuous rain accelerates soil erosion and nutrient leaching, reducing agricultural productivity.
Water, Sanitation, and Health
•	Contamination of water sources: Torrential rains flush pollutants and waste into rivers and wells, increasing risks of diarrheal diseases, dengue, and skin infections.
•	Sanitation breakdown: Latrines and septic systems overflow, spreading pathogens.
•	Health emergencies: Standing water increases vector breeding grounds (mosquitoes), leading to outbreaks of dengue and malaria.
Ecosystems and Forestry
•	Forest stress: Prolonged saturation destabilizes slopes in forested areas, leading to landslides and riverbank erosion.
•	Wetlands: Natural wetlands and lowland areas are overloaded, losing ecological buffering capacity against floods.
 | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
•	Coastal and estuarine communities: Households in low-lying areas around the Nhật Lệ estuary, Quảng Ninh, Bố Trạch, and Lệ Thủy districts face frequent tidal flooding and storm surge. Sea level rise (SLR) exacerbates inundation, forcing relocations.
•	Poor households and informal settlers: Families living close to the shoreline or river mouths often lack storm-resistant housing and drainage infrastructure. They are the first to lose homes and assets when flooding or saline intrusion occurs.
•	Women, children, and the elderly: These groups are more vulnerable during evacuations and recovery, facing higher risks of displacement, food insecurity, and limited access to shelters or social protection.
•	Fisherfolk and aquaculture workers: Livelihoods heavily dependent on coastal ecosystems are disproportionately affected when coastal flooding damages boats, cages, and salt fields.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Housing and Infrastructure
•	Inundation of settlements: Sea water penetrates inland during storm surge and high tides, submerging houses, schools, and clinics in coastal communes.
•	Protective infrastructure stress: Dykes, embankments, and seawalls face overtopping and structural damage, raising costs for reinforcement.
•	Transport networks: Roads near the coast and estuaries are eroded or submerged, disrupting trade, tourism, and emergency response.
Agriculture and Livelihoods
•	Salinization of farmland: Saltwater intrusion reduces soil fertility, damaging rice fields and vegetable crops, especially in Lệ Thủy and Quảng Ninh.
•	Loss of aquaculture productivity: Shrimp ponds and fish cages are inundated or contaminated, reducing yields and incomes.
•	Damage to fisheries: Fishing ports and landing sites are regularly flooded, disrupting operations and reducing safety for fishers.
Water, Sanitation, and Health
•	Drinking water contamination: Wells and shallow groundwater become saline, reducing safe water supply for households and schools.
•	Public health risks: Standing saline water creates breeding grounds for disease vectors, while displacement worsens nutrition and mental health outcomes.
Ecosystems and Nature
•	Coastal erosion: Mangroves, dunes, and beaches are eroded, removing natural buffers and increasing vulnerability to future flooding.
•	Habitat loss: Sea level rise gradually inundates wetlands, affecting biodiversity and the ecological services they provide.
 | Drought: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
•	Poor and rural households: Families relying on rainfed farming and shallow wells face water shortages for both crops and daily consumption. Limited income and assets reduce their ability to cope with repeated droughts.
•	Women and children: Women often shoulder the burden of fetching water during scarcity, while children suffer disproportionately from undernutrition and school absenteeism when households divert resources to cope with water stress.
•	Elderly and chronically ill: Health risks increase under extreme heat and dehydration, with limited access to healthcare in rural areas.
•	Ethnic minority and upland communities: Remote villages in Minh Hóa and Tuyên Hóa districts are highly vulnerable due to weaker water supply infrastructure and reliance on natural springs.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture and Livelihoods
•	Crop failures: Rice, maize, and vegetable yields decline sharply during prolonged dry spells, leading to food insecurity and reduced household income.
•	Livestock stress: Reduced availability of pasture and drinking water leads to livestock mortality, declining productivity, and loss of income.
•	Aquaculture losses: Shrimp and fish ponds suffer from higher water salinity and evaporation, reducing yields.
•	Forest degradation: Drought raises the risk of forest fires and accelerates land degradation, particularly in upland districts.
Water, Sanitation, and Health
•	Drinking water shortages: Wells and small reservoirs dry up, forcing households to rely on unsafe sources.
•	Water quality decline: Concentration of pollutants in reduced water volumes increases risks of diarrheal diseases and skin infections.
•	Heat-related illnesses: Prolonged heat waves linked to drought increase cases of heat stroke, respiratory diseases, and cardiovascular stress.
Housing and Infrastructure
•	Rural water supply systems: Small reservoirs and canals for irrigation and domestic supply run dry or fall below operational levels.
•	Hydropower and energy: Reduced river flows threaten small hydropower output and water availability for energy use.
Economy and Recovery
•	Income shocks: Farmers, fishers, and rural laborers lose primary sources of income, forcing reliance on loans or migration for work.
•	Debt cycles: Repeated droughts increase household indebtedness, trapping vulnerable families in poverty.

Renewable energy - Nearshore Wind Power Development Project by Vingroup”: Overview
•	Type: Nearshore wind (shallow-water/off the coast of Quảng Bình)
•	Proposed capacity: ~3,000 MW, developed in two phases (≈1,500 MW each).
•	Estimated total investment: ~US$3.9 billion. 
Phasing & Grid Connection (as proposed)
•	Phase 1 (2025-2030): ~1,500 MW, with connection envisaged via 500 kV Quảng Bình 1 substation or the 500 kV Quảng Trị-Vũng Áng line, depending on system readiness and approvals.
•	Phase 2 (2031-2035): additional ~1,500 MW, proposed to connect via 500 kV Quảng Bình 2 substation. 
Strategic Rationale
•	Mitigation & energy security: Adds a multi-gigawatt block of zero-fuel-cost electricity to Vietnam's load center in the North-Central region, complementing PDP8's renewable build-out while leveraging recent 500 kV backbone upgrades anchored at Quảng Trạch (Quảng Bình). 
•	Industrial & local value-add: A project of this scale can support port upgrades, fabrication yards, and an in-province supply chain for foundations, towers, and O&M—consistent with Vietnam's push to localize offshore/nearshore wind manufacturing and services. 
Current Status
•	Formal proposal submitted: The Quảng Bình People's Committee confirmed it received Vingroup's proposal for a nearshore wind power plant and published the US$3.9 billion capex estimate. Provincial/state media, as well as energy outlets, subsequently echoed the two-phase, 3,000 MW structure and indicative grid tie-ins. 
•	Regulatory path: As with other large wind projects, progression requires alignment with PDP8 implementation, marine spatial planning, environmental impact assessment, detailed site surveys, and Transmission Operator (EVNNPT) agreements for 500 kV connection capacity. (Policy/sector context.) 
Key Numbers (for quick reference)
•	Capacity: ~3,000 MW (≈1.5 GW in 2025-2030; ≈1.5 GW in 2031-2035).
•	Total investment: ~US$3.9 billion (proposal stage). 
•	Indicative grid nodes: 500 kV Quảng Bình 1, 500 kV Quảng Bình 2, and/or 500 kV Quảng Trị-Vũng Áng line (subject to technical studies/approvals).

climate_hazard:
Extreme heat: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
Elderly and chronically ill people
o	Hue has a growing aging population; older adults face higher risks of heat stroke, dehydration, and cardiovascular strain during heatwaves.
o	Limited access to cooling (air conditioning, shaded housing) increases mortality and morbidity.
Children and school-age populations
o	Heat exposure, which reduces learning capacity, increases absenteeism, and heightens risks of heat rash and dehydration.
o	In rural communes, children often assist with outdoor agricultural tasks, compounding exposure.
Low-income and informal workers
o	Street vendors, construction workers, motorbike taxi drivers, and small-scale farmers, work outdoors with minimal protection.
o	Many live in poorly ventilated housing, intensifying night-time heat stress when recovery is needed.
Women and marginalized groups
o	Women in coastal fishing and farming households shoulder both productive and caregiving work, raising exposure to heat and water stress.
o	Poorer households, especially in peri-urban areas, lack resources for cooling, medical care, or adaptive housing.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture and Fisheries
o	Heat stress reduces crop yields (particularly rice, maize, and vegetables) due to shortened growing cycles and higher evapotranspiration.
o	Livestock (pigs, poultry, cattle) face higher mortality and reduced productivity under prolonged hot conditions.
o	Aquaculture (especially shrimp and fish in Tam Giang-Cau Hai Lagoon) is vulnerable to rising water temperatures, which lower dissolved oxygen, increase algal blooms, and raise disease outbreaks.
Health Sector
o	Increased cases of heat stroke, dehydration, kidney disease, and cardiovascular emergencies.
o	Hospitals and clinics face rising demand for cooling, water, and electricity, stressing infrastructure during heatwaves.
o	Vector-borne diseases (dengue, malaria) may spread more easily as higher temperatures expand mosquito breeding seasons.
Tourism
o	Hue depends heavily on cultural and eco-tourism. Extreme heat reduces visitor comfort, shortens peak tourism seasons, and increases cooling costs for hotels and transport services.
Energy
o	High heat raises electricity demand (air conditioning, refrigeration), risking power shortages.
 | Drought: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
Rural farming households
o	Heavy reliance on rainfed rice, maize, and vegetable cultivation means drought directly reduces yields and incomes.
o	Limited access to irrigation in upland and coastal communes leaves farmers highly exposed.
Poor and marginalized communities
o	Households in A Lưới and Nam Đông (mountain districts) and coastal Phú Vang, Phú Lộc depend on climate-sensitive livelihoods (subsistence farming, fishing).
o	Drought increases food insecurity, out-migration, and indebtedness.
Women and children
o	Women often manage household water collection and care for crops and livestock, so drought increases workload and stress.
o	Children may experience malnutrition or be withdrawn from school to support family labor needs when drought reduces income.
Elderly and chronically ill people
o	Higher vulnerability to dehydration and health complications due to reduced access to safe water.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture
o	Reduced yields of rice, maize, cassava, and cash crops due to water shortages and heat stress.
o	Crop failures increase rural poverty and reduce provincial food security.
o	Salinization risk rises when irrigation flows decline in coastal communes.
Water Supply
o	Hue's reservoirs and rivers (e.g., Hương River) experience reduced flow during extended droughts.
o	Drinking water supply for urban residents and rural communes faces shortages, particularly in dry-season months.
Health Sector
o	Greater incidence of dehydration, kidney issues, and water-borne diseases from reliance on poor-quality water sources.
o	Hospitals experience increased patient loads during prolonged heat and drought.
Energy
o	Reduced river flow lowers hydropower generation capacity in central Vietnam, affecting electricity supply reliability.
 | River flooding: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
Low-income and riverbank communities
o	Many informal or low-income households are located in low-lying floodplains along the Hương River and its tributaries.
o	Poor housing structures (lightweight, non-flood-resistant materials) are easily damaged, leading to repeated loss of assets.
Women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities
o	These groups face higher risks during evacuation and recovery due to limited mobility, health vulnerabilities, and caregiving responsibilities.
o	School closures during flood events interrupt children's education.
Rural farming households
o	Floods damage crops, livestock, and stored food supplies. Recovery is slow for subsistence farmers with little savings or insurance.
o	Fishers and aquaculture households often lose cages, ponds, and stock to river surges.
Urban poor
o	In Hue City, drainage is often overwhelmed, compounding flood risk in densely populated wards, leading to prolonged waterlogging and disease outbreaks.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture
o	Floodwaters destroy rice paddies, vegetable fields, and cash crops, leading to seasonal food insecurity and income losses.
o	Soil fertility may decline due to erosion or sand/silt deposits.
Aquaculture and Fisheries
o	Ponds and cages along rivers are destroyed; escaped stock leads to major financial losses.
o	Lagoon and coastal aquaculture can be indirectly affected when floodwaters alter salinity and nutrient flows.
Health Sector
o	Standing water increases outbreaks of waterborne diseases (diarrhea, cholera, leptospirosis) and vector-borne diseases (dengue, malaria).
o	Hospitals and clinics may be inundated, reducing emergency response capacity.
Infrastructure & Housing
o	Floods damage roads, bridges, schools, health centers, and power supply systems.
o	Repeated flooding accelerates infrastructure degradation, raising maintenance and repair costs.
Tourism
o	Flooding of Hue's cultural heritage sites (e.g., Imperial Citadel, pagodas, mausoleums) disrupts tourism and risks irreversible damage to monuments.
o	Tourist cancellations affect hotel revenues and local service workers.
Industry & Economy
o	Local enterprises, craft villages, and markets face inventory and equipment losses.
o	Business continuity is disrupted by transport delays, damaged facilities, and power outages.
 | Urban flooding: 1. Impacts on Vulnerable Populations
Urban poor and informal settlements
o	Many low-income households live in low-lying wards of Hue City with inadequate drainage.
o	Houses are often built with non-flood-resistant materials, leading to repeated losses of belongings and higher repair costs.
o	Limited savings and lack of insurance make recovery extremely difficult.
Elderly, children, persons with disabilities
o	Difficulty in evacuating during flash floods; higher risk of injury and health complications.
o	Children's schooling disrupted by repeated closures; exposure to unsafe water heightens risk of disease.
Street vendors and informal workers
o	Loss of income when markets, roads, and public spaces are flooded.
o	Workers reliant on daily earnings are particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruption.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Housing and Urban Infrastructure
o	Prolonged inundation damages roads, drainage networks, electricity systems, and housing foundations.
o	Repeated flooding accelerates deterioration of public buildings and residential areas.
Public Health
o	Standing water leads to outbreaks of dengue fever, diarrhea, skin diseases, and leptospirosis.
o	Flooded clinics and hospitals reduce healthcare access during emergencies.
Education
o	Schools in Hue City frequently close during floods; prolonged closures disrupt learning and increase dropout risks.
Transport & Economy
o	Traffic paralysis on key city roads during heavy rain and urban flooding.
o	Tourism, a major economic sector, is disrupted when heritage sites and access roads are flooded.
Cultural Heritage
o	The Imperial Citadel and other UNESCO-listed heritage sites are highly sensitive to water damage.
o	Urban flooding accelerates the deterioration of historical monuments and museums, impacting both cultural identity and tourism revenues.
Small Businesses
o	Shops, restaurants, and hotels in flood-prone wards face damage to inventory, equipment, and facilities.
o	Loss of customer flow during flood days reduces income and increases bankruptcy risks for small enterprises.
3. Systemic Impacts
•	Public services disruption: Flooding reduces the effectiveness of municipal services (waste collection, transport, utilities).

Nature-Based Solutions - Coastal and Wetland Protection Forest Planting: Investment Proposal: Coastal and Wetland Protection Forest Planting in Thua Thien Hue

Project Overview
Thua Thien Hue, a coastal province in Central Vietnam, is highly vulnerable to climate change impacts such as coastal erosion, sea-level rise, and increasingly severe storms. To strengthen natural resilience, the province seeks investment and technical support to implement a large-scale Coastal and Wetland Protection Forest Planting Program.

Project Objectives

Restore and expand coastal protection forests and mangrove wetlands to act as natural barriers against storms, floods, and salinity intrusion.

Enhance carbon sequestration capacity and contribute to Vietnam's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) under the Paris Agreement.

Support biodiversity conservation and improve the ecological services of coastal and wetland ecosystems.

Provide sustainable livelihood opportunities for local communities through community-based forest management and eco-tourism initiatives.

Expected Outcomes

Establishment of new protection forests along vulnerable coastlines and estuaries.

Increased resilience of coastal communities, reducing damages from flooding and storm surges.

Carbon storage and potential generation of carbon credits for participation in domestic and international carbon markets.

Strengthened community engagement and improved socio-economic conditions through green jobs and income diversification.

Investment Needs
The provincial government of Thua Thien Hue is actively seeking international development financing, climate funds, and public-private partnerships to implement this initiative. Potential sources include the Green Climate Fund (GCF), bilateral donors, and private sector investors interested in carbon credits and sustainable development.

Call for Partnership
We invite partners—international organizations, financial institutions, NGOs, and private investors—to collaborate in scaling up this project. By investing in coastal and wetland forest planting in Thua Thien Hue, partners will directly contribute to climate resilience, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable development in one of Vietnam's most vulnerable coastal regions.

Buildings - Upgrading of the Thieu Hoa River Dike System: Project Overview
The Thieu Hoa river basin in Thua Thien Hue plays a critical role in flood control, irrigation, and community protection. However, the existing river dike system is deteriorating and no longer sufficient to cope with increasing flood risks, exacerbated by climate change and upstream hydrological changes. The provincial government seeks investment and technical cooperation to upgrade and reinforce the Thieu Hoa River dike system to ensure long-term resilience and safety for local populations.

Project Objectives

Strengthen and rehabilitate the existing dike infrastructure to withstand more frequent and intense floods.

Safeguard agricultural lands, residential areas, and critical infrastructure from inundation and erosion.

Enhance irrigation capacity to support agricultural productivity and food security.

Integrate climate-resilient design and modern monitoring systems to ensure sustainability and adaptive management.

Expected Outcomes

A modernized and reinforced dike system capable of handling extreme weather events and rising water levels.

Reduced vulnerability of thousands of households living in flood-prone areas.

Protection of farmlands, ensuring stable agricultural production and rural livelihoods.

Improved disaster risk management through the incorporation of early-warning and monitoring technologies.

Investment Needs
The project requires blended financing through international development partners, concessional loans, and public-private partnerships. Priority sources include multilateral institutions (ADB, World Bank), bilateral donors, and climate finance mechanisms such as the Green Climate Fund (GCF). Estimated financing needs cover engineering works, capacity building, and the introduction of climate-resilient design standards.

Call for Partnership
Thua Thien Hue welcomes collaboration with international organizations, financial institutions, and technical partners to realize this project. By investing in the Thieu Hoa River dike system upgrade, partners will contribute directly to disaster risk reduction, sustainable agriculture, and enhanced resilience of vulnerable communities in Central Vietnam.

o	Many live in poorly ventilated housing, intensifying night-time heat stress when recovery is needed.
Women and marginalized groups
o	Women in coastal fishing and farming households shoulder both productive and caregiving work, raising exposure to heat and water stress.
o	Poorer households, especially in peri-urban areas, lack resources for cooling, medical care, or adaptive housing.
2. Impacts on Key Sectors
Agriculture and Fisheries
o	Heat stress reduces crop yields (particularly rice, maize, and vegetables) due to shortened growing cycles and higher evapotranspiration.
o	Livestock (pigs, poultry, cattle) face higher mortality and reduced productivity under prolonged hot conditions.
o	Aquaculture (especially shrimp and fish in Tam Giang-Cau Hai Lagoon) is vulnerable to rising water temperatures, which lower dissolved oxygen, increase algal blooms, and raise disease outbreaks.
Health Sector
o	Increased cases of heat stroke, dehydration, kidney disease, and cardiovascular emergencies.
o	Hospitals and clinics face rising demand for cooling, water, and electricity, stressing infrastructure during heatwaves.
o	Vector-borne diseases (dengue, malaria) may spread more easily as higher temperatures expand mosquito breeding seasons.
Tourism
o	Hue depends heavily on cultural and eco-tourism. Extreme heat reduces visitor comfort, shortens peak tourism seasons, and increases cooling costs for hotels and transport services.
Energy
o	High heat raises electricity demand (air conditioning, refrigeration), risking power shortages.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Renovation and environmental restoration of closed solid waste treatment and landfill sites: Project Overview
Over the past decades, Thua Thien Hue has relied on several landfill sites and waste treatment areas to manage municipal solid waste. Many of these sites have now been closed but continue to pose significant environmental and health risks, including soil and water contamination, methane emissions, and negative impacts on surrounding communities. The provincial government seeks international investment and technical support to rehabilitate and restore these closed landfill areas, transforming them into safe and environmentally friendly spaces.

Project Objectives

Mitigate environmental risks through site remediation, leachate treatment, and methane capture.

Restore degraded land for alternative uses such as green spaces, renewable energy development (e.g., solar farms), or community facilities.

Reduce greenhouse gas emissions in alignment with Vietnam's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and circular economy strategy.

Strengthen local capacity in sustainable waste management and environmental monitoring.

Expected Outcomes

Improved environmental quality (soil, groundwater, and air) in areas previously affected by waste disposal.

Significant reduction of methane emissions through landfill gas capture and management.

Rehabilitated land repurposed for socio-economic and ecological benefits (e.g., parks, community areas, renewable energy projects).

Enhanced public health and living conditions for communities located near former landfill sites.

Investment Needs
The project requires financing and technical expertise for site assessment, remediation works, methane capture infrastructure, and ecological restoration. Potential funding sources include climate finance facilities (Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility), bilateral and multilateral donors, and private sector partners interested in carbon credit generation and green infrastructure development.

Call for Partnership
Thua Thien Hue invites international donors, development agencies, and private investors to collaborate in this effort. By supporting the rehabilitation of closed landfill sites, partners will contribute to climate mitigation, circular economy transition, and improved environmental health for one of Vietnam's most climate-vulnerable provinces.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Development of centralized wastewater collection and treatment systems in urban areas meeting environmental regulations: Project Overview
Urban areas in Thua Thien Hue are rapidly expanding, leading to increased domestic and industrial wastewater discharge. However, existing wastewater treatment infrastructure is limited and insufficient, resulting in untreated effluents being released into rivers and coastal waters, causing environmental degradation, health risks, and threats to Hue's cultural heritage sites. The provincial government is seeking investment and technical cooperation to develop centralized wastewater collection and treatment systems that meet national and international environmental standards before discharge.

Project Objectives

Establish modern, centralized wastewater treatment plants in major urban centers of Thua Thien Hue.

Ensure all wastewater is treated to meet environmental standards before being released into rivers, lagoons, and coastal zones.

Reduce water pollution, improve public health, and protect aquatic ecosystems.

Contribute to the sustainable urban development strategy and the preservation of Hue's UNESCO-recognized cultural heritage.

Expected Outcomes

Significant reduction in untreated wastewater discharged into natural water bodies.

Improved water quality in rivers, lagoons, and coastal areas, enhancing biodiversity and ecosystem health.

Better sanitation and public health for urban populations, particularly vulnerable groups.

Strengthened climate resilience through improved urban environmental infrastructure.

Potential opportunities for resource recovery (e.g., sludge-to-energy, water reuse).

Investment Needs
The project requires large-scale financing for the design, construction, and operation of wastewater collection and treatment systems, including pipelines, pumping stations, and advanced treatment technologies. Priority sources include international development banks (ADB, World Bank), bilateral donors, and climate/environmental finance facilities (Green Climate Fund, GEF). Public-private partnership (PPP) models are also encouraged, particularly with investors in water utilities and green infrastructure.

Call for Partnership
Thua Thien Hue welcomes partnerships with international donors, financial institutions, private sector investors, and technical experts. By investing in this initiative, partners will directly contribute to improving urban environmental quality, protecting public health, and ensuring the sustainable growth of a climate-vulnerable region in Central Vietnam.

Waste management (including waste recycling) - Establishment of centralized wastewater collection and treatment systems in industrial zones/clusters and craft villages, which generate wastewater under the State's responsibility: Project Overview
Industrial parks, clusters, and traditional craft villages in Thua Thien Hue are important drivers of economic growth, but they also generate significant volumes of untreated wastewater, including chemical, textile, food-processing, and aquaculture effluents. Currently, most wastewater from these areas is either inadequately treated or discharged directly into rivers and lagoons, leading to severe environmental risks. Recognizing that such treatment infrastructure falls under state responsibility, the provincial government is seeking investment and partnerships to establish centralized wastewater collection and treatment systems in key industrial and craft production areas.

Project Objectives

Construct and operate centralized wastewater collection and treatment facilities in priority industrial parks, clusters, and craft villages.

Ensure compliance with national and international environmental standards before discharge.

Reduce water pollution and mitigate risks to nearby communities, agricultural land, and sensitive ecosystems (e.g., Tam Giang-Cau Hai Lagoon).

Support sustainable industrial development and improve competitiveness of local enterprises by aligning with green production standards.

Expected Outcomes

Significant reduction of untreated or partially treated industrial wastewater discharged into rivers, lagoons, and groundwater.

Protection of ecosystems, particularly aquatic biodiversity in coastal and lagoon areas.

Improved environmental compliance and social license to operate for enterprises within industrial parks and craft villages.

Strengthened capacity of local authorities to enforce wastewater management regulations.

Contribution to Vietnam's circular economy and climate-resilient industrialization goals.

Investment Needs
This project requires capital investment and technical expertise for the design and construction of wastewater treatment plants, collection pipelines, pumping stations, and sludge management systems. Potential financing sources include:

International development banks (World Bank, ADB, JICA).

Climate/environmental finance facilities (Green Climate Fund, GEF).

Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) with industrial investors and water utility companies.

Bilateral donor support for technology transfer and capacity building.

Call for Partnership
Thua Thien Hue invites international donors, financial institutions, and private sector partners to collaborate in building modern, centralized wastewater treatment systems for industrial parks and craft villages. Investment in this initiative will deliver dual benefits of protecting natural ecosystems and enabling sustainable, low-carbon industrial growth in Central Vietnam.

project_info: Waste management (including waste recycling) - Communal environmental strategy - Ancud Circular: Ancud Circular, the successful model for the recovery of household solid waste in the Country. Today the commune of Ancud in the Chiloé Archipelago has an advantage over the rest of the communes in the country. In 2018, the Ancud municipality started with a small community recycling pilot, but after the health crisis of 2019, a new vision emerged regarding the management of (RSD), since it was urgent to reduce the volumes of waste, which is why they were looking for alternatives to recover waste, both organic and inorganic, which to date Today it has been transformed into the new communal strategy for the management of recoverable waste, which is called “Ancud circular”. Although the valuation data at the national level are not clear and will only be standardized with the implementation of the REP law, the Recovery Report by Commune of Chile, Kyklos and Núcleo Biotechnological PUCV, 2022 on the recovery by commune in 2020 places the commune of Ancud at number 6 at the national level and considering the advances in this topic in the last two years, such as the Circular Recycling Shed, the implementation of differentiated collection in 100% of the urban radius once a week and in the rural sector every 15 days, creation of a clean point and collection of more than 10 materials premiums, education and guided visits to neighborhood associations and educational establishments, among other actions that have been carried out with the community. Our household waste is made up of approximately 50% organic waste, which is why the first focus was to try to reduce organic waste, through the successful #AncudComposta program, which to date has already delivered more than 1,000 home composters to residents of the commune, in addition to more than 7,000 people who have participated in online training on composting and vermicompost. Currently, the differentiated withdrawal of organics from social fairs and municipal fairs is also carried out. In addition to the home composters, this year we expect financing for the Municipal Composting Plant project, which will transform it into a mixed organic waste management system, achieving home/community composting and differentiated collection of organic waste. On the other hand, #AncudRecycle treats all inorganic waste that makes up approximately 30% of the total volume of household waste. The circular warehouse has first-class equipment for waste recovery, a horizontal industrial baler, plastic chipper, shredding machine, and for the implementation of community workshops it has a plastic extruder and injection machine with their respective molds. This strategy will support the City in reducing municipal fleet GHG emissions, in line with targets established in the City's Climate Change Action Plan. project_info: Public and green spaces - Characterization and diagnosis for 53 public spaces and their radius of influence in the municipal capital as part of the Comprehensive Municipal Green Infrastructure System.: The population of San Francisco del Rincón will not have a strategy for implementing comprehensive improvements to the existing public spaces, so they will continue not to comply with the points set out in NOM 001 of SEDATU, remaining as unconnected and useless urban waste. These will lack both a physical and environmental connection, isolating the possibility of functioning as an organic system without implementation of Green Infrastructure. By not having tree inventories or management plans for each space, deficient practices will continue in the maintenance, recovery, removal and reforestation of plant bodies and green areas. Understanding the conditions of the radius of influence of each public space is necessary to prioritize and monitor the elements that contribute to positive and negative social dynamics. Ignoring this contextual reality perpetuates inefficient incidence. Currently, a significant amount of resources are allocated to intervention projects on public space and environmental care strategies, which lack comprehensive diagnoses and strategic scenarios to make public spending more efficient. Finally, there will be no adequate measurement and monitoring of the physical and environmental reality of the municipality, so the drawing of lines of action at the planning level will not be possible.

climate_hazard: Soil degradation/erosion: Without healthy soils the benefits climate change could have for agriculture in the National Park such as increased productivity are lost. It was outlined in the risk assessment that a legacy of historic land management (overgrazing, peat extraction and drainage, recreational pressures) in the Lake District has meant that there are areas of the National Park where soils (which could be peatland, grassland and woodland soils) have been compromised to some extent and as a consequence are vulnerable to damage and erosion from high intensity rain and prolonged periods of drought. As it is likely the Lake District will experience more frequent storms of increasing intensity in the short term with climate change, the risk assessment scored soil health as being highly vulnerable in the short to medium term. In the long term soil health is found to be less vulnerable in order to reflect the burgeoning recognition by policy makers (2020 Agriculture Bill) and land managers (ELMS) currently over the importance of soil health. However in its scoring the risk assessment has also assumed wide-spread implementation of interventions on-the-ground that promote soil health will follow immediately over the next few years. This is because soils take time to recover and it will require interventions now in order to realise greater resilience to climate change in the longer term. | Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): For coastal households the results showed that it was likely that they would be impacted by climate change in the short, medium and long term and in some cases the effects may mean that particular households may need to abandon their properties and move further inland. Despite this the vulnerability score for coastal households in the risk assessment remained at a moderate level. This is because the impact and consequences of sea level rise are recognised as a threat by local authorities and is being prepared for. The North West Shoreline Management Plan (SMP2) covers the coastline from Great Orme in North Wales to the Scottish Border, thus including the National Park's coastline. It incorporates projections of sea level rise into long term plans for coastal defences. The Cumbria Coastal Strategy builds on this and assesses the existing condition of land and flood defences along the Cumbria coast line (including the National Park) and identifies potential future interventions. P a g e 28 Its key objectives are: • to evaluate the risk of flooding and erosion along the Cumbrian coastline • identify properties and infrastructure at risk • identify and evaluate potential long-term solutions • form a robust and objective evidence base • to provide a framework for future infrastructure and development Adaptation strategies including building and enhancing coastal protection structures, such as dykes or sea walls, as well as deploying coastal warning systems. However the success of this planning on lowering the risk of climate change to coastal households is completely dependent on the resource and funding available in the future to implement it. | Increased water demand: The Lake District National Park is a significant water supply source which is of local and regional importance - providing drinking water to around 4 million people in the north west of England. The risk assessment looked at the impact of climate change on both water quality and water quantity at public water supply assets in the National Park. Water quality in the Lake District is highly vulnerable to climate change impacts. High intensity rainfall has the potential to wash soil and nutrients from land into water bodies which is exacerbated by the steep sided topography that surrounds many of the public water supply assets in the National Park (e.g. Thirlmere). In addition rising temperatures were shown in the risk assessment to interact with an increasing nutrient load of water bodies to increase the frequency and scale of algal blooms further deteriorating water quality. Within the results of the risk assessment for water quality the highest level of vulnerability was found to be in the medium term (high vulnerability) with the short and long term scored as being moderately vulnerable. The reason the level of vulnerability of water quality is not high considering the risk factors with climate change just mentioned is because there is commitment by United Utilities (locally responsible water and waste water provider) to resource and invest in a number of interventions (e.g. sustainable land management, blending and treatment technologies) over the short, medium and long term to build resilience and mitigate somewhat this level of risk. This was also the case for water quantity. An increased frequency and duration of droughts in the long term with climate change means that is highly likely that most public water supply assets by 2080 will have suffered disruption due to low water levels, and without mitigation would have consequences for end users. However United Utilities have invested and resourced a number of measures (e.g. drought plans, monitoring of water levels, demand reduction, leakage reduction and efficiency improvements) to mitigate the scale of this impact. This is why the level of vulnerability within the risk assessment is restricted to a moderate impact and not higher. | Urban flooding: The National Park not only manages water so as to make it available for human consumption but its rivers, lakes, woodlands, peatlands and vegetation also work at a landscape scale to store it and prevent communities both within and outside of the National Park boundary suffering from flooding . Increasing frequency of storms and periods of higher rainfall intensity that will occur over the short, medium and long term will make communities in the Lake District highly vulnerable to flooding, and this vulnerability is relevant as soon as the short term. The risk assessment showed that it wasn't just the fact that the volume of rain that will fall in a short period will increase, it will also interact with a number of human created features in the landscape that will exacerbate this risk (e.g. land management practices, urban development on floodplains, artificial manipulation of river courses, expansion of impermeable surfaces). However investment in natural interventions at a landscape scale combined with more hard engineering solutions (e.g. SUDS) associated the flood mitigation schemes that remove or ameliorate these features have the potential to lower the level of vulnerability communities will experience with climate.The vulnerability of inland households to flood risk from climate change was greater than for coastal households. Vulnerability in short term was high, which increased to very high in the long term. This is because inland flooding in the National Park occurs much more frequently and is much more difficult to predict which area will be worst affected. Due to the National Park's mountainous topography flood risk is highly localised, concentrated to households that are located in high risk areas such as those that sit in functional floodplains, close to water courses and or located at the bottom of steep sided valleys. The National Park has a history of damaging flood events with the most recent being those associated with Storm Desmond in 2015. Because of this there is a lot of work and action to help raise awareness and build resilience with communities to flood risk, as well as interventions in catchments to mitigate the scale of flooding when it does occur. | Biodiversity loss: Many species within the Lake District will be pushed out of the National Park as the Lake District's climate envelope changes and there is phenological disruption (i.e. changes to periodic events inbiological life cycles such as bud burst and hibernation). New species may move into the National Park which could be important for the resilience of native species from elsewhere in the UK,however it could also mean invasive plants and animals move in and dominate, as well as a greater variety and incidence of pests and disease.
project_info:
Land-Use - Farming in Protected Landscapes: Farming in Protected Landscapes (FiPL) is a UK government grant program that provides funding to farmers and land managers in England's National Parks and National Landscapes. The program supports projects focused on nature recovery, mitigating climate change, enhancing public access and enjoyment of the landscape, and protecting cultural heritage and the rural economy. Unlike traditional agri-environment schemes, FiPL is a competitive program with funding delivered locally by the National Park and National Landscape authorities, allowing for tailored projects that meet local priorities. In the Lake District the relevant prirorities are:
Nature

Transport - Electrifying the Broads: Electrifying the Broads (Project number 10008242) is a feasibility study funded under Strand 1 of the Clean Maritime Demonstration Competition (2021-22). Four organisations led by RenEnergy, including the Broads Authority, Norfolk Broads Direct and Hydrogen East, partnered to carry out this whole 
systems study with the aim of specifying a demonstrable pathway to decarbonising inland waterways hire cruisers on the Broads. Broads hire cruisers were chosen as a target sector because they represent a significant contributor to the local economy, and are representative of other heavily-used inland waterways recreational vessels making a relatively high contribution to greenhouse gas emissions compared to other inland waterways vessels. 

The Broads offers an ideal context in which to test and measure assumptions, from which valuable high resolution performance and user data will be acquired to form the basis of future designs for the electrification of inland waterways craft. 

Objectives 

Our objectives were to gather geospatial, 
 technological and socio-economic data, to lay the foundations for a demonstration that would help to resolve the challenge of converting an existing fleet to clean energy by electrification. We aimed to resolve a trilemma concerning provision of sufficient onboard electrical energy, sufficient shoreside charging infrastructure to support battery recharging against the costs and benefits for scaling the solutions. Based on our feasibility study, we have concluded that it should be possible to operate a fully electric hire cruiser on the Broads, provided adequate shoreside infrastructure is in place. We recommend proving this with the proposed demonstration project.

Biodiversity loss: Biodiversity loss will have wide-ranging impacts across multiple sectors. In agriculture, the loss of infield trees will reduce shade for livestock, negatively affecting animal welfare and productivity. Forestry will also be impacted, as the decline of natural predators may lead to increased browsing pressure on tree crops, while a reduction in pollinators could hinder pollination and viable seed production. Water supply systems will face challenges due to stressed or degraded peatlands, which can compromise water quality and increase the need for extraction and purification for human consumption.

Conservation efforts will become more urgent as more species require protection. Climate change will drive natural migration, with native species in the park potentially shifting northward or becoming locally extinct, while new species may arrive from southern regions. These changes will disrupt food webs, species abundance, and distribution, all of which will need to adapt to the evolving climate.

Financial and insurance activities will also be affected, as opportunities to invest in ecological solutions may diminish and corporate social responsibility targets become harder to meet. In the realm of professional, scientific, and technical activities, research will become increasingly vital to deepen our understanding of biodiversity's role in addressing climate change.

Education will play a crucial role in responding to the climate and ecological crisis. Biodiversity loss will highlight the need for improved climate education to benefit future generations. Human health and social work activities are closely tied to biodiversity, as engagement with nature has proven benefits for wellbeing. This was starkly illustrated by the incident at Sycamore Gap in September 2023, which underscored the emotional and cultural importance of nature. The landscape of Northumberland National Park continues to draw people from around the world, offering a vital connection to nature that supports both physical and mental health. | Storm: Violent storms like Storm Arwen, which struck Northumberland National Park on 26th November 2021, and Storm Éowyn in January 2025 have far reaching consequences across multiple sectors. In agriculture, high winds damaged buildings and livestock shelters, leaving animals exposed during winter and reducing productivity. The loss of infield trees also diminished shade availability, affecting animal welfare and increasing heat stress during warmer months. Forestry was severely impacted, with over 1,000 hectares of conifer plantations uprooted in a single night due to windthrow. This not only resulted in the loss of valuable timber but disrupted supply chains and long term woodland management plans.

Infrastructure suffered extensively. Overhead electricity and communication lines proved vulnerable, with 45% of properties losing power, some for up to six months. This had effects on residents and visitors, who were unable to use mobile phones or access essential services. Water supply systems, reliant on electric pumps, failed in several areas, requiring emergency water deliveries by tanker. Similarly, sewage and waste management systems were compromised, posing public health risks.

The Otterburn Ranges, which occupy 20% of the National Park and serve as a military training area, experienced damage to infrastructure and power lines, disrupting training operations. Conservation efforts were also set back, as ancient and veteran trees were lost, degrading habitats and biodiversity. Storms often lead to river spates, increasing erosion and sediment loading, which negatively affects aquatic ecosystems.

Transportation networks were severely disrupted, with fallen trees blocking roads and causing financial losses for residents and businesses. In some afforested areas, road closures persisted for over two years following Storm Arwen. project_info:
Nature-Based Solutions - Hadrian's Wall Wetlands Landscape Recovery Project

This is a major nature restoration initiative within Northumberland National Park.

: https://www.northumberlandnationalpark.org.uk/hadrians-wall-wetlands-landmark-nature-recovery-project-aims-to-help-tackle-climate-and-biodiversity-crises/

The Hadrian's Wall Wetlands Landscape Recovery Project is a transformative nature restoration initiative; it aims to restore and enhance over 4,400 hectares of carbon rich landscapes surrounding Hadrian's Wall, integrating climate action, biodiversity recovery, and cultural heritage protection.

The overall objectives are as follows. Restore degraded peatlands and wetlands to enhance carbon sequestration and reduce emissions.
Reconnect fragmented habitats across farmland, forestry, and nature reserves.
Protect and interpret cultural heritage, including 12.8 km of Hadrian's Wall World Heritage Site.
Support sustainable land management and regenerative agriculture.
Engage communities and visitors in nature recovery and climate resilience.


We have received a £750,000 DEFRA grant for the development phase (2023 to 2025) and £490,000 philanthropic pledge for restoration and monitoring.
There has been £143,714 Landscape Enhancement Initiative funding for erosion control and trail restoration; £103,752 Countryside Stewardship revenue and £77,163 capital for sustainable land management at Greenlee. The project aims to secure long-term government and private funding for a 20 year delivery phase.
This will likely include: additional DEFRA and UK government climate funds, carbon market revenues (e.g. peatland and woodland sequestration), ecosystem service payments (e.g. flood mitigation, biodiversity credits) and further partnership contributions.
While the exact total cost for the full 20-year programme is not yet published, it is expected to be multi-million pound, potentially exceeding £10 million, depending on the scale of restoration, monitoring, and community engagement activities.

The project is designed as a 20 year landscape recovery programme, contributing to the UK's net zero goals and enhancing the ecological and cultural value of Hadrian's Wall.

Land-Use - Farming in Protected Landscapes (FiPL) Programme

Most projects mentioned in this application are delivered through a mix of blended financing with the Authority acting as a catalyst/enabler. As the Authority owns less than 0.2% of the National Park, action is delivered through engagement with landowners, with staff sourcing grants and public/private funding to enable projects to happen.: https://www.northumberlandnationalpark.org.uk/nature-landscape/farming/farming-in-protected-landscapes/

Funded by Defra, FiPL supports farmers and land managers to deliver projects that benefit nature, climate, people, and place. The programme runs until March 2026.

Examples of FiPL projects:
Carbon and biodiversity audits, conducted by the Scottish Agricultural College across multiple farms. Helps farmers understand their carbon footprint and biodiversity value. Informs future land management and environmental grant applications.

At High Carrick, a spring was diverted to prevent clean water from mixing with livestock waste.
Reduces sediment and nutrient runoff into the Elsdon Burn. Improves water quality and reduces climate related flood risks.
Grant: £34,574


At Waterhead and Bradley Farm, a water system was installed to enable cattle grazing in areas previously inaccessible. Reduces overgrowth and improves habitat for curlew, lapwing, and snipe.
Supports adaptive land use in response to changing climate conditions.

Projects like Alnham Meadows Enhancement increase species diversity and pollinator habitat.
Enhances carbon sequestration in soils and supports resilient ecosystems.
Links upland and lowland habitats for better landscape connectivity.
Grant: £4,950.60

Bracken control: use of bracken mulchers to manage invasive vegetation. Improves access and reduces fire risk, which is increasing due to climate change. Supports low carbon tourism and landscape resilience.

Electric bike hire: promotes low emission transport for visitors and enhances sustainable tourism infrastructure. Grant: £6,763.69


Funding: Over the last four years, FIPL for the Northumberland National Park area has given out nearly £2 million in funds, worked with 301 farmers and land managers and funded 132 projects.

Land-Use - TBD Within-Range Calcareous Grassland Translocation project: An emerging project would aim to research within-geographic range translation of calcareous grassland species as a proof on concept for assisted colonisation of isolated habitats. This aims to provide evidence for climate adaptation work which could then be extrapolated to supporting species in northwards movements as climate change alters abiotic conditions, resulting in range-shift.

This project is in the very early phases of development, and would be linked to the work of the new Landscape Observatory, a project based within the PDNPA but which links together Protected Landscapes across the UK. This project's first phase of work involves the use of AI mapping to provide detailed models of landscapes to understand their capacity for management, e.g. modelling suitable habitat for a particular species to promote targeted management or translocation. The aim is this can be utilised alongside other evidence gathering to ensure highly evidence based management planning, which is able to be more able to adapt to the impacts of climate change, e.g. through using the Resist-Accept-Direct decision making framework.

project_info: Nature-Based Solutions - Projeto Rio Pirapora: Proposta de SBN aplicadas ao sistema infraestrutural do Parque Rio Pirapora, situado em Maranguape, Estado do Ceará. A área objeto, geoecologicamente, configura-se como um sistema ambiental de vale hidrológico, com características socioambientais de ocupação desordenada, o que implica na configuração de cenários de riscos socioambientais por inundação e movimento de massa, bem como na efetiva poluição do corpo hídrico, perda da biodiversidade local, assentamentos precários e condições de vulnerabilidade das comunidades afetadas. Tais fatores implicam diretamente na qualidade de vida das pessoas, assim como colocam o município num cenário de baixa contribuição para o enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas e o alcance aos Objetivos do Desenvolvimento Sustentável - ODS. Dessa forma, propõe-se a execução de intervenções que viabilizem: o uso de alternativas infraestruturais baseadas na natureza, a adequação do ambiente às boas condições de mobilidade e moradia, o estímulo a governança, participação social e gestão participativa do território e a geração de renda pelo turismo comunitário e empreendedorismo social. Nesse trabalho, são apresentados projetos de intervenção pautados em 4 eixos: infraestrutura da natureza, infraestrutura do cuidado, infraestrutura da sociobiodiversidade local e infraestrutura imaterial, todos com o propósito de gerar melhores condições urbanas, melhores condições de moradia, redução da poluição e da degradação ambiental, valorização das áreas verdes, geração de renda e fortalecimento do turismo de base comunitária. Viabiliza-se pela real possibilidade de retorno financeiro a longo prazo, bem como pelos consideráveis impactos positivos gerados a grupos sociais distintos e ao meio ambiente.

Nature-Based Solutions - Entre Parques: O projeto tem como objetivo principal implementar uma rede integrada de Ruas Verdes Completas em Maranguape, conectando os nove parques urbanos, instituídos pela lei 3.072/2022, às escolas e comunidades vizinhas. A iniciativa busca enfrentar riscos climáticos, especialmente ilhas de calor e alagamentos, por meio de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SBN), articulando mobilidade sustentável, infraestrutura verde, energia limpa e educação ambiental.
O escopo concentra-se nas vias que ligam os parques Horto Florestal, Raimundo Pinto, Raimundo Braga, Pirapora, Valéria, Gereraú, Estação Ferroviária, Santa e EITA, formando um sistema contínuo de circulação segura, inclusiva e educativa. Os principais componentes incluem: (i) mobilidade urbana sustentável, com ciclofaixas, pavimento permeável e calçadas acessíveis; (ii) infraestrutura verde, como arborização, canteiros pluviais e jardins de chuva; (iii) energia limpa e mobiliário urbano, com iluminação solar, bicicletários, bancos e áreas de descanso; (iv) identidade urbana e educação ambiental, por meio de sinalização interativa, mapas, placas sobre fauna e flora e brincadeiras pintadas no chão.
Entre os resultados esperados estão a criação de uma malha urbana verde interligada, ampliação das áreas permeáveis e arborizadas, redução de alagamentos, diminuição da temperatura superficial, estímulo a deslocamentos ativos (a pé ou de bicicleta) e fortalecimento do vínculo comunitário com os parques. Indicadores de sucesso incluem aumento da conectividade verde, maior participação social e ganhos em saúde pública e qualidade ambiental.
Os principais beneficiários serão os moradores do entorno dos parques, especialmente crianças e estudantes, que terão rotas seguras e educativas até as escolas, além de pedestres, ciclistas, comerciantes locais e usuários do transporte público. Para esses grupos, o projeto representa inclusão social, mobilidade segura, lazer e melhoria da qualidade de vida.
Nos impactos positivos, destacam-se três dimensões:
Climática: mitigação das ilhas de calor, aumento da infiltração hídrica, sequestro de carbono e redução de alagamentos;
Socioambiental: ampliação da biodiversidade urbana, fortalecimento da educação ambiental, criação de espaços inclusivos e maior senso de pertencimento comunitário;
Econômica: valorização imobiliária sustentável, dinamização do comércio local e redução de custos públicos com drenagem e saúde, ao promover ambientes mais saudáveis e mobilidade ativa.
Por fim, o projeto está inserido em um programa municipal mais amplo de criação dos nove parques urbanos, funcionando como eixo articulador entre essas áreas e os bairros da cidade. Alinha-se ao Plano Diretor, ao Plano de Governo Municipal e a programas nacionais como o Plano Clima Adaptação, PAC Periferia Viva e Programa Cidades Verdes Resilientes, consolidando Maranguape como referência em desenvolvimento urbano resiliente e de baixo carbono.

Women also tend to assume greater responsibility for caring for children and the elderly during emergency situations, which intensifies the physical and emotional. River flooding: The City of Balanga faces a web of vulnerabilities that heighten its exposure to climate-related hazards, particularly flooding, landslides, and storm surges. Low-income communities, often residing in informal settlements along rivers and coastal zones, are disproportionately at risk due to inadequate housing and limited access to basic services. Children, the elderly, women, and persons with disabilities are especially vulnerable, facing heightened health risks, mobility challenges, and economic instability during and after disasters. The education sector suffers when schools double as evacuation centers, disrupting learning and cases of dropout among displaced youth. Health facilities located in hazard-prone areas risk operational shutdowns, exacerbating disease outbreaks and mental health stress. Livelihoods tied to agriculture and fisheries are threatened by erratic rainfall. Meanwhile, critical infrastructure—such as roads and electricity networks—is susceptible to damage, leading to prolonged service interruptions that affect daily life and emergency response. These overlapping vulnerabilities underscore the urgent need for targeted resilience planning across sectors and communities. | Extreme heat: Extreme heat presents a critical climate hazard for the City of Balanga, exerting direct and indirect stress on the agriculture, forestry, and fisheries sectors. Prolonged periods of elevated temperature accelerate evapotranspiration and soil moisture depletion, leading to reduced productivity of staple crops such as rice, corn, and high-value vegetables. Empirical observations in Metro Bataan have recorded consecutive years of declining rice harvests attributed to heat stress, pest proliferation, and water shortages in irrigation systems. The decline in yield not only undermines farmgate income but also depresses market quality, compounding the vulnerability of smallholder farmers who are heavily reliant on monocropping systems.

The socioeconomic consequences are significant, particularly for subsistence households, women, and elderly farmers whose adaptive capacity is constrained by limited access to irrigation, crop insurance, and climate-resilient technologies. Beyond croplands, extreme heat exacerbates forest degradation in upland barangays, weakening agroforestry systems and reducing the ecological services of forests that regulate downstream water supply. The fisheries and aquaculture sector is similarly impacted, as elevated water temperatures reduce dissolved oxygen levels, trigger algal blooms, and increase the incidence of fish mortality, thereby threatening coastal livelihoods dependent on traditional and small-scale aquaculture practices.

Taken together, the intensification of extreme heat heightens agricultural vulnerability in Balanga, disrupts ecosystem balance, and compromises livelihood stability, underscoring the urgent need for adaptive interventions to safeguard food security and rural income streams.

Land-Use - Local Farm-to-Market Road Program of Balanga City (2025-2029): The Farm-to-Market Road (FMR) Program of Balanga City is a five-year initiative designed to enhance connectivity between agricultural production areas and local markets. Recognizing the importance of resilient infrastructure to agricultural development, the City Government is investing in FMRs to reduce transportation costs, minimize post-harvest losses, and strengthen the livelihood systems of farmers and fisherfolk. More importantly, the program is positioned as a climate adaptation measure that safeguards communities against the increasing risks of flooding, sea level rise, and extreme weather events.

Implementation will proceed in phases from 2025 to 2029. In 2025, priority road segments in agricultural barangays such as Cataning, Cupang, Talisay, and Tortugas will be identified, with initial construction targeting high-demand areas. By 2026, expansion will cover secondary production zones and rehabilitation of existing farm access roads, with particular attention to aquaculture and coastal barangays that are highly vulnerable to climate hazards. In 2027, major links connecting farms to the Balanga Public Market and nearby trading posts will be completed, integrating drainage and elevated road features to ensure year-round access even during heavy rainfall and floods. The year 2028 will focus on upgrading remaining roads into all-weather paved routes, directly connecting producers to food hubs, warehouses, and processing facilities. By 2029, the City anticipates the full completion and turnover of its five-year FMR Network Plan, followed by monitoring and evaluation to assess socio-economic and environmental benefits.

Beyond improving agricultural productivity, the FMR Program has significant impacts on climate change adaptation and mitigation. All-weather farm roads provide safe evacuation routes during disasters, ensuring uninterrupted access to essential services and relief operations. Elevated and well-drained road designs minimize damage from heavy rains and storm surges, making farming communities more resilient to climate variability. By shortening travel time and reducing fuel consumption in the transport of goods, the program also contributes to lowering greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture-related logistics. Furthermore, by connecting farms to markets more efficiently, FMRs reduce the risk of food spoilage, thereby decreasing food waste—a critical aspect of sustainable climate action.

Urban flooding: Flooding in Carmona primarily affects communities located in low-lying and flood-prone barangays, where drainage systems are often inadequate to cope with intense rainfall and overflow of waterways. For households and vulnerable populations—particularly the poor, elderly, children, and persons with disabilities—the impacts are severe. Floodwaters damage homes made of light materials, force frequent evacuations, and disrupt access to essential services. Health risks also rise sharply, with increased exposure to waterborne diseases such as leptospirosis, diarrhea, and dengue.

For the education sector, flooding leads to the suspension of classes and damage to school facilities. Schools are sometimes used as evacuation centers, further disrupting the learning process. Prolonged interruptions affect students' academic performance and add burdens to teachers and parents.

In terms of livelihoods, the impacts are felt strongly in both agriculture and industry. Flooding damages crops, livestock, and fisheries, reducing food supply and income for small farmers. Industrial operations may be halted due to inundated access roads, damaged equipment, or power interruptions, causing productivity losses and wage disruptions for workers. Small businesses, particularly those in informal trade, are highly vulnerable because they lack the resources to quickly recover.

The infrastructure sector also suffers, with roads, bridges, drainage systems, and power lines damaged or rendered unusable. Disrupted transportation isolates communities, delays emergency response, and interrupts the flow of goods and services.

Finally, environmental impacts compound the problem. Flooding carries solid waste and pollutants into waterways, worsening water quality and increasing the cost of rehabilitation. Poor waste disposal practices in some communities further aggravate flooding, creating a vicious cycle that places added stress on vulnerable populations. | Drought: The City of Carmona's DRRMP identifies drought, primarily associated with El Niño, as a recurring climate hazard with wide-ranging impacts on vulnerable populations and sectors.

Drought leads to water scarcity, reducing supply for domestic, industrial, and agricultural use. This shortage disproportionately affects vulnerable groups such as the elderly, children, pregnant women, and persons with disabilities, who are more susceptible to heat-related illnesses and discomfort . In past events, barangays like Milagrosa recorded the highest number of affected households, while smaller populations such as Barangay 7 were less impacted .

In the agriculture sector, drought reduces soil moisture, leading to declines in crop productivity—particularly rice, banana, and mango. This diminishes local food security and forces reliance on external supplies. Farmers also face income losses, while pest infestations and crop diseases become more likely under hotter, drier conditions .

For urban use areas, drought raises the risk of fires, damages infrastructure, and worsens water shortages for households and businesses. Reduced water availability also affects productivity and increases operational costs, while small businesses and informal workers are most vulnerable to disruptions .

Critical facilities—such as hospitals, schools, and evacuation centers—experience strain during prolonged droughts due to increased demand for health services and limited water for sanitation. This stretches manpower and financial resources, potentially compromising essential services .

Overall, drought in Carmona undermines health, livelihoods, and service delivery, hitting the poor and marginalized the hardest while stressing the city's limited natural and financial resources.

While RA 9003 does not obligate LGUs to manage biodegradable waste at the municipal level, IGaCoS recognizes the urgent need to address
gaps in the management of food waste generated by commercial establishments, while some abled resorts and restaurant connect with private collectors who are based outside the city, many of which lack the capacity to treat or dispose of such waste responsibly.

• Develop a system for collection, treatment, and valorization of food and organic waste.
• Explore technologies such as composting, anaerobic digestion, or waste-to-resource innovations (e.g., biogas, organic fertilizer production, black soldier fly intervention).
• Reduce food waste leakage into the environment, thereby improving local sanitation and public health.
• Support the city's sustainable tourism image and strengthen compliance with environmental
regulations.

Expected Outputs:
• Establishment of a food waste treatment facility with appropriate technology.
• Increased volumes of food waste diverted from landfill.
• Production of marketable by-products (e.g., compost, biogas, organic soil conditioner).
• Partnerships with resorts, restaurants, and tourism enterprises for waste segregation and collection.
• Jobs and livelihood opportunities, particularly for women, youth, and informal waste workers.

Target Beneficiaries and Benefits:
• Resorts, restaurants, and other food service providers who will benefit from cost-effective waste management solutions.
• Local communities, who will enjoy improved sanitation and reduced health risks.
• Waste workers, women, and youth, who will have opportunities for skills training, employment, and
entrepreneurship in waste-based industries.
• The environment, through reduced greenhouse gas emissions, improved soil health, and reduced
waste leakage to marine ecosystems.

Coastal flooding (incl. sea level rise): Rising sea levels have consequences for both society and the environment. In the coastal areas, large economic values are at stake because buildings and technical infrastructure are largely located along the coasts (e.g. railway and railway station, sewage treatment plant, sewage and water pipes etc). It is also a health risk issue because the consequences can be unhealthy living environments, lack of accessibility, landslide risk, etc. Coastal natural and cultural environments are at risk of disappearing in the worst case scenario, and industries such as agriculture and tourism can be negatively affected.

Buildings along the coast are at risk of being directly flooded during high water situations already today. In the long term, when the mean sea level rises, the risk of flooding will increase. Water levels that today have a return period of 100 years may occur significantly more frequently in the future. In addition to direct flooding of coastal buildings, there is also a risk that valuable coastal natural environments, such as sandy habitats, will be severely affected by rising sea levels. Many protected natural areas in the municipality are located along the coast and are limited inland by buildings or coastal roads and thus have no way to retreat. At the mouth of Nybro river and Kabusa river, rising sea levels will have a damming effect on the watercourses, especially in connection with high water flows. In the flat catchment areas, this will result in large areas being flooded.

If the sea level generally ends up at a higher level, it means that the groundwater level closest to the coastline will rise to a corresponding extent and that the risk of saltwater intrusion into coastal wells will increase. Saltwater intrusion could become a limiting factor for new construction along the coast if the water and sewage issue is not resolved. A higher groundwater level also affects the foundation depth for buildings and pipes and the suitability of building basements. Groundwater levels must also be taken into account when building, for example, roads, drainage systems and other infrastructure. | Heat stress: How people are affected by heat stress

or respond to risks. These include:
• the elderly
• people with disabilities
• young children
